stories.title: Krishna Drains the Demoness Putana's Life
stories.story:
Gokul slept. The cowherd settlement lay dark, its doors shut, its cattle folded into their pens, and the night itself seemed to hold its breath. Through that darkness a woman moved from house to house, stopping at each doorway and looking in at the sleeping families, and no dog barked and no watchman stirred as she passed.

She was not a woman. She was Putana, a demoness known in many villages only as a name spoken in whispers — a child-killer who moved through the world the way sickness does, quietly, at night, drawn to the very young. Kamsa, the king of Mathura, had sent her to find the child who, he feared, had been born to destroy him. She had come to Gokul hunting, and she went from house to house, searching.

By chance, or by some darker purpose, her wandering brought her to the house of Nanda. There, in a dim room, an infant lay asleep — the baby boy of Nanda and Yashoda, the child the whole settlement had celebrated only days before. Putana lifted him from where he lay, cradled him against her, and gave him her breast.

There was milk in it, and there was something else as well. A poison lay there, meant for just such a child, laid to reach him through the very act that should have nourished him, and to still him as he fed.

The baby's eyes stayed closed, as if in sleep. He did not wake. He did not cry. He closed his mouth over her breast and began to drink, and it must have seemed to her, in that quiet room, the easiest thing she had ever done.

But what he drew from her was not milk alone. He drew out her life along with it, and she felt it going.

"Let go," she cried. "Let go of me."

The child did not let go. He drank on, and her cry rose out of that quiet house, terrible and deep. It rang across the settlement, and the earth shook with it, and the mountains, and the sky, and the very stars and planets in their slow paths trembled at the sound.

Then the life went out of her, and she fell. As she fell, she was no longer the woman who had moved so quietly through the dark. She crashed down in her own form — monstrous, vast, her hair flung loose, her arms and legs thrown wide — and lay sprawled on the ground of Gokul like a great demon struck down out of the sky by a thunderbolt.

The child lay where the fall had left him, whole and unharmed. When the household woke and ran out, they found them there together: the baby they loved, and the dreadful thing that had come for him in the night.

They could make no sense of it. A demon had crept in to feed the child death, and the child had turned the feeding back upon her. Now she lay fallen in the yard, and he lay a little way off, unharmed. By daylight the cowherds carried the great body away, and the settlement slowly returned to its work; the child fed and slept as on any other day.

Long afterward, when the boy had grown and gone from the world, Uddhava, his close friend, would speak of Putana with a strange tenderness. The very demoness who had pressed her poisoned breast to the child with murder in her heart — even she, he said, had been received by that same act as a nurse, and granted a mother's place. What she had meant to do was not undone by this. But in the memory of it, it was not the last word either.
stories.reflection: Putana came to destroy the child, yet the tradition remembers her with tenderness: the very act of violence, offered to him, became her path to a mother's place. The story does not soften her cruelty, but it refuses to make cruelty the last word.
stories.content_note: A demoness attempts to poison an infant and dies; her death is described with restraint.
stories.next_story_tease: Putana was not the last danger to find the baby in Gokul.

stories.title: The Fragrant Smoke
stories.subtitle: The villagers burn Putana's body
stories.story:
Putana came to Gokula wearing the shape of a beautiful young woman. She smiled at the cowherd mothers, offered to hold their babies, and seemed as kind as any nurse — but she was a demoness, and she had come to kill the infant Krishna. The child she meant to destroy drew the life out of her instead, and the lovely stranger fell dead at the edge of the village.

Now her true body lay where she had fallen, and no one in Gokula could look at it for long. Released from the pretty form she had worn, she was enormous — so vast that her fall had crushed the trees in a long stretch around her. Her mouth gaped wide, its teeth like the shafts of a plow; her nostrils opened like cave mouths in a mountain; her eyes were deep pits a man might fall into. The cowherds and their wives stood far off, trembling at the sight, and none of them would draw near.

And there, in the middle of all that horror, was the child. Krishna lay on the dead demon's chest, playing as calmly as if he had been set down in his own courtyard on an ordinary morning. The thing that made grown men step back could not trouble him at all.

Then Yasoda, Krishna's mother, came forward, and Rohini with her — the two mothers of the house — and they gathered up the child. The women bathed him, first with cow's urine and then with the fine dust of the cow pen, their way of washing harm away, and sprinkled him with water. Then they passed their hands over his body and chanted over each part of him in turn — his feet, his hands, his waist, his heart, his throat, his head — asking that every limb be guarded. They called on the Lord who holds the discus to stand before him and the Lord who holds the mace behind him, on the bow and the sword to guard his sides, and on the conch to sound above him; on Garuda, the great bird, to watch the ground, and on the Lord of all to stand all around him. And they named every spirit that preys on children and bade them all stay far away.

Meanwhile Nanda and the other cowherds were on the road home from Mathura. They came into the village to find the vast body stretched across the ground and the child safe in the midst of it, and they marveled. Surely, they said to one another, this was no ordinary boy. Surely he was a great sage, or a master of yoga, to have come through such a thing untouched.

Then they took up their axes. They cut the great body to pieces, carried the pieces away, and set them alight.

And here was the strangest thing. The smoke that rose from the fire was not the smoke of burning flesh. It smelled of aloe — sweet and clean and calm — and it drifted up over all of Gokula. The demoness who had come to kill a child had been given a mother's reward, and the air above the fire seemed to say so.
stories.reflection: The fragrant smoke is the story's quiet astonishment. The one who came to destroy a child is granted a mother's reward, and the text marks it not with a lecture but with a sweetness rising from the fire — grace offered even to the one who meant harm.
stories.content_note: The cowherds cut up and burn a demoness's corpse; described with restraint.
stories.next_story_tease: But the danger to the child was not yet over.

stories.title: The Infant Who Overturned a Cart
stories.story:
A loaded cart is a heavy thing. It is built to carry pots and grain and the whole weight of a household's goods, and it does not turn over by itself. Yet in the village of Gokula, on the day of the ceremony for an infant's first rising, a cart lay overturned and broken, and the only creature near it had been a baby too small to lift a single one of its pots.

The baby was Krishna, the small son of Nanda, chief of the cowherds, and of his wife Yasoda. That morning the brahmins had come to bless the child and had been honored with gifts, and the women of Vraja, the cowherd country round about, had gathered for the rite of his first rising. Yasoda moved among her guests, greeting each one, for a mother who is giving such a ceremony has many duties and her mind was full of them. In the press of it all, the child was set down for a moment in the shade of a cart that stood in the courtyard, heaped high with vessels.

He was hungry, perhaps, or simply tired of being still. He began to cry, and, as babies do when they cry, he kicked.

One small foot struck the underside of the cart above him — a foot as soft and tender as a new leaf, as a fresh sprout of the season, striking wood and iron.

The cart went over. Not gently tipped, but thrown down: its wheels wrenched from the axle, its shaft and yoke broken, its vessels spilled and shattered across the courtyard.

The crash brought everyone running — Yasoda, the women, Nanda and the men — and they stood around the wreckage in a ring of wonder, troubled by a thing none of them could explain. No wind had stirred. No animal had been near. There lay the cart, upended and broken, and in the middle of it sat the child, crying.

The cowherd boys and girls who had been playing close by said what they had seen. The baby did it, they said. He kicked the cart over with his own foot. But the grown men shook their heads. That was child-talk, the sort of thing children invent — how could an infant's foot overturn a cart that strong men could hardly shift?

Yasoda did not stay to argue. She was afraid — afraid of whatever unkind influence might be drawn to a child who had been at the center of such a wonder. She gathered up her crying son and held him close.

The cowherds, strong men all, set the cart upright again and collected what was left of its goods. Then Nanda, troubled and unable to explain what had happened, did what a father does when the world gives no answer: he called the brahmins who knew the sacred chants and had the protective rites recited over his son, with the words of the three Vedas, and he brought out his finest cows, decked in cloth and garlands and gold, and stood with a steady heart while the blessings were spoken over the child.

But no prayer could undo what the courtyard had seen that day, and no one who was there could forget it. A cart overturned by the kick of a baby too small to lift a single pot, and the child himself unhurt in the middle of it, reaching up to be held. The men went back to their herds and the women to their houses, but the question went with them, unasked and unanswered.
stories.reflection: The wonder of the episode is not only the overturned cart but the way the village receives it: the children tell the plain truth and the adults refuse it, because the truth is too large for their idea of what a child can do.
stories.tradition_note: The Harivamsha sets this episode while Yasoda is away bathing at the river and Nanda returns from the forest to find the cart overturned; the Bhagavata Purana places it during the child's birth-rites. The miracle at the heart of both is the same.
stories.next_story_tease: Kamsa's servants were not finished with Gokula, and the next would come not in a human shape but as a storm.

stories.title: The Whirlwind That Stole a Child
stories.story:
On an afternoon in Gokula, Yasoda sat with her son Krishna on her lap, dandling him and looking into his face, the way a mother does when there is nothing to do but be glad of her child. The village hummed around her — cows lowing in their pens, women calling to one another down the lanes. Nothing in the clear air warned her of what was coming.

Then, without warning, the child grew heavy in her arms. She felt it plainly: the small body pressing down on her as though its weight had doubled, so heavy that she could hardly hold him. Astonished, she set him on the ground to see what it could mean.

Before she could think further, the air changed.

A wind came tearing through the lanes of Gokula — a dry, violent wind that lifted the dust of the earth and set it spinning in a harsh wheel of grit. This was no ordinary storm. This was Trinavarta, a demon in the service of Kamsa, the king of Mathura who had sworn that this child would not live, come in the shape of a whirlwind to do the work his master had set him. He came the way such servants come: no face to remember, no warning to give, nothing but wind and dust worn like a body. The spinning grit filled the whole settlement, stealing the light and the sight of everyone in it.

For a long moment Gokula went dark. No one could see the person beside them, or even their own hand before their face. The wind tore at the thatch; the cattle lowed in panic; and the darkness itself seemed to move, spinning where the storm stood. Cowherds stumbled and called out, and mothers reached into the brown air for children they could not see, their voices thin with fright — confusion everywhere, and a fear with no shape to it.

When the dust began to settle, Yasoda looked for her son. He was gone.

For a moment she did not move. He had been in her arms only moments before; she could still feel the weight of him. But the ground where she had set him down was empty, and she stood looking at it, unwilling to believe what her eyes told her.

She searched the spot, and the ground was bare. She searched for any trace he might have left, but the wind had scoured the earth clean. She called his name, and the sound was lost in the settling dust. She looked this way and that through the thinning haze and found nothing, for the whirlwind was already receding, carrying with it the child she had held a moment before. The women of Gokula, hearing her cry, came running with tears on their faces, for the village's dearest child had been taken, and no one could say where the storm had gone.

High above the blinded village, the whirlwind climbed with its small burden — a demon carrying off a child who, moments earlier, had been too heavy for his own mother to hold, rising to do the errand Kamsa had sent him on.
stories.reflection: The detail that the child suddenly felt heavy in Yasoda's arms, just before the whirlwind came, is quietly ominous: the thing that will undo Trinavarta is already present in the very weight that surprised his mother.
stories.content_note: A demon snatches an infant away in a blinding whirlwind; the episode is brief and ends on the moment of loss.
stories.next_story_tease: But the whirlwind had not counted on the weight of the child it carried.
stories.hero_scene: A towering whirlwind of dust and grit sweeps through the lanes of Gokula, blinding everything, while Yasoda reaches through the choking brown air toward the spot where her child had been.

stories.title: Trinavarta Is Crushed by the Child's Weight
stories.story:
One afternoon the sky over Gokula turned strange.

It began as a wind — a dry, rising wind that lifted the dust of the lanes and set the doors to banging. The cattle stirred in their pens and lowed uneasily, and the women at their churning looked up and shaded their eyes. Then the wind thickened and darkened and began to spin, and those who looked up saw that it was no storm at all. Something moved inside it, and it was heading for the house of Nanda, chief of the cowherds.

The something was Trinavarta, a demon who came as a whirlwind, sent by Kamsa, the king of Mathura, to destroy the child Krishna. Before anyone could cry out, he swept down, snatched the baby up from the courtyard, and carried him into the spinning air.

The child vanished into the dust, and the settlement was plunged into a choking darkness. Mothers groped for their own children and called their names, and no one could say where the boy had gone. High above, Trinavarta rose with his prize, and the earth fell away beneath him.

But the demon's climb began to fail.

The child in his arms was growing heavy. He had been nothing — a feather, a leaf — and now he pressed down on the demon like a stone. Trinavarta climbed, and the child grew heavier. He strained to rise higher, and the child grew heavier still, until the whirlwind demon found that he could not move at all. A child is the lightest thing in the world, and yet the sky could not hold this one; the demon who had risen like smoke now hung motionless, pinned by something he could not see or understand. It was as though he held up a mountain. As though he held up the whole weight of the world.

The wind that had borne him aloft so easily now held him fast; he could neither rise nor turn. Then the baby's small hands closed around his throat, and Trinavarta could neither move nor breathe. His eyes started from his head.

And he fell.

He fell out of the sky onto a rock below, and the rock shattered him — the whirlwind broken to pieces on the stone. The cowherds ran to the place, expecting the worst, and found the child lying safe upon the demon's chest, as if the fall had been a cradle and the monster his bedding. The mothers who had lost sight of him in the dust came running too, and found him not only alive but unmarked. They pressed him close and wept with relief, and passed him from hand to hand, turning him over to look for a wound. There was none.

They could hardly believe their eyes. A demon had carried the boy off to his death, and here he was back among them, unhurt, as though the whole thing had been no more than a game of the wind. "What penance have we done?" they asked one another. "What worship, what good deeds, what kindness to living beings, that the child who was taken from us has been given back alive?"

They lifted him up and carried him home. For a long time afterward, the men of Gokula spoke of the wonders they had seen in that broad forest, and Nanda, the cowherd chief, said little — but he had begun to notice how many wonders gathered around this quiet child, and how each one ended the same way: with the boy safe and the danger gone. He did not speak of it, but he watched the child more closely.
stories.reflection: The demon meant to carry the child off into the sky, and instead he was brought down by the very thing he tried to steal — a smallness that held the weight of the world. The rescue is not a struggle of equals; it is the unmasking of what the child already carried.
stories.content_note: A demon is crushed in a fall; the description is brief and not graphic.
stories.hero_scene: A demon in whirlwind form crashes out of a dark, dust-choked sky onto a rock, shattered, while the infant Krishna lies safe and unharmed upon his chest in the aftermath.

stories.title: The Universe in Her Son's Mouth
stories.story:
In Gokula, Yasoda sat nursing her baby, the small son of Nanda and herself. There is no hour more ordinary in a mother's day than the hour when she feeds her child, and this was such an hour: the child on her lap, nearly done with his milk, his drinking slowing. His name was Krishna, and she was looking down at him the way any mother looks at the small face she loves, with its sleepy, contented smile. The afternoon was warm and still around them; dust motes turned slowly in a shaft of light by the door, and from the lane came women's voices and the lowing of cattle.

And the child yawned.

It was only a yawn, the kind every tired baby makes. But as his mouth opened, Yasoda looked into it, and instead of the pink of a child's gums she saw the sky. She saw the wide sky, and the earth spread out beneath it, and the heavens beyond, and the hosts of stars turning in their courses, and the four directions, and the sun and the moon and fire and wind and the great oceans — and every living thing that moves or stands still. The whole universe lay arranged inside the open mouth of the baby she was holding.

She saw all of it, suddenly and at once, and her body began to shake. Her limbs trembled and her breath caught in her throat, and she trembled the way a leaf trembles in a strong wind, for she understood, in that instant, that the small mouth before her opened onto everything. Her arms tightened around him, and still she could not look away.

It lasted no longer than a yawn lasts. Then the moment passed, and Krishna was only a baby again — warm and drowsy against her, his mouth once more too small for anything but a kiss. He could not yet speak a word. He offered no explanation and asked for none. He had only yawned, and let her look.

The walls of the room came back around her, and with them the ordinary sounds of the village — a cow lowing, a neighbor calling, the afternoon light lying across the floor. Yasoda sat a long while without moving, the child asleep in her arms, and she said nothing at all. What she had seen had been given to her without a word, for no reason but that she was his mother and happened to be looking. She had held the sky and the sea and everything that lives inside the open mouth of her own son, and she carried what she had seen the way one carries a thing too large to speak of: quietly, and always.
stories.reflection: The vision is given to a mother in the most domestic of moments, while she is nursing, and it is not sought or asked for. The infinite does not interrupt her love; it shows itself through the very child she is holding.
stories.hero_scene: Yasoda, the child on her lap, stares into his yawning mouth and sees the whole universe within it, the sky and oceans and sun and moon and stars, while she trembles.

stories.title: Garga Secretly Names Rama and Krishna
stories.story:
Most ceremonies are made to be witnessed, but a naming can be a dangerous thing — and when the family priest Garga came to Nanda's house in Gokula, he asked that the rites be done in secret.

Garga had not come on his own. He had been sent by Vasudeva, the man from whose arms the child had been carried to Gokula as a newborn, to perform the rites that every child must receive. The reason for the secrecy lay a few days' journey away, in the city of Mathura, where a king named Kamsa was hunting for the children of Vasudeva's house. He would not have wanted a single one of them to live.

Nanda had not expected the old priest, and the sight of him at the door filled Nanda with joy. He rose at once, pressing his palms together. He washed Garga's feet, seated him with honor, and offered him the welcome due to a guest — and only then, with careful and courteous words, did he make his request. It was no small thing to ask a priest into one's home, and Nanda asked it as a man asks a great favor. Of all who know the things beyond the senses, he said, it is you who should perform these rites. For Garga could read the path of the stars across the sky, and he saw with a knowledge that did not come through the eyes.

Garga answered him plainly, and in a low voice. Kamsa, he said, is a man of evil mind, and he knows of your friendship with Vasudeva. If a naming in Gokula were spoken of, word would travel, and questions would follow, and the child would be in danger. Let this be done quietly, with no one to see and no one to tell.

So it was. There, in that room, without the knowledge of the other cowherds, Garga performed the rites over the two boys of the house. To the elder boy — the son of Rohini, the household's other mother — he gave the name Rama, the boy who would also come to be called Balarama. And to Nanda's son he gave the name Krishna. The two names settled on the sleeping children as lightly as if they had been waiting for them all along.

Then Garga spoke of what he could see, and his words fell soft in the quiet room. This child has not come into the world for the first time. In age after age he appears, and in each age his form takes a different color; he comes under many names, for his names and forms are beyond counting. And before this birth, Garga said, he was born of Vasudeva. The cowherds and all of Gokula will find their welfare in him: through him the good will be shielded from those who do them harm, and the wicked will be kept at bay. He will be the delight of the cowherds and of all Gokula, and the source of every good thing that comes to them. Those who set their hearts on him are fortunate indeed. And he is equal, Garga said at last, to Narayana himself in his qualities.

When the rites were done, Garga left as quietly as he had come, and Nanda spoke to no one of what had been said in that room. The two names were given in secret, and for a while they were held in secret.

Yet the name Krishna, first spoken behind a shut door in Gokula, would one day be spoken in homes and temples across the world.
stories.reflection: Garga's secret naming holds the whole shape of Krishna's early life in miniature — the fear of Kamsa that forces concealment, and the quiet certainty that what is hidden now will not stay hidden.
stories.hero_scene: The sage Garga, seated in Nanda's dim home, performs the naming rites in secret, the two infants before him, as Nanda looks on with his palms pressed together.

stories.title: The Butter Thief of Gokula
stories.story:
The trouble in Gokula did not begin with butter. It began with two boys learning to crawl.

Gokula was a cowherd village, and there Krishna and his brother Rama grew quickly, the way children do. Before long they were dragging themselves through the mud of the cowherd lanes, babbling as they went, and the whole settlement brightened at the sound, for there was nothing the cowherds loved more than the sight of those two small boys in motion. When they had crawled a little way they would turn and creep back toward their mothers with puzzled, half-frightened faces, as if they had traveled a great distance and were surprised to find themselves home again.

Their mothers would gather them up, two boys caked in mud, their limbs stained the color of the lane, and hold them close and look into their faces, at the sweet smiles and the first small teeth, and their hearts would fill. There was no helping it.

Soon the boys were up on their feet, and then the real play began. They would catch the calves of the herd by the tail and let themselves be dragged this way and that across the yard, while the women of the village left their doorways to watch and laugh. Their mothers tried to keep them away from horns and fire, from a boar's tusks and open water, from swooping birds and thorn bushes — and failed, for the boys were too quick and the mothers too fond. In the end the women gave up and simply watched, their minds never quite at rest.

And then Krishna discovered butter.

It began almost innocently. He and his band of cowherd friends would slip into a neighbor's house and let the calves loose at the wrong hour, then stand laughing at the confusion. Soon he knew where the curds and the milk were kept, and the game turned to stealing — stealing of a kind that made the gopis, the cowherd women, want to laugh even as they scolded.

He was clever about it. He chose his hour when the women were deep in their housework, and when the pots hung out of reach in slings among the rafters, he would drag a stool or an upturned mortar beneath them and climb. In the dark of a storeroom he needed no lamp, for the jewels on his own small body caught what little light there was and showed him where the pots hung. He would eat the sweet curd and butter and feed the monkeys who gathered to watch him, and if a monkey refused to eat, he would smash the pot in a temper. And when he could not reach a pot at all, he would march off angry and shout at the small children of the house.

The gopis carried their complaints to Yasoda, his mother. They came with lists of outrages, but even while they complained their eyes were soft with the sight of him, and his small, lovely face undid their anger, so that their scolding came out half in laughter. Yasoda, who had once seen a cart topple at a touch from that same small foot, heard them out with a smile and could not bring herself to scold him.

And so the days went by — butter vanishing, mischief unpunished — and Gokula learned to live with the one thief no one truly wanted to catch.
stories.reflection: The charm of the mischief is that everyone is in on it except the scolding: the gopis complain with delight in their eyes, and Yasoda hears them out and does nothing. The village loves the very trouble it reports.
stories.next_story_tease: And one of those pranks would soon send every cowherd boy running to Yasoda with news.
stories.hero_scene: Toddler Krishna stands on a stool, reaching into a hanging pot of butter in a dim storeroom, the jewels on his small body catching the faint light, while gopis watch with half-fearful, half-delighted eyes.

stories.title: Krishna Shows the Cosmos in His Mouth
stories.story:
The cowherd boys of Gokula came running to Yasoda one afternoon, all talking at once.

"Krishna ate mud," they told her, their faces bright with the importance of the news. "We saw him. He ate dirt while no one was looking."

They were certain of it; they had played with him all afternoon and knew what they had seen. Krishna was Yasoda's son, a small boy who had grown up in her house, but a mother still had to ask. She took him by the hand, drew him to her, and scolded him gently, the way a mother scolds a child she wants to keep safe — not so much angry as wanting the truth.

"Why did you eat mud in secret, when no one was looking?" she asked. "You know it is not good for you."

"I did not eat it, mother," Krishna said, meeting her eyes. "They are saying what is not true."

Yasoda looked at him. There was one sure way to settle it — the oldest trick a mother knows.

"Then open your mouth," she said. "If you have eaten nothing, there will be nothing to see."

And Krishna opened his mouth, and Yasoda looked inside it.

What she saw there has been told for thousands of years. In the small mouth of her small son she saw the whole universe: the earth with its mountains and its oceans, the sky, and the slow turning circle of the stars and planets. She saw water and fire and air and the vast space between them. She saw every living thing, and time itself, and the long tangle of deeds and their results, and all the hidden differences between one being and another — the whole world, moving and still, held between a few small teeth. And still his mouth was small enough to kiss.

What the sages seek through whole lifetimes of study — through the Vedas and the Upanishads and the long disciplines of the mind — Yasoda saw in a single moment, freely given, in her son's open mouth. She stood still, overwhelmed, and her own mind asked the only questions it could form. Is this a dream? she wondered. Is it some divine illusion? Or has a delusion come over my own mind?

She could not hold the vision, so she reached for what had always held her. I am Yasoda, she told herself. Nanda is my husband. This is my son. I am the wife of the chief of the cowherds, mistress of all his wealth. And the child standing before her was only her child again.

Then the vision was veiled from her, as gently as it had come, and the memory of it slipped away with it. She bent down, lifted her son onto her lap, and was simply his mother again. She never knew that she had seen the whole universe in his mouth — and the world, small and ordinary once more, was enough.
stories.reflection: The story shows the infinite and then gently takes it back. Yasoda is not denied the vision because she is unworthy, but because her love needs him small; the mother who has seen the whole cosmos in his mouth is given back the child she can hold, and that is presented not as a loss but as a mercy.
stories.next_story_tease: And the days went back to being ordinary again — which, in that house, meant mischief.

stories.title: Krishna Breaks the Butter Pot
stories.story:
In the cowherd village of Gokula, Yasoda, Krishna's mother, was churning butter. She worked the rope of the churn with both arms; the cloth was bound at her waist, a garland of jasmine kept slipping from her hair, and sweat stood on her face, the small rings at her ears swinging with every pull. The curds turned in the pot, the butter was nearly ready, and the morning promised to be long and quiet. She was glad of it.

Then Krishna came to her, hungry, and stood close, pulling at her until she lifted him onto her lap. As he nursed, she looked down at his face and smiled. It was the still, warm moment of the day.

It did not last. The milk she had set to boil — forgotten in the warmth of that moment — climbed the sides of its pot and began to spill, hissing onto the coals. Yasoda set the child down and ran to it, leaving him alone beside the churn.

Krishna did not take well to being put down. One moment he had been warm and fed and held; the next, he was on the floor. His lower lip began to tremble. He bit it with his small teeth, angry, and looked at the churn pot — the pot full of fresh butter — and broke it. The pot fell apart, and all the butter of the morning's churning lay open before him.

He took up the butter, and since no one was there to stop him, he ate only what pleased him and shared the rest. He climbed onto the upturned mortar and sat there, out of his mother's sight, holding out the butter to a monkey — one of the creatures that wandered freely through the cowherd lanes. The monkey took it from his hand and ate it with as much delight as if it had been a feast.

When Yasoda came back and saw the broken pot and the butter gone, she understood at once who had done it. She picked up a stick.

The boy saw the stick. He scrambled down and ran — as if he were afraid, though anyone watching would have seen that his fear was half a game. And his mother ran after him.

It was a curious chase. The scriptures say that even the yogis, worn out by their long austerities, cannot reach this child with their minds — yet here he was, running through his own courtyard with his mother gaining on him. Her breath came short and her sari swung as she ran, and still she could not quite catch him.

At last he let himself be caught. And when she had him, he did the one thing that undid all her anger: he rubbed his eyes with his small hands — hands black with soot and ash — and cried, leaving black smears down his cheeks, the very picture of a wronged and sorry child. Yasoda, who had come running with a stick, found it hanging loose in her hand, her anger already gone. The butter, the chase, the broken pot — none of it mattered now.
stories.reflection: The comedy is gentle because it turns on a real child's logic: interrupted at the breast, he takes the next sweet thing and shares it, then runs and pretends to cry. Even the line that the yogis cannot reach him lands lightly — the point is not his power but that a mother's chase is the one pursuit he never really outruns.
stories.next_story_tease: Yasoda's anger would not last, and soon she would go looking for a rope.

stories.title: Yashoda Binds Krishna to the Mortar
stories.story:
Yashoda had spent the morning chasing her small son. He had broken her butter pot while her back was turned, and she had run after him with a stick, meaning to teach him a lesson — but the moment she caught him and saw the fear on his small face, the stick dropped from her fingers and lay in the dust. She could not strike him. Her anger was a brief, hot thing, and it always died the moment it met his eyes.

But Krishna had done wrong, and something had to be done. So she put the stick aside and reached instead for a rope. She would tie him up — a gentler punishment, she told herself — and then she could finish her work in peace.

She took the rope and wound it around his waist. It came up short. However she pulled, the rope ended a little short of the knot, short by two fingers' width, no more. She frowned and joined another length of rope to the first. Still two fingers short. She joined a third, then a fourth, fetching coil after coil from the store of her own house, tying rope to rope, and still the gap would not close. All the rope in the house, joined end to end, could not make a loop that would hold him.

She worked on, and the morning grew warm. The sweat stood on her face and along her arms; the hair she had braided at dawn came loose, and the garland slipped from it and hung crooked. Still she tied, and still the rope fell short by those same two fingers.

And then, at last, Krishna looked at his mother. He looked at her wet face, her loosened hair, her hands worn raw from tying ropes for his sake alone, and something in him softened. He was not a child whom any rope could hold. No one in all the worlds could reach him or bind him — not the greatest of the gods, not the mightiest of beings. And yet here was his mother, wearing herself out over a length of rope, for no other reason than that she was his mother and he was her son.

So he let it happen. Of his own accord, moved by nothing but her striving and her love, he stood still and let the rope close around his waist at last. Yashoda bound him to the great wooden mortar, the heavy block on which the household pounded its grain, and this time the knot held.

She wiped her face, satisfied, and turned back to her work. And the child sat bound to the mortar, as quiet as if he had chosen it — because, in the end, he had.
stories.reflection: The wonder is not that Krishna could not be bound, but that he chose to be — that the effort of a mother's love accomplished what the strength of the whole world could not.
stories.tradition_note: The Harivamsha and Vishnu Purana fold this rope-binding into the later uprooting of the twin trees; the Bhagavata gives it as a separate episode.
stories.next_story_tease: Bound at last to the mortar, the child would soon drag it out toward the two great trees at the forest's edge.

stories.title: Krishna Uproots the Twin Arjuna Trees
stories.subtitle: How he came to be called Damodara
stories.story:
Everyone in Gokula knew that the crawling child could not be kept still. Krishna slipped into the cow sheds and came out gray with ash and dust. He rolled in the cow dung and only laughed. Pasted with ashes and powdered dung, his small body shone like a little prince of fire. He wandered into every corner of the village; his father Nanda could not check him, and his mother Yashoda could not keep pace with him. When she caught him and began to scold him, he looked back at her with such innocent eyes that the scolding died on her lips, and she laughed in spite of herself.

One morning, though, the mischief went too far, and Yashoda's patience ran out for good. Worked up with real anger, she took up a length of rope, fastened it around the boy's waist, and tied the other end to a heavy wooden mortar, the great block on which the household pounded its grain. "Now go," she told him, "go where you will — if you can." Then she turned back to her work, certain the matter was settled.

It was from that day, and from that rope, that he came to be called Damodara — the one bound by a rope around his belly. But a rope could not hold him. Dragging the mortar after him, Krishna left the courtyard and made his way toward the edge of the forest, where two great arjuna trees stood side by side — twin trees, tall and straight, grown huge with years, their branches laced together overhead. He meant to surprise the people of Gokula, to play a game that only he understood. The mortar scraped behind him over the packed earth, heavier than he was, yet he dragged it as if it weighed nothing at all. At the edge of the forest the two trees rose before him, straight as two pillars of an unseen gate.

He crawled between them, pulling the mortar through the narrow space. The mortar caught against their roots and held. Krishna pulled, and pulled again, harder. And with a single tug the two trees tore up out of the earth, roots and branches and all, and came crashing down with a sound that carried through the whole of Gokula. Birds burst from the fallen branches. Dust rose in a pale cloud and hung in the air, and for a long moment no one moved. The earth where the trees had stood lay torn open, and their long roots, thick as a man's arm, pointed up at the sky.

The cowherds came running at the noise and stopped short at what they saw. Where two great trees had stood there were only two fallen trunks, their great crowns thrown across the path — and Krishna, still tied to his mortar, laughing, as if to show them all what a child could do.

But those two trees had not always been trees. They were two sons of Kubera, the lord of wealth, whom a sage had cursed to stand rooted in the earth until someone set them free. Tall as they were, broad as their branches spread, they were prisoners, and no one in Gokula had ever guessed it. Year after year the two had stood in their green stillness, leaf and branch instead of arms and legs, waiting for the sage's word to come true. It was to make that word good that Krishna passed between them. A child too small to be trusted out of the yard had, with one pull, ended their long imprisonment and drawn them back into the light.

When the dust settled, the two great trees lay still upon the ground. And between them sat a crawling child, a rope still at his waist, laughing.
stories.reflection: The story holds two wonders in one image: a child too small to walk brings down two great trees, and beneath their crash two cursed beings are set free. The binding meant to restrain him becomes the very thing that liberates.
stories.tradition_note: The Harivamsha and Vishnu Purana fold the earlier rope-binding into this episode; the Bhagavata opens with Krishna already bound — Damodara.

stories.title: The Two Devotees Are Liberated from the Trees
stories.story:
The crash of the falling trees was still rolling across the fields of Gokula when the cowherds came running. What they found stopped them where they stood: Krishna, the crawling boy they all knew, sat between two uprooted arjuna trees, a rope still tied about his waist to the great wooden mortar. He had dragged the heavy mortar between the twin trunks and, with one pull, torn the trees up by the roots.

And then something rose out of the fallen trees, and the cowherds drew back.

Two figures climbed up from between the roots, and they were not men of any village. Light seemed to cling to them; they shone like fire just kindled, and the whole clearing brightened around them. They were Nalakuvara and Manigriva, the two sons of Kubera, the lord of wealth. A sage's curse had held them inside those trunks for years beyond counting, and now it was over at last.

The two beings walked to the child and bowed their heads to the ground before him, their palms joined, and they spoke to him — not as men speak to a small boy, but as servants to their Lord.

They spoke his name as they bowed — Krishna, Krishna. They called him the great yogi, the first and highest of all persons, the one who was there before all things. They called him the one Lord who dwells within every living body, the self of every self, the great and subtle source of all that exists — whom nothing of this world, none of its changing qualities, can ever grasp or hold. To that Vasudeva, the maker of all, they offered their obeisance: obeisance to the supreme goodness, obeisance to the supreme blessing.

And then they asked for the one thing they had waited so long to ask. Let our voices always be given to singing of your deeds, they said. Let our ears always hear of you. Let our hands always work in your service, our minds rest at your feet, our heads bow before the worlds where you dwell, and our eyes look upon those who are devoted to you. Grant us leave, Lord — we are your servants, and we are yours.

Krishna heard them, and his answer was simple. "You are both mine," he told them, "and your hearts are fixed on me. Go now to your own home."

They bowed once more, and then they went — the two radiant beings rising and passing away toward the north, free at last.

The cowherds stood in the clearing a long while, staring from the uprooted trees to the child who sat calm among the roots. They had heard the crash of the falling trees, and they had seen what came out of them. They could not explain any of it. But they understood enough to be afraid, and enough to know that the child in their midst was not simply a child.
stories.reflection: The liberation is quiet on Krishna's side and vast on theirs: they do not ask for riches or revenge, only that their senses be turned forever toward him — and that, once granted, is enough to set them free.
stories.hero_scene: Two radiant, fire-bright figures bow with joined palms before a small crawling Krishna beside two uprooted arjuna trees, light spilling from their forms across a stunned clearing of cowherds.

stories.title: The Fruit-Seller Receives a Gift of Jewels
stories.story:
In the cowherd village of Gokula, a small boy named Krishna was growing up. He was still young enough to be carried, and his days were full of play. When the cowherd women clapped their hands and coaxed him, he danced; when his father asked, he would fetch the stool, the weights, and the wooden sandals and carry them wherever they were wanted, pleased to be of use. The women of the house laughed to see him set off on an errand and come back beaming, and no one who watched him at his play guessed that this child was anything more than an ordinary boy.

One morning a fruit-seller came through the lane — a woman with a basket of fruit and a voice that carried down the street. Come, buy fruits! Sweet fruits! she called, and the fruit in her basket smelled of sun and ripe sweetness. At the sound, heads turned all along the lane, and Krishna was already on his way.

He ran out at once, a fistful of grain clutched in his hand. Gokula kept no coins; in a village that lived on milk and grain, you paid for things by barter, and a handful of grain was the price of fruit. He had watched the fruit-sellers pass through the lanes before, and to a small boy their trade looked like the whole world's business: you give, you get, and everybody is pleased. A fistful of grain made him rich; that was how trade worked.

But his hands were small, and his eagerness was greater than his grip. Before he reached the woman, the grain was running out between his fingers and scattering in the dust, a thin white trail marking the way he had run. By the time he stood before her, his two fists were nearly empty.

The fruit-seller looked down at the child — at the grain spilled on the ground, at the two small hands held up to her — and her heart went out to him. She did not scold. She laughed softly, bent down, and began to fill his hands with fruit, heaping it until no more would stay. He had come to buy with empty hands, and she gave, and asked nothing back.

And then she saw her basket.

Where the fruit had been, the basket now gleamed. It was full to the brim with jewels — gems that caught the morning light and threw it back in every colour. The fruit she had emptied into the child's hands was gone, and in its place lay treasure beyond anything her years of selling fruit had ever held. The basket that had hung heavy on her arm like a day's honest work now weighed like a king's ransom.

She stood still, looking from the jewels to the small boy and back again, and slowly she understood. She had not been selling fruit to an ordinary child at all. She had been giving it, without knowing, to someone who gives back beyond all measure.

But she said nothing of what she understood. She only looked at him, and he looked back at her — a child with his arms full of fruit, and a woman with her basket full of light.
stories.reflection: The exchange turns on a small, human generosity: the woman is not asked for anything but fruit, and she gives it to a child who has already dropped his payment. What comes back is beyond measure, because grace answers the open hand.

stories.title: The Cowherds Decide to Migrate to Vrindavan
stories.story:
In the cowherd village of Gokula, one strange danger after another had fallen on the children — and, again and again, on one child above all. That child was Krishna, the small son of Nanda, the chief of the cowherds. Each time danger came at him, he came through unharmed, and the more often he was saved, the less the village liked it. What they had been calling good fortune was beginning to look like a warning.

The elder Upananda — the oldest of the cowherds, and the one whose judgment the rest trusted — had watched the recent days with growing unease. At last he called the men of the settlement together. Nanda stood at their head, the others gathered round him, and Upananda spoke plainly.

We who wish Gokula well, he said, must leave this place.

Then he set out before them, one by one, what they had all seen with their own eyes. A demoness in a woman's shape had come among them meaning to kill the children, and she had died that same night, while the child she had come to destroy was unharmed. A whirlwind had caught the boy up and carried him into the sky — and brought him down alive. The waggon he had lain beneath as a baby had been overturned by a kick of his foot, its pots and pans flung across the ground. And he had been caught between the two great falling trees, and he had not died.

Set out in a row like that, the pattern could not be mistaken: everything that came near the child was broken or undone, and the child remained. Some of the cowherds called it fortune. Upananda called it an omen.

Before another evil omen falls upon Vraja, he told them, we should go. And there is a place to go: a forest called Vrindavana, fresh and green, with pasture the cattle have never grazed and grass that has never been cropped — new ground, where the omens of Gokula would have no hold. Yoke the carts, he said. Let us go at once, and do not delay.

The cowherds listened, and not one of them argued. One after another they nodded, and the word went round: well said, well said. They had seen too much to shrug off the old man's fears, and the thought of a new forest, thick with fresh grass and safe for the herds, came as a relief after the days they had just lived through.

So the order was given, and the settlement began to move. The carts were yoked and loaded; the old men climbed up, and the children were lifted in after them; the women gathered what each household would need and left the rest behind, for a village, once moved, does not send back for what it left. Every family called in its cattle, and the herds stirred and lowed along the track.

It was no small thing, to uproot a village, but the cowherds did it in a single day and in a single mind. The elders led, the carts followed, the herds came behind, and the whole of Gokula rolled out along the road to Vrindavana — away from the omens, toward the deep grass by the river, where everyone hoped the danger had not yet found them.
stories.reflection: Upananda's wisdom is practical and communal: he does not claim to understand the wonders, only to see that they have become omens, and that the right answer to a sign one cannot read is to move the whole community out of its path.
stories.tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana attributes the decision to the elders with Nanda at their head, alarmed by Putana's death, the overturned waggon and the trees; the Bhagavata has Upananda speak of the omens. Both agree on the departure for Vrindavana.

stories.title: The Wolves That Moved a Village
stories.story:
Krishna and his brother Balarama had grown up in the cowherd country of Vraja, and for seven years the forest by their village had been their playground. They ran through these woods in dark-blue and yellow clothes, their bodies pasted with yellow and white clay, crow feathers in their hair. Some days they wore crowns of leaves and garlands of wild flowers and looked, the cowherds said, like two young trees walking; other days they crowned themselves with lotuses, hung gourds on a string, slung a rope over one shoulder like a sacred thread, and played their flutes as they went. They napped on beds of leaves, galloped about like two young horses, and in all their play they had made the forest beautiful.

But now, standing in it, Krishna saw what the years had cost. The grass was gone and the twigs stripped; the milkmen had pulled up the trees, and fires from the cow sheds had scorched the trunks. The birds had flown from the bare branches, and even the wind that had once blown sweet through the leaves seemed not to stir here anymore. This forest, Krishna said, has become like rice served with no dish to go with it — there, but giving no pleasure.

He turned to his brother. They could not play here any longer, he said; there was no place left even to rest. And the cows suffered too — where the crowded settlement had fouled the grass, the herds grazed poorly and the milk turned poor. It was time to move.

Then he told Balarama of the place he had heard of: a forest on the bank of the Yamuna called Vrindavana. Grass grew thick there, he said, and the ground was free of thorns and biting insects, and the trees bore fruit. Cool winds blew there all year round, as if every season had made its home in that one place. Kadamba trees stood in the groves, and close by rose the great mountain Govardhana, its summit high as Mount Mandara, the mountain of the gods. In the heart of that mountain grew an enormous fig tree, the Bhandira, its branches spreading over a full yojana — a distance that takes the better part of a day to walk — dark against the sky like a rain-cloud. And the Yamuna herself, called Kalindi in the old songs, flowed through the middle of it all, straight as a parting drawn through hair. There, Krishna said, they would look upon the mountain, and the tree, and the river, and be glad.

There was only one difficulty. The milkmen loved their village and would not willingly leave it. So Krishna made his plan. Let us create some calamity, he told his brother, and frighten the milkmen into going.

And as he spoke, the thought became the thing. From the hairs of his body there arose wolves — hundreds of wolves, dark-faced and fierce, each one bearing on its chest the curled mark called Srivatsa, the sign of Vishnu. They poured out of him and ran in every direction, as if the whole settlement of Vraja were to be overrun. They fell upon the calves and the cows and the women, and a great fear seized the milkmen. The wolves gathered themselves into packs of five and ten and twenty and thirty and a hundred and ranged through the village, and the terror of them spread everywhere.

That terror was the whole point. Krishna did not raise these wolves to harm his own people; he raised them to move his people, as a herdsman moves a herd that has eaten one field down to the root. And the fear did its work. Day by day the milkmen lost their hold on the ruined forest, until at last nothing kept them in Vraja — and the whole settlement made ready for the green land on the Yamuna, where the grass still grew deep.
stories.reflection: Krishna does not argue the milkmen out of their home; he frightens them out of it. The wolves are not a punishment but an instrument — a gentle violence aimed at carrying his people from a spoiled place to a better one, the same hand that had beautified the forest now loosening its hold on them.
stories.tradition_note: The Harivamsha tells this migration as Krishna conjuring wolves to frighten the milkmen into moving; the Bhagavata and Vishnu Purana instead attribute the move to omens and portents.

stories.title: Uddhava Remembers Krishna's Cowherd Childhood
stories.story:
Years later, when Uddhava — Krishna's close friend and adviser — looked back on his friend's childhood, what he remembered first was not a god but a boy.

He remembered the calves. There had been a time, he said, when Krishna went out among them day after day, the young ones crowding close as he herded them, and sported in the groves along the Yamuna. The river lay green and quiet behind them, and the child moved at the heart of the herd while the calves pressed around him, as if they knew him and had no wish to be anywhere else. To the people of Vraja he showed his childhood play, and they found it lovely to watch — the way one watches something that will not come again.

He remembered, too, the way Krishna had been in those days: a child who wept and laughed in the same hour, whose glance, when he looked up, had the bright boldness of a lion cub. It was not one mood but all of childhood at once, tears and laughter turning into each other as they only do in the very young. The cowherds never tired of watching him, because in him their own children's days seemed lit from within.

And he remembered the flute. When Krishna played, the cowherds forgot their work and stood listening. The music gathered people round him the way the calves gathered at his feet, and no one wanted the tune to end; it seemed to hold them all in one place, under the trees, until the last note let them go.

But the memory that stayed with Uddhava longest was the strangest one. Kamsa — the cruel king of Mathura, Krishna's own uncle — had never stopped sending his agents against the boy. They came as shape-shifters, demons who could take any form they chose, and they came into the groves of Vrindavan meaning to destroy him. Krishna dispelled them, Uddhava remembered, in sport — as easily as a child knocks aside his toys. There was no battle in it, and no fear. The same boy who herded calves and played the flute simply brushed aside whatever darkness came looking for him, and then went back to his play, as if nothing had come at all.

That was what Uddhava could never put out of his mind: that the tenderness and the power had been one thing. The child who wept and laughed among the calves was the same one before whom the demons melted away. It was the oldest memory he had of Krishna, and it never dimmed; whenever he spoke of him in the years that followed, it was this boy he spoke of first — the child in the grove, with the calves and the flute, before the world knew him as anything else.
stories.reflection: Uddhava's memory holds the childhood and the godhood in a single breath: the same boy herding calves, weeping and laughing, and dispelling demons 'in sport, like toys.' The recollection finds the divine not in the miracles alone but in the tenderness of the ordinary day.
stories.next_story_tease: And among those remembered days was one that began more quietly than the rest, with a child left alone in a courtyard and two trees standing in the yard.

stories.title: Krishna Notices the Twin Arjuna Trees
stories.story:
In the cowherd village of Gokula, there came a morning when the boy Krishna found himself quite alone. His mother Yashoda was deep in the day's work — churning, sweeping, keeping the household in order — and for a while she had no eye to spare for him. So Krishna was left to himself, a small boy with the whole courtyard open before him and nothing to do but look. From the house came the soft, steady beat of the churn — up and down, up and down — and the morning felt slow and wide, with no one hurrying him.

And what he looked at, in that stillness, were the two arjuna trees.

They stood side by side at the edge of the yard, tall and straight, their trunks grown thick with years and their branches lacing together high overhead. Their shade lay cool across half the courtyard, and a small boy could not reach his arms around either trunk. The two leaned companionably, as if they had grown up side by side and meant to stay that way. To anyone else they were only trees — as ordinary as the wall or the well, the kind of thing a village stops seeing. But the child's eyes kept returning to them, the way a child's eyes return to the one thing in a yard that no one else notices, as if the trees were speaking to him in a language just below hearing.

They had not always been trees.

Once, long before, they had been two young men of the highest birth: Nalakuvara and Manigriva, sons of Kubera, the lord of wealth. In their father's bright halls they had lacked for nothing, waited on by the guhyakas — the celestial attendants of his court — and rich and favoured beyond anything the earth could offer, they had grown proud on their fortune. Then a single act of heedless pride threw it all away. The curse of Narada, the wandering sage, brought them down from that height and fixed them here, rooted in the earth as two arjuna trees, their names and their story buried deep inside the wood.

That was what stood in the courtyard that morning, though no one in the village knew it: a secret wearing the shape of the ordinary, waiting with a patience no person could match.

And the child — the only child in the world who could undo such a curse — stood looking up at them. Behind him his mother went on with her work, and the house with its quiet morning. The trees kept their long silence, as they had kept it for ages, and the boy kept looking, not knowing what he saw. But this was the first morning in all those ages that the one who could end their waiting had come within reach of them.
stories.reflection: The whole weight of the episode rests on a child's idle glance. The drama is built from stillness — a boy left alone in a courtyard, two trees, and a hidden history that will not stay hidden. What looks ordinary can carry a long past, waiting only to be seen.
stories.next_story_tease: What the two had done to earn such a fate — and whose curse had fixed them to the earth — was a story of its own.

stories.title: Narada Curses Nalakuvara and Manigriva
stories.story:
The two young men could not have chosen a worse moment to be proud.

Nalakuvara and Manigriva were the sons of Kubera, the lord of wealth, whose home was on the great mountain Kailasa, and they had never known a day of want. One day they drank deep of a heady wine the gods drink, called varuni, until their heads swam. In that state they wandered down to the river Ganga and into the water, where lotus beds grew thick along the bank, and there they played in the river with a company of celestial women, caring for nothing but their own pleasure.

It happened that Narada, the wandering sage, was passing that way. The women saw him first, and shame swept through them: unclothed as they were, and dreading what a curse from such a sage could do, they snatched their garments close and made themselves decent in an instant. But the two brothers, blinded by wine and by the pride of their riches, did not cover themselves, and did not bow. They stood where they were, as if their wealth made them untouchable.

Narada looked at them, and what he felt was not anger but a kind of grief. He began to speak.

Look at the bodies you are so proud of, he said. They will not last. However people may call them divine, in the end every body is worms and ashes, born of a father and a mother like any other, and gone like any other. It is only the pride of wealth that makes a man forget this — and for eyes that such pride has blinded, poverty is the best medicine, the sharpest salve. The poor man does not carry his head stiff with ego; his body is lean with hunger, and he knows he stands on no dignity. It is to the poor that the wise, who look on all beings with an equal eye, are drawn — and it is in such company that a man learns at last to want only the feet of Krishna.

Then Narada turned his words upon the two before him. These two, he said, are the sons of the protector of the world, and yet they lie sunk in darkness. Therefore let them stand as trees — rooted, motionless, unable to move a single step. But he did not wish them lost forever, and the curse carried its own promise. It would not be for all time, he said. After a hundred years as the gods count years — longer than any human reckoning can hold — they would come into the very presence of Krishna, and at his touch their long stillness would end and they would be set free.

So it fell out as the sage said. The two proud young men became twin arjuna trees, and their curse was also their cure: a long rooted silence in which the pride that had blinded them could slowly drain away. And there they stood, season after season, waiting out the hundred years — until at last the years were full, and in a courtyard in the cowherd village of Gokula a child named Krishna came near them one quiet morning, and looked up. The touch that would end their stillness was at last within reach.
stories.reflection: Narada's curse is framed not as revenge but as treatment. Pride, in his telling, is a kind of blindness, and poverty its sharpest cure; the sentence of tree-ness is softened by the promise of Krishna's touch, so that the punishment is turned toward release before it is even carried out.
stories.content_note: The episode involves intoxication and references to unclothed figures; it is told with restraint.

stories.title: The Cowherds Settle in Vrindavan
stories.story:
The road to Vrindavan was full long before the people reached it, because the cattle went first. A whole herd moved out ahead, hundreds of broad, slow backs, and behind them came the cowherds with their families and their carts, every horn and conch they owned blowing as they went, so that the dust of the track and the sound of it rose up together. It was not a flight, and not a festival. It was a village on the move.

Kamsa, the king of Mathura, had learned at last where the child Krishna was being raised, and the cowherds had no wish to stay where the next demon he sent might find them.

The women rode in the carts, freshly adorned for the road, and in one cart sat Yasoda, Krishna's mother, and Rohini, Balarama's mother, side by side. Krishna and Balarama were somewhere in the procession — among the boys who ran ahead and fell behind, or perched on the tail of a wagon, or lost in the warm dust beside the cattle. No one could say where they were at any given moment. That was simply the way of it with those two.

The carts carried more than people. They carried the whole weight of a household — cooking pots and bedding and bundles of grain, the old people who could not walk the whole way, and the small children too young to walk at all. But a cowherd's true wealth moved in front, on four legs, and no one drove the herd hard and no one left it behind.

They were bound for Vrindavan, a place the elders knew, a forest that stayed green and pleasant in every season. The journey was not long, and there was no ceremony about its end. The carts rolled in, the horns blew once more and fell quiet, and the cattle came to a stop.

Then the cowherds looked around, and understood why they had come.

The trees stood thick and cool, their shade lying across the ground like cloth. The hill of Govardhana rose to one side, low and broad, like a guardian set down to watch over the country. And the Yamuna ran past the edge of it all, its banks smooth with sand, the water moving quietly in the light. The old verses remember each of these things by name, because each of them mattered: the forest, the hill, the river.

They made their camp in a crescent of wagons, the way travellers have always made a wall of their carts and called it home. The cattle were loosed to drink, and settled into the grass with deep, satisfied sounds. The fires were lit, and their smoke went up straight into the still evening. The children, set down from the carts at last, ran the length of the new ground as though it had always been theirs.

And in a way it had. In Vrindavan the cowherds set down everything they owned and everything they loved. No one made a speech, and no one raised a flag. The wagons, the herds, the mothers and the boys and the two who were somehow more than boys — all of it came to rest inside that crescent, and the forest, the hill, and the river received them without a word.
stories.reflection: The settling of Vrindavan is told almost without event — a journey, an arrival, a camp — and that quietness is the point. Before any miracle or battle, there was this: a whole people on the road, and a place that received them without ceremony.
stories.next_story_tease: Settled in their new home, the boys would soon take up the herding of calves — and find an enemy waiting among them.

stories.title: Krishna Slays the Calf-Demon Vatsasura
stories.story:
Not long after the cowherds had settled in Vrindavan, the boys of the village were given a new piece of work. The calves had grown old enough to leave the pens, and it was time for them to be taken out to grass with the older herd. So the boys were set to watch over them. It was light work, and it suited them. Krishna and Balarama went out with the rest, and the days settled into an easy rhythm of sun and river and slow-moving cattle.

The pasture lay on the bank of the Yamuna, where the grass grew thick and the water was always near. All day the boys moved through it, and they did not keep watch in silence. The old verses remember how they passed the hours. Sometimes one of them played the flute while the others drifted closer to listen. Sometimes they flung their throwing-ropes at a mark on the ground, testing who could strike truest. And sometimes the two brothers squared off against each other, pawed the earth, and roared, and wrestled like a pair of young bulls while the other boys made a ring and shouted first for one side and then the other. It was play, and it held the long day together.

And it was into this quiet, sunlit routine that the demon came.

He was called Vatsasura. He did not come as himself. He took the shape of a calf — so young, so harmless-looking that no one would look twice — and stepped in among the herd as though he had been born to it. Among all those grazing backs and twitching tails, one more calf was nothing at all. He moved through them slowly, waiting.

But Krishna saw him. Disguise or no disguise, the demon could not pass those eyes. The moment the false calf edged close, Krishna reached out, caught it by the hind legs, and took the tail in the same grip. Then he lifted the creature clean off the grass.

He whirled it. Around his head he swung it, once and again, gathering speed, and then he let it fly, and the creature in its stolen calf's body went tumbling through the air and struck a wood-apple tree with a force no living calf could have survived. It fell lifeless to the ground and lay still beneath the tree, in the very shape it had borrowed, and it did not rise again. Whatever harm he had meant to work among the boys was over before it had begun.

The boys stood astonished for a long, still moment. Then the wonder broke, and they shouted together, "Well done! Well done!"

The old verses close on a marvel of their own: these two, they say, had taken up the herding of calves — and they were the keepers of all the worlds. Yet nothing on the riverbank announced it. The herd went on grazing as though nothing had happened, and the boys went back to their watching, a little quieter than before.
stories.reflection: Krishna's strength shows itself first in the most ordinary work — watching calves on a riverbank. The story does not separate the boy who plays the flute and wrestles like a young bull from the keeper of all the worlds; they are the same pair of hands.
stories.content_note: A demon in calf form is flung against a tree and killed; the violence is brief and not described in detail.
stories.next_story_tease: But Kamsa had more than one creature at his command, and a greater one was already winging toward the pasture.

stories.title: Krishna Slays the Crane-Demon Bakasura
stories.story:
The days in Vrindavan had fallen into a pattern: the boys led the calves out in the morning, the sun climbed, and the river ran. Then one day they came to the pasture and found it was not empty.

Something stood there, huge and still. As the boys drew near, they saw what it was — a crane, but no crane of the river or the reeds. It was enormous, tall as a thing that had grown out of the ground, and it stood planted on the grass, watching. The boys stopped where they were, the calves bunched behind them and lowed, and for a long moment nothing on the riverbank moved. Then they understood: it was not a bird at all, but a demon in the shape of a crane. Baka, the old verses call him — a friend of Kamsa, the king of Mathura who had sent one demon after another against the cowherds' child.

They had no time to warn one another. The great bird struck, and in a single motion it opened its long beak and swallowed Krishna whole.

The boys cried out. Balarama stood frozen, and the rest of them could only stare at the place where their friend had been standing, and at the throat of the monstrous bird. In that black moment they thought they had lost him. A demon had taken the child who never seemed afraid of anything, and the riverbank felt suddenly enormous and empty.

But inside the crane, Krishna was no morsel to be scorched and digested. He was the fire itself. He blazed at the very root of the creature's palate, and the heat climbed, and the great bird that had gulped him down to be rid of him found it could not hold him for another moment. Its beak gaped wide and flung him out onto the grass — whole, unharmed, not even singed. The boys' cries turned, in an instant, to something else.

Then the demon came at him, enraged and beating its wings, and Krishna did not wait for it to reach him. He took hold of the bird by the two halves of its long beak, one in each hand, and tore it apart the way a child splits a stalk of grass. The crane that had swallowed him fell broken to the ground, and did not move again.

The boys could hardly believe what their eyes had seen. They ran to Krishna as though he had come back to them from far away. The old verses catch the moment in a single image: it was as if their very breath, which had left their bodies when he vanished down that throat, now returned to them. And from the sky above, the dwellers of heaven, who had watched it all, let fall a shower of flowers — blossoms drifting slowly down over the children, over the fallen demon, over the quiet water of the Yamuna. The herd grazed on as before, and the boys sat down in the grass to catch their breath, and after a while they led the calves home in the long, level light of evening.
stories.reflection: Bakasura swallows Krishna and discovers, too late, that he has taken in what he cannot contain. But the story's real center is the image of the boys' breath returning — what the demon meant to take, Krishna gives back.
stories.content_note: Krishna is swallowed by a demon crane and tears it apart; the violence is brief and not described in detail.
stories.next_story_tease: The demons were not finished: Aghasura, brother of the slain Putana and Bakasura, was already nursing his revenge.

stories.title: Aghasura Becomes a Giant Python
stories.story:
There is a kind of grief that only wants to make more grief, and Aghasura had it. He was the younger brother of Putana and of Bakasura: the first had come to Krishna's cradle long ago and been destroyed, and the second had come to the pasture not many days since and been torn apart. Their loss sat in him like a splinter. Kamsa, the king of Mathura who had sent one demon after another against the cowherds' child, put him up to the deed, the old verses say — but Aghasura needed little urging. He wanted revenge, and he knew exactly where to find it.

He did not go down to the village in his own shape. He grew, stretching himself out and out until he was a python a yojana long — a yojana is a distance of many miles — and thick as a hill. Then he lay down across the path the boys took each day to the pasture, and he opened his mouth.

It was no ordinary mouth. His lower lip rested on the earth and his upper lip touched the clouds. The space between them was a cave, dark and deep, and his teeth rose like the peaks of a mountain range, so that the whole monstrous thing looked less like a living creature than like a piece of the country itself — a gorge, a cavern, a ridge of stone — lying open in the afternoon light.

That was his trick, and it worked. The boys came down the path with their calves and stopped short at the sight of it, and not one of them was afraid, because not one of them saw a snake. They saw a marvel.

"Look," they said to one another, "a mountain has lain down in the forest." And they argued over it the way children argue over a wonder. Was it a cave cut into the rock, or a cloud that had come down to rest, its edge reddened by the sun? The verses remember the whole happy, foolish debate — how they measured the thing with their eyes and gave it a hundred wrong names, how they stepped closer to peer into the deep shadows of it — while the creature they were praising lay silent and waiting. They even said, in their play, that if it tried to swallow them it would die as Baka had died. And they said it laughing, because they did not believe for a moment that it was alive at all.

Only Krishna knew. He heard their guesses, and he knew in the same instant what the thing was, and whose brother it was, and what it meant to do to him and to his brother Balarama. And he made up his mind, there on the path, that the mouth which had opened to swallow his friends would not close on them.
stories.reflection: The horror of Aghasura lies in how well his disguise works: the boys praise the very mouth that would eat them. Deception here is not a lie told but a truth too strange to be believed, and only Krishna sees through the loveliness to the danger beneath.
stories.content_note: A demon takes the form of a vast python and lies in wait to swallow the boys; the danger is described, but no one is harmed in this episode.
