stories.title: Krishna Kills Aghasura and Revives His Friends
stories.story:
Aghasura was a demon, and he had come to the forest in the shape of an immense python. The forest had gone quiet around him, as though the birds had understood before anyone else what lay stretched along the ground. The cowherd boys of Vrindavan, out with their calves as on any other day, had gone into his open mouth, and now they lay inside him — alive but trapped, not yet swallowed. How they were drawn in, the old verses do not say; only that they went in, and did not come out.

Krishna saw it, and the sight pierced him with pity. These were his friends, his own companions, and they lay in the belly of a demon, helpless, with no one in the world to turn to but him. He was amazed, too, at what fate had done. What use was the life of this wretch, he asked himself — and how could the harm done to these innocents be undone? Could both be answered at once, the death of the evil one and the saving of the good? He saw that they could, in a single stroke, and he did not hesitate. He walked into the demon's mouth.

The gods, watching from behind the clouds, cried out in fear. They had seen what a demon could do to a child, and they did not yet know that they were watching a god undo it.

Inside, Krishna grew. He grew until the demon's throat was blocked, until the great serpent could neither swallow nor breathe. He grew past its teeth and its throat, and the darkness inside it gave way before him. Its eyes bulged, and it writhed this way and that, and its vast body thrashed against the earth as the air was cut off from it. It had meant to hold the whole herd in its belly, and instead it found that it could not even draw a breath. And when its last breath left it, Krishna raised up the boys and their calves, who had lain lifeless inside, and led them out into the open air — alive again.

As the demon died, a great light rose from its body and stood blazing, like a second moon or the sun come up at night, and the light entered Krishna.

Then the sky broke into sound. The gods rained flowers down. The gandharvas, heaven's singers, sang; the apsaras, heaven's dancers, danced; and the brahmins raised their hymns, and all of heaven celebrated the boys' return. And where the demon had fallen, only its dried skin remained, stretched across the ground of Vrindavan, a wonder that would not soon be forgotten. The boys looked at it for a long time before they gathered their calves and started for home.
stories.reflection: The story's emphasis falls not on the killing but on the great light that leaves the demon and enters Krishna, and on the boys walking out alive. Even for an enemy, the account holds out release rather than destruction.
stories.content_note: A demon in python form swallows the cowherd boys and calves; he is overcome without graphic detail.

stories.title: Brahma Steals the Calves and Boys
stories.story:
Brahma, the creator of the worlds, had seen it all. From beyond the world he had watched a small cowherd child walk into the open mouth of a python-demon, and he had watched the same child lead his friends out again, alive. He had seen the great light leave the dead demon and enter the boy, and the wonder of it stayed with him.

He was the firstborn of creation. He had shaped the stars and set the seasons turning, and nothing his hands had made was supposed to surprise him. And yet here was a thing in Vrindavan that his own handiwork could not explain — a village child who had stepped into death and come out holding his friends by the hand. Could it be what it seemed to be? The verses say he wanted to see the beauty of that greatness again, and more besides, and that he wanted to be certain.

So he waited, and the chance came quickly. One day the boys were at their play on a sandbank by the river. It was an ordinary day of the kind Vrindavan knew well — the calves grazing near at hand, the boys spreading out their meal and eating together, the sun warm on the water. In a careless moment the calves strayed, and Krishna went after them alone, to bring them back. The sandbank lay quiet behind him, and the boys, whose sudden fear Krishna had just quieted with a word, were at ease. What was there to fear, with Krishna only a little way off?

And into that quiet Brahma moved. It was not a violent thing. One moment the cowherd boys were there, and the next they were gone, and the calves with them — gathered up and hidden away by a power no one in Vrindavan could see or name. No footfall, no sound; the river went on running as if nothing had been there at all. The creator carried them off as easily as a man gathers a handful of seeds, and set them down in a place beyond the reach of any searching eye. Then he returned to his place in the sky, and watched.

When Krishna came back to the sandbank, the river was the only sound. No boys. No calves. The food they had been eating lay where it had been set down, and no one was left to eat it. He knew at once what had happened, and who had done it, for nothing is hidden from him. And yet, the old verses say, he searched. He went into the deep forest and looked for them, and he did not find them, because they were not there to be found. The all-knowing one went looking for what he already knew, and let the question hang unanswered in the air.

So the day ended with the sandbank empty and one small boy standing alone at the water's edge. He had searched, and he had not found them — and he knew better than anyone why: his friends were not hiding anywhere in that forest. They were gone beyond it, into the keeping of the creator. Krishna looked out across the darkening river and let the night come down. Far away, in the place where Brahma had hidden them, the boys slept on among their calves. And Brahma, watching from above the world, waited to see what the child would do.
stories.reflection: Brahma's test is born not of malice but of wonder: the maker of the universe, unable to account for what he has seen, hides the children away simply to understand what is standing before him. The episode quietly reverses the roles, so that the one who tests is himself the one about to be taught.
stories.next_story_tease: But Krishna would not leave the boys' mothers to grieve for long.
stories.hero_scene: An empty sandbank by the river at dusk, with the boys' half-eaten meal spread on the ground and the boy Krishna standing alone at the water's edge — the only figure left in a landscape from which every calf and cowherd boy has vanished.

stories.title: Krishna Becomes Every Calf and Boy
stories.story:
One day the calves and the cowherd boys of Vrindavan — the little forest village where Krishna was growing up — vanished, and no one could say where they had gone. The boys had walked out that morning with their staffs and their flutes, driving the calves before them, and they simply did not come back. As the afternoon stretched toward evening, mothers stood in their doorways, listening. The cows shifted in their pens and lowed into the quiet for calves that did not answer. The whole village seemed to have lost its young at once.

Krishna had been with the boys, and he alone knew what had become of them. He could have set every child and every calf back in his own place with a word. But he chose a gentler way, one meant not merely to repair what was missing but to give something to the mothers and the cows who were waiting. He became them. Standing at the edge of the pasture, Krishna stretched himself into every vanished calf and every vanished boy, taking on not only each face and pair of limbs but everything that made that child that particular child — his staff and his horn, his flute and the leaf in his hand, his ornaments and his clothes, and deeper than these, his temper, his way of talking, his name, his age, the very way he walked and played. The old verses say that every one of those boys and calves was Krishna himself, whole and complete.

Then each boy gathered his own calf and walked home to his own house. In the cow-pens the cows hurried forward, calling to their calves with a lowing that filled the evening air, and the calves ran to them as though they had never been away. In the houses, mothers rose at the first note of a flute, ran out, and lifted their sons into their arms. They held them close and would not put them down — kissing them, washing them, dressing them, marking their foreheads with tilak, the red mark of blessing, and setting food before them. They asked nothing, and needed no answer. The lost thing had come back, and that was all they wanted.

And the strange, tender part was this: the love did not simply return. It grew. The cows loved their calves, and the women loved their sons, with a warmth greater than they had felt before — because what they held in their arms was Krishna himself, wearing a different child's face, and not one of them suspected it.

So it went for a full year. Morning after morning the boys who were Krishna drove the calves who were Krishna out to the pastures, and evening after evening they came home to mothers who were loving Krishna without knowing it. The affection in those homes climbed the way a vine climbs, leaf by leaf, in a season no one counts. And no one ever guessed — not the mothers, not the cows, not even the boys themselves. All year long the village kissed its children goodnight, and every small forehead under those kisses was Krishna's.
stories.reflection: The episode turns on a quiet paradox: the mothers' love deepened precisely when its object was Krishna, though they did not know it. Love, the story suggests, is not made less real for being offered in ignorance — it is simply received by the one who was always its true object.
stories.next_story_tease: Yet a wildfire was soon to sweep through the forest toward the herd.
stories.hero_scene: In the doorway of a cowherd home a mother lifts her small son high and kisses his head, while in home after home across Vrindavan other mothers do the same with their own boys — every one of them Krishna, wearing a different child's face.

stories.title: Brahma Falls at Krishna's Feet
stories.story:
Brahma, the four-faced creator of the universe, had stolen away the calves and cowherd boys of Vrindavan, for he had seen a greatness in the child Krishna that he wanted to see again — and to be certain of. To Brahma, only a moment had passed since then. In Vrindavan, a year.

When he came back to look for the boys and calves he had hidden, he found them exactly where they had always been — playing on the sandbank by the river, tending their calves, running home at dusk to mothers who held them as though they had been gone a long while. The cows hurried from their pens at the sound of lowing, and the calves ran to them, and the whole herd settled into its evening as if nothing had ever disturbed it. And the love in those homes, the verses say, had grown deeper than before. The cowherd men and women doted on their children with a tenderness that surprised even themselves, and no one could have said why.

Brahma could not tell the difference between what he had hidden and what he now saw. The boys he had carried off — where were they? And these boys, who were they? He stood a long while turning it over, and the more he thought, the less he understood. He reached for the very power of illusion that had hidden the children in the first place and tried to use it again — and the illusion merely looked back at him. It was, the verses say, like a firefly's light at noon, or a darkness trying to settle in the mist of a morning that is already gone.

Then, before his eyes, the children changed. Every cowherd boy on the sandbank appeared no longer as a boy but as a four-armed form holding a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus. On each chest shone the shrivatsa mark, the small sacred curl, and armlets and bracelets glinted on each arm, and from head to foot every form was draped in garlands of fresh tulsi, the holy basil. Each face smiled like moonlight, with a sidelong glance full of kindness, and each form was truth, knowledge, and joy without end. Around them stood all the worlds and all the powers that move them, from the first gods down to the last blade of grass, every one in its own shape. Where a crowd of village children had been playing, there now stood an endless company of the Lord himself — and Brahma, who had made the universe, stood speechless before it.

Brahma's senses froze where they were; he could do nothing but look, unable to say what he was seeing. It was too much for him, and then it was hidden — for Krishna saw what was happening and gently, as one draws a curtain, covered Brahma's sight. When the creator opened his eyes again, it was like a man waking from the dead. The vision was gone. Around him lay the ordinary world, men and animals sitting together with no sign of their natural enmity. And there, before him, stood a small boy with a morsel of food in his hand, searching for his friends as if nothing at all had happened.

Brahma came down from his swan and threw himself on the ground like a golden rod. He touched Krishna's feet with the tips of his four crowns and bathed them with his tears.
stories.reflection: Brahma came to test, and found himself tested. The vision of countless four-armed forms is overwhelming, but what finally undoes him is the plainness that follows it — a child with a morsel of food, looking for his friends. Krishna's true hiding place, the story suggests, is not the spectacle but the ordinary.
stories.next_story_tease: But Brahma had not yet finished speaking.

stories.title: Brahma's Hymn of Forgiveness
stories.story:
Brahma, the four-faced creator of the universe, had come to Vrindavan to see for himself what the child Krishna was — stealing away the village's calves and cowherd boys to draw the truth out of him. Krishna had answered by becoming every one of them, and then by showing Brahma who he truly was. Now the creator lay at the child's feet, and he did not rise quickly. The words came out of him one after another, like water finding its way downhill.

"This body of yours," he began, "is made of your own will. It is not made of matter, as mine is. Who can understand it?" Those who set aside the struggle to know and simply bow and listen, he said, are the ones the truth comes to meet; while those who chase understanding alone and throw devotion away are like men threshing empty husks — all their labour, and nothing left in the hand. Even the purest-hearted, even the great seers, cannot measure your greatness, he said, for it is not the kind of thing that can be measured.

Then he came to what weighed on him most. "Look at my foolishness, Lord," he said. "I was born of passion, and in my ignorance I thought myself a lord apart from you. Forgive me." He measured himself against what stood before him and found the measuring absurd. "Where am I," he asked, "a little body of seven hand-spans, shut inside this shell of a universe — and where is your greatness, in the pores of whose skin whole worlds drift, more worlds than I can count?"

He remembered the day's unfolding and named it aloud. "Today you have shown me your maya," he said — your power of illusion. "First you were one. Then you were all the cowherd boys and calves. Then you were an endless company of four-armed forms, and I worshipped you along with everything that lives. Then you were as many universes. And what remained, when all of it was seen, was only the one — the unlimited."

He spoke, too, of the world itself, and how strange it was. "This whole world," he said, "is as unreal as a dream, and full of sorrow — and yet through your maya it shines as if it were real, resting on you alone."

He called him by his oldest name. "You are Narayana," he said, "the Self of every being, the witness of every world. It was from your navel, when the worlds had dissolved into water, that all of this rose again. Who among gods and sages and men and beasts can say where you have come from?"

And then he marvelled, not at his own smallness but at the good fortune of Vrindavan. "How fortunate are the women who fed you at their breast as if you were their own child, tasting in your milk the nectar of the gods. How fortunate are the people of Nanda's pasture, where you have chosen to live — whose very dust, the dust of your feet, the sacred Vedas go searching for and never find enough of."

At last he came to the end of the hymn and to the one thing he had come to ask. He praised the one who is the joy of the Vrishni lotus, who makes the earth and the cows and the brahmins, the priests and teachers, flourish. "Give me leave, Krishna," he said. "You know everything there is to know." And he walked three times around the child, bowed, and went back to his own realm, leaving behind him a hymn that has not been forgotten since.
stories.reflection: The hymn is remarkable because it is the creator himself measuring his limits. It does not argue Krishna's greatness from above; it works from below, setting a seven-span body against pores that hold universes, and finding that the only honest posture left is praise and a request to be allowed to go.
stories.next_story_tease: And the boys, who had been hidden all the while, would sit down to their meal as if nothing had happened.

stories.title: The Year That Was a Moment
stories.story:
When Brahma, the four-faced creator, had been given leave and was gone, Krishna turned back to the sandbank, and the boys and their calves were there again, just as they had been, as though no hand had ever carried them away.

He set everything back as it had been. He did not announce it; there was no fanfare and no explanation. He simply returned what had been taken, and the world closed over the gap the way water closes over a stone.

And this was the strangest part of the whole affair. A whole year had passed — a year in which the cows had grazed and the seasons had turned, the calves had grown, and the river had risen and fallen again; a year in which the mothers of Vrindavan had poured their love over children who, though they did not know it, had never truly been away. But the boys knew nothing of it. The year sat on them as lightly as a dream that vanishes the moment the eyes open. Their minds, the verses say, were covered by maya, the great illusion, and what they had lost, they could not remember losing — not the days spent hidden away, not the one who had hidden them, not the year itself. All of it was gone from them, as if it had never been.

"Welcome back!" they cried when they saw Krishna, as if he had only just stepped away. "You returned quickly!" They did not ask where he had been, because as far as they knew he had never left them at all, and that certainty was its own quiet mercy.

The calves came wandering back to the boys as though they had only just strayed, and no one thought to wonder at it. Krishna smiled and sat down among them and ate, and they finished the meal they had left unfinished, as though the afternoon had never been broken off. Then they gathered up their things and started home, Krishna calling to the calves as he went, the calves following the sound of his voice. He was decked in peacock feathers and flowers and the bright earth-colours of the woods, his flute sounding as he walked, the boys singing his praises around him, and the eyes of the gopis, watching from the doorways, grew glad at the sight of them.

And as they came into the village they had a story to tell — how that very day Krishna, the son of Yashoda and Nanda, had slain a great serpent. They carried its dried skin with them as proof, the way a hunter carries home the hide, and no one who saw it could doubt the tale.
stories.reflection: The tenderest detail is the return to the story the boys were telling before they vanished — the great serpent, slain 'that very day.' A year of their lives passed without them, and they pick up the thread exactly where they dropped it. Time, the story suggests, is not one thing for everyone, and what Krishna guards can be given back whole.
stories.next_story_tease: And soon the boys would set their hearts on a palm grove whose sweet fruit no one had ever dared to eat.

stories.title: The Fruit No One Had Ever Eaten
stories.story:
The cowherd boys of Vrindavan had been out since morning with their calves, and the afternoon had settled into the slow, warm rhythm they knew well — the calves grazing, the boys at their games in the shade, the sun high and steady. It was an ordinary day, and it would have stayed an ordinary day, but for the wind. When it turned, it carried a scent they knew at once, and it stopped them in the middle of their play. The calves went on grazing, but the boys stood still, lifting their heads like animals catching a trail. Sweet, heavy, faint as a half-remembered dream, the smell drifted from the edge of the forest — from the one place in all their world that no one ever entered.

A little way off stood the palm grove, the talavana. In every season its trees let fall fruit so ripe and fragrant that the smell of it perfumed the air for a long way around. The verses say the fruit kept falling and lay fallen in such plenty that no one could ever have gathered it all — it never stopped coming. Yet it lay where it dropped, season after season, untouched. The ground beneath the palms was soft with over-ripe fruit, and no hand had ever gathered a single piece. No one in Vrindavan had ever tasted it.

The reason was no secret. The grove belonged to a demon named Dhenuka, who wore the form of a donkey, and his kin lived there with him, as fierce as he. He was enormously strong, and he had made men his food, and so the people of Vrindavan kept their distance. Even the grown men, who grazed their herds across every other corner of the forest, gave the grove a wide berth and would not walk past it alone. The fruit ripened and fell and rotted where it lay, and the boys could only look at it from far off, while the fragrance drifted over them and teased them.

That day the longing grew too strong to bear. The smell came again, sweet and insistent, and the boys could not turn away from it. They came running to Krishna and his elder brother Balarama, their words tumbling over one another. "Rama! Rama, mighty-armed! Krishna, destroyer of the wicked!" they cried. They told of the grove where the fruit fell and fell and was never eaten, and of the fierce donkey who guarded it and had made men his food. Their minds were greedy with the fragrance. "Give us that fruit," they begged.

Krishna heard his friends out, and heard the longing in their voices. He did not need to be persuaded, and he did not stop to weigh the danger. When he heard their words, the old verses say, he wished only to do what would please them. So the two brothers set out for the palm grove, the boys following close behind, and the sweet smell of the forbidden fruit grew stronger with every step they took toward it.
stories.reflection: The boys do not try to take the fruit themselves; they know exactly where strength and protection lie, and they ask for what they want with a trust so complete it is almost childlike. The fragrance stands in for every desire that is lovely and safe-looking but guarded by something no one has dared to face.
stories.next_story_tease: But the guardian of the grove would not give up its fruit so easily.
stories.hero_scene: The cowherd boys clustered around Krishna and Balarama at the edge of the palm grove, pointing toward palms heavy with ripe fruit, the sweet fragrance hanging in the warm air as the brothers set out toward the forbidden trees.

stories.title: Balarama and the Donkey Demon
stories.story:
The palm grove stood apart from the life of Vrindavan, the cowherd village where Krishna and his elder brother Balarama were growing up. No herd was ever taken there, and no boy gathered the fruit that lay rotting beneath the trees, for a demon guarded the grove and no one had ever stood against him. But now the cowherd boys had begged the brothers for that fruit — sweet and forbidden — and the brothers did not hesitate at the grove's edge. Balarama walked straight to the nearest palm and laid his arms to its trunk, and when he shook it, the ripe fruit came down in a shower.

He moved from tree to tree, and each one he shook let go of its fruit, until the ground began to fill with it, the fruit striking the earth in a steady, sweet rain. The boys must have laughed at the sound — the soft, quick drumming of fruit falling on fruit, the first time in anyone's memory that the grove had given anything away. For a little while it seemed almost innocent: nothing in it but sunlight, palms, and the smell of ripe fruit.

But the grove had a keeper, and he heard the noise. Deep among the trees dwelt the fierce demon Dhenuka in his donkey's form, feeding on the flesh of deer. He had kept this grove his own for as long as anyone could remember, and he did not share its fruit with anyone. The crashing of the falling fruit called him out of the deep grove, He came rushing through the palms in a fury — huge, and past all reasoning. He did not pause to measure his enemy or to cry a warning; he fell upon Balarama and kicked at him with his hind legs, putting all his strength into the blows.

Balarama caught him by the hind legs. The verses say he whirled the donkey round with a single hand, as easily as play, until the creature expired, and then dashed him against a great palm tree. The tree, struck by that huge-headed body, trembled from crown to root, and the blow shook down fruit like rain poured upon the earth by the wind. Dhenuka fell lifeless to the ground.

The demon who had made men his food, whose very name had kept the whole of Vrindavan out of this grove, lay dead at the foot of the tree he had guarded all his days. It was no wonder, the verses add, for the one who did it is the infinite Lord of all the worlds. The boys watched in silence, and slowly the grove grew quiet again, until there was nothing left stirring in it but the last of the falling fruit.
stories.reflection: There is a strange gentleness in how the verse describes it: Balarama does not labor against Dhenuka, he simply catches him and lets the demon's own fury carry him to his end. The thing that had kept everyone away for so long turns out to be no match for a boy's ease.
stories.tradition_note: The sources differ on the details: the Bhagavata Purana has Balarama shake down the palms and make the kill himself, while the Vishnu Purana has both brothers shake the trees and names Rama (Balarama) alone as the slayer.
stories.content_note: A demon in donkey form is whirled and dashed against a palm tree; the violence is brief and not described in detail.
stories.next_story_tease: But Dhenuka's kin came rushing to avenge him.

stories.title: The Grove Opened to Everyone
stories.story:
The grove did not stay quiet for long. That day Krishna and his brother Balarama, who tended the cattle of Vrindavan, had come at last into the palm grove that everyone else avoided. When Dhenuka, its fierce donkey-demon keeper, came raging out at them, Balarama struck him down, and the grove had barely fallen still when Dhenuka's kin heard what had happened. They were demons of the same form and the same appetite, and they came rushing to avenge him — not one or two but the whole fierce kindred in a body, their hooves drumming on the earth as they poured through the palms. They must have seen the fruit scattered over the ground and the great tree still trembling, and still they came, rage pressing them forward where fear had kept everyone else away for so long. They had guarded this grove as fiercely as their fallen kinsman, and they meant to keep it.

They came all at once, charging at the brothers from every side. Krishna and Balarama did not retreat, and they did not prepare for a long fight. The verses say they moved as if at play, without effort or hurry, and flung the charging donkeys lifeless among the palm trees, one after another, until the last of them lay still. There was no real battle, only a clearing away — the way a hand sweeps fallen leaves from a path. The demons who had been terror itself to everyone who lived nearby were no more than leaves before it.

When it was over, the grove lay strewn with the lifeless bodies of the demons, and the ground, already deep in the fruit Balarama had shaken down, was thick with both. What had been a place of fear was only a quiet grove again, silent but for the wind moving through the palms. The terror that had hung over it for so long was gone, and what remained was the smell of ripe fruit and the shade of the trees.

The gods and the wise heard of the deed and rejoiced. And below, in the grove itself, something simpler and longer-lasting began. The people, their fear gone, came in and ate the palm fruit at last — the fruit that had fallen year after year, untouched and uneaten, now gathered freely and tasted, by anyone who wished it, children and elders alike. The cattle, too, grazed where they had never before dared to venture, cropping the fresh grass beneath the palms, and the grove that had once been spoken of only in warnings became a place people walked through without a second thought.

There was no guardian left to keep anyone out, and so the grove, for the first time, belonged to everybody. Krishna, the verses close, stood among them with his eyes like lotus petals, and the sound of his name and his deeds went out into the world as something auspicious to hear.
stories.reflection: The abundance was always there, falling to the ground season after season; what had kept it out of reach was not scarcity but fear. Once the fear is gone, nothing else changes and everything changes — the same fruit, the same grove, now open to everyone.
stories.content_note: Several demons are flung lifeless among the palms; the violence is brief and not described in detail.

stories.title: Krishna Swallows the Forest Fire
stories.story:
Night lay over Vraja, the cowherd country where Krishna and his brother Balarama lived with the families who kept the cattle. The settlement slept. The cattle lay still in the dark, the cowherds and their households had given themselves to rest after the long day's grazing, and the forest stood quiet around them all, breathing its cool breath over the roofs and the sleeping herds. It was the deep, trusting sleep of people who had never had reason to fear the night, for the forest had always been their shelter. Nothing in that stillness gave any warning.

Then, from the dry heart of the woods, a fire rose. It fed on the parched grass and the undergrowth, and it did not stay where it was born. It came toward the settlement from every side at once, a wall of flame closing in, until there was no direction left to turn that was not burning. Wherever a frightened eye looked there was the glow of it, and the crackle filled the night like a voice, and the heat arrived before the flames, like a warning that came too late. The smoke rose thick and black against the dark sky.

The people woke to heat and light and smoke. The heat reached them even where they lay, terror seized them, and there was no path out, for the fire pressed in from all around. They did the only thing they knew to do. They cried out, all of them together, into the roaring dark, to the two brothers they trusted above all — Krishna, and Balarama, whom everyone called Rama. “Krishna! Krishna! O greatly fortunate one! O Rama of boundless power! We are your own people, your friends — save us from this terrible fire, this fire that no one can cross, this fire like the one that will end all things!”

The verses say the Lord of the world looked on the distress of his own people. He did not rebuke them for their fear, and he did not turn them away. He simply took the fire into himself and drank it up — the whole of it, the flames that had closed around Vraja — until nothing was left burning in the night but the memory of the heat. The wall of destruction was gone, as if it had never risen. The people, who a moment before had stood helpless before the flames, now saw only darkness and the unchanged shapes of their own homes.

The village stood whole. The dark came back over the trees, cool and still, and the people found themselves alive in it — in the silence after the roar, breathing air that no longer stung, wrapped in a night that no longer burned.
stories.reflection: The villagers are shown in their ordinary fear, calling out like people who have nowhere else to turn, and the answer they receive is not a lesson but a rescue. Divine power here is not spectacle; it is the simple act of making a place safe again for the people who sleep in it.
stories.content_note: A forest fire threatens the sleeping settlement; the danger is real but no one is harmed.

stories.title: Pralamba Joins the Games in Disguise
stories.story:
The cowherd boys of Vrindavan were not unused to strangers. Travelers passed through the forest, and boys from the neighboring villages sometimes drifted over to watch their games. But there was something about the new boy that none of them could quite name. He appeared at the edge of their play without anyone noticing him arrive, smiling easily, and before long he was standing among them as though he had always been there.

Krishna and his brother Balarama were tending the herd in the forest, and the days were full of the games cowherd boys invent to pass the time — running and leaping and wrestling, calling the cows by name, weaving little ornaments of grass and wild flowers. The stranger slipped into all of it without effort. He laughed at their jokes and kept pace in their races, and the boys, generous as children are, took him for a friend. There was no reason to look twice at him; he was only another boy, quick with a jest and easy in a race. That was the whole art of the thing.

He was no friend. He was an asura — a demon — named Pralamba, and he had come in the shape of a cowherd boy for a single purpose: to seize the two brothers and destroy them, for their growing fame had begun to trouble the powerful. Adorned with wild flowers and wearing the easy manner of a milk-boy, he moved among the boys studying their weaknesses, casting dreadful looks at Krishna and Balarama when he thought no one was watching, and waiting for his moment. The other boys saw only a pleasant newcomer. Pralamba saw prey.

Krishna knew everything. The verses are plain on this point: even knowing the stranger for what he was, he welcomed his friendship. He did not cry out, he did not warn the others, he did not tear the disguise away. He returned Pralamba's smile with the same quiet friendliness and let the demon believe his trick had worked — and in his heart he had already resolved what must be done with him.

So when the afternoon grew long, Krishna — who knew every game the cowherds played, and how to turn a game to his purpose — called the boys together and proposed something new. They would play the riding game, he told them — carrying one another on their shoulders and racing, the way cowherd boys did. The boys clapped and cheered and rushed to pair off, and Pralamba, delighted at the chance to draw close to the brothers, smiled his borrowed smile and took his place among them.

Krishna watched him move into position — and let him.
stories.reflection: What is striking is how unhurried Krishna is. He knows the demon for what he is and does not flinch or warn; he simply receives the danger as calmly as a host receives a guest, and lets the deception run its course until it turns against the deceiver. The disguised enemy is never as hidden as he believes.
stories.next_story_tease: In the game that followed, the demon would seize his chance — and meet the brother whose weight he could not carry.

stories.title: Balarama Slays the Demon Pralamba
stories.story:
The riding game was a simple one, the kind children everywhere have always played: one boy hoisted another onto his shoulders, and they raced, and the one who lost carried the winner. Krishna and Balarama joined in with the rest. The verses say that when Sridama — another of the cowherd boys — and the other strong boys of the herd stood on Balarama's side, even Krishna was defeated, and good-naturedly he took Sridama on his back. Laughter spread across the clearing as the boys staggered under one another's weight.

Pralamba had chosen to carry Balarama. He was the asura who had slipped into their games disguised as an ordinary cowherd boy, waiting for his chance to carry one of the brothers off. To anyone watching, the pairing looked like an unlucky draw, for Balarama was no light burden. But the demon had made the choice himself, and for his own reasons. All through the games he had studied the two brothers, casting his dreadful looks at them, and he had concluded that Krishna was beyond his reach, too dangerous to touch. The elder brother, he decided, was the one to take. So with Balarama on his shoulders, Pralamba began to move — not back toward the Bhandira tree, where the others were gathering, but away, quickly and quietly, in the opposite direction.

At first Balarama thought little of it. But the demon's steps grew swift, and the laughter of the other boys faded behind them. Then the shoulders beneath him began to swell. The boy he was riding grew — hugely, hideously — until he was no longer a cowherd at all but a great asura in his true form, tall as a tree, dressed in gold and blazing with ornaments, his eyes like chariot wheels and a crown upon his head, and the earth sank under the weight of his feet. He had thrown off his disguise and was carrying Balarama away through the sky like a storm-cloud carrying the moon. For a moment even Balarama was startled.

Then his mind steadied. “Krishna,” he called, “I am being carried off by this great demon, who has thrown aside his illusion and shown his real form. How shall I overcome him?”

Krishna, watching from the clearing, answered him with a smile. He knew, he said, what Balarama truly was; the one being carried was not the weaker of the two. He told his brother to remember his own strength and not to fear.

So Balarama did. He let himself be carried a little longer, gathering himself, and then he raised his fist — a fist the verses compare to a thunderbolt — and brought it down once upon the demon's head. Pralamba fell from the sky and lay still upon the earth like a toppled mountain, and when the cowherd boys came running, they found him there, slain by Balarama's single blow.

The danger was over as suddenly as it had come, and the brothers turned back toward their herd and their friends, unhurried, as though nothing very remarkable had happened at all.
stories.reflection: Balarama's moment of fear matters. Even the strong are allowed a heartbeat of alarm before they remember what they are; what follows is not a struggle but a single, settled blow. The story keeps its power precisely because it does not pretend the danger was never real.
stories.tradition_note: The Harivamsha adds that the celestials gave Balarama the name Baladeva in honour of this feat, and the Vishnu Purana tells the death somewhat differently — Balarama laughing as he squeezes the demon with his knees and beats his head and face with his fists. This account follows the Bhagavata Purana, where the demon falls to a single blow.
stories.content_note: The demon's death is described briefly; the fall is restrained.
stories.next_story_tease: But a fiercer danger than any demon was about to find the herd among the tall reeds.

stories.title: A Fire in the Munja Grass
stories.story:
The herd did not mean to wander. Cows and goats and buffaloes are creatures of appetite, and that day, in the forests around Vrindavan, the cowherd boys were deep in their games — running and leaping and wrestling on the grass, their calls ringing through the trees — and no one was watching the grazing line. So the cattle drifted, from one grove to the next, cropping as they went, until the forest had closed behind them and the boys finally looked up to find the clearing empty.

Krishna, his brother Balarama — whom the cowherds called Rama — and the other boys called for the herd and heard nothing back. The afternoon that had been so full of games suddenly felt very large and very still. They spread out and began to search, the way people who know the land search — reading the ground itself. Here the grass had been cropped short by grazing mouths; there it had been cut and trampled by hooves. Farther on, pressed into the soft earth, a line of hoof-prints led away into the trees. The boys followed the trail the way one follows a dropped thread, deeper and deeper into the wood, and the longer they searched, the deeper the forest's silence grew around them.

The trail led them into a dense thicket of munja grass — tall, sharp-bladed reeds that grew higher than a man and hid whatever moved among them. Deep in that green tangle they found the herd at last: the cattle lost and lowing, turning in circles, no longer sure of the way back. The boys pushed in after them, and Krishna called out to the cows, his voice deep and full, like a cloud gathering before rain. The frightened animals pricked their ears at the sound and began to quiet.

And then the fire came.

Smoke rose first, a grey smudge lifting above the trees, and then the flames themselves, with the wind at their back. It began, the verses say, as if by accident — a wildfire springing up around them on every side. The wind drove it forward. It ate through the dry grass and raced from tree to tree, crackling and roaring, and the heat of it pressed in on the boys and the cattle from all directions. The cows lowed in terror and pressed together, and the boys, who a moment before had been searching and calling, now stood ringed by flame with nowhere left to run.

They did the only thing left to do. They called on the two brothers with all their strength — “Krishna! Krishna! Great hero! O Rama, whose strength never fails!” — and their voices rose above the roar of the burning grass.

And the fire kept coming.
stories.reflection: The danger here is not a demon but something as ordinary as wind and dry grass — which is exactly what makes it frightening. The boys are not weak or foolish; they do everything right, and still the fire surrounds them. Sometimes the test is simply to be where there is no way out, and to know whom to call.
stories.next_story_tease: The fire was closing in — and then Krishna told them to shut their eyes.

stories.title: Krishna Swallows the Wildfire and Saves the Herd
stories.story:
The fire came without warning, and it came from every side at once. One moment the cowherd boys were out in the Vrindavan woods with their cattle — the afternoon hot and still around them, the grass dry from a long stretch of sun — and the next the grass was alight, and the flames were running toward them like a closing hand. They had spent the day as they always spent it, driving the herd from one pasture to the next, the calves at the cows' heels, and now the woods themselves had turned against them.

The boys had nowhere to turn. The smoke bent the trees and darkened the sky, the cattle lowed and bunched together in the middle of the clearing, and the boys, who were only children, saw the fire lean in toward them from all around. It was not the slow, watchful fire of a hearth. It moved with a roar, and the dry grass fed it as fast as it could burn. They called out to Krishna — a cowherd boy among them, but the one they turned to when there was no way out — and their cry was simple: surely those who belong to you, Krishna, do not deserve to perish like this.

Krishna did not argue with them, and he did not run. “Do not fear,” he said. “Close your eyes, and do not open them until I tell you.” And they did. Not one of them asked him how, or why, or whether it would work; they simply shut their eyes, the way a child shuts them when a game requires it — except that this was no game. They stood in the middle of the burning forest, the roar of the fire all around them and the heat on their faces, and not one of them opened his eyes. It was trust, plain and simple, and it was all he asked of them.

What happened next none of them saw. Krishna drew the raging fire into his mouth and drank it down, the whole of it, flame by flame, until the heat and the roar and the smoke were gone. When at last he told them to open their eyes, they were not standing in the burning forest at all. They were at Bhandira, safe — under the great tree where the cowherd boys often gathered — and their cattle stood with them, and not one of them was hurt. There was no smell of smoke left in the air, only the lowing of the cattle, settling.

The boys looked at one another, and at the trees around them, and then at Krishna, and they could find no words for it. They had walked into a ring of fire and had come out of it, and it had cost them nothing but the closing of their eyes. The account says only this: it was his yoga, his power, worked through his maya — the hidden might by which he acts. It does not explain the rest, and perhaps no explanation is wanted.

And then, as if nothing at all had happened, the afternoon went on. The herd was whole, the boys picked up their day where they had left it, and they were home before dark. When they tried, later, to tell the elders what had happened, the words would not come out straight, and the elders smiled and let it go.
stories.reflection: The wonder of the episode is that it is told almost without explanation. Krishna asks for nothing from the boys but the closing of their eyes, and the fire is gone before they open them; the story names the power behind it and then returns, without comment, to an ordinary afternoon.
stories.content_note: A forest fire briefly surrounds the cowherd boys and their cattle; no one is harmed.

stories.title: The Monsoon Pastures
stories.story:
The rains had come to Vrindavan, and the forest had answered them. Where the ground had been dry and tired there was now green; the trees stood heavy with ripening dates and jambu fruit, and water ran bright in the hollows. For weeks the herd had moved through brown grass and dust; now the wood stirred with new life, and the creatures that lived in it went about their days without fear. The verses call this the best of forests in the rains, and the boys could see why. It was into this washed, shining world that Krishna and his elder brother Balarama led the herd.

The cows went slowly, and for a good reason: their udders were heavy with milk, and every step asked care. The forest seemed pleased to receive them — the trees let fall their honey-sweet blossoms as the herd passed, and the deer and the birds did not start or run, as though the boys and their cattle were simply part of the season. There was nothing to guard against that day, no danger waiting in the green shade — only the rains doing what the rains do.

When a sudden shower broke, the boys did what forest people have always done: they sheltered under a spreading tree or in the mouth of a cave and stood listening to the water on the leaves. When the rain passed and the sun came back out over the wet wood, the whole world smelled of earth and green things, and the sweetness of the fallen blossoms hung in the air.

Then they ate. They had brought the simplest of meals — curd and rice — and they set it out on a flat stone near the water and sat down around it together, on the green grass, with the river at their backs and the cows grazing close by. They had been walking since first light, and the food tasted of the walking, and of being young and hungry in the open air. They ate without hurry, the way people eat when nothing in the world is waiting for them. There was nothing more to the feast than that: the food, the stone, the river, and the company.

When the meal was done they lay back on the grass and watched the herd. The cows stood nearby, chewing their cud with eyes half-closed in contentment, and the boys watched them in the same unhurried way, the way one watches a thing that asks nothing of you. All around them the monsoon showed itself — the shining leaves, the full streams, the fruit bending the branches — and it was, the verses say, a beauty of the rains, one that brings happiness in every season and stays in the memory long after it has gone.

No demon came that day. No fire, no danger, no test. There was only the rain-washed forest, the slow cows, the simple food on a stone, and two brothers resting among their friends as the afternoon wore gently on toward evening. They lay there until the shadows began to lengthen; then the cows turned for home, as herds do, and the boys rose and followed, carrying with them an afternoon they would remember without quite knowing why.
stories.reflection: After the demons and the fires, the story pauses for something that needs no rescue and teaches nothing — a meal of curd and rice on a stone, and the sight of contented cows. It is a reminder that the boy-god's life in Vrindavan was also made of such afternoons, and that joy is itself a kind of worship, needing no occasion.
stories.next_story_tease: But the cowherds had begun to wonder at all the boy had done.

stories.title: The Cowherds Wonder at Krishna's Deeds
stories.story:
Govardhan, the great hill that stood over the pastures, was back in its place; the storm had worn itself out; and still the cowherds of Vrindavan could not stop turning the matter over. They gathered in knots at the edges of the pastures, speaking in low voices and glancing now and then toward the boy who sat among the calves as though nothing at all had happened.

How could a child of seven hold up a mountain with one hand? They had seen it with their own eyes — the boy standing beneath the great hill while the rain lashed down and the people and the cattle sheltered under it — and seeing it had not made it any easier to believe. It was not a thing a boy could do. It was not a thing a man could do. And it was not the first strange thing, either. Not by a long way.

So they began to count, the way men count debts they cannot pay. There was Putana, the demon woman who had come to Vrindavan in the shape of a nurse and taken the child to her breast to feed him, and from whom he — a babe whose eyes were barely open — had drawn out the life instead. There was the whirlwind that had snatched him up when he was a year old and carried him high into the sky. There was the morning his mother Yashoda caught him stealing butter and, in her vexation, bound him to a heavy grinding mortar. There were the demons of the forest: the one who had slipped among the calves in the form of a calf, the donkey demon and all his kindred, and Pralamba, whom Balarama had thrown down. And there was the serpent Kaliya, whose venom had poisoned the river and whom the boy had subdued and driven out of the lake.

One by one they set these things down, and the counting only deepened their confusion. A boy of seven, they said, and a mountain lifted. The two things would not sit together in the mind. And yet beneath all the counting lay something else, harder to name — a love for the boy that none of them could set aside, a fondness that held them fast no matter what he did or what he was.

Nanda listened to all of it and said nothing for a long while. Then he spoke, and what he said did not explain the matter away. He gave them back the words of Garga, the family priest — words spoken long ago, when the child was born, and kept quiet ever since.

Nanda had called Garga to Vrindavan to give the child his name. The old sage had come, and he had known at once who the child truly was, and in confidence he had told Nanda what could not be said too loudly. 'This son of yours,' Garga had said, 'was once born of Vasudeva. He takes a body in each age, and many are his names and his forms. He is the delight of the cowherds and of the cattle, and he will be your welfare. In earlier times the good were harried by the wicked, and he will stand between you and every danger. This boy, Nanda, is the equal of Narayana in his qualities.' And having said it, Garga had returned to his own home.

This was what Nanda repeated to the cowherds now, and hearing Garga's words from his lips, they felt their fear loosen. It was a strange comfort — not an answer to how a boy could lift a mountain, but a reason not to be afraid of the question. The wonder did not leave them; it found a place to rest. If the boy among the calves was truly what the old sage had said, then a lifted mountain was no contradiction at all — only one more wonder from a boy who had such wonders in him. And they looked at him with new eyes.
stories.reflection: The cowherds' wonder is never answered with an explanation. Nanda gives them something older and stranger — the memory of a prophecy spoken in confidence years before. It does not explain how a boy lifts a mountain; it tells them who the boy is, which turns the impossible into something to be trusted rather than feared.
stories.tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana gives a different turn to this episode: there the cowherds voice their doubt directly to Krishna, who answers that he is simply their kinsman, neither god nor Yaksha nor demon. The Bhagavata, followed here, has Nanda quiet their wonder by recalling Garga's prophecy instead.
stories.next_story_tease: But the wonder was not finished with them; soon Nanda himself would be taken from the river in the night.

stories.title: Nanda Is Seized by Varuna and Rescued
stories.story:
It happened at night, at the river. Nanda, the chief of the cowherds and the man Krishna called Father, had gone down alone to the Yamuna to bathe while the dark hours still lay over the water. The river was still, the stars lay scattered across its surface, and there was no one else about. The village slept; the only sound was the water closing softly around him as he stood in the shallows.

He had not been long in the water when hands closed on him. A servant of Varuna, the lord of the waters, had come up silently through the dark. He did not know whom he had caught; he took Nanda for an ordinary man, seized him, and drew him down — down through the cold and the silence, to the bottom of the world, where the halls of Varuna stand.

On the bank the cowherds missed him. They had bathed in that river a hundred times and thought nothing of it, but now the dark water seemed to have swallowed one of their own. They called his name, and no one answered. They searched the water with their eyes, and it gave nothing back. Fear took hold of them, and they cried out the only names that seemed to matter: "Krishna! Rama!"

Krishna came at the sound. At the water's edge he understood at once what had happened. He did not hesitate, and he did not wait for help. Without a word he went into the river and down after his father, to the court of the lord of the waters.

There Varuna saw who had come into his presence — and the lord of the waters did not meet the boy as one meets an intruder. He rose and honored him with offerings and with worship, the way a host honors one far greater than himself. Then he bowed, and he spoke.

"Obeisance to you," he said, "who are the supreme Self. My servant was a fool, and did not know what he was doing; he did not understand what was right. Forgive him. And you who see all things, grant your grace to me as well."

Krishna accepted the honor without anger, and Varuna gave Nanda back to him. The boy brought his father up through the water to the bank, where the cowherds stood waiting with their fear.

When they saw Nanda step out of the river, whole and unharmed, the fear let go of them all at once. They pressed around him, asking what had happened, where he had been, whether he was hurt. But Nanda climbed out into the lamplight and the familiar faces, and for a long moment he did not speak. He had seen the lord of all the waters rise and bow to the boy he had raised as his own son, and he did not know how to begin to say it.
stories.reflection: The story turns on a strange reversal: the father is taken, and it is the son who descends to bring him back. Varuna's apology is not to Nanda but to Krishna, and the rescue is less a battle than an act of recognition — the great god honoring the boy before a word of force is spoken.
stories.next_story_tease: And what Nanda had seen beneath the water he would soon tell to all his kinsmen.

stories.title: Krishna Reveals His Supreme Abode
stories.story:
Nanda came back from the river with a story, and he could not keep it to himself. He had been seized in the dark water by a servant of Varuna and carried down to the lord of the waters; and there, before his own eyes, Varuna had risen and honored Krishna, and had bowed to him, and had begged his grace. Nanda told his kinsmen all of it, and the cowherds listened, and something quickened in them.

They had always loved the boy. They had carried him and fed him and scolded him, and all the while, beneath the ordinary love, a question had been waiting. Now it stirred. If the lord of the waters bowed to this child, they whispered to one another, then perhaps the child was more than a child; perhaps the one they called their own was the Lord himself. The thought took hold of them, and with it came a longing they could hardly have put into words: they wanted to see where he truly dwelt.

Krishna knew. He sees everything, and he saw what was stirring in the hearts of his people, and it moved him. He thought of how men and women live — bound by desire, by the small work of every day, by all they have done and left undone, unable by themselves to see past the moment to the light that never fails. And being full of mercy, he resolved to give them what they yearned for, though it was a thing that could not be shown in any ordinary way.

He led them to the water and took them down into the lake of Brahman and let them sink beneath it. There, beyond all darkness, he revealed to them his own abode — the eternal light of Brahman, which is truth, and knowledge, and the infinite. It was not the light of the sun or of the moon, which rise and set; it was the light from which all lights are born, without beginning and without end. The cowherds saw it and were lost in it, and were filled with a bliss beyond anything the world can give.

Then Krishna drew them up again, out of the water and back into the air of Vrindavan. They stood on the bank blinking in the ordinary light, carrying inside them a sight they would never find words for. And when they looked at the boy before them — wet from the river, small and familiar — they knew, as they had not known before, who it was they had been loving all along. The vision did not push them away from him; it only deepened the wonder, and the wonder only deepened the love.
stories.reflection: Krishna does not take his people away to show them heaven; he lets them sink into the light and then brings them back to the riverbank. The vision is given not to detach them from the world but to answer a longing with a glimpse — and then to return them, changed, to the boy they had always known.
stories.next_story_tease: But the world they returned to still held its dangers, and a demon was watching their next night in the forest.

stories.title: Shankhachuda Abducts the Gopis
stories.story:
One evening, when the day's work was done and the heat had gone out of the air, Krishna and Balarama went into the forest with the women of Vraja — the gopis, the cowherd women of the village. It was the kind of evening the two brothers loved best, when they could forget the cattle and the long day and simply be together with the people who loved them. They had walked out together, as they often did of an evening, to hear the night begin. The first stars were coming out, the moon was climbing above the branches, and the two brothers began to sing, honouring the face of the coming night.

It was not an ordinary singing. The verses say the song was sweet and slow, a blessing to the mind and to the ear of every living thing — a sound that could reach into whoever heard it and settle there. The gopis listened, and the song worked on them like a slow, deep calm: their thoughts went away, their hands forgot what they held, and they stood as if in a dream, devoted to the brothers as they were. The song did not hurry anyone; it only held them, and they were glad to be held. Even the forest seemed to lean in to listen.

The brothers went on singing, freely and half-lost in the music, as though the night itself had poured into their voices. And while every eye was on them and every heart was open, the demon Shankhachuda saw his chance.

Shankhachuda served Kubera, the lord of treasure, and he had come to the forest for no good purpose. He was a demon of the kind that had troubled Vrindavan before — strong, watchful, quick to see an opening. Hidden in the shadows at the edge of the glade, beyond the reach of the starlight, patient as a shadow, he had watched the singers and waited for the moment when no one was watching him. Now, in the hush the song had made, he moved. He seized the women and carried them off into the dark.

The spell broke at once. The gopis screamed, and their cry cut through the singing: "Krishna! Rama!"

The brothers turned and saw their own people being carried away into the darkness. They did not stop to reason, and they did not think of weapons or of danger to themselves; the only thought was the women, and the only answer was to run. "Do not fear!" they cried, and the cry itself was a promise. They tore up the trunks of two sal trees, swung them up like clubs, and plunged after the demon like two lions into the night.
stories.reflection: The demon strikes at the one moment the gopis are unguarded — not in weakness, but in absorption, their attention given over entirely to the song. The brothers' answer is immediate and instinctive: a shout of reassurance before any thought of battle, and then a pursuit that will not be turned aside.
stories.next_story_tease: But the demon would not escape — and the jewel he wore was about to change hands.

stories.title: A Jewel for Balarama
stories.story:
The demon Shankhachuda had carried off the women of Vrindavan — the gopis, the cowherd women of the village — and he had not reckoned on being followed. He was a servant of Kubera, the lord of treasure, strong and sure of himself, and for a little while the deed must have seemed safe enough: the forest was deep, the village far behind, and no one, he may have told himself, would come after him so quickly.

But two had come after him, and they were not walking. Through the trees behind him came Krishna and his elder brother Balarama, the cowherd boys of the village, and the verses say what the demon saw when he looked back at them: Time and Death themselves, arriving side by side. The courage went out of him in a rush. He trembled, and he ran — and Krishna ran after him wherever he ran, matching him stride for stride through the dark.

It was not a long chase, but it was a certain one. The demon flung himself this way and that through the trees, branches catching at him as he went, and whichever way he turned, Krishna was there — never quite near enough to be seized, never far enough to be lost. Again and again the demon doubled back, trying to shake the brothers off, and each time they were closer than before, until his breath came hard and the gap between them closed. He had trusted the forest to hide him, and the forest had let him down.

Not far off, Krishna overtook him. He came up beside the fleeing demon and, with a single blow of his fist to the head, struck Shankhachuda down and put an end to him.

Then, with the demon lying still where he had fallen and the women he had taken looking on, Krishna did a small and telling thing. He bent and took the bright jewel from the fallen demon's crest — the ornament Shankhachuda had worn at the crown of his head, gleaming there even as he ran. He did not keep it for himself. He carried it to Balarama and placed it in his brother's hands, openly, where the women could see it given; and that, the women saw, was the whole of it — the one treasure of the demon passing, by Krishna's own hand, to his elder brother, with no ceremony but that.

Then the forest was quiet again. The women were safe, the chase was over, and the jewel that had once shone at a demon's brow rested now in Balarama's hands, a gift given openly before them all, with no one watching from the shadows and nothing left to fear.
stories.reflection: The episode is brief, but its last image is the one that lingers: Krishna lifting the demon's one treasure and, without a moment's hesitation, giving it to Balarama. The victory matters less to the story than the gift — the spoils of the fight passing to the elder brother, in full view of the women who had been taken.
stories.content_note: A demon is struck down with a single blow; the violence is brief and not described in detail.
stories.next_story_tease: But a worse terror was already on its way to the herds, this time in the shape of a bull.

stories.title: A Bull the Colour of Rain
stories.story:
The first warning was a sound — a bellow that rolled across the grazing grounds of Vrindavan and set the herd moving before anyone understood why. Then the cattle saw what had made it, and they did not wait to be told. They scattered in every direction, lowing in fear, for standing at the edge of the pasture was a bull that was no bull.

He was the demon Arishta, come in the shape of a bull to break the cowherds' world. He was the colour of a cloud heavy with rain, with vast horns and eyes like two fiery suns. His tongue kept licking his lips, his tail stood erect, a hump of enormous size rose between his shoulders, his dewlap hung low at his throat, and his face was scarred from years of butting against trees. Wherever he planted a hoof, he tore up the earth. He had haunted the wild forests in this shape, destroying the hermits and ascetics who lived there, and now he had come to Vrindavan.

The cows fled, and the cowherds' cries went up. Krishna, the cowherd boy of Vrindavan, saw his people and their cattle driven to flight by the brute, and he did not run. He walked out onto the pasture and called the demon out, demanding how the lowest of beings dared terrorize the cowherds and their animals, and he slapped his arms together so that the sound rang across the grass, goading the bull on.

Arishta needed no goading. Enraged, he pawed the ground with his hoof, lowered the points of his horns, fixed his reddened eyes on Krishna, and charged.

Krishna did not step aside. He stood where he was and waited for the bull to reach him, then met the rush, seized him by the horns, and flung him a full eighteen paces, so that the great demon landed in a heap on the earth. For a moment the cowherds must have thought the fight was over.

But Arishta rose again, and came again, more furious than before. This time Krishna caught hold of him by the horns and forced him down, pressing the great bull to the ground with his foot. And there, pinned beneath Krishna, the demon in him died — his legs kicked out, his eyes rolled and found no rest, and then he lay still.

When it was over, the herdsmen glorified Krishna, and the gods rained flowers down on him from the sky. The cowherds sang of him as heaven had once sung of Indra's victory over the demon Jambha. The bull that had scattered the herd was finished. The people who had scattered gathered close around Krishna once more, and the cattle, one by one, came drifting back to graze, as if the pasture had already forgotten its fright.
stories.reflection: Arishta is not described as an army but as a single animal, and that is precisely what makes him frightening: he is terror of the ordinary, everyday kind, the thing that can scatter a herd in a heartbeat. Krishna meets him without weapons and without retreat, and the story's comfort is that the fear itself is what gets flung down and finished.
stories.tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana describes the killing differently: Krishna tears off one of the bull's horns and beats him to death with it, after wringing his throat like a wet cloth. The Bhagavata, followed here, has him fling the bull aside and press him to the ground. The two agree on the essentials.
stories.content_note: A bull-demon is slain; the fight is described with some force but not graphically.
stories.next_story_tease: But Kamsa had not finished with Vrindavan, and his next messenger would arrive in the shape of a horse.

stories.title: The Empty Forest
stories.story:
Keshi came to Vrindavan in the shape of a horse, and he came with a purpose. Kamsa, the king who wanted Krishna dead, had sent this demon to do his work, and Keshi had obeyed: he went straight into the forest and set about the cowherds as his master wished.

He was no ordinary horse. His mane tossed like a storm cloud, and his neighing was itself a terror. He had been born in the same hour as Kamsa, so the tales ran, and was as dear to the king as his own life — a peerless fighter who had never met his equal. Now he fell upon the cows and the cowherds, killing and feeding on them, and wherever he ranged the forest fell empty: the people who lived by the woods drew away from it, the paths the herds had worn went unused, and the animals could no longer travel the forest roads. For a time the woods seemed to belong to the demon alone.

Then one day, following the sound of men, the horse came to the settlement of the cowherds. The moment the women and the boys and the men saw him, they set up a cry and fled — to Krishna, their refuge, calling out his name.

Krishna gave them his word and went out to meet the demon. Some of the cowherds cried after him, urging him back. "You are only a boy," they said, "and this one is beyond the strength of us all." But Krishna had already made up his mind.

The horse saw him coming and charged, his mouth open wide as if he meant to drink the sky, his eyes and teeth bared, his neck raised high. Krishna roared like a lion and met the rush. The horse struck at him with his forehooves and bore down on him; Krishna slipped aside from the first rush, caught hold of the demon, whirled him around, and hurled him to the ground.

Keshi rose, angrier than before, and came at him again, his jaws stretched open to bite. This time Krishna stood his ground. Smiling, he thrust his arm into the horse's open mouth, like a hand pushed down a serpent's hole. The demon's teeth met that arm and dropped out, as though they had touched hot iron, and once inside, the arm began to swell, growing until it filled the creature and stopped his breath. Keshi choked. He kicked out his legs and struggled, and then he was still, his body split open like a ripened gourd — or, as some tell it, like a tree torn apart by lightning. Krishna drew his arm out again.

From the sky the gods showered flowers upon him. And from that deed Krishna took a name that stayed with him for good: because he had slain Keshi, the world would call him Keshava — the slayer of Keshi.
stories.reflection: The fight is decided by a strange, almost gentle gesture — Krishna does not strike the horse so much as fill it, letting his arm grow until the creature's own fury chokes it. It is a striking reversal: the demon that came to devour is itself devoured by stillness, and the victory leaves behind not only peace but a name.
stories.tradition_note: The name Keshava, 'slayer of Keshi,' is recorded in the Harivamsha and the Vishnu Purana; the Bhagavata tells the fight itself without pausing on the name.
stories.content_note: A horse-demon is slain as Krishna thrusts his arm into its mouth; the violence is brief and not described in graphic detail.
stories.next_story_tease: And the next danger would come wearing a friend's face.

stories.title: The Thief in the Game
stories.story:
The boys of Vrindavan were deep in their favourite game on the hillside above the grazing herd, and one of them was not a boy.

All through the long afternoon some of the boys played keepers of the calves and some played thieves — stealing a calf away, being caught, and stealing again — in a game that only pretended at danger. It began in laughter, and it usually ended in a tangle of dust and shouting, with the calves bawling and the boys tumbling over one another. And into it, dressed like any cowherd boy, slipped something that did not pretend.

He was Vyoma, the son of the demon Maya, and himself a demon and a master of deception. He wore the face of one of the boys, and no one looked at him twice. He came and went among them as one of them, and one by one he began to lead the children away, the way a thief in the game led off a keeper he had caught — except that the boys he took did not come back. When he drew a child toward the mountain, the child went with him willingly, because it looked for all the world like the game they were all already playing. He carried each one to a cave in the mountain and sealed him inside it, until many of the stolen boys lay hidden in the dark while the game went on around the empty places where they had been. A boy would be there one moment, and the next he was not there at all, and the laughter continued as if nothing had changed.

But Krishna, the cowherd boy who played among them, saw it all, and what he saw stopped him mid-stride. He understood at once what the demon was doing, and he did not let the game go on a moment longer.

Then Krishna put off the shape and size of a boy. He stood in his own form, vast and strong as a king among mountains, and turned on the deceiver. He seized Vyoma with both hands, threw him down upon the earth, and ended the demon there.

And without pausing, he went to the mouth of the mountain cave, broke through the covering that sealed it, and brought the boys out, one after another — first one, then another, then the whole dim crowd of them — from the darkness and the fear they had been shut into, until the mountain had given back everyone it had taken.

The game was over. The thief who had hidden among them lay still on the hillside, and the boys who had been stolen stood blinking in the daylight, counted one by one and whole.
stories.reflection: The most striking thing is where the demon chose to hide: not at the edge of the village but inside the boys' own game, wearing a friend's face. The story does not dwell on the violence; it hurries past it to the cave and the bringing of the children out, as if the rescue, not the slaying, is the point.
stories.content_note: A demon disguised as a cowherd boy carries children off into a cave; the danger is real but ends in their rescue, and the slaying is brief.
stories.next_story_tease: But the cowherds' greatest fear still waited, coiled in the waters of the Yamuna.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna standing huge as a mountain before the cave, breaking open its sealed mouth as the stolen cowherd boys come out into the light, the disguised demon cast down behind him.

stories.title: The Vow at the Poisoned Lake
stories.story:
One morning Krishna went into the forest alone — not with Balarama, his brother, and not with the cowherd boys who usually followed at his heels. Only himself: dark as a rain cloud, a feather in his hair, garlands of fresh kadamba and arjuna blossoms around his neck, and a flute in his hand, walking wherever the cattle led him. The woods of Vrindavan that day seemed made for wandering. Peacocks called from the branches, and low thunder muttered among the hills, as if the season itself leaned close to listen.

He had ranged here before, and the forest always answered him. Plantain groves stood thick and green, the ground was soft with new grass and studded with lotuses, and the air carried the scent of dark-blue lotus from the water. Fountains lay hidden among the trees, and the wind that came off the leaves fanned him as he walked. Sometimes he would stop beneath the great Bhandiraka fig tree, tall enough to seem to brush the sky, its branches bowed with fruit, and let the cowherd boys amuse him with their songs, answering them, note for note, on his flute. It was the kind of place, the old verses say, where a boy might sing to his cows and believe the whole earth was listening.

Then one day, while the cattle grazed and the sun climbed higher, he came down to the bank of the Yamuna. The river lay before him like a woman dressed for a festival — lilies and lotuses on her water, swans and cranes calling over it, landing-stairs worn smooth, a current strong and sweet, her little lakes catching the light, and waterfowl ranging over her in pairs. It should have been the sweetest water in the world.

But the river was not well. There, in a lake along her side, lived Kaliya, the serpent-king, and his venom had seeped into the water until it was no longer fit to drink. Nothing that drank from it could live. The birds had gone quiet over the pool, and for all its beauty the water carried a hidden bitterness that could kill.

Krishna stood at the water's edge and looked into the deep. He did not rage, and he did not turn away. Quietly, the way a boy decides to climb a tree for its fruit, he made up his mind. "I should vanquish this king of serpents," he resolved. "I shall climb the kadamba tree, jump into the lake, and vanquish Kaliya."

It was such a small sentence for so great a deed, and he spoke it without raising his voice. But the resolve was set, and the water, as if it knew, seemed to darken under his gaze.
stories.reflection: The striking thing about the resolve is its quiet. Krishna does not rehearse a battle or boast of strength; he decides the way a boy decides to climb a tree, and the whole deliverance of the river hangs on that calm sentence.
stories.tradition_note: This moment of resolve is particular to the Harivamsha; the Bhagavata Purana moves more directly from the poisoning of the river to the leap.
stories.next_story_tease: But the poisoned water had already begun its silent work on the unsuspecting cowherds and their cattle.
