stories.title: The Brahmanas Refuse Krishna's Request for Food
stories.story:
The cows had been grazing since morning, and by afternoon the boys were hungry. Krishna and his elder brother Balarama were pasturing the cattle not far from home, with the cowherd boys around them, and hunger came over them all alike. It was nothing dramatic — only the ordinary ache of boys who had been out in the fields since dawn, with the sun climbing and the evening meal still far off. The forest was still, the heat of the afternoon lay over everything, and the boys' thoughts kept straying home to the kitchens and to food.

Now, nearby, a company of brahmanas — learned men, masters of the Vedas, the ancient hymns — had gathered to perform a sacrifice. The smoke of their fire rose above the trees, and the sound of their chanting reached the pasture where the boys sat. In those days a sacrifice meant hospitality; a man who could feed the gods at his fire should not find it hard to feed a few hungry boys. So the request Krishna made was not an unreasonable one. He knew the brahmanas were there, and he knew what they were doing, and he sent the boys to them. "Go," he said, "and ask them for food in my name."

The boys went, crossing the fields toward the smoke. They stood before the brahmanas with folded hands and spoke with all the respect they could summon. "O gods of the earth, listen to us," they said. "We come at Krishna's bidding. While pasturing the cows not far from here, Balarama and Krishna have grown hungry, and they ask for food."

The brahmanas heard the request and paid it no mind. They neither said yes nor said no; they simply did not heed it. Their whole attention was given to the machinery of the sacrifice — the proper place, the proper time, the offerings, the chanted mantras, the priests, the fires. Each detail had to be exactly right, and the work of keeping it right left no room for two herd-boys standing at the edge of the rite. They looked at the boys and saw only herd-boys; and behind the herd-boys, in the one who had sent them, they saw only a boy who herded cows.

Yet the one their whole rite was meant for stood a field away, hungry, asking through two boys for a little food. They had given their lives to the books that spoke of him, and when he came asking, they knew him least of all. The supreme Brahman — the one reality their scriptures pointed to — stood within their reach, hidden from them by their own learning. They did not recognize him.

The boys waited, and the silence stretched. They had come with a simple, courteous request, and they had received neither yes nor no — only the sound of mantras going on without them. There was no anger in them, only confusion. They had seen the smoke and heard the chanting and expected generosity; instead they had met a wall of rites that had no room for them. At last they turned and walked back across the fields, empty-handed, to where Krishna and Balarama sat with the cows.

And the brahmanas returned to their fires, satisfied that the rites had been kept correct, and did not know what they had turned away. Their learning had kept the rite perfect. It had also kept them from the one the rite was for.
stories.reflection: The refusal is not hostile; it is distracted. The men are so certain of the forms of worship — the place, the time, the mantras, the fire — that they cannot see the one the worship points to, standing just outside and asking for a little food. Their learning becomes the wall that keeps them from what they study.
stories.next_story_tease: But the brahmanas' wives would prove quicker to answer than their husbands.

stories.title: The Brahmanas' Wives Bring Food to Krishna
stories.story:
The cowherd boys came back empty-handed. Krishna had sent them across the fields to the brahmanas — learned men performing a sacrifice near Vrindavan — to ask for food in his name and Balarama's, and the brahmanas had given them nothing: no yes, no no, only the murmur of their rites going on without them. When the boys told Krishna this, Krishna only laughed. There was no anger in it. He did not scold the men, and he did not repeat the request. "Go to their wives," he said, "and tell them that I have come, with Balarama."

So the boys went a second time, now to the women's quarters of those same houses. There the wives sat, well-adorned in their own homes, going about the quiet work of the afternoon. The boys bowed to them and spoke with the same respect as before. "Obeisance to you, wives of the brahmanas," they said. "Listen to our words. While pasturing the cows with the cowherds, he has come from far away, with Balarama — and he is hungry."

The wives heard the name, and everything in them rose at once. They had always longed for the sight of Krishna — a longing they carried every day without speaking it aloud. They had heard of him, the dark boy of Vrindavan whose name was on everyone's lips, and they had kept that longing lit like a lamp in a dark room. Now, without a word of hesitation, they filled their vessels with food — food of four kinds, rich and fine, prepared with care — and hurried out toward him. There was something of a festival in that sudden movement: doors flung open, feet hurrying, voices rising, as though the whole women's quarter had been waiting all along for exactly this summons.

Their husbands tried to stop them. Their brothers tried, their kinsmen tried, their own sons called after them from the doorways, asking where they thought they were going and before whom. They called it madness, or worse; they reminded the women of their duties, their good names, the scandal of it. But the women did not slow. A longing kept secret for years has a force that reproach cannot match, and not one of them turned back. They went as rivers run to the sea, drawn by a pull that nothing in the house could answer.

What they left behind was not small: houses, husbands, the good opinion of their kin, the settled shape of a whole life — and they left it all without a backward look. There is no heaviness in the telling of it, only eagerness. They were going to meet the one they had wanted for so long without daring to ask, and their feet seemed to know the way, as though they had walked it a thousand times in their thoughts.

So through the groves of Vrindavan they went, their vessels bright in their hands, their veils and bracelets catching the afternoon light, their faces all turned one way — toward the place where Krishna waited with Balarama and the boys and the grazing cows. Some carried the food balanced high; others held it close against them, as though afraid the afternoon might end before they arrived.

It had taken the men an afternoon of silence to answer him. It took their wives no more than a breath.
stories.reflection: The contrast is the point of the story. The learned brahmanas saw only a herd-boy and sent him away; their wives, who had no learning to lean on and only longing to go by, saw what the longing had prepared them to see. They drop everything — home, kin, reputation — because the one they have wanted is finally near.
stories.next_story_tease: But when the wives reached him, they would refuse to go back at all.

stories.title: The Wives Refuse to Return
stories.story:
The brahmanas' wives had crossed a line they could not walk back across. They had left their husbands' great sacrifice, carried food through the forest, and fed Krishna and his cowherd companions with their own hands. They had not come with any thought of returning; they had come only to see him. Now they stood before him in a grove on the banks of the Yamuna, where the ashoka trees were tipped with fresh young leaves, and they looked at him, and they could not look away.

And yet they had known him before they ever saw him. They had heard of the cowherd boy Krishna until his image had taken up its place in their minds and would not leave. Their thoughts were already full of him; their ears had been filled with the sweetness of hearing about him, long before they stood in this grove. So when they saw him, it was not a stranger they found, but the one they had been carrying inside them all along.

He stood among his friends the way a dancer stands at ease — one hand resting on a companion's shoulder, the other slowly twirling a lotus. His skin was dark, his garments gold, a garland of forest flowers at his neck and a peacock feather in his hair. Earrings swung at his cheeks, and his face, bright as a lotus, wore a faint smile. The women drank him in through their eyes and held him there for a long while, and the sorrow that had followed them all the way from home quietly left them.

Then Krishna spoke. "You are welcome," he said. "Sit. Tell me what I can do for you."

But he did not stop at a welcome. The wise, he told them, see clearly what is best for themselves, and so they give him all they have — breath and mind and intelligence, wife and children and wealth, everything a person holds dear. And therefore, he said, they should return now to the place of sacrifice. Their husbands were brahmanas; their place was there.

The women did not lower their eyes. "Do not speak such cruel words," they answered. "We have left everyone — fathers, husbands, sons, brothers, every bond we had — so that we might carry on our heads the garland of tulasi, the sacred basil, that has fallen from your feet. Neither our husbands nor our fathers nor our sons nor our brothers nor any of our people will take us back now. How much less any stranger? For us, who have fallen at your feet, there is no other refuge. Grant us this."

It was the truth, and Krishna saw it. They had staked everything on him, and there was nothing left to return to. He was pleased, and he granted them the grace they had asked for. But he also taught them something to carry back with them. It is not bodily nearness, he told them, that binds a person to him. He is won by remembrance — by hearing of him, and seeing him, and holding him in the mind, and speaking of him. Then he sent them home, and they went, their hearts fixed on him, the way the wise carry what they love with them wherever they go.
stories.reflection: The wives' refusal is not defiance of their husbands but the plain statement of a fact: they have already left everything, and there is no going back. Krishna's answer turns their longing away from his physical presence toward something they can carry anywhere — remembrance.
stories.next_story_tease: But the husbands they returned to would soon see, in their wives' faces, exactly what they themselves had refused.

stories.title: The Brahmanas Repent
stories.story:
In the forest near the cowherd village of Vrindavan, a company of brahmin priests had begun a great sacrifice. Everything was in its place: the right hour, the right offerings, the right verses chanted in the right order, and fires tended by men who knew every rule. They had given themselves to it completely — so completely that when a young cowherd came to them asking for food, a boy sent by his companion Krishna, who waited hungry in the forest with his friends, they waved him away. There were rules to follow. There was no time for a cowherd's errand.

It was their wives who went instead, carrying food through the woods to Krishna and his friends while their husbands stayed behind with the fire. Now the women came home, and the priests looked at them, and something in their faces stopped the men where they stood. Even the one wife whose husband had held her back by force had not truly been stopped: she had closed her eyes and gone to Krishna in her mind, meditating on him exactly as she had heard of him. And Krishna, for his part, had fed the cowherds with the very food the women carried.

Then the full knowledge of it reached them, the way a slow truth reaches a man who has been busy elsewhere. The boy they had refused was Vishnu himself, standing in the forest in the shape of a cowherd — and they had turned him away for the sake of a ritual. What they said to one another was not a proud speech. "Shame on our birth," they said, "and on the three aims it taught us to chase. Shame on our vows. Shame on our great learning." For the power that deludes, they saw now, could bewilder even the wise — even the yogis. And look at these women: no sacred thread, no years of study at a teacher's feet, and yet they loved Krishna, the teacher of all the worlds, with a love that shamed everything the men had spent their lives acquiring.

Then they saw what they had missed. The place of the sacrifice, the hour, the offerings, the verses, the priests, the fires — these were not separate things to be arranged. They were all Krishna himself. He was the one whom the goddess of fortune serves, turning from all others, longing for the touch of his feet; the one who needs nothing at all, and yet grants liberation to all who ask. "Salutations to Krishna," they said, "whose wisdom never falters. He is Vishnu himself, the lord of the lords of yoga, the first being of all — and it is his own power that keeps our minds deluded." They remembered their fault, the insult they had offered him, and they wanted, more than anything, to look upon his face.

But they did not go. They were afraid. Kamsa, the king of Mathura, ruled not far away, and his cruelty was known in every house. So the men who knew every verse of the ritual sat at home and longed for the boy they had turned away, praising him in words they had never once thought to speak beside their fire.
stories.reflection: The brahmanas' lament is really a confession that their ritual had become an end in itself — something performed without remembering whom it was for. The women, who knew none of the rules, had found the one the rules point to.

stories.title: Krishna Vanishes
stories.story:
It was autumn in Vrindavan. On a night when the full moon rose red over the forest, washing the leaves, the paths, and the dark water of the Yamuna in its light, Krishna's flute sounded through the trees — and the cowherd women who heard it set down whatever they held. One left off milking; one left the milk half-boiled over the fire; one turned from a husband she was serving; one from a child she was feeding. They slipped away as they were, earrings swinging, some with their clothes and ornaments only half arranged, so great was their haste. And those who found themselves shut inside their houses stood where they were, closed their eyes, and held him in their minds. Their families called them back; they did not turn. The flute had taken their hearts, and they went where the music led.

Krishna welcomed them in the moonlit grove, and for a while the night held nothing but what they had all come for. And in that happiness a small, secret thought began to grow: that the joy was theirs to keep — that they had earned it, that the one they loved was somehow their own. It was a small thing, the way such a thought always begins: a warmth in the heart, a sense of having been chosen. Krishna saw it.

There was no word, no warning. Where he had stood, there was only empty air. He vanished in the middle of the night, in the middle of their happiness, and the women he loved stood suddenly alone among the trees.

He had not left them to punish them. He had left them to humble them, and to favor them — for the pride rising in them was the one thing that could have spoiled what they had found. And so he, who had come so close, stepped back, so that their love for him could grow deeper than their love of themselves.

In the silence the night turned suddenly vast, and the women understood, as they had not understood before, how much of what they loved was simply him. The flute had stopped. The place where he had stood still held the warmth of him, and that was all that was left. They looked at one another in the red moonlight and could not speak. They had asked the night for so much, and the night had given it; now, in an instant, it had been taken back — not to hurt them, but to show them what it was they had been given. The moon had not dimmed, and the forest had not changed. Only he was gone — and without him, the same night was a different place.
stories.reflection: Krishna's disappearance is the opposite of abandonment. He removes the one thing — pride — that would have soured the gopis' love, so that what remains is only the love itself.
stories.hero_scene: A full moon rising red over the Vrindavan forest at night, and the gopis standing suddenly alone among dark trees, turning to find the space where Krishna stood a moment before now empty.

stories.title: The Gopis Abandon Their Homes
stories.story:
The moon came up full over Vrindavan, washing the eastern sky with a red like the crimson powder worn on festival days. The forest stood soft in that light, the Yamuna carried it in broken pieces on the water, and the air held the deep quiet warmth of an autumn night. Krishna, the young cowherd whose songs the village loved, looked out at the night and the forest, raised his flute, and began to play.

The song called no one by name. It did not beg or command; it only drew, low and sweet, the way a remembered tune draws a listener back to it. It crossed the fields and the lanes and the courtyards of the village, and the cowherd women of Vrindavan heard it, and their hearts went out to meet it. It was the sound they had been waiting for without knowing it, and it made the quiet of the evening feel like a promise.

One woman was milking, and she left the cow standing with the pail half full, without a look back. One was serving the evening meal, and she set the dish down while it was still warm and walked out. One had a child at her breast, and she put the child down and went. One was anointing herself for the night and stopped where she sat; one had kohl half applied to her eyes and left it there, one eye dark and the other bare. Each of them had been in the middle of something, and each of them left it unfinished. The evening's work lay where it had dropped, and the houses stood as though time had stopped inside them.

Husbands caught at their arms, and fathers and brothers called after them, and the hands of their own kin closed over their wrists. It made no difference. The flute went on, unhurried, and the voices behind them rose and fell and were lost under the music. The women went, heedless of everything, because the sound of the flute had taken them and would not let them go.

Some could not go at all. The door was watched, or the house had closed in around them, and no way out could be found. Those women shut their eyes where they stood, some of them before they had even reached the door. The ache of being apart from the one they loved had grown too strong to bear, and when they closed their eyes it burned itself out, and whatever else had been in them went with it. With their eyes shut they went to him, and they found him as surely as the women who had crossed the fields.

By the time the others reached him, the moon stood high over the Yamuna. Krishna saw them coming through the trees — the milkmaid with the pail half full, the one with kohl on a single eye, and those who had never left their courtyards at all but had come to him with their eyes closed. Behind them the village slept on, unaware of who had slipped away from it. Before them the Yamuna lay dark and slow under the moon.
stories.reflection: What stays in the mind is the inventory of unfinished things, the milk half-milked and the eye half-painted. The gopis are not shown renouncing anything with ceremony; they simply drop what they are doing mid-task because the flute interrupted a normal evening and they answered it. The detail that some could not leave at all, and still reached him by closing their eyes, quietly widens the story: the going is outward, but the meeting is not limited by walls.
stories.next_story_tease: But the night was far from over; the dance had not yet begun.

stories.title: Krishna Tests the Gopis
stories.story:
When the cowherd women of Vrindavan, who had come to him through the night, finally reached Krishna that autumn night, he greeted them with a question that was not at all what they had come for. "You are welcome," he said. "What can I do for you? Is all well at home? Tell me why you have come."

Before they could answer, he went on. "This night is fearsome," he said, "and full of fierce creatures. It is not right for women to be here. Go back to the village. Your mothers and fathers, your sons and brothers and husbands, search for you and cannot find you. Do not bring such distress on your own family."

He gestured at the flowering trees silvered by the full moon and the Yamuna breeze moving in the leaves, as if to say: you have seen it, now go. "Return without delay," he said. "Serve your husbands. The calves are crying, and the little ones too; go milk the cows and feed them."

And then he softened. "Or," he said, "if it is love for me that has bound your hearts and brought you here, that is only fitting — every living thing finds its joy in me. But hear me: the highest duty of a woman is to serve her husband faithfully, to do good to her own people, and to care for those who depend on her. A wife must not leave her husband — not even one who is ill-tempered, or unlucky, or old, or dull, or sick, or poor. A love outside marriage brings no heaven and no honor; it is trifling and painful and feared, and it disgraces a woman of good family. And love for me is born of hearing about me, and seeing me, and meditating on me, and speaking of me; it is not born of standing near me. So go back to your homes."

The women stood very still, their hopes broken, a grief they could not cross settling over them. Their faces turned down, their lips gone dry with sighing, they traced lines in the earth with their toes, wiping the tears that streaked the red powder on their chests, saying nothing.

Then one of them found her voice, and the rest followed, their words choked with feeling. "Do not speak such cruel words," they said. "We have left behind every pleasure we had, and come to your feet. Accept us, your own devotees. Do not cast us off — the way the ancient Lord receives those who long for freedom."

"You, who understand duty, have told us that a woman's dharma is to serve her husband and her children and her people. Let it be so. But you are the dearest of all who live in bodies; you are our friend, our very self. Those who are wise give their love to you, who are forever dear — of what use to us are husbands and sons, who bring only sorrow? Be gracious, Lord. Do not cut down the hope we have carried for you so long."

Their voices gathered strength. "Our minds have been carried away by you; they cannot go back into our houses. Our hands no longer do the work of the home, and our feet will not move from beneath your feet. How shall we go back to the village? What would we do there? Quench the fire that your smiling glance and your sweet songs have lit in our hearts — or we will be burned up by the pain of missing you, and reach your feet only through our meditation on you."

At last they asked for the one thing they had come for. "What woman in the three worlds — in heaven, on the earth, or below it — hearing the song of your flute, could keep to the path of duty and not come running? Seeing your face with its smiling eyes and dark curls, your arms that grant fearlessness, your chest that is the home of fortune herself — we are your servants. Place your hand upon our heads. You are the one who takes away the fears of Vrindavan, the friend of the afflicted. Give us your service."
stories.reflection: Krishna's test is a strange kind of kindness: he argues against the gopis with every duty the world recognizes, so that the only answer they have left is the truth — that he is not one more claim among their duties, but the self to which all duties return.
stories.next_story_tease: And Krishna, who had argued against them with every duty in the world, would answer their plea with something far gentler.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna speaking to the gopis in a moonlit forest, his hand raised toward the flowering trees and the Yamuna beyond, while the gopis stand before him with downcast faces, one of them lifting a tear-streaked face to answer him.

stories.title: Krishna Relents and Sports with the Gopis
stories.story:
Across the dark water of the Yamuna, the cowherd women of Vrindavan — the gopis, as they were called — were calling his name. Krishna heard them — he who needed nothing from anyone, who was already complete in himself — and for a long while he listened and did not move, letting the night stay full of their voices.

These were the women who had left their homes at the sound of his flute and followed him to the river on that full-moon night. Earlier that evening, he had tested them: he had sent them back with words meant to turn them away, to see whether their devotion could survive his refusal. It had. They had not gone home. They had grieved, and gone on calling for him, their longing unbroken. And it was that grief, more than anything else, that moved him at last.

Now, hearing how they grieved, he could hold back no longer. Nothing he did that night came from any need of his own. Yet he smiled — not the smile of one who has been won over, but a smile of pure favor — and he came to them, and showed them grace. They had been refused once by his words and again by his silence, and still they had not turned away. They had asked for nothing but him, and that was exactly what they received.

He came down to the cool, sandy bank of the river, into the soft light of the full moon. The moment they saw him, their faces opened like flowers. They began to sing to him, and he sang with them; one voice answered another across the pale sand — a hundred voices braided together in the night — until, for a little while, there was nothing in the world but the two songs answering each other. Grief turned to gladness without a single word being changed.

Then he spread his arms wide and drew them near, and the gopis pressed in around him. He held each one close, the way a person holds what he loves, and answered their affection with the light play of his fingertips. There was laughter, a hand at the fold of a garment — the breathless, easy joy of a long parting ending — and it all happened on sand that stayed cool through the heat of the night.

The gopis asked for nothing more, and they received everything. The women who, a moment before, had believed themselves abandoned, now felt themselves the most blessed women alive. Not because they had earned him — they would have said they had not. But because he had chosen to come back to them, and his coming was enough.
stories.reflection: The source is careful to say Krishna was self-satisfied, complete, in need of nothing — and that the favor he showed was therefore pure gift. The gopis' happiness is not a reward for endurance but the answer to longing that asked for nothing but him.
stories.next_story_tease: But the night's joy would not hold; Krishna was about to slip away from among them.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna on the moonlit sandy bank of the Yamuna, arms spread wide as the gopis press in around him and sing, their faces lifted with relief and joy.

stories.title: The Gopis Search the Forest
stories.story:
One moment Krishna was there among them; the next, the gopis turned and he was gone. No word, no warning — only the empty place where he had stood.

These were the cowherd women of Vrindavan, who had followed him from their homes at the sound of his flute. Now the one they loved had slipped away from them, and they did not go home. They went into the forest, like women out of their senses, searching from wood to wood and singing his name aloud, so that all of Vrindavan could hear. The moonlight fell in pieces through the leaves, and still they went on, bare feet finding the paths between the trees, voices lifting and falling in the dark.

And as they searched, he seemed to rise up in them. His walk, his smile, the way he glanced, the sweet way he spoke — all of it came back through them as they went, until each woman seemed to carry a little of him in her own step and voice. To see them was to see him, scattered among a hundred women.

Because they had no one else to ask, they questioned the trees. "Have you seen Nanda's son?" they asked the great banyan and the holy fig trees — for so the village named Krishna, who had been raised as a son by Nanda, the chief of the cowherds. They asked the flowering trees, the ashoka and the champaka. They asked the tulasi, the holy basil that loves Krishna's feet. They asked the mango and the kadamba and the jasmine, and every other tree and creeper they passed, climbing the great trunks like a friend embracing a friend. "Have you seen him," they said, "the one who stole our hearts with his smiles?"

They even turned on the earth beneath them and demanded to know what penance it had done, that the mere touch of his feet should make it break into blossom. And they asked the doe: has Krishna come this way, his arm resting on a beloved's shoulder, a lotus in his hand, the bees following the scent of his garland? Did the trees bow to him as he passed, blessed by one long, loving glance?

But the forest kept its silence. The trees held their branches still. And the gopis went on from tree to tree, calling the question again and again, because asking was the only thing left to do.

They were not looking for news of him. They were looking for him. And somewhere in the middle of that long night, the search stopped being a search for someone lost and became the only way they knew to keep him near — to keep saying his name, to keep his walk and his smile before their eyes, even while he would not show himself.
stories.reflection: The gopis address trees and creepers as if they could answer, which is the whole heart of the passage: when the beloved vanishes, love turns the whole world into a possible messenger. Their grief does not sit still; it moves, questions, and fills the forest with his name.
stories.next_story_tease: And when the trees gave no answer, their searching turned to something stranger still.
stories.hero_scene: The gopis wandering the moonlit Vrindavan forest, singing Krishna's name aloud and stopping before the great fig and flowering trees to ask, Have you seen Nanda's son?

stories.title: The Gopis Enact Krishna's Lilas
stories.story:
Krishna had vanished from them, and the forest rang with his name. All night the gopis of Vrindavan — the cowherd women of the village, who had loved him since he was a child among them — had searched and called, and the night gave them back nothing but their own voices. At last they began to do the one thing that made their loss bearable. They began to become him.

Each of them took up one of his deeds — the deeds they had heard sung since he was a baby in the cowherd village — and played it out there in the forest, for no audience but the trees and the moon. The forest lay still around them, silvered with moonlight, and the only sound was their own voices. Their calling had the sound of frenzy, and in a way it was frenzy; but it was a frenzy that knew what it was doing. It had a shape, and the shape was him.

One woman lay down on the forest floor and played Putana, the demoness who had once come to the village disguised as a wet-nurse, her breast smeared with poison, meaning to kill the infant Krishna as he fed. Another became Krishna himself and drank from her as he had done, and — so the story ran — he drew the demon's very life out with the milk. They played it through, there under the trees.

Another took the part of a demon again, this time the demon who had come as a wooden cart to crush the sleeping child. She carried off a third gopi, who had become the baby Krishna, and the baby kicked out with one small foot and overturned the cart — the way the real Krishna once had.

Two of them stood side by side and became Krishna and Balarama, his elder brother, and around them the other gopis became the cowherd boys, keeping watch over cattle that were not there and calling to one another the way the herders did at pasture, their voices soft among the trees.

Then one of them raised her arm high above her head, the way Krishna had raised the whole hill of Govardhana on a single finger to shelter the village from the storm, and she called out in a voice that carried through the trees: Do not fear the wind or the rain — I have made you a shelter.

One climbed up onto another and stamped down with her foot, as Krishna had once danced upon the hoods of the serpent Kaliya in the river's poisoned waters. Another pointed into the distance and cried out: O cowherds, see the fierce forest fire! — the fire Krishna had once swallowed whole to save them. And a slim gopi sat down and let herself be tied to a grinding mortar with a garland of flowers, the way the child Krishna had been tied there by his mother for his mischief — and had slipped free even then.

Through it all they went on asking the trees and the creepers of Vrindavan: Have you seen him? And even as they asked, they kept moving, because motion was the only thing that kept the ache from settling. Every part they played was only another way of calling him back — as if, by wearing his deeds, they could hold some piece of him until he returned.
stories.reflection: The gopis' imitation is not mockery but memory made physical. In their frenzy they rehearse the whole of Krishna's childhood — Putana, the cart, Govardhana, Kaliya, the mortar — as a way of keeping him present. Devotion here is not a feeling but a performance, an enactment of everything he has been to them.
stories.next_story_tease: Then the earth itself laid a trail before them.

stories.title: The Favored Gopi's Pride and Krishna's Second Vanishing
stories.story:
All night the gopis, the cowherd women of Vrindavan, had searched the forest for Krishna, the boy of their village. Now the footprints stopped them — clear in the soft earth, and known at once: these were the marks of Krishna, Nanda's son.

The women stood over them the way you might stand over a letter you did not expect. Then they saw what made their breath catch. Beside Krishna's footprints ran another set, smaller and lighter — the steps of one of their own. And where the two sets went on together, the ground was pressed deeper in places, as though he had carried her.

The trees they had begged for news of him had no comfort to give. So the gopis read the story from the earth instead. Here, flowers had been gathered — picked for her, by him, the way a lover gathers blossoms. There, a woman's hair had been dressed and arranged by careful hands. The gopis looked down at the dust of those footprints and called it blessed: blessed is the dust of Govinda's feet — Govinda, the protector of the cows, as they called him.

One of them had been chosen. And none of the others was angry — not quite. They marveled, and they ached. This woman, they told one another, must have worshiped him as no one else had, for him to single her out. He had taken her aside, away from all the rest, and kept her to himself in the deep of the forest. It was a strange and tender thing: Krishna, complete in himself and needing nothing, had still delighted in her company. The thought of it turned in the others like a splinter. They asked themselves what they had done, and what she had done, that he should choose her while the rest of them wandered the wood in the dark. And still they could not look away from the footprints — because the footprints were all of him they had left.

And the one he had chosen felt it too. Standing there, reading what the footprints told, she began to think herself the greatest of all women. Pride crept in where the wonder had been. So when she found Krishna waiting in a farther part of the forest, she did not fall at his feet. She told him she was tired — that she could not walk another step — and that he should carry her wherever he chose.

Krishna answered her gently. Climb onto my shoulder, he said, and I will take you.

She reached for him. She climbed. And at the very moment she would have settled on his shoulder, Krishna was gone — vanished into the air, leaving her with nothing under her hands.

Then her cry went up into the empty forest: O lord, O my beloved — where are you, where are you, mighty-armed one? The forest gave back no answer. She had been lifted to the highest place of all, and she had thought it was her own. Now she stood alone, and understood.
stories.reflection: Krishna vanishes at the exact point of pride, not in anger but as a lesson that cannot be spoken — the favored gopi had begun to possess what could only ever be received. Her cry in the empty forest is the turning: what pride had claimed, loss hands back as longing.
stories.next_story_tease: But her remorse would not go unanswered for long.
stories.hero_scene: The gopis gathered around two trails of footprints in the soft forest earth, one smaller and lighter beside Krishna's, the ground pressed deeper where he carried her, scattered flowers nearby.

stories.title: Krishna Reappears Among the Gopis
stories.story:
He was simply there before them — smiling, his face bright and open as a lotus — and for a moment none of them could move. All night the gopis, the cowherd women of Vrindavan, had searched the forest for Krishna, the boy of their village whom they loved above all else. Twice he had vanished from them, and the second time they had lost even the thin hope that searching would bring him back. Now, when they had nearly stopped looking, he stood among them again.

One moment the grove had held nothing but their sorrow; the next, he was there — and the sorrow was not reasoned away. It simply left them, all at once. They rose as if life itself had come back into their bodies, and their eyes, a moment before downcast and searching, bloomed open with joy.

And because no two of them loved him in the same way, no two of them received him the same way. One took his hand between her two folded palms and held it, the way you hold something too precious to let fall. Another, slender and quick, bent and took from his lips the betel leaf he had been chewing, and kept it cupped in her own palms like a gift she would not share. A third knit her brows at him, flushed with an anger that was really love, silently reproaching him for leaving her to such grief. A fourth did not blink at all, drinking in his face as if she feared that the moment she closed her eyes he would be gone again. And one more did not look with her eyes; she gathered him into her heart through the narrow opening of her closed lids, and kept him there, where he could not leave.

They pressed around him, and he stood among them and let them come.

Then he led them away from the place of their grief to the bright sandbank of the Yamuna. It was autumn, and the moon was full; its light lay on the water and on the sand like something poured out, and it seemed to drive the darkness out of everything that had gone wrong. There, in that light, the ache in their hearts came to rest — the way tired wings come to rest at evening.

He sat down among them — not on any throne, but on the place they had made for him inside their own hearts, the only seat they had to offer. They welcomed him with smiles, with sidelong glances, with the small glad play of their brows: the language of people who have been given back what they thought was lost.

No one rebuked him, and he offered no explanation. Krishna did not say why he had vanished, and the gopis did not ask. Whatever they needed to hear, they would hear soon enough. For this one moment, the answer was simply that he had come back.
stories.reflection: The scene is made of small, individual gestures — a hand held, a bit of betel kept, an unblinking gaze — because the verses want the reunion to be felt one gopi at a time and then all at once. Here grief is not dispelled by argument but by presence.
stories.next_story_tease: But the gopis still carried a question they needed to ask him.

stories.title: Krishna Teaches About Love
stories.story:
On the moonlit sandbank of the Yamuna, the cowherd women of Vrindavan sat close around Krishna, the boy of their village. They had given up everything for him — home, family, the quiet duties the world expected of them — and a little while before, when he had vanished from them and then returned, the question they had carried for so long rose at last to their lips. They wanted to understand the way he loved them in return. Why, they asked, does he love those who love him, and yet seem to hold something back — to give, and then to vanish?

He did not answer with a lesson. He answered with the way love truly behaves.

Some people, he said, serve those who do not serve them back — the way a father and mother serve a child, not because the child can ever repay them, but out of compassion. The parents keep no account of what the child owes. They give because the giving is its own reason, and that is one kind of love: whole and complete, asking nothing in return. And there are others, he went on, who do not serve back at all, even when they are served with everything. So how could anyone expect love from such people, when even a gift freely given wins nothing from them?

But he, he told them, was like neither. When people served him, he did not simply return the favor, the way one trader settles accounts with another, weighing what was given against what is owed. That kind of repayment would end the matter — and he did not want anything to end. What he gave back, he gave in order to draw them further in: to deepen the very love that had reached for him, so that it would not stop, so that its roots would go down and hold.

Then he turned the question around and set it before them. You, he said, have cast aside the world and its claims — even the duties the sacred books lay down — all for my sake, and still you follow me. There is no repaying that. Even if he lived as long as the gods themselves, he told them, he could not repay what they had done for him. So there would be no settling of accounts, no balancing of the ledger — not ever.

And then he gave them the heart of it: their own goodness would return to them of itself. The love they had given was not an investment to be recovered with interest. It had already done its work, and its reward was simply itself. Their love was already theirs — the way a flame is already warm, without needing to be warmed in return.

So he answered their question by taking it away. They had asked how he would repay their love, and he told them there was no question of repayment — because what they had given could not be repaid, and did not need to be. It had already come home.
stories.reflection: Krishna refuses the arithmetic of love. He will not settle accounts with the gopis the way a trader settles a debt, because that would end the matter; instead he deepens the devotion they have already offered. Their love, he tells them, is its own reward — it has already returned to them.
stories.next_story_tease: That night, under the same autumn moon, the answer would be danced rather than spoken.

stories.title: The Great Rasa Dance
stories.story:
The moon that rose over the Yamuna that autumn night was full and white, and the forest lay silver beneath it. The river moved quietly, and the air was mild — the kind of night that asks nothing of anyone. It was the season of clear nights, when the year turns and the moon hangs low and white. Krishna, the cowherd boy of Vrindavan, looked at the night and found it good for dancing. So, on the bank of the river, he began the rasa — the great circle dance of the autumn nights — and the gopis, the cowherd women of the village who loved him, gathered around him.

He did not dance alone at the centre of the circle. He became as many as the women themselves, so that between every two gopis stood a Krishna, and each one felt him near and no other beside her. In him they had found the one they loved beyond all others, and for those hours nothing else existed. The circle was bright with sound before it was bright with anything else — bangles and anklets and little bells keeping time in the dark.

They danced with their whole selves. Their feet found the beat and kept it; their arms swept and lifted; they bent at the waist, their garments swayed, and their earrings swung against their cheeks. Their faces glistened with the effort, their throats flushed as they sang aloud, and their hair came loose, the flowers slipping from it while no one stopped to notice. They sang of him as they danced, their voices rising over the water — songs that belonged to the season, full of the clear night and the turning year. One of them sang with him in a single blended voice, as though the same note came from two throats. Another, weary from the dance, leaned for a moment on his shoulder and did not fall. One, as she moved, kept only the tinkling of her anklets and her girdle for company — and still she sang. In the ring they shone like lightning moving within a circle of clouds.

High above, the women of heaven leaned out to watch, and the sight bewildered them: a ring of mortal women on a riverbank, and at every turn a Krishna beside each of them. The watchers above rained flowers down on the dance. Petals fell on the water, on the grass, on the dark heads of the gopis as they circled, and the night filled with their fragrance.

As the night wore on, the gopis grew tired, and some of them, in the middle of their joy, put on a small show of pride — yet still they sang of his deeds, delighting in the touch of his hands. Where a face was hot from the dance, his hand was there; their weariness seemed to matter to him more than the dance itself. He led them down into the river to wash the heat of the dancing away. They went with him like cattle following their herdsman, and in the water they splashed him, laughing — and he let them.

From the bright chariots above came more flowers, and with them the praise of those who watched. And Krishna, glad and at ease, took his rest among them.

In this way the moonlit nights of autumn passed, one after another. Krishna, who wanted for nothing, kept the company of the cowherd women under the moon, and they kept his. The dance ended as it had begun — not with a word, but with the moon high over the water.
stories.reflection: The multiplication is striking not as a display of power but as a form of attention: Krishna becomes many so that no gopi in the circle is left without him. What the sources linger on is not the miracle itself but the moonlight, the music, and the nearness.

stories.title: Uddhava Arrives Bearing Krishna's Message
stories.story:
The man who came into Vrindavan was no cowherd. The village had been quiet since Krishna left it for the city of Mathura — the cows still grazing, the flute silent — and into that quiet he walked, a stranger who did not belong to it. His name was Uddhava. He was Krishna's close friend, and Krishna had sent him, out of love, back to the home of his boyhood and the people there.

The gopis saw him from across the grove and stopped what they were doing, because there was something about him that made them stare: his dress, his ornaments, even the way he carried himself seemed to belong to someone else — to Krishna, who had gone away from them and had not come back.

They surrounded him at once, astonished. Who is this, they asked one another, so beautiful to look upon, and from where has he come, wearing Krishna's own dress and ornaments? And their astonishment was not only at his beauty. It was at the sudden, aching nearness of the one they had been pining for — as though Krishna had come back to them wearing a stranger's face. For months they had lived in the stillness of his absence, and now here was a man who wore his very clothes, as if the one they longed for had reached out and touched their world again.

They honored him before a word was spoken — received him with shy smiles and sidelong glances and gentle words, the same tenderness they would have given Krishna himself. Then they said what they had already understood: We know you serve our Krishna, they told him — Krishna, lord of the Yadavas, the clan he was born to — and he has sent you out of love for the home he left behind. Otherwise, if it were not for him, we can see nothing in this cowherd village worth the coming of a man like you. What would bring you to Vrindavan, except him?

And there, in that greeting, the grief they had been carrying began to speak. The world, they said, makes friendship for a purpose, and when the purpose is served, the friendship is over. A woman of the streets leaves a man the moment his purse is empty; the kindness she showed him was never for him, only for his money. Subjects abandon a king the moment he can no longer rule; their loyalty was only the price of his protection. Birds forsake a tree the moment its fruit is gone, and guests walk away from a house once the meal is done. Everyone, it seemed, loved only while there was still something to be had.

But they had not loved that way. Their love was the one thing in Vrindavan that had not gone looking for something to be had. Krishna had left them, and still they spoke of no one but him; there was nothing left to gain from him, and still they would not let him go. With speech, and body, and mind fixed on Govinda — the protector of the cows, as they called him — they went on singing the deeds they loved, and weeping, with all shame gone; for grief for him was not a thing to hide.
stories.reflection: The gopis greet Krishna's messenger with their own hard-won knowledge of the world — that most friendship lasts only as long as its usefulness — and measure their own love against it. Theirs is the one attachment that did not break when the object of it went away.
stories.next_story_tease: And as they spoke, one gopi, seeing a honeybee, would pour out her grief to it as though it were Krishna's own messenger.

stories.title: The Gopi's Lament to the Bee
stories.subtitle: Bhramara-gita
stories.story:
Krishna, the cowherd boy of Vrindavan, had gone away to the city of Mathura, and the village was quieter for it. The gopis — the cowherd women who had grown up around him — carried his absence like a weight. One day one of them sat a little apart from the others, turning over her grief, when a honeybee came humming and settled near her feet. Her mind was so full of Krishna that she did not see an insect. She saw a messenger, come from far away, and she spoke to it as though it could carry her words back to him.

O bee, she said, friend of the cheat — do not touch my feet. She knew what it was, she said, the moment she saw it: a courier wearing the saffron of the garlands that had been crushed against other women's breasts, come to mock her before the assembly of the Yadavas, Krishna's own family. Let Krishna carry his favor to those proud women who now have him, she said; I have no need of a messenger from such a place.

Her anger was grief with nowhere else to go. He made us drink once, she said, the nectar of his lips, and it bewitched us — and now he casts us aside like flowers, the way a garland is thrown down when the evening is over. How is it, she asked, that the goddess of fortune waits upon his feet, though she too has lost her heart to him? Why does the bee sing of the lord of the Yadavas here, before us, who have nothing left to offer it? Let it sing instead before his new loves, the ones whose pain he has already eased.

She did not stop. She remembered how he had always charmed and then wounded — taking what was offered and then binding the giver, the way a hunter calls and then strikes — and she said, enough of friendship with the dark one, though his stories are the one thing we can never let go of.

And even as she said enough, she could not leave him. Others, she said, had heard a single drop of the nectar of his deeds and had abandoned home and family to wander like birds. We trusted him, she said, the way a deer trusts a hunter's call — and we have felt the sharp hurt of longing again and again. Dear friend, she said to the bee, if you are truly sent by the one I love, choose what you want and take it, for you are to be honored by me. But how will you carry us back to him, whose side no one can bear to leave, and on whose chest the goddess of fortune sits as his wife?

Then all her reproach collapsed into a single, helpless question. Does he still dwell in the city of Madhu — in Mathura, where he lives now? Does he remember his father's house, and his kinsmen, and the cowherds? Does he ever speak of us, his maidservants? And when — when will he place on my head that arm of his, fragrant with aloe?

She did not expect the bee to answer. The question was not really for the bee at all. It was the same thing she had been asking the empty air every day since he left, and it would go on being asked until he came back.
stories.reflection: The lament's power is that reproach and longing are the same act. The gopi accuses Krishna of abandoning her precisely because she cannot imagine a world without him; every bitter word is only another way of keeping him near.
stories.next_story_tease: The messenger who had come to Vrindavan would soon carry her words, and Krishna's answer, back between them.

stories.title: Uddhava Delivers Krishna's Message and the Gopis Reply
stories.story:
For months the cowherd women of Vrindavan — the gopis — had poured their grief into the empty air after Krishna left for the city of Mathura. They had even pleaded with a honeybee once, mistaking the insect for a courier sent from him. Now at last a real messenger stood before them, a man who had truly travelled from Krishna, carrying words from his own mouth. His name was Uddhava — Krishna's friend and counsellor, a man of learning and restraint — and he had been sent for this one purpose: to bring them some word from the friend who had left them.

Before he spoke a single word of the message, Uddhava did something no one expected: he praised them. Through gifts, vows, and long self-denial, through sacrifice, study, and self-control, he told them, they had offered up sons, husbands, homes, and their own bodies to a single love — and that love had made them peerless. No one on earth had done what they had done. Only then, having honored them, did he speak Krishna's words.

The message was not an apology, and it was not a promise to return. Krishna asked them to see that he had never truly been far from them at all. Just as space and air, fire, water, and earth are found in every living thing, he said, so he was found in all things. He alone created, preserved, and ended the world, and he was pure knowing itself — free of every fault, untouched by the world's qualities. There was nothing outside him to be lost. A beloved who is far away, he said, remains close in the mind of the one who loves; so let them fix their minds wholly on him, and they would soon reach him. This, he said, was the whole heart of the scriptures, of yoga, and of the wise. And then, almost a memory spoken aloud: it was he who had played with them at night in this very forest.

The gopis did not accept it, and they did not refuse it. They answered with a grief so steady it had become its own kind of truth.

Does he remember us? they asked. Does Govinda — the lord of the cows, as they called him — who understands every shade of love, remember the nights when the moon hung bright over Vrindavan, the groves white with blossom, and he danced among us, his ankle-bells ringing, while we praised him with our songs? Will he ever come back to us, scorched by the sorrow he himself made? He has won a kingdom now and slain his enemies; why would he return to women of the forest like us? What are we, who live in the woods, to that great soul? And then the heart of it, the question behind every other question: who could bear to give up the memory of him? These rivers, these hills and forest paths, these cows, the sound of the flute — everything in this place calls back the son of Nanda, the cowherd chief who raised him, again and again. O lord, O husband of the goddess of fortune, O lord of Vrindavan, remover of sorrows.

So the exchange ended not in comfort but in a strange completion. Krishna had asked them to fix their minds on him; they answered that they could not do otherwise — that the world around them would not let them forget, and that forgetting was the one thing their love could not manage. What he had called a path to union, they had already been walking, without choosing it, from the day he left. Uddhava, who had come to teach them, stood silent, and something in the learned man began to turn.
stories.reflection: The gopis cannot be consoled by argument because what they carry is not ignorance but love. Krishna asks for a mind fixed wholly on him, and their reply — that rivers, hills and a flute will not let them forget — is that very fixing, already accomplished. Their longing is the union he describes.
stories.next_story_tease: But their reply undid the messenger, and Uddhava would soon wish to trade his learning for a place in the dust of their feet.
stories.hero_scene: Uddhava standing before the gopis in a Vrindavan grove at dusk, the women gathered around him, their faces lifted as they answer that every river, hill and the sound of the flute will not let them forget Krishna.

stories.title: Uddhava Praises the Gopis and Departs
stories.story:
Uddhava had come to Vrindavan expecting to console. Krishna's own friend and counsellor, sent from Mathura with a message for the gopis — the cowherd women who had loved Krishna since his boyhood in the village — he had thought he would find grief and leave comfort. Instead the learned man stood humbled, and the wish that rose in him was one no teacher was supposed to make. He had listened to the gopis answer Krishna's message, and what he had seen in them rearranged everything he thought he knew about worth.

He did not leave at once. He stayed some months in Vrindavan, easing the sorrow of the women who had become his teachers. Day by day he walked the country, looking at the rivers, the forests, the valleys, and the flowering trees, and day by day he watched the gopis in their state — wholly absorbed in Krishna, their minds carried away by him, so agitated with love that the place itself seemed to shake with their longing. And as he watched, the praise poured out of him. Wherever he looked — a river bend, a stand of trees, a hill in the distance — he saw how thoroughly the place and its people belonged to Krishna, and how thoroughly Krishna belonged to them.

These cowherd women, he said, have reached the highest place any living being can reach. Their hearts are fixed on Krishna, the soul of all things; what good is even a brahmana birth, he asked — the priestly birth that the whole world honours — compared to the taste of the endless stories about him? Consider the distance between the two — where are these simple forest women, and where is the soul of all things? — and yet he has made them his own. The embrace that even the gods long for was given to these women of Vrindavan at the rasa dance, the night-dance of the forest. This blessing, he said, has not been granted even to the goddess of fortune herself, nor to the lotus-scented women of heaven; how then could anyone lesser hope for it? And the Lord bestows his highest good even on the ignorant who serve him, the way the best of medicines heals one who takes it without understanding what it is. These women had thrown away their families and the straight road of duty for the path that the scriptures themselves search for.

And then the wish that turned the whole order upside down. May I become any shrub, any creeper, any herb at all in Vrindavan, blessed by the dust of these gopis' feet. Again and again he bowed to that dust — I bow to the foot-dust of the women of Nanda's village, again and again — the man of learning wanting nothing more than to grow from the roadside where they walked.

When the time came to go, he had one more duty. He comforted Nanda and Yashoda — the cowherd chief and his wife who had raised Krishna — and the cowherds, speaking to them of Krishna, and they honored him as they would a brother, coming to him with offerings in their hands. Their one wish, spoken plainly, was that their minds might rest forever at Krishna's lotus feet, wherever the wandering of their lives might take them. Uddhava bowed toward Krishna, wherever he was, and set out on the road back to Mathura, carrying the news of how the people of Vrindavan loved him still — a devotion he could now measure, because he had felt a share of it himself. When he reached Mathura he told Krishna plainly of the fullness of the devotion he had found among the cowherds.

He had gone to console, and had been the one changed. A counsellor of kings had asked to be a roadside shrub, and no one who heard him thought the wish foolish.
stories.reflection: Uddhava's wish to become a shrub in Vrindavan quietly reverses every ranking he brought with him. The man of learning envies not the gopis' knowledge but their totality — they gave away everything the world calls secure and gained the one thing the scriptures point toward but cannot hand over.
stories.next_story_tease: Not long after Uddhava returned to Mathura, another envoy set out for Vrindavan — a man named Akrura, sent by the king.

stories.title: Akrura Journeys to Vrindavan
stories.story:
The man on the road was the envoy of a tyrant, and yet the nearer he came to Vrindavan, the lighter his errand felt. Akrura had been sent by Kamsa, the king of Mathura, to fetch Krishna and Balarama to the city — the brothers who had been raised among the cowherds of Vrindavan since infancy, hidden there from the king who had murdered his sister's children one by one and hated the two who had escaped him. But in his own heart Akrura was no servant of Kamsa, and as his chariot moved through the country he began to speak to himself, not as a messenger but as a pilgrim.

What good have I ever done, he wondered, that I should have this? What great austerity have I performed, that the rare sight of Krishna — the sight the sages and the gods long for — should be coming to me? He turned the thought over and over, and it kept returning the same answer: it was not a thing he had earned. Even Kamsa, by sending him, had unwittingly shown him grace; the very man who meant harm had handed Akrura the chance to behold Krishna's lotus feet — feet worshipped by Brahma and Shiva, by the goddess of fortune and the sages; feet that had wandered the forest herding cows, marked with the dust of the cowherd women who loved him; feet that give shelter to all who flee before the great serpent of time, and at which Indra and Bali once placed their offerings and won the lordship of the three worlds.

He let himself imagine the meeting, and the imagining became its own kind of prayer. He would see the face at last — the fine cheeks and nose, the smiling glance, the eyes like red lotuses — the one who had come down of his own free will into the line of the Yadus, his own family, to lighten the burden of the earth, whose praises mingle with every auspicious word spoken of his deeds and his births. He pictured himself falling at Krishna's feet, and Krishna's own lotus hand resting on his head in blessing. He saw the embrace: the two strong arms closing around him, and the voice — that voice — saying, "O Akrura." And if that word were ever spoken to him, he thought, then his birth — every birth — would at last be fulfilled. He imagined Krishna looking at him with a smile and eyes soft with kindness, and the thought alone, he felt, would wash away every wrong he had ever carried. He dared to hope Balarama would embrace him too.

And then the fear that every sincere heart knows. I am Kamsa's messenger, he thought. What if Krishna, who sees everything within and without, reads the errand and turns away? But the fear dissolved as quickly as it rose. Krishna is no partisan, he told himself; he has no favorite and no enemy, no one he despises and no one he avoids. He would not hold against a man the chariot he happened to arrive in, or the errand he happened to carry.

So he rode on, his thoughts no longer on the message he carried but on the feet he was travelling toward. The sun sank low, and at Gokula, as the day ended, he came down from the chariot. There in the dust of the road he saw them — the footprints of the Lord, marked with the lotus and other signs, the feet whose dust adorns the crowns of all the protectors of the worlds. He stood before them a long moment, and the journey was already over, because the errand had already become something else.

He had set out to carry a king's order. He had arrived carrying only a longing, and it was enough.
stories.reflection: Akrura's fear that Krishna will read his errand and turn away is the fear of anyone who comes to the divine with mixed motives. The story answers it not with reassurance but with a truth about Krishna himself — that he holds no one as enemy or favorite — which makes the road, and not the message, the real point of the journey.
stories.next_story_tease: The footprints were only the beginning; ahead, at the cow-pens of Vrindavan, the Lord himself was waiting to be seen.
stories.hero_scene: Akrura standing beside his chariot on the road into Gokula at sunset, gazing down at the footprints of Krishna marked with the lotus and other auspicious signs in the dust.

stories.title: Akrura Arrives in Vrindavan and Beholds Krishna
stories.story:
The traveller who came to the cowherd village that evening was Akrura, a nobleman of Mathura, sent by its king, Kamsa, on an errand that concerned Krishna and Balarama. He reached Vrindavan at the hour when the day gives way to night — the sun's rays grown weak, the moon rising tawny in the crimson sky, the birds gone to their nests, and the cows come home lowing to be milked, their calves bound to the stakes, the milkmen calling the kine in by name and kindling the evening fires. It was at this hour that he came down from his chariot and walked in.

At the cow-pens, among the milking cows, he saw them, and he could not stay on his feet. There were two youths — brothers — one dark, one fair, both big-armed and garlanded, their feet marked with the flag, the thunderbolt, the goad, and the lotus. The dark one was Krishna, dark as the leaf of a full-blown lotus; the fair one was Balarama, white as jasmine. They stood at the milking place in the midst of the calves, at the meeting point of boyhood and youth, and their very radiance scattered the last of the evening's gloom. Akrura's face opened with delight.

He did not walk toward them; he fell. Jumping down from the chariot, overwhelmed with love, the hair on his body standing on end and his eyes brimming, he threw himself into the dust where the Lord's feet had been, crying out again and again over the blessed foot-dust that crowns the heads of all the protectors of the worlds. This, he knew, was the highest thing any embodied being could hold — to lie there in that dust, free at last of pretence and fear and grief. Within himself he praised the Lord again and again, remembering who this was — the lotus-eyed one who had once lain on a fig leaf at the end of all things, and who had once stepped over the three worlds as a dwarf.

Krishna saw him coming and understood everything at once. He and Balarama came forward, and as Akrura lay prostrate at their feet, the two of them lifted him up and embraced him. They asked after his welfare, gave him a seat of honor, and offered him a cow, as a guest is offered. Balarama, who knew every courtesy, washed his tired feet from the road. The envoy of a cruel king was received as a brother come home.

Only when he had eaten and rested did the questions begin — and they came not from the youths but from Nanda, the cowherd chief who had raised Krishna. Nanda received the stranger as family, and then asked, gently, how the Yadavas fared — Krishna's own family in Mathura, living as they did under a king with no grace in him, the wretch who had killed his own sister's children while she wept. There was no anger in Nanda's voice, only the concern of one kinsman for others far away under a cruel roof.

And so the man who had arrived as the agent of that very king was received, not as an envoy to be suspected, but as a friend to be fed and questioned with kindness. No one demanded his business. No one asked what message he carried, or pressed him to speak. The cowherds honored him, and he in turn honored Krishna, and for that one evening at least, the errand that hung over them all could wait.

Akrura had expected to look upon Krishna from a distance, as a servant looks upon his lord. Instead he was pulled to his feet, embraced, and seated at the table as kin. The sight he had longed for became a welcome, and the welcome became the message he had really been sent to learn.
stories.reflection: The story turns on hospitality rather than drama. A man who came as the envoy of a tyrant is met with food, a seat of honor and a kinsman's question, before any errand is spoken. In that welcome the fear Akrura carried on the road dissolves — he is received not for what he represents but for who he is.
stories.tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana also describes this meeting, likening Krishna to the leaf of a full-blown lotus and Balarama to jasmine, a swan or the moon; the Harivamsha sets the arrival in a richly described evening in Vraja and adds the image of Krishna among the calves like a bull. The core event is the same across all three.
stories.next_story_tease: But the errand could not wait forever, and before long Akrura would have to speak the truth of why Kamsa had really sent him.
stories.hero_scene: Akrura prostrate in the dust at the feet of Krishna and Balarama beside the milking cows of Vrindavan, the two youths — one dark, one fair, garlanded and radiant — leaning down to lift him up as Nanda and the cowherds watch.

stories.title: Akrura Reveals Kamsa's Plan
stories.story:
The man Kamsa had sent was, of all things, an honest one. Kamsa, the king of Mathura, had sent Akrura to the cowherd village of Vrindavan to summon Krishna and his brother Balarama to the city — the brothers who had been raised there since infancy, far from the court where their own parents were held prisoner. But Akrura was of Krishna's own family, a Yadava as the brothers were, and the moment he beheld Krishna he had bowed to the ground. The errand no longer sat easily in his mouth. Now he stood before Krishna and Balarama, and Krishna welcomed him as a kinsman, though his greeting carried an edge. Why do you ask after our welfare, Krishna said, when the trouble in our own family only grows? And then he asked what message had brought Akrura all this way.

Akrura gave it to him, all of it. He told of Kamsa's long enmity toward the Yadavas, the hatred the king of Mathura had nursed for years. He told of Kamsa's resolve to kill Vasudeva, their father. And he told them the reason he himself had been sent as a messenger: the king meant to use this errand to draw the two brothers to the city, where he could destroy them.

Then, because he was a Yadava himself and could not keep it in, he spoke of their parents. Your father, he said, has grown old in sorrow; his limbs have wasted away, and Kamsa of sinful designs oppresses him still. Out of fear for the king and grief at your absence, his mind burns with anxiety day and night. And Devaki — he would not soften it — your mother is growing lean with grief, like a cow separated from her calf. Her sons never lay at her breast. Her eyes have sunk into their sockets like the moon caught in an eclipse, and she wears soiled garments and spends her days poorly. Since your infancy she has been parted from you, never once hearing your childish talk, never once seeing your moon-like face. If, by giving birth to you, she must only repent, what need had she of a son at all? A woman without children suffers but one grief; a woman whose sons do not accomplish their purpose knows no end of sorrow. As the earth bears you, so Devaki deserves your reverence — save her, a goddess sunk into the water of sorrow.

You vanquished the serpent Kaliya in the waters of the Yamuna, Akrura went on. You lifted the hill Govardhana for the sake of the cows. You destroyed Arishta the bull-demon and wicked Keshi the horse-demon. Now make one more exertion, with the same care, and save your aged parents from their grief. You are the saviour of even your enemies, your prowess like Indra's, your accomplishments without equal — and yet the mother who bore you lives in a grief she never asked for. Though they are aged, your parents now serve another master, and Kamsa insults them on your account. Those who saw your father insulted in Kamsa's own court are all shedding tears. A son is born owing his parents a debt, one the scriptures set down, and it is paid only by care. If you show them this favour, they will lay down their grief — and you will have done your duty.

Krishna had known all of it before Akrura opened his mouth. He took no offence at the words. He simply said, "So be it."

Hearing that, the cowherds of Vrindavan, led by Nanda — the chief who had raised the brothers as his own — resolved to obey Kamsa's summons: they would go to Mathura. They dressed themselves and set about arranging their tributes — buffaloes and bulls, curd, milk, and clarified butter — and the heads of the cowherd clans made ready their offerings. Akrura spent the night without sleep, speaking with Krishna and Balarama, and in the dawn, when the birds began to sound and the last stars faded, the village stirred and prepared to travel.
stories.reflection: Akrura's honesty is the quiet centre of this episode: sent as Kamsa's messenger, he speaks the truth of his own mission and pleads for the parents left behind in Mathura, while Krishna, who already knew it all, listens to the end before he answers.
stories.tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana (5.18) has Krishna answer with a specific vow, that within three nights he would slay Kamsa and his adherents; the Bhagavata Purana, followed here, records the revelation and the reason for the mission without that promise.
stories.next_story_tease: But when Nanda proclaimed the journey to the whole village, the gopis heard it — and their grief would not be silenced.
stories.hero_scene: Akrura speaking earnestly before Krishna and Balarama in Vrindavan, describing the sorrow of Vasudeva and Devaki in Mathura, while the two brothers listen in stillness.

stories.title: The Gopis Grieve at His Leaving
stories.story:
Krishna had grown up in the cowherd village of Vrindavan, in the house of Nanda, the chief of the cowherds; and the gopis — the cowherd women of the village — loved him as the light of their days. So when Nanda gave the word, it fell on them like a blow. Gather all the milk and its products, he told the men; tomorrow we go to Mathura, and we will carry the king his tribute. For Akrura, the king's messenger, had come to carry Krishna away with him — and no one could say when the village would see him again.

Some of the gopis lost the light from their faces, their breath coming short. Others stopped in the middle of their work, lost in the thought of him. Still others stood remembering his smiles, his way of walking, his laughing glances, the softness of his look — and trembled at the separation that was coming. They turned on Akrura.

You showed us his face, they said, framed by those dark curls — the fair cheeks, the fine nose, the little smile that chases away every sorrow — and now you are doing us a cruel wrong, carrying him out of our sight. You are called Akrura, "not cruel," and yet you are cruel indeed: you gave us these eyes, and now you steal away the very thing they were given to see.

Others thought of the city, and their fear sharpened. The night will pass pleasantly for the women of Mathura, they said; their wishes have come true. Tomorrow the eyes of the whole city will feast on him, and we will be left here with nothing. He will hear their sweet, polished speech, and he will never again endure our rustic words. He won our hearts with words sweeter than honey, and now he will wander off, charmed by the bashful smiles of those simple city women. Nanda's son is new to affection; his friendship can break in a moment. We gave up our homes, our kin, our children, our husbands to serve him — and now, how will he ever look at us again?

Let us go and stop Krishna, one of them said. What can our elders and kinsmen do to us now? There stands Akrura, the dry-hearted one, already seated on his chariot, and the proud ones are urging him to hurry.

And they remembered the evenings, which were the hardest of all to remember. At the close of day Krishna used to come back into the village with the cowherds around him — the dust of hooves on his hair and garland, playing his flute, casting his smiling, sidelong glances — and he would steal their hearts all over again. His sweet words, his playful looks, his embraces had made their nights pass like a single moment. Without him, they asked one another, how were we ever to cross the darkness that stretched ahead?

They wept, their bracelets hanging loose upon arms grown thin with sorrow, and the thought of his going lay on the whole village through the night.
stories.reflection: The gopis' grief is remarkable for how precise it is. They name exactly what they will lose — his face, his smile, his flute at evening, the dust of hooves on his hair — and they fear, with reason, that the polished city will outbid their rustic love. Their sorrow is not vague; it is a catalogue of a life.
stories.next_story_tease: But Krishna would not leave them to their weeping without a word.
stories.hero_scene: A cluster of gopis grieving in Vrindavan as word of the journey spreads, one pressing a hand to her heart while others look toward the road to Mathura, Akrura's chariot and the loaded carts in the background.
