stories.title: Krishna Consoles the Gopis
stories.story:
When the sun rose over Vrindavan, the gopis were still weeping.

They were the cowherd women of the village, and Krishna — the boy who had grown up among them — was going away to Mathura that morning. The king of the city had sent for him, and nothing they could do would keep him. Through the dark hours they had sat where his voice had last reached them, calling his name into the night, and the night had given back only the sound of their own crying.

Now the morning was here — the sun climbing over the trees of Vrindavan, the first light falling on the road to Mathura — and the thing they had dreaded began to happen.

Nanda and the cowherds set out behind the chariot with their carts, and the whole village stirred into motion toward the city. The gopis went too. They could not stay behind, and they could not bear to let him go, so they walked on foot after the chariot that carried Krishna. And something strange came over them as they walked: just to follow him a little longer, to keep the shape of him in their eyes, softened their grief into something almost like gladness. Their tears had not quite stopped, but the road itself had become a kind of comfort — each step was a step beside him, and while he was still ahead of them, he was not yet gone.

From the chariot, Krishna saw them. He saw how his leaving had undone them — how they had poured themselves out along the road behind him, weeping and refusing to turn home. And he would not go without a word. He sent messengers back to them with a promise he asked them to keep. He would come back. I will return to you.

The words reached them along the road, his own voice carried back to them, and they were not a comfort offered from a distance — they were something he was asking of them. He had not forgotten them; he was trusting them with a promise. They were to carry it home and keep it there, like a lamp kept burning in an empty house against the family's return.

So they followed for as long as they could — while the banner of his chariot was still to be seen above the road, while the dust of its wheels still hung in the air behind him. They fixed their eyes on that banner and that dust, as though keeping them in sight could keep him there. The road stretched away toward Mathura, and the whole company of the village — the carts, the cowherds, the women on foot — moved along it the way a river moves.

But at last the banner sank out of view, and the last of the dust settled back to earth, and Krishna did not turn back. Then hope went out of them, and they turned homeward. And as they walked, they sang of him — of the deeds he had done, the days they had shared — keeping his name alive on the empty road until he should make good his word. The road that had carried him away from them carried their voices back the other way, and the singing did what weeping could not: it turned their faces homeward while their hearts stayed with him.
stories.reflection: The consolation here is not a speech but a promise, sent back along the road the gopis are refusing to leave. It is the smallest thing in the story, and the largest: one sentence, carried by messengers, that gives them the strength to turn around.
stories.next_story_tease: But at the river Yamuna, Akrura would stop to bathe — and in its waters he would see something he never imagined.
stories.hero_scene: The gopis walking after Krishna's departing chariot on the road out of Vrindavan, their eyes fixed on the chariot's banner and the dust of its wheels, as the sun rises behind them.

stories.title: Akrura Beholds the Divine Vision in the Yamuna
stories.story:
Akrura had been sent to Vrindavan to bring Krishna and his elder brother, Balarama, to Mathura — the city where Kamsa reigned and where their parents, Vasudeva and Devaki, waited, worn down by the king's cruelty. He had told the brothers plainly what lay ahead of them, and neither had flinched. Now, with the two of them riding in his chariot, he came to the banks of the Yamuna. The sun stood high, and the river ran slow and clear, its water bright as a gem. He stopped the chariot and stepped down to wash, as any traveler would, and the two brothers waited on the road above.

Akrura stood at the water's edge, drank a little, and waded in. Murmuring a prayer under his breath, he sank beneath the surface — and what he saw unseated him. There in the river, as though no water lay between them at all, sat the two sons of Vasudeva, still in the chariot, exactly as he had left them on the bank. He broke the surface for air, wondering how the boys could be both on the road and in the river at once, and he dove again.

This time the river opened into something far larger than a riverbed. Before him rose Ananta, the king of serpents — a being of a thousand heads, each crowned with a spreading hood — receiving the praise of all who had gathered around him. And resting at ease in the coils of that great serpent was a figure dark as a rain cloud, clothed in yellow silk, his face serene and lit with the faintest smile, his glance gentle and full of love. In his hands he held a lotus, a conch, a discus, and a mace; a crown rested on his head, and his arms were bright with bracelets and armlets. About him stood his attendants — Sunanda and Nanda — and the sages Sanaka and his brothers; and among the throng were the great devotees of old, Prahlada and Narada. Around them shone the goddesses of fortune and nourishment, of speech and beauty and fame, of contentment and strength and glory, all gathered in attendance on the one who lay upon the serpent.

Then Akrura understood what he was being shown. The boys waiting patiently on the riverbank were not two boys only: what the water had shown him was the truth of them — the Lord himself, resting upon the thousand-hooded serpent, the whole court of heaven gathered about him. He rose from the water trembling with joy, his devotion overflowing, and when he opened his mouth to speak, the words came out broken and thick with feeling. He did not ask how this could be, or whether his eyes had deceived him. He simply praised — the name and the form he had just seen poured out in words that stumbled over one another. For what else can a man do who has looked into a river and found the source of everything looking back at him?

At last he was silent. He climbed the bank, took his place on the chariot beside the brothers, and drove on toward Mathura, keeping the secret of the Yamuna close. The sun kept its place and the river kept flowing, and no one on either bank knew what had happened in between. He had set out that morning to carry two boys to a city; he would arrive carrying the face of the Lord in his memory. Neither of his passengers said a word about it.
stories.reflection: Akrura's vision is given not to a sage in a forest but to a dutiful man washing in a river on a journey, at the most ordinary moment of his day. The story seems to insist that the divine is not hidden in some distant place but waits beneath the surface of what a person is already doing.
stories.tradition_note: The Harivamsha and Vishnu Purana describe Balarama himself as the thousand-hooded serpent with Vishnu resting upon him, while the Bhagavata here presents the serpent Ananta bearing the dark Lord, with both brothers present in the vision. This telling follows the Bhagavata.
stories.next_story_tease: Across the river, Mathura — and Kamsa — awaited them.
stories.hero_scene: Beneath the surface of the Yamuna, Akrura with folded hands gazes up at the thousand-hooded serpent Ananta, and resting in its coils the dark-complexioned Lord in yellow silk, holding a lotus, conch, discus and mace while gods and goddesses gather around him.

stories.title: Akrura Reports to Kamsa
stories.story:
Krishna and his elder brother, Balarama, were on the road to Mathura, where Kamsa — the king who had sent for the brothers — waited for them. They rode in the chariot of Akrura, the king's messenger, and on the way Akrura had stopped at the river Yamuna to bathe. There, beneath the water, he had been shown a vision: Krishna, the boy beside him, revealed as the Lord of all things resting upon the great serpent, the hosts of heaven about him. But one moment the river had shown him everything, and the next it was gone — folded away as suddenly as it had come, the way an actor folds away a play. He rose quickly from the water and found Krishna standing on the bank, as if nothing at all had happened.

"What did you see?" Krishna asked him. "You look as though you have seen something wonderful."

Akrura could barely answer. Everything that can be wondered at, he said — on the earth, in the sky, or in the water — stands in you. He had gone down into the river looking for the source of every wonder, and here it stood before him on the bank: not beneath the water, but there in the boy who had sent him down into it. The vision had been withdrawn, but the one it had revealed had not moved from his side. The river, he understood, had been only a mirror.

He climbed back onto the chariot, still turning it over in his mind, and urged the horses on toward the city. The reins felt strange in his hands; the road ahead felt like the road into a dream.

On the way, villagers gathered here and there to see them pass. The people of Vrindavan had come with the chariot too — Nanda, the old chief of the cowherds, who had raised the brothers, and his men — and they had gone on ahead. Word of the arrival had run before them all, and folk came out along the road to catch sight of the boys of Vrindavan on their way to Mathura at last.

Then Krishna spoke to Akrura. "You go on ahead," he said. "Enter the city first, with your chariot, and go to your own house."

Akrura would not let it go so easily. Come with us, Lord, he pleaded, and make our homes not without a master, for we are householders, and our houses are nothing without you. Purify them with the dust of your feet. The great king Bali won lasting fame by washing those feet, and the water of that washing cleansed the three worlds. O God of gods, whose very name is auspicious to hear and to sing, do not pass our doors. It was the voice of a man who had just seen the whole of creation gathered in one place and could not bear to watch it ride past his own threshold.

But Krishna answered gently and firmly and would not be turned. Akrura had been given an errand, and he knew how to take an answer; so he bowed and drove on ahead, though he would rather have stayed. He entered the city as he had been told, delivered his account to the king who had sent him, and only then, his errand done, turned toward his own house — carrying the wonder of the river quietly inside him, where no one in the city could see it. That afternoon, Krishna entered Mathura with Balarama beside him.
stories.reflection: Akrura had been shown the whole of creation in the river, and then it was hidden again — revealed and withdrawn, as if it were something that could not yet be spoken of openly. He drove on as he was asked, made his report, and kept the wonder privately inside him.
stories.next_story_tease: But Nanda, having delivered his tribute, would prepare to return to Vraja.
stories.hero_scene: Akrura surfacing from the waters of the Yamuna, dazed, while Krishna watches him with calm amusement; behind them the waiting chariot, and ahead the road and gates of Mathura.

stories.title: Nanda Departs for Vraja
stories.story:
The cowherds' time in Mathura had come to an end. Nanda and the men of Vrindavan had come to the city with their tribute — and with them had come the boys they had raised, Krishna and his elder brother, Balarama. Now it was time to turn homeward, back to the pastures and the forests of Vrindavan, where their herds and their houses waited. But one thing remained before they could leave, and it was the hardest thing of all: Krishna was not going home with them.

Nanda had not raised the boys as a favor. He and his wife Yashoda had taken the child and his brother into their home without hesitation, and they had loved them without reserve. They had fed them and cherished them and watched them grow, and in all those years they had never once treated the two as anything less than their own sons. It was the plain truth of that house, and it had never needed to be spoken.

Now the boys stood before them grown, here in the city where Krishna had been born, and it was Krishna himself who came to Nanda and Yashoda to say the words that had waited so long to be said. You two, he said, nourished us and cherished us with such tenderness. You were a father and a mother to us, and you raised us as though we were your own sons. It was gratitude spoken straight, with no ornament, and there was no shame in it — only the plain acknowledgment of a debt that love will not let a man forget.

Then he said what remained to be said. Go back to Vrindavan, dear father. And we, who are pained by this love, will not forget. He promised to come and see his kinsfolk — to return to the people and the place that had made him — and he offered the promise to Nanda and to all the people of Vrindavan together, so that no one would leave carrying only the loss.

Both homes were his now. In Mathura he had been born, Devaki's son, and here in this city lived the parents who had brought him into the world; but Vrindavan was where he had learned to walk and to play, where the man standing before him had carried him through all those years. A promise to return was the one thing that could make the parting bearable on both sides.

Nanda listened, and he could not keep his heart still. He embraced Krishna, and his brother with him, and the love he had carried all those years rose up and overflowed. His eyes filled with tears. The man who had fed these boys, carried them, and sung them to sleep now held them once more, and the tears came without his choosing — love that deep has no other way to say goodbye.

Then Nanda and the cowherds departed, and their eyes were full as they went home.
stories.reflection: The farewell is remarkable for what it does not say. There is no bitterness that Nanda must go home without the boys he raised, only gratitude spoken aloud and a promise to return. The love here is measured in what is given up freely, and in tears that need no explanation.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna and Balarama embracing Nanda as the old cowherd's eyes fill with tears, the people of Vraja gathered around them in Mathura preparing for the long journey home.

stories.title: Kamsa Orders the Gopas Expelled and Vasudeva Punished
stories.story:
The last wrestler had fallen, and the arena lay quiet.

Krishna and Balarama, the young cowherd brothers from Vrindavan, stood unhurt where the fight had been. Kamsa, the king of Mathura, had summoned them to his city and set his champions against them, meaning to be rid of them for good. But one by one his champions had gone down: Chanura and Toshala, whom Krishna had thrown down and struck; Mushtika and Andhra, whom Balarama had brought down with blows like a thundercloud. The great wrestling ground, so lately roaring, now stood empty of fighters, and the crowd began to understand what it was watching.

High above them sat Kamsa, and his face ran with sweat. The painted lines on his brow were washing away, and his lips trembled with a rage that had nowhere left to go. Every breath fed the fire of his fear and his hatred, until the two became one burning thing.

So Kamsa did what a cornered tyrant does: he turned on the helpless.

He raised his voice to his guards, and the words fell on the assembly like a sentence. Turn out of the arena these two sinful, grim-faced young cowherds from the forest, he said. I do not wish to see them. None of the cowherds deserves to remain in my territory. Then he pointed at Nanda — the old chief of the cowherds, the man who had raised Krishna as his own son. This Nanda is wicked, Kamsa said, and bent on doing me harm; bind him with chains and spikes of iron. And Vasudeva, his own kinsman — the father Krishna had been born to — drew the same sentence: Vasudeva is wicked too, Kamsa said; punish him this very day in a manner no aged man deserves. The rest of the cowherds, he added, are all devoted to Krishna; strip them of their cattle and their wealth.

It was not enough that the king had tried to kill the brothers. He reached now for everyone who loved them — the father who had raised them, the father who had begotten them, the whole community that had come up from Vrindavan to see them. The cruelty lay in how precisely it was aimed. He knew exactly where to wound.

Across the arena, Vasudeva heard the sentence passed on himself and on Nanda, and he fixed Kamsa with a long, unblinking gaze. His strength was truth, and he did not flinch. But Krishna saw it all at once — his father Vasudeva insulted, Nanda insulted, his kinsmen in distress, and Devaki, his mother, fallen senseless at the sight — and something in him turned. The wrath that rose in him was not the hot anger of a boy. It was the gathered anger of everything that had been done to his people, and it had found its object at last.

Kamsa's hour had come, though Kamsa could not see it. He sat above the arena, blind with his own rage, and below him Krishna gathered himself and, with the speed of a lion, leaped across the open ground toward the king's pavilion — to put an end to the man who had spent his whole life trying to kill him.
stories.reflection: Kamsa's rage, once his champions fail him, does not collapse into despair; it turns outward and downward, onto the defenseless — the foster father, the kinsman, the whole community. The story marks the precise moment a tyrant stops even pretending to rule and simply lashes out, and it marks Krishna's wrath as the answer that such a man has made inevitable.
stories.tradition_note: This telling follows the Harivamsha, where the provocation that immediately precedes Kamsa's death is his order to expel the cowherds, bind Nanda, and punish Vasudeva.
stories.hero_scene: Kamsa, face flushed and dripping with sweat, rising in fury in his pavilion to point at Nanda and Vasudeva as he orders the cowherds expelled, while Krishna below him begins to leap across the empty arena with the speed of a lion.

stories.title: Garuda Restores Vishnu's Stolen Crown
stories.story:
A shadow crossed the summit of Mount Gomanta — vast and swift, and not the shadow of any cloud. Krishna looked up, and his elder brother Balarama looked up beside him.

Krishna and Balarama had come up from Mathura with the warriors of their clan, for Jarasandha, the emperor of Magadha, was marching against them with a host of kings, and the army had made its stand far from the city, in the high country. While the troops made their preparations below, the two brothers had ranged the flowering forests of the mountain's crown, garlands of wild flowers on their chests, watching the sun and the moon rise and set over the world. Everything around them lay still. Then Garuda came.

Garuda, the great eagle on whose back Vishnu rides, was on his way home from a battlefield. His body still bore the marks of weapons, and he wore the garlands of one who fights on the side of the gods. He flew swiftly, and before him lay something that blazed with light.

Long ago, the tale goes, when Vishnu lay asleep in the ocean of milk, in the abode of Varuna, the lord of the waters, a thief had crept up on him. It was the son of Virochana, one of the daityas — the ancient demon people — and he had taken on the shining form of the king of the gods. While Vishnu slept, he lifted the crown from his head and carried it off. For that crown Garuda fought a dreadful battle with the daityas in the midst of the ocean, and he won it back. But when he looked for Vishnu, Vishnu was nowhere to be found; and so the great bird, the crown resting before him, was passing over the face of the earth toward the realms of the gods, searching as he flew.

Then he saw his master. Vishnu was there below him in a human form — no diadem on his head, no ornament upon him — walking the earth as Krishna. Garuda knew him at once, and he understood why his path had been bent this way. So the great eagle let the crown fall from the sky onto Krishna's head, and it settled there as though it had never been absent, as though it had been fitted to that head from the very beginning. Once placed, it shone on Krishna's brow like the midday sun blazing on the summit of Mount Sumeru.

Krishna's face brightened with pleasure. He turned to his brother. While the preparations for battle are being made on this mountain, he said, I think the work of the gods is near its fulfilment. When I fell asleep in the ocean, the son of Virochana stole away my crown, wearing the form of the king of the gods. Now Garuda has brought it back.

He did not treat the crown as a mere ornament restored. He read it as a sign. I am certain that Jarasandha is near, he said, for the tops of the chariots are already in sight. Look — there shine the moon-white umbrellas and the ordered armies of the kings who have come seeking victory, moving toward us like cranes across the sky.

And he spoke of the emperor Jarasandha almost warmly, as a guest arriving in good time — the first guest of the war, a touchstone against which their strength would be tested.
stories.reflection: The crown is not a piece of lost property so much as a confirmation. Garuda does not merely return what was taken; he returns it at the very moment Krishna needs to know who he is and what is coming. The restored diadem is read not as ornament but as omen — the work of the gods is near, and the enemy is already in sight.

stories.title: Krishna Returns to Mathura
stories.story:
Krishna and Balarama were coming home to Mathura, the city where they had been born but had never truly lived. They had grown up far away, among the cowherds of Vraja; the tyrant Kamsa had summoned them to the city to destroy them, and instead Krishna had destroyed him. Now the brothers were returning in peace, and word of them had run on ahead faster than their horses could carry it. By the time the walls of Mathura came into view, the whole city had risen to meet them.

For five nights they had traveled the road in the company of Damaghosha, a companion of their own people, keeping to the ways of an ordinary traveler. Now the road ended in welcome.

Ugrasena came out first, at the head of the Yadavas — Ugrasena, the old king of Mathura, father of Kamsa himself. Behind him came the traders and the ministers, the boys and the old men, until it seemed no one had been left indoors. They had dressed the city as for a festival. At every crossing of the four streets they had hung garlands and raised flags; the trumpets sounded the note of joy, and praise-singers went through the lanes singing the deeds of the two brothers. The whole of Mathura, it is said, looked as delighted and as beautiful as on the day of Indra's festival. Along the highways the singers called out: the two brothers have arrived at their own city — go out and rejoice.

And their coming seemed to change the very air of the place. Where Krishna and Balarama passed, no one in Mathura was poor, no one went about in soiled clothes, no one lay helpless in the road. The cows and the horses and the elephants grew glad, the birds began to sing glad notes, and men and women felt a quiet happiness they could not name. The winds that blew from the ten directions were clean of dust, and even the images of the gods in the temples seemed to brighten at their approach. People said that all the signs of the golden age had appeared in Mathura with their coming.

Then, seated on a chariot drawn by fine horses, at an auspicious moment, the brothers entered the city. The Yadavas followed them as the gods follow Indra, and the two, their faces full of gladness, passed like the sun and the moon entering a mountain into the house of their father, Vasudeva. There they set aside their weapons of their own accord, and the burden of all they had carried fell away.

Before anything else, they bowed to their father's feet. Then they showed proper honor to king Ugrasena and to all the leading Yadavas gathered there. And the elders welcomed them in return with a warmth that asked nothing of them, and the brothers, light-hearted at last, went in to their mother's apartments. In the days that followed they stayed close to Ugrasena, and they lived in Mathura happily, at peace among their own people.
stories.reflection: The homecoming is told almost entirely through what the city does and feels — the garlands, the clean winds, the auspicious birds — as if Mathura itself were a body returning to health. Krishna and Balarama are welcomed not with a victory parade but with a father's feet to bow to and a mother waiting inside, and that is where the long journey finally ends.

stories.title: Kaishika Offers His Kingdom
stories.story:
Krishna came to the land of Vidarbha as a guest, and by every ordinary measure he came with nothing. He had slain Kamsa, the tyrant of Mathura, yet he had not taken the throne for himself. He held no city, wore no crown, and so had no seat among the kings gathered at Kundina, Bhishmaka's city, for the swayamvara of the princess — the great choosing, at which a princess takes a husband from among the kings who come to seek her. The proud among them had already settled the matter in their own minds, echoing the taunt of the emperor Jarasandha, Krishna's enemy: Devaki's son has never been installed. He holds no city. How shall he sit in the same assembly as kings?

But there were two who saw it differently. Kratha and Kaishika, the brothers who ruled Vidarbha, watched the visitor and thought not of what he lacked but of what they owed him. If we can but see this man anointed king with our own eyes, Kaishika turned it over, our sins will be washed away; his presence will purify our understanding. And since there was no worthier person in all the worlds, what gift could ever be enough? The turning of that question brought them to the only answer worthy of such a guest: the whole of what they ruled.

The answer they settled on was everything. The two brothers went to Krishna and bowed their heads low. Blessed is our birth and our fame today, they said; blessed are our ancestors, since you have come to our house. Then they laid it all at his feet — umbrellas and flagstaffs, throne, army, and flourishing city. Indra himself once anointed you, they reminded him, and you carry the name Upendra from that day — one who stands beside the king of the gods. We now install you in our kingdom. What we two do, no host of kings will be able to undo — not even Jarasandha himself.

There was a reason for the urgency. King Bhishmaka, the father of the maiden, had seen the trouble brewing among the assembled kings and, after consulting the brothers, had readied a fine resting house for Krishna, so that no quarrel over seats could break the gathering apart. Perform the royal anointing today, the brothers urged, and tomorrow be seated at ease on an auspicious throne, installed before all the kings as their emperor, at the bidding of Indra.

So they sent an emissary to the assembly of kings, and there Kaishika rose to speak of what had just occurred. His eldest brother Kratha had conferred the kingdom upon Krishna. But the moment Kratha had said, Sit on this seat, a voice had spoken from the sky — a voice no one could see.

The voice was the envoy of Indra, and his words were plain. Do not offer him the seat on which you have sat, the voice said. For him alone the king of the gods has sent a white seat of gold, built by the celestial architect, crested with gems and marked with the emblem of a lion. Place him upon it among the other kings, and sprinkle him with water, as kings are anointed. Whoever among the kings gathered here for the maiden fails to come shall answer to the king of the gods. Eight jars of celestial gold and jewels, born of the treasure-houses of the god of wealth, will come among you to install this emperor.

Then Kaishika told the kings what had followed. The emissary had set the seat before Krishna — bright as the rising sun — and had returned to the city of the gods. Now let every king here behold the one whom the king of the gods has himself recognized, he said: dreadful, irresistible, wonderful in form, a sight rare in the land of mortals. If we witness this ceremony, the anointing of the God of gods, surely our sins will be destroyed.

The offer had been made, and the heavens had already answered it.
stories.reflection: The brothers' gesture matters because of what it reverses. Jarasandha measures a man by his city and his crown, and finds Krishna lacking; Kratha and Kaishika, looking at the same man, can think only of what they might give him. Their kingdom is not a sacrifice but a recognition — and the answer from the sky confirms that they have seen truly.
stories.next_story_tease: But the white seat was only the beginning; a consecration unlike any on earth was about to fall from the sky itself.
stories.hero_scene: Kratha and Kaishika, the two kings of Vidarbha, bowing low before Krishna as they offer him their umbrellas, throne, army and city, while above them an unseen voice announces the white seat of gold sent by Indra.

stories.title: Krishna's Royal Consecration
stories.story:
The white seat of gold stood among the assembled kings, and Krishna sat upon it. The brothers who ruled Vidarbha, Kratha and Kaishika, had laid their whole kingdom at his feet; and Indra, the king of the gods, had answered from the sky with this seat, sent down for him alone. Around Krishna stood the kings of Vidarbha and the gathered princes of the swayamvara, the princess's great choosing, and overhead the envoy of Indra had already delivered his charge. Nothing remained but the ceremony itself — an abhisheka, a royal anointing, the rite that makes a man a king — and everyone present understood that it would not be performed by human hands alone.

The sign came from the sky. Celestial jars began to pour down from above, like clouds opening after a long drought, and what they poured was no common water: water mixed with gold and gems, with flowers and scented powders, falling over the seated Krishna in a steady, glittering rain. One after another the vessels descended and emptied themselves upon him, until the whole ceremony seemed to be performed not by priests but by the heavens themselves.

Then came the eight jars the voice had promised — vessels born of the treasure-houses of the god of wealth, made of celestial gold and studded with jewels, carrying ornaments that belonged to no mortal treasury. They moved among the kings and joined in the anointing, as though the wealth of the whole earth had been summoned to crown this one man. The kings watched in silence, for this was no ceremony any of them could perform for another.

And Indra himself came down to finish what he had set in motion. The king of the gods, who in an earlier age had anointed Krishna by the name Upendra, now adorned him before the very eyes of the kings and sprinkled him from the sky as the rite required. It was the full abhisheka, performed duly according to the rites laid down in scripture, with Krishna seated on the seat marked with the emblem of a lion — emperor of the kings assembled at Indra's behest.

Kratha and Kaishika had offered their kingdom, and the heavens had answered with a consecration that no earthly king could have granted. No priest raised the water; it rose and fell of itself. No hand carried the crown; it came down with the scented rain, gold and flowers together.

When it was done, the man Jarasandha had mocked as having no throne and no city sat enthroned before kings from every quarter, anointed not by the favor of men but by the gods themselves. The question that had hung over the gathering — how shall he sit among kings? — had been answered at last.
stories.reflection: The consecration is remarkable for how little it depends on human agency. The brothers offer the kingdom, but the sky performs the rite: the water, the gold, the scented powders all descend of their own accord. Indra, who once anointed Krishna as Upendra, now completes the imperial abhisheka before the kings — an honor no earthly sovereign could confer and no earthly sovereign could withhold.
stories.next_story_tease: Yet when Krishna returned to Mathura, he would not keep this empire for himself.

stories.title: Ugrasena Welcomes Krishna Back
stories.story:
Before he left Vidarbha, Krishna told the assembled kings — the kings who had just crowned him emperor — plainly where he was going. I am going home to Mathura, he said, the city of my birth, where king Ugrasena rules.

Garuda, the great eagle who flew at Krishna's side, then asked leave of him. There is a city at the foot of Mount Raivata, on the shore of the ocean, the great bird said — Kushasthali, once held by the rakshasas, the demon people, and now abandoned. It is rich with flowering trees and full of wild creatures. Let me fly west and see whether it is worthy of you. And with that he saluted Krishna and set off toward the setting sun.

Krishna and his kinsmen, the Yadavas, entered Mathura. The news of his crowning had run ahead of him, and it had reached the old king before the man himself did. Ugrasena, the old king of Mathura, had heard how numberless kings had installed Krishna as emperor, how Indra had made peace with him through his envoy Chitrangada, how wealth had been shared out so that no one who came went away empty-handed. And the king of Mathura set about preparing a welcome fit for an emperor.

He made rich offerings at the temples of the gods who guarded the city. He hung the gates of Vasudeva's house with flags and pennons and garlands, and draped Kamsa's old hall of assembly in bright cloth. He anointed the doors of Krishna's sitting room with sweet paste and filled the highways with music and dancing. The whole city bloomed with flags, garlands of wild flowers, and jars of water; sandal water was sprinkled on the roads, lengths of cloth spread on the ground, and sweet incense burned in vessels on either side. The elderly women sang blessings, and the young women moved through their houses in restless expectation.

Then the great conch Panchajanya sounded, and the whole of Mathura came streaming out — women, boys, elders, singers and praise-singers, and a huge army, with Balarama going before them. Ugrasena himself carried the arghya — the offering of honor — and the water for washing Krishna's feet. When the old king caught sight of Krishna — seated on a chariot bright with jewels, a garland of wild flowers on his breast — he stepped down from his own white chariot to walk the rest of the way on foot.

It would not be fitting for me to ride after this, Ugrasena said. You go on the chariot.

But Krishna would not take what the old king was offering. He declined the royal honor, and his words were gentle and final. O king of Mathura, he said, I have installed you and declared you lord of Mathura. I will not now make it otherwise. The empire the kings had given him, the consecration the gods had performed — none of it, he meant, undid what he had already done. So climb back onto your white chariot, he told the old man, and rule the city of Mathura happily, with your sons and grandsons.

And to the king who had lost a son to Krishna's own hand, the conqueror spoke not of victory but of comfort. Kamsa had seized the throne and thrown his own father into prison; Krishna had freed Ugrasena and set him back upon it, and he would not now take the seat from him. The man who entered Mathura as an emperor left its crown exactly where he had placed it — on the head of the old king who had come out on foot to meet him.
stories.reflection: The story turns on a refusal. Krishna enters Mathura as an anointed emperor, welcomed with all the honors a king can offer — and he declines the very throne. The empire the kings and gods conferred is real, but it does not undo his earlier act: Ugrasena is lord of Mathura, and Krishna will not unmake that word. Power here is shown not by taking a crown but by refusing one he had every right to keep.
stories.next_story_tease: But even a king of Mathura had no hall fit for the gods, and Krishna would soon ask Indra for one.

stories.title: Krishna Obtains the Celestial Hall Sudharman
stories.story:
Ugrasena sat once more on the throne of Mathura, and around him his people, the Yadavas, had begun to recover from the long fear of Kamsa — Kamsa, his own son, who had seized the throne and thrown his father into prison before Krishna struck him down. Krishna, who had freed the old king from his confinement and placed the crown back upon his head, stood before him as a servant, not a sovereign. The funeral rites for Kamsa and the rest of the slain were done.

Command boldly what else is to be done, Krishna said to him.

There was a difficulty in the way, and Krishna named it openly. The curse of Yayati, he told the king, has pronounced our race unworthy of dominion. Long ago Yayati's son Yadu refused to take his father's old age upon himself, and for that refusal his descendants were denied the right to rule. The Yadavas could hold their assemblies and their court only because they did not do so in their own name. But with me for your servant, Krishna said, you may issue your orders to the gods themselves. How should kings disobey them?

So he set about proving it. There was a hall in the heavens, the splendid Sudharman — a court of unearthly beauty that belonged to Indra, the king of the gods. Krishna turned to Vayu, the god of wind, and gave him an errand. Go to Indra, he said, and ask him to lay aside his pomp and give up his splendid hall Sudharman to Ugrasena.

Vayu carried the request to the king of the gods, and the answer came back without hesitation. Indra laid aside his pomp and gave up the hall at once. The celestial court that had belonged to the lord of heaven passed into the keeping of the Yadava chiefs, who from that day held their assemblies beneath a roof of jewels that no mortal builder had raised.

It was a strange thing to ask for, and stranger still to receive. Krishna did not demand victory in battle, nor wealth, nor a wider kingdom. He asked for a place — a hall where the Yadavas, whom the curse of Yayati had barred from dominion, could sit and hold their counsel with the dignity of kings. And Indra, who had once anointed Krishna by the name Upendra and had sent the golden seat for his consecration, gave it up without a word of refusal.

The curse had not been lifted; the Yadavas still could not claim a crown in their own right. But beneath the jeweled ceiling of Sudharman they gathered as though they could — and the gods, beginning with the one who had been asked to give up his own splendor, did not dispute it.
stories.reflection: The gift Krishna seeks is not power but a place to stand with dignity. Barred by Yayati's curse from dominion, the Yadavas can hold a court only because Krishna, serving them, commands the gods on their behalf. Indra's instant surrender of Sudharman is the measure of that service: even the lord of heaven lays aside his pomp when asked in Ugrasena's name.
stories.tradition_note: The Harivamsha places the hall Sudharman later, among the splendors Krishna brings to Dwaraka; the Vishnu Purana tells it here, for Ugrasena's court at Mathura.
stories.hero_scene: The celestial hall Sudharman descending into the keeping of the Yadava chiefs, its jeweled columns and golden ceiling shining as Indra lays aside his pomp and yields the splendid court.

stories.title: Narada Reveals the Truth to Kamsa
stories.story:
Kamsa, the king of Mathura, had stopped counting the killers he sent against the cowherd boy of Vraja — the pasture country across the Yamuna where the boy had grown up — because the count only ever rose and the boy never died. Putana, the she-demon who went to nurse a newborn, had been drained of her own life instead. The wagon under which the baby lay had been overturned. The two arjuna trees had been shattered. The serpent Kaliya had been driven out of the Yamuna. Dhenuka, Pralamba, the bull-demon Arishta — all sent, one after another, and each time it was the killer who fell.

And yet the king could steady himself with one certainty. The child the prophecy had named — Devaki’s eighth son, the one foretold to be his death — was gone. Years before, in the prison, he had seized that newborn with his own hands and dashed it against a stone, before it had ever drawn breath as his enemy. He had been so sure of it that he had let the fear loosen its grip, and he had gone on ruling Mathura, cruel and calm.

Whatever this cowherd named Krishna might be — rising through Vraja like a fire no one could put out — he was not the one the prophecy meant. He could not be. That had been settled in blood, long ago.

Then Narada stood before him.

Narada, the wandering sage who moves freely between the worlds, did not flatter the king and did not threaten him. He came as a messenger of fact, nothing more. He told Kamsa the truth plainly, and the truth was worse than any threat could have been: the boy Kamsa feared had never died.

On the night of that birth, Narada said, Vasudeva had carried the newborn across the Yamuna in secret and left him in the care of Nanda and Yashoda, bringing their newborn daughter back to the prison in his place. That daughter — Yashoda’s girl, not Devaki’s son — was the child Kamsa had seized and dashed that night. And the fair one who fought at Krishna’s side, Balarama, was the son of Rohini, hidden in Vraja all these years in the same way.

These two, Narada told him, were his death. The eighth child was alive, grown strong, and living almost within reach — sheltered by a village of cowherds the king had never thought to watch.

Rage shook Kamsa’s senses. Every locked door of the prison, every guard he had posted, every one of Devaki’s infants he had killed there — all of it had been for nothing, because the one child who mattered had been carried out from under his hand, through the dark, while he slept. The fury had to land somewhere, and it landed on Vasudeva.

He seized his sword and had Vasudeva taken. Devaki was bound beside her husband, and both were put back into iron fetters. The man who had saved his son by giving him away would answer for the deception, and Kamsa would see that he did. He would find some other way to reach the boy — he always did. But for now the truth itself had become his enemy, and it would not be put back in chains.
stories.reflection: Narada does not plot and does not accuse; he only states what is true, and the truth alone is enough to shatter the false certainty on which Kamsa's prison was built. The iron fetters Kamsa claps on Vasudeva and Devaki are a confession: he has lost the one thing that kept him calm, and rage is all he has left.
stories.tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana adds that Kamsa, in his fury, also reproached Vasudeva and all the Yadavas in a full assembly; the Bhagavata records only that he seized his sword and bound the couple.
stories.next_story_tease: But knowing the truth only sharpened Kamsa's fear, and he began at once to lay his own plans for the boy.
stories.hero_scene: The sage Narada standing before Kamsa in his court, calmly speaking the truth that undoes the king, while Kamsa's hand moves toward the hilt of his sword and his face darkens with rage.

stories.title: Kamsa Orders the Wrestlers and the Elephant
stories.subtitle: The arena is readied for the two boys of Vraja
stories.story:
When Narada had gone, Kamsa did not rage at once. The truth the sage had left behind — that Krishna and Balarama were alive, and that they were the death Narada had shown him — settled over him like a cold weight, and the king turned it over and over until it hardened into a plan.

He began by walking out to the arena himself, to look over the ground where he meant the thing to happen. It was a fine hall, built by skilled hands: a wide courtyard ringed with pillars of even size, turrets with pleasant rooms, seats raised and royal, passages that could hold a great crowd, and the walls hung with the strong tusks of elephants. Kamsa looked it over and gave his orders — let the platforms and the turrets be hung with garlands and flags and sweet scents, let water-jars of gold be set out in their order, and let the bow festival be announced for the fourteenth day of the month. The city would gather for a celebration.

Then, back in his own rooms, he sent for his wrestlers.

Chanura and Mushtika came, the two strongest men in Mathura, men whose whole lives had been shaped by the king’s favor. Kamsa spoke to them as a patron speaks to men he owns. You are my famous wrestlers, he said. I have showered honors on you; now remember them. In the arena you will face two cowherd boys from the forest, Krishna and Balarama, who have grown up in Vraja. Throw them to the ground and kill them.

Do not look at their size and think it will be easy, he warned. Do not dismiss them as mere boys of fickle nature. These two have been shown to me as my death. If they fall in the ring, my well-being is secure — now and in the time to come.

The wrestlers, eager for a fight and flattered by the king’s words, promised him the thing he wanted to hear. If those two helpless boys come before us, they said, count them already slain. And if they dare withstand us, we will destroy them in your very presence.

Then Kamsa turned to his elephant-master, Mahamatra. There is an elephant, he said — Kuvalayapida, the great bull whose temples run with rut, whose eyes are never sober, who is always in a fury against men. Station him at the gate of the arena. When the sons of Vasudeva arrive, drive him at them, and let him crush the life out of them before they ever reach the ring.

So the king laid his trap. The elephant at the gate, the wrestlers inside, and between them no way out. The city would come for the festival, and the two boys would be invited as guests; and somewhere between the gate and the ring, before the eyes of the whole city, the death Kamsa feared would be brought about.

The king was done with sending demons into the dark. He would not go to Vraja himself, and he would not fight Krishna with his own hands. He would let the elephant and the wrestlers do it for him, and Mathura would watch.
stories.reflection: Fear has turned Kamsa methodical. The same king who once dashed an infant against a stone now arranges an assassination like a festival — layers of planning, a pretext, an audience — because he will not face the thing he fears directly. His cruelty has grown careful, which is what fear does when it has time.
stories.tradition_note: The Harivamsha gives Kamsa a longer and darker speech, in which he declares that Narada has revealed he was not truly Ugrasena's son and that he means to purge Mathura of the Yadavas; the Bhagavata keeps his orders brief and businesslike.
stories.next_story_tease: But the trap still needed the two boys brought to Mathura, and for that Kamsa would turn to a man he believed was his friend.
stories.hero_scene: Kamsa standing in his chamber, issuing orders to the wrestlers Chanura and Mushtika, while beyond the walls the great elephant Kuvalayapida waits to be stationed at the arena gate.

stories.title: Kamsa Sends Akrura to Fetch Krishna
stories.story:
The trap was set, but it had one loose end: the two boys were still in Vraja, and no trap springs on prey that never arrives. So Kamsa turned to the one man he trusted to spring it.

He sent for Akrura, foremost among the Yadavas, called the lord of gifts for the generosity that had made his name spoken of with respect across Mathura. Kamsa took him by the hand, the gesture of a friend to a friend, and his words were warm.

You have always been my friend, he said; there is a matter of importance I would settle through you. Go to Vraja, to Nanda’s settlement, and bring back the two boys, Krishna and Balarama. The bow festival is to be celebrated here, and they should come and see it.

That was the part meant for the city to hear — the festival, the invitation, the honor. But to Akrura he did not bother to hide the rest, because he believed Akrura was wholly his. These two boys, he said, are the means by which the gods have appointed my death. When they are brought here, I will have them killed by the elephant. And when those two are dead, this earth will be free of its thorns at last.

He spoke with the confidence of a man who thought the world was already arranged around his will, and he named the allies who had thrown in their lot with him as if they settled the matter. Kamsa trusted Akrura the way a man trusts his own right hand, and it never occurred to him that the hand he was sending to Vraja might not belong to him. But Akrura was not deceived.

Akrura knew Kamsa — knew what lay behind the soft words and the clasped hand, and knew, as well as any man in Mathura knew, that the king’s invitations had a way of ending. The boys who answered this one were not meant to return. Yet he agreed to go.

His answer was strange and gentle: even men whose hopes have been struck down by fate, he said, go on entertaining their hopes. It was the answer of a man who understood exactly what was being asked of him, and who had decided, for reasons of his own, to make the journey anyway.

So the invitation went out — carried by the most trusted messenger Kamsa had, wrapped in the friendliest words the king could find, and underneath it, spoken plainly, the whole machinery of a death. Kamsa believed he was sending for his doom in order to kill it. He did not yet see that he was sending for the beginning of his own end.
stories.reflection: This is Kamsa at his most dangerous, because he is at his most pleasant. The hand he lays on Akrura's arm and the sweetness in his voice are weapons as much as the elephant and the wrestlers; and the tragedy of the scene is that the generous Akrura sees through all of it and still consents to carry the message.
stories.tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana folds the sending of the horse-demon Kesin into this same plan, to attack the boys in Vraja before they can be brought to Mathura; the Bhagavata has Kamsa give Kesin his orders separately, before summoning Akrura.
stories.next_story_tease: And so the two brothers set out for Mathura, where the whole city was waiting to see them.
stories.hero_scene: Kamsa holding the hand of the noble Akrura in his chamber, speaking to him with soft, friendly words, while Akrura listens with a face that betrays nothing of what he knows.

stories.title: Krishna and Balarama Enter Mathura
stories.story:
Mathura had never looked the way it looked that afternoon, at least not to the two boys who came walking up its road. Krishna and his elder brother Balarama, raised among the cowherds of Vrindavan, had come for the bow festival that King Kamsa had proclaimed, and the city rose before them dressed for the day.

The gateway was of crystal, tall and shining, fitted with doors of gold and golden arches; beyond it lay crossroads of gold, high mansions and terraced gardens, rows of houses and open assembly halls. In the lattice windows doves and peacocks called out to one another. Water pots stood full along the streets, and the ground had been sprinkled with curd and sandalwood; garlands of flowers and strings of lamps hung everywhere among fresh green leaves.

The two brothers entered by the king’s road, surrounded by their cowherd companions, and the news of their coming ran ahead of them faster than they could walk. The women of the city came running to see them.

What the city saw undid its composure. Women came out in the middle of their ordinary tasks, and the tasks fell apart. One had dressed in such haste that her clothes and ornaments were put on inside out. Another had forgotten one of a pair — a single earring, a single anklet. Another had lined only one eye and left the other bare. Some set down their food halfway through eating; some, being rubbed with oil, left off before the bath was done. None of it mattered anymore. They had a single thought, and it pulled them all toward the same street.

Krishna walked among them, and his bold, easy smiles and slow, teasing glances poured over the crowd like nectar. The women drank the sight of him and held him with their eyes, as if they could keep him there by looking. Their skin thrilled with a joy they had no name for, and a sorrow they had carried a long time loosened its hold on them there in the road and fell away.

Those who could not reach the street climbed to the rooftops, their faces open with delight, and from the terraces they showered down curd and unbroken rice and water, garlands and sweet scents, like offerings.

And watching the cowherd women who had this boy to themselves every day, the people of the city called out in wonder: what great austerities — what long fasts and hard penances — must these women have performed, that they can see him whenever they wish?

The two brothers walked on through the rejoicing city, and behind them, in the doorways and on the roofs, the women of Mathura stayed watching until the two of them had passed from sight.
stories.reflection: The heart of the scene is not the grandeur of Mathura but the women's self-forgetfulness — the half-done hair, the single earring, the one lined eye. Joy this complete makes self-consciousness impossible, and the citizens' wondering question to the gopis turns the city's own longing back on itself.
stories.next_story_tease: But the same road held other meetings for them, and the first would not be a friendly one.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna and Balarama walking the king's road into Mathura in the afternoon, surrounded by cowherd companions, while the women of the city lean from windows and rooftops, showering down curd, unbroken rice, garlands and scents.

stories.title: The King's Washerman
stories.story:
Krishna and his elder brother Balarama walked the streets of Mathura at dusk, moving through the crowd the way two young elephants move when they are loosed from their posts — curious, unhurried, and not easy to stand against. They had come that day from the cowherd settlements of Vrindavan to see the city where King Kamsa held his festival. Akrura, the courtier who had driven them there in his chariot, had gone on ahead to the palace, leaving the brothers to wander the streets on their own. They took the city in slowly: the houses leaning close over the lanes, the smell of dye and cooking and dust, the press of strangers, the sheer number of lives going on at once. None of it was theirs, and yet they walked it as if they had every right to be there. Beside them, the crowd moved aside without quite knowing why.

They were in no hurry. They had heard of Mathura all their lives — its gates, its wealth, its cruel and watchful king — and now they meant to see it for themselves, street by street, like boys let loose in a fair that belonged to someone else.

On the road they met a washerman coming toward them, stooped under his bundles of dyed cloth. This was no ordinary man with ordinary washing: he was the king’s washerman, and the cloth he carried was the king’s own — garments dyed in the colors Kamsa favored, gathered from many countries and made bright for the royal household. The dye still seemed to sit freshly on the cloth, red and yellow and deep blue. Krishna stopped him and, without any sharpness in his voice, asked for clothes that would suit the two of them.

The washerman looked them over — their rough dress, their forest manner — and laughed at the request. These clothes belonged to the king, he said; who were they to ask for them? They were boys of the forest, born among the deer and grown up with them, with no notion of what a city or a king might be. Why should such as they desire the robes of a king? And if they valued their lives at all, he added, they would drop the request and be on their way before their words cost them more than they could pay.

The scornful words were still on his lips when Krishna, his anger rising, struck him a single blow of his open hand across the head. The man fell, and lay still upon the earth, and the road fell silent around him, the laughter gone out of the evening as suddenly as it had come.

His attendants, seeing it, dropped their bundles of dyed cloth where they stood and ran, scattering the bright cloth into the dust. Krishna and Balarama stepped forward into the heap of the king’s finest garments and chose for themselves the clothes that pleased them, and the rest they gave away to the cowherds who had travelled with them from Vrindavan. Then the two brothers walked on, deeper into the city, leaving the scattered cloth and the fallen man behind them on the road.

They did not look back. Ahead of them the streets of Mathura went on, bright with lamps and full of people, and the evening had only just begun.
stories.reflection: The washerman is undone less by his refusal than by his contempt: he reads the two strangers by their rough clothes and their forest birth and mistakes both for worthlessness. The episode does not linger over the killing; it moves at once to the bright heap of garments and the brothers walking on, as if what mattered most was not the man's death but what his pride had refused to see.
stories.tradition_note: The Harivamsha and Vishnu Purana identify the washerman as Kamsa's own servant, made insolent by royal favor; the Bhagavata, followed here, has him simply refuse and abuse the two strangers.
stories.content_note: Krishna kills the washerman with a single blow to the head.
stories.next_story_tease: But the two brothers were not done with Mathura's streets, and the next meeting would go very differently.

stories.title: Krishna Straightens the Hunchback Kubja
stories.story:
The woman who came toward Krishna on the street of Mathura was bent nearly double, folded against herself as though she were forever bowing to someone. She carried a small pot of sandal paste and walked with the careful, sideways steps of a person whose body had long ago stopped obeying her. No one in that crowded street paid her any mind. Krishna did.

Krishna and his brother Balarama had only just entered the city. They had come riding in Akrura’s chariot, and now, with the evening sun turning crimson over the rooftops, they were walking Mathura’s broad highways, looking over everything they passed — the stalls and the crowds and the strangers hurrying home. They had grown up in the forest, and nothing here looked like the green world they had left, but they walked through it as though they owned it. The city was Kamsa’s, the king who was no friend to their house, and every road in it ran, in the end, toward his palace. Krishna, who noticed everyone, stopped to look at the bent woman.

Her name was Kubja, the three-bent one. She was a servant in the house of Kamsa, the king, and her work was the making of his unguents; the pot she carried held the sandal paste prepared for the king himself, fragrant and cool and bright. She was small and poor, and the crowd moved around her without seeing her, and she carried the pot carefully, as a servant carries what is not hers to spill. “Who are you,” Krishna asked her, smiling, “and for whom is this paste?”

“I am Kubja, a servant favored by Kamsa,” she said, “and this paste is meant for the king. But who deserves it more than you two?” And before the brothers could answer, she began to anoint them, rubbing the cool sandal onto their arms and chests with her own hands, and the two brothers stood still and let her do it. It was the king’s own unguent, given away on the open street to two strangers — a small, reckless generosity, and Krishna did not forget it.

Krishna was pleased with her. He looked at the crooked woman and decided to return her gift in kind. He was skilled in the art of healing, and he set to work with a craftsman’s care. He set his feet over hers and pressed them down, and with two fingers beneath her chin he lifted her head — and as he lifted, the twist went out of her. He did not pull or strain; he simply set right what had long been wrong. She straightened, joint by joint, and when she stood tall at last she found herself changed: a young and beautiful woman, graceful and sweet of face, no longer folded against herself.

Kubja looked down at her own straight limbs and then up at him, and she could not find the words for what she felt. “Come, hero,” she begged him, “let us go to my house. I cannot bear to let you go.” Krishna answered her gently. He would come to her house, he promised, when his work in the city was done. And so, leaving her standing straight and glad for the first time in her life, he and Balarama went on down the road through the merchants’ street, toward whatever awaited them in the city of the king who was their enemy.
stories.reflection: The episode is striking for how small it is. In the city of the king who sought his life, Krishna's attention falls first on a bent servant woman carrying someone else's sandal paste, and what he gives her is not power or wealth but her own body, made straight. The kindness is entirely private, offered to someone who could do nothing for him.
stories.tradition_note: The Harivamsha has Krishna touch Kubja's haunch to straighten her, and the Vishnu Purana describes him lifting her head by the chin while pressing down her feet; the Bhagavata leaves the gesture brief. This telling keeps the gesture simple, following the Bhagavata's account of the meeting.
stories.next_story_tease: The brothers walked on through Mathura toward Kamsa's wrestling arena.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna, standing before the hunchbacked Kubja on a Mathura street, presses down on her feet with his own and lifts her chin with two fingers, straightening her bent body while she still holds out her pot of sandal paste.

stories.title: Kamsa's Great Bow
stories.story:
In a hall in Mathura stood a bow, and it was the most guarded thing in the city. It was never carried to war; no archer had drawn it in living memory. It stood upright on its stand, decked with offerings, while armed men ringed it day and night, as if it were a king in its own right, or a god the city kept shut away. King Kamsa was preparing a great festival, and the bow was its showpiece; the whole of the king's pride seemed to rest in its unstrung curve. To break it would be to strike at the king himself, and everyone in Mathura knew it.

Two brothers had come to Mathura for that festival, from the cowherd village of Vrindavan: Krishna, and Balarama, his elder brother. They had spent their first day in the city wandering its streets, taking the measure of the place. Now Krishna began to ask the townspeople where the famous bow was kept. The people he asked looked at him strangely, but they answered; and with his brother beside him he went to find it, walking through the streets the way a man walks toward a thing he has already made up his mind about.

He found it in its hall, ringed by its keepers. Without asking leave of anyone, Krishna stepped up to the bow. The guards called out for him to stop, to stand back, but he paid them no mind. For a long moment no one in the hall moved. Then he reached out, took the great bow in his left hand, and lifted it as easily as a child lifts a toy; and before the eyes of everyone who watched, he strung it.

Then he bent it, and the bow broke. It snapped in two at the middle, the way a stalk of sugarcane snaps between the hands, and the sound of the breaking went out in every direction at once, until all of Mathura heard it — the noise of a thing that could not be broken, breaking. The ground itself seemed to carry the report from house to house, and half the city looked up from its work, wondering what had fallen. The echo hung in the air long after the bow lay in pieces.

The guards came at him then, angry and armed, their followers pressing behind them. But Krishna and Balarama took up the two broken halves of the bow, and with those they struck the attackers down — the whole force Kamsa had set to watch over the weapon. One after another the guards fell, and it was over quickly. Then the brothers walked out through the door of the hall, unhurried, and went back into the city as the day's last light began to fail.

The townspeople, who had heard the crack and seen the brothers walk free, could only stare after them. The sun was going down over Mathura, and in the houses that evening the only talk was of the wonderful, impossible thing that had happened that day, and of the two young strangers who had done it and then simply walked away. By nightfall there was not a household that had not heard the tale told twice.
stories.reflection: The bow was not an instrument of war but an object of worship, and that is what makes the act so pointed: Krishna breaks the thing the king has set apart as sacred, then uses its two halves as weapons against the king's own men. Strength here is not only physical; it is a claim of authority, made in public, that the city cannot pretend not to have seen.
stories.tradition_note: The Harivamsha likens the bow to a serpent, and the Vishnu Purana stresses the noise that filled Mathura; the Bhagavata, followed here, has Krishna string it and snap it like a stalk of sugarcane.
stories.content_note: Krishna and Balarama strike down the armed guards with the two halves of the broken bow.
stories.next_story_tease: But the crack of the bow was heard in the palace too, and it would not let the king sleep.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna lifting Kamsa's great bow with one hand and snapping it in two, the broken halves raised as the guards recoil, while the sound of the break echoes out across Mathura at dusk.

stories.title: The King's Sleepless Night
stories.story:
Kamsa, the king of Mathura, had lived for years inside one fear: a voice from the sky at his sister Devaki's wedding had told him that her eighth child would end his reign. The children born to her in his prison he destroyed, one after another; but the eighth, born at last in that same cell, was smuggled out in the night and given to the cowherds of Vrindavan, where he grew up as Krishna, a young man now, with his elder brother Balarama at his side. The two had walked into Kamsa's own city, and the news reached him the way a stone drops into still water: the great bow was broken, and the men he had set to guard it were dead.

He had known they were coming; he had known it for years, and watched for them the way a man watches a door he is afraid will open. He had trusted in the weight of his city, the number of his soldiers, the long favour fortune had shown him. Now, in a single day, they had walked his streets as if the city belonged to them, and the great bow — the bow that was his, the pride of his festival and of his reign — lay in pieces on the floor of its hall.

That night Kamsa did not sleep. He lay in the dark of the palace, and the dark would not settle into rest. Fear kept him awake, and through the fear came omens, one after another, in his waking hours and in the little sleep he could snatch. The palace that had always been his fortress felt, for the first time, like a place with too many shadows and not enough walls. His servants slept, his guards kept their posts, and still he was alone with the dark in a way he had never been before. A man who had spent his life reading the signs of his enemies could read this night as well, and what it said was a verdict he could not turn away from. He turned restlessly, and the bed that had always held him seemed to press back against him.

He looked into a mirror and could not see his own head in it, though his face should have been there, plain as day. The glass was not cracked; the room was not dim. He turned, and turned back, and the figure that stared out at him simply had no head. He looked down at his shadow and saw a hole running through it, a rent in the very shape of him, as if his body had already begun to come apart at the edges. He strained to hear the sound of his own breathing, and heard nothing at all — as if the noise of life had gone out of him while he still stood.

Then the dreams came, brief and terrible. In one he held a dead body in his arms and woke with the cold feel of it still upon him. In another he rode an ass through the long night — a mount for the dead and the disgraced — down a road that had no end. He woke sweating, the dream already fading and the dread of it not fading at all. And over everything settled a heaviness that no torch, no servant, no comfort in the whole palace could lift.

By morning he had seen his own death in every sign — in the glass, in his shadow, in the silence of his breath, in the dreams that would not leave him. They all said the same thing, and Kamsa was not a man who could misunderstand them. He understood them perfectly, and that was the worst of it.
stories.reflection: No sword is drawn against Kamsa in this passage, and that is the point: fear has already begun the work. The man who made a city afraid now finds the world turning its signs against him, and each omen is only the truth he has spent his reign refusing to see.
stories.next_story_tease: But dawn would bring not relief but resolve, and Kamsa would turn his fear into a plan.

stories.title: The Arena at Dawn
stories.story:
King Kamsa of Mathura had planned this day for years. A prophecy said that Krishna — the nephew smuggled out of his prison as a baby and raised among the cowherds of Vrindavan — would end his reign. Now Krishna had come at last to the city with his elder brother Balarama, and in a single day the great bow was broken and the men set to guard it were dead. When the night at last ended and the sun rose up out of the waters, Kamsa gave his order: let the wrestling begin.

He had spent the dark hours with his omens and his dreams, turning them over and over the way a man turns a key in a lock that will not open. But morning had come, and with it he set about turning his dread into a plan. The wrestling festival was to be the great public show of his reign, the day when all of Mathura gathered to watch the king's wrestlers prove their strength. Now it would serve a second purpose, one he kept to himself behind his steady face. He gave the word for everything to be made ready, and the order went out through the palace and into the streets, and the city answered.

All through the city the arena was made ready. Men smoothed the earth of the wrestling ground and raised the banners; drums and kettledrums began to sound, the noise rolling out over the houses until there was no corner of Mathura that did not know the festival had begun. Ropes were drawn around the wrestling ground, and the morning sun climbed slowly over the stands. The sound was meant to be joyful, and it was, in the bright early air — and yet it carried an edge to anyone who knew the king and what his festivals had come to mean.

The people came. Citizens and country folk poured in, priests and warriors at their head, and took their places around the arena until the stands were full and the ground was ringed with faces, the whole city turned out in its best. Their voices rose and fell in a low, expectant murmur, like the sea. Kamsa himself climbed to the royal dais, his ministers around him, and sat looking out over the crowd he had gathered — the crowd that would watch whatever he had arranged for them to watch, and cheer at whatever he told them was worth cheering.

The wrestlers entered and took their places: Chanura and Mushtika, the strongest of the king's fighters, and with them Kuta, Shala, and Toshala — practiced, dangerous men, their oiled bodies shining in the morning light, each waiting for the signal to fight. They moved through the arena with the easy confidence of men who had never been beaten, and the crowd murmured its approval as they passed.

And then, summoned by the king, the cowherds arrived — Nanda, who had raised Krishna from a baby, at their head, with the other men of Vrindavan, come to the city as guests bearing their offerings. They were country men in a king's city, and they looked it, and yet they carried themselves with the quiet dignity of invited guests, their gifts held before them. There were greetings and gifts, and the festival settled into its appointed order, and no one yet spoke of what it was really for.

The stage was set. The drums beat on. And Kamsa, at the centre of it all, watched the gate.
stories.reflection: The story moves from the intimacy of Kamsa's fear out into the great public theatre of the arena — a king turning private dread into spectacle. Everything is told in the language of preparation and display, and the effect is ominous: every drum and banner is being readied for a confrontation no one will announce.
stories.next_story_tease: But the brothers had not yet reached the arena, and between them and its gate stood a creature no wrestler could match.

stories.title: Krishna Slays the Elephant Kuvalayapida
stories.story:
King Kamsa of Mathura had one fear that ruled all his plans: a prophecy said that Krishna — the child of his imprisoned sister, smuggled away as an infant and raised among the cowherds of Vrindavan — would end his reign. Now Krishna had come to the city, his elder brother Balarama with him, and Kamsa had turned his great festival of wrestling into a snare: the contests, the prizes, the galleries packed with citizens, all arranged so that the two he feared could be drawn in and finished. At the gate of the wrestling arena stood an elephant, and it had not wandered there on its own. Kamsa had given the order the day before: let Kuvalayapida, his war elephant, wait at the gate, where no one could enter without passing it.

The arena that morning was the pride of Mathura. It rose on octagonal pillars painted in many colours, hung with festoons of flowers and the banners of every guild, its pavilions bright with gold, its seats and cushioned couches laid out for thousands. At its head, above all the rest, stood Kamsa's own pavilion, shining like a mountain of snow. The king entered in white, great white fans waving on either side of him, and took his place on the throne while the citizens shouted his praises. The wrestlers came in after him, loose-garmented, and took the ground on three sides.

Then Krishna and Balarama came up the road to the gate to the sound of trumpets and the slapping of wrestlers' arms. Krishna had tied back his garments and gathered his curling hair, the way a man settles himself before work. He looked at the elephant's keeper and told him, plainly, to stand aside and make way. The keeper, stung at being spoken to so, answered by goading the beast, and Kuvalayapida came forward, trunk folded, meaning to crush the two of them.

Krishna did not flinch. As the elephant bore down he slipped beneath it, caught hold of its tail, and dragged the huge animal back the length of twenty-five bows as though it were a stray calf. The beast wheeled and turned, and Krishna moved with it — now between its tusks, now under its legs — troubling it the way the wind troubles the sea. He roared like a lion and slapped his arms, and let the elephant's trunk come against his chest. In its rage the animal could scarcely see him; it hunted him by smell and found only empty air.

He struck it and it went down; it rose again. Those who watched said he was playing — that there was something almost childlike in the way he sported with the animal Kamsa had meant to be his doom. Even as he dodged, he smiled, and said that Kamsa, trying to kill him through this elephant, was only hurrying himself toward the land of the dead.

Then the elephant charged a second time, and this time Krishna was finished playing. He caught it as it came, pressed it down, and set his foot on it as a lion settles on its prey. With both hands he tore the tusks from its head and beat the beast with them. The elephant that had been Kamsa's surest weapon bellowed, and in its fury loosed a great flood of must, like a cloud pouring out the rain; then it lay still. Its keepers fell with it.

When it was over, Krishna took up one of the tusks in his hand. Balarama stood beside him, and the cowherds who had come from Vrindavan closed in around the two brothers. Splashed with the elephant's blood and must, they walked into the arena through the gate that had been set to stop them.

Kamsa watched from his high seat as the two he had planned to kill came forward without hurry, carrying the proof of what had happened at the door. The crowd, which had come expecting an afternoon of sport, had already seen more than it had bargained for. The elephant lay broken at the entrance, and the two cowherd boys of Vrindavan were inside.
stories.reflection: The trap Kamsa built was turned against him before the wrestling even began. The elephant he set at the gate became the very weapon — the tusk — that Krishna carried into the arena. What was meant to end the story only showed everyone watching that it could not be ended so easily.
stories.tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana presents the elephant as slain by both brothers together, while the Bhagavata centres the deed on Krishna alone; this story follows the Bhagavata.
stories.content_note: Includes the death of the elephant and its keepers, told without graphic detail.
stories.next_story_tease: And when the two entered, the city would see them for what they were.
