stories.title: A Warning for the Swayamvara
stories.story:
The golden assembly hall of Bhishmaka, king of Kundina, was crowded with kings, come for a swayamvara — the old ceremony in which a princess chooses her husband. Bhishmaka held it for his daughter Rukmini, and more than a few of the suitors had fought Krishna and his elder brother Balarama at Mount Gomanta, and been beaten; they had not forgotten.

When Krishna arrived — the great eagle Garuda and the warriors of his own clan behind him — the brightness seemed to dim. The leading kings exchanged glances and fell silent, stricken by an unease none of them could quite name.

Then Jarasandha of Magadha rose — the strongest of the kings, Krishna's declared enemy — and a hush settled over the hall.

He began quietly, with a warning dressed as counsel. "This Krishna," he said, "is the well-known son of Vasudeva, a man of great energy and prowess. He has not come to look on, but to win the maiden, and he will strain every power he has. Weigh your own strength and weakness, and act by the rules of statecraft."

Then his voice changed, and the kings heard what he truly thought.

"You know well what those two sons of Vasudeva did on Mount Gomanta, and that was without Garuda's help. I cannot say what Krishna will do now that the finest chariot-warriors of his people stand behind him. But when Vishnu seats himself on Garuda and moves to win this maiden, even Indra and all the gods of heaven could not stand against him in the field."

Then Jarasandha told the kings what this suitor had always been.

"When the whole world lay beneath a single ocean," he said, "Vishnu took the form of a boar, raised the drowned earth from the deep, and killed the demon Hiranyaksha. Hiranyakashipu, who could die by nothing in the three worlds — not in sky, earth or sea, not by day or night, not by anything dry or wet — was slain by Vishnu's man-lion form. To Bali, mightiest of the demons, he came as a dwarf, bound him with the noose of a promise, and sent him down to the worlds below.

"At the turning of the ages he was born in secret as the axe-bearing Rama, son of Jamadagni and Renuka, and cut down the thousand-armed Kartavirya, who trusted in the pride of his kingdom. Later he was born as Rama of the Ikshvaku line, son of Dasharatha, and killed Ravana, the terror of the three worlds. In the war that began with Taraka he rode Garuda, eight-armed, and slew demon after demon grown bold on their boons; with his discus, bright as the sun, he killed Kalanemi, who terrified the gods."

The hall was very still. "And nearer still," Jarasandha said, "he lived as a boy among the cowherds of Vrindavan, no one knowing who he was. In the forest he slew the demons Dhenuka, Arishta and Pralamba. In his cowherd form, Devaki's son killed the demon-woman Putana, the horse-demon Keshi, the royal elephant Kuvalayapida, the wrestlers Chanura and Mushtika, and at last Kamsa himself, king of Mathura, with all his followers. All this he did in a boy's body."

"This is my sure understanding," Jarasandha said, "and I came by it at Mathura. I hold Devaki's son to be the first cause of the gods, the slayer of demons, Narayana — the ancient being from whom the universe begins, Truth itself, creator of all that is and all that is not yet, unborn, unconquerable, eternal, lord of the three worlds. Can Garuda be the carrier of a mere man, even a king of kings? When he shows his power for the maiden, what man alive could stand before Garuda? I tell you plainly: Vishnu himself has come to this swayamvara, and a great calamity waits for you. Do what you think proper."

He sat down, and for a long moment no one moved. Then Sunitha rose and added his voice to the king of Magadha's, and the kings understood that the warning would not be argued away.

Outside, the lamps of Kundina were being lit for a festival that suddenly felt smaller. The kings sat on, each alone with the name none of them had wanted to hear, and none could forget.
stories.reflection: It is Jarasandha, Krishna's declared enemy and the man who had bound the kings into war against him, who names Krishna plainly before the assembled princes: not a rival suitor but Vishnu himself. Hatred here produces a clarity the indifferent kings do not share; the enemy sees exactly whom he is fighting, even as he resolves to fight him anyway.
stories.next_story_tease: But the kings did not answer with one voice, for Dantavakra would speak for peace and Salwa for war.
stories.hero_scene: In Bhishmaka's golden assembly hall at Kundina, Jarasandha stands among the seated kings, one hand raised, speaking with heavy certainty, while the assembled monarchs lean forward in alarm beneath the hall's lamps.

stories.title: The Council Divides
stories.story:
When Jarasandha sat down, and Sunitha had risen to back his warning, the kings of the earth — suitors all, come to Kundina to win the princess Rukmini — looked at one another across the golden hall. Into the silence rose Dantavakra, the king of Karusha.

He did not quarrel with the warning. What the king of Magadha and Sunitha had said for their good seemed to him proper; he could not call them false out of malice, pride, or any wish to win the argument himself.

"Krishna has come for the maiden, as we have all come," Dantavakra said. "Why should that surprise us? And why should we find fault with Gomanta, when we chose it ourselves?"

Because of Kamsa's folly, he reminded them, the two brothers had grown up in hiding at Vrindavan. Kamsa had invited them to Mathura and set an infuriated elephant on them; they killed the elephant, walked into the arena, and slew Kamsa, the king of Mathura, with all his followers. "What offence did they commit," Dantavakra asked, "that we grey-headed kings marched on Mathura at another man's bidding?"

The hall stirred uneasily: Dantavakra was telling them their own war back. Faced with the kings' overwhelming army, the brothers had left Mathura and taken refuge on Mount Gomanta. The kings pursued them, laid siege to the hill, and set it on fire — and still those two boys broke out and beat them in the field. "We blame Krishna because he fought instead of dying," Dantavakra said. "As things stand, wherever we go from here we shall pick up a quarrel. Krishna came for the maiden, not for a quarrel with us. Let us make friendship with him instead.

"He is no ordinary man — the first among men and among gods, maker of the worlds, with no malice, no pride, no crookedness in him. The king of gods has come with Garuda to show his true form, and remember: Krishna never marches with his army to destroy his enemies. He comes surrounded by his own clans — the Bhojas, the Vrishnis, the Andhakas and the Yadavas — a sign that he wants friendship, not ruin. Let us greet him as a guest and offer him the water of welcome; make peace with him now, and we may live without fear."

Then Salwa rose — Salwa, the finest speaker in the hall — and the temper of the meeting changed.

"What is the use of this fear?" he asked. "If we had thought it right to make peace, we would have left our weapons at home. Why do we speak ill of our own army and praise another? That is not the way of kings. We were born in great houses and have brought honor to our names; shall we now think like cowards?"

He did not deny the warning; he drew a different answer from it. He too knew Devaki's son for what he was — the eternal Vishnu, adored of all the worlds, teacher of the universe — and what he intended: the protection of the worlds, and the ruin of the kings who stood against him. "A great battle will come between Vishnu and the kings," Salwa said. "Consumed by the fire of his discus, we may go to the house of Yama, king of the dead. No man dies before his time; none escapes when it is done. The demons, for all their penances, fell each in his turn; so the mighty Bali was sent to the worlds below when his hour struck. So why should a king fear what is certain? Let us do what kings are born to do."

The debate broke against that answer and scattered. And through it all, Bhishmaka — king of Kundina, host of the council, father of the maiden and of the proud young Rukmi — had listened in silence, weighing each speech against the one thing he could not bear to lose. Then he rose from his seat among the princes and walked toward the door.

The council was still ringing with argument behind him. Whatever the kings decided, Bhishmaka had made his choice: he would go to Krishna himself, before any war could begin, and win the goodwill of the suitor the whole earth had gathered to deny.
stories.reflection: Every king in the hall seems to know who Krishna is; what divides them is what to do with the knowledge. Dantavakra reads the same facts as a summons to peace, Salwa as a summons to courage, and Bhishmaka, who alone among them is not deciding for an army but for his own children, reads them as a reason to bend. The council's war of words ends not with a king convinced but with a father moved.
stories.next_story_tease: But the kings were not done debating, and soon Shalya would propose summoning the Yavana king Kalayavana.

stories.title: Shalya Proposes Inviting Kalayavana
stories.story:
The kings had come to Kundina for the swayamvara of Rukmini, the princess of the house — the ceremony at which she was to choose her husband — and they were going home with nothing: Krishna had carried her off before any of them could move. Now the defeated suitors gathered one last time in the assembly hall of her father Bhishmaka, restless on their rich seats, before scattering to their own kingdoms.

Bhishmaka, a king learned in the laws of right conduct, rose and asked their forgiveness. "You all know the calamity that has befallen the swayamvara," he said. "Forgive me for what has come of it — the fault was mine." He honored the monarchs of central India and of the east, the west and the north, and sent them home delighted.

But a ring of the greatest kings stayed behind, sensing that something was still to be said: Jarasandha of Magadha, Sunitha, the fiery Dantavakra, Shalya of Soubha, King Mahakurma, Kaishika, the leading kings of the Pravara line, the royal sage Venudari, the king of Kashmir, and the kings of the Deccan.

To them Bhishmaka spoke again, and his words were really meant for his own son, the young Rukmi, who sat apart with his anger still raw. "When I watch my son's ways, my eyes are restless with fear," he said. "And as for these kings — beside Krishna I see boys. His fame and the might of his arms have filled this mortal world. Blessed is Devaki, who bore the lotus-eyed Krishna, most beautiful of beings, adored of all the immortals."

When he fell silent, Shalya of Soubha rose and answered him gently. "Do not grieve for your son, O king. Those who live by the sword meet success or defeat in battle — that is the way of the world, and the law of warriors. Apart from Krishna and his elder brother Balarama, what third person could stand against your son, who wields weapons so mighty that the gods themselves find them hard to handle? Krishna is without birth and without death; in this mortal world even Shiva, who holds the trident, could not defeat him. Your son knew Krishna for the Lord, and so he did not rush into a fight he could not win. There is no shame in that."

Then Shalya paused, and said what he had really come to say. "It is not that no one can defeat him."

Long ago, he told them, the sage Gargya had wished for a son. For twelve years he had lived on powdered iron and practiced hard penances, until Shiva, well pleased, offered him a boon. Gargya asked for a son whom the kings of Mathura could never slay — and the boon was granted. "That son, grown to manhood, is Kalayavana, king of the Yavanas — and the boon makes him unkillable by the kings of Mathura in open battle, and most of all within the city of Mathura itself. Krishna is mighty among the princes of Mathura — yet if Kalayavana comes to battle against him, he can defeat him. If my words seem sound to you, send an emissary to the capital of the Yavana king."

The leading kings heard him out with delight. "We will do it," they said.

Only Jarasandha's heart sank, for he remembered the words Brahma had spoken to him long ago. "Alas," he said. "There was a time when kings, hard pressed by some foreign conqueror, came to me for shelter, and I gave them back their kingdoms, their armies and their treasuries. Now their anger at their old protector makes me beg shelter from a stranger. It is not fitting. Even I — I, who stand in fear of Krishna —" and there his voice failed.

But the will of the kings prevailed, and the emperor who had once sheltered the princes of the earth sent Shalya of Soubha as his envoy to the capital of the Yavanas.
stories.reflection: Shalya's counsel turns the kings' defeat at the swayamvara into a plan against Krishna, and the plan is clever enough that everyone accepts it at once. It is Jarasandha, the mightiest of them, who recoils — because he understands that calling in an ally is also an admission of fear.

stories.title: Shalya Delivers Jarasandha's Message to Kalayavana
stories.story:
A strange wind came up in the capital of the Yavanas that day — cold and fragrant, sweet and unsettling — and the whole court wondered at it. Where could such a wind come from? Then they saw the answer, riding out of the south.

Kalayavana, king of the Yavanas, ruled his city well. He was wise and learned, truthful and devout, master of his own temper, skilled in the arts of war and statecraft, quick to honor his ministers — and no fortress had ever held against him. That day he sat at ease among his counselors, while the learned men of his court spoke of heavenly matters and sang their king's praise.

The car from the south was gold and white, ablaze with jewels, hung with bright flags, drawn by horses swift as thought, decked in tiger-skins — built by the architect of the gods, shining like the sun. On it sat the powerful and handsome king of Soubha: Shalya, an old friend of Kalayavana.

Seeing his friend, Kalayavana rose from his throne, took up the offerings of welcome, and went out to wait at the foot of the car's stair. Shalya climbed down alone, entered the palace in good spirits, and then, seeing the welcome ready in the Yavana king's hands, drew back.

"I am not worthy of these honors," he said. "I am no guest. I am an envoy of the kings, sent to you by the wise Jarasandha, and honors like these belong to kings, not to messengers."

Kalayavana smiled. "I know that the king of Magadha sent you in the name of all the kings. But it is because the whole circle of kings sent you that I honor you — with water for your feet, a seat, and every courtesy. When I honor you, I honor them all. Come, sit beside me on this throne."

So they clasped hands, asked after each other's welfare, and sat at ease together. Then Kalayavana put the question that lay beneath the courtesy. "The kings live without fear," he said, "resting on the strength of that king's arm, as the gods rest under Indra. What could have become impossible for such a man, that he sends you to me? Tell me truly what the king of Magadha commands of me. No matter how hard it is, I will do it."

Then Shalya delivered the message exactly as it had been given to him.

"Krishna has been a thorn in the world since his birth," the message ran. "When I learned of his deeds, I resolved to destroy him. I marched on Mount Gomanta with a host of kings, and at the urging of the king of Chedi I set fire to the mountain itself, to burn Rama and Krishna where they hid. But Rama leaped down from the burning summit into the middle of that army, golden sword in hand. He moved through the kings like a serpent; chariot, horse and foot went down before him, and with his great ploughshare he caught up their war-elephants and turned them against their own lines, until the host broke itself. Then Krishna followed — discus bright as the sun, black iron club in hand — and fell upon them as a lion falls on deer, with a leap that shook the mountain. And the mountain itself seemed to whirl; a shower came down on the flames, the fire died, and the hill sank back into the earth as if dancing."

Shalya paused. The tale of a defeat had one last turn. "Enter the city of Mathura with your army," Jarasandha had said, "and set up your glory there."

When the envoy fell silent, the Yavana court was still. The king had been handed a war, and a city that was his for the taking — if he dared take it.
stories.reflection: The embassy moves by courtesy: Kalayavana honors the envoy and, through him, the whole circle of kings, and only then does the appeal arrive. Jarasandha's message is a confession of defeat at Gomanta turned into an invitation for another king to finish what he could not.
stories.next_story_tease: Kalayavana would answer the appeal by marching on Mathura that very day.

stories.title: Kalayavana Marches on Mathura
stories.story:
Kalayavana, king of the Yavanas, held in his hands the strangest honor of his life: the kings of the earth had asked him to defeat Krishna, the hero of Mathura, whom no king had yet beaten in war. He was not a man given to doubt, and the request only confirmed what he already believed of himself.

"Happily honored am I," he said, "and my life is crowned with success. Numberless kings have begged me to vanquish Krishna, who is invincible in the three worlds, even to gods and demons — and they have already declared my victory. Whatever comes of it, I will carry out the command of the emperor Jarasandha. Even my defeat in such a cause will count as success. The stars are auspicious today, and today I march on Mathura, to defeat Krishna in the field."

He loaded Shalya with precious gems and fine clothes, scattered gifts among the priests, and made offerings to the sacred fire. Then, when the rites of blessing were done, he set out with his army; and Shalya, his errand achieved, embraced the king of the Yavanas and rode home with the answer for the kings.

Few in the host that marched behind Kalayavana knew the story of their king's birth, though all India was about to learn it. The sage Gargya, mocked as powerless by his own brother-in-law before an assembly of the Yadavas, had not forgiven the laughter. He went to the shore of the western sea and did penance, living on iron sand, until Shiva was pleased and granted his prayer: a son who would be a terror to the tribe of Yadu. The childless king of the Yavanas befriended the sage, and by the king's wife Gargya begot a son — a boy black as a bee, with a chest hard as the point of a thunderbolt — and they named him Kalayavana. The old king set the boy on his throne and went into the forest to live as a hermit.

Once he was king, Kalayavana asked the wandering sage Narada who the mightiest heroes on earth were. "The Yadavas," Narada answered — and the king of the Yavanas never forgot the name. They were the only enemies he thought worth marching against.

So he gathered a countless host of foreign warriors — elephants, horsemen, chariots and foot — and drove it against Mathura, wearying the beast that carried him each day but never seeming to tire himself. The whole army moved at the pace of his restlessness. The name of Kalayavana ran ahead of it like fire: he was coming to Mathura, he would not turn back until Krishna was beaten in the field, and he had sworn that even his own defeat would not count as failure.
stories.reflection: Kalayavana's boast contains its own admission — even his discomfiture, he says, will count as success. A king who sets out expecting that nothing he does can be failure has already stopped weighing his chances.
stories.tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana tells this march differently: there, Kalayavana learns from Narada that the Yadavas are the mightiest heroes on earth and advances on his own, with no embassy from Jarasandha. This account follows the Harivamsha.
stories.next_story_tease: As the Yavana host drew near Mathura, Krishna prepared a warning sealed in a jar.

stories.title: The Serpent-Jar Stratagem Against Kalayavana
stories.story:
Before they understood what it was, the people of Mathura saw the host: a swarm of kings and foreign warriors covering the plain like locusts, with a river that had never flowed before running behind it — a river born of the filth of its horses and camels, which men would afterward call Aswasakrit.

Everyone knew its leader's story by now. The sage Gargya, dishonored before his king by his own brother-in-law, had abandoned his home in anger and gone to do penance, living on pounded iron for twelve years until Shiva granted him a boon: an all-powerful son who could defeat in battle the descendants of the Vrishnis and the Andhakas. The childless king of the Yavanas heard of the boon, invited Gargya into his kingdom, and consoled him. And by Gopali, a heavenly maiden in the guise of a milkmaid, Gargya begot the child Kalayavana. The boy was raised in the king's own palace like a son, and when the old king died, Kalayavana ruled in his place.

As his power grew, the kings of the foreign tribes near the mountains — the Shakas, the Tukharas, and hundreds of others — placed themselves under his shelter. Clad in every kind of dress and armed with every kind of weapon, they rode with him. The earth shook under his horses, elephants, asses and camels, and the dust of his army hid the sun.

Krishna had taken no notice of Kalayavana while he grew up among the Yavanas, for Narada had told him long ago about the boon. But when he heard that this army was coming, he called his kinsmen together. "A great calamity has found us," he said. "This enemy is unkillable by us, because of the boon Shiva gave his father. I tried every peaceful means to win him over — conciliation and the rest — but he wants war, and pride has made him deaf. Narada told me his intent: he means to live in this very city. And I tell you the same — we cannot stay. Jarasandha will never forgive us. The other kings, angry over the fall of Kamsa, have taken shelter under him and work against us, and many of our kinsmen have already been slain. We will never prosper here."

Even as he planned the retreat, Krishna tried one last thing. He sealed a dreadful black serpent — black as soot, coiled in the dark of a clay jar — and sent it to the king of the Yavanas by his own envoy. "Krishna is like a deadly serpent," the envoy said, and set the jar before Kalayavana.

The king of the Yavanas looked at the sealed jar and understood at once what the Yadavas meant to say. Without a word, he had the jar filled with fierce ants. The sharp-beaked ants devoured the serpent down to ash; the jar was sealed anew, and sent back the way it had come.

So the warning returned to Mathura empty — a serpent turned to ash, and a king who could not be frightened. Whatever answer Krishna sent next would have to be stronger than fear.
stories.reflection: The exchange of sealed jars is a conversation without words, each side answering a threat with a sharper one. Krishna's warning is devoured before it is even delivered — a reminder that a terror meant for the proud may only harden them.
stories.next_story_tease: But the exchange of warnings was not over; Jarasandha's mace was already hurtling toward Mathura.

stories.title: Jarasandha Hurls His Mace toward Mathura
stories.story:
From the heights of Girivraja, the mountain-girt capital of Magadha, its king lifted a mace and began to whirl it — once, and again, and ninety-nine turns in all — until the iron seemed less a weapon than the shape of his anger. Then, with everything he had behind it, he hurled it toward Mathura.

The king was Jarasandha, and his quarrel with Krishna was old. Years before, Krishna had slain Kamsa, the cruel king of Mathura, who had married Jarasandha's daughters — and the king of Magadha had never forgiven it. Men who knew them both said it was not a grudge to be taken lightly.

Jarasandha was the son of Vrihadratha, and the story of his rise was told wherever kings gathered. When the great ascetic Chandakausika came into the land of the Magadhas, King Vrihadratha went out to receive him with his ministers, his priest, his wives, and his young son, and in his joy he offered the sage his whole kingdom, and the boy along with it. The sage was pleased. Instead of taking the gift, he gave a prophecy: the boy would grow in prosperity and might beyond every other king; weapons hurled at him, even by the gods themselves, would cause him no pain; he would outshine all who wore crowns, as the sun dims every lesser light; and the kings of the earth would live under his command.

Vrihadratha set the boy on the throne, and, having lost all taste for the world, retired into the woods with his two wives. The prophecy kept its word. Jarasandha ruled his own people like a father, and by his valour he brought king after king under his sway.

And it was this man's mace that now flew toward Mathura, the city where Krishna lived. The weapon fell just outside the city — ninety-nine yojanas from the heights where it had been thrown, a yojana being a measure of many miles — and the place where it struck, lying close to Mathura, came to be called Gadavasan. The citizens saw the whole matter clearly and went to Krishna with the news of its fall.

The name of Jarasandha explained the weight of it. He had two champions, Hansa and Dimvaka, whom no weapon could slay and whose counsel in statecraft and right was counted the finest among men; the two of them together with Jarasandha were held a match, men said, for the three worlds and all that lived in them. It was for that reason that the warrior clans of Krishna's own people — the Vrishnis, the Andhakas, the Kukkurras — had never judged it wise to fight him. And now his strength lay in the earth near Mathura: a throw that had crossed the whole distance between the two cities was also a warning that the army behind the throw could cross it.

Krishna heard the citizens out. The mace lay at Gadavasan, close to the city's edge, and the warning was complete in itself: a weapon that could cover such a distance could be followed by the army that owned it. The citizens had brought their news; what it meant now rested with Krishna.
stories.reflection: A mace hurled across the country was a king's way of drawing a line: the distance from Girivraja to Mathura, measured by his own strength, as a notice that the enmity over Kamsa's death would not quietly fade. The weapon itself was a warning, and it was also an announcement of the long conflict to come.
stories.next_story_tease: But the king of Magadha was only beginning; the time would come when Krishna proposed meeting that strength directly.

stories.title: Krishna Proposes Slaying Jarasandha as Prelude to the Rajasuya
stories.story:
Yudhishthira, the eldest of the five Pandava princes, had set his heart on the Rajasuya — the great sacrifice by which a king declared himself sovereign over the other kings of the earth. But one obstacle stood between him and that sacrifice, and the obstacle could not be conquered in battle: Jarasandha, king of Magadha, whose strength no army had yet broken.

In Yudhishthira's hall, Krishna — his cousin and most trusted adviser — spoke of him plainly. Jarasandha had lost Hansa and Dimvaka, the two great champions who had stood beside him, and Kamsa, the Mathura king who had married into his house, was dead with all his followers. The time had come, Krishna said, to destroy Jarasandha himself. Yet he was not a king who could be overcome in open war — even all the gods and the demons together could not conquer him in battle. There was one way he could be beaten: a personal struggle, man against man, with bare arms.

"In me is policy," said Krishna, "in Bhima is strength, and in Arjuna is triumph. So let us achieve the destruction of the king of Magadha as the prelude to the Rajasuya. If we three approach him secretly, he will surely meet one of us in combat; and from fear of disgrace, from greed, and from pride in his own strength, he will call Bhima to the fight. Then Bhima, mighty-armed, will end him the way death ends a man however swollen with pride. If you know my heart," he said to Yudhishthira, "if you have any faith in me, hand over Bhima and Arjuna to me as a pledge, and lose no time."

Yudhishthira looked at his two brothers, who stood with cheerful faces, and answered. "Say not so. You are the lord of the Pandavas; we depend on you, and what you advise is wise counsel." The man who stood under Krishna's command, he said, could already count Jarasandha as slain, the captive kings as set free, and the Rajasuya as accomplished. Then he spoke of leadership itself: troops under a good leader do excellent service, while a force without one is inert; wise men lead water into low fields where it will do its work, and fishermen drain a tank by opening a hole at the right point. So, he said, let Krishna go before them — he whose strength is wisdom — let Arjuna follow Krishna, and Bhima follow Arjuna; and policy, good fortune, and might would carry the enterprise through.

So the three set out for Magadha, dressed as brahmanas — the holy men who live by study and prayer — so that they could approach the king without being known. Friends and kinsmen sent them off with blessings. As for the people who saw them pass, they looked at Krishna and Arjuna, never once defeated in battle, with Bhima at their head, and said that Jarasandha was as good as slain.

Their road ran long. They passed from the country of the Kurus through Kuru-jangala and by a lake of lotuses, crossed the hills of Kalakuta and the rivers Gandaki, Sadanira, and Sarkaravarta, forded the delightful Sarayu, and saw the country of Eastern Kosala. From there they went on to Mithila, crossed the Mala and the Charamanwati, then the Ganges and the Sone, and came at last to Magadha, in the heart of the land of Kushamva. Climbing the hills of Goratha, they looked down on the city of Magadha, always filled with cattle, wealth, and water, and handsome with its numberless dwellings — the stronghold of the man they had come to meet. Three brahmanas stood at the edge of the enemy's country with nothing but their bare arms, and the great enterprise lay spread below them.
stories.reflection: Krishna's plan rested on reading Jarasandha's character: a king certain that no weapon can harm him will still step down to meet bare arms, summoned by his own pride. Policy, strength, and triumph each had a man assigned to it, as if the victory were already divided into its parts before the journey even began.
stories.tradition_note: The Bhagavata Purana (10.71) presents this same plan as Uddhava's counsel to Krishna rather than Krishna's own proposal; the Mahabharata version, followed here, attributes it to Krishna himself.
stories.next_story_tease: In Girivraja, the three disguised Brahmanas would announce themselves in a way no one expected.

stories.title: Krishna and the Pandavas Break the Chaityaka Peak
stories.story:
Krishna and the two Pandava princes, his cousins Bhima and Arjuna, had come to Girivraja to humble the pride of Jarasandha, the king of Magadha who kept conquered rulers captive in his city. They began by breaking a mountain.

Krishna showed Arjuna the capital as they drew near: filled with flocks and herds, its water never failing, adorned with fine mansions in excellent order, free from every kind of calamity. Five great hills protected it — Vaihara, Varaha, Vrishava, Rishigiri, and the beautiful Chaitya — their high peaks grown over with tall trees of cool shade, their slopes hidden in flowering lodhra woods, each hill linked to the next so that the city lay ringed in stone. The Chaitya peak had its own long memory: there the sage Gautama had once raised his son Kakshivat, and in olden times the mighty kings of Anga and Vanga had come to the sage's hermitage and lingered in joy. A king who owned such a city, Krishna said, believed nothing could touch him. "But today," he said, "we shall humble his pride by slaying him."

They entered the capital and walked to its gate — and instead of passing through, they set their hands to the high Chaityaka peak, the hill worshipped by the royal line of Vrihadratha and by every citizen of the Magadhas. Long ago the old king Vrihadratha had slain a man-eating demon named Rishava, and from the demon's hide he had made three drums and placed them there, drums of such a kind that once beaten their sound lasted a full month. It was at that very place, where the garlanded drums used to sound, that the three men broke the great peak down, pulling at the immovable rock with their bare arms — the old, honoured hill that the whole city had worshipped with perfumes and flower wreaths. By that deed, men said afterward, they seemed to set their feet upon the head of their enemy; and with joyful hearts they entered the city.

But the city read the omen before it saw the men. The learned brahmanas of Girivraja saw many evil signs and carried the news to Jarasandha. His priest made the king mount an elephant and walked about him whirling lighted brands, and Jarasandha, to turn the portents aside, began a sacrifice with vows and fasts. The holy hill of his fathers had fallen at his gate, and all his rites could not undo what the omens promised.

Meanwhile the three — unarmed, with only their bare arms for weapons — walked the capital in the robes of brahmanas, the wandering holy men of the land. They passed shops rich with foods and flower garlands and every sort of ware a man could wish for, and they snatched the garlands outright from the flower-sellers, as if the city were already theirs to take from. Wearing bright robes, garlands, and earrings, their arms smeared with sandal paste and thick as the trunks of sala trees, they moved through the wondering crowds like Himalayan lions walking among cattle. People stared at guests so vast of chest and neck, and word of them ran ahead to the king.

They passed through three crowded gates and came proudly and cheerfully to Jarasandha's door. The king rose in haste to receive them, with water for their feet, honey, and the offerings of the arghya, the rite by which guests are honoured, and gifts of cattle, with every courtesy his court could offer. "You are welcome," said the great king.

But of the three guests only one answered him. Bhima and Arjuna stood silent at Krishna's side, and the welcome hung in the air unanswered.
stories.reflection: The broken peak was the first move of the whole enterprise, and it was deliberate: a king's own sacred hill, torn down at his gate, announced that these strangers had not come to beg but to humble him. The omens the priests read afterwards only told the city, in another language, what its own eyes had already seen.
stories.next_story_tease: The silence of the two disguised brothers would need an explanation.

stories.title: Krishna Speaks for the Silent Disguised Brothers
stories.story:
The three strangers in the robes of brahmanas, the priestly holy men of the land, had come to the court of Girivraja with a purpose no one there knew: Krishna and the Pandava princes, his cousins Bhima and Arjuna, had entered the king's city in disguise to free the rulers Jarasandha of Magadha held captive there, or to bring him down in combat. And Jarasandha, who had received countless guests in his long reign, did everything a host should do. He rose in haste when the three were brought before him; he gave them water for their feet, honey and the offerings of welcome, gifts of cattle, and every honour his court could offer. "You are welcome," said the great king.

And his two younger guests said nothing at all.

The king had come to this meeting in a season of ill omens. The learned brahmanas of Girivraja had seen evil signs and reported them to him; to ward the evils off, Jarasandha had begun a sacrifice with vows and fasts, while his priest made him mount an elephant and walked about him whirling lighted brands. The holy hill of his fathers had been torn down at his gate — the omen on every tongue — and now three strangers stood in his hall where the trouble had arrived, and one of them was about to speak for all three.

The moment stretched. These were no ordinary holy men. They had walked the public road of the capital as though the city were already theirs — past shops heavy with every sort of ware, snatching garlands from the flower-vendors as they went. The people of Magadha had drawn back from the size of them: heroes built like elephants, with necks broad as tree trunks and wide chests, their arms smelling of sandal paste. Through three gates crowded with men they had come, proud and cheerful, to the king. Now they stood before him, and his welcome had fallen into a silence he had not expected.

Krishna spoke for the three. "Great king," he said, "these two are bound by a vow. Therefore they will not speak. They will remain silent until midnight, and after that hour they will speak with you."

The explanation was simple and complete. The king had received guests who could not answer him — not a single word until the night hour when their vow released them. Whatever Jarasandha wished to ask — who these men were, where they had come from, what errand had brought them to the capital of Magadha — would have to wait on the guests themselves. Until then they were simply guests under his roof, owing him nothing but their presence while the night ran down.

The court of Girivraja settled into waiting. The welcome had been given, the vow had spoken for the two silent men, and the first true words between Jarasandha and the strangers would come only when midnight released them.
stories.reflection: A vow of silence was a clever shield: it let Krishna's party enter the enemy's court, accept its honours, and give away nothing — not a word, not a name — until the hour they themselves chose. Jarasandha's hospitality was turned into a waiting game, and the waiting belonged to the host.
stories.next_story_tease: When midnight came, Jarasandha would question the strangers about their disguise.

stories.title: The Rules of an Enemy's Gate
stories.story:
The five hills of Girivraja ringed the capital of Magadha like the fingers of a cupped hand, and inside that ring ruled Jarasandha, the king who kept conquered rulers captive in his city. To that city three men had come who meant to make him answer for it — Krishna and the Pandava princes, his cousins Bhima and Arjuna. They had come dressed as holy men, but they had not come to beg.

Best loved of the hills was Chaitya, worshipped by the citizens and by the royal line of Vrihadratha; and it was that hill, at the point where the great drums of the old kings used to sound, that the three had torn down with their bare arms before ever entering the gate. Then, in the robes of wandering brahmanas, they had walked through the crowded streets past shops heavy with food and flowers, and the people of Magadha, seeing such giants in holy men's dress, had wondered what sort of guests these were.

Inside the city the omens had already been speaking. Learned brahmanas had reported evil signs to Jarasandha; his priest had set him on an elephant and walked about him with lighted brands; and the king had begun a sacrifice to turn the portents aside. Yet when the three strangers presented themselves at his house, he rose in haste and gave them full honour — water for their feet, honey, the offerings of welcome, gifts of cattle — and bade them welcome. Bhima and Arjuna stood silent while Krishna spoke for them. But Jarasandha was not a man to let a strange entry pass unremarked, and when the ceremony of welcome was over he looked at his guests and asked what they meant by coming into his city by no proper gate.

Krishna answered without heat, as though stating a rule everyone knew. "The rule stands written," he said, "that an enemy's house is entered through a wrong gate, and a friend's house through the right one. Know also that this is the vow we keep: having entered a foe's dwelling for the sake of our purpose, we do not accept the worship offered to us."

The water for the feet stood untouched. The gifts lay where they had been laid. In the most courteous words imaginable, the king of Magadha had just been told that these men were not his guests but his enemies — that they had entered his house the way one enters an enemy's house, and that they refused his friendship outright. Whatever courtesy had passed between them was finished.

Jarasandha heard it out in silence. And in that silence the three of them stood in the hall of the king they had come to fight, with the challenge itself still waiting to be spoken.
stories.reflection: Krishna answers a charge of bad manners with a precise code of his own: a friend's house and a foe's house are not entered the same way, and a guest who refuses the offered worship is declaring, openly and without rudeness, that he has come as an enemy. The courtliness of the reply only sharpens the threat beneath it.
stories.next_story_tease: But Jarasandha, certain of his own innocence, would demand to know what injury he had ever done them.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna standing calm in Jarasandha's hall, the untouched water for the feet and the gifts of welcome lying between him and the seated king, with Bhima and Arjuna silent behind him in mendicants' robes.

stories.title: The Hand Krishna Held Back
stories.story:
The three guests had refused the king's welcome, and the refusal hung in the hall like a line drawn between Jarasandha of Magadha and the strangers before him. They had come to his city disguised as brahmanas, the holy men whom every king is bound to honour; he had received them with every honour; and they had set his courtesy aside. Whatever they were, they were plainly not what they seemed — and Jarasandha, who had conquered and imprisoned so many rulers, did not raise his hand against them. He asked his question first. "I have searched my memory," he said, "and I cannot recall that I ever did you an injury. When I have done you no wrong, why do you treat me, who am innocent, as your enemy? Answer me truly — that is the way of honest men."

Krishna's answer changed the air of the hall. "We did not come of our own will," he said. "A king at the head of a royal line sent us against you. You have brought many of the rulers of the world here as captives to your city. After such a wrong, how can you call yourself innocent? You treat other kings with cruelty and keep them for a sacrifice to the god Rudra, whom some name Sankara. The slaughter of human beings as an offering to the gods is never seen anywhere. Why then do you mean to perform a sacrifice to that god by killing men? You would make rulers of your own warrior class into animals for the altar."

Then he told them plainly who stood before him. "Know that we are no brahmanas. I am Krishna, and these two are Bhima and Arjuna, the sons of Pandu. King of Magadha, we challenge you. Stand and fight. Either set free every king you hold, or make your way to the realm of Yama, the lord of the dead." He spoke of what waits for a warrior who dies in open fight: heaven, gained as surely as victory — the road by which Indra, king of the gods, rose to his place by vanquishing the demons. And he spoke of kings who had thought themselves beyond reach — Damvodhava, Kartavirya, Uttara, and Vrihadratha — all swept away with their armies for looking down on those above them. "Do not scorn other men," Krishna said. "Valour lives in every man, and there are many whose strength equals or passes yours. Put aside your pride in the presence of your equals."

Jarasandha's answer was unshaken. He had never made a captive of a king he had not first conquered, he said; every ruler kept in his city had been defeated in open war. It was the duty of his order — the Kshatriyas, the warrior kings — to bring others under their sway by the showing of strength and then to hold them. "Having gathered these monarchs to offer them as sacrifice to the god, how shall I, out of fear, set them free today?" He would not bargain, and he would not bend: troops against troops, he said, or alone against one of them, or against two, or against all three at once.

They might have fallen on him together then, and one alone would have been enough — for Krishna himself was more than a match for the king of Magadha, and the strength of his whole line could have ended the matter then and there. But Krishna held back. He was devoted to truth, and he remembered the decree of Brahma, the creator: Jarasandha was destined to fall in battle by the hand of Bhima, and not by the hand of any Yadava. He would not take what destiny had given to another.

So Bhima, the son of Pandu, stepped forward to meet the king of Magadha, and Krishna drew back his own hand and stood aside. The long duel began — a fight in which Krishna would take no part, because this death had another name written on it, and he would not write over it with his own.
stories.reflection: The hinge of the episode is Krishna's restraint — the king of Magadha stands within his reach, yet he will not take what destiny has assigned to another hand. His power shows itself as much in what he refuses to do as in what he does.
stories.next_story_tease: But even as the duel began, a new enemy was already marching against Mathura — the Yavana king Kalayavana.
stories.hero_scene: Bhima stepping forward to face Jarasandha in the middle of the great hall, while Krishna stands back with arms folded, deliberately refusing a fight that destiny has assigned to another.

stories.title: The Captured Host of Kalayavana
stories.story:
The war was over almost before it had begun. Kalayavana, king of the Yavanas, had marched against Mathura to destroy the Yadavas, Krishna's own people, and his army never marched home again. What became of that host was a strange sight: horses, elephants and chariots, the whole captured army, filing peacefully into the Yadavas' city of Dwaraka at Krishna's command, its banners furled, its weapons turned to new masters. Krishna placed it all in the hands of Ugrasena, the king of the Yadavas. From that day the Yadus had no more fear of invasion; the war elephants that had carried it now stood stalled where they could harm no one.

How had such a thing come about? The army's master had followed Krishna into the mountains and had not come out again. The one who ended him was no soldier but a sleeper, a king who had lain in a cave through the turning of whole eras, waiting out the world.

His name was Muchukunda. When he woke in the dark of the cave, the first thing his eyes found was Krishna standing before him, and he knew him at once for the Lord of all things. He bowed and praised him, and Krishna granted him his wish. "Go to the realms of heaven," Krishna said, "and enjoy every pleasure they hold. When that time is over, you will be born again in a noble family, remembering all your past lives; and at the last you will win release from the wheel of birth and death." Muchukunda prostrated himself and went out of the cave. The men he met in the daylight seemed small to him, shrunken in body and in spirit, and he understood that the world he had known was finished and the dark age of the world had come. He set out for Gandhamadana, the mountain shrine of Nara-Narayana, to live in penance; and in time everything Krishna had promised came to pass, exactly as he had said.

Muchukunda was not the only one that cave changed. Kalayavana, the Yavana king who had marched on Mathura, entered those hills after Krishna and never left them; and free of the man who had threatened them, the Yadavas gathered up what his host had left behind. Krishna went back to Mathura, took the enemy's army as his own, and led it to Dwaraka, where Ugrasena received it.

With the fighting done, Balarama, Krishna's elder brother, grew restless to see his own people again. He went to Vraja, the cowherd country where the brothers had grown up, to the cow-pens of Nanda, the old herdsman who had raised them. He moved among the herdsmen and their women with affection and respect. The elders embraced him; he embraced the younger ones; with those of his own age he talked and laughed. The cowherds showered him with kind words. But the gopis spoke to him with a show of anger, and beneath the teasing there was something real.

"And how is the fickle one?" they asked. "Is Krishna well, he who forgets his friends as easily as he makes them? Does he laugh with the ladies of the city at our country ways? Does he ever think of us, who used to sing his songs with him? Will he not come here once again, even to see his mother?"

Then the questions turned inward, and the pretence fell away. "Father, mother, brother, husband, kin, what did we not give up for his sake?" they said. "But what is the use of saying it? His tale without us, and our tale without him, are two different tales."

Balarama carried their words back with him when he left the cow-pens, with news of a captured host, a city made safe, a war finished. And in Vraja, the women who had loved Krishna first went on waiting for the song he no longer sang among them.
stories.reflection: The episode pairs a great victory with a small, human wound: the safety Krishna wins for the Yadavas costs Vraja his presence. The gopis' jealousy is teasing, but their last words carry real pain — a reminder that the price of a kingdom is sometimes paid in the homes it leaves behind.
stories.next_story_tease: The Yadavas' relief would not last, for Jarasandha, hearing of his daughters' widowhood, was already gathering his armies.

stories.title: Twenty-Three Armies Against Mathura
stories.story:
Asti and Prapti, the daughters of Jarasandha, king of Magadha, came to their father's court the way grief comes: slowly, and with everything already known. They had been given in marriage to Kamsa of Mathura; now they stood before him as widows and told him of it. Jarasandha heard the unwelcome news, and grief and anger rose in him together.

He had owed Kamsa a debt. The dead man had been his son-in-law and his ally, a king who had chained up his own father and ruled Mathura with Jarasandha's backing, holding the Yadava clans in check while Jarasandha filled his prisons with the kings of the world. Now the Yadavas had killed him. Krishna and Balarama had struck Kamsa down, and Ugrasena, the father Kamsa had imprisoned, had become king in his place, with the Bhojas, the Vrishnis and the Andhakas, the clans of the Yadavas, gathered around him. The debt was unpaid, and Jarasandha resolved to make the earth free of Yadavas, to wipe the whole race away in a single campaign. Burning like fire, making every possible arrangement, in no time at all the king of Magadha was marching on Mathura.

And the kings he had conquered marched with him. Some came for fear of Jarasandha, some out of jealousy of Krishna, some because he had beaten them and they had nowhere else to stand. His friends, his relatives and his allies came too, each at the head of his own army. Dantavakra of Karusha came, and the powerful king of Chedi; the king of Kalinga; Bhishmaka with his son Rukmi; the kings of Anga and Vanga, of Koshala and Kashi and Dasharna; Bhagadatta, the lord of the Yavanas; Suvala of Gandhara; Duryodhana and the other sons of Dhritarashtra. King after king, chariot-warriors every one, they followed him, each camping in his own place.

They entered the province of Shurasena, a land of barley fields and woodlands, and the order went out: lay siege on every side to this city. Twenty-three akshauhinis ringed Mathura, and an akshauhini was an army of its own, thousands upon thousands of chariots, elephants and horses. So great was the host that the horizon turned to dust and metal, and the ground beneath the city's walls trembled under the weight of it.

From the walls, Krishna watched the host settle around Mathura like a sea risen over its banks. He had come into the world in a human body on purpose, to work in it as a man works, and a man who means to solve a problem does not wave it away. He did not wish the army gone, or turn the siege aside with a gesture. He looked at it long and carefully, the way a man looks at a thing he means to solve, weighing the twenty-three armies, and the kings behind them, and the city, and the people inside it.

Around the walls, the fires of the besieging host burned through the night, ringing Mathura like a second horizon. The siege had begun, and the first night of it belonged to the besiegers. Inside the city, Krishna was still thinking, for a king who looks on such an army must first decide what he is willing to do.
stories.reflection: Krishna meets the greatest army ever raised against him not with a miracle but with deliberation. The old phrase kāraṇa-mānuṣaḥ — one whose humanity is his instrument — is the point: he refuses to solve the siege by sheer divinity, choosing instead to think, plan, and act as a man among men.
stories.tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana compresses this whole conflict into one line — Jarasandha attacked eighteen times and was routed each time — while the Harivamsha narrates the march and the siege separately and gives the invading force six divisions. This story follows the Bhagavata Purana's number of twenty-three akshauhinis.
stories.next_story_tease: And as Krishna thought, a divine chariot with celestial weapons was descending from the sky toward Mathura.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna on the walls of Mathura gazing out at Jarasandha's encircling army of twenty-three akshauhinis, spread across the plain like a risen sea, its campfires already burning against the dusk.

stories.title: A Divine Chariot and Weapons Descend for Krishna
stories.story:
Mathura was ringed by the greatest army the age had seen. Jarasandha of Magadha had come with twenty-three divisions to avenge Kamsa, the tyrant king of Mathura whom the brothers Krishna and Balarama had struck down, and he had sworn that no Yadava would be left alive beneath the sun. Day and night the fires of the besiegers ringed the walls.

Krishna stood looking out at the host, and while he looked, he thought. These warring kings lay heavy on the earth; this gathering itself was another weight laid upon her. "I will destroy this force," he said within himself, "this weight heaped on the earth. It was to lift such burdens that I came down, and while I do this work, another part of me is ever at work, keeping what is right safe in the world." And as he finished the thought, the sky answered him.

Out of the empty air above Mathura two chariots descended, bright as the sun itself. Each had its driver at the reins, and each carried the ancient weapons of a warrior, bows, quivers, maces, armor, things old beyond memory yet gleaming as though made that morning. No one had sent them and no one had summoned them. They came of their own accord, sinking down out of the light like the answer to a question not yet spoken, and came to rest before the two brothers.

Krishna turned to Balarama. "Look, brother," he said. "Calamity has come upon the Yadavas, and they look to you. It was for this that we two were born, to bring ease to the good."

The brothers armed themselves, and the ancient weapons fitted them as if they had been shaped for them all along. Then the two chariots rolled out through the gates of Mathura, past the citizens who had come running into the streets, and out onto the open ground between the walls and the enemy host.

Krishna's chariot was driven by Daruka, his charioteer. As the wheels cleared the gate, Krishna raised to his lips the great conch at his side and blew it once. The sound rolled across the plain like thunder walking the earth, deep and unhurried, filling the whole space between the city and the camps.

In the tents of the Magadha king, in the ranks of the allied kings, in the hearts of the soldiers who had come to wipe the Yadavas from the face of the earth, terror entered and took hold. Men looked at one another and did not know why their hands trembled.

Two chariots stood before the greatest army the age had seen, and for a moment the army did not move. The sun stood high over Mathura. The conch's echo went on fading over the fields.

Then the battle began.
stories.reflection: The chariots come down of their own accord, at the exact moment Krishna resolves to act — as if heaven had been waiting for his decision. His weighing of the earth's burden is described in wholly human terms, and the divine answer arrives only when the human resolve is complete.
stories.next_story_tease: Jarasandha's host rolled forward to meet the two chariots, and the greatest battle of the age began.
stories.hero_scene: Two sun-bright chariots descending out of the sky over Mathura, their drivers holding ancient divine weapons, while Krishna and Balarama below look up at the falling light; beyond the walls, the vast enemy camp darkens the plain to the horizon.

stories.title: The Yadavas Rout Jarasandha's Army and Spare Him
stories.story:
The gates of Mathura swung open, and the two brothers rode out to meet an ocean. Krishna and Balarama, the heroes of the Yadava house, were going out against the army that had ringed their city, the twenty-three divisions of Jarasandha, king of Magadha. Jarasandha, seeing them come, cupped his hands to his mouth and shouted abuse across the field, insults for Krishna, and for Balarama a challenge: if you have any courage, come and fight, summon your fortitude and show it.

Behind the brothers, on the towers and terraces of Mathura, the women of the city had gathered to watch, and more than one fainted where she stood, overcome with grief and fear at the sight of that enormous host.

Krishna's chariot drove into the thick of it, and there he fought as he alone could. Like a wheel of fire that burns in an unbroken circle, his arrows streamed out, nock, draw, loose, without pause and without gap. Elephants crashed down among their own ranks. Horses went down in the press. Chariots splintered like dry branches under a storm. Men said afterward that Jarasandha's army was an ocean without a shore, that no one could have crossed it; but the one who rode into it was not to be measured by any ordinary measure. High above, where the armies could not see them, the gods and the singers of heaven gathered from all quarters to watch, and their presence filled the sky over the field with a strange, still brightness.

In the middle of it all, Balarama sought out Jarasandha himself. The Magadha king had lost his chariot, his horses and his charioteer in the press, and stood alone on the field. Balarama seized him the way a lion seizes a lion, by the shoulders, so that the king of Magadha hung helpless in his grip. Around him his army lay in ruins; his allies were dead or had fled. The Vrishni soldiers closed in, ropes were brought, and Jarasandha, the enemy of the Yadava house, was bound where he stood.

Then Krishna stayed the binding. "The king of Magadha is not to be killed," he said. "He will gather forces again."

Balarama's hands went still. Krishna spoke to the captive in words plain and clear, and then he let him go. Jarasandha stood a long moment in his shame. Then he turned and walked off the field, and no one stopped him.

All around him his host was gone. Krishna, his own strength unbroken, had crossed that ocean as if it had been a pond. The news ran ahead of him, and the people of Mathura poured out through the gates to meet him, carried on a wave of joy. Conches and kettledrums sounded from the walls; the streets were sprinkled with water and hung with banners; women stood on the rooftops and showered the returning chariots with garlands, curds and unbroken rice. The sun set on a city that had braced itself to die at dawn and could not stop celebrating at dusk. And the weapons that had come down from the sky for the battle were seen no more, as if they had never been.

Seventeen times after that day Jarasandha came again to Mathura, each time with an army of akshauhinis, great formations of thousands of chariots, elephants and horses, and seventeen times Krishna broke his host and sent him home. He returned to Magadha with his life, and that was all he carried back.

The city sang on into the night. The king who had sworn to leave no Yadava alive had walked away alive himself, spared by the very men he had come to destroy, for a purpose that no one on that field could yet see.
stories.reflection: Krishna lets Jarasandha walk away at the height of victory, knowing the man will return seventeen times. His mercy is not softness but strategy: Jarasandha's death belongs to a design larger than this one day's battle, and the release is the first move of it.
stories.tradition_note: The Harivamsha splits this episode differently: there the fighting runs twenty-seven days, and it is a voice from the sky — not Krishna — that stays Balarama's hand and declares that Jarasandha must not yet die. The Bhagavata Purana, followed here, has Krishna himself release the captive.
stories.content_note: Battle scene: the rout of an army is described with restraint, but includes slaughter imagery.
stories.next_story_tease: But even as Mathura celebrated, a new enemy — one protected by a boon no weapon could break — was already marching out of the north.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna on his chariot in the thick of battle, bow drawn and arrows streaming in an unbroken arc like a wheel of fire, while behind him Balarama holds the captured Jarasandha by the shoulders and Krishna's raised hand stays the binding.

stories.title: Kalayavana Is Burned by Muchukunda's Glance
stories.story:
There is a cave in the mountains above Mathura, and in it a king had been sleeping longer than the oldest tree. Toward that cave Krishna ran one afternoon, with an army at his heels that no one in the world could defeat. And in that cave the army's master met his end, though not by any weapon.

The army belonged to Kalayavana, king of the Yavanas, a foreign people from beyond the lands Krishna knew. His story began long before his birth, in the house of a teacher. Gargya, who taught the Andhaka and Vrishni families, kept a vow of lifelong purity, and his wife's brother mocked him cruelly for it before the king until he could bear the shame no longer. He left the city and turned to penance. For twelve years he lived on iron filings and prayed to Mahadeva, the great god who carries the trident. At last the god answered: Gargya would have a son, all-powerful, who would trouble the Vrishnis and Andhakas in battle.

The king of the Yavanas had no son. When he heard of the boon, he brought Gargya to his own land and set women to attend him, and one of them, a heavenly dancer named Gopali in the form of a milkmaid, conceived a child through him. That child was Kalayavana. Raised as the king's own son, he took the throne when the old king died.

Kalayavana grew, and his name with him. Kings of the Shakas and Tukharas and many other foreign peoples came from the lands near the great mountains to shelter under him. When he marched on Mathura at last, his host covered the earth like locusts, and its dust hid the sun.

Krishna had heard the story from the sage Narada, and because of the boon he had never met the Yavana in battle. Now he called his kinsmen together. "Great trouble has come upon the Vrishnis and Andhakas," he told them. "This enemy cannot be slain by us, because of the boon the trident-holder gave him. I tried conciliation and every other means short of war; he will have battle, for pride has made him deaf. Narada has told me plainly that we cannot live here, and I say the same to you. Jarasandha does not forgive, and the kings who shelter under him have not forgiven the death of Kamsa. We will never prosper in this city."

Still, he tried one last ruse. He sent Kalayavana a sealed jar holding a black serpent. "Krishna is like a deadly serpent," the envoy said. Kalayavana understood at once: he filled the jar with countless sharp-jawed ants, and they devoured the serpent to ashes.

Then Krishna did the thing that looked like flight. He left Mathura, and Kalayavana pursued him, exactly as Krishna intended.

Narada had told the Yavana how to know his man: the mark on his chest, the jewel at his throat, the face that was always glad. When he saw Krishna before him he knew him at once. He ran at him. Krishna turned and ran on, and at every step the Yavana felt his prize within reach. "Running is not fitting for one born in the Yadu clan!" he shouted after him. Krishna did not answer. He went on, and entered the mountain cave.

Inside, in the dark, a man lay asleep.

Kalayavana looked at him and laughed. "This one has led me far," he said, "and now he lies here like a holy man pretending to sleep." Certain it was Krishna, for who else would hide in a cave while a king hunted him, he walked up and kicked the sleeper.

Slowly, as if rising from the bottom of a deep well, he opened his eyes. The glance he turned on the Yavana was angry, angry at being woken, angry at being kicked, angry at a world that had forgotten to leave him alone. Where that glance fell, Kalayavana caught fire, and in a moment he was ash.

The king whose dust had hidden the sun left behind only a small mound of ashes. And the sleeper, awake at last, sat up and looked at the young man standing quietly before him.
stories.reflection: Krishna wins this battle by running, and the boon that made Kalayavana unbeatable in war means nothing against a power he never thought to guard against. The enemy who could not be slain by any weapon is undone by a sleeper's opened eyes.
stories.tradition_note: The Bhagavata Purana tells the cave episode briefly, without the story of Gargya's penance and Kalayavana's birth; that background comes from the Harivamsha, which is followed here.
stories.content_note: Includes a death by burning (a character reduced to ashes by a glance), described without graphic detail.
stories.next_story_tease: But who was the sleeper whose glance could burn a king to ashes?
stories.hero_scene: In the darkness of the cave, Kalayavana's foot still lifted from the kick, frozen before the great slowly-opening eyes of Muchukunda; a single glance blazing across the dark, while Krishna watches from the cave mouth.

stories.title: Muchukunda's Story
stories.subtitle: Muchukunda, an Ikshvaku king who once guarded the gods against the asuras, was granted deep sleep as his reward.
stories.story:
The man who had been asleep for ages sat up in the darkness of the cave, and waking felt like being born. A king had kicked him awake a moment before, and that king was gone; all that remained of him was a heap of ashes on the floor. A young man stood watching, Krishna, of the Yadavas, the one who had led the angry king to this cave. For a long moment neither of them spoke, and Muchukunda understood, without being told, that this was not the man who had kicked him.

This was Muchukunda, son of Mandhata, of the line of Ikshvaku, a king of an age so old that it had passed away while he slept. The story of how he came to sleep through the ruin of his own world began in heaven, in a war.

Long ago, when the gods fought the asuras, their ancient enemies, the hosts of heaven led by Indra asked this mortal king to stand guard for them. They chose him because he was strong, and because a king of the Ikshvaku line, once he gave his word, kept it. Muchukunda fought for the gods and guarded them through battles longer than the lives of ordinary men.

When the war was over, the gods came to release him. They met him at the mouth of the cave, Indra and the hosts of heaven, and told him the truth gently, the way one tells a friend something hard. The world he had left was gone. His kingdom no longer waited for him; its enemies were cut down, and there was nothing left for a warrior king to defend. His sons, his queens, his kinsmen, his ministers and his counselors were all scattered or sleeping. "Time is stronger than the strong," they said. "The Lord of all stands beyond even time, and nothing can stand against him."

Then they offered him the boon they had promised. "Choose whatever you wish," they said, "and good go with you. Ask anything except final release from the turning of birth and death, for that is not ours to give."

A man who has guarded heaven, and come home to find his whole world gone, may ask for anything. Muchukunda bowed to the gods, and he asked for sleep.

Not the sleep of a night, or even of a season. He asked to lie down in the earth and sleep without waking, undisturbed, until the proper time came round for him to wake. The gods granted it, and Muchukunda, son of Mandhata, the king who had guarded heaven, lay down in the cave and slept.

And he slept. The years turned to ages, and the ages turned to whole eras of the world. Kingdoms rose and fell; Mathura was besieged and delivered; kings who found their way into his cave and disturbed his rest burned to ash at his feet. Through all of it Muchukunda lay in the dark, breathing slowly, dreaming of nothing, waiting for a time he had not been told about.

Now he was awake. He sat in the cave with the ashes of a king before him and a young man with a quiet face standing in the dark, and he understood, without being told, that the one who had woken him was not the one who had kicked him.

He opened his mouth to ask who the stranger was.
stories.reflection: Muchukunda chose sleep when he could have chosen anything — a king who had spent his strength guarding heaven asking only to rest until the world needed him again. The boon he took was patience itself, a waiting for the right time.
stories.next_story_tease: When Muchukunda finally opened his eyes, he found Krishna standing before him.
stories.hero_scene: Muchukunda lying down to sleep in the mouth of the mountain cave while the ages prepare to pass over him; behind him the gods of heaven fade into the light, and the dark of the cave swallows the sleeping king.

stories.title: Krishna Grants Muchukunda His Boon
stories.story:
Muchukunda, a king of the Ikshvaku line — one of the oldest royal families in the world — woke slowly, the way a man surfaces from a sleep that has lasted for ages. The cave smelled of smoke and ash, and near its mouth lay a heap of ashes where something, or someone, had been burned away. He had slept through the turning of the world, but he understood what he saw well enough: the one who had pursued Krishna into this mountain was gone now, consumed, as it seemed, by his own wickedness.

What stood before him was a young man such as he had never seen: dark as a laden rain cloud, dressed in yellow silk, four-armed, glowing as though light came from within him, a garland of forest flowers looped across his chest, and a smile of pure affection on his face. Muchukunda pressed his palms together. The long watch he had kept for the gods against the asuras — the demons who were heaven's old enemies — had worn his senses thin, but he could still ask the question that mattered. "Are you the fire that burns within all things?" he said. "I think you must be the best of the three great gods who rule the worlds. I cannot look at you steadily — your splendor is more than my eyes can bear."

The young man spoke, and his voice was easy, as if he were telling an old story. Through many births, he said, he had measured the dust of the earth and known the deeds of all three times — what was, what is, and what has not yet come. But let the king hear about today. For the relief of a world grown heavy with evil kings, Kalanemi had been slain, and Kamsa, and Pralamba, and the others who hated the good. "And for your sake," Krishna said, "I came into this cave. Ask me for a boon, best of kings — whatever you desire, I will give it."

A gift, offered freely. Muchukunda had once conquered the four directions and sat on a golden throne while lesser kings bowed before him. He had been young and drunk on kingship, and the years of that drunkenness had passed like a bad dream. He had seen what it all came to: the body a king is praised for is only a jar of clay, and in the end it is called worms and ashes and dust. "When a man is ready to leave the turning world," he said, "it is then that he meets the good. I count it your grace, Lord, that the kingdom fell away from me of its own accord, for I desire no boon but the service of your feet — the one gift even the poorest may ask. Blessings bind. They are woven of desire and fear and the dull pride of having, and they keep a man tethered to what fades. Give me none of them. Only take me as your refuge."

Krishna heard him out, and when he answered there was something like pleasure in his voice. "That you were not tempted by the boons I offered," he said, "know it to be your true wakefulness. Men who are not devoted may discipline their breath and their minds for years and still not reach me. Wander the earth as you please — only keep your mind resting in me. You lived by the warrior's law and slew creatures in the chase; that debt is settled. In your next birth, king, you will be born a brahmana — of the class of priests and teachers — a friend to all beings, and you will come to me alone."

Muchukunda had asked for nothing, and so he had received everything there was to receive. He rose from the stone floor of the cave and went out into a world that looked new to him — a wanderer now, with nothing to carry but the one thing he had chosen. Behind him the ashes in the cave settled into stillness, and the long sleep of the king of the Ikshvakus was over at last.
stories.reflection: Muchukunda asks for nothing, and that refusal is the whole of his request. A man who once conquered the directions has learned that every earthly gain ends as ordure, worms, and ash, so the only boon he wants is to be released from wanting. Krishna names that refusal itself a kind of wakefulness: the king who slept for ages is, at last, fully awake.
stories.next_story_tease: But even as Muchukunda walked out into the light, the king of Magadha was marching on Mathura once more.

stories.title: Krishna and Balarama Elude Jarasandha
stories.story:
Jarasandha, the king of Magadha, had marched on Mathura before, and every time the brothers who held the city had turned him back. He could not forgive it. Krishna and Balarama had slain the tyrant Kamsa and ended the reign that had kept Mathura in fear, and Jarasandha had sworn that the city would not stay theirs. Now he came once more, with an army so vast that it covered the plain like a rising flood. There would be no more turning back, he told his generals. This time the brothers would learn what it cost to defy him.

And this time the two brothers did not wait to meet him. Krishna had already set the city's wealth moving — the herds and the treasure, carried away with the men he had chosen for the task. Then, with the enemy's vanguard in sight, he and Balarama abandoned whatever remained and ran. The two of them, who had faced every host the Magadha king could bring and never given ground, fled on foot as though terror had finally caught them. They did not look back. They did not slow down. They ran as men run when everything is lost.

The king of Magadha laughed out loud when he saw it. This was the pair who had broken his armies season after season; now they were running like startled deer, and their flight told him the long quarrel was ending at last. Jarasandha gave chase, and his soldiers chased with him, sure that nothing could save the brothers now. Krishna and Balarama ran until their breath burned and their legs would carry them no farther, and when they reached the great mountain that stood alone above the plain — Mount Pravarshana — they climbed, exhausted, and hid among its rocks and trees.

Jarasandha's men ringed the hill. They searched the slopes for footprints, for any trace of the two who had vanished into the scrub, and they found nothing at all. The king of Magadha did what besiegers do when the quarry will not come out: he set the mountain on fire. Flames raced up the grass and the dry brush, and the smoke rose in thick columns until the whole flank of Pravarshana burned like a torch. Let them burn with it, Jarasandha thought, and he turned his army toward home, certain that he had seen the last of them.

But on the burning slope, Krishna and Balarama were not waiting for the fire to reach them. They sprang from the blazing hillside and leapt eleven yojanas — an old measure of distance, and a leap so far that no eye could follow where they came down — landing beyond the ring of Jarasandha's soldiers, unseen, in the quiet darkness at the mountain's foot. While the smoke still climbed behind them, they made their way across the country and back to Dwaraka, their city by the sea, where their people had made their home behind walls of water that guarded them better than any wall of stone.

Back in Magadha, Jarasandha told the story of how he had smoked the brothers out of Pravarshana and left them ashes, and he believed every word of it. What he did not know — could not know — was that the whole pursuit had been shaped from the beginning: the flight that looked like fear, the hill that looked like a trap, the fire that looked like an ending. Krishna and Balarama had chosen to be thought dead, because a king who believes his enemy is gone will stop looking. And so the brothers walked the streets of Dwaraka, unharmed and unlooked for, while the king of Magadha celebrated a victory that had never happened.
stories.reflection: Jarasandha's laughter is the hinge of the episode: he believes he has won because he saw the brothers run, and Krishna lets him keep the belief. The whole escape turns on an enemy defeating himself — the fire, the ashes, the triumphant return home all belong to a story that was never true, while the brothers slip, unseen, toward a city the sea will guard better than any army.
stories.tradition_note: The Bhagavata shows the brothers reaching their sea-girt city after eluding Jarasandha; the Harivamsha places the resolve to abandon Mathura and the founding of Dwaraka at this point in the story.
stories.next_story_tease: But in the fortress of Girivraja, twenty thousand captive kings were still waiting on their release.
