stories.title: The Captive Kings Appeal to Krishna
stories.story:
One morning in the hall where Krishna held his court at Dwaraka, when the brahmanas — the priests and learned men of the city — sat at ease and the business of the day had quieted, a stranger was brought in. He was not a merchant, not a soldier, not a king's man; dust lay on his clothes from a long road and hard travel. The guards let him pass because he asked, with a stranger's urgency, to see Krishna. He crossed the hall, bowed low before him, and pressed his palms together.

He had come, he said, from the kings of the earth. When Jarasandha of Magadha had set out to conquer the world, he had demanded that every king bow to him. Those who submitted kept their thrones; those who refused were taken by force and shut away in his fortress at Girivraja, in the heart of Magadha. Twenty thousand kings, the man said, lay imprisoned there — kings who had once commanded armies of their own and now sat in darkness, waiting for something that no army could bring them.

Then he delivered their words, and the hall grew still. "This world," the captive kings said, "is a place where the strong cut short the hopes of the weak whenever it pleases them. We have learned it at last. The happiness of a king is only a dream that depends on others; we carried its burden in bodies that knew fear from dawn to dawn. Now, Lord, we have given all of that up. We take refuge in you from the terror of this world. Your feet remove the sorrow of those who bow down — free us from the bond of Magadha. Jarasandha holds us with the strength of ten thousand elephants and keeps us shut in his house like a lion penning sheep."

And they reminded Krishna who Jarasandha was. Eighteen times, they said, this king had been broken by Krishna in battle, with his discus raised, and still he swelled with pride; still he oppressed the people who looked to Krishna for protection. "You have come down into this world for the sake of the good and the restraint of the wicked," the kings said. "If a man may cross your command and nothing follows, then we do not know what this world is. Ordain an end to it, unconquered one."

The messenger fell silent. Twenty thousand kings had sent their plea in the mouth of one unknown man, and the plea lay now at Krishna's feet. The brahmanas looked at one another; the courtiers looked at the floor; no one spoke. The whole hall waited for Krishna to answer, and in that stillness twenty thousand prisoners hung on a single word.
stories.reflection: The captive kings speak in the language of total dependence: rulers who once commanded armies now own nothing but their fear and their choice of refuge. Their appeal carries a quiet inversion — the strong, they say, decide who lives in this world, so the weak can only choose where to turn. That they turn to Krishna is itself a claim about where true strength lies.
stories.next_story_tease: Uddhava, however, would counsel that no army could break Jarasandha — only a single combat could.

stories.title: Uddhava's Counsel to Slay Jarasandha
stories.story:
Uddhava, Krishna's close friend and adviser, could speak plainly, and he did so now in the quiet of Dwaraka. The Rajasuya, he began, was no common rite. It was the sacrifice by which a king had himself acknowledged as emperor of the world, and the scriptures were clear about who might offer it: only a king who had conquered the circle of the directions, who had brought every quarter of the earth to bow before him. One quarter had never bowed. Magadha stood across the path of every conqueror, and at the heart of Magadha stood Jarasandha, holding twenty thousand kings in his prison at Girivraja and calling himself lord of all the earth.

For Krishna, Uddhava said, this was one deed that served two ends. Bring Jarasandha down, and the directions would lie open for the sacrifice; bring him down, and the captive kings would go free. There was no need to choose between the rite and the rescue — they were the same road, and it led to the same gate.

But how? Jarasandha was no ordinary enemy, and Uddhava did not pretend otherwise. His strength, he reminded Krishna, was the strength of ten thousand elephants. Send against him a hundred akshauhinis — the full war-host of a king, chariots and elephants and foot-soldiers together — and he would still not fall. Such a man cannot be overwhelmed; he can only be met. Only one man alive was his match, and that man was Bhima, the strongest of the five Pandava brothers, Krishna's cousins. In a duel of two chariots, on a field with no army to hide behind and no retreat to run to, Bhima could finish what no host on earth could finish. That was the only way: not war, but single combat, man against man, and the stronger man would walk away.

And here was the shape of it. Bhima would go to Girivraja dressed as a brahmana — a man of the priestly class — passing himself off as a mendicant come to beg alms of the great king. And the alms he would ask for would be a duel; Jarasandha, who prided himself on his strength and had never in his life refused a challenge, would grant it. Let the two fight it out, chariot against chariot, with Krishna there to see it done.

Uddhava's voice carried no heat. He was not proposing a gamble; he was reading a map. The slaying of Jarasandha, he said, would serve a great purpose — for the kings he held in prison, for the sacrifice that waited on a conquered world, for the peace of every kingdom between the seas. The women of those captive courts already sang of the day their enemy would fall and their husbands walk free; the gopis of Vrindavan sang of Krishna, and Sita the daughter of Janaka sang of him, and the sages who had made him their refuge. All the world that looked to him was waiting on this one deed. The man who could not be broken by armies would be broken by the one thing he had never learned to fear: an equal.

Krishna listened, and the plan settled into place like a stone dropping into still water. Bhima would go in a brahmana's dress; Arjuna, his brother, would go with Krishna to see it through; and the long quarrel with Magadha would end where Jarasandha had made his strength a prison — on a field of single combat, with no one left to save him but himself.
stories.reflection: Uddhava's counsel is precise rather than clever: it matches the one man who can fight Jarasandha to the only kind of contest in which the king can fall. The advice also binds two aims into one deed — the rite demands a conquered world, and the conquest here is a rescue. Strategy, duty, and mercy turn out to be the same road.
stories.tradition_note: The Mahabharata (2.20) attributes this plan to Krishna himself; in the Bhagavata it is Uddhava who counsels it. The two versions are kept separate here, as the attribution difference is material.
stories.next_story_tease: Soon, to the sound of drums and conches, Krishna would set out from Dwaraka for Indraprastha with a vast host at his back.

stories.title: The Road to Indraprastha
stories.subtitle: Krishna leaves Dwaraka with a vast procession for Yudhishthira's Rajasuya.
stories.story:
The morning Krishna left Dwaraka, the conches sounded before the sun cleared the sea. They began at the palace and were answered from the gates, and by the time the first light touched the city's white towers, every street knew that its lord was going out on a journey — and that no one remembered a departure like it.

He had spoken of it the evening before, quietly, the way he did everything that mattered. Yudhishthira, the eldest of the five Pandava brothers and Krishna's cousin, was preparing the Rajasuya, the great imperial sacrifice, and had sent for Krishna to come to Indraprastha. There was more in the invitation than ceremony. The sacrifice asked that every king of the land acknowledge Yudhishthira's eminence, and one king, Jarasandha of Magadha, would never bow to any man's glory. He stood between them and the sacrifice; but that was for later. First came the road.

Krishna entrusted Dwaraka to his elder brother Balarama, who would guard the city and its people while he was gone. Then he mounted his chariot — the one that bore the banner of Garuda, the great eagle of the gods — and gave the word.

What followed was less a departure than the city turning itself inside out. The army came first — chariots by the hundred, horsemen, elephants in their ornaments, foot soldiers in ordered ranks, so many that the plain beyond the gates could not hold them. The music began: drums of every kind — the mridanga and the bheri and the deep-voiced anaka — with conches and the curved gomukha horns joining in, until the sound rolled back off the walls and out over the sea. Banners climbed the morning air, and the sun caught on weapons, armor, and the crests of the allied kings who had chosen to ride with Krishna.

Behind the army came the inner procession. The women of the palace followed — Krishna's queens, with their children and attendants — borne on gilded palanquins with silk curtains drawn against the dust, and after them the long trains of oxen, camels, mules, and she-elephants carrying the household's goods. The whole mass of it shone and moved and sounded like an ocean stirred by great fish, and at its head rode one chariot under the Garuda banner — and in that chariot sat Krishna himself, calm as the eye of the storm.

Halfway down the road, the sage Narada met them — the tireless traveler of the gods, welcome in every court. He bowed before Krishna and paid his homage, and Krishna returned the honor with words that pleased him. Then Narada rose through the sky, carrying the sight of Krishna in his heart, and the procession went on.

Krishna had also sent a royal messenger ahead, to the kings whose lands the road would cross — a courtesy, and a signal too, so that no ruler along the way would mistake an army for an invasion. The messenger carried his word from court to court, and the kings made ready to receive their guest.

The land rolled past them: Anarta, where Dwaraka stood, then the dry country of Sauvira, the wastes of Maru, and Vinashana, where an old river was said to vanish into the earth. They crossed the Drishadvati and then the Sarasvati, rivers of the older stories, and everywhere they passed, towns emptied into the streets to watch — the local kings riding out to greet Krishna and ride a stretch of the way beside him, children running alongside the elephants, women watching from the rooftops.

It took many days. But the road was the easy part; what waited at its end was not. Indraprastha lay ahead, and the Rajasuya, and the question of Jarasandha — and Krishna was going there with the whole weight of his city at his back, to settle all of it.
stories.reflection: The scale of the procession is not vanity. A king does not travel so heavily when his journey carries other kingdoms' fates; Krishna leaves his own city guarded and goes as a guest to another king's sacrifice, and the grandeur of the march says plainly how much is at stake — a sacrifice that could crown Yudhishthira's rule, or open a war with Magadha.
stories.next_story_tease: But the sacrifice would wait; there was an older imprisonment in Magadha to break first.

stories.title: A Son Crowned, the Kings Freed
stories.subtitle: After Jarasandha's fall, Krishna sets his son on the throne of Magadha and opens the prison.
stories.story:
The city of Girivraja was still settling after the fall of its king when Krishna did something the court had not expected. Jarasandha was dead — Bhima, Krishna's cousin and the strongest of the five Pandava brothers, had slain him in single combat outside the city, after a duel long enough to shatter two great maces — and in the hush that followed, everyone waited to see what the victors would do with a conquered capital. Magadha had been the terror of kings for a generation: its armies had marched across the world and carried its enemies home in chains. Some braced for fire, or plunder, or a war carried into the houses of the defeated. What they got instead was a coronation.

Jarasandha's son was a young man named Sahadeva. He had not chosen his father's wars, had not dragged kings from their thrones, had not filled the dungeons beneath the city. Krishna called him forward before the assembled court and installed him as lord of the Magadhas — the house of Jarasandha set back on the seat its king had made terrible. The ministers and elders of Magadha, who had expected a reckoning, watched the crown come down on the head of the one man in the city whose hands were clean of all of it. A conquered capital does not often get its own line of kings back, and the court did not quite know what to make of the mercy.

But the crowning was only half of what Krishna had come to do. The other half lay underneath their feet.

For years Jarasandha had kept his prisoners in Girivraja — kings he had vanquished in battle and carried away from their own thrones, warrior-kings of many lands who had ruled their own courts and now sat in darkness. He had not held them for ransom. He had gathered them for one terrible purpose: he meant to offer them up, one great day, as a sacrifice to Rudra — Shiva, the great god — the kings of the world led up like animals to feed a god who had never asked for them.

Krishna went down to them himself, and the prison was opened. One by one the captive kings came out into a light they had not seen in years — blinking, leaning on one another, slow to trust that the doors were truly open and that no guard would drag them back. Some wept. Some knelt. When the last of them stood in the daylight, Jarasandha's whole design lay undone: the kings of a hundred lands walking free out of the city that had swallowed them, no condition asked, no oath extracted, no price set on their freedom.

Girivraja that day saw both halves of a victory arranged side by side: a new king crowned in the hall above, and in the courtyard below, the old king's prisoners taking their first free steps. The kingdom of Magadha did not fall — it was handed back to its own people, with a son of their own line on the throne. It was the cruelty of the old reign that ended, not the kingdom itself.

And with the kings freed, the last obstacle on the road to the Rajasuya — the great imperial sacrifice — was gone. The captives who had been meant to die for a sacrifice would instead return to their own kingdoms, and when they reached their courts they carried a story with them: that the man who had conquered their lands had been answered at last, and that the man who had freed them had asked nothing for it but their freedom — and that on the day Magadha lost its terrible king, it found a gentler one.
stories.reflection: The crowning of Sahadeva is the quieter half of a victory. Bhima's duel ended Jarasandha, but it is Krishna who decides what comes after — a son restored to his father's throne and prisoners walking free. Justice that removes a king's cruelty without erasing his kingdom is the harder kind, and this story shows it being chosen on purpose.
stories.next_story_tease: But how Jarasandha came to that duel had not yet been told.
stories.hero_scene: In the court of Girivraja, Krishna places the crown on young Sahadeva's head as the assembled court watches, while below, the kings Jarasandha had imprisoned step out of their cells into the first daylight they have seen in years.

stories.title: Three Brahmanas at the King's Door
stories.subtitle: Krishna, Bhima and Arjuna come to Girivraja in disguise to ask alms of Jarasandha.
stories.story:
Three brahmanas — holy men of the priestly class, who lived by teaching and by alms — came to the gate of Girivraja, the hill-girt city of Magadha, at the hour of hospitality, when a householder's door stood open to any guest, and asked to see the king. They wore the marks of their calling and carried themselves like men of peace, and they asked only for alms, the oldest and simplest request a traveler can make. But the king they had come to see was Jarasandha, lord of Magadha, and the three brahmanas were not brahmanas at all.

They were Krishna, Bhima, and Arjuna — Bhima and Arjuna two of the five Pandava brothers, and Krishna their cousin. Jarasandha was the one king who stood between them and the Rajasuya, the great sacrifice by which Yudhishthira, the eldest of the Pandavas, meant to be honored as king of kings; and they had already learned what every army in the world had learned: Jarasandha could not be beaten in open battle. His strength and his hosts were too great for any force to carry his walls. But a duel — single combat, one man against one man — was a different matter, and it was for that the three had set out, on a plan Krishna had argued for and Yudhishthira had finally accepted.

The road had been long. From the country of the Kurus they had crossed Kuru-jangala, passed the lake of lotuses and the hills of Kalakuta, forded the Gandaki and the Sarayu, walked through the eastern lands and past Mithila, and crossed the Ganges and the Sone before the hills of Goratha rose ahead of them. There at last they saw the city of Magadha standing on its height, filled with cattle and grain and water — the seat of the man they had come to meet.

At that hour they presented themselves at his house, and Jarasandha received them as he received every suppliant. He was a king famed for his giving — the sort of generosity that becomes a story in itself — a man of whom it was said he would part with anything a guest asked of him, even his own head. The three made their request in the proper form. Know that guests have come to you, they said, suppliants from far away. Grant us what we desire, and may it be well with you.

Jarasandha looked at them as they stood before him, and something in the looking changed. He was no fool. He studied their voices, their bearing, the marks on their forearms — the scars a bowstring leaves on a man who has spent his life drawing one. These were no brahmanas, he understood. These were royal men wearing a brahmana's guise.

He did not turn them away. Instead he thought of Bali, the great king who had given the earth itself to Vishnu when the god came to him as a dwarf brahmana asking for a step of ground — and had lost his kingdom and kept his fame. A warrior's life is brief, Jarasandha reflected; the body falls away like a thing discarded. What is a king's life worth if it is not spent winning fame that outlives him — and what fame is greater than a gift given to brahmanas? He had heard how Harishchandra and Rantideva, and humbler givers out of the old tales, had won eternal honor with perishable bodies by giving.

So when he spoke, his answer was large. Ask, he told them. Choose whatever you desire, and I will give it — I would give you my very head.

The three brahmanas heard the words of the king of Magadha, and if any of them felt the weight of being offered everything by a man who did not know what they meant to ask, they did not show it. The boon had not yet been named. Jarasandha stood at his own door, generous as his fame promised, and waited to hear what three strangers who were no strangers would demand of him.
stories.reflection: The story gives Jarasandha his due: he recognizes the three men by voice and by the bowstring scars on their arms, and still offers them whatever they ask. His famous generosity is not a mask — it is the very quality the disguise relies on, and the tale lets him see through one deception while standing openly inside the other.
stories.next_story_tease: The masks would not stay on much longer.

stories.title: The Disguise Cast Off
stories.subtitle: Krishna names himself and his companions, and Jarasandha chooses his opponent.
stories.story:
Jarasandha, the king of Magadha, had given his word to the three strangers in his hall: ask, and it is yours — even my head. He was a king whose open hand was famous in every land, and he meant every word. What he did not know was that the three brahmanas were Krishna and his cousins Bhima and Arjuna, come in disguise from the country of the Kurus; and what they meant to ask of him was not alms.

Now the moment had come to say what they had crossed half the world to ask. Give us battle, said Krishna. That is our request. If you think fit, let it be single combat, man to man — we are not suppliants for grain or gold. We are warriors, and we have come desiring war, and nothing else.

And because the time for masks was over, he went on and named them, one by one, in the king's own hall. This man is Bhima, a son of Pandu — and this is his brother Arjuna. And know me: I am Krishna, their cousin, and your enemy.

He spoke the names the way a host introduces his guests at a feast, and in that hall the courtesy died. These were not three wandering brahmanas who had come to test a king's charity. These were the men who had crossed his lands, walked through his gate, and stood in his hall to tell him they had come to fight him. And Krishna did not soften it. You have brought the warrior kings of the world here as captives, he said — kings of every country your armies reached — and you keep them to offer in sacrifice to Rudra, the fierce god. The slaughter of human beings as an offering to the gods was never seen among the virtuous. Set those kings free — or make your own journey to Yama, king of the dead.

Jarasandha threw back his head and laughed aloud. It was not a small laugh, and it was not kind. He answered that he could not recollect ever having wronged the three; that even searching his memory he found no injury done to them. A warrior king, he said, does not imprison a king who has not first been vanquished in fair war. Every man in his prison had been beaten in battle before he was chained — that was the law of his order, to bring others under his power by strength and then hold them. And if he were to free them now because three men came to his door and asked, what would remain of the duty he had kept all his life? Then he turned on Krishna, and his words went for the throat.

I will not fight you, he said. You are a coward. When the pressure came, you abandoned your own city of Mathura and fled to the sea — you hid yourself in the salt water and called it a kingdom. Your valor fails you in the field; there is no honor in crossing blades with a man who ran from his own capital. You are not worth my mace.

But the other two he measured differently. Arjuna, he judged, would not be a fighter for him — not his match. Bhima, though: Bhima was his equal in years and his equal in strength. That was the one he wanted, the fight that would mean something. So the king of Magadha made his choice. He had a great mace brought and handed it to Bhima, took a second mace for himself, and without another word walked out of his hall and through his city gates, down to the level ground outside the walls where kings settled such accounts.

Bhima followed him. Behind them came Krishna and Arjuna, and behind them, gathering as word spread through the streets, came the city of Girivraja itself — to see the strongest man in Magadha meet the man who had come for his prisoners, with nothing left between them but the duel.
stories.reflection: Jarasandha's taunt — that Krishna fled Mathura and hid by the sea — is the insult of a man who measures courage only by what he would do himself. Krishna does not answer it; he has already answered it by walking into Girivraja disguised, which is the kind of nerve that gets a man inside an enemy's gates without losing a single soldier.

stories.title: The Duel of Equal Champions
stories.story:
On the open ground outside Girivraja, two men faced each other with maces in their hands, and the dust between them might as well have been a battlefield. Jarasandha, the king of Magadha, had ruled that city for years on a strength no one had ever matched. Bhima, the second of the five Pandava brothers, had come there with his brother Arjuna and their cousin Krishna, disguised, to free the kings Jarasandha held prisoner; and when Krishna threw off the disguise and demanded battle, Jarasandha had looked the three of them over and chosen Bhima as his opponent. It was the choice of a man who wants to break the strongest one first.

Now they stood facing each other, and for a long moment neither moved. Then both raised their great maces and closed in. The first blows would have finished lesser men: the clubs came down with the full weight of both arms behind them, and the sound of their meeting rolled across the field like the clash of a thunderbolt, sharp and dry.

The two champions began to circle, moving in wide, intricate patterns, turning now left, now right, like wrestlers who had spent a lifetime reading each other's feet. Each watched for the instant the rhythm would break — a shoulder dipping too far, a heel sliding in the dust. Neither found it. Every step was answered, every rush met, every opening closed the moment it appeared.

Then the maces began to give way. Blow after blow, the great clubs of both men shattered under the force of the exchange, splintering like brittle twigs, until each champion was left holding a ruined staff.

Anger did the rest. Dropping what was left of their weapons, the two men fell on each other with their bare hands, striking with fists hard as iron. The blows landed on shoulders and chests and sides, and the sound of fist on flesh was harsh and heavy across the field. Neither man gave ground. Bhima's strength had never met its match; Jarasandha's had never met its equal. They were matched in skill, matched in strength, matched in the fire that drives a fighter, and every advantage one of them seized, the other answered before it could be pressed.

By the time the light began to slant over the city walls, the duel was still not decided. Both champions stood breathing hard, bruised and battered, their ruined maces lying in the dust where they had dropped them. Neither had fallen, and neither would fall.

And so the great duel of the two champions remained unfinished — not for lack of fury, but because fury alone could not break the balance between them. Bhima looked across at his enemy and saw something like himself: the same pride, the same iron fists, the same refusal to fall. The fight could have gone on until the next dawn, and the one after that, and still neither man would have yielded.

Only one man on that field knew the duel could not end this way. Krishna had not crossed the country to watch two equal champions wear each other down; he had come to end a threat. He watched in silence, waiting for the moment that would end it.
stories.reflection: The duel is left unfinished not because either man weakens but because they are exactly matched; Bhima's strength meets a strength like his own, and endurance alone cannot break the deadlock. Krishna watches, knowing that a fight this even can never be won by fighting.
stories.content_note: A sustained mace and fist duel; intense but described without graphic detail.
stories.next_story_tease: But Krishna had not come to Girivraja to watch a duel that could never end; he knew the one secret that could finish it.

stories.title: The Twig That Ended a Duel
stories.story:
Outside the walls of Girivraja, the duel had reached a standstill. The maces had shattered, the two champions had fallen to trading blows with their bare hands, and everyone who watched understood the same thing: this fight had no end in it. Bhima, the strongest of the Pandava brothers, and Jarasandha, the king of Magadha, were too evenly matched. Skill for skill, strength for strength, fury for fury, neither could finish the other, and both were too proud to stop.

Krishna, the brothers' cousin, who had planned this challenge, watched it all. He had not come to Girivraja to watch two champions wear each other down. He had come to end a threat — and he knew something no one else on that field knew: Jarasandha could never be killed by the ordinary means of war.

The secret lay in the king's birth. Jarasandha had been born in two halves, and the demoness Jara had joined the halves together; the joining was what gave him life, and it was the same joining that left him vulnerable. A body so put together could not be felled by any blow, however mighty. It could only be undone along the seam where it had been joined.

So instead of watching, Krishna acted. While the two champions circled each other in the dust, he bent down and picked up a twig from the ground. Then, in Bhima's sight, he snapped it in two, cleanly, and let the halves fall. It was a small gesture, the kind no one else would have marked. But Bhima's eyes caught it, and understanding broke over him like daylight.

He turned back to Jarasandha. The king of Magadha came at him with a rush, fists raised, expecting the same iron exchange as before. This time Bhima did not meet the rush head-on. He dropped low. One of the king's legs he pinned to the earth with his own foot; the other he caught in both arms. Then he heaved with all his strength.

It was not a blow, and that was the whole point: no blow could have done it. Along the seam where the two halves of his body had been joined at birth, Bhima tore the king of Magadha apart — and the man who had seemed unkillable was killed at last.

A great cry of lamentation rose up, a cry of horror and grief that rolled over the city like thunder: the lord of Magadha was dead. The cry spread from the field to the streets, and the earth of Girivraja seemed to settle under the news.

When it was over, Bhima stood over the body of the man he could never have beaten in a fair fight. He had not won by greater strength. He had won because Krishna knew the secret of the king's birth, and had shown him, with a snapped twig, the only way to use it.
stories.reflection: The duel of equal strength could never be won by strength; the king who seemed unkillable is undone not by a harder blow but by a secret known to one man. Krishna does not fight the battle himself. He sees the truth that ends it, and shows Bhima how to act on it.
stories.content_note: Jarasandha is killed by being torn in two; described with restraint, without graphic detail.

stories.title: The Kings Emerge From the Mountain
stories.story:
For years the mountain at Girivraja had held more kings inside it than many kingdoms could count. Jarasandha, the king of Magadha, had not killed every ruler he conquered. Some he carried home and sealed inside a prison carved into the rock, where men who had once commanded armies and sat on thrones wasted away in the dark, forgotten by the world that had once feared them.

Then the prison was opened. Jarasandha had fallen in the duel outside his own walls — the single combat he himself had chosen, against Bhima, strongest of the five Pandava brothers, who had come with his cousin Krishna to win the prisoners free. When the king was dead, Krishna walked to the prison rock and opened its gates.

The men who came out were hardly recognizable as kings. Hunger had eaten the flesh from their bodies and dried the color from their faces, and long confinement had worn them thin, so that they walked out into the daylight like men who had forgotten what a crown feels like. Twenty thousand eight hundred of them — more kings than most of the world had ever seen gathered in one place. And every one of them stopped at the sight of the dark figure waiting outside the gate.

Krishna stood before them in his own form, and the sight of him was like open air to men who had lived years in the dark. He was dark and four-armed, with the mark of Srivatsa, the curl of fortune, on his chest, and his eyes were like the heart of a lotus in bloom. His lotus hands held the mace, the conch, and the discus; a jewel blazed at his throat; a garland of wildflowers hung over his shoulders. The kings breathed him in; they reached toward him with their arms; and the long weariness of their captivity dissolved in the joy of seeing him. Then, one after another, they bowed and pressed their heads to his feet.

When they spoke, they did not speak of revenge. We do not resent the king of Magadha, they told him. A ruler swollen with the pride of power does not find what is good for him. Such men mistake a mirage for a pool of water and die of thirst staring at it. We were the same. Our fortunes blinded us, and we fought one another for conquest. See what has become of those fortunes now — you have shaken them away. What is a kingdom, after all, to a body that falls and suffers and ends? Show us the way to your feet, for that alone is worth having.

And with a single voice rising from the dust of the prison yard, they praised him by name: Krishna, Vasudeva, Hari, the Supreme Self.

Krishna answered them. It is well that you have resolved rightly, you who speak the truth, he said. Remember the kings whom pride undid: Haihaya fell, and Nahusha, and Vena, and Ravana, and Naraka. Know that this body, and everything born of it, comes to an end. Return to your people and carry on their line. Take happiness and sorrow, birth and death, as they come; do not cling to the body; find your joy within; and keep your vows.

Then he turned to Sahadeva, the youngest of the Pandava brothers, and had the kings bathed, fed fine food, and dressed in fresh garments and ornaments. Krishna himself came forward and honored them, and the kings stood before him clean and adorned, their dull eyes bright again. Chariots were brought, yoked with good horses and decked with jewels and gold, and onto those chariots the kings were lifted.

So the twenty thousand eight hundred kings were freed at last from their long hardship by Krishna, and they rode home through the country that had forgotten them. And when they reached their people, they told them everything: the years of darkness in the mountain, the duel outside the gates, and the dark four-armed figure who had stood waiting for them in the light.
stories.reflection: The kings' first words are not curses on Jarasandha but confessions of their own pride; captivity has taught them what their crowns could not. Krishna sends them home not as subjects but as kings again, and what they carry back is not wealth but a story.
stories.next_story_tease: Soon after, with enemies pressing on Mathura, Krishna would begin looking for a new home for his people.

stories.title: Krishna Chooses the Site of Dwaraka
stories.story:
Krishna called the Yadus — his own warrior clan — together in the assembly at Mathura and told them what most of them had been unwilling to say out loud: the city of their birth could not hold them much longer.

This city has been the home of the Yadus, he said. We were born here and brought up in Vraja, the cow-country of our boyhood. Our griefs have ended and our enemies have been defeated — but our hostilities with the kings have begun, and our battle with Jarasandha has commenced. Our army and our animals are beyond counting; we have jewels and friends in plenty. Yet Mathura is small, and an enemy can enter it too easily. If a crore — ten million — of princes and soldiers live crowded together here, dissension will find its way among them. It is time we laid out a city elsewhere.

The Yadavas heard him out and answered with one delighted voice. Krishna, they said, do what you think proper for us all.

When the elders of the Vrishnis, the chief family among the Yadavas, consulted among themselves, they spoke of the danger openly. Jarasandha, they said, could never be slain by them, and his power was very great. Many armies of many kings had been destroyed at Mathura, and still his soldiers were so many that the Yadus could not hope to destroy them even in a hundred years. And then word came that made the decision for them: Jarasandha was marching on Mathura, and at his side rode Kalayavana, a fierce foreign king, with a great and irrepressible army behind them.

The Yadus resolved to retreat. Krishna rose in the assembly and said: Today is an auspicious day. We leave Mathura this very day, with our army and our followers.

They left the city in a flood of gold and dust, headed by Vasudeva, Krishna's father, with wives in the chariots and elephants swaying under their burdens, the noise of the column rolling out like the waves of the ocean. They carried their wealth, their kinsmen, and their friends; golden chariots, infuriated elephants, horses trotting with gold on their harnesses. They set out toward the west, and they marched until the ocean rose on the horizon.

The shore they reached was beautiful enough to feel like a reward. It was tangled with creepers and climbing vines, rich in coconut trees, sweet with the scent of ketaki flowers and palmyra palms, and the Yadavas looked around them as if they had stepped into a celestial region.

But Krishna had not come there merely to camp. He walked the shore searching for the place where a city could stand, and he found an extensive tract of land on the bank of the ocean. Its soil was coppery and mixed with gravel, well suited for beasts of burden, and it carried every favorable mark a city could want, as if the Goddess of Prosperity herself had chosen to preside over it. The sea breeze fanned it, and the ocean watered it. Nearby rose the charming mountain Raivata, its slopes rich with gems, a place great men had long resorted to. There the sage Drona, the great teacher of princes, had lived for many years, and there the archer king Ekalavya had dwelt; and on the mountain's flank lay a level stretch of ground, laid out square like a board of dice, that men called by the name of Dwaravati.

Krishna chose that site for his city. The Yadavas, who had wanted nothing more than to encamp their soldiers there, pitched their tents for the night, and the shore filled with the smoke and voices of a people making themselves at home.

That night Krishna walked among the tents without a trace of anxiety. He thought of the city that would rise on that coppery ground, of the houses that would line its streets, and of the names he would give them, one by one.

And so the Yadavas secured Dwaravati, and lived there happily with their friends, the way the gods live in their own city: a city still to be built, but already a home.
stories.reflection: Krishna chooses the new city the way a gardener chooses ground, reading the soil, the breeze and the mountain. But he does not seize the land as a conqueror; he puts the proposal to the Yadus first, and the city is founded on their consent as much as on his vision.
stories.tradition_note: The Bhagavata Purana places the founding of Dwaraka after the slaying of Jarasandha. This Harivamsha account, followed here, tells the move differently: the Yadus leave Mathura because Jarasandha and Kalayavana are advancing on the city.
stories.next_story_tease: The tents were barely pitched before Krishna set about making the new city worthy of the name Dwaravati.

stories.title: Krishna Enriches Dwaraka
stories.subtitle: Wealth rains on every house, and the gods' own assembly hall is brought down from heaven.
stories.story:
The city was rising from the shore of the western sea, but the people raising it had almost nothing of their own.

Krishna had led the Yadavas, his own clan, to this coast after years of wandering and enmity, and chosen the coppery ground near Mount Raivata for their new home. He rose with the sun, bathed at the edge of the forest, and walked the ground himself before a single stone was laid. On an auspicious day, under the star Rohini, he gave gifts to the brahmanas, the priests, and asked their blessing; then the building began — courtyards and promenades, well-levelled roads and inner apartments, the four gates named Shudraksha, Aindra, Bhallata and Pushpadantaka, and temples for Brahma, for the god of sacrifice, for Indra, and for the deities who preside over fire and water.

Where the sea crowded the site, Krishna asked the ocean to draw back twelve yojanas, and the water obeyed. The architect of the gods himself came down to lend his hand, and the city took shape as something men could speak of beside Amaravati, the capital of heaven.

Krishna set the old king Ugrasena at the head of it all. "Take Ugrasena before you," he told the Yadavas, "and enjoy this place without anxiety, like the celestials."

Yet as he watched the walls rise, one thought kept returning to him: his people were building themselves a home out of nothing, and they were poor. He wanted every household in his new city to feel rich.

He acted without delay. He summoned Sankha, the keeper of treasure, and gave him a single command: let wealth fall into every house of Dwaraka. Not into a treasury at the centre, not into a storehouse behind guarded walls — into every house. Sankha obeyed, and riches came down on the city like rain, filling courtyards and granaries, until no family in Dwaraka stood empty-handed.

Then Krishna's thought turned higher. The kings of heaven took counsel in a great hall called Sudharma, and no city on earth had anything to match it. His people, so lately wanderers, had no hall of their own where the whole clan could gather and decide matters together. So he sent the wind on the errand: Vayu, the god of air, was to go to the celestial regions, ask for the hall Sudharma, and bring it back to Dwaraka.

The wind went, and the wind returned, and the gods' own assembly hall came to rest above the city of the Yadavas. From that day, when the elders of the Yadu race met to settle their affairs, they met in a hall that had once held the councils of heaven.

The refuge by the sea had become a capital. Wealth lay in every house, the hall of the gods stood among the people, and the clan that had reached that shore with little more than courage was now named in the same breath as the cities of the celestials. Krishna had asked only that his people live without fear — and what he had fetched from heaven was no throne for himself but a place where the whole community could sit together and decide its own affairs.

So Dwaraka grew rich in a single season, and the wealth did not gather at one door. It lay scattered through every household, like seed sown in a city that meant to stand for a long time.
stories.reflection: Krishna's first concern in his new city is not the height of his own walls but the emptiness of his people's hands, and so the wealth is not hoarded at the centre but showered into every house. The one treasure he fetches from heaven is not a throne but an assembly hall — as if a people who had lived as wanderers were being told they would now deliberate like gods.
stories.next_story_tease: But Indra had not finished with Dwaraka — he sent the celestial architect to make the beautiful city more exquisite still.
stories.hero_scene: Heaps of gold and gems raining down into the courtyards of the newly built Dwaraka while Krishna watches from the ramparts, and far off over the sea the wind-god Vayu descending out of heaven carrying the celestial assembly hall Sudharma in his wake.

stories.title: Vishwakarma Adorns Dwaraka for Krishna
stories.subtitle: At Indra's bidding, the celestial architect remakes the city in the image of Amaravati.
stories.story:
Krishna came back to Dwaraka on Garuda's back — Garuda, the great eagle who carried him through the sky — and even from the air the city looked like something from the other world. Sporting grounds and gardens, turrets and courtyards covered the ground the sea had surrendered, spread wide and filled with echoes on every side. And he had not yet seen Dwaraka at its best, for the king of heaven had plans for his city.

When Indra heard that Krishna had returned, he sent for Vishwakarma, the architect of the gods. "If you wish to please me," Indra said, "make Krishna's beautiful city more beautiful still. Ring it with hundreds of gardens and build it after the fashion of the cities of heaven. Adorn it with the finest gems of the three worlds — for Krishna, who takes up the works of the gods, is forever plunging into the dreadful ocean of war. His home should shine as his deeds do."

Vishwakarma went down to Dwaraka and set to work, and when he finished, the city had been remade in the image of Amaravati, the city of the gods.

Krishna entered, and what he saw would have filled any eye. The city stood ringed by ditches full of lotus-stalks, like the Ganges and the Sindhu, with swans sporting on the water. Along the rooftops ran walls of gold, so that Dwaraka looked the way the sky looks when it is covered with gold-hued clouds. On the east shone a gate of gold and jewels, and beyond it rose the hill Raivataka with its pleasant table-lands and caves; to the south the bushes were draped in creepers of five colours, to the west in creepers the colour of a rainbow, and to the north the yellow mountain Venuman stood watch over the city.

Forests crowded the city on every side — Chitrak, Panchavarna, Panchajanya, Sarvartuka, and the great woods of Bhargava and Pushpaka, huge as Mount Meru, their creepers running down to the very roots of the trees, with ashoka and mandara flowering among them. And the sacred river Mandakini, bright with lotus leaves and gems, came down and entered Dwaraka by fifty mouths, gladdening everyone who lived there.

Within the walls stood eight thousand chariots, hung with nets of bells and flying banners. The city ran eight yojanas in length and twelve across, held twice that number of quarters, and was crossed by eight great highways and sixteen meeting places; Vishwakarma had laid seven broad roads for the movement of soldiers — a city so well made, men said, that even its women could defend it.

The palaces of the Yadavas rose with golden and jewelled stairs. Their turrets carried flags, their domes were of gold, and their rooftops, bright with golden flowers and five-coloured patterns, put one in mind of mountains with sunlit summits and caves. They shone like forest-fire and filled the sky with light like the sun's and the moon's, and the whole city — cloud upon cloud of houses — stood beneath the sky like a heaven filled with bright clouds.

And at the heart of all this splendour, Vishwakarma built the house of Krishna himself: four yojanas long and four broad, set about with palaces and hills made for delight. And beside it rose a golden palace of surpassing beauty, the loveliest in the whole city, which he built for Rukmini, Krishna's queen.

Everything the architect did at Dwaraka he did at the bidding of the king of heaven. And Krishna, looking on the palaces of his people and the city the gods had adorned for him, was well pleased; and when all was accomplished, he entered the city to live in it.
stories.reflection: What is striking is that Dwaraka's beauty is not Krishna's boast but Indra's gift — the king of heaven sends his own architect to adorn the city of a mortal king, as though heaven itself could not bear that Krishna's home should lag behind its own. The verses catalogue the splendour almost breathlessly, and among all the golden houses the one they pause on is Rukmini's.
stories.tradition_note: The Harivamsha tells of Vishwakarma and Dwaraka more than once; in this passage he comes at Indra's request to beautify a city that already stands.
stories.next_story_tease: And the celestial architect was not done with Dwaraka yet.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna entering the golden city of Dwaraka on Garuda's back, the river Mandakini flowing in through fifty mouths, swans sporting on lotus-filled moats, gardens on every side, and the golden domes of the palaces rising like the summits of mountains under a sky filled with effulgence.

stories.title: Vishvakarma Builds Dwaraka for Krishna
stories.story:
Mathura could not hold forever. That was the arithmetic Krishna carried with him as he looked out from its walls, and it was not the fear of a soldier but the calculation of a ruler.

Krishna and the Yadavas, his clan, had made the city their home. Now a foreign king named Kalayavana had marched on Mathura with an enormous army, numberless as the dust, and ringed the city, his soldiers stretched to every horizon. Krishna knew that if he stayed to fight, a second enemy would fall on them from behind — Jarasandha, their mighty enemy, whose armies would arrive the moment the battle began. Two wars at once, and Mathura's people would pay the price. A ruler who loved his people could not spend them so cheaply. There was no shame in retreat, if retreat saved the people for whom a king exists at all.

So Krishna made a different kind of choice. He would not meet two armies with one. He would move his people to a place no army could easily follow. He chose a site in the sea and asked the ocean to withdraw its waters over a stretch twelve yojanas wide, and the ocean gave way, leaving the seabed bare for the work to come.

On an auspicious day, chosen under a favourable star, he made offerings to the brahmanas, the priests, and had them perform the rites of blessing, and then he set the work in motion. He summoned Vishvakarma, the divine architect, in his mind, and the architect came to him there by the water, ready to build. By his art the city rose from the water — Dwaraka, a fortress in the sea, with high ramparts, turrets of silver and gold, and gardens of celestial trees and vines, and courtyards laid out with a craftsman's care. It was a city so skilfully made it seemed the work of a god, because it was. Every wall showed the divine architect's craft; nothing in it was ordinary, and nothing was wasted. Indra, king of the gods, sent the Sudharma assembly hall and the Parijata tree; Varuna, lord of the waters, sent swift white horses. So the new city was furnished with the best of heaven and of the deep.

Then, by his mystic power, Krishna conveyed all the people there — the whole of the Yadava clan, with their families and their goods — from Mathura to the new city by the sea. In a single day the city was full of life, and Mathura stood behind them, quiet at last. They had left their old home not in flight but in good order, and they took up the new one in the same spirit.

Krishna had planned it as carefully as any battle. He told the Yadavas that the site he had chosen was like the very abode of the gods, and that the city would be known by the name of Dwaravati, as Indra's city is known as Amaravati. He laid out the courtyards and the promenades and the well-levelled roads, and he gave each family land for a house. Temples were raised for the gods in their proper places, and four great gates opened onto the sea and the land, and the Yadavas marked out their plots with ropes and measured their streets, until the fort began to look like a home.

What Krishna had built was not merely a wall. It was a place where his people could live without looking over their shoulders — a home that would shelter them for years to come.
stories.reflection: Krishna's choice is a statesman's, not a warrior's. Faced with two enemies at once, he does not seek the glory of a great battle; he withdraws his people to a fortress in the sea and asks the divine architect to raise a city. Protection, the story suggests, can be built as surely as it can be won.
stories.hero_scene: The sea-fortress of Dwaraka rising from the withdrawn waters — golden domes and high ramparts gleaming above the sea — while Krishna looks on from the shore as the divine architect Vishvakarma raises the city into being.

stories.title: News of Rukmini's Swayamvara
stories.subtitle: Spies bring word from Kundina, and Krishna sets out with the Yadava host.
stories.story:
The news reached them at the house of Balarama, Krishna's elder brother, where all the leading Yadavas had gathered at Krishna's word.

The men who brought it were scouts who had been watching the movements of the kings, and what they carried would set every throne in the land in motion. Rukmi, prince of the Bhoja line, had summoned a great meeting of kings at the city of Kundina, and rulers from every province were already hurrying there. Word was passing from mouth to mouth: on the third day from then, Rukmini — Rukmi's sister, adorned with golden ornaments and said to be the fairest woman in the three worlds — would hold her swayamvara, the ceremony in which a princess chooses a husband from among the kings gathered to win her.

The scouts did not hide the scale of the gathering, and their words carried an edge of prophecy: that meeting of kings, they said, would be the ruin of those very kings. The rulers were coming on elephants, horses and chariots, proud as lions and tigers and spoiling for a quarrel with one another. Hundreds of their encampments would soon cover the plain before Kundina, and the kings who feared the Yadavas would sit there in safety, trusting in their numbers.

"Every king on earth is assembling," the scouts said. "Why should we sit here alone and downcast? Let us take up our armies and set out for victory."

The words struck Krishna like a dart to the heart, and he did not linger. At the head of his army he set out at once, and the Yadavas mounted their chariots and followed him. Krishna shone at the head of that host, discus and mace uplifted; behind him streamed chariot after chariot, bright as the sun and ringing with bells.

But before he left, he gave counsel to Ugrasena, the old king. "Wait here with my brother," he said. "Once the city is emptied by our departure, those kings who fear us and yet make merry at Kundina may march against it at Jarasandha's bidding. The city must not be left unguarded."

Hearing this, the old king answered with a voice that trembled. "If you go and leave us behind," he said, "we shall not be able to live here happily, or anywhere else — like a woman without her husband. Under the shelter of your arms we do not fear even Indra and the gods, let alone the kings of the earth. Wherever you go, we shall follow you, for the sake of victory."

And Krishna smiled. "I will do whatever you wish," he said. "Of that there is no doubt."

So the departure became a shared journey: the old king refusing to be left behind, and Krishna, who had meant to guard the city, yielding to the affection of his people. The army moved out of Mathura, banner after banner falling into line, until the whole strength of the Yadava clan was on the road — and the way to Kundina lay open before them, where Rukmini was waiting to choose.
stories.reflection: The verses say the news struck Krishna like a dart to the heart, and they do not explain why — the restraint is part of the art, as though something more than politics had been touched. The scene is doubled by Ugrasena's refusal to be left behind: the old king's devotion answers Krishna's care for the city, and a planned departure becomes a journey they take together.
stories.next_story_tease: Krishna reached Kundina as the sun was turning red, and the assembled kings saw who had come.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna setting out from Mathura at the head of the Yadava host, discus and mace uplifted, the army streaming behind him in sun-bright cars, while the aged king Ugrasena follows — refusing to be left behind.

stories.title: Krishna Summons Garuda at Bhishmaka's House
stories.subtitle: The king of birds appears at a thought, and the assembled kings learn who has come to the swayamvara.
stories.story:
Krishna reached Kundina, the capital of Vidarbha, as the sun, low in the west, turned the colour of heated iron. Rukmini, princess of Vidarbha, was to choose a husband at her swayamvara — the ceremony in which a princess takes the hand of the king she chooses — and every king who hoped to win her had come. The plain before the city had become a sea of tents, with the smoke of a hundred camps rising into the evening air.

For a moment Krishna was moved by what the old teachings call a rajasika impulse — a restless stirring of pride, the wish to make the assembled kings understand who had arrived. It was not a mean wish, and it was not sinful; it was the desire to show his strength. And Krishna had a way of showing strength that no king in that arena could match.

He thought of Garuda, the king of birds, the great eagle who bore him through the sky. A thought was enough; no messenger was needed. The moment Garuda came into his mind, the eagle took a form that could be plainly seen and came to Krishna, beating wings strong enough to trouble the wind itself. And every man gathered there — kings, warriors, servants, all of them — trembled, bent low, and fell to the earth, writhing like serpents that had lost the power to rise.

Krishna alone stood firm as a mountain, and he knew, before he saw, that the king of birds had arrived. Then he saw him: Garuda, garlanded and anointed with heavenly perfumes, shaking the ground with his wings; golden-feathered, bright as a mountain veined with ore; the weapons on his back lying face-downward, like serpents seeking the touch of their master's hand; dark serpents trailing from his talons. This was the bird who had once fetched the nectar of immortality from heaven, the dread of the serpent race and of the demons called Daityas, whose image stood on the flag above Krishna's chariot. Now he stood before his lord like a servant bringing a gift.

Krishna welcomed him with pleasure. "Welcome, foremost of birds," he said. "We are going to the swayamvara — come with us. Hundreds of mighty kings have gathered there with their elephants, horses and chariots. We shall behold those high-souled ones."

So the chariot set out again, with Garuda flying beside it and the warriors of the Yadavas following, and when they reached the city, all the kings who had come for the swayamvara were filled with delight at the sight of them. Armed though they were, they hurried to make ready quarters for Krishna, as though the terror of the king of birds had already passed and left only wonder behind.

Bhishmaka himself, king of Kundina and father of Rukmini, rose from among the kings and came to welcome him. He brought water to wash Krishna's feet and rinse his mouth, offered the honour due to a guest, and gave him a place in his own city. And as Shiva is said to enter Kailasa, his mountain home, Krishna entered with his army the house that had been kept ready for him, and was honoured there with food and drink, with jewels and with affection, and he lived happily in the house of Bhishmaka.

The kings who had fallen before the king of birds — the same kings who now pressed forward, delighted, to make room for Krishna — had been shown, without a single word of threat, what stood beside him. The swayamvara had not yet begun, and already the assembly knew who had come to it.
stories.reflection: The verses are candid that this is display — a rajasika impulse, pride without sin. Krishna arrives at the swayamvara and announces himself with the king of birds, so that every king in the arena understands, before a word is spoken, who has come. And the scene ends in the quietest possible key: Bhishmaka washing Krishna's feet and honouring him, and Krishna at rest in the house prepared for him.
stories.tradition_note: The Harivamsha names Rukmini's father both Bhishmaka and Kaishika; this retelling follows the title of the episode and uses Bhishmaka throughout.
stories.next_story_tease: But in Bhishmaka's house, Rukmini had her own counsel to give Krishna.
stories.hero_scene: Garuda appearing before Krishna among the encamped kings of the swayamvara — wings shaking the earth, golden feathers bright as a mountain of minerals, black serpents dragged in his talons — while warriors lie fallen and trembling on the ground and Krishna alone stands firm like a mountain.

stories.title: A Swayamvara That Was Never Meant to Be
stories.story:
The king of Kundina had agreed to a swayamvara he did not want. Bhishmaka had let his son Rukmi send out the invitations — every throne in the land summoned to Kundina, where the princess Rukmini would choose a husband. Now the kings came by every road: chariots, elephants, horses and foot-soldiers poured into the city until the streets seemed to dance with armed men, and with every arrival Bhishmaka felt the affair slipping further out of his hands. He had hoped to give Rukmini to Krishna alone; his son had flung her choice open to every king who cared to come.

So Bhishmaka came to Krishna, seeking him out as a man seeks the one person who might set a disaster right. "My son, out of a child's folly, wishes to give away his sister in a swayamvara," he said. "I do not like it. I want my daughter to choose the one she sees, and no other. Forgive my son's bad conduct, I beg of you."

Krishna's answer was not gentle. "If your son is this arrogant while he is still a boy," he said, "how arrogant will he be when he grows old? A king who speaks a falsehood, even before a single king, burns himself up in the end. Truthfulness is the first duty of a king; Brahma, the creator of the world, proclaimed it long ago. So how can your son utter a lie before all these kings gathered in your city?"

His voice grew harder still. "You say you knew nothing of this great gathering — yet kings bright as the sun and moon sit at your tables, and chariots, elephants, horses and foot-soldiers have danced through Kundina. How can you not know your son's work? Perhaps you thought my coming would not suit you, and offered no welcome to one you deemed unworthy. The law-givers say that whoever stands in the way of a maiden's choice wastes himself in hell — that is why I did not enter your assembly hall, nor accept your welcome. Kaishika, a king of this land who delights in guests, gave rest to my followers; and I, with Garuda beside me, live here as in the city of the gods."

Bhishmaka bowed low. "Forgive me," he said. "We are blind with ignorance — give us eyes to see. But now we have you, and under your shelter I am afraid of nothing."

Then Krishna softened. "The beauty of your daughter Rukmini has drawn me to this place," he said. "I will not tell you to give her to me and to no one else. But hear what the gods decreed long ago, when they gathered on the summit of Mount Sumeru: 'Go down to the world of men with your husband. Be born in the house of Bhishmaka at Kundina, and be united with Krishna.' I tell you this plainly, king. Do whatever seems right to you, after due thought."

"But know this," he went on. "Your daughter Rukmini is no ordinary woman. She is the goddess Lakshmi herself — fortune in human form — born among mortals at the word of Brahma. She must not be given away in a swayamvara where all the kings are assembled. Invite one bridegroom and give her to him with proper rites — that is the duty of a warrior king. You cannot give Lakshmi away in a public choice."

He paused, and when he spoke again there was something almost like a smile in his voice. "To place an obstacle in the way of that swayamvara, Garuda has been sent here by the king of the gods. And I too have come — to witness this festival of kings, and to see your daughter, the beautiful lotus among women."

Bhishmaka heard it all in silence: that his daughter was not his to give away at all, that the gods had settled her fate on a mountain-top before she was born, that the ceremony his son had proclaimed across the land could never bind her. He had come to Krishna fearing a disaster; he left knowing that what he had feared was the will of the gods themselves.
stories.reflection: The revelation reframes the entire swayamvara: Rukmini is not a prize to be contested but a goddess whose destiny was fixed before her birth, and so no assembly of kings can undo it. Krishna's sternness with Bhishmaka — about falsehood, hospitality, and the law — clears the ground for the gentle truth he then delivers.
stories.next_story_tease: Before he left Kundina, Krishna would show Bhishmaka what he truly was.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna, facing King Bhishmaka in the quiet of Kundina, one hand raised as he speaks the revelation — that Rukmini is the goddess Lakshmi, born to be united with Keshava — while Garuda waits behind him in the fading light.

stories.title: A Farewell of a Thousand Arms
stories.story:
The conversation was over, and Krishna rose to leave. He had come to Kundina as a guest, and at last he had spoken plainly to King Bhishmaka of what the gods had decided long ago on the peak of Mount Sumeru: that Rukmini, the king's daughter, was Lakshmi herself, the goddess of fortune, born into this house to be joined to him. The king, who had been afraid for his daughter and ashamed of his son's scheming, had bowed low and asked only for the wisdom to see clearly. Krishna had given him that answer. Now the kings who had gathered for Rukmini's swayamvara — the ceremony in which she was to choose a husband — were stirring in the city, and Krishna had a road before him.

Then, as he stood, the sight Bhishmaka saw stopped him where he was. The young man before him was the same young man who had sat in his hall all these days, asking for nothing. But he was not one shape any longer. He was every shape at once — vast and quiet and older than the world. He had a thousand feet and a thousand eyes and a thousand arms, and his eyes were like red lotuses. The shape of a man was there, and inside it the shape of everything: every direction at once, every being that breathed, every star the sky had ever held. Bhishmaka, king of Kundina, stood in the presence of the universe wearing a human face, and in one blinding instant he understood who had been a guest in his house.

He did not speak of his daughter then, nor of the swayamvara, nor of his son, nor of the kings outside the walls. All of that fell away from him like dust. He bowed lower than he had ever bowed to any king — lower than he had bowed a moment before, when he had begged forgiveness — and he began to praise.

He praised the one who had no beginning and no cause, who had existed before the first dawn and would remain after the last, and who had made himself known in the house of a mortal king. The words came out of him slowly at first, then faster, as if the vision had unlocked something in his chest that had been waiting all his life to be spoken. He had thought he was entertaining a guest: a young prince from Mathura who spoke well and carried himself like a king. Now he knew he had been sheltering the one from whom everything flows, and his praise broke over that knowledge like a wave.

Then it was over. Krishna stood before him again as he had stood all along — a young man, gracious, ready to leave. The thousand arms were one pair of arms; the thousand eyes were two. The vision had not been snatched away so much as folded back up, the way a vast sky folds into a single point at nightfall.

Bhishmaka straightened slowly and said nothing. There was nothing left to say. He had been shown what his daughter was, and he had been shown who her destined husband was, and the two truths together had rearranged his world. His son had wanted a grand ceremony; the gods had wanted something else entirely. And the king, who had spent the past days anxious and afraid, found that he was no longer afraid of anything.

Outside, the kings who had come to win Rukmini were waiting. As Krishna came out they rose and followed him, drawn by something they could not name. They did not know what Bhishmaka had seen. They had only seen Krishna — and even that was enough to move them.

Bhishmaka watched them go from his doorway, and what he had seen stayed with him all his days. A king does not forget the day the universe visits his house.
stories.reflection: The cosmic form appears not as a spectacle for a crowd but as a private revelation to one anxious father — the divine answering Bhishmaka's plea for 'eyes of wisdom' by literally showing him what he could not otherwise see. That the vision is followed by Krishna quietly returning to human shape suggests the form is a gift of sight, not a display.
stories.next_story_tease: Once the kings had gone, the swayamvara's true decision passed to Rukmini herself.
stories.hero_scene: Bhishmaka on his knees before Krishna, who stands revealed in his universal form — a thousand feet, a thousand eyes, a thousand arms, eyes like red lotuses — filling the dim hall of Kundina with light while the mortal shape he wore moments ago seems to hang over him like a garment.

stories.title: The Choice Rukmini Made in Secret
stories.story:
After Krishna left Kundina, the kings who had ridden to the swayamvara — the ceremony in which Rukmini, the princess of the house, was to have chosen a husband — gathered one last time in the hall of Bhishmaka, Rukmini's father and king of Kundina, eager to be on the road home. Bhishmaka, who knew the laws of right conduct as well as any king alive, stood before them and asked their forgiveness. "You all know the misfortune that has fallen on this swayamvara," he said. "Forgive me for what has grown out of my own wrongdoing."

He honored them, welcomed them, and sent them on their way — the monarchs of central India and the kings of the east, the west, and the north. Mighty chariot-warriors all, they returned his courtesy gladly and rode off relieved to leave a ceremony that had come to nothing. A few stayed behind with Bhishmaka — Jarasandha among them, and Sunitha, and Dantavakra, and the king of Soubha, and others of the Deccan — lingering as if they sensed that the mystery of Kundina was not finished yet.

But the true decision of that swayamvara was not being made in the assembly hall. It was being made in the women's quarters, where the princess at the center of everything had heard what the kings had not.

Rukmini had never set eyes on Krishna. She knew him only through what travelers said of him — his beauty, his courage, his kindness — reports that had reached Kundina from Mathura, where the young prince had made his name, and her heart had already answered them. Everything her brother Rukmi had planned — the invitations, the gathering of kings, the grand ceremony where she would walk in and choose — had been built on the idea that she was a prize to be won. But standing in the shadow of that enormous plan was a girl who had already chosen for herself, and her choice ran with her father's secret hope and with the will of the gods: Krishna.

Now she went to her friends with her face bent down — not the shame of wrongdoing, but the burning shyness of a girl confessing a feeling too large to keep inside. The wise and gentle Rukmini, whom the kings of the earth had come to court, stood among the women who had grown up beside her and spoke the plainest words she had ever spoken.

"I tell you truly," she said, "I will not be the wife of anyone but Krishna, whose eyes are like lotuses."

That was all. She did not argue, did not explain, did not defend herself. She had heard of the one man in the world, and every other suitor who had ridden into Kundina for her sake had become, in that single moment, impossible. Her friends heard the quiet certainty in her voice and knew there was nothing to say against it. The princess who had drawn half the kings of the earth would stand before none of them and place a garland on his neck, because her choice was made — and it was made in the only way such a choice can truly be made: by herself, in secret, with no ceremony to help her.

The swayamvara her brother had announced across the land would be held or it would not; the kings would come or they would not; none of it mattered now. What mattered was that Rukmini had chosen, and the one she had chosen was Krishna. Whatever her brother arranged and whatever the kings demanded, the bride had already decided — and a bride's decision, made like this, no assembly of kings could undo.

In the quiet of the women's quarters, with the evening settling over Kundina, Rukmini sat among her friends and held her secret close. To the city outside, nothing had changed. To her, everything had.
stories.reflection: The story turns on the contrast between the public machinery of the swayamvara and a private word spoken among friends: all the kings, invitations, and ceremonies are scaffolding around a choice that Rukmini makes alone, for herself. Her shyness is not hesitation — the certainty is already complete before she speaks it aloud.
stories.next_story_tease: What Rukmini declared in the women's quarters, Krishna would answer with a chariot before the eyes of the assembled kings.
stories.hero_scene: Rukmini among her friends in the women's quarters of Kundina, her face bent down in shyness as she confesses that she will accept no husband but the lotus-eyed Krishna, evening light falling through the lattice onto the circle of young women.

stories.title: Two Weddings in One Memory
stories.subtitle: Uddhava recalls how Krishna carried off Rukmini and won Satya
stories.story:
Years later, Uddhava, Krishna's close friend and adviser, sat in the palace at Dwaraka and remembered the great days of Krishna's life — and two weddings came back to him in a single memory, the way a man recalls two victories of a long-ago war in one breath.

The first began with a summons. Bhishmaka's daughter, the princess Rukmini — the bride the kings of the earth had gathered in Kundina to compete for — had sent for Krishna, and he had answered. Her choice was already made, and it was known only to her and to the man she had called. So when Krishna came to Kundina he came as a bridegroom answering a bride, not as a suitor entering a contest.

The kings who had ridden to her swayamvara — the ceremony in which she was to choose among them — saw none of that. They saw the crowd, the ceremony, the prize they had come to win. And while they watched and waited, sure that the day must end with one of them crowned, Krishna carried off his bride.

It was a gandharva marriage, the oldest and simplest of rites, in which a man and a woman take each other by consent alone — no priest, no fire, no assembly. In the sight of all the gathered kings, who could only look on, he took Rukmini as his wife by that rite, and the swayamvara that had drawn half the thrones of the earth ended without a single garland being placed. She was his share — the bride the gods had destined for him — and he claimed her openly, with the whole company of suitors for his witnesses.

But Uddhava's memory did not stop there, because Krishna's life had not stopped there. The same recollection that held Rukmini held another bride as well: Nagnajiti, the princess called Satya, whose swayamvara was held in her own kingdom, in a hall ringed by the proudest kings of the age. There had been no secret summons for Satya's hand, no message carried to Dwaraka in the dark. She was offered openly as a prize to the strongest, and the kings who came for her were arrogant and sure, each of them certain the garland would be his.

Krishna came to that swayamvara too, and he did not need to be summoned. As the proud kings pressed forward he met them and humbled them, one after another, until the pride of that assembly lay broken at his feet. The kings who had come to win a princess went home having lost something of themselves, and Satya, Nagnajiti, went with Krishna as his bride.

Two weddings, remembered together: one a secret answered openly, one a contest won by strength. In the first, a princess chose him in the dark and he came for her while the suitors stared; in the second, he walked into the hall of the proud and won his bride before their eyes. The rites were different — the whispered consent of a gandharva marriage, then a victory in front of a crowd — but the shape was the same: Krishna married the women the gods had joined to him, and the kings of the earth, for all their armies and their pride, could only watch.

That is how Uddhava remembered it, years afterward: the princess who was carried off and the princess who was won, Rukmini and Satya, two weddings folded into one memory of a man no king could stop.
stories.reflection: Uddhava's recollection deliberately pairs the two marriages, and the pairing says something about Krishna: Rukmini is taken by the quiet rite of consent while the suitors watch, Satya is won by openly humbling the proud. One is a whisper, the other a conquest — yet in both, the initiative is entirely his, and the assembled kings are reduced to spectators.
stories.tradition_note: This account comes from Uddhava's recollection in the Bhagavata Purana, which condenses Rukmini's carrying off and Satya's swayamvara into a single memory; the Harivamsha tells each of the two marriages at length.
stories.next_story_tease: But the story of that summons goes back further — to the day in Kundina when Rukmini first made her choice and entrusted it to a brahmana messenger bound for Dwaraka.
stories.hero_scene: Uddhava, in the palace at Dwaraka, remembering: Krishna lifting Rukmini onto his chariot before the staring assembly of suitors at Kundina, and in the same memory standing victorious in the swayamvara hall of Nagnajiti with the humbled kings around him.
