stories.title: Satadhanva Murders Satrajit for the Jewel
stories.story:
Krishna was away from Dwaraka, visiting the elders of the Kuru court in Hastinapura, when the plan was made. In his absence two men of the city found their moment: Akrura and Kritavarma, who had watched Satrajit's fortunes rise with the Syamantaka — the sun-given jewel that hung at his throat — and had never forgiven him for it. Akrura had long wished for Satyabhama, Satrajit's daughter, and once the jewel came to Satrajit's keeping he had begun to wish for that as well. The beautiful daughter and the brilliant stone, he felt, had both been denied him unfairly. Satrajit had broken his word to them, they claimed; he had promised them a jewel among women and then scorned them, and now the Syamantaka hung around his neck while they went without. Envy, in Dwaraka, had learned to dress itself as a broken promise.

They did not act with their own hands. They found Satadhanva, of the Bhoja line, a man of strength and little conscience, and they put the thought into him as one sharpens a blade and hands it over. Satrajit had broken his word, they said; the jewel should be seized; the deed would be easy, and the reward beyond price. Satadhanva listened. He was a man who had always wanted what belonged to others, and the Syamantaka was the most beautiful thing in Dwaraka.

That night, while the city slept, he crept into Satrajit's house. He struck down the sleeping Satrajit, took the jewel from its place, and was gone before the household could gather itself. The women of the house cried out into the empty dark, and their wailing was swallowed by the stillness of the night. The city's wealthiest man lay dead, and the Syamantaka had changed hands for the second time.

Satadhanva did not keep the jewel for himself. He carried it to Akrura, who received the Syamantaka as his due. But Akrura was a cautious man. He made Satadhanva swear he would never reveal where the jewel had gone, and promised in return: "If Krishna attacks you, I will follow you. The whole of Dwaraka is now under my control." So the oath bound the two of them together — the murderer and the man who had set him on, each holding the other's secret, each believing himself the cleverer.

Through the long night the Syamantaka lay hidden in Akrura's keeping, and in Satrajit's house the women wept. By morning the theft was known and the murderer was not — the jewel had simply vanished with the life it had cost. Only two men in Dwaraka knew where it was, and they had sworn to carry the secret to their graves.

But the house they had robbed was not empty. Satrajit had a daughter, and she was already making ready for the road.
stories.reflection: The murder is dressed in grievance — a broken promise, a seized prize — but underneath it is simple greed: Akrura wanted what Satrajit had, and Satadhanva was willing to take it for him. The jewel that had raised Satrajit's fortunes drew the blade that ended them; nothing about the Syamantaka ever stayed neutral.
stories.content_note: Satrajit is murdered in his sleep; the violence is described with restraint.
stories.next_story_tease: Satyabhama would find her father before the city did — and her grief would carry the truth to Krishna.
stories.hero_scene: At dead of night, Satadhanva moving through the dark house of Satrajit with the Syamantaka in his hand, the city asleep outside and the deed already done.

stories.title: Satyabhama Reports Her Father's Murder
stories.subtitle: She finds her father slain and hastens to Hastinapura to tell Krishna, who laments with Balarama.
stories.story:
Satrajit's daughter found him first. Morning had come into the house in Dwaraka, and Satyabhama — Krishna's wife, and the murdered man's daughter — found her father dead, slain in the night. The Syamantaka was gone from its place: the great jewel that Krishna had once given to Satrajit, and that the house had been proud of ever since. She cried out, "Father, father!" and the sound of her own voice told her it was true; she felt herself slain along with him, as though the grief had cut her down where she stood. For a long moment the world held only the body on the floor and the empty space where the jewel had been.

But the shock did not leave her helpless. The man who had done this had the whole night's start, and her husband was far away in Hastinapura, the City of the Elephant. There was no time to wait for the city to wake or the funeral rites to be prepared. So Satyabhama did for her father what could be done: she laid his body in a great vat of oil, where it would keep safe until the proper rites, and then she left Dwaraka and rode for Hastinapura. The road was long, and she rode it as though the news would spoil in her keeping, as though a faster telling would hurt less. The dust rose around her, and she did not slow for it. When the gates of Hastinapura rose before her at last, she passed through them without stopping, and asked for her husband before she had caught her breath.

She found Krishna and told him everything: how Satadhanva had come in the night and struck her father down, how the Syamantaka had been taken from the house, how she had left the body in oil and ridden through the dust to bring the word herself. Standing at his side, she wept. And Krishna, hearing it, wept too — he who had held the griefs of the world in his keeping wept for this one as though it were the only grief that had ever touched him.

He grieved, and Balarama, his elder brother, grieved with him. The old chronicles pause over it, wondering: the two of them mourned their kinsman following the ways of human beings, as a son-in-law and a brother mourn. There was nothing distant in that weeping and everything human in it — that morning, they were only family.

The mourning did not last long. When it was over, something had settled in Krishna's eyes: the quiet of a man who has been handed a name he will not forget. Satadhanva had taken a life and a jewel from his family. He would be allowed to keep neither.
stories.reflection: The detail that Krishna and Balarama wept "following human ways" is the heart of the episode — the lords of the universe grieve without distance, as any family would. Satyabhama's journey carries the story forward: she becomes the bearer of her own loss, and the grief she brings will not go unanswered.

stories.title: A Hundred Yojanas and No Jewel
stories.story:
Satadhanva rode as though the road were endless and the distance nothing. His mare, Vijnatahridaya, could carry him a hundred yojanas without rest — each yojana a journey of many miles — and behind him came the two men he feared most in the world: Krishna and Balarama of Dwaraka, out to avenge the murder of Satrajit and to recover the Syamantaka jewel.

Days earlier, Satyabhama — Krishna's wife and Satrajit's daughter — had found her father slain in his house in Dwaraka, and the Syamantaka, the great jewel Krishna had once given him, stolen. Every sign pointed to Satadhanva of the Bhoja clan. There was no time for counsel: the moment Krishna was home, he and Balarama mounted their chariot and gave chase, determined to run the killer down before he could reach a friendly court and slip beyond their reach.

The chase carried them out of the Vrishni lands and onto the long roads that led toward Mithila. A hundred yojanas the mare covered, mile after mile, the brothers pressing close behind — farther from Dwaraka than either had ever had cause to ride before. But no creature can outrun exhaustion forever. In a grove on the approach to Mithila, Vijnatahridaya stumbled and stood still, her strength spent and her breath failing; and there rider and horse came to a stop, the chariot closing in behind them.

Krishna looked at the trembling mare, then at his brother. "Wait here," he said. "I will go on foot and take the jewel from him myself." Balarama held the chariot, and Krishna went forward alone, the discus in his hand — the same discus that had ended the lives of demons greater than Satadhanva.

The fugitive had no fight left in him. Krishna overtook him on the edge of Mithila and struck him down with the discus, and the murderer of Satrajit lay dead in the very field where he had hoped to find safety. Krishna bent over the body and searched it; he searched the folds of the fallen man's clothes, and the saddle of the spent mare. There was no jewel. The Syamantaka was not on Satadhanva.

He came back to his brother with empty hands. "Give me the jewel," said Balarama. "I have not got it," Krishna answered. The words fell between the two brothers like a stone. Balarama's face darkened, and his anger rose as it rarely did. "Shame on you," he said, "shame on you. I forgive you because you are my brother — but I will go away from here. I have nothing more to do with you, or with the Vrishnis of Dwaraka." And he turned his back on the chariot and walked into Mithila alone.

King Janaka of Mithila received him with honor, rising from his seat at the sight of his guest and loading him with gifts worthy of a king's affection. Balarama stayed on in Mithila for months, and in that time he found a pupil: Duryodhana, the young prince of Hastinapura, who had come to Janaka's court and received from Balarama the finest instruction in the use of the mace that any teacher could give.

Krishna returned to Dwaraka alone — the murderer punished, the jewel still lost. A pursuit that had begun with a murdered father-in-law had ended with a dead fugitive, a parted brother, and a gem that seemed to have vanished into thin air. But Krishna did not believe in vanishing gems. Somewhere in Dwaraka, someone was keeping a secret about the Syamantaka; and he had already begun to guess whose keeping it had passed into.
stories.reflection: The chase that spans a hundred yojanas ends in nothing: the killer is dead, but the jewel is not on him, and Balarama walks away rather than ride home empty-handed beside his brother. Krishna's pursuit was just, yet justice alone does not return what was stolen — the story turns on the gap between punishing the thief and recovering the loss.
stories.tradition_note: The Bhagavata has Balarama simply go on to Mithila to visit King Janaka, his dearest friend; the Harivamsha presents the parting as a rift, with Balarama angry that Krishna could not produce the jewel. Both agree that Satadhanva was killed near Mithila and that no jewel was found.
stories.next_story_tease: Somewhere in Dwaraka, a secret was being kept about the missing jewel.

stories.title: The Jewel in Akrura's Keeping
stories.story:
Krishna had come home from Mithila with the killer of Satrajit dead and the Syamantaka jewel still missing. In the weeks that followed he saw that the fallen Satadhanva received the rites owed to the dead — for the man, whatever he had done, was of the Bhojas, a clan of Dwaraka's own family. But the jewel was the thing the city whispered about. Satadhanva had died with empty hands. So where was it?

That season the rains failed. The earth grew dry and the sky hardened, and the old men of Dwaraka said the sky would not open until Akrura came home — Akrura, an elder of Krishna's own family, who had been away from the city for months. When at last he returned, the rains came back with him, and the Kukuras and Andhakas, the clans that made up Dwaraka, saw their old saying come true: wherever Akrura went, good fortune followed.

Krishna had asked himself the same question the city whispered — and he had answered it long before, in a promise made in the dark. Satadhanva had not kept the jewel. On the night Satrajit was slain, it had passed from the killer's hands into the keeping of Akrura; and Akrura had made Satadhanva swear, before he fled, that no one would ever learn where the gem had gone.

And Akrura had kept his word so well that his own good fortune gave him away. He had thrown himself into a vast undertaking, gathering jewels and goods for a sacrifice so long and so lavish that the city called it the Akrura Yajna, and he had taken to wearing armor as though he expected danger. To most of Dwaraka it was the piety of a great lord; to Krishna it was a confession in another language.

Now Krishna did what he did best with secrets: he brought them into the light without breaking the man who kept them. He honored Akrura before the assembly, greeted him as a friend, and spoke with him of old times; and then, gently, he put the matter before him. "The jewel was entrusted to you by Satadhanva, was it not?" he said. "Satrajit had no son, so the gem will pass in time to his daughter's sons; and until then, no one else could hold it safely. Keep it, then, virtuous one — but show it to the kinsmen, and bring peace to this house."

And Akrura, moved by the gentleness of the words, brought out the Syamantaka and showed it to the assembled kinsmen. Krishna held the jewel up before them all, letting its light fall on every face, and the stain of suspicion that had clung to him since Satrajit's death — the whispered talk that he had taken the gem for himself — dissolved in that light. Then he gave the jewel back to Akrura, who received it with wonder; and Krishna let it go with a delighted heart, as though the treasure had never been the point at all.

The city breathed again. Balarama, who had been living in Mithila in high honor as King Janaka's guest, was brought home by the car-warriors of the Vrishni clan, Krishna himself among those who rode to fetch him; and brother and brother were reconciled. Akrura, confirmed in Krishna's friendship, gave his own sister Sushila to Krishna in marriage. And the rains, the old men noted with satisfaction, continued to fall.

The Syamantaka had returned to Dwaraka — not to Krishna's keeping, but to the man who had hidden it: trusted, in the end, because he had been trusted.
stories.reflection: Krishna's way with the jewel is characteristic: he does not seize it or expose the hider. He asks, in public, with honor intact, and lets the truth do the work — clearing his own name not by force but by bringing the secret into the light, then giving the treasure back so that reconciliation matters more than possession.
stories.tradition_note: In the Harivamsha, Akrura had long coveted the jewel and had sworn to Satadhanva never to reveal where it lay; Krishna returns it to him with a delighted heart, and Akrura seals the reconciliation by giving his sister Sushila in marriage.
stories.next_story_tease: But while the jewel was being restored, a demon far to the east was stealing the earrings of the mother of the gods.

stories.title: Indra's Plea at Dwaraka
stories.story:
The wind that afternoon carried a fragrance no garden of Dwaraka had ever grown, and flowers fell from a sky that had been clear a moment before. In the great assembly hall called Dasharha — whose golden doors opened onto a courtyard a full yojana, many miles, across — Krishna and the leading men of the Yadavas, his own people, sat at their daily business. Then a great noise filled the air, and through a net of light they saw the king of the gods descending on his white elephant Airavata, the gods gathered about him.

Balarama and Krishna went out at once to receive him, with King Ugrasena, the ruler of their people, and the chiefs of the Vrishni and Andhaka houses. Indra came down from the elephant, embraced Krishna, Balarama, and the king in order of age and rank, and — honored by both brothers — entered the hall and accepted the offerings of hospitality. When he was seated, he reached out and touched Krishna's face: the face of his younger brother, as the old telling has it. And he spoke.

"By you, Krishna," said Indra, "the tyrants of the world have fallen one by one — Arishta, Dhenuka, Chanura, Mushtika, Kesin, Kamsa, Kuvalayapida, and Putana, the child-killer. By your arm the three worlds are kept safe, and the gods receive their share of every sacrifice. But hear why I have come. The demon Naraka, son of the Earth, king of Pragjyotisha, has grown swollen with a boon granted him by Brahma the Creator. He has stolen the earrings of my mother Aditi, which drip nectar. He has taken the umbrella of Varuna, the god of the waters, which no rain can wet, and the jewel that crowns Mount Mandara. He has carried off the daughters of gods, sages, demons, and kings — sixteen thousand and a hundred maidens, all wearing the single braid of the unwed — and shut them in a house he built for them on Mount Mani. And now, Krishna, he sends word that he will have my elephant Airavata."

The hall was silent. "No creature can slay him," Indra went on, "but you are not bound by what binds other creatures. Garuda will carry you to his city. Slay him, Krishna, and come back."

Krishna rose and took Indra by the hand, and thought of Garuda; and the great bird, who can range anywhere and take on any strength, stood in the courtyard. Krishna seated Satyabhama, his queen, on the bird's back, mounted behind her, and rose into the sky, turning east toward Pragjyotisha, where razor-edged nooses guarded the demon's walls and four terrible keepers watched: Hayagriva, Nisunda, Panchanada, and Muru with his thousand sons. Indra mounted Airavata and, in the sight of all Dwaraka, returned to the world of the gods.

The city stood looking after them until the sky was empty: Krishna of Dwaraka flying east to war, his queen at his back, against a demon who had robbed the mother of the gods. Then the fragrance faded from the air, and the people of Dwaraka returned to their day — waiting, as they always did, for Krishna to come home.
stories.reflection: The king of the gods does not come to Dwaraka as a commander but as a supplicant, listing the oppressors Krishna has already removed and then naming the one he cannot. Indra's visit makes plain what the Yadavas have always suspected: their city is where heaven itself sends its hardest battles.
stories.next_story_tease: But before the demon's fall, a quiet gift at a mountain festival would stir a storm in Krishna's own household.

stories.title: A Flower for Rukmini
stories.story:
Mount Raivataka had never seen such a gathering. Krishna had come there with Rukmini — his first wife, the daughter of King Bhishmaka — for the festival that closed a vow she had undertaken, and with them had come his sixteen thousand wives, each in the splendor of her rank, along with his sons and brothers, who had gone on ahead. For days the mountain rang with the sounds of giving: priests received what they asked for, beggars went away loaded with gifts, and those who kept religious vows went away satisfied. When the fasting was over, Krishna honored Rukmini before them all.

While he sat there with Rukmini at his side and the other queens circled around them, the sage Narada arrived on the mountain — Narada, the wandering singer who carries news between heaven and earth. Krishna rose and received him with the honors owed to a great sage, and Narada, honored in his turn, gave his host a single flower: a blossom of the Parijata, the heavenly coral tree, which no earthly garden could ever grow.

Krishna took the flower, and because Rukmini sat beside him, he placed it in her hand. She understood at once. Raising the blossom, she set it in her hair, and Rukmini — the most beautiful woman in the three worlds, men said — seemed doubly beautiful with the celestial flower among her tresses.

Then Narada spoke, and his words were a praise of Rukmini and of the flower he had brought. It would never wither, he said. For a full year it would breathe whatever fragrance she wished; it would give her warmth or coolness at her word, and from it would flow juices of every taste. Whatever flower she longed for, the Parijata would become; whatever color she wished to see, it would take on; it would grow thin or plump as she willed. It would light her nights like a lamp, drive off unwholesome smells, and give her garlands of Santanaka flowers and clothes that never wore out. When she wished, it would sing with music; and it kept hunger, thirst, and weariness far from her. It was the root of good luck and of piety, and it would not let a mind that had won it wander toward any evil path.

Only one thing was asked in return. When a full year was complete, the flower would leave her — such was its nature, set by the Creator — and even the wives of the gods, Uma and Aditi and Sachi and Savitri and Sri herself, wore it for no longer than a year.

Then came the words that changed the temper of the gathering. "O goddess," said Narada, turning to Rukmini, "among the sixteen thousand wives of Krishna, I count you the foremost and the most beloved." The queens around them heard it. Some bowed their heads; others felt the praise land like a blow, and the bright air of Raivataka turned a shade cooler for them.

Rukmini kept the flower in her hair, and the festival went on. But the flower, which never withered, had been given its year; and the words of the sage, spoken once, would be remembered longer than any blossom.
stories.reflection: Narada's gift honors Rukmini, but the praise is public, delivered before all sixteen thousand queens, and the episode quietly sets the stage for the jealousy that follows. The flower is described as inexhaustible in its powers yet limited to a single year — a reminder that even heaven's gifts are bounded, while the words spoken over them are not.
stories.next_story_tease: But in another part of the mountain, a proud queen had heard every word.

stories.title: The Queen Who Cast Off Her Jewels
stories.story:
The maids were still speaking when Satyabhama's hands went to her clasps. Before their report was finished, the necklaces and bangles that had gleamed on her at dawn lay in a heap at her feet; and then she shut herself into the loneliest room of her mansion on the mountain.

The report had come from the festival on Mount Raivataka, where Krishna had taken Rukmini — his chief queen, the daughter of King Bhishmaka — for the ceremony that ended a vow she had been keeping. All sixteen thousand of Krishna's wives had gone up the mountain, each in the finery of her rank, and the festival had been days of giving: priests, beggars, and holy men had gone away satisfied, and when the fasting ended, Krishna had honored Rukmini before the whole gathering.

It was there that the wandering sage Narada had come to Krishna, and the tale of what followed had flown through every tent and mansion before the evening was out. Narada had given Krishna a single blossom of the Parijata, the heavenly coral tree; and Krishna, with Rukmini at his side, had passed it to her. She had set the flower in her hair, and Narada had praised her before them all. The flower would never wither, the maids reported; it would scent the air as she wished for a full year, give warmth or coolness at her word, light her nights like a lamp, and take whatever color or shape she desired. Even the wives of the gods — Sachi, Aditi, Savitri, and Uma — wore such flowers, and never for more than a year.

Satyabhama, the daughter of Satrajit, was proud, and her pride stood on a single foundation: that she was the wife Krishna loved best. Now a flower from the gardens of heaven had been set on Rukmini's head, the greatest of sages had called Rukmini the foremost of Krishna's wives, and the whole mountain was talking of nothing else. Such good fortune falling on a co-wife was more than she could bear. Anger rose in her like a flame.

She sat in the midst of her handmaids, who knelt silent and did not dare to speak. Through the windows, the sounds of the festival drifted up the hill — the songs, the blessings, the laughter of guests who had come to honor a happiness that was not hers. The room she had chosen was far from all of it. There Satyabhama sat, her jewel boxes empty, her anger burning slowly, like a fire that has been fed and left to itself.

She did not know — how could she? — that even then, Krishna had noticed her empty place in the circle of his wives. The festival went on without her, and the praises of Rukmini continued. But the queen who had cast off her ornaments sat waiting in her anger; and it was only a matter of time before someone who loved her came looking for her.
stories.reflection: Satyabhama's jealousy is the shadow side of her love: she measures Krishna's regard by what can be seen, and a flower on another queen's head becomes a verdict on her own worth. The pride of being loved best is a fragile crown, and this is the first moment it slips — a small, human crack in the grandeur of Dwaraka.
stories.next_story_tease: Krishna, reading the storm in her silence, slipped away from the festival toward her mansion.

stories.title: The Fan and the Falling Tears
stories.story:
Krishna, the lord of Dwaraka, had brought his queens to a festival on Mount Raivataka. The day belonged to Rukmini, his first wife: the sage Narada — a wanderer who moved freely between the worlds — had arrived with a flower from the gardens of heaven, the Parijata, and the flower had gone to Rukmini. Now Narada sat with her, praising it, and one face was missing from the circle of Krishna's wives. Satyabhama was gone — and Krishna knew, before anyone told him, where she had gone and why.

Under some pretext he rose and left the festival, walking quickly toward the mansion on the hill that Vishvakarma, the gods' master builder, had raised for Satyabhama. He had left his son Pradyumna to entertain Narada, and his charioteer Daruka waited at the gate. Krishna entered alone. His queen, he knew, was burning with jealous anger, and the knowledge made his steps slower and heavier as he climbed.

From the doorway he saw her in the room her maids called the apartment of anger, in the midst of her handmaids, sighing hot and fast. She laughed a mocking laugh at a lotus she held near her face, nipping its petals with her nails. She traced lines on the floor with one toe. She sat with her face resting on her palm. She took sandal paste from a maid's hand, touched it to her breast, and flung it aside as if it had stung her. She lay down on her bed, then sat up, then lay down again. Krishna watched the whole restless theater — a woman determined to be angry at the only man she loved — and did not announce himself.

At last she laid her head on the pillow and drew her veil over her face. This was his moment. He signed to the handmaids to keep silence, crossed the room with careful steps, took up a fan, and stood beside her, fanning her slowly and laughing a little under his breath.

The Parijata flower had left its perfume on him, and the fragrance drifted through the chamber — heavenly, rare, unmistakable. Satyabhama smelled it and wondered. She threw the veil back. "What is this?" Without a single glance at her husband she questioned her maids about the scent. They could only kneel, faces to the floor and palms pressed together. Perhaps the earth herself had breathed out one of her own precious perfumes, she thought — and then, looking about her, her eyes fell on Krishna. "Ah — you," she said, and her eyes brimmed at once, love and jealousy crowding each other. Pouting and sighing, she turned her face away. Then she frowned, and with her eyes lifted she said: "You look very beautiful." The tears she had been holding spilled down her cheeks like dew shaken from lotus petals.

Krishna went to her at once and caught the falling tears in his hands, then wiped with his own fingers the tears that reached her breast. "Why do tears fall from your eyes like dew from a pair of lotuses?" he asked gently. "Why does your face wear the look of the full moon in a morning sky, or of a lotus at noon? And why, today, are you dressed in plain white — the color a lady wears only when she worships the gods — instead of the safflower-sprinkled, gold-dusted silks you love?"

She had no answer yet, and so he gave her his own. "As flame lives in fire," he said, "so my love lives in you — and in you alone."
stories.reflection: Krishna does not meet Satyabhama's jealousy with correction or a defense of his conduct; he slips past her guards, takes up the fan, and asks her why she is sad — the question of a lover, not a lord. The protest that his love dwells in her alone is all the more tender for coming while she is still turned away, still unwilling to look at him.
stories.next_story_tease: The flower, it turned out, was not the wound; the wound was being left out — and Krishna answered it with a promise far larger than a single flower.

stories.title: The Promise of the Whole Tree
stories.story:
The trouble on Mount Raivataka had begun with a flower. Satyabhama, Krishna's queen, had shut herself into her rooms because of the Parijata that the sage Narada had brought — a flower from heaven that had found its way to Rukmini's hair, and not to hers. Krishna had followed her, and by gentleness had won his way past her silence. Now he sat close to her and asked her to name the grief itself. Her sorrow, he said, seemed to burn through all his limbs. If there was no harm in it, if it was fitting for a husband who loved her to hear it, he begged her on his life to reveal it.

At last she spoke, her voice choked with tears. "It was you yourself who raised me to honor and good fortune in the old days, and they grew famous through the world. Because I was the wife you loved best, I held my head higher than anyone. But my maids tell me that today I am laughed at — by your other wives, and by strangers too. The Parijata flower that Narada gave you, you gave to your dear Rukmini, and thought nothing of me. By giving her that priceless thing you have shown everyone where your heart lies. Narada praised her in your hearing, and you were pleased to hear your beloved praised. And even if the sage had his reasons — why was my name never spoken in all of it?"

"And if I am to repent of having tasted the sweetness of your love," she went on, her voice rising, "then I would rather have none of it. Grant me leave to go. I could not have believed, even in a dream, that you would honor another above me — yet it has come to pass, awake, before everyone's eyes. Perhaps the sage Narada has grown fond of her; what cuts me is that you sat there through it all. You have always told me that people live for honor. Dishonored as I am, I have no wish to live. My protector has become my terror."

"Cast off by you, I shall wither like a white lily. How could I look again on these Raivataka hills in their spring flowers? How could I breathe this breeze, ringing with cuckoo song and fragrant with blossom? How could I watch the sea below the hill, where I once rested on your lap in the water? You told me once, 'Daughter of Satrajit, there is no wife dearer to me than you.' What is left of that promise now? Who remembers it?" Her voice broke into bitter laughter. "I never knew you for a cheat before. Now I find you fickle and false, partial to my rival. I read your thoughts in your face, thief, however you try to hide them. Your tongue is honey — and your heart is guile."

Then Krishna spoke. "Say no such thing, dearest ruler of my heart. What more can I tell you, my darling? Know that I am yours entirely. To please me, the sage Narada, whose deeds are beyond reproach, gave her that flower out of generous feeling and regard — I did not give it with my own hands."

And then Krishna made the promise that answered everything. "What is a single flower?" he said. "I shall fetch the Parijata tree itself — the best of all trees, from the gardens of paradise — and keep it in your mansion. So be it. From this day, it is my first concern."

The storm in Satyabhama's eyes faltered. She had asked, in her grief, only to be remembered; he had answered by promising her a tree from heaven — not the flower that had wounded her, but the whole tree it had grown from, to be rooted in her own courtyard. Whatever she had expected from her accusation, it was not this.
stories.reflection: Satyabhama's long accusation is a precise anatomy of a wounded pride, and its sharpest lines are those of a woman testing whether she is still loved. Krishna's answer is not to argue with any of it but to outbid the wound: against one flower he sets a whole tree of paradise, as if the only way to prove where his heart lives is to give more than the rival received.
stories.next_story_tease: But the tree belonged to Indra's heaven, and to bring it down Krishna would have to ask a king of gods who had no wish to part with it.

stories.title: A Message Carried to Heaven
stories.story:
Narada was preparing to leave Dwaraka when Krishna, the lord of the city, stopped him with an errand to heaven. The sage who moved so freely between the worlds had come at just the right moment, for Krishna had made a promise to his queen Satyabhama — and the promise required the one thing no man could simply take: the Parijata tree itself, which grew only in Indra's paradise.

"Go to heaven," Krishna said, "and speak with the courtiers of Indra's court. Remind the king of the gods of the love between us from the old days, which you know well — and tell him this is my request, not my command. The Parijata tree was created long ago by the great sage Kashyapa for the happiness of Aditi, mother of the gods. It is the finest of all trees; it grants religious merit and boundless fortune, and it was given once as a gift to the goddesses themselves when they fulfilled their vows. My wives have heard of it, and they wish to give it away in their turn, to earn the merit of generous deeds and to please me. Ask Indra, therefore, to send the tree down to Dwaraka. It will be restored to heaven once the ceremony of giving is over."

He paused, and added: "Put all your skill into persuading the lord of the immortals to part with the tree. It will bring honor to your powers as an ambassador — and I know that everything you undertake is attended with success."

Narada smiled. "Very well," he said. "I will speak to the lord of the gods as you ask. But I am certain he will never part with the Parijata." And then, because the sage had seen more of the worlds than anyone, he told Krishna the tree's long history.

"The gods and the demons won the Parijata when they churned the ocean with the great mountain Mandara, seeking the treasures of the deep. When the tree rose from the waters, the great god Shiva wanted to carry it away to his mountain Mandara. Indra went to him in person and entreated him: 'This is Sachi's pleasure tree; let it stay in her gardens.' Shiva granted the boon — 'So be it' — and did not take the tree to the mountain. That is how Indra saved the Parijata from Shiva's own hands, by calling it his queen's."

"Nor was that all. Later, to please his wife Uma, Shiva created on the slopes of Mandara a forest of Parijata trees a full four miles across — a wood lit by its own light, into which neither the rays of the sun nor the cool beams of the moon nor even the breath of the wind could enter, and where heat and cold came and went at the pleasure of the mountain's daughter. None could enter it but the god and the goddess, their followers, and myself. There the Parijatas rained gems and jewels at a mere thought, and Shiva's own attendants took their pleasure in the wood by their lord's leave."

"Once," Narada said, "a mighty and dreadful demon named Andhaka, swollen with pride in a boon he had won, dared to force his way into that forest — and Shiva struck him down, though the demon was ten times stronger than the great demon Vritra and could not be slain by any created being. I tell you truly, Krishna: Indra, the thousand-eyed king of heaven, will never give you the Parijata, won at such cost. It grants queen Sachi every wish she makes, and it fulfils the desires of Indra himself."

Krishna heard the sage out in silence. Then he gave his answer. "If the lord of the immortals will not give up the tree at your request, I shall hurl my mace at his breast."

And so the request, it turned out, carried a warning folded inside it. Narada set out for heaven bearing both — a brother's plea, spoken out of the old friendship between the two houses, and a warrior's threat, spoken in the same breath. Which one Indra would hear first was now the only question.
stories.reflection: Narada's long recollection shows how dearly the Parijata was won — the gods churned an ocean for it, and Shiva himself was talked out of taking it — so Indra's grip on the tree is old and possessive. Krishna's message is a masterpiece of two registers: he asks as a brother first, and warns as a warrior only at the edge, leaving heaven's king to choose which Krishna he will meet.
stories.next_story_tease: In heaven, Indra listened to the message with gathering anger — and answered it with a challenge.

stories.title: A Challenge Sent to Dwaraka
stories.subtitle: Indra refuses to part with the Parijata tree
stories.story:
In the court of heaven, the sage Narada stood before Indra, the king of the gods, and the message he carried was not the one Indra had hoped to hear. His brother Krishna, the lord of Dwaraka, wanted the Parijata — the tree he had promised his wife Satyabhama — the very tree that bloomed in Indra's pleasure garden, the Nandana forest, where its blossoms were said to scent the air of heaven.

The request had been made as one brother makes to another. Krishna expected indulgence, Narada reported, because he was Indra's younger brother, and he had sent his words with courtesy. But he had sent a warning too: neither god nor demon, neither the musicians of heaven nor the great serpents of the deep — no power in any of the worlds — would turn him from his pledge. If Indra refused the tree when it was asked in friendship, Krishna would come to heaven himself and hurl his mace at the breast of the king of the gods, the breast where queen Sachi lays her fragrant ointments.

Indra heard him out, and the grievances of a lifetime gathered behind his eyes. Had he not forgiven Krishna again and again, remembering only that the boy was his brother? When the Khandava forest burned, Krishna had driven Arjuna's chariot and kept Indra's rain clouds away, letting the great fire rage on. When Krishna lifted the Govardhana hill to shelter the cowherds of Vrindavan, he had done it by setting aside the worship that belonged to the lord of rain. When Indra had asked his help against the demon Vritra, Krishna had answered only that he was impartial and looked on all creatures equally — and so Indra had slain Vritra with his own arms. And in every war between the gods and the demons, Krishna fought as his own will pleased, never troubling himself about the authority of the king of heaven.

Narada listened, and then spoke plainly. He had tried to turn Krishna from this course, he said; he had set reason after reason before him, and the lord of Dwaraka had heeded none. To Indra he offered the counsel of a friend: it seemed better to let the Parijata be transplanted to Dwaraka than to let a quarrel split the house of heaven.

But Indra's mind was already made up. "Let the sage carry this answer to Krishna," he said. "Our father Kashyapa and our mother Aditi have gone into the waters on a sojourn, and this matter should rightly be laid before them — for what has my brother done but abuse his elder, and that at the urging of his wife? Shame on women," the king of the gods said, "and shame on the influence of pride — that even Vishnu, led by his wife, should insult me this day." He remembered what his parents and Brahma himself had taught him: that there is no friend like a brother, and that a wise, well-behaved brother is dearer to a man than thousands of sons. "The demons fight me because they are not my brothers," he said. "Only a brother could wound me so. I will not be the one to begin a rupture among kin. Let my brother's challenge be set before our parents when they return."

Narada waited until the king of the gods had said all he meant to say. When Indra fell silent, his answer stood clear and final. "Until I am conquered in battle by Krishna," he declared, "I will not part with the Parijata tree. Go, and tell him I am prepared for the quarrel."

So Narada bowed and left the court of heaven, carrying the challenge back to Dwaraka. And the king of the gods, who had once unleashed storms upon the world for the sake of his pride, sat waiting for the brother who had promised to come.
stories.reflection: The quarrel is framed entirely in the language of kinship: Krishna asks as a younger brother, Indra refuses as an elder one, and each grievance Indra recites is a memory of being set aside by someone he loves. The refusal is less about a tree than about a brother who has never once deferred to him.
stories.next_story_tease: The challenge reached Dwaraka, and Krishna prepared to come to heaven in person.
stories.hero_scene: In the great court of heaven, the sage Narada stands before the seated king of the gods, who listens with gathering anger as the messenger relays Krishna's demand for the Parijata tree, the air of the celestial hall heavy with the weight of the coming quarrel.

stories.title: Battle at Heaven's Eastern Gate
stories.subtitle: Indra challenges Krishna for the Parijata tree
stories.story:
Krishna, the lord of Dwaraka, came to heaven the way daylight comes to a garden — openly, and before the eyes of everyone. Indra had refused to part with the Parijata tree, the heavenly tree Krishna had promised his queen Satyabhama, and so Krishna had come to take it himself.

He had left Dwaraka that morning under the pretext of a hunt, riding out to the Raivataka mountain with Satyaki, his friend and fellow warrior. There he handed his chariot to his charioteer, Daruka, told him to wait and groom the horses, and promised to re-enter the city on that very car by evening. Then, with Satyaki beside him, he mounted the great bird Garuda, king of all birds, and his son Pradyumna followed behind in a chariot swift enough to course over the hills. In the space of a breath, Krishna stood in the Nandana forest, the pleasure park of the gods, where hosts of celestial warriors kept watch with weapons in hand and the finest trees of heaven grew in long, ordered avenues.

He did not linger. Before the guards could gather themselves, Krishna tore the Parijata tree from the earth and set it on Garuda's back. And then a strange thing happened: the tree seemed to awaken, and to bow before the one who had taken it, as a living thing bows in homage. "Do not fear," Krishna said to it gently. When he was sure it was firmly placed, he circled the stronghold of the gods once, the great tree riding behind him on the king of birds, its branches still heavy with blossom.

The keepers of the garden did not wait to see more. They ran to Indra with the news, and the sound of their running reached the king's court before their words did: the finest tree in heaven was being carried away.

Indra came out mounted on Airavata, his great elephant, with his son Jayanta following on a chariot, and found Krishna at the eastern gate of heaven. "Krishna," the king of the gods called out, "what is this?"

Krishna, seated on Garuda, bowed his head in salute to his elder. "I am only taking away this excellent tree," he said, "for a ceremony your sister-in-law Satyabhama wishes to hold."

But Indra had given his answer to Narada, and he would not soften it now. "You should not take away this tree without challenging me to fight," he said. "Strike the first blow at me, Krishna — keep your promise, and hurl your mace at me."

So the brothers began. Krishna loosed arrows fierce as thunder at the great elephant; Indra loosed arrows of heavenly make at Garuda and cut Krishna's shafts from the air as they flew. Krishna, smiling, cut off Indra's in turn, and the two lords of earth and sky stood in the open sky severing each other's arrows, bowstring answering bowstring. At the twang of Sharanga, Krishna's own bow, and the thunder of Indra's together, the dwellers of heaven themselves swooned away.

While the duel raged, Jayanta slipped toward Garuda and tried to pull the Parijata from the bird's back. "Stop him," Krishna said to Pradyumna, and at once his son turned and barred the way. The two young warriors faced each other from their chariots — Jayanta piercing Pradyumna with sharp arrows, Pradyumna answering shaft for shaft — until a fierce combat blazed between the son of Indra and the son of Krishna, as though the quarrel of the fathers had passed whole into the hands of the sons. The gods and the sages, the perfected Siddhas and the singing Charanas, all looked on, struck with wonder at what they saw.

And then, from the host of heaven, a new champion began to advance — a messenger of the gods named Pravara, of great strength, making straight for the tree on Garuda's back. Krishna marked him and spoke one quiet word to Satyaki. "Oppose him, even from where you stand." And Satyaki, who had never refused his lord anything, moved to meet the champion of heaven.
stories.reflection: The battle begins with courtesies — Krishna salutes his elder before trading arrows with him — and what follows is a family quarrel fought with divine weapons, watched by all of heaven. The courtesy makes the rupture more striking: neither brother wants to begin the enmity, and neither will step back.
stories.tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana tells this episode differently: there, Krishna disarms the gods with his discus and spares Indra, while the Harivamsha has Indra ride out on Airavata and demand a formal battle. This story follows the Harivamsha.
stories.content_note: An archery battle between Krishna and Indra and their sons; described without gore.

stories.title: The Warrior Who Could Not Be Killed
stories.subtitle: Satyaki duels Indra's champion Pravara
stories.story:
Among the warriors of heaven there was one whom no weapon could slay. His name was Pravara, and his story was strange for a fighter of the gods: he had been born a Brahmana — a priest and scholar — on the great island of Jambu, where mortal men live, and he had won his way to heaven through the merit of his penances. There he had earned the friendship of Indra himself, and Brahma, the creator, had granted him a boon: that he could never be killed. In the service of the king of the gods he had become a messenger of heaven, accomplished in mighty weapons, able to subdue all foes. And now, in the battle over the Parijata — the tree that Krishna, the lord of Dwaraka, had promised his queen Satyabhama and come to heaven to take — Pravara came forward to prove his worth.

He moved straight for the tree on Garuda's back, and Krishna marked him at once. "Satyaki," he said, "oppose him, even from where you stand."

Satyaki was no stranger to impossible work. He was a warrior of Krishna's own clan and had stood beside him through the wars of Mathura and Dwaraka; he had never yet refused Krishna anything. He nocked an arrow and rode to meet the champion of the gods, while the host of heaven fell back on either side to give the two warriors room.

The duel that followed was like no other in that long morning. Pravara was a master of the bow, and the boon of Brahma hung over him like a second skin. Shaft after shaft Satyaki loosed, and shaft after shaft Pravara met in mid-air, cutting the arrows down before they could reach him. When Satyaki's bow sang, Pravara's answered; and again and again the champion of heaven struck the bow from Satyaki's hand, disarming him before the eyes of the watching gods.

A lesser man would have been broken by the shame of it. Satyaki only bent, retrieved his bow from the air or the dust, and returned to the fight. His arrows flew straighter for each humiliation, and though he could not wound the immortal champion, he gave him no rest, closing the ground between them again and again so that Pravara had no moment to look past him. The gods and sages who had gathered to watch the brothers' quarrel found themselves watching this instead — a mortal warrior holding his own, by pure refusal to yield, against a man who could not lose. They saw the bows flash and the chariots turn in the narrow sky, and not one of them could say when Satyaki had last given ground.

Then Pravara tired of the game. He had not come to heaven to trade arrows with a mortal, however stubborn. Turning his mount, he made for the Parijata, reaching for the tree that rode on Garuda's back.

And the king of birds, who had borne the tree through the whole battle without moving, moved at last.

One blow of Garuda's wings — one vast, sweeping stroke — and the champion of heaven was gone. Pravara and his chariot together were hurled a full four miles back through the sky, tumbling end over end, until they struck the ground and lay still. The warrior whom no weapon could slay had been felled not by arrow or mace, but by a wing. His chariot lay where it had struck, and he lay senseless within it.

The gods stared. The duel between the brothers paused, as if heaven itself needed a moment to understand what it had seen. And Satyaki, bow still in hand, took his place beside the tree — the one guard of the Parijata that no champion of heaven, it seemed, could pass. And while heaven still stared at its fallen champion, the king of birds was already turning his eyes toward the elephant below.
stories.reflection: Pravara's boon protected him from every weapon in creation, and Garuda's wing was not a weapon in any sense the boon had imagined. The duel is a reminder that Satyaki's loyalty is as much a part of this story as any god's power — he holds the line not because he can win, but because he will not stop.
stories.content_note: A duel with arrows and a blow from Garuda's wing that hurls Pravara and his chariot four miles; described without gore.

stories.title: The Fall of Airavata
stories.subtitle: Garuda brings down the king of elephants
stories.story:
A single tree had set heaven and earth at war. The Parijata grew only in the garden of Indra, king of the gods, and Krishna had lifted it out of that garden and was carrying it home to Dwaraka, the city he ruled on earth. Indra would not let it go, and so through the long morning the two of them fought across the sky above heaven — Krishna riding Garuda, the king of birds, and Indra on his great elephant, the air between them crossed and recrossed with arrows.

The elephant was no ordinary mount. His name was Airavata, and he was the banner of the king of the gods — the beast that had carried Indra through a hundred wars against the demons, the asuras, whose very presence on a battlefield was said to mean that heaven would not lose. His tusks were the pride of the sky-world, and the sound of him was like the sound of a storm coming.

Krishna had marked him early. In the first exchange of the fight he drove arrows into the elephant's flanks, sharp arrows fierce as thunder, and Airavata only stood, shaking them off the way a mountain shakes off rain.

But there was one on the field who served no order of heaven. Garuda had carried the Parijata on his back through the whole of the battle, patient as the sky, while arrows rattled against his feathers like hail on a roof. Now the king of birds turned his attention to the elephant.

He wasted no time with arrows. He struck Airavata on the head with his claws, and the great talons sank deep — fearful talons, made for tearing, that had once held serpents large enough to drink rivers. The elephant screamed and reared, sorely wounded, shaking his vast head to throw the bird off. But Garuda held on and struck again, until the greatest beast of heaven began to stagger in the empty air.

And then the heights gave way.

Airavata lost his footing in the sky itself. The king of elephants fell from the top of the world, turning slowly as he dropped — past the gates and the gardens of the gods, past the avenues of the Nandana, the pleasure-forest of heaven where the tree had stood that very morning — down through the blue air, until he struck the peak of the Parijatra mountain and lay there, the pride of heaven brought to earth.

For a moment the battle stopped. The gods stared at the mountain where their banner had fallen; the sages and the hosts of heaven fell silent. Indra stayed beside his great elephant, and even the arrows between the two of them ceased to fly. The sound of the fall seemed to ring on in the air long after the dust had settled.

The day was not done. The sun still stood high, and the quarrel was far from settled. But the king of the gods stood in the open sky with no mount beneath him, while far below, on the peak of the Parijatra, the elephant who had been the pride of heaven lay where the bird who carried Krishna had put him.
stories.reflection: Airavata was the visible power of the king of the gods, the beast whose presence promised victory — and he is brought down not by a divine weapon but by claws, by the older strength of the bird who carries Krishna. In the quarrel between the brothers, the measure of power belongs not to the thunderbolt but to the one who bears it.
stories.content_note: Garuda wounds Indra's elephant with his claws and the elephant falls from heaven; described with restraint.

stories.title: A Boon Won in the Night
stories.story:
The truce at nightfall was Krishna's doing.

All day, over the Parijata — the wish-giving tree of heaven, uprooted from Indra's own garden — the king of the gods had fought from the back of his elephant Airavata, and Garuda, the great bird who carried Krishna, had met him with beak and claw until the great beast swayed, bleeding, in the sky. Now the sun had gone down behind the Parijatra mountain, the battle had begun again, and Krishna, looking across at the wounded elephant, raised his hand.

“Airavata is sorely wounded,” he called to Indra, “and night grows apace. Let us refrain from fighting now. Do as you wish tomorrow morning.”

The king of the gods saw the sense in it and agreed.

The mountain on which they camped had made itself small when Krishna came, sinking into the earth until it was no bigger than a stone for grinding sandal — a bow of reverence from a peak that knew whose weight it carried. Indra raised a shelter of stones for the night near the sacred lake of Pushkara, and there Brahma came to him, and the sage Kashyapa with his wife Aditi, and the hosts of heaven: the Sadhyas and the Vasus, the Ashwin twins, the Adityas and the Rudras. Krishna stayed on the far side of the mountain with his son Pradyumna and the warrior Satyaki, and behind them, resting on Garuda's back, stood the great Parijata itself, its blossoms pale in the failing light.

Before the night settled, Krishna turned to the mountain under him. It had bowed itself for his sake, and he would not let such reverence pass unmarked. “You shall be called Sanapada,” he said, “and you shall be auspicious and holy as the Himalaya. Abound in gems; outshine Meru itself. I shall be glad to see you, always, full of precious stones.”

Then, saluting Shiva — the god whose emblem is the bull — Krishna thought of the Ganga. At his thought the great river, whose source lies at the feet of Vishnu, came flowing up the mountain to him. He worshipped her, bathed in her water, and then, taking up that sacred water and leaves of the bilva tree, he made his offering and invited Rudra, lord of all lords, to be present.

Shiva came, with the goddess Uma at his side and his followers around him, appearing on the surface of the Ganga's water and on the bilva leaves themselves. Krishna worshipped him with flowers of the Parijata, the very tree that the long day's battle had been about — and then, in a voice that carried across the dark water, he began the god's praise.

“You are Rudra,” he said, “who binds every being in the web of the world and sets it free again, and who makes yourself known through the sound that fills the universe when life begins. You are self-manifest and without beginning. You are Pasupati, lord of all creatures — of those who hold to life and of those who have renounced it. You are the performer of all acts, and no master of the universe stands above you; the learned call you the God of gods, the giver of life and the contentment of all the great masters. Because all that is visible is born from you, they name you Bhava — self-created, creator of all creators — and because the defeated gods and demons themselves crowned you, you are Maheswara, the maker of the universe. I place myself wholly in your protection. Crown me with fame — me, who am devoted to your devotees and beloved of your beloved.”

The night held still. When the hymn was done, the god of gods looked on Krishna and spoke.

“O best of gods, you shall obtain the things you desire. You shall carry away the Parijata tree. And you shall be invincible.”

Then Shiva and Uma faded back into the night from which they had come, and Krishna was left on the moonlit bank with the water moving at his feet. The tree still rested on Garuda's back — and now he knew it would go home with him.
stories.reflection: Krishna spends the pause in the fighting not in readiness but in worship, saluting the god whose devotee he declares himself to be. The boon he wins is quietly telling: he asks that the Parijata be carried away and that he remain invincible — as though the night's devotion, not the day's arrows, were the real weapon in the quarrel.
stories.next_story_tease: But Shiva had not finished speaking: before the night was over he would tell Krishna what lay hidden beneath the mountain.

stories.title: The Stronghold Beneath the Mountain
stories.story:
The mountain had one more secret, and Shiva had not yet finished speaking.

All that night Krishna had kept a vigil of worship on the Parijatra. He had called the Ganga up to the mountain, bathed in her water, and offered Shiva the sacred water and the leaves of the bilva; he had praised the god until the god of gods appeared with the goddess Uma at his side upon the river and the leaves themselves, and granted him his boon — he would carry the wish-giving tree home with him, and no enemy would ever conquer him. His son Pradyumna and the warrior Satyaki kept watch nearby, and behind them the great Parijata rested on Garuda's back in the darkness. The hymn was done. The boon had been spoken. Still Shiva lingered on the dark water, and still he spoke.

“On the summit of this mountain,” he said, “there is a stronghold of the Danavas, a clan of demons, called Satpura. Hidden inside that fastness live mighty Danavas of wicked soul. By a boon of Brahma, the creator, no weapon of the gods can touch them, and no god can prevail against them. Do you, O Krishna, slay them.”

The words fell into the night like a stone into still water. All day the war over the tree had been fought in the open sky, arrow against claw, for a prize that could be seen and carried. Here was a different war — one the gods could not fight at all. Beneath the very ground where Krishna stood, in the fastness of Satpura, an army of demons waited, shielded from every god by a boon older than the quarrel over the Parijata; and the charge of slaying them had been given to Krishna alone.

He had come to the mountain for a tree, and the tree was already promised to him. The night was asking him for a war the gods could not fight — and it was a command, not a choice.

Before the first grey of dawn, on the summit where the stronghold's gate lay hidden, a shrine was raised, and Krishna was enshrined within it. The mountain that had made itself small as a grinding stone at his coming held his presence from that night forward — a place of worship now, made holy by the one it sheltered, and a watch set over the fastness in its heart.

Whatever the Danavas plotted in their safe hiding, they would scheme now under an eye their boon could not shield them from. When morning came, the fight with Indra would resume on the slopes below, and the Parijata would still be the prize. But the night had given Krishna more than a boon: it had given him a task — and before the sun rose, he had taken it up.
stories.reflection: The revelation sits oddly against the boon of the night before: Krishna is promised the Parijata, yet the stronghold he is shown is one the gods themselves cannot enter by Brahma's boon. The shrine on the summit reads like a claim — the mountain that bowed to Krishna now holds his presence, as though the hidden enemy were answered by an equally hidden protection.
stories.next_story_tease: Dawn would bring the fight with Indra again — and Krishna carried the night's promise that the Parijata would go home with him.

stories.title: The Parijata Comes to Dwaraka
stories.story:
The Parijata was coming to Dwaraka — on loan from heaven, and with a mother's condition attached.

The quarrel between Krishna and Indra over the tree had been ended not by a victor but by the elders of the gods: the sage Kashyapa and his wife Aditi, who were parents to both. When the night had passed, Aditi spoke to Krishna. “Take this Parijata,” she said. “Go to Dwaraka and perform the auspicious festival so longed for by your wife. But when that ceremony is over, you are to bring this tree back and place it as before in the garden of Nandana.”

Krishna accepted the tree and its condition together. His son Pradyumna and the warrior Satyaki, who had guarded the Parijata through all the fighting, kept their watch as it traveled, and Garuda, the great bird, bore the tree without complaint, its blossoms swaying above the clouds. On the way home Krishna set the tree down at Raivataka, the mountain that looked out toward the sea and the city, before carrying it the last stretch into Dwaraka itself.

Word of the tree ran ahead of them. When Krishna arrived over the city, he blew his conch, and the sound delighted every inhabitant of Dwaraka. He alighted from Garuda, and with Satyabhama, his wife, at his side he walked to her garden and planted the great Parijata there, where its roots would hold the earth of the city and its branches rise toward the sky it had come from.

Then the wonder of it began to spread. The fragrance of the tree perfumed the earth for three furlongs in every direction, drifting through the streets of Dwaraka like a rumor of another world. Anyone who came near it could remember the lives they had lived before this one; and when the Yadavas, Krishna's own people, looked into its blossoms, they saw themselves as they had been before this world — in their old, celestial forms. Heaven, it seemed, had taken root in Satyabhama's garden.

Satyabhama received the tree joyfully. This was the festival she had longed for, the reason the tree had been carried down from heaven at all; and here it stood in her own garden, blooming in the air of Dwaraka. Whatever the ceremony required — flower, shade, or fragrance — the Parijata would provide.

Only the condition hung over the joy, soft as the tree's own scent: the tree was a loan, not a gift. When the rite was done, it was to return to the garden of Nandana, to the heaven from which it had been uprooted. For now, the city had its wonder — a tree from the gods' own garden rooted in mortal earth, flowering at Satyabhama's door.
stories.reflection: The tree is a gift with a return address: Aditi lends what Indra could not keep by force, and Satyabhama's joy is framed by a condition. The wonder of the tree — past-life memory, celestial forms — belongs to the Vishnu Purana's telling, while the loan belongs to the Harivamsha's; both agree on the marvel itself, heaven rooted in a mortal garden.
stories.tradition_note: The Harivamsha has Aditi grant the Parijata on condition that it return to the garden of Nandana after Satyabhama's rite, while the Vishnu Purana has Indra himself consent to the tree remaining on earth as long as Krishna abides there.
stories.next_story_tease: The battle that had uprooted the tree, and the parents who stopped it, were yet to be told in full.

stories.title: A Mother's Hands Between Two Brothers
stories.story:
Before the Parijata could be carried home to Dwaraka, the quarrel over it had to be settled — and the settling came close to unmaking the world.

On the Parijatra mountain, in the first light, the battle over the tree began again, and this time the world itself reeled. Krishna and Indra fought from their cars, and though neither ever struck the other directly, their weapons sought everything around them: Krishna's arrows scattered Indra's soldiers, ten shafts apiece for the horses of the king of gods; Indra's arrows covered the horses of Krishna's car and buried Garuda's wings in a storm of shafts; a thousand arrows cloaked the great elephant. And as the two heroes fought, the earth shook like a boat adrift in water, the quarters blazed with an unnatural light, mountains trembled, hundreds of trees were uprooted, and even people at their prayers fell where they stood. Hurricanes tore the sky. Rivers turned and ran backward. Fire burned even in water; planets clashed in the heavens; hundreds of stars dropped from the sky, and the elephants of the quarters quivered in their stalls. Cranes wheeled overhead crying dreadfully, and it seemed that earth, heaven, and sky had all vanished from view.

In that breaking world, the ascetics recited their sacred mantras, and the brahmanas, the learned priests, sat deep in meditation, praying for the sake of all creatures.

Then Brahma, the creator, spoke to Kashyapa. “Go, with your wife Aditi,” he said, “and prevent your two sons.”

The sage obeyed, and came with Aditi to the battlefield. The moment Krishna and Indra saw their parents, the fury fell away from both of them. They climbed down from their cars, laid down their arms, and saluted the feet of Kashyapa and Aditi.

Aditi took them both by the hands. “Born of the same parents,” she said, “you are trying to slay each other as if you were not brothers. Let pass what has happened. If you think you should obey the words of your mother and your father, lay down your arms and hear what I say.”

“Let it be so,” they said, and the two of them walked together to the bank of the Jahnvi, as the Ganga is also called.

There, at the water's edge, Indra spoke. “O Krishna, you are the Lord and Creator of the universe, and I have been placed by you in my kingdom. Having yourself established me here, why do you disregard me? Having accepted me as your elder brother, why do you wish to destroy me?”

Krishna did not answer with weapons. The two bathed together in the Jahnvi, and returned to Kashyapa and Aditi; and the ascetics gave that place a name — the union ground of dear ones — for there the two brothers were united with their parents. Before the assembled celestials, Krishna promised safety to Indra; and the gods, shining in their true forms, repaired to heaven, with Kashyapa, Aditi, Indra, and Krishna riding together on one car. Sachi, Indra's queen, adored the sage and his wife.

The battle was over; the quarrel was healed. And when the night had passed, Aditi, who had seen her sons nearly destroy the world over a tree, took the tree itself out of the quarrel. Krishna would carry it to Dwaraka, she said, for the festival his wife longed for — and when that rite was done, he would bring it back to the garden of Nandana, where it had always stood. So the war that had shaken the three worlds ended not with a victor but with a mother's gift: the tree was given, not taken, and the two brothers parted at peace.
stories.reflection: The battle ends not with a victor but with a mother's hands holding both her sons'. Indra's question — you placed me in this kingdom, you call me elder brother, why would you destroy me? — is the real resolution: the quarrel was never about power but about kinship, and once the brothers bathe together in the Jahnvi, the war simply stops being possible.
stories.next_story_tease: Back in Dwaraka, Satyabhama was readying a rite that would put even the gift of the Parijata to a stranger test.

stories.title: The Garland That Bound and Released
stories.subtitle: Satyabhama's Punyaka rite and the gift to Narada
stories.story:
Satyabhama, Krishna's wife, lifted a garland over her husband's head. It was not meant as decoration: flowers and all, it was a binding — the knot of a rite that would hand him to a wandering sage and then buy him back again, all within the same afternoon.

It began with a summons. Satyabhama wished to keep the Punyaka, a ceremony in which a wife gives away her dearest possession and then ransoms it back; and Krishna thought of the one guest the rite needed — Narada, the wandering sage who moves freely between the worlds. The sage appeared as though the thought itself were a road. When the appointed hour came, Satyabhama and Krishna bathed the great sage, anointed him with scents, hung garlands on him, and fed him with their own hands.

Then the rite proper began. Satyabhama set a garland of flowers around Krishna's neck and bound him to the Parijata, the heavenly tree that grew in her garden in Dwaraka. With his permission she dedicated him to Narada, and then she gave away her gifts: sesame seeds that gleamed like jewels, gold mixed with rice and other grains, mountains of gold, and a thousand cows — wealth poured out in such measure that the ceremony looked less like worship than like a festival of giving. The women of the household looked on as the sage accepted it all, and a joke hung in the air, waiting to be played out.

Narada accepted everything, delighted. “O Keshava,” he said, “given to me by Satyabhama together with water, you have become mine. Follow me, and do what I say.”

“This is the first stage,” Krishna answered, and began to follow him.

The sage walked a few paces, cracked a few jokes, and said, “Wait here, I am going.” Then, instead of going, he lifted the garland from Krishna's neck. “To release yourself,” he said, “give me a Kapila cow with her calf, and the skin of a black antelope filled with sesame seeds and gold. This means of release has been laid down by the god whose emblem is the bull.”

“So be it,” said Krishna, and offered the fee on the spot. Then he smiled at the sage. “Narada, you who are conversant with religion, I have been greatly pleased with you. Ask for a boon, and I will grant it.”

Narada asked that the eternal Vishnu might always be pleased with him and grant him a place beside him; and that if he were ever born again, it would be of no woman, but as a Brahmana, of the priestly line.

“So it will be,” said Krishna.

The rite did not end with the release. Satyabhama had invited all sixteen thousand of Krishna's wives to the Punyaka ceremony, and when it closed she shared out among them the celestial garments and ornaments that Shachi, Indra's queen, had once given to Krishna — heaven's own finery, passed from hand to hand in Dwaraka.

And the Parijata, at a word from Krishna, began to display its own accomplishments, flowering and working its wonders while friends and relations gathered to watch. Krishna had brought his family from far and near: the five Pandava brothers, his cousins, with their mother Kunti and their wife Draupadi; his sister Subhadra; his aunt Shrutasrava with her son; and Bhishmaka, the father of his queen Rukmini, with his. For a year Krishna stayed in Dwaraka, happy in the company of Arjuna and the ladies of his household, the days turning gently around the blooming tree, which flowered in the city as though it had never left heaven.

At the end of that year he carried the Parijata back to the city of the celestials — returning the tree to heaven, and with it, in some measure, the peace between the two brothers who had lately faced each other in battle.
stories.reflection: The whole rite runs on a divine joke: the lord of the universe is bound by a garland, sold for gold and cows, and ransomed back at a price fixed by Shiva. Krishna plays along without once breaking the mood, and the ceremony ends in generosity instead of solemnity — devotion, in this telling, is not afraid to laugh at itself.
stories.next_story_tease: When the tree came home to heaven, Krishna would make a vow before Indra that set a ten-day countdown to war.

stories.title: The Vow Before Indra
stories.subtitle: Krishna returns the Parijata to heaven
stories.story:
When Krishna carried the Parijata tree back to heaven, more came home than a tree. That very tree had once set him and Indra at war with each other — a quarrel that ended only when Kashyapa and Aditi, sent by Brahma, stopped the fighting, and the two gods bathed in the sacred river Jahnvi and made peace. A year of festival in Dwaraka had passed since then. Now Krishna set the tree back in the garden it had left, and in the court of heaven he bowed to Indra, then to Aditi and Kashyapa — a son's greeting at his parents' door. The court that had watched them fight now watched them stand together, and the sight carried its own peace.

Aditi received it exactly that way. After Krishna had bowed to her, she spoke. "May you both always entertain such brotherly feeling," she said. "You are to satisfy this desire of mine."

"It shall be so," said Krishna.

Then, having honored his parents, he turned to the king of gods, and his words changed the mood of the meeting. "O king of gods," he said, "I have been commanded by Shiva to destroy all the unslayable Danavas who live on earth. From today, within ten days, I will kill all those Asuras. At the time of that battle, Pravara, together with the heroic Jayanta, must wait in the sky to slay the Danavas. Of them, one is a god in human form, and the other is the son of a god."

It was a strange vow, and Indra knew why. These Danavas — demons of an ancient line — were unslayable by the gods. They carried a boon from Brahma, and no weapon of heaven could touch them; that was why they had lived so long on earth, proud and untroubled. Yet here was Krishna promising to finish them within ten days, and asking that his two chosen watchers stand ready in the sky when he did — as though the ruin of the invincible were a thing that could be scheduled. The gods gathered closer at the words, for it was not every day that the lord who lived among mortals set a date for war. Indra had long known these Danavas as a burden heaven could not lift; now, for the first time, he heard someone promise to lift it.

Krishna explained it plainly. "Although those Danavas, proud of the boon conferred on them by Brahma, cannot be killed by the gods," he said, "we will kill them, for I am now a man."

There was the whole secret, and it turned the vow from a boast into a promise. The boon that shielded the Danavas from every god left them helpless against a man — and Krishna, who had just spent a year at festival among mortals, spoke of that human form as his weapon. He was the man who would do what heaven could not, and the gods had only to watch the sky when the killing began.

Indra, pleased, answered, "So it will be." Then the king of gods and the lord of Dwaraka embraced — the quarrel over the Parijata finished at last with an embrace, and a different war agreed upon in the same breath, one to be fought on earth within ten days. Far below, the Danavas went on living as though no such promise existed. The ten days had begun to run, and the earth did not yet know it.
stories.reflection: The vow's logic is the striking thing: the Danavas' invincibility is a gift from Brahma, and it is precisely that gift which makes them killable — by a man. Krishna speaks of his human form not as a weakness but as the one door the boon left open, and the embrace with Indra seals both reconciliation and war in a single moment.
stories.next_story_tease: Within those ten days, Krishna would be drawn to a sacrifice at Shatpura where the Danavas were already making demands.
