stories.title: The Demand at the Sacrifice
stories.subtitle: The Danavas of Shatpura claim a share of Brahmadatta's yajna
stories.story:
"Give us our share in the sacrifice. We will drink the Soma of the rite, and Brahmadatta must give us his daughters."

The demand reached the sacrificial ground of Shatpura in the middle of a year-long sacrifice. It came from Nikumbha and the other Danavas of the city — demons made fearless by the boon they carried — who gathered on the bank of the sacred river Avarta. They did not frame their words as a request. They claimed a share of the offerings, the most valuable of the jewels Brahmadatta possessed, and his daughters, who were said to be many and beautiful. "If he transgresses this order," they announced, "we will not allow him to celebrate this sacrifice. This is our order."

Brahmadatta, who conducted the rite, was a Vajasaneya brahmana — a priest of the school of the sage Yajnavalkya, learned in the four Vedas and in the six branches of sacred knowledge. He answered the Danavas as his learning taught him: no portion of sacrificial offerings had ever been laid down for them in the Vedas, and if they doubted it, they could ask the great sages seated at the rite. His daughters would be given in marriage to proper bridegrooms, as the same Vedas required. "If you come to terms," he said, "I may give you my entire collection of jewels. If you show your force, I will not give even that — for Devaki's son is my supporter."

The Danavas chose force. They scattered the vessels of the sacrifice and began to carry off his daughters.

It happened that Krishna's own parents were at Shatpura. Brahmadatta was an old friend and teacher of Vasudeva, Krishna's father — and a teacher is guarded by his pupil, just as Indra guards Brihaspati, the teacher of the gods. So Vasudeva had come to protect the rite, and Devaki, Krishna's mother, with him. Around them sat the greatest of the sages — Vyasa, Yajnavalkya, Sumantu, Jaimini and others of firm devotion — and Devaki moved among the beggars of the sacrifice, giving each one what he asked for, from the wealth of Vasudeva. Such was the household the Danavas had chosen to challenge: the teacher of Krishna's father, guarded by the mother of Krishna. The sacrifice was rich in food and in gifts — and it was precisely that richness the Danavas meant to tear apart.

When Vasudeva saw the Asuras robbing the sacrifice, he thought of his sons — Krishna, Balabhadra and Gada. The moment he thought of them, Krishna knew everything. "Proceed, my son," he said to Pradyumna, "and save the maidens by your power of illusion. I myself will soon go to Shatpura with the Yadava army."

Pradyumna was there within a moment. By illusion he carried the maidens away, left likenesses of them in their place before the Danavas, and told Devaki, "Be not afraid." Well satisfied, the Danavas carried off the false maidens and entered their city in triumph, while Brahmadatta's true daughters were safe. The trick had saved the maidens and bought the sacrifice its peace — for a little while.

The great sacrifice went on according to the rites, and its fame spread. All the kings Brahmadatta had invited arrived and camped near Shatpura: Jarasandha, Shishupala, Dantavakra, the five Pandava brothers, the hundred sons of Dhritarashtra, Rukmi, Shalya, Shakuni, and many another ruler besides. The year of offerings had grown a ring of armies around it, and with every new arrival the camp grew thicker and the air heavier.
stories.reflection: Brahmadatta's defiance rests on one sentence: no share of the offerings was ever laid down for the Asuras in the Vedas, and his daughters will be given to proper bridegrooms, not to force. He stakes everything on the order of the rite and on the name of Devaki's son — and the rescue comes not as a miracle but as a son obeying his father's summons.
stories.next_story_tease: Narada, watching the kings gather around the sacrifice, decided that the assembly needed a conflict — and set out for Nikumbha's house.
stories.hero_scene: Nikumbha and the Danavas scattering the articles of Brahmadatta's sacrifice on the bank of the river Avarta while Devaki looks on, and Pradyumna arriving with his illusive powers to carry the maidens to safety.

stories.title: The Sage Who Brought the War
stories.subtitle: Narada incites the kings against the Yadavas
stories.story:
"At this sacrifice all the warrior kings and the Yadavas have assembled. Surely this will lead to a conflict. I shall therefore try to bring it about."

That was the thought of Narada, the wandering sage, as he looked over the encampment at Shatpura — the sage who moved among gods, kings and demons as though they were rooms of a single house, and whose words carried weight in every one of them. The kings had come from every quarter — Jarasandha, Shishupala, Dantavakra, the Pandavas, the sons of Dhritarashtra, Rukmi, Shalya, Shakuni and many more — and camped around the sacrificial ground where Brahmadatta's year-long rite still burned. On one side of that circle stood the Yadavas of Dwaraka; on the other, the kings. And inside the city, the Danavas who had tried to seize Brahmadatta's daughters still nursed their grievance. Where another sage might have foreseen bloodshed and spoken a warning, Narada walked straight to Nikumbha's house.

The Danavas received him with honor, seated him, and waited. Narada wasted no words. "Having caused a dissension with the Yadavas," he said, "how are you sitting here at ease? Do you not know that Brahmadatta is the friend of Krishna's father?"

Then he told Nikumbha what was coming to the sacrifice. All five hundred wives of Brahmadatta had been brought to the sacrificial ground to honor Krishna, the son of Vasudeva — wives from priestly, warrior, merchant and farming families alike. Years before, each of them had worshipped the sage Durvasa, and he had granted them a boon: one by one, each would bear a son and a daughter. By virtue of that boon they had all given birth to daughters of matchless beauty — tender, ever youthful, their bodies carrying the fragrance of every flower. Narada let the picture hang in the air, then drew the conclusion for them: jewels would open the ears of the kings, and maidens would seal the bargain.

The point was not lost on Nikumbha. These were the maidens who would come with the Yadavas — more of them, and lovelier, than the daughters the Danavas had failed to seize.

"O hero," Narada went on, "invite in proper order the help of the other kings." The Asuras understood the lesson. If the kings who had come for the sacrifice could be turned — bought with jewels, promised maidens — then the Yadavas would find no friends at Shatpura, and the Danavas would meet them with an army of their own. The Danavas set about their work, and Narada, his errand at Nikumbha's house done, passed back through the encampment.

There he did the other half of his work. The great sage persuaded the heroic sons of Pandu to hold back from the coming war, so that when the armies met, the Pandavas would not be counted on the Yadavas' side. It was a careful mercy, or a careful cruelty — and Narada left it at that.

So the stage was set at Shatpura. The Danavas had their allies among the kings, the kings had their price, the Pandavas had been set apart, and the Yadavas were walking toward a sacrifice that had quietly become a trap. Nothing had been decided by battle, and yet everything had been arranged for one — which was exactly the kind of work Narada did best. And he had done it all without ever raising his voice.
stories.reflection: Narada here turns the blessing he received in Dwaraka toward the opposite end: he does not merely foresee the clash at Shatpura, he resolves to bring it about. The same gifts that let him joke with the lord of the universe let him arm the Asuras and disarm the Pandavas.
stories.next_story_tease: Before the assembled kings could act, Nikumbha would use his illusive powers to carry the Yadava heroes one by one into a cave beneath Shatpura.

stories.title: The Cave That Swallowed the Heroes
stories.subtitle: Nikumbha's illusion empties the Yadava ranks, one hero at a time.
stories.story:
As the clear sun rose over the plain, the mountain gave birth to an army. From the mouth of the cave of Shatpura the Danavas came roaring — a host spilling out on asses, elephants, crocodiles, hares, horses, buffaloes, lions and tortoises, with chariots drawn by the same wild beasts, and the sound of trumpets, wheels and conches rising like a storm that had learned to march.

The war had begun over the sacrifice of the brahmana Brahmadatta, when the Danavas of Shatpura claimed his daughters and the kings of the earth took their side. Now the Yadavas of Dwaraka, who had come to defend the rite, stood on the plain before the cave — and they had come prepared for everything but this.

Krishna, his elder brother Baladeva, and Satyaki had ridden to the field on Garuda, the king of birds; they had bathed in the sacred river Avarta and worshipped Shiva before the first arrow flew. Pradyumna, Krishna's son, stood at the head of the army, while the Pandavas kept guard over the sacrifice ground behind them. At Krishna's mandate the war-bugles sounded, and Samba and Gada drew the host up in the shape of a great crocodile, while Sharana, Uddhava, Viprithu, Prithu, Sudangshthra, Vichakshu and the rest held the rear with Aniruddha. Above, hidden where only Krishna could see them, hovered Indra's son Jayanta and the brahmana Pravara, summoned by a single thought.

The kings of the earth had chosen their sides. With the Asuras stood the followers of the Chedi king Shishupala, the hundred brothers of the Kuru house led by Duryodhana, and rulers such as Bhagadatta, Shalya, Shakuni and Jarasandha. At the head of the whole host came Nikumbha, as the lord of the gods rides out at the head of the celestial host — only darker — and behind him the Asura ranks filled earth and sky with their lion-like cries.

The battle opened with arrows like serpents. Nikumbha's shafts fell on the Yadava army like a rain of poison, and Anadhrishti, commander of the Yadava host, could not bear it. He answered shaft for shaft, his feathered arrows clearing the enemy's ranks, until the air grew so thick with missiles that Nikumbha himself, with his chariot, his standard and his horses, vanished from sight. That was an insult the great Asura could not forgive. Anger kindled in him, and with it the resolve to fight with what no arrow could touch.

That was when the field learned its true enemy. Nikumbha, foremost of those who wield illusion, was not hiding. He was working. By his powers of illusion he bewildered Anadhrishti where he stood, carried him to the cave of Shatpura, and imprisoned him there. Then he returned to the field and did it again — Kritavarma, Charudeshna, Vaitarana of Bhoja's race, Sanatkumar, Arksha the son of Jambavati, Nishatha and Ulmukha — and after them, one by one, countless more Yadava heroes, each led dazed and helpless into the dreadful cave while Nikumbha himself stayed so completely hidden that no one could see him come or go.

It was a war fought by subtraction. The Yadava ranks did not fall. They vanished. A captain would be standing there shouting orders, the dust would shift, and he was gone, swallowed by the mountain. The army could answer spears and arrows; it could not answer a man who was never where it looked.

When the truth of it sank in, rage came to the Yadava side such as the plain had not seen. Krishna, Baladeva, Satyaki, Samba, the irrepressible Aniruddha, and Pradyumna most of all, who had watched his kinsmen led into the dark, were filled with anger. They had come to fight a war; they found themselves watching a prison being filled.

Krishna looked at the cave, and then at the host that had done this. He set string to his great bow, Sarnga — and the note it made silenced the battlefield.
stories.reflection: The battle turns on an enemy who fights by theft rather than slaughter, taking warriors whole instead of killing them. Against a power that hides itself, no formation avails, and the story's edge is that the fury which finally answers it belongs not to the army but to Krishna alone.
stories.content_note: Battle violence with restraint: warriors are captured and imprisoned rather than killed.
stories.next_story_tease: But the Sarnga bow was already strung.

stories.title: Fire Ranging on Grass
stories.subtitle: The Sarnga bow answers the Asura host at Shatpura.
stories.story:
When Krishna set string to the Sarnga bow, the Asuras saw their death approaching — and, being Asuras, they charged straight into it.

Anadhrishti and the other Yadava captains had been swallowed by the cave of Shatpura, taken one by one through the illusion of Nikumbha, the leader of the Danavas. The Yadava army still stood, but its heart lay imprisoned in the mountain. Only one answer was left, and Krishna gave it: he drew the Sarnga and moved among the Danavas.

He moved as fire ranges over dry grass — not running, not pausing, simply advancing, and everything ahead of him burned. Wherever he stepped, the Danava host found itself standing in the path of a blaze. The Danavas did not understand what they were seeing. To them he was one man with a bow, and they had a mountain's worth of weapons. They seized thousands of spiked clubs and iron maces, fiery lances and burning axes; they tore up great rocks and boulders; they hurled maddened elephants, chariots and horses — and ran at him with all of it, like locusts driven by the noose of Death into a burning fire. The whole arsenal of the mountain came down on Krishna in one tremendous shower.

The fire of Narayana — Krishna's own fire — consumed it all. The flung weapons, the stones, the elephants, the chariots: everything met the blaze of his arrows and was gone. And Krishna, smiling, baffled them all, standing under the downpour as a bull stands in autumn rain, patient, unhurt, untouched.

Then the host tried to run. Some broke for the sky, rising on whatever dark power they had left, seeking the one direction an army believes is safe: upward, into the open air.

It was not safe. The sky was not empty. Above the field, hidden where only Krishna could see them, waited Indra's son Jayanta and the brahmana Pravara, called up by a single thought before the battle began. As soon as any Asura rose into the sky, their arrows met him, and he fell. The survivors looked up and understood, too late, that the one direction they had left unguarded was guarded. The sky had become a wall.

Caught between the fire on the ground and the silent archers above, the Danavas had nowhere left to turn. Their numbers, their weapons, their fury — all of it ash in the path of one archer. The plain filled with the wreck of their courage; their roar died into the dust, and the rout that Nikumbha's illusion had postponed came at last, in full.

Krishna lowered the Sarnga. The fire had done its ranging, and the grass was gone. Beyond the smoke stood the cave of Shatpura, still holding its prisoners.

The battle was won. The cave was not.
stories.reflection: The rout has the shape of a parable about fear: the host that charges a burning fire, and the few who escape, are met by the one force they forgot, the sky, where Jayanta and Pravara have waited unseen all along. Krishna's calm throughout, smiling and bearing the shower like a bull in rain, is the story's true wonder.
stories.content_note: Battle violence described with restraint; no graphic detail.
stories.next_story_tease: The rout was complete, and only the question of what would be done with the conquered city remained.

stories.title: Shatpura for Brahmadatta
stories.subtitle: After the victory, the conqueror gives the city away.
stories.story:
The kings who had gambled on the Asura side now sat as prisoners in the Yadavas' camp, and when the Danavas of Shatpura saw it, fear finally entered their hearts.

They had been routed by Krishna and the Yadavas and had fled in every direction. Now their allies were captives and their stronghold surrounded, and the war they had promised to win was lost. Nikumbha alone refused to accept it. Filled with anger, he turned on his own fleeing host. "Why do you break your promise and run?" he cried. "You swore to avenge the destruction of your kinsmen. If you are slain in battle, you will live happily in heaven among the gods. But if you flee, whose face will you look upon in your own house? What will your wives say? Shame on you, all of you!"

Burning with shame, the Asuras turned back and threw themselves at the Yadavas with double fury. It did not save them. At the sacrificial ground, where the pavilions of the rite still stood, the five Pandava brothers — Yudhishthira, Bhima, Arjuna, Nakula and Sahadeva, who had guarded the sacrifice from the first — cut down all who came; and those who tried to escape by rising into the sky were slain by Indra's son Jayanta and the brahmana Pravara, still on watch above the field. The field ran red; a river of blood flowed down from the mountain Govinda, and its fish were the swords of the fallen.

Only Nikumbha kept the old courage. Seeing his comrades slain and the enemy's power growing, he leaped up and fought on, and Jayanta and Pravara met him with arrows like thunderbolts. The great Asura struck Pravara down with his iron club, and the brahmana fell to earth; but Indra's son caught him up in his arms, embraced him, found him still alive, and set him down before turning on the Asura. Arrow after arrow he buried in Nikumbha's body, until the wounded Nikumbha, thinking of the slayer of his kinsmen whom he had sworn to avenge, broke off the fight and vanished, making his way to where Krishna stood. And Indra himself, seated on Airavata, his white elephant, came down with the gods to witness the battle; and embracing his victorious son and Pravara, he had the trumpets of heaven sounded over the field.

When the last Asura had fallen or fled, the plain fell silent. The war was over.

Krishna then did what conquerors are not expected to do. He gave the victory away. The kings who had been taken with their followers — the rulers who had sided with the Danavas — were brought before him. Instead of punishment they received jewels and fine raiment from his hand. For them the war ended not in chains but in gifts.

To the Yadavas, his own people, he gave the hundreds of maidens of the conquered demon city. To the Pandavas, who had guarded the sacrifice and fought beside him, he gave six thousand chariots with their horses — a gift that made the five brothers wealthy beyond any campaign.

And then came the last and strangest gift. In the conquered city of Shatpura — the lair from which the Danavas had poured out to war — there lived a brahmana named Brahmadatta. Krishna summoned him and granted him the city itself, caves, walls and all.

The warriors around him must have wondered. They had bled for this ground, watched their captains vanish into that mountain, seen their friends carried off — and Krishna placed it all in the hands of a priest. Yet perhaps the explanation lay in the gift itself: he had not conquered Shatpura to hold it. He had conquered it to give it away.

So the Asura city, which had known only war, passed into the keeping of a man of peace, while the Yadavas, laden with honor and chariots, turned their faces toward home.
stories.reflection: The distribution is the true conquest: after a war fought with bows and illusions, Krishna's first act is to undo what wars do, restoring captives, honoring the kings who opposed him, enriching the allies, and handing the enemy's stronghold to a brahmana. Spoils in his hands become gifts, and the conquered city becomes a bequest.
stories.next_story_tease: Aboard the boats that carried them onward, the Yadavas were about to learn a song from heaven.

stories.title: Heaven Sings at Sea
stories.subtitle: The celestial Chhalikya song comes down to the Yadava fleet.
stories.story:
The war at Shatpura, the city of the demons, was over. Krishna and his people, the Yadavas, were at sea — the fleet that carried the Yadava court had sailed out into open water — and there, at Krishna's command, a celebration began such as the world had never heard.

It began with Balarama, Krishna's elder brother. Warmed by wine, his eyes gently reddened, he sat sporting with Revati, the daughter of King Revata, looking at her face and finding in it all the delight he needed. Seeing his brother so content, Krishna summoned the Apsaras, the dancers of heaven, and the beautiful women came to the boats to please Balarama and Revati. They had dressed themselves as the women of the Yadava country. They saluted the couple first, and then, as the couple wished and the Yadavas asked, they danced in time, displaying gesture after gesture of the celestial dance, and sang, in the Yadava tongue, songs set to a thousand tunes.

And the songs they sang were the deeds of Krishna himself. They sang of Kamsa's destruction and the fall of Pralamba and Chanura; of the child tied to the mortar, who earned the name Damodara; of Putana's end and the great trees pulled up by the roots; of the serpent Kaliya pressed down in the lake; of Govardhan held aloft on one hand for the sake of Gokula; of the hump-backed woman cured, the dwarf form assumed, the wolves sent against the forest, the flying city Saubha brought down, Subhadra carried away from her brothers, the battle with Valahaka and Jamvumali, and the jewels taken from Indra himself. Every wonder of his life came back to him as song, sung before the whole company — and Balarama, delighted, began to sing with Revati, clapping the time.

Krishna, to please his brother, sang with Satyabhama. Arjuna, who had come aboard for the sea voyage, joined his sister Subhadra and Krishna in the singing. Then the whole fleet joined in — Gada and Sarana, Pradyumna, Samba and Satyaki, Charudeshna; Balarama's sons Nishatha and Ulmukha; the commander Akrura, Sankha, and all the leading heroes of the Yadava house — and sang together in one great chorus. By Krishna's power the boats themselves grew to hold them all, and the music carried over the water until the whole world was filled with joy and the sins of those who listened were washed away.

Then Narada came down — the wandering singer of heaven, guest of the celestials — bearing his vina, the stringed instrument he carried on all his travels. He played, and he sang for Krishna with such intensity that a portion of his matted hair melted away in the heat of his own devotion. He composed songs on the spot and sang them again and again with every gesture his body could make. He smiled on Balarama and Revati, on Krishna and Arjuna, on Satyabhama and Subhadra; and though Krishna's wives were patient by nature, the sage who loved a joke made them laugh whether they wished to or not. He sang tunes high and low, laughed aloud, and wept tears of joy.

And Krishna himself danced. To the music of his own flute he performed the dance called the Hallishaka before them all, and the Apsaras answered him step for step — the beautiful Rambha rising to dance before Balarama and Krishna, and Urvashi with her.

The celestial song called the Chhalikya, which until that day had been heard only in heaven, was brought down then and sung for mankind — and the world listened from its rooftops and its boats.

When the music finally ended, the dancers of heaven moved through the company at Krishna's command, giving away the best jewels of the earth, beautiful raiments and garlands, until every guest was laden with gifts. And the fleet sailed on, singing: heaven's song riding on mortal water, where a boy's deeds were remembered, and the war was, for one night, nothing but a song.
stories.reflection: The soiree turns the war's end into a festival of memory: every great deed of Krishna's life is sung back to him, and the celestial Chhalikya is brought down to human ears. Heaven does not stay above, it comes aboard the boats, dances, and weeps with joy, and the story's quiet point is that the divine rejoices to be remembered by the world it saved.
stories.next_story_tease: The celebration ended, and Nikumbha still lived.

stories.title: A Thousand Nikumbhas, One True Head
stories.story:
The Yadavas had won their war, and while they were busy at their sports the demon Nikumbha found his chance. The garden of Bhanu's women's quarters was supposed to be unapproachable; that was precisely why it stood unguarded. Years before, Pradyumna, the son of Krishna, had carried off Prabhavati, the daughter of Nikumbha's brother Vajranabha, and the demon had never forgiven the insult. Now he slipped in, seized Bhanumati, the beautiful daughter of Bhanu, and was gone before the weeping could even begin.

When the lamentation reached the men's quarters, Vasudeva — Krishna's father — and the elder Ahuka rushed out in fury and found only an empty garden. They went straight to Krishna. He asked no questions and called no council: with his friend Arjuna beside him he mounted Garuda, his great winged carrier; he ordered Pradyumna, whose banner bore the makara, a creature of the sea, to follow in his chariot; and he set off in pursuit. They caught Nikumbha long before he could reach the city of Vajra and the safety of his kinsmen.

The fight that followed was stranger than any of them had expected. Nikumbha fought smiling, a heavy club in his right hand and the weeping Bhanumati in his left, and because of her no one could strike him. Krishna, Pradyumna and Arjuna could have killed the demon a dozen times over; none of them could bear to wound the maiden. Arjuna, the finest of archers, solved the riddle the way a skilled man handles a serpent coiled around a camel: he struck the serpent and left the camel alone. His arrows, thin as reeds, found the demon again and again without ever touching the girl.

Then Nikumbha changed the game, for illusion was his art. In a single breath he and the maiden vanished so completely that even his pursuers could not tell where they had gone. A yellow vulture crossed the sky, and Arjuna's arrows bit into it — the demon, transformed, was fleeing. The chase carried them across all seven continents, until at last Nikumbha dropped onto the summit of Mount Gokarna, on the bank of the river Chela Ganga — a mountain guarded by the power of Mahadeva, the great god Shiva, which no god, demon or ascetic could cross.

He had chosen well — but not well enough. Pradyumna, himself a master of illusion, slipped past the demon's guard and snatched Bhanumati away, while Krishna and Arjuna drove Nikumbha back with arrows until he fled from the northern slope of the mountain to the southern. With Krishna's permission Pradyumna carried the maiden home to Dwaraka and returned at once, to find Krishna and Arjuna waiting at the mouth of the cave where Nikumbha had vanished — the hidden entrance to Shatpura, the city of his demon kin.

All night the three kept watch there. At dawn the demon came out to fight. Arjuna's arrows from the Gandiva, his great bow, sealed the passage — but Nikumbha broke through them, seized his thorn-covered club, and struck Arjuna full on the head. Blood poured from the hero's mouth and he fell senseless; the master of illusions snatched him up and carried him off. And then, all at once, the earth and the sky were full of demons.

Thousands of Nikumbhas filled the heavens — on the earth and in the sky, in every direction, identical faces, identical clubs, identical smiles. Every eye saw a thousand demons. Krishna saw only one. With a sight older than the world and its illusions, he perceived the true form of the creator of illusions standing among his own echoes, and the discus left his hand and flew true. It cut off the head of the real Nikumbha — and in that instant every false Nikumbha dissolved like mist at sunrise. The demon who had filled the sky with himself was gone, and Arjuna, whom he had carried off, was free.

The gates of Shatpura stood open and empty behind them. Krishna gathered his friend up onto Garuda, and they turned toward Dwaraka — leaving behind a city whose master had been destroyed by the very illusion he had trusted.
stories.reflection: The thousand Nikumbhas are defeated not by force but by perception: Krishna wins the moment he sees through the illusion to the single true form behind it. Notice too that the whole pursuit was shaped by compassion — the heroes refused to strike until the maiden could be spared, so the killing blow came only when the fight could be finished cleanly.
stories.content_note: Mild battle violence: a hero is knocked unconscious and a demon is beheaded by the discus; described without graphic detail.
stories.next_story_tease: But Nikumbha had a brother, and that brother had already begun to ask the universe for a gift that would threaten all three worlds.

stories.title: Vajranabha Demands the Three Worlds
stories.story:
On the summit of Mount Sumeru, the mountain at the centre of the world, a demon king named Vajranabha sat in penance so severe that its heat reached the throne of Brahma, the creator of all worlds. Vajranabha was no ordinary demon, and he wanted no ordinary power: he wanted to be unkillable, and he wanted a home that nothing could enter. When Brahma, pleased by his penance, appeared before him and offered a boon, the demon asked for two gifts — that even the gods might never be able to kill him, and that he might possess the city Vajra, where even the air could not enter without his will: a city that gave its lord whatever he desired before he had even thought of it, ringed by gardens and walls, surrounded by branch cities, full of peerless gems.

Brahma granted both gifts, and Vajranabha moved into Vajra. Millions of demons came to live there under his protection, filling the central city, its gardens and its charming branch cities — healthy, well-fed and contented — while their king enjoyed the boon he had demanded. No enemy had ever been known to pass those walls, and no one in the three worlds had found the door.

For a time that satisfied him. Then pride finished what penance had begun, and the king of the demons decided that the three worlds were not the gods' to keep. He stood before Indra, the king of heaven, and announced his claim. 'All three worlds,' he said, 'belong to the high-born sons of Kashyapa — and I am one of them. I wish to govern them. If you do not approve of my proposal, give me battle.'

Indra answered with patience instead of war. He consulted Brihaspati, the wise priest of the gods, and then replied: 'Our father, the ascetic Kashyapa, is now engaged in a sacrifice. When it is finished, he will do what is fair.' Vajranabha carried the same demand to Kashyapa himself — the ancient sage who was father to gods and demons alike — and heard the same words: go back to Vajra, live self-controlled, and wait for the sacrifice to end.

The demon returned to his city to wait — and while he waited, the gods were not idle. Indra went secretly to Dwaraka and told Krishna everything Vajranabha had said. Krishna's answer was calm and complete: 'My father's horse-sacrifice is at hand — the grandest rite a king can offer. When it is over, I will kill Vajranabha. But since even the wind cannot enter his city unless he wishes it, we will find our own way in.'

And the way in was already taking shape. During the horse-sacrifice, a wandering actor named Bhadra so charmed the assembled sages with his art that they offered him any boon he desired. It is said that Krishna's wish moved his heart, and the goddess of learning herself guided his tongue — for Bhadra asked for strange gifts: to range freely over the earth and the sky, to be slain by no creature that moves or stands still, to take any form he pleased, to be never touched by age, and to find the sages always pleased with him. The sages said, 'So be it' — and Bhadra became the one being in all creation who could go anywhere and be welcomed everywhere. He began to wander the cities of the demon kings, performing for them, and on every festival day he came to Dwaraka, where the Yadavas received him as a guest of honour.

The plan was quiet, and it was already complete. And in heaven, Indra was speaking to the swans — the celestial birds who carry the gods and the pious across the sky, and are themselves children of Kashyapa, brothers to the gods. To them he spoke of the great duty that now lay before the gods: the destruction of their enemies.
stories.reflection: The boon that made Vajranabha untouchable also made him predictable: a king who cannot be killed and a city that cannot be entered will be defeated through exactly that logic — by someone who can go anywhere and take any form. Boons answer words, not intentions, and pride read his own wish as a promise of safety.
stories.next_story_tease: The actor's boon was the key to Vajra — and soon the Yadavas would carry it through the city's unbreachable gates disguised as a company of players.

stories.title: The Play That Drained a City
stories.story:
The demon king Vajranabha could not be killed, and his city of Vajra could not be entered — even the wind could not pass its walls unless he willed it. So Krishna chose a way in that had nothing to do with walls: a play. By the time the company of actors reached the lands of the demons, its fame ran ahead of it. Everywhere they performed, the demons rose from their seats, delighted, and pressed jewels into their hands; in the city of Supura the people were so enchanted that they begged for more. What the demons never guessed was that the troupe's newest players were not actors at all — they were Pradyumna, the son of Krishna, with Gada, Shamba and the other Yadava heroes in the costumes of the stage, led by Bhadra, the actor who had been granted the boon to wander freely through all three worlds.

When Vajranabha heard of the marvellous actors, he did what any patron of the arts would do: he sent a messenger and invited them in. The demons of the branch cities brought the troupe to the city of Vajra, lodged them in a house built by the celestial architect, and supplied everything they could need, by the hundred. Vajranabha raised a beautiful pavilion and made a festival of the visit. The women of his family watched from behind a screen, where they could see everything; the king himself sat among his kinsmen. And the actors began.

First came the instruments — bells, flutes and drums — and then the women of the troupe sang the celestial song called the Chhalikya, the very music the Yadavas had brought down from heaven. They sang of the descent of the Ganga, the heavenly river, in seven scales and three modes and in the springtime raga called Vasanta — so sweetly that the demons rose again and again to heap rewards on them. Then came the Ramayana itself: they acted the birth of Vishnu, who came into the world to destroy the demon king Ravana, and how the young sage Rishyashringa was brought to King Dasharatha's court. The demons were startled by the likeness of the players — it seemed impossible that actors should resemble Rama, Lakshmana and Bharata so closely — and they rose from their seats, called out their praise, and gave away necklaces of gold and precious stone, bracelets and cloth.

After the Ramayana, Pradyumna himself, still in the guise of an actor, conducted the prologue with Gada and Shamba, and then sang the hymn of the Ganga's descent with beautiful gestures. Then came the drama called Rambhabhisara. Shura played Ravana, Monovati played Rambha — the dancer of heaven whom Ravana had wronged — Pradyumna played Nalakuvara, and Shamba was his jester. By their powers of illusion the Yadavas conjured the very scene of Mount Kailasha, and acted how the furious Nalakuvara cursed the wicked Ravana, and how Rambha was consoled.

The demons of Vajra were enchanted. Costly garments, jewelled necklaces, chariots that rode the sky, celestial elephants, cool sandalwood and rare perfumes — and at last the fabled gem Chintamani, which grants whatever its owner thinks of — all of it rained down upon the actors, scene after scene, until the treasuries of the demon lords ran dry. Even the women of the demon chiefs gave away their jewels. The demons were being emptied of their riches, in the very act of trying to spend them.

Only slowly did they understand what they had done. They had paid their enemies to entertain them — and the Yadavas, welcomed through gates that no army could ever have breached, had walked into the unbreachable city of Vajra.

Behind the screen, where the women of the demon king's own family sat watching, a quieter message was arriving. Vajranabha's daughter Prabhavati had heard from her friend Suchimukhi — a goose, who could fly where she pleased — and Suchimukhi whispered that she had been to Dwaraka and seen Pradyumna himself, and that he had appointed this very evening to meet her. 'The Yadavas never speak an untruth,' said the goose, 'and Pradyumna has given his word. Tonight you will see your love.'
stories.reflection: The city that no army could enter was entered by applause: the demons paid their enemies to entertain them and never suspected that the pleasure they bought was their own ruin. There is something almost courteous in the way the Yadavas take Vajra — not by storm, but by invitation.
stories.next_story_tease: The emptied treasuries were only the beginning, for Vajranabha had already set his heart on conquering heaven.

stories.title: A Father's Warning, a Son's March
stories.story:
The great sacrifice of Kashyapa was over, and the gods and demons had returned to their own worlds — all but one. Vajranabha, the lord of the unbreachable city of Vajra, had decided that the three worlds belonged to him, and he had gone home to prepare for war. He came to his father Kashyapa expecting a blessing — and received a warning instead.

'Indra, the king of heaven, is the eldest of you all,' said Kashyapa, 'and the foremost in accomplishments. He is mighty through his own penance, devoted to the learned and the holy, the king of the whole world and the refuge of the good. He holds his sovereignty because he works for the well-being of all creatures. You will not vanquish him, Vajranabha — you yourself will be killed, as surely as a man who rouses a serpent's anger meets his own end.'

Vajranabha heard the words as a man in love with death hears a physician's warning — and refused the remedy. He saluted Kashyapa, turned away, and began to gather his kinsmen, his warriors, his friends. He would conquer the three worlds — and he would begin with heaven itself.

But the gods were already ahead of him. Indra and Krishna had sent the swans — the celestial birds, children of Kashyapa and brothers of the gods — to bring about Vajranabha's destruction. When the swans carried word that the demon was marching on heaven, the Yadava heroes held a worried council in the city of Vajra, where they waited with their wives. 'Vajranabha will be killed by Pradyumna,' they said. 'But his daughter is Pradyumna's wife, and Sunabha's daughters are wives of our heroes — all with child, their time near. What are we to do?'

They sent the swans back to Indra and Krishna with the question, and the gods answered with a promise: 'Do not fear. You will have beautiful sons, as gifted as Kama, the god of love himself — even in the womb they will master the sacred scriptures — and your sons will grow to youth at once, masters of every art and every scripture.'

The swans carried the promise to the city of Vajra. There Prabhavati bore Pradyumna a son, omniscient and youthful like his father; a month later Chandravati bore Chandraprabha, who resembled Gada; and Gunavati bore Gunavan — all youthful, omniscient, wonderful. The boys mastered every scripture as they grew and played freely on the palace turrets, where the demons on watch in the sky saw them — shown to them by the very wish of Indra and Krishna.

The watchers carried the news at once to Vajranabha, who was making ready to conquer heaven. 'Arrest them!' cried the demon king. 'They have trespassed into my house!' Soldiers ringed the quarters, and cries rose on every side: 'Seize them! Kill them!' The mothers, who loved their sons, began to weep.

Pradyumna stood firm among them. 'So long as we are alive and steady, you need not fear. The demons will not be able to touch us.' Then he turned to the bewildered Prabhavati. 'Your father and uncles and brothers wait outside with clubs in their hands, and for your sake they deserve our respect and honour — but the time is dreadful. If we endure this, we die; if we fight, we succeed. Consult your two sisters, and tell us what we should do, for we are under your orders.'

Prabhavati knelt, her hands on her forehead, weeping. 'Take up your arms and protect yourself. If you survive, you will see your wife and your sons. Remember the noble Rukmini, your mother, and your young son Aniruddha, and save yourself. A great sage gave me a boon — that I would lead a blameless life, never be a widow, and my sons would live — and I hope his words will not fail.' She rinsed her mouth, and placed a sword in her husband's hands.

Beyond the city, the armies of Vajranabha were gathering for the march on heaven. Within it, a woman who carried a sage's promise had armed her husband for the war that would test it.
stories.reflection: Kashyapa's warning is not a threat but an account of how sovereignty actually works: Indra rules because he serves the well-being of all creatures, not because he is the strongest. Vajranabha hears only the prophecy of death and marches toward it. Set against his pride is Prabhavati, a daughter of the enemy who arms her Yadava husband on the strength of a rishi's word — boon against boon, promise against promise.
stories.next_story_tease: Meanwhile Dwaraka was preparing a different kind of return — one that would bring the parijata tree and the captive maidens of Naraka's house back to Krishna's city.

stories.title: Homecoming with the Parijata
stories.story:
The war against Naraka, the demon king, was over — and Krishna was flying home. From the back of Garuda, the great bird who carried him, he looked down on Dwarka, his city by the sea — and the city looked back at him like a long-awaited answer.

He saw his own house rising among hundreds of palaces — the dark palace of the Yadavas, its gates bright with a million white jeweled pillars, gems lustrous as fire, and golden seats set here and there for his court. For his welcome a great palace had been raised entirely of gold, with pillars of crystal, ringed by lakes full of lotuses and fragrant red lotuses, where peacocks and koel birds called from the trees and golden stairways led down to the water. The celestial architect Viswakarma had enclosed the whole with stone walls a hundred yards high, girded with ditches — a plot half a yojana on every side, measured, men said, against the palace of Indra himself.

Then Krishna raised the Panchajanya — his great conch — to his lips and blew. The sound made the hair of his enemies stand on end; the ocean was stirred to its depths and the sky resounded; and to those who heard it in Dwarka it was the most wonderful sound in the world. At the note of the conch, and at the sight of Garuda circling down, his own kinsmen, the Kukuras and the Andhakas, felt their sorrow fall away. There he was — Krishna, bright as the sun, conch, discus and club in his hands, seated on the great bird. The citizens' joy spilled over: trumpets sounded, bugles blew, and men raised leonine shouts of triumph, while the Kukuras, the Andhakas and the other Yadava clans crowded toward him, their joy overflowing.

King Ugrasena, the ruler of the Yadavas, set Vasudeva — Krishna's father — before him and made his way to Vasudeva's palace to the sound of conches and trumpets. In their houses Devaki, Krishna's mother, and Rohini and the other women of the household moved about with joy. A few moments later Krishna arrived at the house prepared for him.

He alighted at the entrance and showed proper respect to all the Yadus, his elders and kinsmen. Balarama, his elder brother, honoured him, and Ahuka, Gada and Pradyumna and the rest; and so welcomed, Krishna entered his residence with the mountain of jewels beside him. Pradyumna, his son, carried in the Parijata, the tree that was Indra's own favourite. By the power of that celestial tree the heroes saw their own forms made beautiful, and took great delight. Praised by the rejoicing Yadava chiefs, Krishna passed into the house Viswakarma had built, placed the mountain of jewels with its shining summits in his inner apartments, and then, with his kinsmen about him, worshipped the celestial tree and planted it in its proper place.

There remained one more homecoming. With his kinsmen's permission, Krishna honoured every maiden he had brought back from Naraka's house — the women the demon king had held captive — giving them raiments, ornaments, servants, riches and every object of enjoyment. Devaki, his mother, with Rohini and the other women of the house, had already received them with honour. By good fortune Satyabhama ruled over all the women of the household, while Rukmini, his queen, was in charge of the relatives. And to each of those women Krishna allotted her own house, her own tank, her own garden.

So the city that had sent him to war received him home with trumpets and gold; and the women Naraka had hidden away came out into the light of Dwarka, each with a place to call her own. The Parijata, planted in its proper place, began to change the air of the city, and the mountain of jewels stood in the inner apartments like a promise kept.
stories.reflection: The return to Dwarka is complete only when the women Naraka had kept captive are given homes of their own. The treasure Krishna brings back is not measured in jewels but in the shape it gives to freedom: separate houses, tanks and gardens, one for each of the maidens.
stories.next_story_tease: But beyond the rejoicing city, the war was not over: Rudra's terrible fever-demon, Jvara, still waited on the field where the Asuras had fled.

stories.title: When Fever Consumed Baladeva
stories.story:
Krishna had marched on Sonitpura, the city of Vana, the thousand-armed demon king, to win back his young grandson whom Vana held prisoner — and Vana's great army had come out to stop him. All day the host had held the field. Now it broke before four fighters moving together like one storm, and the battle showed its true face.

Krishna's elder brother Balarama fought with a plough, and his ploughshare was like a hook: he drew the enemy close and ground them down with his heavy mace, raging as if he meant to swallow the whole field. Krishna's son Pradyumna kept the demons at bay with his arrows. Krishna himself — dark as a storm cloud — blew his conch and fought every way at once, conch, discus and club always in his hands. The great eagle Garuda struck among them too, beating the demons with his wings and tearing at them with beak and claws until he sent them to the realm of Yama, king of the dead. Pounded by that rain of arrows and overpowered by those four, the demon army turned and fled.

Seeing his host routed, one of Shiva's own followers came walking onto the field to protect it: Jvara, the demon of fever. He sighed again and again like a man out of his wits, and his shape was stranger than any demon's — three legs, three heads, six arms, and nine faces. He carried a weapon that consumed whatever it touched. He roared like a thousand storm clouds, and as he came he yawned and nodded, his hair standing on end, his eyes filthy and terrible. He twisted his many faces into something still more terrible and shouted at Balarama: "Why are you so proud of your strength? Do you not see that I have come to this field? Wait a few moments. You stood against me in this battle — you will not return with your life."

Smiling, showing a fist dreadful as the fire that ends a world, Jvara ran at Balarama. But Balarama was too quick: he wheeled in one swift circle after another, and the demon could find no opening. At last, aiming at that body huge as a mountain, Jvara hurled his burning weapon. It struck Balarama on the breast. Then it dropped from his breast and fell on the summit of Mount Sumeru, far beyond the field, and shattered the great mountain into pieces. But a remnant of the fire stayed where it had struck — and it began to consume Krishna's elder brother.

The warrior who had stood unshaken against whole armies now reeled about the field, sighing and yawning without end, his eyes wide, his hair on end, his senses swimming. Almost losing hold of himself, he cried out: "Krishna! I am being consumed — I am being consumed completely. How shall I be saved?"

Krishna smiled. "No fear," he said.

And he embraced his brother. At that embrace, at the touch of Krishna, the burning that had begun to eat Balarama went out. He was saved, there in his brother's arms.

Then Krishna turned, angry now, to the demon. "Jvara," he said, "come and fight with me. Show me the full extent of your strength and power in this battle."

The fever-demon raised his burning weapon again — and the field went still.
stories.reflection: The mightiest warrior on that field is not laid low by an army but by fever, something small and formless; and the cure is not a weapon but an embrace. Krishna answers his brother's despair with two words, 'No fear,' and the burning goes out at his touch.

stories.title: The Grapple with the Fever-Demon
stories.story:
Vana, the thousand-armed demon king, had met Krishna and his kinsmen in battle outside his city of Sonitpura, and to help Vana the god Shiva had sent creatures of his own to fight — among them Jvara, the demon of fever. Jvara's burning weapon had very nearly consumed Balarama, Krishna's elder brother, before Krishna put the fire out with an embrace. Now the field lay empty around the two of them, and Krishna had called the demon out. "Come and fight with me," he had said. "Show me the full extent of your strength and power in this battle."

Jvara — three-legged, three-headed, six-armed, nine-faced, and never without his consuming weapon — answered with the weapon already burning. Around them the field had emptied: the demon army had fled, and only the two of them stood face to face in the middle of it.

With his right hand Jvara hurled his great burning weapon straight at Krishna's body. It struck home, and for a few moments Krishna felt it burning. Then the fire went out. It had touched him, spent itself against him, and died — the way fire dies when it meets what it cannot consume.

Then Jvara came at him, his long arms reaching like serpents. He struck Krishna on the neck and dealt him a blow across the breast, and there in the middle of the field a great duel began between the fever-demon and the man who would not be moved. The sound of their blows rolled across the plain like thunder against a mountain summit. Blow for blow they traded strokes that would have felled whole armies. The demon could range through the sky; Krishna stood planted on his ground. And strange to hear above the din, words kept coming out of the fight as if one fighter were teaching the other: "Do not strike this way. Strike this way."

For a long moment Krishna — who in truth was the lord of the universe, hidden in the body of a man — fought as if his own end were possible, as if this one body were all he had. Then he caught the fever-demon in his arms and began to crush him, grinding the golden, sky-ranging Jvara the way a pestle grinds grain, until the demon's strength ran out of him like water from a broken jar. The whole duel had lasted a moment. That moment decided everything.

At last Krishna threw the broken Jvara down upon the earth, and for a moment he believed the field was won.

But the fever-demon, released from that crushing embrace, did not flee the field. He did what no beaten enemy had done before: he entered Krishna's body and was gone.
stories.reflection: In the midst of the duel come strange words of instruction, 'Do not strike this way, strike this way,' as though the fight itself were a lesson being given and received. And Krishna, wearing a mortal body, lets the burning touch him for a few moments before it goes out: even what wounds him is held within his own order.
stories.content_note: A wrestling duel between Krishna and the demon Jvara; described without gore.

stories.title: Fever Driven Out by Fever
stories.story:
In the great battle outside Sonitpura, the city of the thousand-armed demon king Vana, Krishna had faced the strangest of all Vana's defenders: Jvara, the demon of fever, whom the god Shiva had made and sent to fight. Krishna had caught the demon in his arms and ground him down until he hung limp. Certain that he was finished, he threw Jvara to the earth.

He was wrong — and the mistake cost him more than any blow of the battle had. Released from that crushing grip, the fever-demon of unspent strength did not leave the field. He slipped into Krishna's own body.

Possessed by fever, Krishna's movements slowed. The man who had taken enemy cities had to steady himself again and again with one hand on the ground. Sleep pressed upon him, his steps faltered, his hair stood on end, and he sighed and yawned without ceasing. The fighter who had just crushed a demon in his arms was brought low by the demon's last trick — and it was a long time before he regained his natural state.

Then, knowing what was in him, Krishna did what no one else could have done. From his own strength he called forth a fever of his own: a second Jvara, dreadful to every creature, made for one purpose — the destruction of the first.

The fever he had made seized the first Jvara by force, dragged him out of Krishna's body, and set him before his maker. So the fever that had entered Krishna was driven out by fever itself.

Krishna struck the demon down to the ground and was about to tear him to pieces. Bewildered, Jvara cried out: "Krishna, it is for you to protect me!"

And as Krishna's hand hung raised, a voice without a body spoke from the sky: "Do not kill this Jvara. He is worthy of being protected by you."

Krishna heard, and let the fever-demon go. Jvara prostrated himself, his head bowed at Krishna's feet. "Grant me this one boon," he said. "Let me alone be the fever in this world, and let no other fever flourish beside me."

"It is proper to grant a boon to one who prays for it," Krishna said, "and you have asked for my protection. So be it, Jvara. As before, you will be the only fever — and the one I created will dissolve back into me."

The fever Krishna had made — the cure that had driven out the sickness — dissolved into its source and vanished, as everything made from him returns to him. Then Krishna told the demon how he would move through the world from that day on, and gave him one promise more: any person who greets Krishna with respect and reads this account of the great battle with attention will be freed from fever.

"So be it," said Jvara, delighted. He saluted Krishna and took himself from the field, and this time the burning did not follow him home.
stories.reflection: The episode turns on a strange symmetry: fever is driven out by fever, the cure created from the same energy as the disease and then dissolved back into its source. And even the demon who had possessed him, once he asked for protection, was spared: in Krishna's world, even fever is answered when it prays.
stories.next_story_tease: But Jvara was not done: before he left the field, the spared demon would receive the terms of his rule over every living thing.

stories.title: The Only Fever in the World
stories.subtitle: Krishna spares the defeated Jvara and grants him dominion over fever
stories.story:
The great battle of Sonitpura had stopped. An invisible voice had spoken out of the sky, and god and demon alike on that field had gone still.

It was a war that had drawn the gods themselves in: Krishna had come against Vana, the thousand-armed king who served Shiva, and Shiva had sent his own creatures to fight for Vana. One of them was Jvara, the fever. Earlier, the burning demon had slipped inside Krishna's body — for a while Krishna's steps had grown heavy, his hair had stood on end, he had yawned and sighed without cease and steadied himself with one hand on the ground, until at last he shook the weakness off. He had drawn the demon out by creating from his own strength a second fever, more dreadful than the first, which had seized Jvara and dragged him from Krishna's body. Now the creature lay pinned under Krishna's hand, and Krishna, angry, had thrown him to the earth and was about to tear him apart — when the voice spoke: "Do not kill this Jvara. He is worthy of being protected by you."

Krishna heard, and let the fever go. Jvara rose and prostrated himself at Krishna's feet. "Grant me this one boon," he said. "Let me be the only fever in this world, and let no other flourish beside me."

"It is proper to grant a boon to one who asks for it," Krishna said, "and you have asked for my protection. Go in peace, Jvara. You will have what you pray for. As before, you will be the only fever — and may the one I created dissolve in me."

And the counter-fever Krishna had made melted back into his own being, as frost melts into the morning.

Then Krishna told the fever how it would live from that day on. "Divide yourself into three parts. With one, enter the four-legged animals; with the second, the trees and stones and all things that do not move; with the third, human beings. And of that third part, take a fourth portion, and let it live always among the birds." So among people the fever would come in four forms — returning every day, after two days, after three days, and after four. In trees it would live as the blight that pales the leaves, in fruit as blight, in lotuses as frost, in the earth as drought, in water as the weed that chokes it, in peacocks as the growing crest, in mountains as mineral, in cattle as sickness. "By your very sight and touch," Krishna said, "animals will lose their lives. Only gods and men will be able to withstand you."

Jvara was delighted. He folded his hands and saluted Krishna. "I am blessed that you give me rule over all creatures and things. I was made long ago by Shiva himself; now, vanquished by you in battle, I am your servant. Command me, and I will obey."

"Then hear the wish I cherish," Krishna said. "Any man who greets me with respect and reads this account of the great battle with full attention will be freed from fever."

"So be it," said Jvara. He saluted Krishna and left the battlefield — carrying with him, in the very shape of his existence, the mercy that had spared him.
stories.reflection: Jvara asks not for safety but for supremacy — he wants to remain the only fever in the world — and Krishna grants the wish while redrawing its limits: the fever may range everywhere, but it returns in measured forms, and the telling of its defeat is promised to free men from it. Mercy, here, is not the erasure of an enemy but the reshaping of his power.
stories.next_story_tease: But the fever was only one of Vana's defenders — Shiva himself was already riding toward the battlefield.
stories.hero_scene: On the Sonitpura battlefield the defeated Jvara, a gaunt burning figure, prostrates with bent head at Krishna's feet while Krishna, radiant, raises a hand in blessing and the counter-fever he created dissolves into mist behind him.

stories.title: The Lion-Drawn Car Enters Battle
stories.subtitle: Shiva and Kartikeya ride out to protect Vana
stories.story:
Krishna, his brother Balarama and his son Pradyumna had ridden the great eagle Garuda into the war at Sonitpura, where Vana, the thousand-armed demon king, had come out with all his host to stop them. Half of that host was running now — and the rest was burning.

The three heroes, blazing like three fires, had swept down on the demon ranks with a downpour of arrows. Fire from Krishna's discus ran among them and consumed thousands; the survivors scattered, dropping their mail coats, their swords, their daggers, their darts and their axes as they ran.

Vana himself galloped after his fleeing soldiers, shouting them back: "Born of the demon race, will you fly from the field in fear? Think of what you are! Think of the years you have spent at Shiva's side — and then decide whether to run. I stand here before you!" But the demons, beside themselves with terror, paid him no heed and fled. Kumbhanda, Vana's powerful minister and friend, tried his own appeal: "Look! Shiva himself is here, and Kartikeya, and Vana — abandon hope of your lives and fight!" The words were still in the air when the last of the runners vanished. Of all that great army, only the Pramathas — Shiva's own wild attendants — stood their ground, ready to fight again.

Then Shiva's anger rose. His eyes reddened to see his soldiers routed, and to protect Vana he mounted his shining chariot and made ready for battle. Kartikeya, Shiva's son, climbed into a car that blazed like fire. And Shiva's own chariot came rolling onto the field — drawn by lions, thundering as if it meant to devour the sky, like the full moon breaking free of clouds.

It was ringed by strange companions. Some wore the faces of lions, tigers, serpents, horses, camels, asses, peacocks, rams, cats and sheep. Some had matted hair; some were dressed in bark or the skins of beasts; some were beautiful and carried shining weapons and flowers; others were small and grim, with great teeth and a hunger that never left them. They blew conch-shells and bugles as they came, and ranged themselves about Shiva's car, waiting at ease while the lion-drawn chariot bore their lord toward Krishna.

Krishna saw the car coming and rode Garuda to meet it. Shiva, who always stood at the front of any fight, struck him in anger with hundreds of winged arrows, and Krishna answered with the great weapons Indra had given him. The earth shook under the exchange; the elephants trembled and lifted their heads; streams were shaken loose on the mountains and their summits came tumbling down; fire-brands fell from the sky, and jackals howled their ill-omened cries.

Brahma, the grandfather of the worlds, came with the gods around him to watch, and the shining companies of the sky gathered in the air to see the encounter.

Then Krishna loosed Indra's own weapon at Shiva. Burning, it flew straight at the car where the god stood — and in the same breath hundreds and thousands of arrows rose to answer it. Angered, Shiva let fly his dreadful fiery weapon, and the sight was strange beyond telling: Krishna and the three other heroes beside him were buried under arrows, and the sky over Sonitpura turned the colour of the end of the world.
stories.reflection: The moment Shiva enters, the war stops being a siege and becomes a confrontation between gods themselves. The ghosts with their animal faces and their conch-shells are a reminder that Shiva's power is not tidy — it is wild, old, and loyal — and Krishna rides out to meet it without hesitation while the whole sky gathers to watch.
stories.next_story_tease: Yet before that duel could be decided, a strange figure would step between Krishna and his discus.
stories.hero_scene: Shiva's lion-drawn car rolls onto the Sonitpura battlefield like the full moon freed from clouds, ringed by a host of ghosts with the faces of lions, tigers, serpents and horses blowing conch-shells, while Krishna on Garuda rides to meet it.

stories.title: The Goddess Who Stood Between
stories.subtitle: Kottavi intervenes, and Krishna puts away his discus
stories.story:
Krishna and Shiva had drawn apart at last, and their great duel was over. But the war at Sonitpura — where Krishna had come to fight Vana, the thousand-armed demon king whom Shiva protected — was not over. It had only changed hands, and the younger commanders took it up.

Kartikeya, Shiva's son, drove the chariot that Kumbhanda had brought him straight at Krishna, his brother Balarama and his son Pradyumna, and struck them with hundreds of sharp arrows. Bathed in blood, the three heroes fought back like three fires. When they struck Kartikeya with the three weapons given them by the Wind-god, the Fire-god and Indra, he met them with three weapons of his own — and the heroes, by their power of illusion, swallowed even those.

Then Kartikeya, blazing and biting his lips, took up the Brahmashira, the dreadful weapon of Brahma himself, blazing like a thousand suns, able to destroy the world. The moment it was loosed, creatures lost their senses from its heat and fled on every side, and the whole universe seemed to wail. Krishna saw it and raised his discus, the weapon that answers all weapons; and as clouds cover the sun in the rainy season, so the discus covered the light of the Brahmashira and left it shorn of its power.

Kartikeya's eyes reddened with anger, and he blazed up like fire fed with butter. He seized his golden spear — the Sakti, hung with bells, sure of aim, bright as a fire-brand — and hurled it with a shout that chilled his enemies' hearts. The spear flew up into the sky, hung there as if it were alive and searching for Krishna, and rushed down at him. The gods themselves despaired: "Perhaps Krishna will be consumed." But as the great spear came at him, Krishna shouted, as if he were scolding the weapon itself — and struck it down to the ground. "Well done! Well done!" rose from every side, and Indra with all the celestials sent up a roar of triumph.

Then Krishna took up his discus to finish the fight, and was about to let it fly — when a goddess came and stood before him. Her name was Kottavi, and Shiva had summoned her to shield his son. She stood between Krishna and Kartikeya and would not move. She was unclothed, as her ancient form was, and no warrior would strike through a woman who stood unarmed in the weapon's path.

Krishna was baffled. "Go!" he said. "Fly from this place! Why do you throw yourself in the way of certain destruction?"

But Kottavi heard him and did not stir. To shield Kartikeya, she would not even cover herself while she stood before him.

"Take Kartikeya and go," Krishna said. "It will be well for us today if you do this. Otherwise, if I hold back from the fight, he will fight me."

And looking on the goddess who would not move, Krishna put away his discus.

Then Kottavi led Kartikeya away to Shiva, and the great danger passed. When Vana saw the young war-god released and drawing back from the field, he himself felt the urge to fight Krishna. His ghosts, his yaksha spirits and his soldiers had fled on every side; of all his broken army only the Pramathas, Shiva's attendants, remained. And so Vana marched out with his great demon commanders about him, while his priests and elders — learned in the scriptures — performed rites of victory over him with prayers, chants and herbs, calling for the ruin of his enemies.
stories.reflection: Krishna's discus has never hesitated before a weapon, but it stops before a woman who stands unarmed. The episode turns on a strange kind of strength: the goddess does not fight, she merely refuses to move, and in that refusal the shape of the battle is changed.
stories.content_note: The episode centers on the goddess Kottavi appearing unclothed on the battlefield; the source treats this matter-of-factly, and the story describes it with restraint.
stories.next_story_tease: With Kartikeya withdrawn, Vana himself now took the field, roaring of his thousand arms.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna, discus raised to strike, frozen mid-throw as the goddess Kottavi stands unclothed and unafraid before the young Kartikeya, her form gleaming between them like a golden spear.

stories.title: The Boast of a Thousand Arms
stories.subtitle: Vana vaunts, and Krishna answers with the Sarnga bow
stories.story:
Krishna, lord of Dwaraka, had marched on the city of Sonitpura to free his grandson Aniruddha, who lay bound in the palace of its king. Now that king, Vana of the thousand arms, had come out to meet him, and the war would be decided on the open field.

"Wait! Wait!" Vana shouted across it. "You will not escape me alive to Dwaraka and see your friends there. You have eight arms — how will you fight me, who have a thousand? Slain with all your friends here in Shonita, you will remember Dwaraka too late. Today you will see my thousand arms, bright with weapons and ornaments, multiply into a million."

His words rolled over the field like the waves of a storm-driven sea, and his angry eyes shone like two suns rising.

From the top of the palace, Narada laughed aloud, so loudly that the sky seemed to split in two. The sage, who loved to watch the doings of the world, shifted about on his seat, eager to miss nothing of the battle.

Krishna answered him from the back of Garuda, the great eagle, with the patience of a man who had heard many boasts. "Why do you roar like this, Vana? Heroes do not vaunt. If words could win a battle, yours would have won it already. Come — either defeat me, or be defeated and lie on the earth for good."

The fight that followed was unlike anything the field had seen. Krishna struck first, with arrows that cut Vana to the quick. Vana answered with burning arrows, and then with iron clubs and maces, spears and javelins, until Krishna was buried beneath the storm of weapons. Thousand-armed Vana fought easily; Krishna, with his eight arms, fought on. Seeing that skill was against him, Vana grew blind with rage and loosed the great weapon that Brahma the creator had shaped long ago for the demon king Hiranyakashipu. Darkness swallowed every quarter of the sky. Dread omens crowded the air. The world itself seemed to pass out of sight. The demons who watched cried, "Well done! Well done!" while the gods cried out, "Alas!" A rain of burning arrows poured down, and while Krishna burned beneath it, even the wind and the clouds held still.

Then Krishna took up the weapon of Indra, king of the gods — and the moment it was ready, the darkness fell away, the fire died, and the demons lost heart. Seeing their weapon undone, the watching gods laughed and roared like lions.

Beside himself with rage, Vana shouted curses at Krishna on Garuda's back and buried him once more under maces and clubs. Krishna parried every blow — and then, from his great bow Sarnga, he loosed arrows like thunderbolts. They shattered Vana's chariot, with its horses and banners, all together. His shining crown fell, and his coat of mail, his bow and his shield, struck from him one after another, and winged arrows struck him on the breast. Cut to the quick, the king of the thousand arms lost his senses and went down among the wreckage of his chariot.

From the palace roof, Narada leapt up clapping. "Great fortune! Great fortune! Blessed is my life, for I have seen Krishna's prowess this day. Finish what you came for — destroy Vana!"

And high above the field, the standards fought their own battle. The horses of gods and demons clashed beneath them, and Garuda and the peacock of Vana's banner struck at each other with wings, beaks and talons — until the great eagle, leaping up in anger, caught the peacock's head in his beak, and the banner of Sonitpura came down.
stories.reflection: Narada's laughter at the boast and his applause at the defeat frame the whole duel as a spectacle: the ascetic watches from the palace rooftop, and the mightiest warriors of the universe perform for him. The hundred arms multiply into a million only in Vana's own telling — in the end, it is one bow that dismantles them.
stories.next_story_tease: But Vana's life was not yet decided — the goddess would step between them once more.
stories.hero_scene: Vana's thousand arms spread in fury as Krishna's arrows from the Sarnga bow shatter his chariot, crown, mail, bow and shield, while Narada claps from the palace rooftop and Garuda battles the peacock overhead.

stories.title: Kottavi Stands Between Krishna and Vana
stories.story:
The war had come to Sonitpura because Krishna's grandson Aniruddha had been taken from Dwaraka and bound with serpent-nooses in the palace of Vana, king of the thousand arms. Now the city had fallen, the young man was free, and the last of the fighting was being done on the open field.

High above it, the standards themselves were fighting. Garuda and the great peacock of Vana's banner clashed in the air, striking with wings, beaks and talons, until the eagle caught the peacock's head in his beak and flung it down. Beneath them, Vana had risen for the second time that day. His chariot lay in splinters — horses and standards shattered by arrows from Krishna's bow Sarnga — and his crown, his coat of mail, his bow and his shield lay scattered in the dust. He came on anyway, a thousand arms, and every one of them held a weapon.

Krishna faced him from Garuda's back. "Wait, wait!" Vana roared, his eyes wild with fury. "You will not escape me alive to Dwaraka today. You have eight arms — how will you fight me, who have a thousand? Today you will see my arms multiply into a million."

"Heroes do not vaunt," Krishna answered. "If words could win battles, you would have won already. Come, Vana — either defeat me, or be vanquished and lie down on the earth for good."

The duel flared up once more, and the field shook to its edges. Vana loosed the great weapon that Brahma had made for Hiranyakashipu, and darkness fell over all the quarters; burning arrows rained down, and even wind and cloud held still. The demons watching applauded, and the gods cried out in alarm. Krishna took up the weapon of Indra, king of the gods; the darkness was torn away, the fire went out, and the watching gods laughed like lions. Beyond all reason now, Vana heaped maces and spears on Krishna — and Krishna struck him on the breast with winged arrows, and the thousand-armed king of Sonitpura lost consciousness and fell.

From the palace roof, Narada clapped his hands. "What a battle!" he called out. "Blessed is my birth, for I have seen such prowess today. Do not stay your hand, Krishna — finish it!"

The discus was already in Krishna's hand when a goddess stepped between them — Kottavi, whom some called Lamva. She came unclothed, with nothing to protect her but the fierce dignity of an old promise. "I gave this boy my word long ago," she said. "I granted him a boon, that I would protect him. I will not see that boon broken now."

Krishna looked at her, and the discus did not move. "Then hear my vow, goddess. I will cut off Vana's thousand arms today, every one of them, and let them fall to the earth. Your son will live, even if Vana is left with only two."

She could not find fault with mercy that came shaped like that. And so it was done: the discus passed through the field of arms like light through a forest, and where it went, weapons fell and arms fell with them, until the king who had fought with a thousand hands stood at the end of it with two — alive, breathing, shorn of his terrible power but not of his life. The goddess's boon was honoured, and Krishna's vow was honoured too.

The field fell silent, watching Vana stare at his two empty hands. And high above, unseen by any, the god Shiva watched as well — for Shiva, too, had once given Vana his word.
stories.reflection: Krishna's mercy here is exact and strange: he takes away the thing that made Vana terrible, the thousand arms, and leaves the life. Kottavi's boon and Krishna's own vow meet in a single act of measured severity, and both promises are kept in the same stroke.
stories.content_note: Depicts a battle and the severing of Vana's thousand arms; described with restraint, not graphic.
stories.next_story_tease: But Shiva, too, had promised Vana his protection — and he was watching the field.
stories.hero_scene: The unclothed goddess Kottavi standing between Krishna on Garuda and the fallen Vana, her arms spread in protection while Krishna's discus hovers in the air, severed arms and weapons strewn across the battlefield behind them.
