stories.title: The Serpent of Ambika Forest
stories.subtitle: Nanda is swallowed and freed
stories.story:
A cry cut through the Ambika forest in the small hours of the night, and every cowherd of Vraja woke at once. "Krishna! Krishna!" Nanda's voice rang through the trees. "A great serpent has taken me!"

There was no mistaking that voice, or the terror in it. The cowherds had come to a forest sacred to the goddess Ambika to keep a vow, and they had lain down to sleep under the great trees while their cattle grazed at the edge of the clearing. Nanda, the chief of the herdsmen, who had raised Krishna as his own son, slept at the centre of the camp — and when the cowherds came running with firebrands snatched from the campfire, they saw why he had cried out.

A serpent of impossible size lay coiled across the clearing, and Nanda was wrapped inside its folds. The creature had not eaten in a long time; hunger had driven it from the deep forest toward the sleeping men, and it had taken their leader like a mouse in a nest. It was already swallowing, its jaws working over Nanda's shoulders, and its coils tightened with every breath it drew.

The cowherds did not stop to think. They fell on the serpent together — beating it, scorching it, pressing the smoking ends of their firebrands into its scales, shouting all the while. The great snake shuddered and hissed; the smell of burning scales filled the clearing. But it did not let go. The fire that made the cowherds flinch back only made the serpent draw Nanda deeper, and Nanda's cries grew fainter as the great jaws worked.

Then Krishna came through the ring of desperate men. There was no weapon in his hand, no anger in his face. The cowherds fell back to let him pass, and he walked up to the serpent as if it were a stray calf, and touched it with his bare foot.

The touch undid what all their fire could not. The serpent released Nanda at once, its coils falling slack, and Nanda tumbled out onto the grass — shaken, breathless, alive. And where the monstrous body had lain, there now stood a being of molten light, as though the firebrands had taken hold and burned the beast away, leaving only what had been hidden inside it all along.

Krishna studied the radiant figure, which bowed low before him. "Who are you?" he asked. "You shine with a beauty that is wonderful to see."

"I was Sudarshana, a Vidyadhara," the being said, "one of the sky-farers. I was proud of my form and prouder still of my beauty, and one day I laughed at the sages of the Angirasa lineage to their faces. They cursed me — but theirs was a compassionate curse, laid on me as a grace I did not yet understand. It bound me in the body of this serpent, to crawl and to hunger until the touch of the blessed one should free me. That touch is yours, and this is the day. Your foot has burned away the evil of the curse, and I stand released."

"Then go," Krishna said. "The curse is finished."

Sudarshana praised him then — the one who takes away the fear of all who come to him for refuge — and when his words ran out, he circled Krishna, bowed again at his feet, and rose into the dark sky until the night swallowed him.

The cowherds stood a long time in silence. The firebrands still smoked in their hands. Nanda sat on the grass, whole, drawing breath after breath. They had grown up with Krishna — had watched him graze the calves, had scolded him and loved him as their own — but they had never seen anything like this. What kind of boy was it whose foot could turn a devouring serpent into a shining god?

They finished their vow as the sun rose, and on the road back to Vraja they told the story at every village they passed. Each telling made it more wonderful — and each telling left them a little more certain that the boy who walked with them was not merely a boy.
stories.reflection: The curse the sages laid on Sudarshana had been a grace all along — punishment as a waiting-room for Krishna's touch. The same night reads three ways: terror for Nanda, astonishment for the cowherds, gratitude for the freed Vidyadhara, and all three are held together by one boy's bare foot.
stories.next_story_tease: The serpent gone and the vow fulfilled, Krishna's road was already turning another way — toward Mathura.

stories.title: The Weaver and the Garland-Maker
stories.subtitle: Two craftsmen of Mathura honour the brothers
stories.story:
Mathura had never seen boys like the two who walked its royal road that evening. Men and women stopped to look; children ran ahead to look again. They moved like young elephants, unhurried and easy, and the dust of the road only made them shine the more.

They had come from Vrindavan in the chariot of Akrura, whom Kamsa, the king of Mathura, had sent to fetch them; Akrura had left them at the city's edge to enter on foot. Now they walked the royal road through Kamsa's streets as if they had been born to them — Krishna and Balarama, brothers, cowherd boys in plain cloth, on the day before the city would learn what they were. Men and women regarded them with pleasure and fell in behind them, the way a town follows a festival it has not yet understood.

It was a weaver who first dared to stop them. He looked at the two brothers — at the homespun cloth they wore, at the road dust on their shoulders — and it grieved him that such forms should go so plainly dressed. He brought out his finest cloth and, glad beyond measure, cut and fitted garments for them both, rich cloth of many colours, each garment marked with its own device. When Krishna and Balarama stood dressed in the weaver's work, they shone, and the weaver saw that he had dressed something more than two travellers. Krishna was pleased with him, and to the weaver he gave a rare gift: a form like his own, so that the man who had clothed the lord's body would bear the lord's likeness in his own.

From the weaver's shop they went on through streets that grew quieter as the evening deepened, until they came to the house of Sudama, the garland-maker. Sudama looked once at his two visitors and seemed to know at once who stood in his doorway. He brought them in, set seats for them, washed their feet, and offered them water and all the honours of a guest. He pressed garlands on them and sandal paste, and his hands trembled with delight as he worked.

"Our birth is made fruitful today," he said, standing before them with folded hands. "Our family is purified. You two are the cause of this whole world, and you look on all that lives with the same eye, for you are the soul of everything that breathes. Tell your servant: what shall we do for you?"

Krishna and Balarama accepted the garlands and the paste, and were pleased. Then Sudama was asked what he himself wanted — and the garland-maker, who had given everything he had and asked for nothing, named one thing only.

"Unshakable devotion," he said. "A love of you that nothing can move."

"It is yours," Krishna said. "And with it, take this: fortune that never leaves you, prosperity that grows in your line for generations." Nor did the blessing end with this life: at the end of his days, a heavenly region awaited the man who had honoured the lord before he fully knew him.

Word of the two strangers spread through Mathura that night. The weaver told his neighbours, and Sudama told his customers, and the garland-scented shop carried the story out into the streets. Kamsa's city had been told to fear the cowherd boys from Vrindavan; instead it learned that they had walked its royal road like kings and blessed its craftsmen, that a weaver's needle and a garland-maker's flowers had been enough to earn the favour of the two who were the world's cause. The city waited, uncertain and wondering, to see what they would do next.
stories.reflection: The two gifts mirror each other: the weaver receives a form like the Lord's because he dressed the Lord's body, and the flower-seller asks only for devotion because he has already laid every other offering at Krishna's feet. Each man is answered exactly with what he offered.
stories.tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana tells of the flower-seller alone, and frames his reward as fortune that never forsakes him and a heavenly region at the end; the Bhagavata adds the weaver and names Sudama's boon unshakable devotion.
stories.next_story_tease: But while Mathura wondered, in a dry well far away a king lay trapped in a lizard's body — and his long wait was almost over.

stories.title: Krishna Liberates King Nriga
stories.story:
In the days when Krishna lived in the city of Dwaraka, the young men of his own people, the Yadavas, still played as boys play anywhere. One morning they ran out through the gates into the open fields and played until the sun stood high, chasing one another through the long grass and the dust until their legs ached. By afternoon they were thirsty, and thirsty boys think of water. They went searching for it, calling to one another across the empty fields, and in their searching they came upon a well.

It was dry. But it was not empty.

At the bottom lay a lizard — not a lizard such as any of them had ever seen, but a creature the size of a hill, one no well should ever have held. There it lay in the dark, still as the stone around it, its hide gleaming faintly in the light from the well's mouth. It had the stillness of something waiting. The boys stood at the rim and stared down at it, and for a long moment no one spoke. Then, being boys and never ones to leave a wonder alone, they decided to haul it up.

They knotted ropes of leather and thread, lowered them into the dark, and bound the great creature. Then they pulled — all of them together, heels set, calling to one another — and it did not so much as stir. They pulled until their hands burned and their breath came hard, and still it lay where it was, patient as stone. At last they had to stand back, breathless and baffled, wondering what such a creature could be and how it had ever come to rest in a dry well.

Word of it reached Krishna, and he came to the well, the boys making way for him. He stood at the edge and looked down into the dark, and he did not trouble himself with ropes. He reached in with his left hand, took hold of the creature, and drew it up into the light. The moment his hand touched it, the lizard was gone — and the boys, who had strained and failed, saw that his touch alone had been enough.

In its place stood a man, and he shone. He stood in the sunlight with the brilliance of molten gold, a splendour that seemed not of this world, and the boys fell back from him, shielding their eyes. For a long moment no one could look at him directly. The whole morning's play was forgotten; the well, the field, and the dust of the road all seemed to stand still around him.

Krishna was not surprised. He knew already who stood before him and by what deed he had come to this. But he asked the question aloud, so that the answer would be heard not by him alone but by everyone gathered at the well. “What deed,” he asked, “has brought you to this state — you, who did not deserve such a thing?”

The radiant man lifted his head. He was Nriga, a king of ancient days, and before the wondering crowd he began to speak, the boys pressing closer and forgetting, for a little while, their thirst. And the story he told, of how a king had come to crouch in a dry well, was one the whole city would learn.
stories.reflection: The scene withholds more than it gives. We are not told, here, why a king crouched in a dry well in a lizard's skin; we are shown only that the touch of Krishna's hand was enough to end it. Liberation, in this telling, does not wait for an explanation — it comes first, and only afterward asks, so that the telling can become a gift to everyone listening.
stories.tradition_note: This episode is told only in the Bhagavata Purana; it has no parallel in the other major sources.

stories.title: Nriga's Story of the Disputed Cow
stories.subtitle: How a king famed for giving fell into a lizard's body
stories.story:
The being who stood before Krishna had been a lizard until moments ago — a lizard the size of a hill, at the bottom of a dry well, drawn out at last by Krishna's left hand and restored by his touch to a king of molten-gold splendour. The Yadava princes — Krishna's own kinsmen — still stared. The people of Dwaraka pressed close. And Krishna asked the question everyone wanted answered: how had a being so evidently blessed come to spend his years at the bottom of a well?

The king bowed. “What is unknown to you, lord,” he said, “you who are the witness of every heart? But if you wish the world to know, I will tell it. I am Nriga, of the line of Ikshvaku.”

And Nriga told his story.

He had been a king famed above all kings for one thing: giving cows. As many cows as there are grains of sand on the earth, as stars in the sky — so many had he given. Milch cows and young cows, gentle cows of fine colour and form, tawny cows with horns tipped in gold — he had given them to brahmanas of good conduct, to men who kept their vows, to households bowed down by want. And not cows alone: land and gold, houses and horses, elephants and beds, sesame and silver, and maidens with their servants. His wealth had flowed outward his whole life, and the fame of it had travelled ahead of him into every kingdom.

Then came the accident — one cow among thousands. A cow belonging to a leading brahmana of his realm strayed from its owner's herd and mingled with the royal cattle, and in the great round of giving it was led out and given to another brahmana.

“Its owner saw it as it was led away,” Nriga said, “and he cried out, ‘That cow is mine!’ The brahmana who had received it cried out as well, that it was his by gift. Both stood before me, each seeking his own right, and both claimed the cow.”

Nriga understood at once what had happened. He offered each man recompense — whatever he had won by righteous toil — and begged them both to forgive a servant who had not known what he gave.

“Neither would accept,” Nriga said. “The owner would not take another cow, or gold, or land, in place of his own. ‘I will not accept it, king,’ he said, and walked away. The other would not give the gift back. The two could not be reconciled, and I could not undo what my own hand had done.”

The story might have ended there, in a dispute no court could settle. It did not. In that very moment, Nriga said, Yama's messengers came for him, took him from his palace, and brought him before Yama, the lord of the dead, who weighs every life. And Yama gave the king of givers a choice.

“You carry both merit and fault from this life,” Yama said. “Your giving was vast; your error is real. Which will you taste first — the good or the bad?”

Nriga answered without hesitation. “Let me taste the bad first.”

He did not explain why, and the old telling does not say. He chose, and his choice took the shape of a lizard. “I fell from my palace into this body,” Nriga said, “and the dry well became my kingdom. Year after year I lay at the bottom of it — a king who had given away thousands of cows, unable to give anything at all, not even a prayer, in a lizard's throat. And all those years, the merit of my giving waited.”

He fell silent. The Yadava princes looked at the radiant king and tried to see the lizard in him. Krishna listened without moving.

“And now,” Nriga said at last, “you have touched me. And I think — I hope — the waiting is over.”
stories.reflection: Nriga is no villain: a famously generous king, undone by an accident that no compensation could repair. His choice to suffer the bad first is the quiet heroism of the tale — he would rather taste his error than postpone it, trusting that the merit of a life of giving would keep its own appointment.
stories.next_story_tease: His story told, Nriga bowed at Krishna's feet — and the ending the lizard-years had delayed was already descending from the sky.

stories.title: Nriga Ascends, and Krishna Warns the City
stories.subtitle: The lizard-king's merit claims its ending
stories.story:
The king who stood before Krishna had been a lizard an hour before — a lizard the size of a hill, at the bottom of a dry well outside Dwaraka, until Krishna drew him out and his true form returned. He was Nriga, a king of ancient days, once famed for giving away more cows than there are stars in the sky, and he had just finished telling how one mistaken gift had cost him so many years in a well. Now the words were running out, and praise was taking their place.

“What is there that you do not know, lord?” he said. “Yet I, who lay so long in blindness at the bottom of a well, have come to see you with my own eyes — you whom the wise seek in the depths of their hearts, whom the scriptures only glimpse, the lord beyond the reach of the senses. The very sight of you is the end of birth and of fear.”

Then he asked for what he had been waiting to ask. “Permit me, Krishna,” he said, “to go to the celestial world, where the merit of my giving has been waiting all these years.” He bowed, circled Krishna, and touched Krishna's feet with his head. Then he stood, and waited.

But Krishna did not send him off in silence. He turned to the citizens of Dwaraka, who had gathered to watch the wonder, and what he said to them was meant to outlast the day.

“The property of a brahmana,” Krishna said, “even a little of it, enjoyed without right, is fire that cannot be digested. I do not count the poison halahala the deadliest thing in the world, for even that has an antidote: poison kills the one who eats it, and water quenches fire. But the wealth of a brahmana, taken without leave, destroys three generations of the house that takes it.”

He went on, and his voice carried to the farthest listeners. “Kings, blinded by their royal fortune, do not see their own fall. For every handful of dust they seize, and for every tear of those they rob, they and their houses pay in years — unchecked, unrepentant, until the reckoning comes. Whoever takes the livelihood of a brahmana, whether it was given by his own hand or another's — may such wealth never come near me, for men who covet it become short-lived. And you, my people: never do harm to a brahmana, even one who has erred. As I bow to the brahmanas, attentive and well-disposed, so should you. Wealth torn from a brahmana drags the taker down.”

The words fell on the gathered citizens and settled into them. Then, while the silence was still new, a celestial car descended — bright and fragrant, shining as if it were made of the morning itself — and came to rest before Nriga.

Nriga looked at Krishna once more. Then he stepped into the car, and the car rose. It climbed above the walls of Dwaraka, above the roofs and the upturned faces, and Nriga's form grew small and bright against the sky until it was only a point of light — and then nothing.

The citizens stood looking up long after it was gone.
stories.reflection: Krishna's warning is carefully framed: he does not exalt brahmanas as a class so much as mark how the powerful consume what they never earned, and how a single unknowing wrong, even inside a life of great charity, still exacts its price. The poison metaphor — worse than halahala, because no antidote exists — carries the whole weight of the teaching.
stories.next_story_tease: But far from Dwaraka, in the kingdom of Karusha, a king had begun to call himself the true Vasudeva — and his claim would not go unanswered.

stories.title: Paundraka Demands Krishna's Insignia
stories.story:
In the kingdom of Karusha there lived a king who came to believe he was God.

It happened slowly, the way such things usually do. Paundraka's courtiers called him Vasudeva — the Lord descended to earth — and he liked the sound of it. Priests who wanted his favour agreed that he was the one Lord, that there was no other. One by one the voices of flattery closed around him, until the king lost all memory of his real self and accepted the title as simply true. He was Vasudeva, and in his own mind the whole world existed for his sake.

There was one difficulty, and it grew larger the longer he thought about it. The real Vasudeva was alive, and he wore the marks of the Lord openly, in the city of Dwaraka. Those marks — the discus, the conch, the other divine signs that the true Lord alone should carry — had become Paundraka's obsession. In his mind they belonged to him and to him alone, and that a Yadava prince named Krishna walked about bearing them was an insult too great to be endured. And so the king of Karusha did what any king certain of his own divinity would do: he sent a messenger to Dwaraka with a demand.

The journey was long, but the messenger made it in haste, and the demand lost nothing in the carrying. He entered Krishna's assembly, where the chiefs of the Yadavas sat with their lord, and delivered his master's words without flinching. Paundraka, king of Karusha, was Vasudeva, the one descended Lord; there was no other. The divine marks Krishna wore were Paundraka's, worn out of folly. Let Krishna give them up, surrender the name of Vasudeva and the character that went with it, and come to Karusha to do homage — and he would be given the means to live.

There is no gracious way to receive such a message, and the Yadavas did not try to find one. They laughed until the hall rang, at the thought of the king of Karusha demanding that Krishna hand over the signs of the Lord.

Krishna answered with a smile. “Go back to your master,” he said, “and tell him the discus is already on its way to him. I will hurl these very signs at the fool and slay him, and his face will soon lie covered by cranes and vultures.”

The messenger bowed and carried the reply back to Karusha — the whole of it, every word, with nothing softened. And Paundraka, who had been waiting for good news, heard the message out in silence. He had been certain of his own divinity, and the thought that the demand might be refused had never once crossed his mind. That was the nature of his delusion: it left no room for the possibility that the embassy had been absurd from the first word.

In the assembly of Dwaraka the laughter died slowly, and the chiefs of the Yadavas sat looking at their lord, because everyone in that hall knew that Krishna's promises were not the sort that fail. The discus would go to Karusha. The fool would meet it. The only question was when.
stories.reflection: The comedy of the episode is also its point: Paundraka asked Krishna to surrender the very marks that made him what he claimed to be. Divinity demanded as tribute reveals itself as costume, and the laughter of the assembly is the story's honest verdict on borrowed glory.
stories.next_story_tease: But the discus Krishna promised the messenger was already on its way — the impostor's borrowed glory was about to meet its end.

stories.title: Krishna Slays Paundraka and the King of Kashi
stories.story:
In the kingdoms east of Dwaraka there ruled a king who came to believe he was Krishna — or rather, that Krishna was himself. Paundraka had been an ordinary king once, no better and no worse than a hundred others, but flattery had undone him. His courtiers and priests, too eager to please him, told him he was Vasudeva, the Lord descended to earth, until he forgot who he really was and accepted the title as true. It was a strange kind of theft, because the man he was stealing from was the very man he claimed to be.

He dressed himself in yellow silk like Krishna's and marked his chest with the shrivatsa, the sacred curl that marked the true Lord. He took up the conch, the discus, the sword and the mace, strung the great bow called Sharnga, and raised a banner bearing an eagle. In every particular he made himself look like Krishna, so that a man who saw him from a distance might honestly have mistaken one for the other. And it was no disguise worn for a single hour: he wore it so long and so completely that he could no longer tell where the pretence ended and he began.

At last he sent a messenger to Krishna with a demand. Let Krishna relinquish the discus, lay aside Paundraka's insignia, his name, and the character of Vasudeva, and come to Karusha to do him homage — and he, Paundraka, would grant him the means to live. The impostor was offering, with perfect seriousness, to spare the man he was copying and to keep him as a dependent.

Krishna heard the message and laughed. “Go back to Paundraka,” he told the messenger, “and tell him I will send him my discus. He will rightly understand my meaning. I will come to his city with it, and I will deliver it to him, and there will be no delay.” The discus, Krishna knew, could be delivered in only one way, and Paundraka would soon discover what that way was.

Paundraka was not alone in his delusion. The king of Kashi had made himself his friend and ally, a rear-guard at his back, ready to defend him. So Krishna marched against them both, and the two armies met before the walls of Kashi, where the impostor and his ally would learn whether a borrowed name could stand in a real battle.

When Krishna saw Paundraka in the field — wearing the borrowed yellow silk and the borrowed banner, looking so like himself that the likeness was almost a mockery — he laughed again. Then he fought. With mace and discus and a stream of arrows he scattered the combined army of the two kings, the way a fire at the end of an age sweeps through a field, until the ground before the city was cleared of everything that had stood against him.

He turned to Paundraka. “O Paundraka,” he said, “I will now make you give up my name, which you, a fool, have falsely taken.” With sharp arrows he struck Paundraka from his chariot, and with the discus he cut off his head. Then he turned on the king of Kashi, cut off that king's head with his arrows, and sent it flying over the walls and into the city, where it fell at the palace gate.

So the false Vasudeva died as he had lived, with his whole mind fixed on Krishna. And that, the old story says, was the strange mercy of it. Because Paundraka had thought of Krishna without ceasing, even if only in envious imitation, that constant thought had quietly burned away every bond that held him. The man who stole Krishna's name ended by arriving at the very place he had spent his whole life pretending to stand.
stories.reflection: Paundraka is the reverse of everything a devotee should be, yet the sources close his story with a startling grace: because his mind never left Krishna, even in enmity and imitation, the impostor was freed. The costume he wore in mockery became, in the end, the only true thing about him.
stories.tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana extends the episode: after the two kings fall, the son of the king of Kashi sends a magical being against Krishna, and Krishna's discus destroys it and sets the city of Varanasi ablaze. This story follows the Bhagavata Purana, which ends with the two beheadings.
stories.content_note: Paundraka and the king of Kashi are beheaded in battle; the violence is described with restraint.

stories.title: The Fire That Burned Varanasi
stories.story:
The king of Kashi was dead — struck down before his own walls by Krishna, together with the impostor Paundraka whom he had sheltered. His queen and his kin mourned him, and his son Sudakshina performed the rites for his father's passing. But grief was not the only thing in the young prince's heart. When the ceremonies were done, he took his teachers with him and went to worship Shiva at Avimukta, in the sacred heart of Kashi, the city also called Varanasi. He fasted and chanted, pressing his worship upon the Lord of that place with the single-mindedness of a man who has already chosen his request — and he prayed as a man who intends to be answered.

Shiva was pleased with him and offered a boon. Sudakshina asked for the southern fire — the fire of black magic, tended by brahmana priests, that would accomplish his purpose against the man he called impious: Krishna of Dwaraka. He wanted no wealth and no protection, but a weapon: a fire that would burn one enemy and spare everything else. The boon was granted, and from the fire pit there rose a demon of living flame.

It was terrible to look upon, the old telling says — fangs set in a face of iron, brows knotted, a tongue that licked out like a serpent's, feet the size of palm trunks that shook the earth with every step. The priests who served that fire stood with Sudakshina and watched it take shape, and their own faces were white. The conjured thing set out across the country, walking toward Dwaraka — not like a beast, but like a purpose: unhurried, straight, and hungry. Everything in its path knew that it meant burning.

In Dwaraka the citizens saw it from the walls, and their courage failed. They ran through the streets to the assembly hall, where Krishna sat playing dice with his companions, and the cry went up: the fire of black magic is coming. Krishna looked up from the dice. His people were afraid, and his own household trembled with them.

Krishna needed no report of what came toward them. He is the witness of all things, within and without; he heard the distress of his people and saw the fear of his own. His discus Sudarshana blazed into being — like ten million suns, like the fire that ends a world — and went to meet the demon.

It struck the conjured thing and broke it. With its face shattered, the demon turned and fled back along the road it had come, back to the city that had raised it. It fell upon Varanasi and burned Sudakshina and the priests who had made it. The black magic consumed its own master.

But the discus was not finished. It entered Varanasi itself — through the ramparts, past the assembly halls and the markets, along streets that had never known an enemy — and burned the whole city. The city that had been inaccessible even to the gods was wrapped in flames, with all its princes and their followers.

The fire Sudakshina had raised to burn Dwaraka had burned his own city instead, and the discus had done in a single night what no army and no god had ever done. Where Varanasi had stood, there was ash and silence.
stories.reflection: The story turns on a terrible symmetry: the fire raised for Dwaraka fell on its raiser, and the discus that broke the conjured demon then ended the city that had sent it. A harm intended for another comes home to the one who sets it in motion, and even a city inviolable to the gods could not stand against the power of Vishnu's weapon.
stories.tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana tells the same episode without naming the Kashi king's son and gives the whole burning to the discus alone; the Bhagavata Purana names the prince Sudakshina.
stories.content_note: A conjured fire-demon and the burning of a city; described with restraint, but may warrant a word of context for younger listeners.
stories.next_story_tease: The embers of Varanasi had barely cooled when a new storm gathered far to the north — one that began at a svayamvara in Hastinapura.

stories.title: Samba Carries Off Duryodhana's Daughter
stories.story:
A svayamvara is supposed to end with the bride choosing her husband. Samba chose first.

Lakshmana, the daughter of Duryodhana, had come of age, and the roads to Hastinapura, the great city of the Kurus, were crowded with princes gathered to offer themselves at her svayamvara. It is a festival of waiting: the princess moves among the assembled kings with a garland in her hand, and the choice is hers alone. For a young man with more pride than patience, it was an invitation to be bold — and among the waiting princes came Samba, the son of Krishna and Jambavati, a young Yadava of Dwaraka, handsome and headstrong, with more confidence than caution. Whatever moved him — love, pride, or the sheer pleasure of daring — he did not wait to be chosen. He lifted Lakshmana into his chariot and drove away with her, and before the guards could move, before the ceremony could recover, the chariot was gone through the gate.

The Kurus were furious. "This boy is ill-mannered!" "Bind him!" "What will the Vrishnis dare to do?" The house of Kuru had never thought much of the kings of Dwaraka — the Vrishnis, as the Yadavas of Dwaraka were also called — and there were those at Hastinapura who said openly that the Yadu race had no claim to royal dignity. Now a boy of that house had treated their princess like plunder, and the insult was doubled. The great chiefs flung themselves into their chariots and gave chase — Karna, the Kurus' most famous warrior, Shala, Bhuri, Yajnaketu, and Duryodhana himself, shouting "Stop! Stop!" as their wheels thundered over the ground after the abductor.

Samba was a great chariot-warrior, and he had not stolen a bride to be caught easily. He wheeled his horses, strung his bow, and shot into the pursuers — four arrows into the horses of each of the foremost chariots, a single arrow into each charioteer — and wounded them all. For a moment the might of the Kurus flinched before a boy.

But there were too many of them, and they came on in a ring, closing the open ground from every side. They cut down his four horses and brought his chariot to a halt. Chariot-less and ringed by enemies, Samba was seized and bound — the verses note that it cost the Kurus great effort — and led back to Hastinapura a prisoner, with Lakshmana taken from him.

The news of the capture flew to Dwaraka faster than any chariot. When the Yadavas heard that one of their princes had been bound by the Kurus, their wrath kindled, and the councils of Dwaraka grew hot with talk of war.

Samba had gambled everything on boldness and lost. The price of his audacity now lay in the hands of Duryodhana, and in Dwaraka proud men were already sharpening their anger.
stories.reflection: Samba's crime was not that he loved Lakshmana but that he treated her choice as his own — seizing her at the svayamvara as if a bride's hand were a prize to be taken. The Kurus' fury was genuine, and so was their contempt for his manners; the story leaves the question of who was right to the consequences that follow.
stories.tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana adds Bhishma and Drona to the pursuing chiefs; the Bhagavata Purana names Karna, Shala, Bhuri, Yajnaketu and Duryodhana, which this story follows.
stories.next_story_tease: Yet even as the Yadavas' anger smoldered, Dwaraka was about to receive a guest who came with a question stranger than any war: how one man could fill sixteen thousand homes at once.

stories.title: Sixteen Thousand Homes, One Krishna
stories.story:
Narada had heard an impossible thing: that Krishna, with a single body, had married sixteen thousand women and kept a household for each. The sage, who wanders the three worlds and is astonished by little, was astonished by this. He came to Dwaraka to see it with his own eyes.

The city itself was the first marvel — nine hundred thousand palaces of crystal and silver, the verses say, streets laid out with care, squares and marketplaces full of life. But the inner palace was something more: sixteen thousand mansions with coral pillars and beryl floors, hung with canopies of pearls, lit by jeweled lamps that left no corner dark, peacocks calling from the roofs, maidservants moving through the rooms in gold necklaces and fine robes.

Narada entered the first mansion — the palace of Rukmini. There was Krishna, resting on a couch while his queen fanned him. The moment he saw the sage he rose, bowed, and seated him with honor; he washed Narada's feet and took the water of that washing onto his own head — the one whom the worlds worship did reverence to a guest. Then he asked what he could do for the sage.

Narada's answer was praise of a strange kind. "Nothing in you is wonderful, Lord of all worlds," he said, "for friendship toward every being, firmness toward the cruel, a life descended freely for the good of the world — these are simply what you are. I have seen your feet, the refuge of all who fall. Let me never lose the memory of you."

Narada rose and went to the second mansion — and there was Krishna again, playing dice with the lady of that house, and with Uddhava, his close friend and adviser. "When did you arrive, sage?" they asked him, as if he had only just come.

In the third mansion Krishna sat with small children laughing in his lap. In the fourth he poured offerings into the sacred fire, performing the five great sacrifices of a householder. In the fifth he sat in the twilight stillness, murmuring the sacred words of the Veda. In the sixth he was riding out among horses, elephants, and chariots. In the seventh he sat in counsel with his ministers, Uddhava among them. In the eighth he was giving adorned cows to the foremost brahmanas. In the ninth he laughed at a jest with his beloved. In the tenth he sat alone, absorbed in the vast silent Being behind all change. And still the mansions went on: here he made war with some kings and peace with others; there he performed the thread ceremonies and the weddings of his sons and daughters and kept the festivals of his children; elsewhere he worshipped all the gods with great sacrifices, or rode to the hunt on a Sindhu horse.

In all sixteen thousand mansions, the same. In every home Krishna was wholly present, and nowhere was he less.

After the first few mansions Narada stopped being surprised at the sight of him and began instead to test what he saw. In one home Krishna was mid-sentence with a minister; in the next, mid-verse of a chant; yet when Narada entered, each Krishna looked up as though the sage were the only guest in the world, and greeted him with the same complete attention. The same Krishna. The same fullness.

At last Narada came before him and laughed, like a man who has seen a trick he cannot explain. "I know your yoga-maya now," he said — the power by which Krishna was one, yet wholly present in every home at once. "Even the clever cannot see it. Permit me to depart, Lord, to the worlds that are flooded with your glory."

Krishna let him go. Narada left Dwaraka with his question dissolved: he had come to measure how one man could be husband to sixteen thousand wives, and he had learned that the question was wrongly put. In every home Krishna had been complete; nothing of him had been shared thin, nothing diminished. Some things, the sage had discovered, are not lessened by being given everywhere at once.
stories.reflection: Narada's wonder is the point: he comes to Krishna's sixteen thousand households as a puzzle of logistics and finds the puzzle itself dissolved — in each home Krishna is wholly present, and nothing of him is divided or lessened. The story does not explain yoga-maya; it shows it, room by room, and lets the seeing be the understanding.
stories.next_story_tease: But even as he took leave, Narada knew the wonder was deeper than he could name — and his song of Krishna's glory was about to begin.

stories.title: Narada Marvels at Krishna's Yoga-Maya
stories.story:
Narada stood looking back at Dwaraka for a long time before he turned away. For days he had walked through the sixteen thousand mansions of Krishna's queens, and in every mansion he had found the same thing — Krishna himself, whole and unhurried, doing whatever the moment required. In one hall he sat at ease among his ministers; in another he listened to a singer in a garden; here he stood beside a queen at the evening lamp, and there he laughed with children in a courtyard. Not a copy, not a shadow — the same person, fully there, as though no other palace existed in the world.

The sage had wandered every world there is. He had watched the gods at their councils and the demons at their schemes, kings at their wars and ascetics at their penances; he had seen illusions that fooled even the wise. Nothing had ever undone him the way Dwaraka did. He could not keep it inside, and he could not explain it: he had come to test a rumor, and he was leaving inside a mystery he would spend the rest of his journeys trying to sing.

He found Krishna, and stood before him smiling in spite of himself. He had rehearsed nothing; the words came out the way wonder does, before he had decided to speak them.

"I understand your yoga-maya now," he said — yoga-maya, the power by which Krishna was one, yet wholly present in sixteen thousand homes at once. "Even the masters of illusion cannot see it. Serving your feet has opened my eyes to it, and my mind can barely hold what it has seen."

Krishna took the words the way he took everything — fully, and without a ripple of vanity. In Dwaraka he followed the path of men: rising with the sun, ruling a city, living a mortal king's life among mortals. And yet the power he carried through those ordinary days was the power that holds every world in being. He did not argue with the praise, nor wave it away; he accepted it the way a lamp accepts the light it has always given. What he said next was less an order than a release.

"Wander the worlds, Narada," he said. "Sing of what you have seen wherever you go. Let the telling of it purify whoever hears."

So Narada departed, and for a long while Dwaraka saw no more of him. But the rest of the worlds saw more of him than they ever had. He went singing, and his songs carried the wonder he had found: that the lord of all could be in sixteen thousand places at once and be, in each, entirely himself — that the same hand which held a lamp in one palace reached for a child in another, and that no distance between them was real.

Wherever he went, people stopped to listen — farmers in the fields and merchants at their stalls, women at the well and children on the road. All of them heard how the king of Dwaraka moved through his days like a man, yet held the worlds in his palm. And the old texts say of such telling what they say of few things: whoever sings of these deeds, or hears them sung, or simply delights in them, finds his heart turning toward the path that has no end.

Krishna, left to his city, went on being what he was: a king among the Yadus, a husband to his queens, a man who met each morning the ordinary duties of a place that did not know it sheltered the wonder Narada had carried away, singing.
stories.reflection: Narada's wonder is the story's real subject: the lord of all worlds living the ordinary life of a king, and that ordinariness itself being the miracle. What he cannot explain, he carries out into the world as song — praise becomes the only adequate response to such a mystery.
stories.next_story_tease: Krishna, meanwhile, was already living the next quiet chapter of his days — the ordered worship of a king's morning in Dwaraka.
stories.hero_scene: Narada, smiling in wonder with folded hands before Krishna in a lamp-lit hall of Dwaraka, as Krishna gestures him out into the world to sing.

stories.title: Krishna's Dawn Worship in Dwaraka
stories.story:
The birds of Dwaraka sang the sun up before it showed itself, a chorus at every window, as if the day belonged to Krishna. Inside the palace, in the deep quiet of the brahma-muhurta — the last dark hours before dawn — Rukmini lay awake beside him, sorry to see the night end, for when her husband rose, the day took him from her side.

But rise he did, as he rose every day. In the first grey light Krishna touched the water and cleansed himself for what came next. Then he sat and turned inward, to the one reality that shines of itself, that has no second and no end, that no impurity can touch — and for a while the palace, the city, the sea beyond it, all fell away. It was not an escape from the day but the day's foundation; everything that followed stood on that stillness.

He bathed in clear water, according to the rite, performing each act as though it were the only act in the world — unhurried, complete, attentive. He put on fresh garments and performed the sandhya worship at the turning of night into day, feeding the sacred fire with offerings while his speech stayed still and his mind rode the chant. He saluted the rising sun, and offered the first worship of the day to his own senses, asking them to serve him rather than rule him.

Then the giving began. Every day, the texts say, Krishna gave away herds of milk-giving cows — cows with horns of gold and hooves of silver, strung with pearls, each with linen and sesame beside it, everything a household could need. The brahmanas came forward in turn, each receiving from the king's own hand, and his face showed no fatigue at the giving, only the same unhurried attention he gave to everything. He honored the cows and the brahmanas, the gods and the elders, his teachers, and every living being that came before him. He adorned himself, and those who saw him said the ornament of the human world had dressed itself in its own finery.

He looked into the mirror, as the custom of kings was, and saw the auspicious things set before him: clarified butter, cows and bulls, brahmanas, the images of the gods. He gave garlands, betel leaf and unguents to the brahmanas who waited on him, and they blessed him and went their way.

The sun was fully up. His charioteer brought the great chariot to the gate, and Krishna took his driver's hand and mounted, while the women of the inner palace watched him go with shy, loving glances. Through the streets of Dwaraka he rode, and the city rose around him like one living thing, until he came to the hall of Sudharma — the ancient assembly hall of the Yadus.

There the lords of the Vrishnis were gathered, Uddhava and Satyaki among them. Krishna took the highest seat, and the hall seemed to gather its light around him, as though the four directions brightened where he sat. The ministers brought their humor, jesting with their king as trusted friends do, and the sound of the mridanga drum and the vina lute rose with flute, cymbal and conch and filled the hall.

So the day of the lord of Dwaraka began — not in display but in order: water and fire, silence and song, gifts given and people heard. Those who watched him at his worship said he performed it not as a king performing for his court, but as one who served the Lord in every person who came before him.
stories.reflection: The wonder of the episode is its plainness: the lord of the universe performs the small disciplines of an ordinary king's day — ablutions, meditation, charity, court — and the disciplines are not beneath him but the very shape of his days. Devotion here is not spectacle but faithful repetition.
stories.next_story_tease: Far from Dwaraka, in a poor village, a brahmana who had once been Krishna's schoolmate was about to set out on a long journey.

stories.title: Four Handfuls of Flat Rice
stories.subtitle: Sudama's Poverty and Journey
stories.story:
Of all the brahmanas who kept their vows in that poor village, none was more learned than Sudama, and none lived in greater want. He had chosen a life of the mind and the spirit, and the world had repaid the choice with hunger. His house stood at the edge of the village with empty stores. Whatever came to him by chance — a measure of grain from a harvest, a coin from a passing traveler — went to feed the fire and the family, and it was never enough. Some days there was no grain at all. His body grew thin, and his clothes wore thin with it, and his wife's face lost its color, the way faces do when they are always hoping and always short.

She bore it as long as she could. Then one day she came to him, her voice low and her eyes on the ground, and said what had been on her mind for months.

"You were Krishna's friend," she said, "before either of you had anything. You know this. He is the lord of Dwaraka now, ruler of the Bhoja, the Vrishni and the Andhaka peoples, and fortune never leaves his side. Go to him. He will see you, and he will give us wealth, and this house will know ease again."

Sudama heard her out and said nothing. He was a man who had long ago stopped asking the world for things; it was hard to begin again, even with a friend. But his wife did not stop. She asked again and again, day after day, and at last the thought took root in him. If Krishna was truly his friend, what harm could there be in one journey?

He resolved to go. Once the resolve was made, he did not linger over it; whatever waited in Dwaraka — a welcome or a door closed in his face — had to be better than standing still.

But he would not go empty-handed. A guest does not come to a king's door with nothing. Sudama went to the brahmanas of the village and asked — humbly, for he had never been good at asking — for something to carry. He asked for no gold and no fine cloth; the plainest gift would do. They gave what they had: four handfuls of flattened rice — plain rice, pressed flat, the poor man's food, the kind of gift a neighbor brings a neighbor. He tied the four handfuls in a piece of rag and set out for Dwaraka.

The road was long and he was weak. He walked through country he had never seen, past fields and forests, resting where he could, and as he walked he turned one question over and over: how would he even gain sight of Krishna? The lord of a great city, surrounded by guards and ministers and queens — would such a man see a ragged brahmana standing at his gate? Sudama had no answer. He only walked, the little bundle in his hand, and trusted the friend he remembered — a boy who had shared his lessons and his hunger, and who had never once made him feel small.

At last the towers of Dwaraka rose on the horizon, and the sea glittered beyond them. He crossed the outer groves, passed the three gates of the city, past merchants and chariots and men in armor, until he stood before the palace of the king who had sixteen thousand queens — the king who had once been a boy at their teacher's house, hungry and ragged like him.
stories.reflection: Sudama's poverty is not merely hardship; it is also the condition that lets the story happen. The wife who refuses to let pride waste a friendship, and the poor man who would rather carry a gift of flat rice than come empty-handed, set the whole meeting in motion. The gift's smallness is the point — friendship is measured by the giving, not the gift.
stories.next_story_tease: Inside the palace, Krishna had already seen him — and was rising from his couch.

stories.title: Krishna Embraces His Old Friend
stories.story:
Sudama had walked a long road to reach this gate — all the way from his poor village to the king's palace in Dwaraka — carrying nothing but four handfuls of flattened rice tied in a rag. Years before, he and Krishna had been schoolboys together, studying at their teacher's house. Now Krishna was a king, and Sudama was so poor that this small bundle was the only gift he could bring. He stood at the palace gate and knew he was out of place.

The palace of Krishna housed sixteen thousand queens, and the building that held them was a city of its own — courtyards and corridors, gardens and lamps, guards who had seen every kind of man come and go but who looked at the ragged brahmana and saw something they could not place. But no one turned him away, and no one asked his business, as though the palace itself were waiting for him.

Sudama did not have to wonder what to do next. From somewhere deep inside the palace, Krishna saw him — saw him from afar, through rooms and walls and the whole long passage of years since they had been boys together. He rose from the couch where he sat with Rukmini and hurried to the gate — the king of Dwaraka, running to meet a guest in rags.

He embraced him. The tears came to Krishna's eyes — the old texts say it plainly: the tears of joy — as he held his old friend, the best of brahmanas, thin and weary from the road. Sudama, who had feared he might not even be recognized, found himself wrapped in his friend's arms. Krishna held him a long moment, and when he drew back his hands stayed on Sudama's shoulders, as if he could not quite believe the road had brought him.

Krishna would not let him stand. He took him by the hand and seated him on his own couch. And then the servants of the palace could scarcely believe what their eyes reported: the king himself knelt and washed the feet of the ragged guest, and took the water and bore it to his own head, honoring it as the holiest of things. In all the palace, no one moved; the servants stood frozen, watching their king serve his guest. He had fragrant incense brought and rows of lamps lit, and he received his friend with joy, as though a treasure had come to the palace rather than a poor man. A poor man's gift, a king's welcome — somewhere between the two, the old friendship simply resumed.

The women of the inner palace saw it, and the wonder of it stopped them where they stood. Krishna, whose fame was spotless, whose word held the worlds together, had seated a penniless brahmana on his own couch and washed his feet with his own hands. They had seen kings bow to him and learned men worship him; they had never seen him honor anyone like this. "What good deed has this man performed," they whispered to one another, "that our king should cherish him so — a man with nothing, while the queen of fortune herself serves him?"

Rukmini herself came and stood beside them, and took up a fan, and fanned the weary brahmana — she, the goddess of fortune, cooling the man who had arrived at her palace with nothing but a rag of flattened rice.

And the two friends sat and talked. Not of kingdoms, not of wealth. They talked of the old days, of the years when they had studied together in their teacher's house — the mornings, the lessons, the small adventures of boys — and the palace around them, for all its splendor, faded to nothing next to that.

The women of the palace watched the king of Dwaraka sit and talk and laugh with a guest who had arrived in rags, and they understood — many of them for the first time — what kind of king they served.
stories.reflection: The palace women's question — what merit has this beggar performed? — is the story's hinge. By every worldly measure Sudama deserves nothing, yet Krishna honors him as a treasure. The episode turns the usual logic of honor upside down: the king bows to the poor man, and the goddess of fortune fans him, because friendship, not rank, is what the lord of Dwaraka counts.
stories.next_story_tease: Then Krishna asked what gift his old friend had carried all the way from home.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna, risen from his couch, embracing the emaciated, ragged Sudama with tears on his face, while Rukmini stands beside them with a fan and the women of the palace look on in astonishment.

stories.title: Krishna Eats Sudama's Flat Rice
stories.story:
Sudama was a brahmana — one of the priestly class — and he was poor. He had set out for Dwaraka with very little in his hands: a single handful of flattened rice, tied in the fold of his cloth, the only gift he could bring to his friend Krishna, who was now lord of a city of gold.

Krishna had once been his friend; this much Sudama held to, though time and fortune had carried them far apart. Krishna had come into kingship and wealth — a palace, a household, a city that glittered on the sea. Sudama had stayed poor, with a wife at home and a house where the grain did not always last. Flattened rice was the food of the very poor, pressed flat and carried in a rag; it was all he had to offer, and he knew how small it would look in that place.

He had meant, somewhere in his heart, to ask for help. A poor man does not cross half the kingdom for nothing. But the nearer he came to Dwaraka, the smaller his request seemed, until it lodged in his throat like a stone he could neither swallow nor speak.

The city, when he reached it, was more than he had imagined — towers and gold, and the sound of the sea against the walls — and he walked through it feeling smaller with every step, clutching the little knot of rice against his side. Krishna did not wait for Sudama to be announced. When he heard who had come, he went out himself and received his friend with the warmth of old affection, led him in, and seated him where he himself sat. Sudama looked around at the splendor of that house and felt his poverty more keenly than he ever had at home.

Krishna could see into his friend's heart, and he knew why Sudama had come and what he carried. Gently he asked what gift his friend had brought him. "Even a trifle, offered with love, pleases me," Krishna said — "a leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water. Whatever is given with devotion, I accept."

Sudama was ashamed, and he offered nothing. He could not bring himself to untie the knot in his cloth; the rice, so carefully carried all that way, now seemed too small to show and too poor to give. So Krishna reached over and took the handful of rice from the fold of his friend's cloth himself. "What you have brought me," he said, "is what pleases me most." He ate one mouthful, and it gave him the delight of a feast. He reached for a second.

Then the goddess of fortune, watching and pleased, stayed his hand. "This much," she said, "is enough to grant every riches in the world." Sudama heard the words, but he could not see how one mouthful of a poor man's rice could mean such a thing.

He stayed that night in Krishna's house, and in the morning he set out for home. He had asked for nothing; not one word of his need had crossed his lips. He returned the way he had come, on foot and empty-handed, carrying only the memory of his friend's welcome — and that welcome, he found, was worth more than any treasure he might have been bold enough to name. Something had been given and received in that room, and though he could not put a name to it, he carried it home as surely as he had carried the rice. The shame that had walked with him all the way to Dwaraka did not walk with him back.
stories.reflection: The story turns on what Sudama does not say. Face to face with the friend he came to ask for help, he is too ashamed to speak of his need, and he offers only the handful of rice he carried in a rag. Krishna's delight in that handful — and the goddess of fortune's word that it already contains every riches — suggests that what is given with love is never small.

stories.title: Sudama Finds His Hut a Palace
stories.story:
Sudama walked the long road home from Dwaraka with empty hands, and his heart was strange with wonder. He had gone to see his old friend Krishna carrying a poor man's gift, a single handful of flattened rice, and Krishna had eaten it with delight, as if it were a feast prepared for a king. Any man in his place would have asked for help that night in the palace; his poverty had followed him all the way to Dwaraka, whispering of everything he lacked. But when he stood before Krishna, the words would not come. He could not ask for anything at all.

Now the villages of his own country were appearing one by one along the road, and he turned the marvel over in his mind. "Where am I," he asked himself, "poor and burdened with faults, and where is Krishna, the very home of fortune?" All his life he had measured the distance between them, and it had always seemed like the distance between mud and the moon. Yet Krishna had taken his handful of rice with love, and had given him back something he had not dared to imagine, and had done it without being asked, as though it were nothing.

Walking, he began to understand why. If he had asked for wealth and received it, would he have remembered? Wealth has a way of loosening a poor man's grip on everything else; it fills the hands and empties the heart. Krishna, who knew him through and through, had given him prosperity unasked, and in the giving had kept him still his friend. For the wise say that the Lord does not hand his devotee the riches that would pull the heart away; he gives what the heart can carry. And to Sudama he had given everything, because Sudama had asked for nothing but to remain his friend. "May this friendship, this companionship, this service to him," he prayed as he walked, "be mine in birth after birth."

He was still turning such thoughts when he came to the edge of his own village, and stopped, for he no longer knew it. Where his humble hut had stood there now rose a cluster of celestial mansions, ringed with gardens and clear lakes, their waters loud with the calling of birds. Well-dressed men and graceful women moved through the courtyards as though the place had always been theirs. Sudama stood in the road, a poor man in a worn cloth, and could not believe his eyes.

His wife heard that he had come, and hurried out to meet him, radiant as the goddess of fortune among her attendants. When she saw him her eyes filled with tears of love, and whatever hand had worked this change while he was away, she was still the same wife; she drew him, half laughing and half weeping, through the gates.

Inside, the wonder deepened. The beds were heaped soft as foam, spread with ivory and gold; jeweled lamps glowed in the rooms; the walls of crystal and emerald gave back the light of a hundred riches. Sudama, who had slept on a mud floor all his life, walked through his own house as though through a dream.

And there, among the golden couches, the truth of it settled on him at last. The Lord gives generously even to one who asks; how much more to a friend who asks for nothing? Krishna had taken his single meager handful of flattened rice with joy and repaid it with a kingdom — and he had given it in such a way that the giving never came between them: unasked, unannounced, as natural as the return of an old friend.

That night, standing in the jewel-lit splendor of his own home, the poor man who had gone to Dwaraka with empty hands found that he was rich beyond all measuring. Not in palaces, not in gold, but in this: that Krishna treasured even a handful of flattened rice, and had turned an old friend's poverty into a palace without waiting to be asked.
stories.reflection: Sudama's poverty is not ended by the palace but redefined by it. The story's quietest point is that Krishna gives generously even to those who ask, yet gives most safely to the friend who asks for nothing, and Sudama's prayer is not for wealth but that the friendship itself should continue birth after birth.
stories.next_story_tease: The same grace was about to move on a grander stage, when Vasudeva himself would be initiated into a great sacrifice at Samanta-panchaka.

stories.title: Vasudeva's Sacrifice
stories.story:
The holy field of Samanta-panchaka lay open to the sky, a plain long consecrated by the rites of the wise, and that season the sages were doing something rare: they had chosen a man as their own. Vasudeva, Krishna's father, had come to them with a question about the highest duty, and the asking itself had pleased them. Now they took him as their disciple, and Vasudeva in turn chose them, as such rites direct, to be his priests, and they prepared to initiate him into a great sacrifice.

The field itself had its own gravity. For ages the wise had come to Samanta-panchaka to offer their rites, and the very ground was held to be blessed, so that a sacrifice performed there stood in a place already full of offerings. The sage Narada was among the gathered sages, watching the preparations take shape with quiet pleasure.

Word of the rite went out to every house of the Yadavas — Krishna's own people — and the clans came. From every direction the great families of the Vrishnis and the Yadavas converged on the plain, filling it with color and the low murmur of a whole people gathered for one purpose. When the initiation began, the Vrishnis arrived wearing lotus garlands, and Vasudeva's queens came with them, delighted, bright with gold and fine garments. The air filled with the sound of mridangas and drums, conches and kettledrums, until the whole field seemed to be singing. The priests anointed Vasudeva as the rite required, touched his body with fragrant unguents, and dressed him in silks and bracelets, necklaces, anklets and earrings, until the man who had come asking questions stood at the heart of the ceremony like a king at his crowning. His priests, too, were robed in jeweled silk, and the whole assembly shone under the open sky.

Among the kinsmen stood the two who made the gathering complete: Krishna and his elder brother Balarama, each surrounded by his own family and his own sons — sons among their father's people, the extraordinary standing quietly in an ordinary family gathering.

Vasudeva performed the rites as the tradition prescribed, the subsidiary offerings — the daily fire-offerings of agnihotra, and the rest — one after another, unhurried, with the great sages guiding every step. For days the fires burned, and the field breathed smoke and saffron and the scent of ghee, and the chant of the priests rose and fell with the sun. Then came the giving. At the proper time, as the scriptures direct, he gave the priests their dakshina, rich gifts of cows and land and maidens, so that the men who had conducted the sacrifice went away honored beyond anything they had asked. The queens made their offerings in turn, and the rite closed with the avabhritha bath, the final purification that brings a sacrifice to its end. When Vasudeva had bathed in that last water, he gave garments and ornaments to the bards and to the women who had graced the field; to his own kinsmen, with their wives and their sons, he gave abundant gifts, holding nothing back. Nor did he forget the wider circle: the assembled priests, the hosts of gods, men and ancestors, and the celestial singers called caranas, all were honored in their turn, so that no one who had taken part went away empty-handed.

When the drums had fallen silent and the fires had received their last oblations, Vasudeva stood on that holy field, cleansed by the bath and crowned with the dust of the rite. He looked across the plain at his sons, Krishna and Balarama, each at the head of his own house, and it seemed to him that the sacrifice had already given him everything a man could ask. The field of Samanta-panchaka had seen many great rites; it had rarely seen one so simply complete: a father purified, his sons beside him, and nothing held back from anyone who had come.
stories.reflection: The account lingers not on the meaning of the rites but on the scene itself: the anointing, the music, the giving that leaves no one empty-handed. Its quiet center is the sight of Krishna and Balarama standing among their father's kinsmen, the extraordinary present in an ordinary family gathering.
stories.next_story_tease: But in Dwaraka, a mother's grief was waiting, older than any sacrifice and not yet healed.

stories.title: Devaki Asks for Her Slain Sons
stories.story:
In Dwaraka, everyone told the story of the boy who had come back from the dead. But for Devaki it was never a story.

Years before, when Krishna and Balarama had finished their studies, their teacher had asked for his fee: his own son, dead and gone, was to be brought back to him. The two brothers had gone to the world of the dead and done it, returning the boy to his father's arms. People marveled at the tale; it was told at feasts and retold to children. And Devaki heard it the way a woman hears a thing when it touches her own loss.

She had borne eight children, and six of them she had never seen grow. Kamsa, her own brother, had killed them one by one as soon as they were born, for he lived in fear that one of her sons would grow up to take his kingdom and his life. She had held each child only long enough to lose it. She had never watched one of those six take a step or speak a word; her whole memory of them was grief, worn smooth by years of silence. Only the last two — Balarama, and then Krishna — had been spared that fate; they had grown up in safety, and they were the sons who now lived beside her in Dwaraka.

Surrounded by palaces and grandsons, she had learned not to speak of the six. The loss did not diminish with distance; it simply became the shape of her days, a room in the house of her mind she had learned to walk past quickly.

But the story of the teacher's son undid that silence. A father had wept for one dead boy, and his sons had brought him back. She had wept for six, and no one had ever brought them back — not the priests with their rites, not the years with their healing, not even the gods. The tale that made everyone else marvel opened Devaki's old wound again, and this time she did not turn away from it.

She went to Krishna and Balarama with tears on her face, and she did not demand; she asked. "When your teacher commanded you," she said, "you went to the world of the dead and fetched back a son, long dead, and returned him to his father. That was the fee he asked, and you paid it. Grant my wish the same way. Bring back my sons — the ones my brother slew. I held each of them only long enough to lose him."

The two brothers looked at their mother. They did not tell her it was impossible. They did not say that the dead cannot be returned, that the years cannot be undone. They had fetched a dead son once, for a teacher's fee. She was their mother, and her wish was older than the palace she lived in, older than the kingdom, older than the grief she had carried all these years.

And in their silence Devaki understood that she had been heard. Whatever her sons intended, they had not refused her; they had not turned away. Standing before her sons in the bright halls of Dwaraka, with the tears still on her face, she felt the weight of years lift just a little, like a door opening in that room of her mind she had walked past for so long. For the first time in years, she let herself hope.
stories.reflection: What is striking is how quiet the request is. Devaki does not rage or reproach; she reminds her sons of what they once did for a stranger's son and asks, almost gently, for the same for her own. In this telling, grief does not thunder; it remembers, and asks.
stories.next_story_tease: To answer her, the two brothers would descend beneath the world, to the kingdom of the daitya king Bali.
stories.hero_scene: Devaki, tears on her face, stands before Krishna and Balarama in the palace at Dwaraka, her hands clasped as she asks them to bring back the six sons Kamsa slew, and the two brothers look at their mother in silence.

stories.title: Krishna and Balarama Visit Bali in Sutala
stories.story:
Krishna and his elder brother Balarama did not travel by any road that day. Where they were going, beneath the world, no path led; they descended by their own mystic power into the vast, splendid realm called Sutala, the kingdom of Bali, king of the daityas — the ancient demon race. A demon by birth, Bali was a devotee by heart.

Bali knew them the moment they appeared. He rose from his seat at once, for before him stood Krishna, whom his heart had worshipped all his life, and Balarama beside him, and he bowed low, his whole family bowing with him, his heart overflowing with the joy of the sight. He brought forward a noble seat and settled the two upon it, and then he worshipped them with everything his kingdom held precious: garments of great worth, ornaments, cooling unguents, and all the riches of his realm laid out like an offering. He washed their feet with his own hands, his kin around him, and again and again he lifted those lotus feet to his head, his mind dissolved in love. It seemed to him that no king in any world had ever entertained such guests, and he did not intend to let the moment pass unhonored.

"Your sight is hard to obtain, even for the gods," Bali said. "Gods and demons, the minstrels of heaven and the sages of the sky — some approach you with enmity and some with longing, and none can fully know you. From the dark well of this world, where no one thinks to seek you, you have drawn me up and set my feet upon your path. Instruct me, lord. Make me free of fault."

Krishna looked at the king of Sutala with the affection he gives to devotion, wherever it is found — in a palace above the earth or in a kingdom beneath it. Then he told him what he had come for.

"These six sons," he said, "were once the six sons of the sage Marichi. They laughed at Brahma, the creator god, and for that fault they were cursed to be born as demons. Born in Devaki's womb, they were slain by Kamsa — the very children my mother weeps for. They dwell here, near your own city, waiting to be released from the curse. I will take them back with me, to end my mother's grief."

He said it without drama, as one stating what had always been true. The six sons of Marichi had passed through many births to arrive at this one — waiting, in the shadows of a demon king's realm, for the two brothers to come and fetch them home. Their deaths at Kamsa's hands had never been an ending, only a pause.

Bali listened, and understood that the visit had never been about him — and yet he was not diminished by that understanding. It was enough that the Lord had entered his kingdom, enough that he had sat on his seat and accepted his worship. The six sons, waiting in the shadows of his realm, were about to be given back to the light, and Bali had been allowed to witness it.

So, having spoken, Krishna took the six sons into his keeping. Bali pressed his head once more to those feet that had come down into his kingdom, and the two brothers rose from Sutala with the six sons beside them, carrying a mother's grief, and its answer, back toward the world above.
stories.reflection: The descent to Sutala reads almost like a mirror of the world above: it is a demon king, not a mortal one, who shows what devotion looks like, asking nothing for himself and only to be made whole by the Lord's presence. The revelation of the sons' origin is given almost as an aside, as if to say that even their deaths were a thread in a longer design.
stories.next_story_tease: Back in Dwaraka, a mother was waiting with open arms for the six sons she had lost.

stories.title: The Six Sons Restored to Devaki
stories.story:
Krishna and Balarama returned to Dwaraka carrying six small children, and the city that had witnessed every kind of wonder fell quiet at the sight. Two grown men — one dark, one fair — walking up the coast road with infants in their arms, six of them, small and silent, as though the brothers had gone down into the earth and come back with the morning held in their hands. Word of them traveled faster than their feet: children, the city whispered, they have brought children back from the underworld.

The children were Devaki's sons. Years before, her brother Kamsa had taken each of her first six children at birth and killed them, one by one, because a prophecy had warned him that a child of Devaki would one day end his reign. She had carried that grief ever since — a weight worn smooth by time but never lifted. She had borne Krishna and Balarama, the seventh and the eighth, and had loved them with all her strength; but the six were always there, six small absences standing in the shadow of her heart.

And now Krishna and Balarama had descended to Sutala, the netherworld kingdom where King Bali reigned, and had brought the six back to the world above. The journey home was long, and the brothers carried the children turn by turn, so that not one of them was ever out of someone's arms — as if the earth had once taken these children and they meant to be sure it did not take them again.

Word ran ahead of them through the streets, and Devaki came out of the palace as they reached the gate. She came forward slowly, the way people move when they are afraid to believe, and the women of the palace followed her with their hands pressed to their mouths. She stopped a little way off and counted them — one, two, three, four, five, six — and then her milk came, the body remembering what the heart had kept locked for so many years. She took them into her arms, all six at once, and nursed them, her breasts flowing, holding each small head to her, weeping and laughing together, while the courtyard stood silent around her. No one moved. The guards, the ministers, the women of the palace — they watched a mother receive her children, and there was nothing to say.

When the six had drunk their fill, they drew back from her and stood. Then, before the eyes of everyone gathered there, they bowed — first to Krishna, then to Devaki, their mother, then to Vasudeva, their father, and at last to Balarama. And released at last from the curse that had taken them at birth, they rose from the ground and ascended, slowly, like light climbing a wall, until they reached the abode of the gods and were gone.

Devaki stood with empty arms, milk still on her lips, watching the sky where her sons had vanished. She had held them for a single evening — long enough to feed them, long enough to know them — and the old grief went out of her like a breath she had been holding for years. Beside her, Vasudeva watched his sons climb the sky and said nothing; there was nothing a father could add. The court watched her, and then looked up at the sky, and understood what they had seen: a debt of love, paid in full.

Dwaraka kept this in its memory for a long time after — six children carried down into the earth and carried back up again, and a mother whose arms were, for one night, the place where a curse was dissolved.
stories.reflection: Devaki is given her sons not to keep but to hold once: the restoration lasts a single evening of milk and touch, and then the children leave. The story honors a mother's love by letting it finish what a curse began — the six are freed through her embrace, not through any power, and her grief is answered by release rather than by possession.
stories.next_story_tease: But Krishna's journeys were not finished: in Mithila, two men were preparing for the same guest, each certain the visit was meant for him alone.
stories.hero_scene: The six sons, having drunk Devaki's milk, rising into the sky above the palace courtyard of Dwaraka as Devaki stands below with empty arms and milk still on her lips, while Krishna and Balarama watch and the whole court gazes upward in wonder.
