stories.title: When Balarama Came Home to Vraja
stories.story:
For the first time in years, Balarama took the road to Vraja alone, and he went with his younger brother Krishna's blessing. Vraja was the cowherd country where the two brothers had grown up — before Mathura, before Dwaraka, the golden city by the sea where they now lived.

The village had not forgotten them, and the news that Balarama was coming ran ahead of him like fire in dry grass. By the time he reached the cow-pens, the gopas and gopis of Vraja — the cowherds and the milkmaids — had gathered, and they came at him all at once: the old cowherds pressing forward to embrace him, the women laughing and weeping at the same time, hands reaching for his arms as if they could not quite believe the sight.

The elders who had watched him grow up spoke first. Welcome, they said, you whom we raised among us. We have heard of your deeds — how you met the great fish Panchajana in the ocean and destroyed it; how you fought Jarasandha and the kings with him at Gomanta; how you entered Mathura, and the earth itself was steadied by it. Every tale that had reached the village, they laid before him like offerings.

Balarama answered them with something better than a list of victories. "You are dearer to us than our own kin," he told the cowherds. "We were reared in your houses. We took our meals with you and tended the cattle beside you. We spent our boyhood sporting on these very grounds. Whatever we are, we became here, among you. You are our firm friends."

Then the gopis came forward, and all their questions were of one person. Does Krishna remember his father Nanda, who raised him? they asked. Does he remember his mother Yashoda, who held him as a child? Does he remember his friends, the boys he played with, the women who sang for him? Their voices were half teasing and half raw. He left us so suddenly, they said, cutting the thread of friendship as if it had never been woven. How do the wise ladies of Dwaraka trust the words of one so quick to charm and so quick to leave? And yet even as they spoke they could not bear to hear of anything else — when one of them tried to turn the talk to other things, the rest cried out: what other stories can we hear, when our hearts are still with him?

Balarama listened to it all, and then he gave them what they truly wanted. He carried Krishna's messages in his own heart, all the way from Dwaraka — and the words he spoke for his brother went straight to the gopis' hearts. The village learned that Krishna remembered everything: the father who had raised him, the mother who had loved him, the friends of his boyhood, the nights of song by the Yamuna. He had not forgotten; the distance was not of his choosing; the love was kept, as surely as they had kept it.

And then Balarama stayed. For two months he remained in Vraja, through the spring months of Madhu and Madhava. He sported with the gopis in the groves of the Yamuna; the days passed in play and song, and the nights in the light of the full moon, with the wind carrying the scent of flowers through the trees. Vraja had its prince back, and the women who had pined for Krishna learned that his brother carried his heart in his words. When at last the time came to leave, there was not a house in the village that did not stand at its door to watch him go.
stories.reflection: The gopis' question — does Krishna remember us? — is answered not with assurances but with messages carried in a brother's heart, and with two months of staying. Balarama's visit heals the wound of the departure not by explaining it but by showing that the love survived the distance.
stories.next_story_tease: But one night in those two months, Balarama would summon the Yamuna herself — and the river would learn what it cost to refuse him.

stories.title: The Night the Yamuna Was Dragged
stories.story:
The wine came to him from a tree.

It happened during the two months that Balarama, Krishna's elder brother, had come to spend in Vraja, the cowherd country where the brothers had grown up. Deep in the forest, where he was sporting with the gopis by the Yamuna, the goddess Varuni — the goddess of wine, sent by Varuna, the lord of the waters — flowed out of the hollow of an old tree. The fragrance of that honey-stream rode the wind to where the cowherds sat, and Balarama, who had never needed an excuse for joy, drank. Around him the gandharvas, the musicians of heaven, sang; overhead the sky sounded with drums, and flowers rained down on the grove. The evening had turned to gold.

By the time the moon rose, the wine had done its work, and the whole grove seemed brighter for it. Balarama wore a single earring and a garland of wildflowers; his blue cloth hung loose about him; his eyes shone, and the women sang his deeds back to him as he laughed among them. He was, the cowherds said, like the moon in an autumn night — all light and play.

Then he turned to the river. The Yamuna ran broad and dark through the groves, and Balarama, standing at her bank, called to her by name. He spoke to her as one speaks to a friend whose company he longs for: "O great river, you who flow to the ocean, come in your bodily form, and let us sport together in your waters."

The river kept her silence. Perhaps she thought the words were only the wine speaking; perhaps a river that had flowed to the sea since the beginning of the world did not know how to answer a summons. He called again — "Will you not come? Will you not come?" — and when the Yamuna still gave no answer, the mood of the evening changed.

The joy in Balarama's face did not fade slowly; it simply went out, and in its place came the wrath of the plough-bearer — for Balarama's weapon was the great plough he carried, the farmer's tool that in his hands was a weapon of war. He seized it and drove its point into the river's bank, and he dragged. The earth groaned. The bank tore open. The water, wrenched from its ancient course, followed the plough like a woman dragged by the hand — currents tangling, fish and water-creatures flung about in bewilderment, the white geese scattering in panic. The river that had chosen its own path since the beginning of time now flowed where Balarama chose.

And the Yamuna, afraid at last, begged his pardon. "Rama, Rama, mighty-armed," she said, "I did not know your valour. Forgive me — forgive the river that did not know the glory of the Blessed One."

Her words went into him like water into dry ground. His anger was gone as quickly as it had come. He released her. He stepped into her waters, bathed, and sported as he had first asked to do, at his ease in the current, and the night settled back into its old peace. The gopis and cowherds on the bank, who had watched with their hearts in their mouths, let out their breath at last. When he came out he put on blue garments and a golden garland, and the river lay quiet and restored along her course.

Long afterward, the cowherds of Vraja would point to the path where the river had been dragged — the scar in the land, the channel pulled from its old course — and say: there. That is where the Yamuna learned Balarama's name. And of the night itself they would say only this: that it passed like a single moment, as all nights pass in Vraja when the heart is full.
stories.reflection: The river is dragged not out of cruelty but out of a drunkard's insistence on being answered, and the moment she names his power he lets her go. Even the wrath of the plough-bearer turns out to be a form of play — he wanted her company, and once she gave him her fear and her pardon, he was satisfied.
stories.next_story_tease: Far from the Yamuna's banks, meanwhile, a raging ape was laying waste to the land in the name of his slain friend.
stories.hero_scene: Night on the Yamuna: the intoxicated Balarama, garlanded and blue-clad, driving his great plough into the river's bank and dragging her from her course, the water and its creatures tumbling in bewilderment behind the ploughshare.

stories.title: The Ape Who Avenged Narakasura
stories.story:
When the demon king Narakasura fell to Krishna's discus, he left behind a friend who would not let the world forget it.

Dvivida was an ape of the mountains, vast and powerful, and he had loved the slain demon king like a brother. Where Narakasura's other allies made their peace or hid themselves, Dvivida chose vengeance — and he had the strength to make vengeance terrible. He would repay his friend's death, he swore, with the ruin of everything Krishna loved. He was not a demon of the cities, who plots in shadows; he was a force of the wild, and he struck in the open, where everyone could see and no one could stop him.

The land he chose to punish was Anarta, the country of the Yadavas. And he began.

He set fire to the cities and the villages, and watched the flames climb. He went to the mountains and tore them up by their roots, and hurled them down upon the regions below, crushing whatever lay beneath. He waded into the middle of the ocean and stood there, scooped up the sea with his two arms, and flung it over the coastal lands until the shore drowned. The hermitages of the sages — the quiet places where holy men kept their fires and their vows — he tore apart, breaking their trees and scattering their offerings, defiling the sacred fires themselves, and the holy men were driven from the places they had kept for a lifetime. He seized men and women and hurled them into the caves of the mountains. He laid waste to the whole country, and the women of good families learned to fear the shadow of the ape.

The terror had a shape and a name. Farmers abandoned their fields; villages emptied at the first cry of alarm; the roads filled with people walking with everything they owned on their heads, not knowing which direction would be far enough. No army could catch him. He moved like a storm, and like a storm he was gone before the dust settled, leaving behind only smoke, torn earth, and the sea lying where the land had been.

For the ape, it was a kind of joy. Every village that burned was a stone laid on Narakasura's pyre; every hermitage broken was a blow struck for his friend. He was doing what the dead king would have wanted, and he meant to keep doing it until there was nothing left of Anarta to save.

And then, one day, in the middle of the country he had made his own, Dvivida came upon a sight he had not expected. Standing in the ruin — quiet, unhurried, a garland of lotuses around his neck — was the lord of the Yadavas himself. Not the one who had slain his friend. The other one: Balarama, Krishna's elder brother, the plough-bearer whose weapon was a great iron plough, come to see what had been done to his people's land.

The ape stopped. Behind him the fires still burned, and the hands that had torn up mountains hung at his sides. For a long moment neither of them moved; only the smoke of the burning passed between them. For the first time since Narakasura died, Dvivida looked at a man and did not see prey. Then he showed his teeth — not in fear, but in the joy of a fighter who had finally found an opponent.
stories.reflection: Dvivida's destruction is terrible precisely because it is faithful: he is repaying a friendship, and every act of ruin is, in his own mind, an act of love for the dead. The story sets revenge and ruin against the quiet arrival of Balarama, and the whole country holds its breath at the meeting.
stories.content_note: The ape Dvivida ravages the land: villages burn, mountains are hurled down on regions, coastal lands are flooded, and villagers are seized and assaulted. The destruction is described with restraint, but may warrant parental awareness for younger listeners.
stories.next_story_tease: The ape and the plough-bearer were about to settle everything between them.
stories.hero_scene: In the wreckage of Anarta: the vast ape Dvivida, smoke rising from burning villages behind him, faces the quiet, lotus-garlanded Balarama across the torn ground, the whole land holding its breath.

stories.title: The Ape Who Mocked Balarama
stories.story:
The hill of Raivataka had never known a stranger visitor. Balarama — Krishna's elder brother, and the strongest man of the Yadava clan — had brought the women of his household up from Dwaraka for a day of ease: the wine jars open, a song on his lips, the sea breeze moving through the groves. Then the leaves above him shook, a branch bent like a bow, and an ape the size of a young elephant dropped onto a limb overhead. The singing stopped.

For months this same ape had been the terror of the land. His name was Dvivida, and he had been the dearest friend of Narakasura, the demon king whom Krishna had slain; in his grief and fury he had sworn to make the whole world pay. He had interrupted the sacrifices and subverted the rites. He had set fire to forests, villages and towns. He had hurled rocks down upon cities, lifted up mountains and cast them into the ocean, and churned the sea until it rose over its bounds and swept away the settlements on its shores. He could change his shape at will, and he had enlarged himself until he could walk through the standing corn like a man walking through grass, crushing the harvests beneath him. The whole land, disordered by this maddened ape, had lost its peace and its sacred study. And now he had followed the Yadavas to their pleasure hill.

He did not come to fight. He came to mock. Rocking on his branch, he grinned at Balarama, rolled his eyes at the young women, flicked his brows and pulled faces at them until they drew back, half offended and half afraid. Balarama, whose head was light with the wine they called varuni, felt the anger rise, hot and sudden. He seized a stone and hurled it.

The ape caught it out of the air — and laughed.

Mocked before the women of his own household, Balarama rose to his feet and took up his mace and his plough, the two weapons that had been with him since the pastures of Vrindavan. The ape, drunk on his own daring, struck at Balarama's head. The blow fell as harmlessly as red chalk flung at a mountain. And Balarama answered — with his mace, blow after blow, until the ape's great body was broken in a hundred places.

Still the beast came on. He tore up trees and rocks and hurled them in a blind rain that fell harmlessly around the plough-bearer. And Balarama, disgusted at last, cast aside his weapons and seized the ape with his bare arms, like a man taking hold of a storm. What followed was not a duel but a settling. The ape's arms, thick as palm trunks, beat uselessly against that grip. When Balarama brought him down, the earth herself shuddered — the mountains trembled, the forests swayed, as if the ground knew what had been lifted from it. The ape lay where he had fallen, blood at his lips, and did not rise again.

In the sky, voices shouted victory and homage; the gods rained flowers on the hill.

The women came out of the groves, and the songs began again, quieter than before. And down in the country, in the villages Dvivida had burned, the smoke that rose was only cooking smoke once more. The sea returned to its bed. The harvests stood. The land, which for months had lived in the shadow of a maddened animal, remembered how to be a land again.

They said afterward that the hill of Raivataka carried a scar where the great ape had fallen. But hills heal, as countries do — and the memory of that afternoon stayed longer with the Yadavas than the scar did: the day their lord stood in a grove with his weapons laid by and finished with his bare hands what no army had been able to finish in a year.
stories.reflection: Dvivida's end comes not from a weapon Balarama keeps ready but from the strength he has never needed to display: the mace and plough are laid aside before the ape is seized with bare hands. The land is freed not by armies but by one man's patience finally spent — and the hill keeps the scar, though the peace outlasts it.
stories.tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana tells the same duel differently: there Dvivida first steals Balarama's plough and club and breaks the wine cups, and Balarama fells him with a single blow of the fist on the forehead. This account follows the Bhagavata Purana, where the ape is struck down with mace and plough and finally seized with bare arms.
stories.content_note: Mild violence — a demon-ape is slain in combat; not graphic.
stories.next_story_tease: Before the season turned, Balarama would ride out again — this time to a city that answered courtesy with insult.
stories.hero_scene: On Raivataka hill, Balarama — mace and plough cast aside — seizes the towering ape Dvivida with his bare arms and brings him crashing to earth as the hill trembles, the women of the household watching from the grove, flowers raining from a sky ringing with victory cries.

stories.title: An Envoy Answered with Mockery
stories.story:
Balarama — Krishna's elder brother — came to Hastinapura, the city of the Kurus, as a peacemaker, and for a few hours it looked as though the peace would hold.

Samba, a young prince of the Yadava clan — Balarama's own people — lay in a Kaurava dungeon. The young warriors of Dwaraka, the Yadavas' city by the sea, had already strapped on their armor and were clamoring for war; Balarama had quieted them with a single word. He would go himself, he said, and bring the boy home with courtesy. Counselors like Uddhava, Krishna's trusted adviser, urged restraint, and the warriors urged steel, but it was Balarama who settled it: he set out alone, in a chariot radiant as the sun, and when he reached the city of the elephants he did not ride through its gates in pride. He stopped in the outer grove and sent word that he had come.

The elders came out to meet him — Dhritarashtra, the old king of the Kurus; Bhishma, the grandsire of their house; Drona, their teacher of arms; and Bahlika, their elder kinsman. They were plainly glad to see him. They received him with the cow of welcome and the water of honor, and they asked after the welfare of his kinsmen, as kinsmen ask after kinsmen. Everything, so far, was grace.

Balarama delivered his errand simply. Ugrasena, king of the Yadavas, had sent him. The Kurus held one of their princes captive — seized, as the Yadavas saw it, unjustly, seized by many against one — and the Yadava king asked only that Samba be released. It was a modest request, made in a modest voice, and it was met with laughter.

Duryodhana and his brothers answered for the Kurus. The Yadavas, they said, were cowherds who had climbed above their station. Bound to the Kurus by marriage, eating at their tables, sleeping under their roofs — and now sending envoys and making demands, as if the royal insignia they had taken up were theirs by right rather than by gift. "Enough of the Yadavas' kingship," they said. "These claims fit you the way nectar fits a serpent." And even if the Yadavas took offense — what then? The Kurus named their own champions, Bhishma, Drona, Arjuna, and asked, laughing, whether even Indra, the king of the gods, could stand against them while such men stood on the field. No, they said. Samba stays.

The words were not addressed to Balarama. They were spoken about him, and past him, as though he were already gone.

Balarama heard it all. He saw the wickedness of the Kurus laid bare — their pride running in a dozen different directions, none of them toward peace — and he understood, with a sudden clarity, that these men would never release Samba for any courtesy, because they had no idea whom they were insulting. They mocked the house of Ugrasena, the Yadava king — the king before whom the rulers of the earth bowed down. "The Vrishnis eat land given by the Kurus!" they jeered. And Balarama looked at them and thought of the pride of men made mad by wealth, stumbling like drunkards down a road they cannot see.

But he said nothing of it. He had come with open hands, and he would not answer mockery with steel — not here, not yet. He rose, and the laughter died in the hall, and the elders watched the great plough-bearer walk out past them without another word.

The chariot rolled out of the grove, and the gates of Hastinapura shut behind it on a peace that had never really begun. Behind him the mockery was already being retold with relish, in the very halls that had honored him that morning. Balarama carried one thing out of Hastinapura that day, and it did not cool on the long road home: the anger of a man who has been laughed at in front of the people he loves.
stories.reflection: The insult cuts deeper because it comes after a true welcome — the cow and the water of honor are offered before the mockery begins. The Kauravas measure the Yadavas by birth and borrowed land; Balarama measures them by a kingship they cannot see. The two sides are not even arguing about the same thing.
stories.next_story_tease: The anger he carried out of Hastinapura was not the kind that cools.

stories.title: The City Dragged Toward the Ganga
stories.story:
Hastinapura was still laughing when the earth began to groan.

That morning Balarama — the elder brother of Krishna — had ridden to Hastinapura to ask the Kurus to release Samba, a young prince of his own house who lay in their prison. He had been answered with laughter: mocked for the cowherds he came from, mocked for the peace he had come to make, mocked in front of elders who had welcomed him and then let the mockery stand. He had not gone far. The anger that had banked itself since morning came up at last, and his eyes went red with it. He turned back toward the city, carrying with him the one thing a city cannot withstand: a man who has stopped caring about the cost.

He drove the blade of his plough deep into the earth, beneath the very ramparts of Hastinapura. "Today," he said, "I will make the earth free of the Kauravas." And he leaned into the plough and pulled.

The city moved.

Walled and towered, gate and street and all, Hastinapura — the city of the elephant — tilted, swayed, and began to slide toward the Ganga like a boat torn loose from its mooring. Inside the walls the streets tipped, the houses groaned, and the great hall where the Yadavas had been mocked an hour before pitched like a deck. The river waited below, patient and deep, and it was plain to every soul in the city that in a few more paces Hastinapura would plunge into it like a stone into a well.

Then the gates flew open, and the Kurus came out — not in war-array, but with their families, terrified, clutching children, scrambling over one another, the great gates standing open and empty behind them. They ran to Balarama and fell at his feet and poured out their hearts: "Rama, Rama, support of all, we did not know your power. You are the one cause of creation and preservation and destruction; you yourself bear this earth upon your head, O thousand-headed one. Your anger is for the instruction of the world, not born of hatred or envy. Homage to you, soul of all beings."

Duryodhana himself came forward and yielded. Samba was brought up out of his cell, and with him Lakshmana — the Kuru princess whom Samba had carried off to make his bride, and for whose sake the whole trouble had begun — and both were placed in Balarama's keeping. Then the Kuru king, humbled as he had never been, made his peace in the coin of kings: a herd of elephants, every one of them sixty years old, and six thousand golden chariots blazing like the sun. He even asked, he who was proud of his skill with the mace, to be taken as Balarama's pupil in club-fighting; and Balarama accepted him. An odd peace, sealed between the man who had mocked and the man he had mocked, on the tilted ground of a city that had almost drowned.

Balarama accepted the gifts, released the city, and set it back upon its foundations. Then he turned for home, and in Dwaraka, in the assembly of the Yadus, among kinsmen who loved him, he told the whole tale — how he had gone for peace and been answered with pride, and how the pride had been answered with the plough.

And Hastinapura — they say its walls have leaned toward the river ever since that day, the way a man leans after a blow. Some marks a city carries the way a body carries a scar: for as long as the city stands, every traveler who comes up by the river can read in that tilt what one man with a plough could do when he was pushed past patience.
stories.reflection: What frees Samba is not the argument that failed the day before but the visible proof of what Balarama is: the city is not conquered but lifted, and the Kurus' surrender takes the form of recognition — they call his anger instruction, not vengeance. Even Duryodhana's pride finds a way to bend, becoming a pupil's humility before the very mace he had mocked.
stories.tradition_note: The Harivamsha records that Duryodhana, after surrendering Samba, became Balarama's pupil in club-fighting; that detail is included here. The Vishnu Purana has Balarama plunge the ploughshare beneath the city's ramparts with eyes red with rage, and the city drawn toward him.
stories.next_story_tease: The plough had saved a city — but a blade of grass would soon cost its wielder more than any war.
stories.hero_scene: On the plain beside the Ganga, Balarama leans into his great plough, its blade driven deep beneath Hastinapura's ramparts, and the entire walled city tilts like a boat on the river while terrified citizens pour from its gates.

stories.title: The Suta Who Would Not Rise
stories.story:
The talk in Dwaraka had turned to the coming war — the Kurus and the Pandavas, two branches of one royal family, sharpening blades against each other — and Balarama, the elder brother of Krishna, who had no taste for what was coming, went walking.

He was a pilgrim in those days. He bathed at Prabhasa, and made his offerings to the gods, the seers and the ancestors. He visited the holy waters one after another — Prithudaka, Bindu-saras, Tritakupa, Sudarshana — and the tirthas — the holy bathing places — strung along the Yamuna and the Ganga like beads on a thread. At last he came to the forest of Naimisha, where the sages were holding a long sacrifice, a satra that ran on season after season.

The sages saw him coming and rose to meet him, every one of them, like a field of grass bending to the wind. They honored him, seated him with his company, and made him welcome among them. It was then that Balarama's eyes found the one man in that whole assembly who had not risen.

He was a suta — a bard, of the charioteer line rather than the priestly line — and he sat among the brahmanas, the priests and scholars of the rite, on a seat of honor, unmoving. He had not stirred when Balarama arrived. He had not offered the folded hands of greeting. His name was Romaharshana, and the long sacrifice had made him great: he had been a pupil of the blessed seer Vyasa himself, and he had learned much, and he sat there full of his learning, in the seat the sages had given him, and rose for no one.

Balarama looked at him, and the anger came up like a tide. A suta — however learned, however honored — seated above the brahmanas, refusing to rise in their own sacrifice, before the very sages who had raised him. Untamed, undisciplined, vainly proud of his scholarship. Balarama spoke so that all could hear: "This is the very purpose for which I was born into this world." He bent and plucked one blade of kusha grass — the sacred grass used in their rites — from the earth, charged it with his power, and struck the suta down.

Romaharshana fell, and did not rise.

Then the cry went up — "Ha! Ha!" — a sound of grief that ran through the forest like wind through dry leaves. The sages came crowding around the fallen man, and they turned to Balarama with faces he had not expected. Not anger. Grief, and dismay. "O prince of the Yadus," they said, "we ourselves gave him this seat. It was we who raised him to the brahmana's seat; it was our gift that made him what he was. What you have done, you have done without knowledge. You have slain a brahmana. This is brahma-hatya — the killing of a brahmana — and there is no heavier sin."

Balarama stood over the man he had struck down and heard them. He had been certain — he had said so aloud, that this was the very purpose of his birth. And the sages, who had honored him to his face, told him that in that single stroke, done without knowledge, he had committed the one sin that stains even the stain-removers.

"If there is any purifier of this sin," they said, "O purifier of the worlds, tell us — and we will show you the way to it."

The forest was quiet. The long sacrifice had stopped. Balarama, who had come to Naimisha for peace and for purity, stood in the middle of it over the body of a man he had been certain it was right to kill — and heard, from the mouths of the sages, that the certainty itself had been his error.
stories.reflection: The episode keeps two judgments alive at once: Balarama sees a suta who will not rise, while the sages see a brahmana they themselves raised up. What is striking is that the slaying is called "done without knowledge" — the sin is real, yet the certainty that produced it was the error. Even the purifier of worlds can act from ignorance, and must be purified in turn.
stories.content_note: Mild violence: a man is struck dead (with a blade of grass, no gore). The episode turns on caste and honor, and the sages themselves dispute the act.
stories.next_story_tease: The sages would show him the penance for his unwitting sin — and it began with a demon who defiled their sacrifice.

stories.title: The Sages Prescribe Balarama's Penance
stories.story:
At Naimisha the grove had gone quiet. The suta Romaharshana lay where he had fallen, in the very enclosure where he had been reciting the ancient tales, and the cry the sages had raised still hung in the air like smoke: brahma-hatya — the slaying of a brahmana, a man of the priestly order. And the man who had struck the blow stood before them, waiting.

He was Balarama — Krishna's elder brother, who had come to the Naimisha forest as a pilgrim and been welcomed to the sages' great sacrifice, a rite that ran on season after season. When he had arrived among them, Romaharshana alone had remained seated, the one man in all that assembly who had not risen to greet him, and the answer had been terrible and swift: one blade of kusha grass, and the voice that had filled the grove fell silent forever. The suta had been dear to the sages, a voice that had carried the ancient lore across the years. Now the heaviest sin of the old law lay on Balarama, and every man in that grove knew its weight, for the killing of a brahmana is the sin that even the gods are said to fear.

The sages did not rage at him. They had cried out at the deed; now they drew together and spoke of atonement, as elders speak to one who has failed, and what they prescribed was no small thing. They told him of the demon Balvala, son of Ilvala, who had plagued their sacrifice for as long as any of them could remember. At every parvan — at the close of each cycle of rites, at the time of the new moon and of the full — the demon came down from the sky and rained filth and impurity upon the fire, defiling what years of penance had made pure, so that the sacrifice had to be begun again from the first offering. Year after year their rites had been broken by him, and they had been powerless to stop it. "Slay that cruel one," the sages said, "and that shall be the first part of your penance." Then they spoke the second part: for twelve months Balarama must wander through all of Bharatavarsha, the sacred land, bathing at its holy fords and washing the stain from himself in its waters, until the turning of the year had cleansed him.

Balarama heard the whole of it without flinching. He might have argued that the suta had dishonored the sages first, that respect had been broken before his blade was drawn; he said none of it. The killing had been his; the cleansing would be his as well. He stood before the sages and accepted — the slaying of the demon and the year of wandering both — and the old text is careful to say that he undertook the expiation for the benefit of the world, not only for himself.

So the penance was set, and the grove settled back toward its long rite with a new understanding: the man who had broken the silence of Naimisha would answer for it at the next parvan, when Balvala came again to rain his filth upon the fire. The sages returned to their seats. Balarama remained among them, watching the flame that the demon had defiled so many times, waiting for the season of his atonement to begin.
stories.reflection: The sages answer bloodshed not with punishment but with a task: the sin is to be washed out in action — by facing the demon who has plagued their rites, and by a year of walking the sacred land. Balarama accepts without defense or argument, and the old text says he did it for the benefit of the world; the burden, once accepted, turns outward and becomes service.
stories.next_story_tease: At the next parvan the demon would come again to defile the fire — and Balarama's penance would meet him.

stories.title: Balarama Slays the Demon Balvala
stories.story:
The morning of the parvan — the day that closed one cycle of the sages' rites — rose clear over the forest of Naimisha, where a great sacrifice had been running season after season, and the sages fed their fire and offered the day's oblations as they had done a hundred times before. Then, without warning, the sky above the sacrificial hall turned dark — not with cloud, but with a shape. From that darkness a rain began to fall, hissing into the fire and soiling the offerings: a rain of filth and impurity. The demon Balvala had come again.

It was exactly what the sages had described when they set the penance of Balarama — Krishna's elder brother, who had come to Naimisha as a pilgrim and, in a flash of anger, struck down their suta Romaharshana with one blade of grass. The demon was the son of Ilvala, cruel and ancient, a rover of the sky who at every parvan descended to defile their sacrifice at the very moment of its completion. For years they had endured him, powerless, watching their rites broken time and again by a hand they could not reach — the fire smothered, the offerings spoiled, the work of penance undone and begun again. And now they had in their midst the man whose penance was this demon's end. Every eye in the grove turned to Balarama, and he understood at once: this was the first half of his atonement, coming to meet him.

He saw the demon clearly — a body huge and black, like a mountain of crushed collyrium, drifting over the enclosure while the defilement rained down from him. And at the sight Balarama remembered his weapons, the plough and the mace that had torn apart the armies of the demons, and he did not wait. He raised the plough, and with its tip he caught the sky-roaming Balvala and dragged him down out of the air, and the demon fell to the earth before the fire. Balarama finished the work with his mace, and the defiler of Naimisha lay still at last, and the rain of impurity stopped as suddenly as it had begun.

The grove filled with the sages' joy, and it was a joy with years of helplessness behind it. They crowded around Balarama, praising him and calling down blessings that never fail; they laid upon him the vaijayanti, the celestial garland strung with lotuses that do not fade, and gave him garments from heaven itself. The fire that had been defiled so many times burned clean and bright above the demon's body, and the sacrifice went on as it had always been meant to go on.

With the sages' leave, Balarama set out from Naimisha the next morning, walking with the brahmanas, the priest-sages of the rite, toward the river Kaushiki — the first steps of the twelve-month pilgrimage that would carry him through all the holy fords of Bharatavarsha, the sacred land. The demon was dead. The penance had begun.
stories.reflection: There is a strange economy in the episode: the same hands that committed brahma-hatya at Naimisha are the hands that free the sages' sacrifice, as if the penance and the service were one act. The sages' gift of the unfading garland and their unfailing blessings suggest that in their eyes the cleansing had already begun with the deed.
stories.content_note: Demon-slaying: Balvala is dragged from the sky by the plough and his skull is crushed by the mace; described without graphic detail.
stories.next_story_tease: Far away, on the slope of Govardhana hill, the king of the gods was descending to ask a favour of Krishna.

stories.title: Indra Asks Krishna to Befriend Arjuna
stories.story:
The rain that had lashed Vrindavan for seven nights had ceased at last, and Govardhana hill stood again in the valley where it had always stood — lifted, held, and set down by the hand of Krishna, a cowherd boy of Vrindavan. The cattle were safe beneath it, and the village was drying in the sun. Then the sky over Govardhana opened a second time, and what descended was no storm: an elephant, vast as a cloud that holds its water, with the king of the gods upon its back.

Indra had watched the mountain rise with his own eyes, and wonder had overcome his anger. He had seen the worship offered to him set aside, and the village turn instead to the hill; he had answered with a deluge meant to break the cowherds — seven nights of rain that even gods and demons could not withstand. But the boy had held up the mountain through all of it, and the cows had sheltered and survived. Now the fury in the king of heaven had turned to awe, and he wanted to see this Krishna for himself.

He left his elephant at the foot of the hill, and Airavata stood patient as a rainless cloud, the rut trickling down its temples. Indra approached the boy seated at ease beneath the mountain, where he had been playing in the forest, living the small human life of a cowherd's day. What the king of heaven saw shook him: the curl of hair called the Srivatsa, the mark of Vishnu, upon the boy's breast; skin dark as a blue lotus; a crown bright as the sun above his brow; celestial earrings at his ears; a necklace of jewels on his chest. And above Krishna's head, invisible to mortal eyes, the great bird Garuda, king of birds, spread his wings to shade him from the sun. The god who had come to humble a village stood before the protector of all the worlds in the clothes of a milkman — and first he was ashamed, and then he was glad.

He spoke, and his voice was deep as thunder, and he did not pretend. He had been enraged when his worship was set aside, he said, and he had sent the rain — but Krishna had put it down by his own power, in Indra's very presence, holding the weight of the mountain like a house in the sky. "Whose mind would not fill with wonder?" the king of the gods asked. "As gold is the foremost of metals, so you are the foremost of the celestials. You alone are eternal among the gods, and I see no second who could carry what you have carried." Then, standing on the green ground of Vrindavan, Indra asked for something stranger than praise: he spoke of a son.

"A portion of myself," he said, "has been born on earth as Arjuna, the son of Kunti — your own cousin, of the same line of kings. In the coming war of the Bharatas, he will be your friend and your help in battle. Befriend him. Teach him what you know of the spirit. And regard him always, and take care of him as you take care of me."

Krishna heard him out, and his answer was simple and final: he knew Arjuna, and he would befriend him as long as he continued upon the earth.

So the king of the gods returned to heaven with his anger spent and a promise warm in his keeping, and the cowherds of Vrindavan went back to their herds beneath a clean sky — leaving the boy Krishna on the green slope of Govardhana with a friend he had not yet met.
stories.reflection: Indra comes down to praise, but the heart of the visit is a request — that Krishna befriend a boy he has never met. The king of heaven asks the cowherd to love his son as he himself is loved, and Krishna's flat promise, "as long as I continue upon the earth," quietly measures the whole span of the friendship that follows.
stories.tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana adds that Indra first bathed Krishna with water from Airavata and installed him as Govinda, king of the cows, while the cattle poured out their milk in celebration; the Harivamsha version, followed here, moves directly from praise to the request concerning Arjuna.
stories.next_story_tease: Years later, in the amphitheatre of Panchala, a young brahmana would rise to string a bow no king could bend — and Krishna would remember the promise.

stories.title: Krishna Rejoices as Arjuna Wins Draupadi
stories.story:
In the amphitheatre of Panchala, the great bow lay on its stand in the middle of the ground, and it had already beaten every king in the land. One after another the monarchs had risen, strained against it, and sat down again in failure; the bow would not bend for them. The target wheel turned high overhead, and through the hole in its rim hung a mark, waiting for the one man in the world who could send an arrow through it.

That day the prize was Draupadi, the daughter of Drupada, king of Panchala: she was to be won by the man who could string the bow and shoot the mark, and the amphitheatre held half the kings of the earth come to try. Rukma had failed, and Sunitha, and Vakra. Karna, the great archer of the charioteer's house, had failed. Duryodhana had failed. Salya, mighty among the kings, had failed. And the brahmins who had come as guests watched the royal suitors sink back one by one, while the whole hall grew heavy with their disappointment.

Among the guests sat Krishna, a prince of the Yadavas — the one man in the amphitheatre who knew that the young brahmins near the priests' seats were not what they seemed. The middle one was Arjuna, his cousin, one of the five Pandava brothers the world believed dead. Years before, on a green hill in Vrindavan, Krishna had promised to befriend Arjuna for as long as he lived.

Then a young man rose from among the brahmins seated in the assembly, and a clamour went up. Some of the priests tried to stop him — how could a young brahmin, unpractised in arms, string a bow that the great warriors of the royal houses could not? If he failed, the whole company of brahmins would be mocked before the assembled kings. But others spoke for him. Did not Rama, son of Jamadagni, once defeat the whole warrior class? Did not the sage Agastya drink the fathomless ocean by his own power? Never despise a brahmin's strength, they said, for brahmins are strong in a strength of their own. Let the youth bend the bow. And the brahmins, in their hundreds, blessed him as he walked forward.

The young man was Arjuna, the middle of the five Pandava brothers, disguised as a priest. He walked around the bow, bent his head to Ishana — one of the names of Shiva, the giver of boons — and remembered Krishna. Then he took up the bow that the kings of the earth could not string, and strung it in the blink of an eye. He took up the five arrows, shot through the hole in the wheel, and the mark fell to the ground.

The sky itself applauded. The gods showered celestial flowers on the head of the young victor; thousands of brahmins waved their upper garments in joy; the musicians struck up together, and the bards sang his praises — while all around the hall, the kings who had failed cried out in grief and despair. Drupada, watching, was filled with joy and ready to lend his armies to the victor. In the uproar, Yudhishthira, the eldest of the five brothers, slipped quietly away with the twins, Nakula and Sahadeva.

And Krishna, who had watched it all from among the crowd, saw the mark fallen and his cousin standing there shining like Indra himself — and his heart filled with joy. He moved through the celebrating throng, carrying a white robe and a garland of flowers, the honours of a victor, and placed them on Arjuna. No one in that hall understood the gesture. No one needed to.

When Arjuna left the lists, every brahmin in the hall saluted him with reverence, and close behind him walked Draupadi, who had become his wife — while the defeated kings of the earth watched the unknown young brahmin walk out of the amphitheatre with the prize.
stories.reflection: Krishna's joy is different from the amphitheatre's roar: everyone else marvels at the feat or grieves over it, but Krishna moves through the crowd carrying a white robe and a garland — not celebrating the deed but honoring the man, with a private gesture in the middle of a public triumph. It is the first gift of a friendship promised years before on the slope of Govardhana, and the promise has begun to keep itself.
stories.next_story_tease: Before the day was out, Krishna would whisper the truth of the disguised Pandavas to Balarama.

stories.title: Krishna Names the Disguised Pandavas
stories.story:
Krishna saw them the moment they crossed the floor of the amphitheatre: five young brahmins in a hall full of kings who had eyes only for Draupadi. Where other princes saw ascetics in deerskins, he saw mighty elephants moving toward a lake overgrown with lotuses — fire lying under ashes, alive and unspent. Krishna, a prince of the Yadavas, had come with his brother Balarama to watch.

It was the svayamvara of Draupadi, daughter of Drupada, king of Panchala — the great ceremony at which a princess chooses her own husband, and Drupada had made the choosing a test no one could pass. Every royal house had come; one after another the kings had failed to string the great bow, tossed to the ground by it and left panting, crowns loosened and garlands disordered. Only Karna — known to the world as a charioteer's son, though in truth the child of the sun god — had strung it easily. But Draupadi's voice rang through the hall: "I will not choose a charioteer's son for my lord." Laughing in vexation, he flung the drawn bow aside. Then a brahmin seated among the priests rose, strung the stiff bow as if it were a reed, and put an arrow through the golden mark. Krishna, filled with joy, had greeted him with a white robe and a garland of flowers — that was moments ago. Now Drupada stood to give his daughter to that brahmin, and the kings of the earth were on their feet in fury.

"Passing us by and treating the assembled monarchs as straw," they cried, "this Drupada desires to bestow his daughter on a brahmin! Let us slay him!" They seized their weapons and rushed at the king of Panchala, who, pale with fear, sought the protection of the brahmins. Mighty Bhima tore up a large tree as an elephant might, stripped off its leaves, and stood with it beside Arjuna like the king of the dead with his great mace; and Arjuna, shaking off all fear, stood with his bow ready to receive the assailants.

And then, in the middle of the uproar, Krishna turned to Balarama and began, very quietly, to name the five brahmins.

"That hero there," he said, "who moves like a lion and draws the great bow in his hand — a bow four full cubits long, each cubit the span from a man's elbow to his fingertips — is Arjuna. No doubt of it. That other hero, who tore up the tree and now stands ready to drive off the monarchs, is Bhima — Vrikodara, the wolf-bellied; no one alive but Bhima could do such a feat today. And the youth of lotus-petal eyes, four cubits tall, gentle and fair, with the bright nose, who left the amphitheatre a little while ago — that is Yudhishthira, Dharma's son, the eldest. The two others, like the war-god Kartikeya, are, I suspect, the sons of the twin gods the Ashvins. I had heard that the sons of Pandu and their mother Pritha — Kunti — escaped the burning of the house of lac."

Balarama, whose skin was the colour of a cloud that holds no rain, looked where his brother pointed, and his face cleared. "What good fortune," he said, "that our father's sister Pritha — Kunti — is alive, and her sons with her."

Krishna had known since the five first came into view. Watching them drawn toward Draupadi, he had murmured to Balarama, "That is Yudhishthira; that is Bhima with Jishnu; and those are the twins." Balarama had surveyed them slowly and cast a glance of quiet satisfaction at his brother. The two Yadava princes watched the uprooted tree and the drawn bow with the calm of men who had just found a family they thought lost.

Around them the amphitheatre seethed. Biting their lips in wrath, the monarchs saw only two insolent brahmins — not five princes of the Kuru line who had escaped a burning house, survived the wilderness, and walked into the world's greatest gathering in borrowed robes. The kings saw what they expected to see. Krishna saw what was.

And for now, he said nothing.
stories.reflection: Krishna's recognition is a private gift, not an announcement: he names each brother to Balarama in the middle of a roaring hall and then keeps the secret, so the Pandavas can remain hidden until they choose to be seen. The scene turns on restraint — knowing who someone is, and letting them stay disguised, is its own act of friendship.
stories.next_story_tease: But the insulted kings were not ready to let the matter end in a bride given to a Brahmana.

stories.title: Krishna Stills the Angry Kings
stories.story:
"Slay him!" The cry rose from the kings of the earth as one voice. King Drupada of Panchala had risen to give his daughter, the princess Draupadi, to the unknown young brahmin who had strung the great bow and shot the mark — in truth Arjuna, a Pandava prince in disguise, though no king in the hall knew it. The kings he had invited and feasted felt the insult like a wound. "He passes us by and treats the assembled monarchs as straw!" they shouted. "He would bestow his daughter on a brahmin! The svayamvara — the choosing of a royal bride — belongs to the warrior class, and a brahmin has no claim on a warrior princess. Let us slay him, and his son with him!" They seized their weapons and rushed at the king of Panchala, who went pale with fear and took shelter among the brahmins.

The brahmins were not afraid. They shook their deerskins and coconut-shell pots, shouting back, "Fear not — we will fight!" Arjuna, in his brahmin's robes, smiled at them and raised a hand. "Stand aside and watch," he said. "With arrow after arrow I will check these angry kings, as a charm checks a snake." Then he took up the great bow he had won and stood immovable as a mountain, Bhima at his side.

Karna came first — the finest archer among the kings, known to the world as a charioteer's son but in truth the child of the sun god. He flung himself at Jishnu — the poets' name for Arjuna — with all his fire, while Salya, king of Madra, charged Bhima. Arjuna drew his bow and pierced Karna with sharp arrows until he fainted. When Karna came to himself he fought with greater care than before, and the two raged at each other until, wrapped in each other's showers of arrows, they vanished from the watching crowd. Only heroes could read the words they flung — "Behold the strength of my arms!" — "Mark how I have countered that feat!" Then Karna paused and called across the field. "Foremost of brahmins," he said, "I am pleased by the strength of your arms. Are you the science of weapons made flesh — or Rama, best of brahmin warriors? Are you Indra himself, or Vishnu in a brahmin's form, come to fight me?"

"Karna," Arjuna answered, "I am none of these. I am only a brahmin, and the foremost of all warriors who carry weapons. By my teacher's grace I am master of the Brahma weapon and of the Paurandara — the great weapons of Brahma and Indra. I have come to vanquish you; wait, then, a little." And Karna, reflecting that a brahmin's sacred power is ever invincible, drew back from the fight.

On the other side of the field, Salya and Bhima had locked together like two elephants in rut, striking with fists and knees, throwing each other down and hauling each other up, until the lists rang with the crash of their bodies, two masses of granite meeting. Then Bhima lifted the king of Madra in his arms and hurled him down — yet set him down so gently that Salya was hardly hurt. Strength and mercy in one feat, and all who saw it wondered. The monarchs drew back, alarmed, crowding about the two brahmins. "These bulls among brahmins are wonderful warriors!" they murmured. "Who could fight Karna except Rama, or Drona the great teacher of arms, or Kiriti the son of Pandu — and who could face Duryodhana except Krishna, the son of Devaki?"

Then Krishna himself rose. He had watched Bhima's feat, and what he had suspected from the first stood confirmed: these two were the sons of Kunti — his own cousins, whom the world believed dead. Gently, addressing the assembled monarchs, he said one thing: "This maiden has been justly won." And the monarchs, accomplished in battle, desisted from the fight. The storm over the amphitheatre broke apart; the kings lowered their weapons; and the unknown brahmin walked out with the daughter of Drupada beside him — while Krishna and Balarama watched from the crowd, their silence full of joy.
stories.reflection: The duel proves what the brothers are; only Krishna's word settles what they are not — a threat. Strength wins the field with bows and an uprooted tree, but the peace is won with a single sentence spoken gently at the right moment, and the monarchs accept it. There is a kind of power that consists in knowing when not to fight.
stories.content_note: Battle violence, described with restraint.
stories.next_story_tease: That evening the five brothers carried their bride back to the potter's house — but someone had already guessed who they were.

stories.title: Fire, Even Covered, Can Be Known
stories.story:
"Enjoy it all," Kunti called from the inner room, without looking out. Her five sons — princes of the Kuru line living disguised as brahmins since their narrow escape from a house set to burn them — had come home to the potter's house that evening and told their mother they had brought alms that day. Kunti, who had not yet seen her sons, answered as the mother of brahmin boys should when the day's begging comes in: "Enjoy it all, whatever you have obtained."

The moment after, she saw the alms — and cried out, "Oh, what have I said?" For that morning, at the svayamvara of King Drupada, her son Arjuna had strung the bow no king could bend and won the hand of Draupadi, the king's daughter. The brothers had brought the princess home in triumph and, still keeping up their disguise, announced to their mother only that they had "brought alms." Now Kunti saw what the alms was: she had commanded her five sons to enjoy, all together, the daughter of the king of Panchala.

Afraid of the wrong that might follow, Kunti took the cheerful princess by the hand and went to Yudhishthira, her eldest son. "Your younger brothers told me that the alms they had obtained was the daughter of the king of Panchala," she said, "and in ignorance, my son, I said, 'Enjoy it all.' Tell me how my words may not become a lie, how no sin may touch this princess, and how she may not be troubled."

Yudhishthira reflected for a moment and consoled his mother. Then he turned to Arjuna. "By you, Arjuna, the king's daughter was won," he said. "It is proper, then, that you should wed her. Kindle the sacred fire and take her hand with the due rites." But Arjuna shook his head. "King, do not make me share in sin," he said. "What you command does not follow virtue; that is the path the sinful walk. You must wed first, then the strong-armed Bhima, then myself, then Nakula, and last of all Sahadeva. We are all obedient to you — command us as you wish."

The brothers looked at one another, and at Draupadi; and the beauty of the princess of Panchala, fashioned by the Creator himself, entered their hearts, and desire pressed upon their senses. Yudhishthira, watching his younger brothers, understood what was passing in their minds. He remembered the words of the sage Krishna-Dwaipayana — the great seer Vyasa — and, from fear of a division among the brothers, he spoke: "The auspicious Draupadi shall be the common wife of us all."

It was then that two more visitors came to the potter's house. Krishna, suspecting that the five men he had seen at the svayamvara were none other than the lost princes of the Kuru line, had come with his elder brother Balarama. They entered and found Yudhishthira of the long, strong arms seated at the heart of the room, his younger brothers around him glowing like fire. Krishna went to the eldest, touched the feet of Kunti's son in greeting, and said, "I am Krishna." Balarama did the same. The delight of the five brothers at the sight of their cousins was plain to see; and the two Yadava princes also touched the feet of Kunti, their father's sister.

Then Yudhishthira, gazing at Krishna, asked the question that had been burning in him. "How, Vasudeva," he said, "did you find us, living as we are in disguise?"

Krishna smiled. "Fire, even if it is covered, can be known," he said. "Who else among men but the Pandavas could show such might? Sons of Pandu, by sheer good fortune you escaped that fierce fire; and by sheer good fortune the wicked son of Dhritarashtra and his counselors did not gain their wish. Blessings on you — and grow in prosperity like a fire in a cave, spreading little by little on every side. And now, lest any of the monarchs recognize you, let us return."

And the two Yadava princes went out again into the evening as quietly as they had come, leaving the potter's house to keep its secret a little longer.
stories.reflection: Krishna's answer — that fire, even covered, can be known — cuts both ways. The disguise holds not because the brothers are invisible, but because the people who see through it choose to protect the secret instead of revealing it. Recognition and restraint are both acts of friendship, and the visit ends the moment it might betray them.
stories.next_story_tease: In the days that followed, the potter's house prepared for a wedding — and Krishna prepared a gift.

stories.title: Krishna's Wedding Gifts
stories.story:
The wedding was done, and with it every fear left Drupada. The king of Panchala no longer stood in fear even of the gods, for his daughter Draupadi was married at last — married to the five Pandava brothers, the princes of the Kuru line whom the world still believed dead, burned years before in the house of lac. All that had seemed lost to Drupada's house had returned in a single season. The ladies of his household went to Kunti, the mother of the five brothers, and worshipped her feet, naming themselves one by one; and Draupadi, in red silk with the auspicious thread of the wedding still around her wrists, saluted her mother-in-law with reverence and stood before her with her palms joined.

Kunti looked at her daughter-in-law and blessed her, naming the great devoted wives of story and heaven. "Be to your husband," she said, "as Sachi is to Indra, king of the gods; as Swaha is to Vibhavasu, the fire-god; as Rohini is to Soma, the moon; as Damayanti was to Nala; as Arundhati is to the sage Vasishtha; as Lakshmi is to Narayana. Bear long-lived and heroic children, and be installed as queen of the kingdom and capital of the Kuru country beside your husband Yudhishthira the just. And as I rejoice today, seeing you in your red silk, so may I rejoice again when I see you the mother of a son."

Then the gifts began to arrive, and the courtyards of Drupada's palace slowly filled. Krishna — the brothers' cousin, who had recognized them at the svayamvara and kept their secret — sent presents to the newly married Pandavas: ornaments of gold set with pearls and with the deep blue stone called lapis lazuli; costly robes woven in distant countries; soft blankets and hides of great value; beds, carpets, and carriages; vessels by the hundred, set with gems and diamonds; serving women by the thousand, brought from many lands, beautiful and young and skilled, and decked with every ornament; well-trained elephants from the country of Madra; excellent horses in costly harness; and chariots drawn by horses of wonderful colour. And Krishna — whom the poets call the slayer of the demon Madhu — sent, too, coins of pure gold beyond counting, by the tens of millions, laid out in separate heaps.

It was a royal fortune, sent to men who had come to Panchala with nothing but their bows and their disguises — the wealth of an alliance declared openly at last, after years of hiding. The brothers who had escaped a burning house and begged their bread as brahmins stood among mountains of gifts sent by a cousin who had recognized them in a crowd and never once said their names aloud. Gift followed gift, and still the heaps of gold stood apart, each mound its own small treasury.

And Yudhishthira the just, eager to honour Govinda — Krishna — accepted all those presents with great joy, taking them as they were meant: not payment, not dowry, but the welcome of one house laid at the feet of another, and a promise that the hidden princes would not stay hidden much longer.
stories.reflection: The catalogue of gifts is almost excessive — gold by crores, servants by thousands — yet the source records no message sent with them, only the presents themselves. The wealth says what Krishna cannot say aloud in a hall of spies: these are my people. And Yudhishthira's joy in accepting, desirous of gratifying Govinda, completes the exchange — the pleasure of receiving is itself the gift returned.
stories.next_story_tease: But Krishna knew the brothers could not stay hidden forever — and he would soon counsel them toward a kingdom of their own.

stories.title: The Counsel at Panchala
stories.subtitle: Vidura brings word from Hastinapura, and Krishna's opinion decides the Pandavas' next move.
stories.story:
Vidura came to Panchala with word from Hastinapura, and the message he carried had been waiting in the air ever since the wedding fires died down. The five sons of Pandu had found shelter in King Drupada's house — a father-in-law, a home, and a wife in Draupadi, whom all five brothers shared. But Vidura, their own father's brother and the wisest voice in the Kuru court, spoke now of what lay behind them: the throne of Hastinapura, theirs by right, and the question that would not stay buried. Would the sons of Pandu press that claim?

Drupada heard him out, and his answer was careful. It was proper, he said, for the princes to return to their ancestral kingdom — but it was not proper for him, their host, to urge it. If Yudhishthira and Bhima and Arjuna and the twins themselves wished to go, and if Balarama and Krishna, who knew every rule of right conduct, were of the same mind, then let the Pandavas go. Those two, he added, had always worked for what was good and pleasant for Pandu's sons.

Yudhishthira answered with all the warmth of a son. "We are, O king, with all our younger brothers, at your command. We shall cheerfully do whatever pleases you."

Then Krishna spoke, and his words settled the room. "I am of opinion that the Pandavas should go. But we should all abide by the opinion of King Drupada, who is versed in every rule of right conduct."

It was a rare sentence: an opinion offered, then set aside for another man's judgment. Drupada received it as the honour it was, and agreed with what Krishna thought — for the sons of Pandu had grown as dear to him as they were to Krishna. And then he said the thing that has been remembered about that quiet council ever since: "Not even Yudhishthira himself seeks the welfare of the Pandavas as earnestly as Krishna does."

The decision moved with the speed of a command. At Drupada's bidding the Pandavas set out with Krishna and Vidura, taking Draupadi and their mother Kunti with them, and journeyed toward the city named for the elephant, stopping along the way as though the road itself wanted to delay a homecoming that had been too long in coming.

Word of their approach raced ahead of them. Dhritarashtra, the king of Hastinapura and the brothers' uncle, sent his own sons out to receive them, with Drona and Kripa — the masters who had trained every prince of the house in arms — riding at their head. Surrounded by that honour guard, the Pandavas entered the city, and the streets filled with people who had come out to see them. "Here returns the prince who has always protected us as if we were his own kin," some cried. And others called out with the fierce love of a city for its own: "If we have ever given alms, if we have ever poured offerings of ghee into the sacred fire, if we have earned any merit at all — let the Pandavas live in our town for a hundred years."

At the palace the brothers bowed to Dhritarashtra and to the wise Bhishma, the eldest of their line, and to all who deserved that honour, and asked after the welfare of every citizen present. When they were summoned to the court, Dhritarashtra gave them what no one had dared hope for — not a welcome merely, but a settlement. "Go to Khandavaprastha," he said, "so that no quarrel may arise again between you and your cousins. If you settle there, no one will be able to do you harm. Protected by Arjuna as the gods are by the thunderbolt, dwell in Khandavaprastha and take half the kingdom."

The brothers agreed, content with half a kingdom. They honoured the king and set out from Hastinapura toward a stretch of unreclaimed desert they would have to turn into a home. It did not look like much of a throne. But Krishna had counselled the journey, and when the brothers set out into the wilds, Krishna went with them — the desert would not be faced alone.
stories.reflection: Drupada's parting tribute is striking: he measures Krishna's care for the Pandavas against the love of their own eldest brother and finds it no less. In a court where everyone has an interest in the brothers — the Kauravas, the citizens, even their new father-in-law — Krishna alone wants for them exactly what they would want for themselves, and gives his opinion in a form that leaves the final word to others.
stories.next_story_tease: The unreclaimed desert was a strange gift — and Krishna would not leave the Pandavas to it until it had become a city.

stories.title: Founding Indraprastha
stories.subtitle: Krishna helps raise a capital from the wilds of Khandavaprastha, and then takes his leave.
stories.story:
Half a kingdom sounds like a fortune until you stand on it. The land their uncle Dhritarashtra had given the Pandavas — Khandavaprastha — was unreclaimed desert: thorn and dust and emptiness, no walls, no palace, no street that could be called a street. The brothers had come there content, asking only that no quarrel should arise again between them and their cousins. But contentment does not build cities. Work does.

Krishna had not gone home. Of all those who had urged the brothers toward Hastinapura, he was the one who came with them into the wilderness, and he stayed. With Krishna at their head, the Pandavas set about making the desert theirs. They called in the sage Vyasa, their own grandfather, and with his help chose a sacred and auspicious stretch of ground for the settlement. There they performed the ceremonies that hallow a piece of land, and measured out the ground on which their city would stand. Every step was deliberate: first the ground made holy, then the ground made level, then the ground made home.

What rose from that measuring was not a camp but a capital. Around it they dug a trench wide as the sea, and over it walls climbed toward the sky, white as fleecy clouds or the rays of the moon. Those who saw the finished city said it gleamed like Bhogavati, the jewelled city of the great serpents beneath the earth — so bright did it shine against the desert it had replaced. The storytellers would call what the Pandavas had made a second heaven. It was the first thing in many years that belonged wholly to them: since their father's death they had been guests and wanderers, schooled in Hastinapura on sufferance, sheltered in Panchala as refugees. Now the city on that measured ground answered to their name alone. It came to be called Indraprastha, and the name sounded like a promise to men who had grown up living on the goodwill of others. For the first time, the ground they stood on was theirs.

And when the walls stood, Krishna took his leave. He had seen the ground hallowed and measured, the city raised, and his friends standing inside their own gates; there was nothing left to wait for. With Balarama beside him he set out for the west, toward Dwaraka. Little is recorded of the parting itself, because there was little to say. The brothers stood at the gate and watched the two cousins drive away, the dust settling slowly on the road west. Behind them the white walls of Indraprastha threw long shadows across the desert that used to be empty. And what they carried back into their new city was not the emptiness of guests left behind, but the ease of men who had been settled, at last, in their own home.
stories.reflection: Krishna does not merely wish the Pandavas well — he stays until the city stands, helping choose the ground, hallow it, measure it, raise its walls, and only then takes his leave. The gift of the kingdom was Dhritarashtra's, but the gift of a home worth ruling was made together, and the parting that follows is confident precisely because the work is complete.
stories.next_story_tease: In the years that followed, Arjuna would leave the new city for a long wandering through the holy places — and Krishna would hear of it before any word was sent.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna standing with the Pandavas on the raw ground of Khandavaprastha, pointing across the measured land as the white walls of the new city rise behind them — a trench wide as the sea ringing the site, towers white as fleecy clouds, while Balarama waits at the roadside for the journey home.

stories.title: Reunion at Prabhasa
stories.subtitle: In the middle of his exile, Arjuna is met on the western shore by the friend of his oldest story — the two who were Nara and Narayana of old.
stories.story:
Somewhere along the shores of the western ocean, a wanderer came to a place that felt like home, though he had never been there.

Arjuna, one of the five Pandava brothers and the finest archer of his age, was passing the years of a long exile in pilgrimage, moving from one sacred water to the next and bathing where the old stories said the gods had bathed. At last he reached Prabhasa, a beautiful stretch of coast held holy by every traveller. He had told no one he was coming and sent no word ahead. The old account calls him the invisible Arjuna: he went from shrine to shrine without herald, telling no one where he was bound.

But Krishna heard of it.

From Dwaraka, his city by the sea, Krishna — Arjuna's cousin and oldest friend — heard that the wanderer had reached Prabhasa, and he went to him at once, across the land and down to the shore, to the place where his friend stood. They met and embraced on the sacred ground, two friends asking after each other's welfare with the easy closeness of men who had never needed distance between them. The storytellers add a strange and beautiful note: these dear friends, they say, were none other than the sages Nara and Narayana of old, two ancient seers bound to each other through the ages. Anyone watching the pair on that shore would have understood why the tale was told.

They sat down together, and Krishna asked the question that mattered. "Why, Arjuna, do you wander over the earth, visiting all these sacred waters and holy places?"

Arjuna told him everything — the long roads, the rivers, the reasons that had sent him out into the world. Krishna heard him out and answered only, "This is as it should be." No lecture, no plan to shorten the exile, no argument. His friend had chosen a hard road, and Krishna honoured the choice.

The two spent their time at Prabhasa as they pleased, sporting together by the sea. Then Krishna drew him onward to Raivataka mountain, where they would pass some days. Everything had been seen to beforehand: at Krishna's command, craftsmen had adorned the mountain, and food had been gathered in plenty. Arjuna watched the actors and the dancers, dismissed them all with proper thanks, and lay down on an excellent bed prepared for him. As he lay there in the dark he described to Krishna everything he had seen in his wandering — the sacred waters, the lakes, the mountains, the rivers, the forests — and his friend listened. In the middle of his telling, sleep stole upon him.

He woke to sweet songs and the singing of the vina, a stringed instrument, and the blessings of the bards — a king's morning, arranged for a guest who had been living like a pilgrim. After the morning's rites, Krishna greeted him warmly, and Arjuna rode out on a golden car toward Dwaraka, the city of the Yadavas, Krishna's own people.

The city had dressed itself for him. At Krishna's command every garden and house had been adorned, and the citizens, eager to see the son of Kunti, poured into the streets by the hundreds of thousands. In the squares, women and men of the Bhojas, the Vrishnis, and the Andhakas — the clans of Krishna's family — crowded together to welcome him, and the young men of the Yadava tribe embraced him again and again, old friends greeting the wanderer returned. Arjuna honoured the elders who deserved it and took their blessings in turn. Then he went to Krishna's mansion, filled with gems and every comfort, and made his home there — and there he stayed, with Krishna, for many days.

No one hurried him. The exile would resume; the road was still waiting. But for those days, the invisible Arjuna was simply the guest of his oldest friend, in the most beautiful house in Dwaraka.
stories.reflection: The storyteller names Krishna and Arjuna as Nara and Narayana of old, and the embrace at Prabhasa carries that weight: the friendship is older than either man's fame. Krishna asks why his friend wanders, listens to everything, and answers only, "This is as it should be" — acceptance rather than rescue, which is exactly what Arjuna, in the middle of his own long exile, most needed.
stories.next_story_tease: At the festival on Raivataka, Krishna would notice where his friend's gaze kept lingering — and would counsel him to act.
stories.hero_scene: On the sacred seashore at Prabhasa, Krishna and Arjuna embrace in greeting, the western ocean stretching behind them — two friends who were said to be the Rishis Nara and Narayana of old, meeting again in the middle of the wanderer's exile.

stories.title: Krishna Counsels Arjuna to Abduct Subhadra
stories.story:
The festival on Raivataka had everything a festival should have, and more of it than anyone could take in at once.

The mountain near Dwaraka belonged to Krishna's family, the Yadavas, and both branches of the clan — the Vrishnis and the Andhakas — had gathered there to make merry. Musicians struck up, dancers danced, singers sang, and the young men of the clan, bright with ornaments, rode about in cars decked with gold. Mansions set with gems and gay artificial trees rose around the hill, and citizens came by the hundreds and thousands, some on foot, some in fine chariots, with their wives and followers. Balarama, Krishna's elder brother, roamed the ground in high spirits, his wife Revati beside him and musicians trailing after. Pradyumna and Samba, Krishna's young sons, went about garlanded with bright flowers, as carefree as young gods. King Ugrasena, the old ruler of the Yadavas, moved through it all with his queens and his train, and the heroes of both clans — Satyaki, Uddhava, Akrura, and a hundred more — each with his own following, crowded the hill until it rang. It was a festival loud enough to forget yourself in, and no one thought of anything but the day.

Through it all two friends walked together, seeing everything: Krishna, and Arjuna — the Pandava prince who was spending his years of wandering as Krishna's guest in Dwaraka. As they strolled they came upon a young woman in the midst of her maids: Subhadra, daughter of Vasudeva and so Krishna's own sister, decked in every ornament and lovely to look upon.

Arjuna stopped in mid-stride. The great archer, who had faced a hundred dangers without flinching, stood fixed as a post, and could not look away. Love had taken him — the poets would say the god of love himself had loosed his arrow — and it showed all over his face. The drums and the singing went on around them, but Arjuna no longer heard them. The whole bright festival had narrowed to a single figure.

Krishna noticed at once, because Krishna noticed everything. He looked at his friend, struck dumb mid-step, and smiled.

"How is this?" he asked. "Can the heart of a man who roams the forests be troubled by the god of love? This is my sister, Arjuna — my father's favourite daughter. Tell me if your heart is set on her, and I shall speak to my father myself."

Arjuna answered as an honest man in love must. She was Vasudeva's daughter and Krishna's sister, he said, and with so much beauty, whom could she not fascinate? What heart would not be stirred?

And so, warm and unhurried, Krishna turned matchmaker. There was an old and honoured way among the Kshatriyas, the warrior class, he reminded his friend: a suitor of proven courage might carry off his bride, and the marriage, once made, was accepted by all. Waiting for a choosing-ceremony was uncertain — who could say what a girl might decide when the time came? "Therefore, Arjuna, carry away my beautiful sister," Krishna said. "For who knows what she may do at a self-choice?"

It was counsel given with a smile, between friends, and it settled everything. There was nothing solemn about it; Krishna made the bold sound as simple as breathing.

Subhadra, meanwhile, knew nothing of the two men who had stopped to look at her, or of the plan already taking shape behind Krishna's easy manner. She stood among her maids at the bright centre of the festival, and the day went on around her, untouched.
stories.reflection: The comedy sits beside the warmth: the mightiest archer of his age stopped still by a glance, and Krishna too fond of him to leave him stranded there. Friendship here looks like a knowing smile and an offer to manage everything — and a nudge toward a bolder path than waiting.
stories.hero_scene: Arjuna stopped in the middle of the Raivataka festival, gazing at Subhadra decked in ornaments among her maids, while Krishna stands beside him watching with a knowing smile.
