stories.title: Nuptial Gifts for Indraprastha
stories.subtitle: Krishna brings the Yadava host to honour Subhadra's new home.
stories.story:
When the twelve years of his exile were complete, Arjuna came home — and he did not come back alone. Beside him was Subhadra, the sister of Krishna, whom he had carried away from Dwaraka and married there. They returned to Khandavaprastha, the Pandavas' half-kingdom, where the brothers had raised the new city of Indraprastha. It was a homecoming with two edges: the city gained back a prince, and the household gained a new bride.

Arjuna went first to the king — his eldest brother, Yudhishthira — then paid his respects to the brahmin priests, and at last went in to Draupadi, the wife the five brothers shared. She met him with the sharpness of a woman who had waited twelve years and heard where her husband had been. "Why do you linger here, son of Kunti?" she said. "Go to the daughter of the Satwata race! A second tie always loosens the first upon a bundle of firewood!"

The Satwatas were Krishna's own clan — and the old proverb carried her fear plainly: a new bond, she felt, would loosen the old one. Arjuna pacified her and asked her forgiveness, again and again. And then Subhadra herself finished what his words had begun.

She came into the inner rooms dressed not as a queen but in the simple garb of a cowherd woman — Arjuna's own doing, so that she entered as a sister to the household, not a rival for its first lady. She looked, the account says, handsomer in that dress. First she bowed to Pritha — Kunti, Arjuna's mother — and Kunti, overcome with affection, drew the girl's head to her and breathed in the scent of her hair, the old mother's gesture of blessing, and poured blessings on her without end. Then Subhadra hastened to Draupadi, bowed before her, and said: "I am your maid."

Draupadi rose at once and embraced her — the sister of Krishna — with pure affection. "Let your husband be without a foe!" she blessed her.

"So be it!" said Subhadra, her heart delighted.

From that time the Pandavas lived happily, and Kunti too was happy. And when Krishna heard that Arjuna had reached Indraprastha with his sister, and that the household had made its peace, he came there himself, so that the whole world could see the marriage sealed in friendship.

He came with Balarama, his elder brother; with Pradyumna, his son; with Uddhava, his trusted friend and adviser; and with the heroes of the Vrishni and Andhaka clans. A great army guarded him on the road, and they brought nuptial presents with them, as a family celebrates a wedding it had not been able to attend. King Yudhishthira, hearing that Krishna was near, sent the twins, Nakula and Sahadeva, out to receive him, and the Vrishni host entered the city in splendour. The streets had been swept and watered and hung with floral wreaths, and sprinkled with sandalwood water, fragrant and cool; flags flew over the gates, and every part of the town was filled with the sweet scent of the day.

Then the gifts were given. Krishna gave the Pandavas a thousand cars of gold furnished with rows of bells, ten thousand cows, mares and mules, and serving women — the gifts a family sends when a daughter goes to a new house. It was giving on the scale of Dwaraka itself, open-handed and glad.

The Pandavas received their kinsman's gifts, and the household that had been uneasy for one bright afternoon settled into the happiness that would carry it for years. The city stood fragrant and adorned, its streets full of Yadavas and Kurus mingling like one family. And under all the gold and the garlands lay the moment the whole procession had come to honour: a bride who had said, "I am your maid," and the blessing that answered her — "Let your husband be without a foe."
stories.reflection: Subhadra's answer to Draupadi — "I am thy maid" — dissolves the jealousy in a moment, and Draupadi's blessing follows at once: "Let thy husband be without a foe." The household's peace is made not by Krishna's gifts but by the two women's grace; the great procession of cars and cows that follows only makes the alliance visible to the world.
stories.tradition_note: The nuptial gifts in this episode are for Subhadra's marriage and are distinct from the wedding presents Krishna earlier sent after Draupadi's wedding (Mahabharata 1.201). The Bhagavata Purana tells the Subhadra episode more briefly.
stories.next_story_tease: Before long the new household would welcome a child — and Krishna would be there for the rites.

stories.title: Birth Rites for Abhimanyu
stories.story:
The rites of infancy are a family's quiet business, but for the son Subhadra bore at Indraprastha, they were performed by Krishna's own hands. He had come to the Pandavas' new capital with the whole wedding host, bearing gifts for the household his sister had joined — and when the celebration was over, he stayed. Krishna remained there with Arjuna, and the two friends were in no hurry to part.

The household had not always been at ease. When Arjuna first brought Subhadra home from Dwaraka, Draupadi, wife to all five brothers, had met him with the sharpness of a woman who felt her place taken. "Why do you linger here, son of Kunti?" she had asked. "Go to the daughter of the Satwata race! A second tie always loosens the first upon a bundle of firewood." Arjuna had pacified her and begged her forgiveness, and Subhadra, sent into the inner rooms dressed simply, in the rough clothes of a cowherd woman rather than the finery of a queen, had gone straight to Draupadi and bowed. "I am your maid," she said. Draupadi had risen and embraced the sister of Krishna, and blessed the marriage: "Let your husband be without a foe." From that day, the old account says, the household lived happily, and Kunti too was happy.

Now the household was growing. Subhadra, Krishna's own sister, gave birth to a son. The news ran through Indraprastha, and the child was called Abhimanyu — a name spoken with pride in both houses from his first hour, for the blood of the Yadavas now ran in the line of the Pandavas.

Upon his birth, Krishna performed the usual rites of infancy himself: the ceremonies that welcome a child into the world, give him his name, and lay the first blessing on his days. He did it as an uncle does, for a child he already loved. No vision was seen, no miracle recorded; the old account only says that the rites were done, and the child began to grow up like the moon in its bright fortnight.

And the child grew dear to Krishna. In those first years Abhimanyu was not yet the warrior the world would remember — he was simply his uncle's joy, a brightening in the palace that no one could miss. Indraprastha had many splendours then: the wealth of the new capital, the court of the five brothers, the friendship between the Yadavas and the sons of Pandu. But this small one was watched over most closely of all. In his laughter, in his first steps, in the way he reached for his uncle, the two houses that had joined at Subhadra's wedding were joined again, in the most ordinary and lasting way.

Krishna stayed on through the child's earliest years, and when at last he spoke of returning to Dwaraka, the parting was a real one. He left behind a sister happy in her new home, a friend in Arjuna, and a nephew whose first rites his own hands had performed — the uncle who had come for a wedding and stayed for the child.
stories.reflection: The rites are performed without spectacle — no prophecy, no miracle — and that is the point: Krishna gives the child the most ordinary of services, the welcome a family gives a new life. The story's devotion lives in the uncle's plain attendance, not in any display.
stories.next_story_tease: That summer, Krishna was still at Indraprastha when Arjuna proposed an outing to the banks of the Yamuna.

stories.title: The Stranger on the Yamuna
stories.story:
The summer days had come to Indraprastha, the shining new city where the five Pandava brothers ruled. One morning Arjuna went to Krishna — his cousin and closest friend, visiting from his own city of Dwaraka — and said, “The summer days are here. Let us go down to the Yamuna and spend the day there with our friends, sporting in the groves and the water; we will be home by evening.” Krishna answered that this was his wish too. And so, with the leave of Yudhishthira, the eldest of the brothers and their king, the party set out, leaving behind a city that was thriving as never before.

Under Yudhishthira the just, the neighbouring kings had been brought under the Pandavas’ sway, and the people lived happily, delighting in their king not only because he ruled them but from sincere affection. He was devoted to the scriptures, performed the great sacrifices, and sheltered the good. His brothers could be easy with one another under such a king, and Krishna, who came often, was more brother than guest.

They chose a fine spot on the Yamuna, overgrown with tall trees and crowned with high pleasure mansions, so that the place looked like a city of heaven. Everything a day of enjoyment could want had been gathered there: costly food and drink, flower garlands, perfumes, and inner rooms bright with gems. At a word from Krishna and Arjuna, the women of the party did as they pleased — some in the woods, some in the waters, some within the mansions. Draupadi, the Pandavas’ queen, and Subhadra, Krishna’s sister, light with wine, gave away their rich robes and ornaments to the women sporting about them. Some danced, some sang, some laughed and jested, some drank the fine wines, some playfully blocked one another’s way; flutes and lutes and drums filled the groves, until the whole place seemed the very picture of Prosperity. For one day in high summer, the world seemed to have arranged itself purely for enjoyment.

In the midst of it all, Arjuna and Krishna slipped away to a quiet spot a little apart from the others and sat down on two costly seats. There the two friends talked of old campaigns — victories won side by side, old enemies remembered, and the easy silences of men who have trusted each other with their lives. They passed the afternoon like the Ashvins, the twin gods of heaven, at ease, while the music and laughter of the grove reached them from a distance, softened.

Then a Brahmana came toward them. He was still some way off when the two friends felt the change: the noise of the day seemed to fall back from him, and the grove grew quieter as he walked. He stood as tall as a Sala tree. His complexion was like molten gold; his beard was bright yellow tinged with green; his height and build were in just proportion; his locks were matted. He came on steadily — a figure blazing with splendour, the foremost of the Brahmanas, the priest-sages — and he did not look like a man who had come to share their sport. When he reached the two heroes, the idle day was over.
stories.reflection: The day is all brightness and ease — music, wine, generosity, two friends at their leisure — and the stranger cuts across it like a shadow at noon. The story lets pleasure stand at its full height before the omen walks into the grove, as if to say that the world's golden hours are exactly when the unknown arrives.
stories.next_story_tease: But the Brahmana who approached them had not come for sport — he had come hungry.
stories.hero_scene: On a grassy bank of the Yamuna under tall trees, Krishna and Arjuna sit on two costly seats deep in conversation, while behind them the pleasure mansions rise and the river sparkles — and a towering Brahmana with molten-gold skin and a yellow-green beard walks toward them through the grove.

stories.title: Agni Asks for the Khandava Forest
stories.story:
Krishna and Arjuna were resting on the bank of the Yamuna when the Brahmana with the matted locks stood before them and asked for food — not politely, but as a starving man asks. “I am a Brahmana with a boundless hunger,” he said, “and I ask you both to satisfy me.” “Tell us what food will satisfy you,” the two friends answered, “and we will do our best to give it to you.”

“I do not desire ordinary food,” said the Brahmana, and his voice had changed. “Know that I am Agni, the fire itself. The food I want is the great forest of Khandava, which lies near where you sit — but Indra, the king of the gods, protects it. In that forest lives Takshaka the serpent, who is Indra’s friend, with his followers and his family, and for Takshaka’s sake Indra shields the whole wood and every creature in it. Whenever I blaze up to consume it, he pours rain down upon me from the clouds, and I fail. So I have come to you two, for you are both masters of weapons. If you will help me, I will surely eat that forest at last. Hold off Indra’s showers, and let no creature slip past you while I burn.”

These were the same matted locks the stranger had worn when he walked out of the summer grove; only now, as he spoke of blazing, something behind his eyes seemed to kindle. Two men who had fed armies and cities stood before a god who asked to be fed with a forest.

But why did the god of fire hunger so? The tale, the sages say, goes back to a king named Swetaki, a man of such strength and prowess that men compared him to Indra himself; no one on earth, it was said, ever equalled him in sacrifices, in charity, or in wisdom. Year after year Swetaki performed the five great sacrifices and many another, with vast gifts to the Brahmanas — until at last the priests who served him grew weak, their eyes inflamed by the endless smoke, and they left him, refusing to serve at his rites again. The king begged them to come back, but they would not, for their eyes still pained them. At the urging of those very priests he invited others in their place and finished the sacrifice he had begun. Then he set his heart on a greater work still: a sacrifice that would last a hundred years. This time not a single priest would help him. He bowed to them, spoke them fair, pressed gifts upon them; all refused. At last the king grew angry and told them plainly: “If I were a fallen man, or one who had failed you in homage and service, you would be right to abandon me. But I am neither, and you have no fair reason to block my sacrifice. If you turn from me out of spite alone, I will go to other priests, win them over with sweet words and gifts, and lay my cause before them.” The priests, who knew well that they could not serve at so vast a rite, pretended to be angry in their turn. “Your sacrifices never end,” they told him.

And there the old tale stops. On the bank of the Yamuna, the two friends looked from the blazing Brahmana to the great dark forest across the water — the wood that Indra’s friendship had kept unburned for so long. The fire-god was asking them to stand between him and the rain. To refuse was possible; the request was only a request. But Agni had called them the two foremost of heroes on earth, and he had asked them for food. The two friends looked at each other, then at the forest — and the summer air was very still.
stories.reflection: Agni comes not as a god commanding but as a guest asking, and in that framing the heroes' weapons become an answer to hunger. The fiercest event in the story — the burning of a forest — begins with a request, the oldest courtesy of the world.
stories.tradition_note: The tale of King Swetaki, told here to explain Agni's craving for the Khandava forest, continues in the source beyond the passage excerpted here.

stories.title: The Earth Shall Drink Their Blood
stories.story:
The Kamyaka forest had never seen such an assembly of wrathful kin. The five Pandava brothers were living there as exiles, having lost their kingdom in a rigged game of dice against their cousins; and now their kin and friends came to them, burning with anger. The Bhojas, the Vrishnis and the Andhakas came; the kinsmen of Panchala came; Dhrishtaketu, king of Chedi, came; the celebrated and powerful Kaikeya brothers came. In the hearing of all they reproached the sons of Dhritarashtra, and then asked the only question worth asking: “What should we do?” The warriors of the Kshatriya line, with Krishna — their cousin and their dearest friend — at their head, seated themselves in a ring around Yudhishthira the just.

Respectfully saluting Yudhishthira, Krishna spoke, and his voice was heavy with mourning; and the words he spoke were a vow. “The earth shall drink the blood of Duryodhana and Karna, of Dussasana and the wicked Sakuni! Slaying them in battle, and defeating their followers along with their royal allies, we shall set Yudhishthira the just back on his throne. The wicked deserve to be slain. This is eternal morality.” The four he named were the men behind the Pandavas’ ruin: Duryodhana, eldest of the cheating cousins; his brother Dussasana; Karna, their ally and Arjuna’s great rival; and Sakuni, the crafty uncle of the Kauravas, who had loaded the dice.

The forest listened. But Krishna’s anger was not spent. As he thought of the wrongs done to the Pandavas, he fell into such a passion that he seemed bent upon consuming all created things; those nearest him could feel it, like the heat of a fire. Then Arjuna, who loved him, set himself to pacify him. Beholding Krishna angry, he began to recite the feats Krishna had achieved in his former lives — for the man who stood wrathful in the exiles’ camp was, Arjuna said, the soul of all things: immeasurable, eternal, of infinite energy, the lord of the Prajapatis themselves, the supreme ruler of the worlds, Vishnu of profound wisdom.

“In days long past,” Arjuna said, “you wandered on the Gandhamadana mountains for ten thousand years, a hermit whose home was wherever evening fell. You lived on water alone for eleven thousand years by the lake of Pushkara. On the high hills of Vadari you stood for a hundred years on one leg, arms upraised, living on air. On the banks of the Saraswati your twelve years of sacrifice left your body so wasted that it was like a bundle of veins. On the plains of Prabhasa you stood on one leg for a thousand years of the gods. All asceticism rests in you, and you are the embodiment of every sacrifice.”

Then he spoke of what Krishna had done with all that power. Naraka, the demon son of the Earth, had been slain and his earrings taken, and the demon himself offered up as the horse of the first horse-sacrifice. The Daityas and the Danavas — the demon hosts of old — had been destroyed in battle, until Krishna set Indra on the throne of the universe and took birth himself among men. He spoke the names like a litany: Ahvriti slain at Jaruthi, Kratha, Sisupala with his adherents, Jarasandha, Saivya, Satadhanwan. On a war-car that roared like clouds and blazed like the sun, Krishna had defeated Rukmi in battle and won the daughter of Bhoja for his queen. He had slain Indradyumna, and the Yavana king Kaseruman, and Salwa the lord of Saubha, and had destroyed the city of Saubha itself. And even as a child, with three steps alone, he had filled heaven, the sky, and the earth.

Arjuna’s voice went on, reciting the old deeds as one recites a litany — and as he spoke, the wrath of Krishna, which had seemed ready to consume all creation, began to be held, like a fire held in the hands of a friend. The kinsmen sat silent in their ring. The vow stood spoken, and every leaf of the forest had heard it. But the anger was not yet gone from Krishna’s eyes; Arjuna’s words had not yet done their full work.
stories.reflection: The vow is spoken for the sake of the just king in exile, and Krishna's wrath is inseparable from his friendship: the same heart that delights in his friends burns at their wrongs. Arjuna's answer is not argument but remembrance — he recites who Krishna is, holding the fire in the vessel of a thousand lifetimes.
stories.tradition_note: Krishna's vow here is echoed later, before the war of Kurukshetra, in a similar promise.
stories.next_story_tease: But Arjuna's recitation had only begun to do its work on the wrathful Krishna.

stories.title: Nara and Narayana
stories.subtitle: Arjuna soothes Krishna's wrath with the tale of his own ancient deeds
stories.story:
In the Kamyaka forest, Krishna’s anger frightened his own kinsmen. Krishna was the Pandavas’ cousin and their dearest friend, and the Pandavas — Yudhishthira and his four brothers — had been cheated of their kingdom at dice and sent to live as exiles in the wild. By the time the news reached Krishna, the fury in him had grown into something terrible: a heat that seemed ready to burn the world down around the wrongs that had been done to his friends.

Their friends had come to the forest from near and far — the Bhojas, the Vrishnis and the Andhakas, the kinsmen of Panchala, Dhrishtaketu the king of Chedi, the Kaikeya brothers — and had seated themselves in a wide ring around Yudhishthira the just, with Krishna at their head. In that ring Krishna had already spoken his vow: the earth would drink the blood of Duryodhana and Karna, of Dussasana and the wicked Sakuni, and Yudhishthira would sit on his throne again. But the vow did not cool his blood. As he thought of the wrongs of the Pandavas, he fell into such a passion that he seemed bent upon consuming all created things; those nearest him could feel it, like standing too close to a fire. So Arjuna exerted himself to pacify him.

Arjuna did not argue, and he did not plead. Beholding Krishna angry, he began instead to recite the feats Krishna had achieved in his former lives — the penances and the battles of the soul of all things: immeasurable, eternal, of infinite energy, the lord of the Prajapatis, the supreme ruler of the worlds, Vishnu of profound wisdom.

He told of the ten thousand years Krishna had wandered on the Gandhamadana mountains, a hermit whose home was wherever evening fell; of the eleven thousand years lived on water alone by the lake of Pushkara; of the hundred years on the high hills of Vadari, standing on one leg with arms upraised, living upon air; of the twelve years of sacrifice on the banks of the Saraswati, until his body, stripped of its upper garment, was nothing but a bundle of veins; of the thousand celestial years he had stood on one leg on the plains of Prabhasa. He told of the slaying of Naraka, the demon son of the Earth, and of the first horse-sacrifice that followed; of the Daityas and Danavas destroyed in battle until the sovereignty of the universe rested in Indra’s hands; of the three steps by which, even as a child, Krishna had filled heaven, the firmament and the earth; and of the sinful demons slain by the hundred in each of his thousand incarnations.

Then Arjuna spoke directly to his friend. “All asceticism rests in you,” he said, “and you are the embodiment of all sacrifices — the cause of creation and its course, the mover of all minds, the beginning and end of all things. You are mine, and I am yours, and all that is mine is yours also.” When Arjuna fell silent, Krishna answered him. “He who hates you hates me,” he said, “and he who follows you follows me. Irrepressible one — you are Nara, and I am Narayana. We are the two sages, Nara and Narayana, born into the world of men for one purpose: you are from me, and I am from you.”

The fire in Krishna’s eyes sank. The wrath that had seemed ready to consume creation gathered itself back into the shape of a man sitting quietly among his friends. He did not unsay the vow — the earth would still drink the blood of Duryodhana and Karna, and Yudhishthira would still be crowned — but he spoke of it now without fury, as a thing already accomplished. And the kinsmen who had watched the storm pass looked at Arjuna with wonder. He had not argued Krishna out of his anger, nor pleaded with him. He had simply reminded Krishna of who Krishna was — and for Krishna, that had been enough.
stories.reflection: Arjuna does not argue Krishna out of his anger; he reminds him of who he is. The catalogue of ancient feats — penances of ten thousand years, three steps that filled the three worlds — says that the power now blazing in wrath has always existed and has always been used with purpose. And the claim goes deeper: the two friends are Nara and Narayana, one soul in two bodies: an injury to Arjuna is an injury to Krishna.
stories.next_story_tease: But the day's work was not done: Draupadi still wept, and Krishna had yet to speak to her.
stories.hero_scene: In a forest clearing ringed by seated kings and warriors, the angry Krishna half-rises from his place while Arjuna, one hand raised in calm, recites his friend's ancient deeds — the air between them seeming to burn and cool at once, and the faces of the gathered Yadavas lit by the dying light.

stories.title: A Promise for a Weeping Queen
stories.subtitle: What Krishna swore to Draupadi in the Kamyaka forest
stories.story:
Some sorrows cannot be answered with plans for war. In the Kamyaka forest, while the gathered kinsmen talked of vengeance, Draupadi sat apart and wept.

Her husbands — the five Pandava brothers — had lost everything at dice: kingdom, wealth, dignity — and were living as exiles in the great forest, far from everything they had known. All morning the clearing had been full of their friends, come from near and far with hearts hot with anger against the sons of Dhritarashtra: the Bhojas, the Vrishnis and the Andhakas, the relatives of Panchala, the king of Chedi, the Kaikeya brothers. They had sat in a wide ring around Yudhishthira, and Krishna, their cousin and their friend, at their head, had sworn that the earth would drink the blood of the men who had wronged them, and that Yudhishthira would sit on the throne again. But that was talk of battles still to come, and it is cold comfort to a woman who has already lost. She was the princess of Panchala, the wife of the five brothers, and she had tasted enough of the Kauravas’ cruelty to know that vows are cheap until they are kept. Her anger had names: Duryodhana and his brother Dussasana, Karna their ally, Sakuni the master of the loaded dice. And each of them sat safely in Hastinapura, the Kuru capital, while she wept on the forest grass.

Krishna saw her tears, and he did not offer her patience, and he did not offer her philosophy. He spoke to the weeping queen, and his words were a promise laid against the future like a stone.

“Fair lady,” he said, “the wives of those with whom you are angry shall weep even as you weep now, when they see their husbands lying dead on the ground. And I promise you this: you shall once more be the queen of kings. The heavens might fall, or the Himalaya split apart, the earth might be rent, or the waters of the ocean might dry up — but my words shall never prove empty.”

For a moment the forest seemed to hold its breath. It was an odd comfort to offer a woman wronged before a court: not “bear it patiently,” but “they will weep as you weep now, and you will sit on a throne again.” Krishna did not soften the wrong, nor blur the memory of it; he swore it would be answered, measure for measure, and he staked the order of nature itself on his word. And this, everyone could hear, was not the speech of a man soothing a woman — it was a king giving his word before witnesses.

The weeping Draupadi heard him, and her tears slowed on her face. Those who knew Krishna knew that his word, once given, was firmer than the ground under their feet; even Arjuna, standing among the allies, said nothing, for there was nothing to add to a vow that had taken the sky for its surety. In the evening the talk in the camp turned from grief to plans — of armies and alliances, and of the war that waited at the end of the thirteen years. But those who had heard Krishna’s words to Draupadi carried something else away with them: the memory of a queen weeping in exile, and the man who had promised her a throne, with the fall of heaven as the only price of his failing. And she, for her part, began that evening to believe it — for she knew, as everyone there knew, that Krishna had never in his life spoken a word that the world had not, in the end, been forced to keep.
stories.reflection: Krishna does not tell Draupadi to be patient or to forget. He answers grief with a counter-vow, matching the wrong done to her with a future so certain that he stakes the order of nature on it — heaven falling, oceans drying up — before he will let his word fail. Consolation here is not softness; it is the same iron promise that will later be kept on the battlefield.
stories.next_story_tease: Then Krishna turned to Yudhishthira with a confession that had been burning in him since Dwaraka.

stories.title: Had I Been at Dwaraka
stories.story:
“Had I been at Dwaraka,” Krishna told Yudhishthira, “this evil would not have befallen you.” The words came out of him like a confession, there in the Kamyaka forest where the exiled Pandavas sat with their allies around them. Everyone in that circle knew the story: how Yudhishthira had been drawn into a gambling match at Hastinapura; how the dice had been loaded; how he had staked and lost his wealth, his brothers, himself, and at last the queen herself; and how the Pandavas had been sent into exile for thirteen years. And everyone knew, too, that Krishna had not been there to stop it. He had been away in the country of Anarta, around his own city of Dwaraka, fighting the forces of Salwa, who had brought war to his gates.

“Coming to that gambling match uninvited — even if Dhritarashtra himself, or Duryodhana, or the other Kauravas, had not asked me,” he went on, “I would have stopped the game before it began, by setting out all its evils before them. I would have summoned Bhishma and Drona and Kripa, and Vahlika, to my aid.”

He laid out for Yudhishthira exactly what he would have done, as if the scene still played out behind his eyes. He would have stood before Dhritarashtra and told him plainly that his sons should have nothing to do with dice. He would have shown the evils by which the son of Virasena had once been deprived of his kingdom. He would have described how a man who takes up the game goes on playing, from the mere wish to win, until ruin takes him — how through dice men lose their possessions in a single day, fall into distress, are robbed of wealth they never even tasted, and exchange harsh words with those they love. “Desire for women, dice, hunting and drinking,” he said, “the cravings that take hold of people through temptation — the wise regard these as the four evils that rob a man of his prosperity, and those learned in the scriptures hold that ruin waits upon them all.”

And he did not stop at counsel. If Dhritarashtra had accepted his words, Krishna said, the welfare of the Kurus and virtue itself would both have been secured. But if the old king had rejected his gentle counsel — offered like medicine — Krishna would have compelled him by force. And if the men who waited at his court, professing to be his friends but in truth his foes, had supported him in the folly, Krishna would have slain them all, along with the gamblers, there in the hall itself.

“O Yudhishthira,” he said, and his voice was rough with grief, “it is because I was away from the country of Anarta that you have fallen into this distress born of dice.” And he told Yudhishthira how he had learned of the calamity: arriving at Dwaraka, he had heard everything from Yuyudhana, his friend and kinsman, and with his heart sore and shaken he had ridden at once, wishing only to see his friend. “Alas, best of the Bharata line,” he said, “you have all fallen into dire distress. I see you and your brothers plunged in misfortune.”

It was strange, the Pandavas thought, to hear the man who had just sworn that the earth would drink their enemies’ blood speak now like a man shouldering blame. He did not console them with assurances; he grieved with them — and he grieved for his own absence, for the single moment when his friends had needed him and he had been elsewhere, fighting his own war at Saubha, while the dice fell without him there to catch them. But the lament, for all its grief, was also a promise in disguise: whatever game came next, Krishna would not be absent from it.
stories.reflection: Krishna's lament is both grief and claim. He names the four evils — women, dice, hunting, drinking — as the root of the ruin, but he also insists that his own presence would have changed everything, by counsel or by force. It is a friend's confession of where power truly lies: not in being everywhere, but in the one moment a friend is absent and disaster slips in.
stories.next_story_tease: And the forest would soon test that friendship again, when a furious sage and ten thousand disciples arrived without warning.

stories.title: A Prayer Heard in Dwaraka
stories.subtitle: How Draupadi's prayer crossed the miles to Krishna's side
stories.story:
Krishna lay asleep in Dwaraka, his city by the sea, with Rukmini, his wife, resting beside him. Far away, in the Kamyaka forest where the five Pandava brothers lived in exile with their wife, Draupadi, a heart was failing. And at that very moment ten thousand ascetics were walking toward the brothers' hermitage.

At their head came the sage Durvasa — a guest any household dreaded, famous for a temper that blazed up like fire and curses that never missed. He had chosen his moment with care, making certain that the Pandavas were resting at their ease and that Draupadi had finished her meal before he set out with his followers. Yudhishthira, the eldest brother, went forward to greet him with palms joined, offered him the finest seat, and gave the whole company a respectful welcome. "Return quickly after your bath," he said, "and the meal will be waiting." Durvasa, never troubling himself to wonder how such a feast would be provided, went down to the stream with all ten thousand disciples to bathe.

But Draupadi knew what her husband had promised, and her heart sank. The vessel that fed the Pandavas was a gift of the sun: it stayed full until she had finished her meal, and empty afterward. She had eaten long ago. There was no food in it now, and no way to fill it — and a guest like Durvasa could not be turned away with apologies.

After much anxious thought she could see no way out. So she did what she had done in her darkest hour before: she prayed. Inwardly she called on Krishna — the son of Devaki, whose face was dark as the leaf of the blue lotus, whose eyes were red as the heart of a lily, who wore yellow robes and the bright Kaustubha gem at his breast. "You who saved me once from Dussasana, when the whole court sat silent," she said in her heart, "save me now from this."

The prayer was answered before it was finished. In Dwaraka, Krishna rose from Rukmini's bed — she slept on, unaware — and came to the forest. Draupadi bowed before him in joy and told him everything: the arrival of the sages, the empty vessel, her fear of Durvasa's wrath. And Krishna, who had crossed half the world at the thought of her trouble, said only: "I am very hungry. Give me something to eat, and then go about your work."

She stared at him. "The sun-given vessel stays full only until I have eaten from it," she said. "I ate long ago. There is nothing in it now."

"This is no time for jokes," said Krishna. "I am truly hungry. Bring me the vessel and show it to me."

She had it brought. He looked inside, and there, stuck to the rim, was a single grain of rice with a scrap of vegetable clinging to it. He took it and swallowed it. "Let Hari, the soul of the universe, be pleased," he said, "and let the god who receives the offerings at every sacrifice be satisfied with this."

Then he turned to Bhima, the strong second brother, who stood nearby. "Go quickly," he said, "and invite the sages to dinner."

Bhima hurried to the nearest stream — clear, cool water — where Durvasa and his ten thousand had plunged in and were rubbing themselves after their bath. And there they stopped, one after another, staring at one another: their stomachs were full to the throat, though they had eaten nothing. "We told the king to prepare our meal and came here for a bath," they said. "How can we eat now? The feast has been prepared for nothing."

Durvasa understood at last, and his face clouded. "By making the king prepare a feast we cannot touch," he said, "we have done Yudhishthira a great wrong."
stories.reflection: The hinge of the story is timing: the prayer is answered before it is finished, Krishna leaving Rukmini's side the instant the thought forms in the forest. And the miracle is almost comically small — not a feast conjured from the sky, but one leftover grain swallowed at the rim of an empty pot. His protection here is not spectacle; it is presence, arriving exactly when there was no other help.
stories.tradition_note: The sun-given vessel that fed the Pandavas until Draupadi had eaten is the same vessel the epic elsewhere calls the Akshaya-patra, and Durvasa's visit is one of several episodes that turn on its power.
stories.next_story_tease: Now Durvasa and his disciples had to face the king whose feast their own bellies had already consumed.

stories.title: A Single Grain for Ten Thousand
stories.subtitle: How Krishna fed the sage Durvasa and his ten thousand disciples with one grain of rice.
stories.story:
Ten thousand guests, and nothing to set before them.

In the years when the five Pandava brothers lived in exile in the Kamyaka forest with their wife, Draupadi, the sage Durvasa arrived at their hermitage one day — and behind him came ten thousand disciples. He had not been expected, and there was no time to prepare. Ten thousand guests is a number that empties a granary and breaks a cook's heart.

Yudhishthira, the eldest brother — a king without a kingdom — went forward to receive him. He joined his palms, offered the sage an excellent seat, and spoke with perfect courtesy. Bathe in the river, he said, and return quickly; the food will be ready. It was a gracious invitation, and a desperate one. There was no food to be had, and to send such a guest away unfed was unthinkable.

Durvasa — a guest whose anger no one wished to test — suspected nothing of how the king would feed him and his host of followers. He went down to the stream to bathe, and the ten thousand went with him. Draupadi had already finished the day's meal, and the cooking vessel stood nearly empty.

Draupadi turned the problem over and over and found no way to feed ten thousand men. At last she did the only thing left to her: she prayed. Inwardly she called on Krishna, their cousin and dearest friend, who lived far away in his city of Dwaraka. She remembered his face, dark as the leaf of the blue lotus; his eyes, red as the heart of a lily; his yellow robes and the bright Kaustubha gem at his breast. And she begged him to come to her help.

And Krishna came. He brought no carts of provisions and no army of cooks. He asked simply for whatever there was to eat, and Draupadi brought him the vessel. He looked inside, and there, sticking to the rim, was a single grain of rice and a scrap of vegetable. One grain — not even a mouthful. He took it and swallowed it. "May Hari be pleased," he said, "and may the god who shares the offerings at every sacrifice be filled."

That was all. A single grain, offered and accepted, and nothing more.

Down at the river, something strange happened. Durvasa and his ten thousand disciples had plunged into the water and were rubbing themselves after their bath, when one by one they stopped. Every one of them felt, suddenly and unmistakably, that his stomach was full — completely, comfortably full, as after a rich feast. There was nothing more to ask for and nothing more to want. A guest who is already full cannot in courtesy sit down to a meal, and a guest who wants nothing cannot ask for more. To return now and claim a feast they could not eat would be absurd — almost a small shame.

So the sage and his ten thousand disciples did not return to the hermitage at all. They took the road out of the forest, full and wondering, and not one of them could say how it had come about. Behind them, in the quiet hermitage, stood a pot that had held nothing but a single grain — and it had been enough.
stories.reflection: The humor is quiet and exact — a sage with ten thousand disciples slipping away rather than admit he is already full. But the heart of it is the single grain: Krishna does not multiply abundance so much as accept what is offered with complete trust, and the scarcity simply stops being scarcity.

stories.title: Virtuous Men Never Suffer
stories.story:
The ten thousand disciples of the sage Durvasa went down to the stream to bathe, and when they came out of the water they were full — not of the feast they had been promised, but full in a way none of them could explain, their stomachs heavy to the throat. The sage looked at his followers, and his followers looked at one another. Durvasa understood first. A feast had been promised them and they could not touch it; what king would forgive such an insult to his hospitality? The wrath of Yudhishthira, they feared, would fall on them like fire. And so, without a word of farewell, the whole company slipped away from the Kamyaka forest as quietly as it had come, fleeing the anger they believed they had earned.

The Pandavas were left standing in the sudden quiet. A few hours earlier the forest had been loud with the arrival of ten thousand guests, and Yudhishthira had gone forward with joined palms to welcome them, promising a meal for every man. It was a promise no host should ever have made: the sun-given vessel from which the brothers ate each day was empty, for Draupadi had already taken her food, and not a grain remained for a feast.

Draupadi, alone with her worry, had done the only thing she could. She had called on Krishna — their cousin, far away in Dwaraka — and reminded him of the day in the Kuru court when Dussasana had dragged her by the hair and the whole hall had sat silent. "As you protected me then," she had prayed, "extricate me now from this difficulty." And Krishna had come. He had looked into the empty vessel and found what a desperate eye could not: a single grain of rice and a leaf of vegetable clinging to its rim. That grain he had eaten. And in that same hour the sages bathing in the stream felt their hunger die in their stomachs.

Now Krishna stood before the brothers, and they did not know how to thank him. He spoke first, and his words were simple. Knowing their danger from that wrathful sage, he said, he had been implored by Draupadi to come, and therefore he had come speedily. There was no need for fear now; Durvasa was gone. And then he gave them the deeper assurance, the one they would carry long after the forest grew quiet again: "Virtuous men never suffer."

It was a strange comfort to hold, because their lives had been full of suffering — the poisoned feast, the lost kingdom, the exile, their wife dragged before an assembly of enemies who had shamed her. Yet the words came from someone who had crossed the whole distance from Dwaraka in the time it takes to say a name, and standing in his presence the brothers found that they could believe them.

He asked only one thing of them: their permission to return home. The Pandavas gave it freely and watched him go.

When he had disappeared among the trees, the forest seemed to breathe again. The sages were gone, the feast that could not have been made had somehow been served, and the danger that had filled the afternoon had lifted like mist off the river. Yudhishthira looked at the empty vessel, at the stream where the ascetics had bathed, at the sky gone soft with evening — and understood, at last, that they had never been as alone as they had felt.
stories.reflection: Krishna's reassurance is striking for what it does not say: no rebuke of the sage, no drama about the miracle, only the quiet certainty that virtuous men never suffer. The relief comes not from Durvasa's retreat but from the discovery of who had been standing behind them all along.
stories.next_story_tease: Back in Mathura, Krishna would soon send a trusted friend to Hastinapura to learn the truth of the Pandavas' suffering.

stories.title: An Errand for Akrura
stories.story:
Krishna walked through the streets of Mathura and stopped at the house of Akrura — an elder of his own family, and one of the truest friends he had. With him came his brother Balarama and Uddhava, his trusted friend and adviser. Krishna had not sent for Akrura, nor summoned him to the palace; he came himself, on foot, to the door of a friend.

When Akrura saw them approaching, he went out to meet them and bowed low before Krishna and Balarama, and they received his reverence and returned it. With his own hands he washed their feet, held that water to his head as if it were the holiest thing he would ever touch, and then seated them and took their feet in his lap, rubbing them with the tenderness of a man who had waited a long time for this visit. "Blessed are our dwellings," he said, "that the teacher of the world has entered them."

"By good fortune," he said, "Kamsa is slain with all his followers, and this family is yours." Then his praise poured out like a river that had been dammed too long. These two, he said, were the foremost of persons, the cause and the substance of the world. Krishna creates, sustains and dissolves the universe with his own powers; whenever the ancient path of the Vedas is lost among men, he restores it for the good of all; and now he had come down into the house of Vasudeva, his father, to lighten the burden of the earth, spreading glory over his own family. Even the kings of the gods, he said, found Krishna's way hard to reach — and yet here he stood, inside the walls of a devotee's house. "What wise man," Akrura asked, "would seek refuge anywhere but in you — dear to your devotees, true in speech, a friend who remembers a kindness and grants every wish?" He spoke of the bonds that hold a man — son, wife, wealth, house, the body itself — and begged Krishna to cut them all.

Krishna heard him out, and then answered. Great souls like Akrura, he said, are the ones to be served, the most worthy of all. The holy places are not made of water, nor are the gods made of clay and stone. The true sacred presence lives in people — in a friend who wishes you well, in a heart that has bowed to the good. He might have said more, but he had come on other business, and now he spoke of it.

After their father Pandu died, Krishna told him, his five children had been left with their mother, deep in sorrow, and the blind king of Hastinapura dealt with his brother's sons out of a mean and troubled mind, guided by his wicked son Duryodhana. The boys had been brought to the capital after their father's death; they were there not by choice, and the king's house was not their home. "Go to Hastinapura," Krishna said, "and learn how the Pandavas fare — whether things go well with them or ill." Learn, and come back and tell me, was the meaning of it: not a war, not a proclamation, but a friend sent to look with his own eyes and report honestly.

Akrura bowed his head. He asked for no guard, no retinue, no letter of authority; a friend's eyes were the only credential he needed. He would go, and he would watch, and he would remember everything. Krishna, Balarama and Uddhava left him standing at his own door, and the house that had held the lord of the world felt, for a moment, like the center of the earth.
stories.reflection: The episode's quiet teaching is in Krishna's praise: holiness lives in people, not in things, and Akrura's bowed heart is a truer sacred place than any shrine of water or stone. The errand that follows shows the same instinct — the protection Krishna offers the Pandavas begins with one friend sent to look, and to tell the truth of what he sees.
stories.next_story_tease: In Hastinapura, a sorrowful woman waited to hear that someone from home still remembered her.

stories.title: A Doe Among Wolves
stories.story:
Hastinapura was full of eyes, and Kunti had learned to live under them. The palace of the Kurus was a place of whispers and rivalries, and in the years since her husband Pandu's death she had felt herself watched from every side — the widow of the dead king, the mother of five boys the court had never wanted. They were the sons of Pandu, and the kingdom their father had left was now held by his blind brother. Then word came that her brother Akrura had arrived from Mathura, and for the first time in many months, Kunti let herself hope.

Akrura did what courtesy required, and more. He greeted the elders of the house — Bahlika with his son, the sage Bharadvaja, Gautama, the old friends of the family — and then he settled in and watched. He stayed for months, asking little, seeing everything. He marked how the sons of Pandu shone: their brilliance, their strength, their courage, their humility, every good quality that had survived their father's death. And he marked, too, what the sons of Dhritarashtra had done to them — the poison mixed into their food, the cruelties that had no name in the law but were known to every whisper in the palace.

Then Kunti came to him, and she did not come composed. She was weeping. In the months of Akrura's stay she had kept her composure, as a queen of the Kurus must, but this was her brother, and with him the composure failed. Among her rivals, she told him, she was like a doe among wolves; every day she measured her children's danger by the faces that surrounded them. Then she asked the question that had pressed on her heart since the day she learned her brother was in the city. "Do they still remember us?" she said — her parents, her brothers, the home she had left behind in Mathura. "Do my father and brothers still think of me?" She did not ask for wealth or power or a return to favor; she asked only to be remembered, to know that the world she had left behind still held her name.

And then, as if the question had carried her to the edge of a deeper need, she turned from the messenger to the one he had come from. "The blessed Krishna, my brother's son," she said, "is the refuge, dear to his devotees. Krishna, Krishna," she cried, "great yogin, soul of the universe, protector of all beings! I see no refuge for us but your lotus feet." She spoke of him as her nephew, the boy of Mathura who was, she knew, more than any boy. "Salutation to Krishna, the pure one, the supreme self." If her parents had forgotten her, Krishna had not. If the wolves of Hastinapura closed in, the refuge was still there, as close as a name spoken through tears.

Akrura and Vidura stood with her, sharing her sorrow, taking it into themselves. Vidura — the wise uncle of the Kurus who had always loved the Pandavas — and Akrura, who had come straight from Krishna's side. Between the two of them they could give her what the palace never would: the assurance that she was not alone. She had spoken her grief aloud at last, and she had been heard; and being heard, the walls of the palace seemed to stand a little further off.

That night Kunti slept more peacefully than she had in months. Her words were on their way to Mathura, carried by a brother who had seen everything — toward a city where someone still remembered her name.
stories.reflection: Kunti's grief is doubled: she is a widow among enemies, and her only refuge is a nephew far away. The story does not soften this — her prayer is said through tears, in the middle of a hostile court — and that is exactly why it is moving: the doe among wolves has nothing but her devotion, and the devotion is enough.
stories.next_story_tease: Before he left the city, Akrura had one more word for the blind king.

stories.title: No One Dwells Here Forever
stories.story:
Before he left Hastinapura, Akrura asked to see the king. Krishna of Mathura had sent him to the city to learn how his cousins, the five Pandava brothers, were faring in the palace of their uncle, the blind king Dhritarashtra — and Akrura had learned it well: the poison, the cruelties, the slow grinding-down of five boys and their mother. Now, with that knowledge sitting in him like a stone, he went to the one man who could change it. Dhritarashtra sat on the throne his brother Pandu had left empty, and loved his own sons with a love that had gone crooked.

Akrura did not flatter him. He spoke as a friend of the house, plainly. "Rule the earth by righteousness," he said, "and win your subjects by good conduct. Act otherwise, and you will be blamed in every mouth and walk into darkness." Then he said the thing that kings rarely hear: no one dwells in this world forever with anyone. A being is born alone, and dies alone; no retinue follows a man out of the world, and the guards who surround a throne cannot surround a grave. The wealth a man gathers by wrong means is carried off by others of little wit; the man who nourishes his sons on unrighteousness, thinking himself clever, takes the guilt onto his own shoulders and is finally abandoned by those very sons. "Therefore this world, O king," Akrura said, "is a dream, a waking illusion, a fantasy of the mind. Do not anchor your soul to it."

Dhritarashtra heard him out. The truth of it was undeniable, and the old king admitted as much. "Even so, gentle one," he said, "your sweet words do not rest in my heart, because my heart is unsteady." He knew what was right; he loved his sons more than he could hold to what was right. His love for them sat on his mind like a weight, and the truth could not move it. And then he spoke the deeper helplessness, the one that makes counsel useless: "What man can undo the ordinance of the Lord?" The lord who, entering his own creation through his inscrutable power, sets in motion the wheel of the world — who could stand against that wheel, and who could call a man guilty for being crushed beneath it? He bowed to that power, unknowable in its play, and fell silent.

Akrura left the city as he had come, and the blind king remained on his throne, the truth ringing in his ears and no room for it in his heart. The counsel had been given; whether it would be kept was another matter, and Akrura knew better than to wait for the answer.

Back in Mathura, he went straight to Krishna and to Balarama, Krishna's elder brother, and told them everything — what he had seen of the Pandavas, what the sons of Dhritarashtra had done, and what the blind king had confessed when the truth was set before him. He told them how the king had heard every word of the counsel, and acknowledged the truth of every word, and how the acknowledgment had changed nothing in his heart. He reported it all without softening a word. Krishna listened. Balarama listened. The news did not surprise them, but it was news that had to be carried, and it had been carried by a friend's eyes and a friend's honesty.

The kingdom of the Kurus went on as it had. But from that day, nothing between Hastinapura and Mathura was quite what it had been. A message had passed between the two cities — not of war, not yet — and the road that carried it ran both ways.
stories.reflection: Dhritarashtra hears the truth and agrees with it, yet cannot act on it — the story's most honest moment. Akrura's counsel fails in the usual sense, and the failure is recorded without judgment: some truths find no hold in a heart that loves wrongly, and the wise know better than to wait for the answer.
stories.next_story_tease: Before long, Krishna himself would walk into the Pandavas' court at Indraprastha.

stories.title: A Visit That Made Them Whole
stories.story:
The city of Indraprastha was not expecting a guest that day, and the news ran through it like wind through an open hall. Krishna, who ruled the far coast at Dwaraka, had come to see the Pandavas — the five brothers who were kings now in the city they had built beside the Yamuna, where Yudhishthira's rule had already made the kingdom prosperous. He came without an army and without a summons. The old telling says simply that he came to see them, and the brothers went out to meet him before any court ceremony could be arranged.

Yudhishthira rose at once, and Bhima with him, and they embraced him with both arms, the way men embrace a brother who has crossed a hundred lands to stand in their doorway. The touch of him, the tellers say, seemed to wash away the weariness of every hard year they had carried. Krishna paid his respects first to Yudhishthira and to Bhima, then to the others as they pressed forward, and Draupadi led him herself to the finest seat in the hall. Satyaki, a young warrior of Krishna's own clan who had ridden with him from Dwaraka, was received with the same warmth, honored and greeted by each of the brothers in turn.

But it was Kunti who spoke for them all. She had been mother to these boys through the years of wandering and want, when Krishna had been the one cousin who remembered them, who came to them, who wrote to them in their exile. Now she stood before him, the queen of a great house, and her composure broke. Weeping, her voice choked with love, she said, "Now we are safe, for you have remembered us."

Her tears were not grief. They were the relief of a woman who had watched her sons survive everything and had asked only one thing of the world: that they not be forgotten. The boy who had come to their forest hut in the years of hiding was now the master of Dwaraka, and he was still the same friend.

Yudhishthira asked him to stay through the rains, and Krishna stayed. Four months he remained at Indraprastha, through the slow green season when the roads dissolved and the world turned inward. He did not come as a king to be entertained. He lived among them, at ease — sitting with Yudhishthira over the long questions of kingship, testing grips with Bhima, walking the gardens with Arjuna, letting the twins argue with him about horses and swords. The old telling closes the account with a plain sentence: he delighted them all.

In those four months he was simply what he had always been to them: a cousin visiting, a friend at leisure, the one ally who had never once asked what the friendship was worth. The palace of Indraprastha, so often a stage for plots and prophecies, became for a season only a house where someone beloved was staying — and no one in it wanted the rains to end.

When at last he left, he took nothing with him but their goodbyes, and left behind a household that had been, for a little while, whole.
stories.reflection: Kunti's words — "now we are safe, for you have remembered us" — define the Pandavas' bond with Krishna more exactly than any treaty: safety as being remembered. The story's quiet power is that nothing is accomplished in it; a visit, an embrace, a season of joy — and that is precisely the point.
stories.next_story_tease: But the friendship was about to be tested in fire: the forest of Khandava was waiting, and Agni would not be denied.

stories.title: Krishna Grants the Khadava Forest to Agni
stories.story:
The Pandavas — the five royal brothers of Indraprastha — had a guest among them who was more than a guest. Krishna, their cousin and closest friend, had come to stay with them, and the old telling says that wherever he lived among them, he wished only for their good. It was during such a stay that Agni, the god of fire, set his heart on the great forest of Khadava.

The woodland was ancient, thick and deep, older than memory, and Agni wished to consume it — to feed on it as fire feeds, until nothing was left but ash. Yet the forest was not torn from him by force, nor won from him by prayer. It was given to him freely, by two men who stood at its edge.

One of those men was Krishna, and he took up the reins of Arjuna's chariot with his own hands, to serve as his friend's charioteer. It was a small thing to watch, a friend taking the reins; but it placed Krishna exactly where the moment needed him. Arjuna, for his part, would need a steady hand, for to give a forest to fire means to let the fire have its way — to watch the great woodland turn to flame, tree by tree, the smoke rising in a black column over the land, the heat rolling out across the plain until it pressed against the face. There is no sound quite like a forest burning in earnest: the crack of sap, the hiss of green wood surrendering, the long sigh of a trunk giving way.

And so it happened. With Krishna holding the reins and Arjuna ready with his bow, the forest of Khadava was given over to Agni. The god of fire fell upon it and consumed it, until the ancient trees were gone and only ash remained, glowing faintly where the forest had stood.

Agni was pleased, and a pleased god does not leave empty-handed those who have served him. To Arjuna he gave the great bow called Gandiva, a weapon whose name would be spoken with awe for generations; white horses, swift and gleaming; a chariot that no enemy could stop; and quivers that would never run empty — however many arrows Arjuna drew, there would always be another waiting at his fingertips.

Out of the burning itself came one more gift. Maya, a master builder, had been caught in the forest as the fire swept through it, and his life was spared. In gratitude he raised for the Pandavas their great assembly hall — a hall so beautiful that those who entered it could not say whether it had been built by human hands or by something finer.

So an ancient forest went to ash within a season, and from that ash came the bow and the horses, the chariot and the endless quivers, and in time the great hall that kings would come to envy. The fire had taken much, and given much in return; and Krishna, who had asked nothing for himself, had simply held the reins while his friend gave the forest away.
stories.reflection: The Khadava forest is one of those episodes where destruction and founding turn out to be the same thing. Agni consumed an ancient woodland, and from the ash the Pandavas received the weapons and the hall on which their power would rest — while Krishna's whole part was simply to hold the reins.
stories.tradition_note: The Bhagavata Purana condenses this episode to a few verses; the Mahabharata tells the burning of the Khadava forest at far greater length.
stories.next_story_tease: The hall Maya built for the Pandavas would soon host the great Rajasuya sacrifice.

stories.title: The City That Rose to Meet Him
stories.story:
News traveled ahead of the chariots. Krishna was coming — not for a visit this time, but for the Rajasuya, the great sacrifice through which Yudhishthira, king of the Pandavas at Indraprastha, meant to be acknowledged as a king of kings. And the city of Indraprastha met him the way a festival meets the sun.

The streets had been swept and sprinkled with water fragrant with elephant musk. Banners streamed from every rooftop, golden arches stood at the crossings, and at each doorway stood the full pitchers of water that are the old sign of welcome. From the palace Yudhishthira came out to meet him with his teachers and his friends, and the sound that went before them was music and the chanting of the Vedas together. When Krishna stepped down, the heart of the king of the Pandavas melted. Yudhishthira took him in both arms and held him, and the embrace said everything a court could not.

Bhima embraced him next, smiling through eyes blurred with love — Krishna was his mother's sister's son, his own cousin. Arjuna folded him in his arms. The twins, Nakula and Sahadeva, bowed and touched his feet. Around them the bards and the heralds sang his praises, and the whole assembly seemed to press inward, each person wanting to be nearer to him. Of that welcome the old telling says simply that Krishna stood at its center like the jewel crowning a hundred good names.

The women of the city had dropped their household work the moment the news came. Down the king's road they hurried, hair-braids coming loose and garments slipping in their eagerness, to stand where they could watch him pass, and from the rooftops they showered him with flowers, welcoming him with smiles, embracing him in their hearts. Those who caught sight of Krishna's queens — Rukmini, Satyabhama, Bhadra, Jambavati — murmured to one another that the ladies of the Vrishni house moved among them like the stars around the moon. What had those women done, they asked, to be looked on by one whose glance made a festival of the eyes of all the world?

In the palace, Kunti rose from her couch and went to meet her sister's son. Krishna bowed to his aunt and to the elder women of the household, and Kunti led him into the house with her own hands. At her mother-in-law's bidding, Draupadi welcomed each of Krishna's queens — Kalindi, Mitravinda, Saibya, Nagnajiti, and the rest — and settled them in the women's quarters with every honor.

Yudhishthira gave Krishna the best of the palace, and when Krishna was seated at ease, the king spoke. In the Mahabharata's telling his words are plain. "It is because of you that the whole earth is under my rule," he said. "Through your grace I have gathered this wealth, and I wish to give it away as the rites ordain — to the brahmin priests and to the sacred fire. Grant me leave to perform the sacrifice with you and my brothers. Better still, take your own place at the head of it, for if you perform it, I shall be cleansed of every sin."

Krishna answered with the affection of a friend who wants nothing from the friendship. "You deserve imperial dignity. Let the great sacrifice be performed by you; if you perform it and gain its fruit, we will all count ourselves crowned with success. I am always seeking your good. Perform the sacrifice you desire — and give me some office in it, for I should obey all your commands."

"Then my resolve is already crowned with fruit," Yudhishthira said, "since you have come just as I wished."

So the son of Pandu set himself, with his brothers, to gathering everything the Rajasuya would need, and an arrival of embraces and showers of flowers became the beginning of the greatest sacrifice the age would see. For a few days more, though, there was only this: a king's city gladdened by the presence of its truest friend, like a dark region made bright by the sun.
stories.reflection: The Rajasuya is often remembered as the summit of Yudhishthira's glory, but this story records the arrival as pure affection — a city that empties its households to see one man pass. The political begins as the personal: the king who would conquer the world first asks his cousin to bless the undertaking.
stories.tradition_note: The Mahabharata frames the same arrival differently — Krishna coming with a mass of treasure for Yudhishthira and a Yadava army under Vasudeva's command. This account follows the Bhagavata's framing of the arrival as a reunion of love.
stories.next_story_tease: Yet not long before this day of glory, the same friendship had nearly been broken by an elopement — Arjuna had carried off Krishna's sister from the very heart of Dwaraka.

stories.title: The Renunciant Who Carried Off a Bride
stories.story:
Arjuna heard the rumor on the pilgrim road, and it turned his wandering into a rescue. He was one of the five Pandava brothers, walking the holy places during his long exile from their city of Indraprastha. At Dwaraka, far to the west, Balarama — Krishna's elder brother — had decided to give their sister Subhadra in marriage to Duryodhana, the cousin who hated Arjuna's brothers. The plan was kept close, but Arjuna heard of it anyway, and the thought of it burned in him.

He had seen Subhadra once, and the sight had stayed with him like a name written in light. He was not about to let her be given to the enemy of his house. And so the man who had faced armies without blinking did a strange thing: he put aside the warrior's dress, took the triple staff of a wandering holy man, and entered Dwaraka as a renunciant, in the one garb where his own mother's kin would never think to look for him.

It was the rainy season, and he stayed through its months, waiting for his moment. The Yadavas took the young ascetic in without question, as wandering holy men are always received. One day he was brought into a house and offered guest-gifts, and there he saw her — Subhadra, whose beauty, the old telling says, stole the hearts of heroes. And she, seeing him, desired him, for he was the one who stole the hearts of women. Neither of them spoke of it aloud. They did not need to.

Then came the day of a great festival, when the gods' image was carried out of the city in procession. The chariots rolled through the gate, the crowds followed, and Subhadra rode in one of them. In the joyful confusion — guards' eyes on the procession, no one watching the quiet renunciant — Arjuna saw his chance. He seized his bow, took the reins, and carried her off, holding back the warriors who rushed to stop him.

The news ran back to Dwaraka before the wheels had settled, and Balarama — the elder, the mighty — broke. His anger rose like the sea at full moon, sudden and immense. The warriors of Vrishni spoke of pursuit and punishment, of the insult to their house, and for a while it seemed the road behind Arjuna would fill with armed men.

Then Krishna spoke, and his words turned the storm. What Arjuna had done was not an insult but an honor. The house of Vrishni was not for sale: no daughter of theirs was to be given away like an animal, no one was to be sold like goods, and a bride's self-choice was a gamble no father should make for his daughter. Arjuna had seen the fault in every gentler way and had taken the maiden by force, as warriors may — and who could fault him? He was the son of Kunti, born in the line of Bharata; no one in all the worlds could vanquish him except the three-eyed god Shiva. "Go to him," Krishna said. "Stop him with words, not weapons, and bring him back. If he rides home after defeating us, our fame is gone. There is no disgrace in friendship."

The Yadavas went out and stopped Arjuna — with words, not weapons — and he turned his chariot back to Dwaraka. There, welcomed and honored by the sons of Vrishni, he was united in marriage with Subhadra. And the anger that had risen like a tide went out: Balarama, appeased, sent rich wedding gifts for the bride and the groom, and the house of Vrishni made the marriage its own.

When at last Arjuna brought his bride home to Indraprastha, the welcome there was warmer than the road had been long. Draupadi, who had waited through his travels, met her new rival with a jealousy that dissolved within the day: Subhadra came to her and said, "I am your maid," and Draupadi rose, embraced her, and answered, "Let your husband be without a foe." Kunti, from excess of affection, blessed the girl who had become her daughter. And from that day, the old telling says, the Pandavas' household lived happily.
stories.reflection: Krishna's defense of the elopement is remarkable for what it protects: not Arjuna's honor but his family's. The argument that a bride must not be given like an animal or sold like goods turns a scandal into a principle — the Yadavas did not lose face, they gained the alliance of the Pandavas, and the anger that might have ended in war ended in wedding gifts.
stories.tradition_note: The Mahabharata gives the decisive speech for the alliance to Vasudeva, Krishna's father, and adds the full story of Subhadra's welcome at Indraprastha; the Bhagavata condenses the episode and credits Krishna himself with pacifying Balarama. This account follows the Bhagavata's shape.
stories.next_story_tease: At the great sacrifice that followed, the man who had stolen Subhadra would watch Krishna take the humblest office in the hall.

stories.title: The Highest Hands at the Lowest Work
stories.story:
Yudhishthira's Rajasuya — the great sacrifice meant to crown him king of kings — was in its last days at Indraprastha. On the final day, when the king himself was to be sprinkled with the consecrating waters, the inner enclosure of the sacrifice held the most extraordinary gathering the age had seen. The great sages had come with the invited kings — men who had lived on mountain air and silence — and sat at ease beside the thrones, with Narada at their head, a wanderer who had watched more ages begin and end than the kings had counted years. They argued and tested one another's wisdom like hawks darting at meat thrown into the air, and the enclosure, crowded with kings and seers, shone like the night sky thick with stars. No one who had not taken the vows of the sacrifice came near that platform; Yudhishthira's offering had drawn the whole world, and the whole world had come in its best.

Narada looked at the king's prosperity, born of the sacrifice, and was glad. Then he looked at the vast company of warrior-kings, the pride of every royal house in the land, and grew thoughtful. He remembered words he had heard long ago in the mansion of Brahma, when the gods had been commanded to be born on earth, to meet one another in the field of war, and to return. This was no mere gathering of princes, he knew, but a meeting of gods in mortal bodies — and the one who moved among them as a man was the one he had known as the source of all things: Narayana, the lord of all, born into the line of the Yadavas, who had himself given that command. So the seer sat at the sacrifice with awe, and saw what no one else in that brilliant hall could see: that many who sat here together in friendship would one day meet again on a battlefield, and the earth would be the lighter for it.

And into the middle of that glory came the moment no telling of the Rajasuya leaves out.

Krishna — he who was himself the center of all worlds, round whom every creature moved — was washing the feet of the priests. He did it himself, taking the lowliest task of the sacrifice, the office no proud man would take, because he wished the rite to bear excellent fruit. No one had asked him; no one could have commanded him. He chose it, and did it so quietly that the old telling records it without fuss, as if it were the most natural thing in the world.

Then Bhishma, the grandsire of the Kurus and the most honored voice in the hall, rose and spoke to Yudhishthira. "Let an offering of honor be given to the kings, each as he deserves," he said. "Six kinds of men are owed such honor: the teacher, the priest of the sacrifice, a kinsman, a student who has finished his studies, a friend, and a king. But let the first offering go to the foremost among those present. As the sun among all lights, so is this one among us in strength and prowess. This hall is lit and gladdened by him, as a sunless region is by the sun, or still air by a breeze."

Yudhishthira asked whom he meant, and Bhishma answered from his knowledge of men: Krishna. So at the grandsire's command, Sahadeva, the youngest of the five brothers, brought the first offering of the finest things the sacrifice could give, set it before Krishna of the Vrishni line, and Krishna accepted it as the rites prescribe.

The hall had seen him kneel with the water at the priests' feet; now it saw him raised above every king — and no one found the two things strange. The bent back at the water and the lifted vessel of honor belonged to the same man, and that was the truest thing the Rajasuya showed that day.

But among the seated kings, one had watched the first offering with a face like a closed fist. His grievance was older than the sacrifice, and it would not wait for the consecration.
stories.reflection: The juxtaposition is the meaning: the same man takes the lowest office in the sacrifice and then receives its highest honor, and no one finds the two in tension. Narada's vision — that the assembly was a concourse of gods gathered to thin the burdened earth — gives the scene its quiet weight: the one serving at the feet of priests is the one who set the whole gathering in motion.
stories.next_story_tease: One king's old grievance, smoldering through the honors, was about to turn the assembly to battle.

stories.title: Shishupala Incites the Kings to Battle
stories.story:
Krishna had received the first honor of the Rajasuya — Yudhishthira's great sacrifice at Indraprastha — and the hall changed in a single breath from a place of ceremony into a place of war. The kings of the earth had come to the sacrifice from every direction, to witness the rite, to share in its glory, to be counted among its guests. And when the first offering of honor went to Krishna, before any of them, the assembly had felt the sting of it. They carried that sting through the long rites, and the air of the hall grew thick with it.

Then Shishupala, the king of Chedi, rose and gave the anger a voice. "When I am here to lead you all," he cried, "what are you thinking of? Come, let us stand in battle against the Vrishnis — Krishna's own people — and the Pandavas!"

The words found their mark at once. The great company of kings, already restless with wrath, stirred like a sea whipped up by storm winds, and all around the hall the countless troops that had ridden in with their masters seemed to gather themselves for a rush.

Krishna saw it before anyone else. Seated in his place, he understood what was coming, and he did not move. He neither rose nor reached for a weapon nor called for his chariot. He waited, as a man waits when he has already seen the end of a thing.

Yudhishthira saw the same storm and read it differently. This was his sacrifice, his city, his guests, and the ruin of any one of them would be his. He leaned toward Bhishma, the grandsire of the Kurus, who sat near him like a mountain among men. "This vast ocean of kings has been stirred to wrath," he said. "Tell me, Grandsire, what I should do, so that my sacrifice may not be obstructed and my people may not be hurt."

Bhishma answered as though the matter were already settled. "Fear nothing, tiger of the Kurus. Can the dog slay the lion? As dogs in a pack gather around a sleeping lion and bark, so are all these lords of the earth. They are barking in rage at the sleeping lion of the Vrishni race. Krishna is that lion now, asleep; and until he wakes, this king of the Chedis makes these monarchs look like lions."

The old man's voice did not rise, and the whole hall leaned in to hear him. "This Shishupala, with little wisdom, means to drag all these kings after him, through him who is the soul of the universe, down to the country of the dead. For Krishna — who is Vishnu come to earth — has long meant to take back into himself the strength that burns in this Shishupala. And look how the minds of the king of Chedis and of all who follow him have turned crooked: the one who means to gather them to himself first clouds their judgment. Krishna is the maker and the end of every living creature."

He fell silent, and the silence was heavier than the shouting had been. Kings glanced at one another, no longer certain whether the rage they felt was their own or something placed inside them.

But the king of Chedis had heard every word, and it had not cooled him. He turned on the grandsire, and when he spoke, his words were stern and rough — the words of a man who means to answer a prophecy with war.
stories.reflection: Bhishma's calm before a hall of furious kings is not a dismissal of their numbers; it is a reading of their anger as a prelude. The more the monarchs rage, the closer he knows the end to be — the fury of the hall is not the danger but the sign.
stories.next_story_tease: Shishupala, however, had heard every word — and his answer was already forming on his lips.
