stories.title: The Pandavas Entrust the Peace Mission
stories.story:
War with their cousins was almost certain now, and in the camp at Upaplavya the five Pandava brothers had gathered around Krishna, their cousin and friend, to make one last appeal for peace. Duryodhana, who sat in Hastinapura, the city of the Kurus, had taken their kingdom from them with loaded dice, and for days the tent had argued the only question that divided the house — whether to stretch out a hand to Hastinapura or to raise weapons against it.

Now, in the lamplight, the brothers pressed their last great plea upon Krishna: carry our cause to Hastinapura, and bring back either the kingdom or an answer that ends this waiting. One after another they spoke for the mission, Bhima and his younger brother Nakula each entrusting the family's hope to him, until Arjuna rose, and the night's argument took its final shape.

"Yudhishthira has said what needed to be said," Arjuna began. "But it seems to me, Krishna, that you do not believe peace can be won easily — whether because of Dhritarashtra's greed or because of the weakness we are in now. You think that human effort alone is fruitless, and that without a man putting forth his own strength nothing is ever achieved. That may be true, and it may not always be true. But nothing should be counted impossible."

He leaned forward, and his voice changed from argument to entreaty. "If peace is proposed in the right way, it can be made. Strive, then, to bring it about with our enemy. You are the greatest friend of both the Pandavas and the Kurus — even as the creator of all beings is the friend of gods and demons alike. Do what is good for both houses. And for you, our good is not hard to accomplish: the moment you set foot in Hastinapura, it will be done."

Then the harder edge of the night surfaced. Whatever Krishna wished — peace or war — his wish would be honoured by the Pandavas, Arjuna said; the choice was his alone. But let him remember what had brought them to this pass. Duryodhana, unable to bear the sight of Yudhishthira's good fortune and finding no honest means against it, had robbed them of their kingdom by the dishonesty of dice. "What warrior," Arjuna asked, "born to the sword and challenged to combat, would turn away from the fight even if he were sure to die? When I saw us vanquished by foul means and banished to the woods, I thought Duryodhana deserved to die at my hands."

Yet he did not press that course. If Krishna judged that the time for war had come, let it be begun soon and without more deliberation. But if the road of peace still lay open, Krishna alone could walk it — for he was kin to both houses and trusted in both courts.

"Surely you know," Arjuna said, "how Draupadi was insulted in the midst of the assembly by Duryodhana, and how we bore it with patience. That such a man will deal justly with the Pandavas, I cannot believe. Wise words will be lost on him like seed sown in barren soil. Therefore do, without delay, what you think proper and beneficial for the Pandavas — what should be done next."

He fell silent. The mission had been entrusted: the kingdom's last claim, the family's dignity, and the question of peace or war now rested in Krishna's hands, and every eye in the tent turned to him, waiting for the answer that would set the road to Hastinapura — or to battle. Outside, the night pressed against the canvas, and the camp settled into its watch. Inside, the brothers waited, and the waiting itself had become a kind of faith: whatever Krishna decided, they would follow him — to the Kuru city, or to the field of arms.
stories.reflection: Arjuna's speech carries both directions of the Pandavas' hope: he entreats Krishna to win peace and in the same breath reminds him that Duryodhana cannot be trusted, that wise counsel will fall on him like seed in barren soil. The brothers are not naive — they simply believe that whatever Krishna chooses will be right, which is why the night ends not with a decision but with an expectation.
stories.next_story_tease: It remained for Krishna to answer whether he would carry the Pandavas' plea to Hastinapura.
stories.hero_scene: By night in the camp at Upaplavya, Arjuna stands before Krishna with one hand raised, arguing for the peace mission, while Bhima and Nakula wait behind him and the tent glows with lamp-light.

stories.title: Krishna Accepts the Peace Mission
stories.story:
In the Pandava camp at Upaplavya the night of talk had come to its end. The brothers had pressed their plea — that Krishna, their cousin and friend, and a friend of the Kurus too, should carry their cause to Hastinapura and ask for peace — and when they had all finished, Arjuna spoke once more, and this time his words were few and direct.

"You are now the best friend of all the Kurus," he said. "Kin to both sides, you are the dear friend of both. It is for you to make peace between the Pandavas and the sons of Dhritarashtra — and you are able to do it. Go to Hastinapura for peace, and tell our ever-angry cousin Duryodhana plainly what must be said: if he will not listen to counsel that is wise and good for him, he will bring his own ruin upon himself."

Krishna answered without hesitation. "Yes," he said. "I will go to king Dhritarashtra, seeking what is right, what may benefit us, and what is good for the Kurus."

The decision was made that night, and with the next dawn Krishna prepared for the road. It was the month of Kartika; autumn was over, the season of dew had set in, and the fields around Upaplavya stood thick with ripened grain. He bathed and anointed himself, worshipped the sun and the sacred fire, touched the tail of a bull, bowed to the brahmin priests who blessed his going, walked round the fire, and cast his eyes on the auspicious things set out before him — the careful rites of a man beginning a great journey.

Then he remembered Yudhishthira's request and called to his kinsman Satyaki, who sat near him. "Have my chariot made ready," he said, "and let my conch and discus, my mace, my quivers and darts, and every weapon of attack and defence be placed on it. Duryodhana is wicked at heart, and so are Karna, the great bowman at his side, and Shakuni, who threw the dice against Yudhishthira — and even a contemptible enemy should never be underrated by a strong man."

His attendants understood and set to work, and the chariot they readied blazed like the fire that ends a world, and could move as fast as thought. Its two wheels gleamed like the sun and the moon; its sides were painted with moons, both crescent and full, and with fish, beasts and birds; garlands of flowers hung from it, and pearls and gems were set on every side. A tall flagstaff rose from it hung with bright pennons, tiger-skins lay across its frame, and the very sight of it raised the hearts of the Yadavas, Krishna's own people. To it they harnessed the four great horses — Saivya, Sugriva, Meghapushpa and Valahaka — bathed and decked in beautiful gear. And then, as if the sky had noticed, Garuda, king of the birds, came down and perched on the flagstaff, and it rattled under his weight.

Krishna mounted the chariot, which stood high as a mountain and sounded deep as a kettledrum, and took Satyaki up beside him, and the wheels began to turn, filling the earth and the sky with their rattle. The sky was cloudless, the wind blew fair, and the dust settled out of the air. Birds of good omen crossed the road from the right — cranes, peacocks and swans crying as they flew; the altar fire, fed with offerings, blazed up toward the right; and the great seers Vasishtha and Vamadeva stood on Krishna's right to honour his going.

Yudhishthira followed his cousin's chariot, and with him came Bhima, Arjuna and the twins Nakula and Sahadeva; behind them walked the allies — Chekitana, Dhrishtaketu the ruler of the Chedis, Drupada, and the king of Kasi. They accompanied the chariot a little way, and then let it go, and stood watching the last chance for peace roll northward toward the city of the Kurus, its wheels thundering under the bright autumn sky.
stories.reflection: Krishna accepts the mission in three clauses — what is righteous, what is beneficial, and what is good for the Kurus — as if the three could be one. And then he arms his chariot for a peace mission, because he knows whom he is going to meet: the same Krishna who promises reconciliation also tells Satyaki that no foe, however contemptible, should ever be disregarded.
stories.next_story_tease: The road to Hastinapura lay open before him, and in the Kuru city the brothers waited to receive their guest.

stories.title: The Chariot Krishna Rode to Hastinapura
stories.story:
It was the month of Kartika, under the star Revati; autumn had gone and the season of dew had come, and the earth around Upaplavya lay covered with abundant crops. The night had passed, a bright sun rose in the east, and on such a morning everyone in the camp understood what the day would bring, for Krishna had promised to ride out on the road to Hastinapura, the city of the Kurus, and ask for peace. For months the Pandavas had lived on borrowed hope, and all of that hope now rested on a single journey. Arjuna had begged him to go; Yudhishthira had weighed every word; and Krishna had given his word to the Kurus that he would come.

Before the sun was high he finished his morning rites: bathed and anointed, he worshipped both the Sun and Fire, touched the tail of a bull, bowed to the brahmins who blessed his going, walked round the sacred fire, and cast his eyes on the auspicious articles set before him. Then he remembered Yudhishthira's request and called to Satyaki, his kinsman, who sat near him.

"Let my chariot be made ready," he said, "and let my conch and discus, along with my mace, my quivers and darts, and every weapon of offence and defence be placed upon it. For Duryodhana is wicked at heart, and so are Karna, the great bowman at his side, and Shakuni, who rolled the dice against Yudhishthira — and even a contemptible enemy should never be disregarded by a powerful man."

His attendants understood Krishna's wishes and went to work at once. The chariot they yoked was a marvel: its two wheels shone like the sun and the moon, its sides were painted with moons both crescent and full, and with fishes, beasts and birds, and it was hung with garlands of many flowers and studded with pearls and gems. Gold covered it, and a fine flagstaff carried bright pennons; tiger-skins lay across it; and the very sight of it raised the hearts of the Yadavas, Krishna's own people. To it they brought the four great horses — Saivya, Sugriva, Meghapushpa and Valahaka — bathed and harnessed in beautiful gear.

Then, as if the sky itself had answered, Garuda, king of the birds, came down and perched on the flagstaff, and it rattled under his weight. Krishna mounted the great chariot, which stood high as a mountain and moved as if at the rider's will, and its wheels turned with a sound deep as a kettledrum and loud as thunder. He took Satyaki up beside him, and the chariot set out, filling the earth and the sky with the rattle of its wheels.

The sky above him was cloudless, and auspicious winds blew round him, and the air, freed of dust, grew pure. Birds and beasts of good omen wheeled past on his right hand and followed him, and cranes and peacocks and swans cried out in good omen. The fire of the altar, fed with offerings and prayers, blazed up cheerfully toward the right, free of smoke. And on his right side stood the great sages Vasishtha and Vamadeva, with many another sage of earth and heaven, to honour his going.

Behind the chariot came the Pandavas — Yudhishthira, Bhima, Arjuna, and the twins Nakula and Sahadeva — and with them walked Chekitana, and Dhrishtaketu the ruler of the Chedis, and Drupada, and the king of Kasi, and the great warrior Sikhandin. It seemed the whole earth was moving with that one chariot, and the sound of its wheels rolled ahead of it like a promise, all the way to the gates of Hastinapura.
stories.reflection: Krishna rides out for peace with every weapon laid on the chariot: he will offer peace with open hands, but he will not go unarmed into a court where Duryodhana, Karna and Shakuni hold the king's ear. The preparation is not a contradiction of the mission; it is its honesty.
stories.next_story_tease: Before the chariot had gone far, Yudhishthira came walking behind it, carrying messages for the ones he loved.

stories.title: Messages for Kunti and the Elders
stories.story:
Krishna had not ridden far when he heard Yudhishthira's voice behind him and reined in. The eldest Pandava had followed the chariot some distance on foot, and now he came up beside it, carrying the weight of everything he had not managed to say at parting.

He had not followed alone, though the others were gone by now. When the chariot rolled out of Upaplavya, the whole camp had gone a little way with it — Bhima and Arjuna and the twins Nakula and Sahadeva, and after them the allied kings, Chekitana and Dhrishtaketu, Drupada and the king of Kasi, and the warrior Sikhandin. One by one they had fallen back and turned for home, until only the eldest Pandava was left on the road, still walking after the chariot.

"The lady who brought us from our infancy," Yudhishthira began, and Krishna knew at once whom he meant. Kunti, their mother, had remained in Hastinapura when her five sons went out to the world of exile and danger, and she had grieved for them every day since. Whatever was said in councils about kingdoms and armies, this was the message that had to travel first.

"Ask after her welfare," Yudhishthira said. "Salute her and embrace her, and comfort her again and again, for she is bowed down with grief for her sons."

Krishna waited, for the eldest Pandava had not finished. And indeed Yudhishthira went on, naming the elders of the Kuru house one by one, and each name carried its own weight. "Salute the Kuru king Dhritarashtra for me," he said, the blind father who had watched his own son swallow a kingdom and done nothing to stop it. "And Bhishma," the grandfather who had taught them the use of arms and was bound now to the other side by his vow. "And Drona, and Kripa," the teachers who had shaped them as warriors. "And salute Vidura," Yudhishthira said, and his voice changed, "who is full of great wisdom" — the wise uncle who had stood by the Pandavas in that cold court when no one else dared.

Krishna took the messages into his keeping, one by one, and promised that each would be delivered exactly as it had been given: the embrace for the mother, the salutations for the king, the honours for the elders, the warm regard for Vidura. Nothing had been asked for himself; Yudhishthira had sent no demand, no warning, no word of his own rights. Only the grief of his mother and the courtesy owed to the old.

Then Yudhishthira stepped back from the chariot and stood in the road, and Krishna drove on. Behind him the eldest Pandava remained where he was, watching the chariot shrink toward the horizon, and the messages he had entrusted to it went ahead of him like a small, careful map of everything the coming days might break: a mother who stood to lose her sons whichever way the war went, teachers bound by oath to the wrong side, a wise uncle who could see the catastrophe and could not prevent it. The chariot carried all of it with it, rolling on toward Hastinapura.

It carried one thing more. Krishna had his own word to keep on that road. To Arjuna, who had pleaded that he carry peace between the two houses, he had answered that he would go to king Dhritarashtra — seeking what was right, what might benefit the Pandavas, and what was good for the Kurus. The private messages and that public errand rode together now, in the same chariot, toward the same city.
stories.reflection: At the moment when war hangs in the balance, Yudhishthira's first thought is not for his claim to a throne but for his mother's grief and for the elders he still honours. The messages are a small map of the tragedy to come: a mother who loses either way, teachers bound to the side they cannot leave, a wise uncle powerless to stop what he can foresee.
stories.next_story_tease: But there was one more parting word to come, from Arjuna, and it carried the weight of everything the mission stood against.

stories.title: Arjuna's Warning and Bhima's Roar
stories.story:
Krishna was leaving Upaplavya, where the five Pandava brothers were camped, to carry their offer of peace to their cousins in Hastinapura. The chariot had not yet cleared the camp when Arjuna walked beside it and spoke again, in a voice that carried over the rattle of the wheels.

Krishna turned to listen. Everything Arjuna had said before had been a plea: the words of a friend who wanted no war between the two branches of one family, who had begged Krishna to go and bring peace between the Pandavas and the sons of Dhritarashtra. He had asked Krishna to carry one more word to their cousin Duryodhana, whose anger never cooled — that if he refused good counsel, he would be the maker of his own ruin. But this was a different kind of word. This was what a man says when he has finished asking.

"If Dhritarashtra's son," Arjuna said, "who always chooses the crooked path, acts otherwise, then I shall surely annihilate the whole race of the Kshatriyas, the warrior class itself."

There was no heat in the words, and that made them heavier. He did not rehearse the wrongs of thirteen years or count Duryodhana's crimes. He said only that if the man who always chose the crooked path chose it once more, the warrior race itself would be ended — by his hand, in a war that would leave no one to boast of victory. The warning was exact, and it was total: peace was on offer, and refusal had been priced.

Krishna had already agreed to the errand. He would go to Dhritarashtra, the king of the Kurus, seeking what was right, what would serve the Pandavas, and what was for the good of the Kurus as well. The warning did not change his purpose; it only made plain what the errand was riding against.

Then Bhima heard it, and Bhima, the mightiest of the five brothers, answered in his own way. He set his feet on the earth, drew a breath that seemed to take in half the morning, and let out a terrible shout. It went out across the camp and the fields and the road — a sound with no words in it and no need of them, the whole of Arjuna's promise given a body and a voice.

The bowmen who heard it trembled where they stood, their hands unsteady on their bows. The steeds and the elephants, it was said, lost all command of themselves and stood shaking as the sound rolled over them. Men who stood near felt the very ground tremble, and the birds of omen that had followed the chariot scattered. It was the sound of a war that had not yet begun — the war itself announcing its presence at the edge of the camp, so that every man who heard it knew, without being told, what a refusal would sound like. The shout seemed to hang in the air long after the sound of it had died.

Krishna drove on, carrying the plea for peace and, beside it, the shape of what refusal would cost. Behind him the brothers stood on the road and watched the chariot go, and between them and it the morning still trembled with the echo of Bhima's shout. In Hastinapura, when Duryodhana made his choice, he would be choosing within the hearing of that roar.
stories.reflection: The warning and the plea travel in the same chariot. Arjuna's words are not the opposite of the peace mission but its shadow: Duryodhana must hear what refusal will cost before his choice can mean anything. Peace is being offered not as a favour he may take for granted, but as a choice he is still free to refuse — and the refusal has been priced.
stories.next_story_tease: Farther along the road, a company of sages waited to greet the envoy of peace.

stories.title: When Krishna Met Parashurama
stories.story:
Krishna had not travelled far from Upaplavya, the camp of the Pandava brothers, when he saw ahead on the road a company of sages. Even from a distance they seemed to carry a light of their own — the radiance of men who had burned away the world's desires in long austerity. He reined in the chariot, and before the horses had fully stopped he had alighted and gone to bow before them. He travelled as the envoy of kings, but before sages every envoy bows first.

Among the sages stood Narada, the tireless traveller of the three worlds, and his presence carried its own meaning: whatever happened on this road would be known everywhere. The others, too, had that stillness about them, and Krishna honoured the whole company as it was due — and waited for their word.

Then one of the sages came forward, and the air seemed to change around him. It was Parashurama, son of the sage Jamadagni — the warrior-sage of an older age, feared by every warrior in the world, feared since before the fathers of the men now gathering were born. He came to Krishna and embraced him, and the embrace was not a formality between two great men; it was the greeting of an elder who had come a long way on purpose.

"We are desirous," Parashurama said, "of beholding all the Kshatriyas of the earth assembled from every side." The great gathering at Hastinapura would draw every king and every warrior of the world to one place, and the sages had not wanted to miss it. But they had not come only to watch. "And we are anxious," the sage went on, "to hear the words of peace that will be spoken by you unto the Kurus, in the presence of all."

There was something in the words that made the moment larger than a roadside courtesy. These were men who had renounced the world, yet they had journeyed to hear a speech about peace. They would take no side in the quarrel; they had come to stand as listeners where the fate of the earth was about to be spoken aloud. And it was Parashurama, the terror of warriors since an age gone by, who said that what mattered was the word Krishna would speak.

Krishna received the blessing and the embrace, remounted the chariot, and gathered the reins. As the chariot rolled on toward Hastinapura, the sages stayed where they were, a company of witnesses in the dust of the road — a kind of promise that whatever words were spoken at the gathering of the Kurus would not be spoken unheard. Their light faded behind the chariot. Ahead lay the city, and the assembly, and the words that everyone had come to hear.
stories.reflection: The sages come as witnesses, not as advisors: they want to see the warriors of the earth gathered and to hear the words of peace spoken before them. That the ancient Parashurama, Jamadagni's son, should journey to listen rather than to act is its own quiet argument that in the coming days, the words spoken at Hastinapura may matter more than any sword.
stories.next_story_tease: With the sages' blessings behind him, Krishna turned his face toward the city of the Kurus.

stories.title: Krishna's Auspicious Journey to Hastinapura
stories.story:
From Upaplavya, the Pandavas' camp, Krishna set out on the errand Yudhishthira had asked of him. Ten car-warriors rode behind his chariot, fully armed and ready to meet hostile heroes; a thousand foot-soldiers and a thousand horsemen followed, with attendants by the hundred carrying provisions in abundance. Ahead lay Hastinapura, the capital of the Kurus. And for those who watched him go, the sky itself began to speak.

Though no cloud stood in it, thunder rolled and lightning flashed. Fleecy clouds in the clear sky rained down behind him. The seven great rivers — the Sindhu among them — that flow eastward turned and ran the other way. The directions themselves seemed reversed, and nothing could be told apart. Fires blazed up from the earth, and the earth trembled again and again. Wells and water jars by the hundred swelled up and ran over. Darkness covered the whole universe, and dust filled the air until neither one point of the horizon nor another could be distinguished. Loud roars rolled through the sky, and no being was visible from whom they came. And a south-westerly wind, harsh with thunder, tore up trees by the thousands and crushed the city of Hastinapura.

But the road that Krishna travelled turned gentle. Delicious breezes blew, and everything around him became auspicious. Showers of lotuses and fragrant flowers fell where he passed. The way itself grew delightful, free of prickly grass and thorns. Wherever he stayed, brahmin priests by the thousand glorified him and worshipped him with dishes of curds, ghee, and honey, and with gifts of wealth, and the women, coming out onto the road, strewed wild flowers of great fragrance in his path. The same departure was ruin for the Kuru capital and blessing for every place his chariot touched.

He passed through villages abounding in bees, pleasing to the eye and restful to the heart, and through cities and kingdoms of every kind, until he came to a delightful spot called Salibhavana, filled with every sort of crop. The citizens of Upaplavya — always cheerful, well protected, free from any fear of invaders — came out of their town and stood together on the way, eager to see Krishna; and when he arrived, they worshipped him with all the honours due to a guest.

At last, when Krishna came to Vrikasthala, the sun reddened the sky with long, straggling rays of light. Alighting from his chariot, he performed the traveller's washing and set himself to his evening prayers. Daruka, his charioteer, freed the horses and tended them as a master charioteer should, loosening the yokes and traces and letting them rest. Then Krishna said, "Here we must pass the night — for the sake of Yudhishthira's mission."

Reading his intention, the attendants soon raised a shelter and prepared, in a short time, excellent food and drink. The brahmins of the village — noble and high-born, modest, devoted to the learning of the Vedas — came to honour him with blessings and auspicious words, and pressed their own houses, rich as they were, upon him. "Enough," Krishna told them, and he paid each one the respect due to his rank, walked with them to their homes, and returned in their company to his own tent. He fed the brahmins with sweetmeats and took his meal with them, and passed the night there content — at the very threshold of the city whose sky had darkened at his coming.
stories.reflection: The omens at Krishna's departure split the world in two: ruin gathers over Hastinapura while his own path turns auspicious, as though the sky itself chose sides. The same journey is disaster for one city and blessing for every village along the way — his presence, not the weather, decides what happens where.
stories.next_story_tease: In Hastinapura, Duryodhana was already raising a reception fit for a king — pavilions, gems, and garlands meant to dazzle the arriving guest.

stories.title: Duryodhana's Lavish Pavilions That Krishna Ignores
stories.story:
News of Krishna's coming reached the Kuru palace before Krishna did. Krishna was on his way to Hastinapura to plead for peace between the Pandavas and their cousins, and Dhritarashtra, the blind king, learned from his spies that the envoy had set out — and his hair stood on end. He called for Bhishma, the grandsire of his house; for Drona, who had taught the princes of both families the art of war; for Sanjaya, his trusted counsellor; and for the wise Vidura. And he spoke to them, with Duryodhana, his son, and the royal advisers listening.

"What strange and wonderful news we hear," the king said. "Men, women, and children speak of nothing else, in the houses where people gather and in the open squares. All say that Krishna of great prowess is coming here for the sake of the Pandavas. He deserves honour and worship at our hands. A guest so honoured grants happiness; a guest slighted brings misery — and if Krishna is pleased with our offerings, all our wishes may be granted through his grace before the assembled kings. So make every arrangement for his reception without delay. Let pavilions be set up along the road, furnished with every comfort, so that he may be pleased with us. Bhishma, what do you think in this matter?"

Bhishma and the others applauded the king's words. "Excellent," they said.

So Duryodhana chose delightful spots at proper intervals along the route, and there rose pavilion after pavilion, glittering with gems of every kind. The king sent fine seats, attendants, perfumes and ornaments, rich robes, the best of food, drinks of many kinds, and fragrant garlands — and at Vrikasthala, where Krishna would pass the night, he raised one pavilion more beautiful than all the rest. When everything stood ready, Duryodhana informed his father that all was prepared.

The road from Vrikasthala to the capital had become a pageant. Pavilions rose at every interval like small palaces of jewels, and the air along the way carried the weight of garlands, scents, and vessels of drink laid out for a king's welcome. Travellers and townsfolk alike slowed to look at what Duryodhana had built, and the talk was all of the wealth being spent to receive one man.

Then Krishna arrived at the capital of the Kurus.

And he passed all of it by — the gem-studded pavilions, the seats, the garlands, the costly feast raised in his honour — without casting a single glance at it. Not one of the gems of diverse kinds drew his eyes. Duryodhana had built as though the visitor could be dazzled into alliance, as though magnificence itself were the language in which the Kurus and the Pandavas could still be reconciled. But Krishna needed nothing, and his chariot rolled past the last pavilion and on toward the city — leaving a court that had measured him in gold to wonder, at his silent passing, what measure would have been right.
stories.reflection: The reception is measured entirely in riches, and Krishna's answer is perfect indifference: the gifts say everything about the giver and nothing about the guest. A man who needs nothing cannot be won by display — only by the truthfulness of the one who receives him.
stories.next_story_tease: When Dhritarashtra began planning gifts meant to bind Krishna, Vidura would name the deception openly.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna's chariot passes gem-studded pavilions hung with garlands along the road to Hastinapura, his eyes fixed straight ahead, while the assembled display of seats, vessels, and ornaments stands ignored and unused.

stories.title: Vidura Exposes the Plan to Bribe Krishna
stories.story:
Dhritarashtra had begun to list the treasures he would heap upon Krishna — gold, jewels, gifts beyond measure, everything a king could give a guest. The blind king planned to win over the visitor the whole court called the lord of the three worlds, and most of the assembly took this for wisdom. Vidura heard it and could hold his peace no longer.

Vidura was the blind king's brother, and the one man in that hall who told him the truth. "Great king," he said, "the three worlds respect you, and everyone who knows you holds you dear. Your years are many, and your mind is calm, so that what you say can never be against the scriptures or against right reason. Your subjects are certain that virtue lives in you as surely as letters live cut in stone, as light lives in the sun, as waves live in the ocean. Every person you honour is made happy by it. So hold fast to those virtues, with your friends and kinsmen beside you. Choose sincerity. Do not, out of folly, bring destruction on your sons, your grandsons, your friends, your kinsmen — on all that you hold dear."

Then he came to the point. "It is much that you wish to give Krishna as your guest. Know that he deserves all this and far more — the whole earth itself. But I swear by my own soul that you do not wish to give it either from virtue or for the sake of pleasing him. All this betrays only deception, falsehood, and insincerity."

The words fell on the hall like a stone into still water. Vidura went on, unsparing. "By your outward acts, O king, I know your secret purpose. The five Pandavas ask only for five villages. You will not give them even that — and so you are not truly willing for peace. You hope to win the hero of Vrishni's race to your side with wealth, and in this way to separate Krishna from the Pandavas. But neither wealth, nor attention, nor worship can do that. I know Krishna's greatness, and I know the firmness of Arjuna's devotion. Arjuna is Krishna's very life, and Krishna will never give him up."

And then he told the king what Krishna would actually accept. "Only a vessel of water, only the washing of his feet, only the usual enquiries after the welfare of those he will meet — nothing more. Give him the one thing he comes seeking: peace between you and Duryodhana on one side and the Pandavas on the other. Follow his counsel, O king. You are their father; the Pandavas are your sons, young in years beside you. Behave as a father to them, and they will honour you as sons."

In a single speech Vidura had named the plan and the heart beneath it: the gifts were not generosity but a bid to prise Krishna loose from the Pandavas; the peace Krishna had crossed half the country to offer was real; and the guest himself could not be bought at any price. The question that hung in the air of the Kuru hall was whether anyone there was willing to hear it.
stories.reflection: Vidura's service is to name what everyone else politely ignored: the king's gifts are not generosity but an attempt to separate Krishna from the Pandavas. His certainty rests on character, not suspicion — he knows Krishna's magnanimity and Arjuna's devotion, so he knows no price exists that could come between them.
stories.next_story_tease: But Duryodhana had already formed a resolution of his own — to imprison the ambassador who was coming to make peace.
stories.hero_scene: Vidura stands before the seated Dhritarashtra in the Kuru hall, one hand raised as he names the king's secret purpose, while the counsellors fall silent around them.

stories.title: Duryodhana Resolves to Imprison Krishna
stories.subtitle: Bhishma Departs in Anger
stories.story:
The debate over Krishna's welcome had barely settled when Duryodhana rose, and to the surprise of the hall he agreed with Vidura on one point alone: that Krishna could never be separated from the Pandavas.

"All that Vidura has said about Krishna is truly said," Duryodhana declared. "Krishna is devoted to the Pandavas and can never be torn from them. So let no wealth be bestowed on him. He is not unworthy of our worship, of course — but this is neither the time nor the place for it. If we honour him now, he will only think we worship him out of fear, and no warrior who respects himself brings such disgrace upon his own head. Krishna deserves the reverence of the three worlds. But war has been decided, and war should never be put off by hospitality. Give him nothing."

Then Bhishma, the grandsire of the Kuru house, answered in his deep old voice. "Worshipped or not worshipped, Krishna never becomes angry," he said. "But no one may treat him with disrespect, for he is not a man to be slighted. Whatever he sets his mind to, no one can frustrate, by any means, with all his power. Do without hesitation what Krishna of the mighty arms advises, and bring about peace with the Pandavas through him. He has a virtuous soul, and he will speak only what is right and profitable. So answer him, with all your friends, only with what is agreeable to him."

Duryodhana's answer came like a blow. "Grandsire, I cannot by any means live sharing this swelling prosperity of mine with the Pandavas. Listen — this is the great resolution I have formed. I will imprison Krishna, who is the refuge of the Pandavas. He comes here tomorrow morning, and once he is confined, the Vrishnis, Krishna's own clan, and the Pandavas — aye, the whole earth — will submit to me. Tell me how it may be done, so that Krishna does not guess our purpose and no danger overtakes us."

A silence fell over the hall. Even Dhritarashtra, who had yielded to his son in so much, recoiled. At the fearful words about imprisoning Krishna, the king and all his counsellors were deeply pained. "Never say such a thing again," he said to Duryodhana. "This is not the ancient custom. Krishna comes to us as an ambassador. He is our kin, dear to us, and he has done us no wrong. How then does he deserve imprisonment?"

But the old king's protest only released the older man's wrath. Bhishma rose from his seat. "This wicked son of yours has his hour upon him, Dhritarashtra," he said. "Set before good and evil, he chooses evil, though his own well-wishers beg him otherwise — and you follow in the wake of this wicked wretch, treading the thorny path, setting at naught the words of every friend. This son of yours, with all his counsellors, will come into contact with Krishna of unstained acts and be destroyed in a moment. I will not listen to the words of this sinful wretch who has abandoned all virtue."

And having said this, the aged chief of the Bharata race, blazing with anger, rose and left the hall — the assembly staring after him, the blind king stricken, the prince unmoved. And the plan to imprison the ambassador stood in the middle of the hall, like a storm that had not yet broken.
stories.reflection: Duryodhana's resolution turns diplomacy into a siege: he will imprison the ambassador who came to make peace, confident that holding one man will bend the whole earth. Bhishma's rage is the measure of the folly — he walks out rather than listen, naming the ruin he already sees coming.
stories.next_story_tease: At dawn, Krishna would enter Hastinapura and walk into the middle of that broken council to meet Dhritarashtra.

stories.title: A City Rises to Receive Krishna
stories.story:
Word of Krishna's coming had travelled ahead of him, and Hastinapura made ready as though for its greatest festival. The main streets were hung with jewels and gems, and no man, woman or child stayed indoors, so eager was everyone to see the visitor who had ridden so far on an errand of peace.

His errand touched every family in the city. Krishna had come to plead with the sons of the blind king Dhritarashtra, who held the Kuru kingdom, for his cousins, the five Pandava brothers, who had been cheated out of that kingdom and driven into the forest.

The welcome began before he reached the gates. All of Dhritarashtra's sons except Duryodhana had ridden out to meet him in their finest robes, and with them came Bhishma, the revered elder of the Kuru house, Drona and Kripa, the teachers of the princes, and the other elders of the court. Behind them the people followed by the thousand, some in chariots and fine carriages, most on foot.

Krishna had risen before dawn, said his morning prayers, and taken leave of his cousins at their camp; and all along the road the townspeople had come out to see him pass. At Vrikasthala they pressed about his chariot so thickly that only when he was gone did they turn back to their homes. Soon after, Bhishma and Drona and the sons of Dhritarashtra met him on the open road, and he entered the city in the midst of them all.

The citizens lined the streets and bent their heads to the ground, singing his praise as he passed. Ladies leaned from the windows of the great houses, crowding so thickly that the tall mansions seemed ready to bend beneath their weight. And though Krishna's horses were among the swiftest in the world, they could barely move through that dense river of people.

At last he came to the palace of the blind king and passed through three outer halls into the chamber where Dhritarashtra sat. The king, who could not see his guest, rose to his feet as Krishna entered, and with him rose Bhishma, Drona, Kripa, Somadatta and king Vahlika, for all of them stood to honour him. Krishna bowed first to the king and to Bhishma, greeted the other elders in the order of their years, and spoke warmly to Drona and his son, to Vahlika, Kripa and Somadatta.

In the centre of the chamber stood a wide golden seat set with jewels. At the king's request Krishna took it, and the priests brought the offerings of a royal welcome — a cow, honey, curds and water — and performed the rites with care. Krishna stayed a while among the Kurus, laughing and jesting with each as age and closeness allowed, while the blind king who had risen for him sat honoured and glad. When he had taken his leave, Krishna greeted the assembled court and went on to the house of Vidura — the king's younger brother, and the truest friend the exiled Pandavas had in Hastinapura.

Vidura received him with every good thing his house could offer. What use, he asked, in trying to put into words the joy he felt at this coming? Then he asked the question that had been on his heart all day: how did the Pandavas fare? And Krishna, who knew how dearly Vidura loved his nephews, told him everything — how they lived in the forest, how they bore their exile, what they hoped.

So the day that had begun with a city pouring into the streets to honour one man ended quietly, in Vidura's house, with Krishna speaking freely of his cousins. The plea for peace that had brought him to Hastinapura was still waiting to be spoken aloud.
stories.reflection: The whole city rises to honour Krishna, and he returns the honour in exact order of age and standing, paying the court its due before a single word of his mission is spoken. His first night in Hastinapura is spent not among kings but with Vidura, the one man in the palace who loves the Pandavas; even his welcome is a quiet alignment.
stories.next_story_tease: The same afternoon, Krishna went to the house of his aunt Kunti, who had not seen her sons in a long time.

stories.title: Kunti Pours Out Her Grief
stories.story:
That afternoon Krishna went to the house of his aunt Kunti — the mother of the five Pandava brothers, who were living in the forest while their cousins held the kingdom. Krishna had come straight from her sons, and she had been waiting for him since word of his arrival reached her.

When he stood at her door, she could not hold back. She threw her arms around his neck and wept, remembering her sons, and the tears she had held back for months came freely at the sight of him. Only after Krishna had received the rites of hospitality and taken his seat did she speak, her face drawn, her voice choked with tears.

Her sons, she said, had been gentle children. From their earliest years they had waited with reverence on their elders, held together in friendship, mastered both their anger and their joy, and spoken only the truth. Robbed of their kingdom by trickery, they had gone quietly into the forest, though they deserved to live among friends and servants. "They left their old mother behind," she wept, "and went into the woods. How do they live now, in that deep forest full of lions and tigers and elephants?"

They had lost their father as small children, and she had raised them alone. At home they slept in high rooms on soft blankets and deerskin, and woke each morning to the grunt of elephants and the neighing of horses, the clatter of chariot wheels, the music of conches and cymbals, the singing of women and the praise-songs of the bards, with the blessings of priests at dawn. How could sons who woke to such music sleep now in a wilderness that rang with the howls of beasts? The thought was more than she could bear.

Then, one by one, she asked after them, as though the telling might bring them nearer. How was Yudhishthira, her eldest — gentle, golden-skinned, the most learned of the Kurus, bearing without complaint the weight of a kingdom he could not use? How was Bhima, strong as ten thousand elephants and swift as the wind, who had slain the demons Hidimva and Vaka, who fed on men, and the warrior Kichaka besides — terrible in anger, yet quick to obey his elder brother? How was Arjuna, who could loose five hundred arrows in a single stretch, the finest bowman of his age, whose skill men compared to the fabled king Kartavirya's?

Krishna answered her gently. "What woman in the world is like you?" he asked. "You have borne both happiness and sorrow with a patience few can match; bear this waiting too. Your sons are well, and they send you their love through me. The time is coming — sooner than you think — when you will see them again as lords of the whole world, their foe slain and their fortunes restored."

The words were spoken softly, but Kunti knew the man who spoke them. She let her tears fall at last, a little lighter for being spent, for her sons were alive and well, and someone who loved them had come to speak for them.
stories.reflection: Kunti's lament is unbearable precisely because it is concrete: she remembers the music her sons woke to and the beds they slept in, and measures their suffering against it. Krishna does not scold her out of her grief; he answers it with a certainty, that her sons will return as lords of the world, consolation grounded in what will come to pass rather than in hope.
stories.next_story_tease: That same day Krishna came to Duryodhana's palace, where a feast had been prepared for him.
stories.hero_scene: In a dim chamber in Hastinapura, Kunti stands with her arms around Krishna's neck, weeping, her face buried against his shoulder as her tears fall, while Krishna stands still and gentle, receiving her grief.

stories.title: Krishna Refuses Duryodhana's Feast
stories.story:
From his aunt Kunti's house, Krishna went to the palace of Duryodhana — the eldest of the blind king's hundred sons, and the prince who now held the kingdom his cousins had lost. Everyone in Hastinapura knew why Krishna had come, and Duryodhana meant to receive him as an honoured guest before a single word of peace could be spoken.

The palace was furnished with great wealth, its halls set with beautiful seats, fit, men said, for the king of the gods himself. Krishna crossed three wide courtyards, unhindered by the waiting servants, and entered the great hall — high as a hill, bright as a summer cloud. There, in the midst of a thousand kings and surrounded by the whole Kuru court, sat Duryodhana on his throne, his brother Dussasana at his side, and with them Karna, the great archer who had sworn his friendship to Duryodhana, and Sakuni, the uncle who had cheated the Pandavas out of their kingdom at dice.

At Krishna's entry, Duryodhana rose, and his counsellors rose with him. Krishna greeted the sons of Dhritarashtra, the counsellors, and every king present, each according to his age, and took the golden throne that had been set for him, its seat covered with a carpet embroidered in gold. The king offered him a cow, honey, curds and water, and placed at his service palaces, mansions and the whole kingdom. The Kauravas and the assembled kings honoured him as he sat there.

Then, the worship over, Duryodhana invited Krishna to eat at his house. Krishna did not accept.

The king pressed him, his voice gentle with something else moving behind it, his eyes on Karna as he spoke. Why would Krishna not accept the feast prepared for him — the fine foods and drinks, the robes and beds kept ready? He had promised his help to both sides and wished both parties well; he was of Dhritarashtra's own kin, and the old king loved him. "Tell me the true reason for this refusal," Duryodhana said.

Krishna raised his right arm and answered in a voice deep as thunder, calm and clear: "An envoy, O king, eats and accepts gifts only when his mission has succeeded. When my work here is done, you may feast me and my companions."

Duryodhana answered that such words ill became Krishna. Whether the mission succeeded or failed, the feast was offered out of kinship, and there was no quarrel between them, no war.

But Krishna had not finished. "Not from pride, not from anger, not from malice, nor for any gain would I turn aside from what is right," he said. "A man eats another's food when he is in need — or when love moves him to it. I am in no need, and you have shown me no love. From the day they were born, you have hated your own cousins, the gentle Pandavas, who never did you harm and who hold fast to virtue. Who can injure such men? He who hates them hates me, and he who loves them loves me. Know this: the Pandavas and I have but one soul between us. The food of a house that hates my very self could not pass my lips. I will eat at the house of Vidura, where the food is offered in love."

In a hall prepared for a thousand kings, Krishna had chosen the simple table of Vidura's house — the one table in Hastinapura where he could eat without denying his own words. The refusal was not discourtesy. The friend of the Pandavas would not sit down to the feast of the man who had spent his life hating them.
stories.reflection: Krishna's refusal of Duryodhana's food is not a diplomatic slight but a statement of identity: he and the Pandavas, he says, have but a common soul, and one does not eat at the table of a man who hates one's own self. It is also a quiet correction of Duryodhana's arithmetic, which counts feasts and favours where Krishna counts only love and virtue.
stories.next_story_tease: That night, at the table Krishna had chosen, Vidura would tell him the truth about the court he had come to save.
stories.hero_scene: In Duryodhana's jewel-bright court before a thousand kings, Krishna raises his mighty right arm and refuses the feast, while Duryodhana watches with Karna and Sakuni at his side and the assembled kings look on.

stories.title: Vidura's Warning in the Night
stories.story:
At nightfall Krishna ate at the house of Vidura, as he had promised in Duryodhana's hall. Vidura was the blind king's younger brother, and the one man in that palace whom the exiled Pandavas could call a true friend. When the meal was over and the house had grown quiet, the meaning of Krishna's choice came clear, and the man who had welcomed him with joy now spoke with dread. Krishna had come to Hastinapura to plead for his cousins, and Vidura meant to tell him, before he went to the court, exactly what waited there.

"Your coming here was not well judged, Krishna," Vidura said. "Dhritarashtra's son obeys neither the laws of kingship nor the laws of goodness. He is wicked and quick to anger; he craves honour while he insults others; he turns from the counsel of the aged. He thinks himself wise, but he is a fool — a slave to his desires, ungrateful, suspicious of his truest friends, in love with what he knows to be wrong. Were you yourself to point out his true good, he would cast it aside out of pride and rage. He believes that Bhishma, Drona and Kripa, that Karna, Drona's son and king Jayadratha can win him anything he wants — and so he has never once set his heart on peace."

Krishna listened, and Vidura went on. Duryodhana and his brothers, with Karna at their head, truly believed that the Pandavas could not even look upon Bhishma and Drona, let alone fight them. The short-sighted prince, with his great army assembled, already counted his purpose achieved; he had decided that Karna alone could defeat his enemies. So he would never make peace. Krishna might desire peace and brotherhood between the two houses, but Dhritarashtra's sons had resolved to give the Pandavas nothing that was theirs. "Among men so resolved," Vidura said, "your words will be wasted — like a song sung to the deaf."

Nor did Vidura think Krishna should enter that assembly at all. The Kauravas had gathered a mighty force and feared no one; they truly believed that Indra at the head of all the gods could not overcome them. Duryodhana sat in the midst of his elephants, his chariots and his heroes and counted the whole earth already his; what he held, he would never give back. "Alas," Vidura said, "for Duryodhana's sake the destruction of the earth is at hand." All the kings of the earth had chosen their side and were eager to fight the Pandavas; many were old enemies of Krishna, and all, fearing him, had bound themselves to Karna and the sons of Dhritarashtra. They had their suspicions of Krishna himself. "It does not seem right to me," Vidura said, "that you should walk into the midst of them."

The night was still. Krishna had heard every word — the long tale of Duryodhana's faults, the certainty of war, the plea that he turn back. He did not argue with any of it. Vidura knew this court as no one else did, and Krishna had not come to Hastinapura to be persuaded out of listening.
stories.reflection: Vidura's warning is a portrait of a man already overtaken by fate: every vice he names is a reason Duryodhana cannot be persuaded, and every reason is also a prophecy of war. Krishna listens without argument, because the value of the warning is not that it changes his purpose, but that it is true.
stories.next_story_tease: But Krishna would answer Vidura's warning with a resolve of his own.
stories.hero_scene: Late at night in Vidura's quiet house, the lamp burning low, Vidura leans forward with a grave face as he warns Krishna, who sits in calm stillness listening to every word.

stories.title: The Merit of Striving for Peace
stories.story:
The city of Hastinapura slept, and the lamps in Vidura's house burned low. Krishna and Vidura — the blind king's brother, the wisest man in the Kuru court — still sat talking. Krishna had come to plead for peace between Dhritarashtra's sons and his cousins the Pandavas, and Vidura had just told him plainly what waited: Duryodhana's wickedness, and the enmity of every warrior king who had chosen his side.

Krishna listened to it all without surprise. Then he answered, and his answer was not a defence of his plan but a statement of why he had come at all.

"Everything you have said is true, Vidura," he said. "You have spoken to me as a father and mother speak, and your words are worthy of you — consistent with virtue, with good sense, and with truth. But hear the reason for my coming. I know well the wickedness of Dhritarashtra's son, and the enmity of the kings who stand with him — and still I have come. Great is the merit of him who frees the whole earth from the meshes of death: this earth, with its elephants, its chariots and its horses, already overshadowed by a dreadful calamity."

He spoke of merit as a man speaks of something he has weighed. If a man strives with all his might to do a good deed and fails, Krishna said, the merit of the striving is still his. And if a man only plans an evil deed in his heart but never does it, the evil can never touch him. The scales of the world are not read by outcomes alone.

"I will strive sincerely, Vidura, to bring about peace between the Kurus and the Srinjayas — between Dhritarashtra's sons and the Pandavas with the allies who would fight beside them — who are about to slaughter one another. That calamity hangs over them all because of the Kurus' own conduct; it is the doing of Duryodhana and Karna, and the other kings only follow where those two lead. The wise call a man a wretch who will not lift a hand to save a friend sinking in misfortune. Striving with all his might — even seizing his friend by the hair, if he must — one should hold him back from a wrongful act. He who does so wins praise, not blame."

So Krishna had come: not because he expected the court to listen, but because when kinsmen fall out, a true friend speaks between them. If Duryodhana judged him wrongly, he would still have his own conscience. He had come so that no one could ever say that Krishna, though able to help, had made no attempt to stop the two houses from destroying one another; and having striven for peace, he would stand free of blame before all the kings.

"If the foolish Duryodhana will not accept my words, he will only be inviting his own fate," Krishna went on. "But if I can bring peace to the Kurus without sacrificing the interests of the Pandavas, my conduct will be highly meritorious, and the Kauravas themselves will be saved from the meshes of death. If Dhritarashtra's sons reflect coolly on what I shall say — words full of wisdom and consistent with righteousness — then peace will be made, and they will honour me as its author."

Then, with the calm of a man who had settled a long argument in his own heart, he added what Vidura was meant to carry back into the night. "But if they seek to injure me, know this: all the kings of the earth united are no match for me — like a herd of deer before an enraged lion."

There was nothing more to say. The lamps flickered, the city slept on, and Krishna lay down for the night. Whatever the morning brought, he would meet it having done the one thing within his power: he had come, and he would speak.

Vidura stayed wakeful long after, weighing the man who had come to plead for peace and, in the same breath, had told him he could not be harmed if the plea was refused. Between those two truths lay everything that was about to happen to the world.
stories.reflection: Krishna's answer to Vidura turns the peace mission into a matter of conscience: merit belongs to the striving itself, not to the outcome. He does not come to the Kurus expecting to be heard — he comes so that the attempt is made, and so that no one, least of all himself, can later say it was not.
stories.next_story_tease: At dawn, Krishna would ride out into the streets of Hastinapura toward the Kuru assembly.

stories.title: Krishna Enters the Kuru Assembly
stories.story:
Before the sun was fully up, the sound of conches and cymbals drifted into Vidura's house, where Krishna had spent the night in talk. A band of singers and bards with sweet voices had gathered at the door to wake him with music; and Hastinapura, which had slept through the darkest hours, stirred with the first news that the messenger of peace was awake.

Krishna rose and performed the rites of morning — the cleansing bath, his prayers, offerings of melted butter poured on the sacred fire. He dressed and began his worship of the rising sun; and while he was still at his devotions, Duryodhana and Sakuni, the uncle who had cheated the Pandavas at dice, came to him.

"The king is seated in his court," they said, "with all the Kurus led by Bhishma, and with all the kings of the earth. They are all asking for you, as the gods in heaven ask for their king Indra."

Krishna greeted them both courteously; and when the sun had climbed a little higher, he summoned a number of learned priests and made them presents of gold, robes, cows and horses. Then his charioteer Daruka came and saluted him, and soon returned with his master's chariot — a great shining car hung with rows of tinkling bells, drawn by swift horses, its wheels rumbling like distant thunder.

Krishna walked around the sacred fire and the band of priests, put on the jewel called Kaustubha, and mounted the chariot, surrounded by the Kurus and guarded by his own Vrishni kinsmen. Vidura followed in his own chariot; Duryodhana and Sakuni shared one; and Satyaki and Kritavarman, the boldest warriors of Krishna's clan, rode behind with the rest, on chariots, on horses and on elephants.

They came out onto a broad street that had been swept and watered for the occasion. Cymbals clashed, conches were blown, and every other instrument poured out its music. Young warriors, the pride of Krishna's line, surrounded the chariot; thousands of soldiers in bright dress, bearing swords, lances and axes, marched before it; five hundred elephants followed, and chariots beyond counting. All the citizens of Hastinapura, young and old, men and women, had come into the streets to see him; terraces and balconies were crowded with ladies, and every window held a face. Honoured by the Kurus, answering the greetings of all as each deserved, Krishna moved slowly down the street, his eyes on everyone.

At last he reached the Kuru court, and his attendants blew their conches and trumpets until the sky rang with the sound. The whole assembly of kings trembled with delight at the thought of seeing him; and when they heard the rumble of his chariot, like the roll of rain-heavy clouds, the kings rose, their joy so deep that the hair of their bodies stood on end.

At the gate Krishna alighted from his chariot and entered the great hall — bright with gold, high as a bank of summer cloud. He walked in with Vidura on one side and Satyaki on the other, and beside him even the splendour of the hall seemed to dim. The kings made way for him; the sages who had come to the assembly were given their seats; and Krishna, the guest the whole city had poured into the streets to see, took his place in the midst of the court.

There he sat, the calm centre of a hall that had dressed itself in all its glory to receive him — a glory that seemed, in that moment, borrowed from his presence rather than lent to it.
stories.reflection: The procession into the Kuru court is honor laid on like cloth of gold, and Krishna accepts all of it — the music, the crowds, the trembling delight of the kings — without once bending toward its vanity. He is the guest the whole city turned out to see, yet the calm at the center of that splendour belongs to a man who has come on other business entirely.
stories.next_story_tease: Once the assembly had settled into silence, Krishna rose to make his plea for peace.
stories.hero_scene: At the gate of the Kuru court in Hastinapura, Krishna, wearing the Kaustubha gem, alights from his blazing car and enters the cloud-like hall arm-in-arm with Vidura and Satyaki on either side, his radiance overshadowing the splendour of all the assembled Kurus.

stories.title: Krishna's Plea Before the Assembly
stories.story:
The last of the kings had taken his seat, and silence settled over the great hall of the Kurus at Hastinapura. Into that silence Krishna rose to speak. He had come as an envoy of peace from the five Pandavas — his cousins, and the nephews of the blind king Dhritarashtra — to settle the quarrel between the two branches of one family before it became a war. Every king in the hall leaned forward to hear him.

Though he spoke to Dhritarashtra, he meant the whole assembly to hear. "I have come so that peace may be established between the Kurus and the Pandavas, without the slaughter of heroes," Krishna said. "I have no other words to offer, O king. Everything worth knowing in this world, you already know."

Then he reminded the blind king what his family was supposed to be. The Kuru line, he said, had long stood first among royal houses for its learning and its conduct: joy in another's happiness, grief at another's misery, eagerness to relieve distress, harm done to none, sincerity, forgiveness, truth — these had always prevailed among the Kurus. "What a pity it would be if anyone of such a race did wrong," Krishna said, "and a greater pity still if that man were you. You should be the first to restrain the Kurus when they deal deceitfully with strangers, or with their own kin."

Then he came to the point, and the hall heard the name it had been waiting for. "Your wicked sons, led by Duryodhana, have cast off virtue and profit, set aside all morality, and, maddened by greed, are doing their worst to their own nearest kin," he said. "The danger that threatens everyone has its origin in the conduct of the Kurus. If you grow indifferent to it, it will end in a slaughter that touches all. But if you are willing, you may still allay it — peace is not hard to reach."

Peace, Krishna said, rested on two men alone: the king, and himself. "Set your sons right, O king, and I will set the Pandavas right," he said. "Whatever you command, your sons and their followers should obey. If they live in obedience to you, that is the best they can do. Let the sons of Pandu be your allies. Protected by them, Indra himself, at the head of the gods of heaven, could not vanquish you — how then could any earthly king withstand you?"

Then he drew the king a picture of a world that need not burn. He named the warriors who would face each other across a battlefield — on one side Bhishma, Drona, Kripa, Karna, Ashwatthama, Vikarna, Somadatta, Vahlika, the chief of the Sindhus, the king of the Kalingas, and Sudakshina of the Kamvojas; on the other, Yudhishthira, Bhimasena, Arjuna, the twins Nakula and Sahadeva, Satyaki, and Yuyutsu. What man of sound mind, Krishna asked, would choose to fight such a host? But make both houses your own, he said, and the sovereignty of the world would be yours, with every ruler on earth seeking your alliance. Protected by sons, grandsons, fathers, brothers, and friends, the king would live out his days in happiness.

"In battle, great king, nothing is to be seen but destruction," Krishna said. "If the Pandavas are slaughtered, or if your own mighty sons fall, tell me what happiness will be left to you. All of them are brave and skilled in arms, and all of them long for battle. Save them from the danger that threatens them. When the war is over, you will not behold all the Kurus, nor all the Pandavas. You will see the heroes of both sides thinned and weakened, warriors struck down by warriors, until the kings gathered here, hot with wrath, have destroyed one another."

When Krishna finished, the hall was stiller than it had been at his first word. He had laid before the blind king the whole arithmetic of war — every warrior counted, every alliance weighed, every happiness that might survive the slaughter set against the one that would not. The choice, plainly, was Dhritarashtra's to make.
stories.reflection: Krishna's plea is built on a single repeated question: in the ruin of both houses, what happiness would remain to the king? He offers Dhritarashtra sovereignty won by alliance instead of battle, and leaves the choice entirely in his hands — the peace mission succeeds or fails on whether the blind king can see what has been put before him.
stories.next_story_tease: Into that silence, the sage Parashurama rose to tell the assembly a story from the age of the world.

stories.title: Parashurama Reveals Nara and Narayana
stories.subtitle: The legend of Dambhodbhava
stories.story:
For a long moment no one in the great hall dared to answer Krishna's speech. The kings sat without moving, and the silence stretched out like a held breath. Then a voice rose out of it — old and calm. It was Parashurama, a warrior-sage of an age long past, and he spoke straight to Duryodhana, the prince whose answer would decide whether the peace held.

"Listen to my words," Parashurama said. "They come with an example to point them, and if my speech commends itself to you, take your own good from it."

And he told the assembly about a king of long ago named Dambhodbhava, whose rule stretched over the whole earth. Every morning, when the night had passed, the king called the priests and warriors of his court — the Brahmanas and Kshatriyas, as they were called — and put the same question to them: "Among all men, priest or warrior, merchant or labourer, is there anyone who is my equal in battle, or my better?" Then he would wander the earth, drunk on his own pride.

The wise priests, learned in the Vedas, the oldest sacred teachings, counselled him to set his pride aside, but the king went on asking the same question day after day. At last some of them, their anger roused, answered him plainly. "There are two beings who stand above all men and are always victorious in battle," they said. "You will never equal either of them, if you go looking for them."

The king asked where these heroes might be found, and into what family they were born. "They are ascetics named Nara and Narayana," the priests replied — holy men who had given up comfort to live as hermits, testing themselves with fasting and hardship. "Both were born into the line of men. Go and fight them, if you will. They are keeping the hardest of austerities even now, in a hidden corner of Mount Gandhamadana."

The king could not bear even the rumor of such rivals. He gathered his whole army, marched to the rugged and frightening slopes of Gandhamadana, and searched the forests until he found the two hermits — thin with hunger and thirst, worn by cold winds and burning sun. Dambhodbhava approached them, touched their feet in respect, and asked after their welfare. The two sages received him kindly, setting before him fruits and roots, a seat and water. and asked his business. "Whatever you wish," they said, "let it be done."

"The whole earth has been conquered by the strength of my arms," he declared. "All my enemies are dead. I have come to this mountain because I wish to fight you both. Grant me this — I have carried the wish for a long time."

"Wrath and greed have no place in this hermitage," the sages replied. "There are no weapons here, and nothing of malice or wrong. Seek your battle elsewhere — the earth is full of warriors."

But the king pressed them, and they soothed him and overlooked his rudeness. Still he repeated his summons. At last Nara picked up a handful of grass-blades. "Since you want battle so badly, come, warrior, and fight!" he said. "Take up all your arms and array your troops. I will cure you of your eagerness for it."

Dambhodbhava answered that he had come to fight, and would fight even against such a weapon. With all his troops he covered every side of the mountain with a shower of arrows. And the hermit, with nothing but those blades of grass, turned aside every shaft they loosed. Then Nara loosed his own weapon, a blade of grass that could not be countered — and what followed silenced every boast that had ever rung through Dambhodbhava's court. The king who had measured himself against the whole world found his measure at last.

Parashurama paused, letting the assembly understand his tale before he spoke. "Those who were Nara and Narayana in the ages past," he said at last, "are now Arjuna and Krishna. Know, O king, who these two are. If you believe me and do not mistrust my words, take up a virtuous resolve and make peace with the sons of Pandu."

The kings of the earth looked at the two men sitting among them — the envoy who had come to plead for peace, and Arjuna beside him — and it seemed to them that they heard the oldest names in the world laid over the newest faces.
stories.reflection: The tale of Dambhodbhava is a lesson in misplaced pride delivered through the oldest of mirrors: the king who measured himself against every man on earth never once thought to ask what the gods' own companions might be. Parashurama leaves the assembly in no doubt about who sits before them — the question now is whether Duryodhana will believe it.
stories.next_story_tease: The appeal would be carried one step further, directly to Duryodhana himself.

stories.title: Krishna's Appeal to Duryodhana
stories.story:
Of all the doors Krishna knocked on during his peace mission to Hastinapura, the hardest was Duryodhana's. Bhishma, the grandsire of both houses, had listened to him. Drona, who had taught all the princes to fight, had listened. The wise Vidura, the blind king's own brother, had never needed persuading. Even Dhritarashtra himself found everything Krishna said true, reasonable, and good for the world — except that it asked of him a resolve he did not possess.

"I am not my own master," the king confessed. "Duryodhana never does what pleases me. He pays no heed to the words of Gandhari, his mother, or of wise Vidura, or of friends like Bhishma, all of whom wish him well. Counsel that stubborn, senseless prince yourself, Krishna. If you do, you will have done the noble thing a friend should do."

So Krishna — who understood what was right, and also what was practical — went and stood before the angry prince in the crowded assembly, and spoke to him in sweet words, meant for Duryodhana's own good and for the good of all who followed him.

"You are born into a race famous for its wisdom," he began. "Act righteously, as I will show you. You have learning and good conduct; you are adorned with every fine quality. It is only the wicked-souled, the cruel, and the shameless who act in the way that seems good to you. The righteous keep their hearts steady on virtue and good sense; the unrighteous turn perverse. The path you keep to is that perverse path. To persist in it is sinful and terrible, and it leads to death itself — and all for nothing, for you cannot even hold to it for long."

He did not scold. He reasoned, the way a man reasons with a kinsman whose ruin he can already see. If Duryodhana turned back from what promised only sorrow, he would escape the sinful, disreputable deeds of his brothers, his followers, and his counsellors. "Make peace with the sons of Pandu," Krishna urged. "They are wise and brave, tireless in effort and deep in learning, and every one of them has his soul under his own control. Such a peace would please your father; it would please the grandsire Bhishma, Drona, the noble Kripa, Somadatta, wise Vahlika, Ashwatthama, Vikarna, Sanjaya, Vivinsati, and many another of your kinsmen and friends. The whole world would prosper by it."

Then the sweet words grew heavier, and the whole assembly heard what a friend was willing to say. "You are modest, of noble birth, learned, and kind of heart. Obey your father and your mother. Good sons always hold their fathers' commands to be for their good, and when calamity comes upon a man, he remembers what his father told him. Peace with the Pandavas commends itself to your father. Let it commend itself to you and your counsellors as well. The man who listens to his friends and then does not act is consumed at last by his own neglect, like a man who swallows the poisonous fruit called Kimpaka. He who keeps putting off good counsel until it is too late is left to repent. But he who hears wisdom and accepts it at once, setting aside his own opinion, wins happiness all his days."

He ended where he had begun, on kinship. "He who rejects the words of well-meaning friends is soon brought low by his enemies. Turning from the righteous, he follows the wicked, and makes his own friends weep for him. He abandons wise counsellors for foolish ones, and falls into great distress. The companion of sinners, who behaves falsely and never heeds good friends, who honors strangers but hates his own kin — he is soon cast off by the Earth. You have quarrelled with your own kin, and you seek shelter with the sinful, the incapable, and the foolish. What other man on earth would do such a thing?"

Krishna fell silent. Around the two of them the court of the Kurus held its breath: the guest who had spoken like a friend, and the prince who had been asked, at last, to choose.
stories.reflection: Krishna's appeal never leaves the ground of kinship and self-interest: he argues for peace as the path of wisdom, obedience, and survival, not as surrender. The tragedy of the scene is that the strongest argument in the hall is addressed to a man who has already decided, and everyone present knows it.
stories.next_story_tease: But Duryodhana was already shaping his answer, and it would fit on the point of a needle.

stories.title: Duryodhana's Refusal: Not a Needle-Point of Land
stories.story:
Krishna's words had barely settled over the assembly when Duryodhana rose to answer. He was the eldest of the blind king's hundred sons, and the leader of the Kuru side in the quarrel. He had listened to the sweet counsel with a face like stone, and now the court heard, in reply, not a rebuttal but a declaration.

"You should weigh every circumstance before you speak, Krishna," he began, and the very formality of the address did not hide its edge. "You find fault with me alone — you, and Vidura, and my father the king, and my teacher Drona, and the grandsire Bhishma. Yet I cannot find the least fault in myself, not even a minute one, not after the longest reflection. As for the game at dice that they accepted joyfully — the Pandavas were vanquished, and their kingdom was won by Shakuni. What blame can be mine in that? The wealth that was won from them, I ordered returned. And that they were defeated at dice a second time, and had to go to the woods — can that be any fault of ours?"

He spread his hands, the picture of a man unfairly accused. "What fault do they lay at our door, that they count us their enemies? Though they are really weak, why do the Pandavas so cheerfully pick a quarrel with us, as if they were strong? What have we done to them?"

Then the injured tone hardened into pride. "We will not bow down to them in fear, whatever fierce deeds or alarming words they threaten. We would not bow down to Indra himself — let alone the sons of Pandu. I do not see the man, faithful to the ways of a warrior, who could venture to conquer us in battle. Let alone the Pandavas — the very gods could not vanquish Bhishma, Kripa, Drona, and Karna in a fight."

And now the assembly heard the heart of it, spoken plainly. "If we are cut down with weapons in our hands, keeping the customs of our order, when our end comes — even that will carry us to heaven. This is the highest duty of a warrior: to lay himself down on the field of battle, on a bed of arrows. If we win that bed of arrows without ever bowing to our enemies, it will never grieve us. Who, born in a noble race and true to the warrior's way, would bow to an enemy out of fear, only to save his life?"

He called up the old saying of the sage Matanga, and the words rang through the hall like a sword drawn from its sheath. "A warrior should always stand erect and never bow, for it is effort alone that makes a man. Better to break at the knots than to bend. A man like me bows only to priests, for the sake of piety — and to no one else."

Then came the close, each sentence a door shutting. "The share of the kingdom that my father once gave them shall never again be theirs as long as I live. While king Dhritarashtra lives, both they and we should put up our weapons and live in dependence on him. The kingdom that was given away long ago, when I was a child dependent on others, out of ignorance or fear, cannot be given away again. It shall not be won back by the Pandavas."

Duryodhana paused and looked straight at Krishna, and the court heard the words that would be remembered as long as the Bharatas told this story. "As long as I live, Krishna, not even so much of our land as the point of a sharp needle could cover shall be given by us to the Pandavas."

There it was. Not a province, not a village, not a field — a needle's point. The peace mission had asked for five villages, for a token, for anything that would let the cousins live without war; and the answer measured the whole earth by a needle's point and found it too much. The assembly sat in silence; even those who had long expected the refusal felt its finality settle over the hall like dust.
stories.reflection: Duryodhana's refusal is not stammered but recited — an argument with its own logic, grounded in pride and a warrior's code of never bending. What makes it chilling is its clarity: he genuinely believes the dice game was not his fault, and he genuinely believes a bed of arrows is a happy fate. Pride here speaks fluently in the language of honor.
stories.next_story_tease: Krishna's patience had limits, and the needle's point had just crossed them.
stories.hero_scene: Duryodhana stands erect in the Kuru assembly, hand raised in refusal, addressing Krishna with cold defiance while the silent court watches; before him the space of the hall seems to shrink to the point of a needle.
