stories.title: Cast Away Your Fears
stories.story:
The sun went down on Kurukshetra, and the war did not stop with it. Duryodhana, king of the Kauravas, watched his army dying around him in the dark and rode to his two greatest champions — Drona, the teacher of arms who had trained the Kuru princes, and Karna, the warrior everyone knew as a charioteer's son.

"This war was set on foot by the two of you," he said, "in your rage, after the king of the Sindhus fell to Arjuna's arrows. Now you watch my army being slaughtered as though it were nothing — you, who could overcome the Pandavas alone. If you meant to abandon me, you should have said so at the beginning. You told me the two of you would vanquish the sons of Pandu, and I believed you. I would never have provoked this war if you had told me otherwise."

The words stung like a goad, and the two champions went back into battle like snakes driven on with sticks. They hurled themselves at the Pandavas, and the Pandavas, closing their ranks, advanced to meet them with all their troops. Drona pierced Satyaki, Krishna's kinsman, with ten arrows; Karna pierced him with ten more; Duryodhana with seven; Vrishasena with ten; and Sakuni, Duryodhana's uncle, with seven, until Satyaki stood walled in by enemies. The Somakas answered by piercing Drona from every side with showers of arrows, and Drona, enraged, began to take the lives of the warriors around him the way the sun burns away the darkness.

A great uproar rose among the Panchalas as he slaughtered them. Some abandoned their sons, their fathers, their brothers and uncles, and fled for their lives; others, beside themselves, ran straight at Drona himself. That night the Pandava host fled, throwing down their blazing torches, in the very sight of Bhima and Arjuna and Krishna, of the twins Nakula and Sahadeva, of Yudhishthira their eldest brother, and of Dhrishtadyumna, the Panchala prince. The world lay swallowed in darkness; only the lamps of the Kaurava troops showed where the fugitives ran, and Drona and Karna pursued them, scattering arrows on all sides.

Seeing the Panchalas slaughtered and routed, Krishna grew cheerless, and he spoke to Arjuna. "Dhrishtadyumna and Satyaki went out against Drona and Karna with the Panchalas behind them, shooting shaft after shaft," he said. "Our host is broken and routed. The flight has been checked, but it cannot be rallied. So hear me, warriors of the Pandavas: cast away your fears. Draw the army up in good order, and the two of us will go forward now, weapons raised, and stand against Drona and Karna."

Then Krishna saw Bhima advancing, and he spoke again, to put heart back into Arjuna. "There is Bhima, who loves a battle, coming against those two great bowmen," he said, "and Drona and Karna are ringed about by the Somakas and the Pandavas. With him behind you, and with all the great warriors of the Pandavas, fight now, son of Pandu, and your troops will take courage from it."

Then the two of them — Arjuna, with Krishna at his side — drove forward and took their station at the head of the battle. The vast force of Yudhishthira saw them, turned, and came streaming back to the place where Drona and Karna were grinding down their foes. At dead of night the two hosts met like two oceans swelling at the rising of the moon. The warriors of the Kaurava host threw away their blazing lamps and fought on, fearless and mad, while the world lay under gloom and dust.

Krishna's voice had done what shouting could not: the fear went out of the Pandava host, and the night went back to being a battle.
stories.reflection: The rally works because Krishna does not shame the fleeing host; he names the fear and sets his own courage beside it. Leadership here is standing at the head of the battle with the frightened, not above them.
stories.content_note: Night battle with a routed host and heavy casualties; violence is kept restrained but parents may want to know the episode is set in the war's bloodiest stretch.
stories.next_story_tease: Yet even as the night raged, Krishna still held Arjuna back from Karna.

stories.title: The Time Has Not Come
stories.story:
The night battle at Kurukshetra had many terrors, and Karna — the Kurus' champion, whom everyone knew as a charioteer's son — was the greatest of them. He struck Dhrishtadyumna, the Panchala prince, full on the chest with ten shafts that pierced deep, and Dhrishtadyumna answered with five, crying, "Wait! Wait!" The two great bowmen shrouded each other in that dreadful combat with showers of arrows, each bow drawn to its full stretch.

Then Karna sent the charioteer and the four horses of Dhrishtadyumna to the world of the dead, cut his main bow with keen arrows, and left him standing in a broken chariot. Deprived of chariot, horses, and driver, Dhrishtadyumna jumped to the ground, seized a mace, and — though Karna's straight shafts struck him all the while — came close enough to slay Karna's four horses in turn. Then he climbed onto Arjuna's chariot and would have gone back at Karna, but Yudhishthira, the eldest of the Pandavas, ordered him to hold.

Karna filled the dark with his leonine shouts, the twang of his bow, and the blast of his conch. The Panchalas and the Somakas, seeing their prince brought low, snatched up every weapon to hand and rushed at him with no thought for their lives. But Karna's driver had yoked fresh horses — white as conch shells, of the swift Sindhu breed, well broken and fast — and Karna, sure of aim, beat down the Panchala warriors like a cloud pouring rain upon a mountain. The Panchala host fled like a doe before a lion.

Horsemen fell from their horses, riders from their elephants, chariot-warriors from their chariots, all around. Karna's arrows cut down the fleeing on every side, and many fled without even feeling that they had been struck. In their terror they took the stirring of a straw for Karna himself, and ran from their own friends, mistaking them for him. And Karna pursued the broken host, shooting shafts as he went.

King Yudhishthira, seeing his army fly, turned to Arjuna. "Look at Karna standing there like the god Rudra with his bow in hand," he said, "scorching everything around him like the blazing sun at this dead of night. These cries you hear are the cries of our helpless friends, torn by his shafts. He aims and looses in one motion, with no pause between the two acts. He will destroy us all. Do now, Arjuna, what you judge should next be done about the slaughter of Karna — for the time may have come."

Arjuna turned to Krishna. "Yudhishthira is frightened today by the prowess of Karna," he said, "and our army is flying, broken by Drona and terrified of Karna. I see him careering without fear, and I cannot bear it, any more than a snake can bear the tread of a man upon its body. Take me to the spot where that great warrior stands. I will either kill him — or let him kill me."

But Krishna looked out across the field and held him back. "I see Karna, that tiger among men, careering in battle like the lord of the gods himself," he said. "There is no one else who could stand against him. But I do not think the time has come for you to meet the charioteer's son. The blazing dart Indra gave him is still with him, kept and unused. Let Ghatotkacha — Bhima's son by the demoness Hidimva — go out against him instead."

And Krishna, turning, spoke to Ghatotkacha, who stood in the dark like a storm waiting to be loosed. "Go," he said, "and slay Karna in battle, at this dead of night." The command was simple. The purpose behind it was not: the dart that had been saved for Arjuna was still burning in Karna's keeping, and Krishna meant for it to be spent on Ghatotkacha before the time ever came for the two of them to meet.
stories.reflection: Krishna's refusal to let Arjuna meet Karna is strategy wearing the face of grace: he sends another to draw the weapon that was saved for his friend, so that when the time does come, Karna will face Arjuna with his one infallible dart spent. The plan protects Arjuna and asks everything of Ghatotkacha in return.
stories.content_note: Depicts Karna's night-time slaughter of fleeing warriors, including severed limbs; softened here but the episode is the war's most violent stretch.
stories.next_story_tease: But another Rakshasa, Alayudha, had come to fight beside Karna that night.

stories.title: A Detour That Was No Detour
stories.subtitle: Krishna sends Ghatotkacha against Alayudha
stories.story:
By the light of a thousand torches the night battle of Kurukshetra raged on, and in the thick of it Krishna saw something that needed correcting: Bhima, his great mace swinging, was being overwhelmed by a demon taller than his chariot.

The demon was Alayudha, brother of Vaka — the same man-eating Vaka Bhima had slain in the forest years before — and he had come to the Kaurava side with a grudge and with strength to match it. Bhima held his ground, but the fight was going out of him. Krishna, watching from his chariot, did not ride to Bhima's aid. He rode instead to Ghatotkacha.

Ghatotkacha was Bhima's own son, born of the demoness Hidimva, and that night he was locked in combat with Karna, the Kurus' champion, holding back the greatest of the Kaurava warriors. Krishna reined in beside him and spoke. "Look," he said. "Bhima is being violently beaten down by the demon Alayudha, in the sight of all the troops — and of you. Leave Karna for now, and quickly slay Alayudha. You can come back to Karna afterwards."

It was an order that looked like a detour. Ghatotkacha obeyed it without a question: he broke away from Karna, turned, and met Alayudha in the middle of the field. The two demons closed with each other, and the night rang with a duel of giants such as that plain had not seen.

While they fought, the battle went on around them in its separate currents. Satyaki, Nakula, and Sahadeva drove their arrows through Alayudha's demon warriors; Arjuna loosed shafts on every side and overthrew whole ranks of the enemy. Karna, still furious at being abandoned, fell upon the Panchalas under Dhrishtadyumna and Shikhandin, their princes; and Bhima, seeing his comrades cut down, rushed at Karna in turn. Nakula, Sahadeva, and Satyaki, their first work done, rode to join that fight, while the Panchalas turned to face Drona. Only the two demons fought alone, and the whole field seemed to pause around them.

Alayudha struck the first telling blow: a gigantic iron club crashed down on Ghatotkacha's head. The son of Bhima staggered, sat down motionless, and for a moment the watching armies thought the night was over. But he shook himself awake, seized a mace decked with gold and hung with a hundred bells, blazing like fire, and hurled it. The mace smashed through Alayudha's horses, his driver, and his loud-rattling chariot, crushing them all to pieces.

Then Alayudha did what demons do when their strength fails them: he turned to illusion. Leaping from the wreck of his chariot, he poured out a shower of blood until the sky itself seemed a mass of black clouds torn by lightning, with thunder rolling and strange cries filling the air. Ghatotkacha rose into the sky and broke the illusion with one of his own. Alayudha answered with a heavy shower of stones; Ghatotkacha met it with a shower of arrows. Spears, maces, swords, clubs, and axes flew between them; they tore up great trees — banyan and peepul and champaka — and hurled mountain-summits at each other, until the clash of wood and rock was like rolling thunder. Men who watched said it was like the old combat of Vali and Sugriva, the monkey kings.

At last, stripped of every weapon, the two giants rushed at each other and seized each other by the hair. Wounded and bleeding, with blood and sweat streaming down them, they looked like two mighty storm clouds pouring rain. Then Ghatotkacha whirled his enemy high overhead, dashed him down upon the earth, and struck the head from him. Standing over the fallen demon, he roared.

The Panchalas and the Pandavas answered with leonine shouts. Thousands of drums were beaten, ten thousands of conches blown, and the night — illumined with torches all around and ringing with music — declared the victory of the Pandavas. Krishna had sent Ghatotkacha to kill Alayudha, and Ghatotkacha had done it, exactly as told.
stories.reflection: Krishna's command looks like a detour — leave Karna, kill the other giant first — but it is the shortest road to the same end. Ghatotkacha is trusted not with one enemy but with the whole shape of the night's work, and he carries it out without asking why.
stories.content_note: A night battle between two Rakshasas described with restraint; ends with Alayudha beheaded, without graphic detail.
stories.next_story_tease: But Karna's infallible dart was still waiting in his quiver.
stories.hero_scene: By torchlight on the night battlefield, the giant Ghatotkacha whirls the wounded Alayudha overhead and dashes him down, while Krishna watches from his chariot and the armies pause around them.

stories.title: The Dance of the Spent Dart
stories.subtitle: Krishna rejoices while the Pandavas mourn
stories.story:
Ghatotkacha lay where he had fallen — Bhima's son, born of the demoness Hidimva, slain at last by the dart Karna had saved for Arjuna. The Pandavas stood weeping over his body, and their troops, seeing their champion fall, began to fly away in panic. And Krishna danced.

He shouted like a lion. He embraced Arjuna. He tied up the horses, roared aloud, and began to dance on the platform of the chariot in a transport of joy, like a tree shaken by a storm, slapping his own armpits and crying out his delight.

Arjuna, whose heart was full of grief, could hardly bear the sight. "Krishna," he said, "you show great joy at a time made for sorrow — the death of Hidimva's son. Our troops are fleeing at the sight of Ghatotkacha slain, and we are all filled with fear. The cause must be very grave indeed if it makes you light-hearted at such a moment. If it is no secret, tell me truly what has lifted your gloom. This joy of yours seems to me like the drying up of the ocean, or Mount Meru itself learning to move."

Krishna's answer came without hesitation. "Great is the joy I feel," he said. "Listen, Arjuna, and what I tell you will drive the sorrow from your heart and put delight in it. Know that Karna, his dart spent on Ghatotkacha, is already as good as slain in battle."

And then he explained. No man alive could stand before Karna while that dart was in his hand; armed with it he looked like Kartikeya, the war-god himself. With his natural armour and his ear-rings he could have conquered the three worlds single-handed — neither Indra, king of the gods, nor Varuna of the waters, nor Yama of the dead would have dared come near him. Even Arjuna bending his great bow, the Gandiva, even Krishna himself lifting the great discus Sudarshana, could not have overcome him.

But by good fortune the armour had been taken from him; by good fortune the ear-rings had been taken from him; and now, by good fortune, the dart itself was spent — on Ghatotkacha. Long ago Karna had cut away his natural armour and his shining ear-rings and given them to Indra in exchange for the dart, and from that day he had carried the weapon that never missed, always thinking of Arjuna as already slain. "But now," Krishna said, "that dart has slain Ghatotkacha, and it is gone. Karna is like an angry snake of deadly poison charmed into stillness, or a fire that has sunk to a mild flame. Stripped of his armour, his ear-rings, and the dart Indra gave him, he is like a man again — no longer like a god."

Yet Krishna would not let Arjuna grow careless. Even without the dart, no one else could slay Karna. Devoted to the priests, truthful in speech, given to prayer and penance, kind even to his enemies — heroic as a lion, blazing like the noon sun — he could not be vanquished even by the gods, and he would mangle them until their flesh and blood fell thick upon the field. "But one moment will come when he can be slain," Krishna said. "When his chariot wheels sink into the earth, take that moment, and slay him in his helplessness. I will make you a sign beforehand. When you see it, act."

So the night ended with the Pandavas weeping for Ghatotkacha, and Arjuna slowly understanding that the grief and the joy were one event. The boy who had fought so fiercely had spent, with his life, the one weapon that could have killed Arjuna — and his death had bought the war. Krishna had danced because he saw Arjuna standing alive, and because he already saw Karna, shorn of his armour and his charm, walking toward the moment when his own chariot wheel would sink into the earth.
stories.reflection: Krishna's joy is not callousness but recognition: Ghatotkacha's death has already done its work before the body has fallen. The episode shows how Krishna counts costs the Pandavas cannot yet count — and it lets Arjuna's grief stand, answered rather than erased.
stories.content_note: The episode turns on the death of Ghatotkacha, described as a fallen mountain with no graphic detail; the focus is on Krishna's unexplained joy.
stories.next_story_tease: In the same chariot, Arjuna would ask how such enemies had ever been slain.
stories.hero_scene: On the torchlit night field, Krishna dances on the terrace of his chariot, arms raised in a leonine shout, while behind him the Pandavas weep over Ghatotkacha's fallen form and Arjuna stands puzzled in grief.

stories.title: The Deaths Krishna Arranged
stories.subtitle: How Jarasandha, Ekalavya, and Sisupala fell
stories.story:
The Pandava army was fleeing through the night when Krishna, in the chariot with Arjuna, answered what had been pressing on his friend. "How, Krishna," Arjuna asked, "were those lords of the earth — Jarasandha, the emperor of Magadha, and the others — slain, and by what means, and for our good?"

Had Jarasandha, the king of the Chedis, and the mighty son of the Nishada king not fallen, they would have become terrible. Duryodhana would certainly have chosen them — they had always hated the Pandavas — and all three would have joined the Kauravas. Heroes and mighty bowmen every one, they would have guarded Dhritarashtra's sons — Duryodhana and his hundred brothers — as the gods guard their own; with Karna beside them they could have conquered the whole earth.

"Listen, Arjuna," Krishna said, "to the means by which they were slain. Without such means the very gods could not have conquered them in battle; each of them could fight the whole host of heaven, guarded by the gods who watch over the world."

Jarasandha first. Once, hard pressed by Balarama, Jarasandha had hurled a mace that could have slain every creature on earth — blazing like fire, driven with the force of Indra's thunderbolt. Balarama met it with the great weapon called Sthunakarna, and the mace, its force destroyed, fell to the earth and split the ground open, making the very mountains tremble. In that blow the demoness Jara fell too, with her son and her kinsmen — the same Jara who, long ago, had joined the two halves of the child and given him his name. Deprived of his mace, Jarasandha was afterwards slain by Bhima, in Arjuna's own presence. "If the valiant Jarasandha had stood armed with his mace," Krishna said, "the very gods, with Indra at their head, could not have slain him in battle."

Then the son of the Nishada king: Ekalavya. His skill could not be baffled, for Drona had taken his thumb by a trick, claiming the rights of the teacher Ekalavya honored as his own. Proud and steady, his fingers cased in leathern gloves, he shone like a second Rama. With his thumb he could not have been vanquished by gods, demons, ogres, and serpents together — he could shoot day and night, and no mere man could even look at him. "For your good," Krishna said simply, "I slew him on the field of battle."

And the king of the Chedis, Sisupala — he too could not have been vanquished by gods and demons together, and Krishna slew him before Arjuna's own eyes. "I was born to slay him," Krishna said, "as I was born to slay the other enemies of the gods, with your assistance, from the wish to do good to the world."

Then Krishna widened his account until it took in the whole war. Hidimva, Vaka, and Kirmira — demons of might equal to Ravana's, destroyers of priests and of sacrifices — had all been slain by Bhima. Alayudha, master of great illusions, had been slain by Hidimva's son. And Hidimva's son himself — Ghatotkacha, whose body still lay on the field — Krishna had slain by means, through Karna and his dart. "If Karna had not slain him with his dart in the great battle," he said, "I myself would have had to slay Bhima's son. From the wish to do you good, I did not slay him before." Enemy of priests and of sacrifices, destroyer of the sacred rites, of sinful soul, he was slain — and by that same act the dart Indra had given Karna was rendered futile.

"They that are destroyers of righteousness are all slayable by me," Krishna said. "That is the vow I made, for the establishing of righteousness. Wherever the Vedas and truth and self-restraint and purity and righteousness and modesty and prosperity and wisdom and forgiveness are to be met with, there I myself always remain."

Then he turned back to the war before them. "Do not be anxious about the slaughter of Karna," he said; "I will tell you the means by which you will slay him, and Vrikodara — Bhima, the Wolf-Belly — will bring down Suyodhana, Duryodhana himself." But the uproar of the enemy army was growing, and troops were flying away on every side. What needed saying had been said, and the chariot had to move again.
stories.reflection: Krishna's list of slain kings is also an account of his own vow: he stands wherever righteousness stands, and he will use any means — guile, a preceptor's ruse, a Rakshasa's dart — to clear the field for it. The hardest sentence is the quietest: Ghatotkacha's death was never an accident of war but a price Krishna had already agreed to pay.
stories.tradition_note: The epic's account of Ekalavya's end — a thumb taken by Drona's guile and death on the battlefield — differs from later folk retellings; this story follows the Mahabharata as excerpted in the evidence pack.
stories.content_note: Recounts the deaths of several kings and Rakshasas, all described without graphic detail; one episode involves a thumb cut off by guile.
stories.next_story_tease: Then Krishna spoke of a protection Arjuna had never known he had.

stories.title: The Protection Arjuna Never Knew
stories.subtitle: Why Karna's dart never found its mark
stories.story:
All through the war at Kurukshetra, Karna, the greatest archer of the Kaurava army, had carried one weapon that he never once hurled at Arjuna. It was a dart — given to him long ago by Indra, king of the gods, in exchange for the armour Karna had worn since birth and the ear-rings that belonged to it. The dart never missed. Whichever single warrior it was aimed at would fall. It was the one thing that could end the whole war in a single stroke, and from the day Indra gave it, it was meant for Arjuna.

Many times across the battles, Arjuna had come within reach. Many times Karna's hand had closed on the dart. And every time — before he could hurl it — something went wrong.

Krishna finally explained why, on a night when the two armies fought on in darkness. Speaking to Satyaki, his close friend and a warrior on the Pandava side, as the uproar of the night battle died down for a moment, he said, "Whenever Karna reached for that dart and fixed his eyes on Arjuna, I clouded his mind. That is why the dart was never hurled at Arjuna."

That was the whole secret — not armour, not luck, not a vow. In the instant between drawing back the arm and letting the dart fly, Karna's thoughts would wander, the moment would slip past him, and the danger would pass before anyone on the Pandava side even knew it had come. Protection can work like that: invisible, unfelt, finished before it is ever noticed.

Then Krishna said something that had no strategy in it at all. "I do not hold my father, my mother, my brothers — not even my own life — so worthy of protection as Arjuna in battle."

His father. His mother. His brothers. His own life. Arjuna stood above them all.

The words made sense of something the whole army had seen that night and not understood. When Ghatotkacha fell — Bhima's son, killed in the darkness by that very dart, spent at last on someone other than Arjuna — the Pandava host had wept. Krishna had danced. He had seemed heartless, dancing while others mourned. But he had been looking at Arjuna, alive on the field; the dart that could have taken Arjuna's life was gone forever. "Seeing Arjuna, like one returned from the dead, still standing on the field," Krishna told Satyaki, "this joy seized me."

The armour, the ear-rings, the dart: one by one they had been stripped from Karna, and the last of the three was spent on the night Krishna had chosen. Arjuna never learned how close the war had come to ending in a single instant, because the danger had never been allowed to arrive.

On the dark field, Krishna sat in his chariot with Arjuna alive beside him. He had protected what he valued most in the world, by means no one could see, at a cost he had already counted. And somewhere out in the night, Karna still carried his bow — not yet knowing that the weapon he trusted was gone, and that he himself, who had given away the armour of his birth, was as mortal now as any man on the field.
stories.reflection: Krishna's protection of Arjuna is almost invisible: it works by clouding Karna's mind at the exact instant of the throw, so the danger dissolves before anyone knows it existed. His confession to Satyaki — Arjuna above father, mother, brothers, his own life — turns the night's strategy into a statement of love.
stories.next_story_tease: Dawn would bring its own griefs, and Krishna would console the eldest Pandava.
stories.hero_scene: On the dark battlefield, Krishna sits in the chariot with Arjuna alive beside him, while in the distance the faint figure of Karna stands at his chariot, one hand resting on the spent quiver that no longer holds the dart.

stories.title: Rise, O King, and Fight
stories.subtitle: Krishna consoles the grieving Yudhishthira
stories.story:
The armies fought on into the night, and in the darkness the war took its cruelest turn. Karna had carried through every battle a dart given to him by Indra — kept all those months for Krishna or for Arjuna; a weapon that could slay any single warrior it was aimed at, one that even the gods could not turn aside. In the black hour of night it was spent at last, not on Arjuna but on Ghatotkacha, the son of Bhima and of Hidimba, a princess of the rakshasas, a fierce and powerful race. Ghatotkacha fell, a loss that the blind Kaurava king Dhritarashtra would later wave away as nothing — as insignificant, he would say, as the crushing of straw.

Now the Kaurava troops — the army of the Pandavas' cousins and enemies — were wild with joy at the death of the young rakshasa prince. They raised loud shouts in the darkness and flung themselves at the Pandava ranks. King Yudhishthira, the eldest of the five Pandava brothers, watched his army begin to give way — and something in him gave way too. He turned to his brother Bhima. "Resist the Kaurava host," he said. "The slaughter of Hidimba's son has left me stunned." Bhima rode out to hold the enemy, and the king sat down on his chariot, his face wet with tears, sighing again and again. The man who had borne exile and loss without flinching sat staring at Karna's arrows, utterly without cheer.

Krishna saw him and came to him. "Let not such grief be yours," he said. "Despair like this does not become you, as it might an ordinary man. Rise, O king, and fight. Bear the heavy burden. If you lose heart, our victory becomes uncertain."

The words reached Yudhishthira through the noise of the night, and he wiped his eyes with his hands and answered. The path of duty was not unknown to him — but first he spoke of Ghatotkacha, and what he said was not a lesson; it was a reckoning of love. While the Pandavas had lived as exiles in the forests, Ghatotkacha, then little more than a child, had served them in a hundred ways. When Arjuna went away to win celestial weapons, Ghatotkacha came to them at Kamyaka forest and stayed until Arjuna returned. Through wild and trackless country he had carried the tired princess of Panchala — Draupadi, wife of the five brothers — on his own back. Skilled in every kind of warfare, he had done hard and difficult things for the king's sake, feats no one else could do.

"My love for Ghatotkacha," said Yudhishthira, "is twice the love I bear my youngest brother, Sahadeva. He was devoted to me, and I was dear to him. That is why grief scorches me. Look at our troops — afflicted, routed. Look at our great chariot-warriors broken before Karna's shafts."

His voice broke, and for a moment the night held its silence. All around, the battle pressed on: Karna's arrows still darkening the air, the Pandava host still reeling. But in the circle of that chariot there was only the king's grief and the friend who had come to answer it. Krishna had not asked the king to forget the boy. He had asked him to stand — to bear the burden, to keep the victory from slipping away. So he waited, letting the grief speak itself out, for he knew that the king's love for the dead youth was not something to be argued away.

The war did not stop for Yudhishthira's sorrow. The Kaurava shouts still rang across the dark field, and the Pandava line still had to hold. But the counsel had been spoken, and the king who had wiped his eyes with his own hands had answered out of love rather than out of despair. That, in the dark of that night, was the first step of bearing the burden again.
stories.reflection: Krishna does not belittle the king's grief; he refuses to let it become despair. Yudhishthira's answer matters because he does not deny his sorrow — he measures it openly, weighing Ghatotkacha's services against his own duty — and that honest accounting is what lets him stand again.
stories.next_story_tease: But on the field where the night was still loud, Krishna had already begun to think of other means against Drona.

stories.title: The Ashvatthama Stratagem
stories.story:
Drona, the great teacher of weapons who had trained the warriors of both armies, was cutting through the Pandava host, and nothing could stand before him. The Panchalas and the Srinjayas — allies of the Pandavas from the land of Panchala — rushed at him in waves, yelling as they came, and his arrows struck them down as fast as they arrived. Mighty warriors they were, full of courage, and even as he cut them down they did not yet fear him; still they came on, and still they fell. Steeds and men went down in such numbers that the field came to look like a battlefield of the gods in some older age. Fear crept into the hearts of the five Pandava brothers, and hope drained out of them. Drona alone seemed enough to undo them all. The day was theirs to lose, and he was taking it from them hour by hour.

"He will swallow us all," they said to one another, "like a fire swallowing a heap of dry straw in spring. No one can even look at him in battle. And Arjuna — the one man who is his match — will not fight him." For Drona had been Arjuna's own teacher, the man who had taught him the bow, and Arjuna, who honoured the ways of right conduct, would not raise his weapon against the man who had given him his skill.

It was Krishna who answered their despair. "This greatest of bowmen cannot be defeated by force," he said, "not even by the gods, with Indra at their head. But when he lays aside his weapons, even mortal men can slay him. Set aside the path of strict virtue for once, sons of Pandu, and find some way — before Drona destroys us all. When his son Ashvatthama falls, he will stop fighting. Let some man tell him that Ashvatthama has been slain."

It was not the kind of counsel the brothers had expected from him, and it landed among them like a stone dropped into still water. Arjuna would not agree to it; he heard the plan and refused. Others approved of it. And Yudhishthira — the eldest, the brother whose word was truth itself — agreed only with the greatest difficulty. To save his brothers he would have to become, for a little while, the bearer of a falsehood, and he accepted that burden with his head bowed. It was the hardest thing he had yet agreed to in the whole war.

So it was done, in a way that split the truth down the middle. Bhima, the mightiest of the brothers, took up his mace and struck down a war-elephant of their own army — a huge, terrible, foe-crushing beast named Ashvatthama, which belonged to Indravarman, chief of the Malava people. Their own elephant, felled by their own hand, not to win any fight but to make a single sentence true. Then Bhima approached Drona in the midst of the battle and, with some bashfulness in his voice, cried aloud: "Ashvatthama has been slain."

The words were true of the elephant lying dead behind him. They were spoken to a father who would hear them as the name of his son. There is a difference between a lie and a truth spoken to deceive, and the whole weight of that difference sat in Bhima's voice. Drona had heard a thousand war-cries that day and never once turned from his work. But this one name, spoken low, would do what no weapon on that field could do. On the width of a name shared between a man and a beast, the whole battle was about to turn.
stories.reflection: The man who taught Arjuna the way of dharma on this same field now counsels him to lay that virtue aside, and the text refuses to smooth it over: Arjuna rejects the plan, Yudhishthira accepts it only with great difficulty, and the lie is built out of something technically true. The episode leaves the reader standing in exactly that discomfort, without a verdict.
stories.content_note: Battle violence and a wartime deception.
stories.next_story_tease: The battle did not end with Drona; ahead waited Karna, and an arrow meant for Arjuna alone.
stories.hero_scene: In the dust and noise of the battlefield, Bhima lowers his mace beside the fallen elephant named Ashvatthaman while, at a distance, the chariot of the aged Drona waits as the words of his son's death are carried toward him.

stories.title: The Untruth That Was Nearly True
stories.subtitle: Krishna urges Yudhishthira to speak the lie that would stop Drona
stories.story:
Drona came on like a fire racing through dry straw, and no one could stand before him. Teacher to both armies, he had been enraged by the fall of Bhurishravas and Jayadratha, two great champions of the Kaurava side, and now he turned his full fury on the Panchalas and the Srinjayas, the Pandavas' allies. His shafts and darts cut them down as they charged. Again and again the finest warriors of the Pandava army rushed at him; again and again they fell, until the field grew crowded with the fallen and the ground turned dark beneath the horses' feet. Fear entered the hearts of the five Pandava brothers, and their hope of victory drained away. No one dared even look at him in battle, and Arjuna — the one man who was his match — would not fight his own teacher, for he honoured the ways of right conduct.

Seeing the brothers afflicted and afraid, Krishna, who had their welfare at heart, spoke. This greatest of bowmen, he said, could never be conquered by force — not even by the gods, with Indra at their head. But when he lays aside his weapons, even mortal men can slay him. "Cast aside the path of strict virtue for once, sons of Pandu," Krishna said, "and find some way to win, so that Drona does not slaughter us all. When his son Ashvatthama falls, he will stop fighting, I think. Let some man go and tell him that Ashvatthama has been slain."

To Yudhishthira — the eldest, called the son of Dharma for his justice, whose whole life had been the keeping of his word — Krishna said it even more plainly. "If Drona fights on in rage for even half a day, I tell you truly, your army will be annihilated. Save us from Drona. In such a strait as this, falsehood is better than truth."

Arjuna would not approve of the plan. Others approved. But Yudhishthira accepted it only with the greatest difficulty.

Then Bhima, the mighty-armed, took up his mace and slew a war-elephant of their own army — a huge, terrible, foe-crushing beast named Ashvatthama, belonging to Indravarman, chief of the Malavas. The beast was built for the front of a charge, and its fall shook the ground. Then Bhima approached Drona in the midst of the battle and, with some bashfulness, began to shout aloud: "Ashvatthama has been slain!" Keeping the true fact within his own mind, he spoke the untrue words across the field.

Hearing them, Drona felt his limbs go weak, as sand dissolves in water. But he remembered the prowess of his son and soon came to regard the news as false; recovering himself, he took comfort, knowing that no foe could stand against Ashvatthama. Then, filled with rage, he rushed at Dhrishtadyumna, the young prince of Panchala, and buried him under a thousand sharp arrows. Twenty thousand Panchala chariot-warriors in turn covered Drona with their shafts, until he vanished from sight in a storm of arrows. Drona scattered their arrows, invoked the Brahma weapon, a celestial weapon of immense power, and stood blazing like a smokeless fire. He struck down the Panchala warriors where they stood, and the great ones of that army fell like trees torn up by a storm. Twenty thousand Panchala chariot-warriors were slain that day; a warrior named Vasudana was cut down by a single broad-headed arrow; and with them fell five hundred soldiers of the Matsya country, six thousand elephants, and ten thousand horses.

The lie that was meant to end him had only fed his fury. Drona stood on the field as if he meant to wipe out the warrior class itself, and the great seers — Viswamitra, Jamadagni, Bharadwaja, Gautama, Vasishtha, Kasyapa, and Atri — gathered to look upon him. Even they could not turn the great teacher from his course.
stories.reflection: The half-truth is told with almost unbearable care: Bhima keeps the true fact within his mind, Yudhishthira accepts the plan only with great difficulty, and Arjuna refuses it outright. What the episode makes visible is the cost of the lie — Drona's doubt lasts only a moment, and the deception that was meant to disarm him releases instead his full, terrible power.
stories.content_note: Depicts the heavy carnage of Drona's onslaught (described with restraint) and the moral cost of the Ashvatthama deception; may warrant parental awareness for younger children.
stories.next_story_tease: Krishna's stratagem had not ended Drona's fury, and on the other side of the field Karna was already tearing the Pandava divisions apart.
stories.hero_scene: Before the towering, blazing figure of Drona on his golden car, Bhima calls out with downcast, bashful face the words 'Ashvatthama is slain,' while behind him the huge slain elephant lies on the miry field and Krishna watches from the Pandava chariot.

stories.title: The Field Seen From Krishna's Chariot
stories.subtitle: Krishna points out Karna's rampage and urges Arjuna forward
stories.story:
All around them, the war between the Pandavas and their cousins, the Kauravas, pressed in from every side. From the chariot where the two of them stood, Krishna showed Arjuna the battle as only he could see it. He pointed across the field. "There," he said. "Your brother Yudhishthira is being hunted by many great bowmen of the Kaurava army, all bent on killing him. The mighty warriors of Panchala, allies of the Pandavas and hard to defeat in battle, are racing after the king to save him."

Arjuna looked, and Krishna read the confusion of the fight for him, piece by piece. Duryodhana himself — the Kaurava king and the Pandavas' chief enemy — was pursuing Yudhishthira with a great force of chariots, he and his brothers, warriors whose weapons stung like poisonous snakes. Elephants, horses, chariots, and foot-soldiers of the Kauravas all pressed toward the king, greedy as poor men after a precious jewel. Satyaki and Bhima had checked them for a moment, but the host was too vast; now it rolled toward Yudhishthira again like floodwater in the rainy season rushing to the sea, the warriors roaring like lions, blowing their conch-shell trumpets, shaking their bows.

"I consider Yudhishthira as good as dead," Krishna said, "caught in Duryodhana's grip — a man already poured out as an offering on the sacrificial fire." So mighty was that host, he said, that even Indra, king of the gods, could scarcely escape its arrows. Who could bear the fury of Duryodhana himself, who loosed his shafts in ceaseless showers and, when angry, seemed like death? The arrows of the great Kaurava bowmen — Duryodhana, Ashvatthama, Kripa, and Karna, the deadliest of them all — could break down mountains.

Then Krishna told Arjuna why the danger was graver than it looked. Not long before, Karna had forced king Yudhishthira to turn his back and flee the field. Karna fought with immense skill and speed of hand, more than a match for the eldest Pandava — especially with Duryodhana beside him. And Yudhishthira, worn thin by his fasts, strong in spirit but not in a warrior's bodily strength, had been caught by Karna's assault in terrible peril. "I think the king has fallen," Krishna said. "Bhima, who is fierce in battle, stands silent while the Kauravas roar with triumph and blow their conches. I think Pandu's son Yudhishthira is dead."

Then he pointed again — to Karna, urging the Kaurava chariot-warriors forward, shooting as he came, with arrows and clubs and every weapon he carried. The king's banner was no longer to be seen; Karna's shafts had likely struck it down. Before the very eyes of the two youngest Pandava brothers, the twins, and of Satyaki, Shikhandi, Dhrishtadyumna, and Bhima — before all the Panchala and Cedi troops — Karna was destroying the Pandava division with his arrows, the way an elephant destroys a bed of lotuses. Arjuna's chariot-warriors were fleeing; wounded elephants were stampeding in every direction, crying out in pain. Karna's own standard, bearing the device of the elephant's rope, moved all over the field; and there he was, rushing at Bhima himself, scattering hundreds of arrows as he came, routing the Panchala warriors as he went.

"Set your heart rightly on the battle," Krishna said. "Advance against that leader of chariot-warriors."
stories.reflection: Krishna's words do not merely report the battle; they arrange it — first the pursued king, then the overwhelming numbers, then Karna's particular menace — until Arjuna can see with his charioteer's eyes that hesitation has become the only real enemy. The urgency is built entirely from what is visible on the field, not from exhortation.
stories.next_story_tease: But before Arjuna could advance, the field rose up against him in the person of Drona's son.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna, standing in the chariot beside Arjuna, points across the battlefield towards the distant figure of king Yudhishthira, while on the far side Karna's standard bearing the elephant's rope moves over the field, scattering the Pandava division like an elephant destroying an assemblage of lotuses.

stories.title: Comfort the King First
stories.subtitle: Krishna advises Arjuna to see the wounded Yudhishthira before facing Karna
stories.story:
The war between the Pandavas and their cousins, the Kauravas, had come to its hardest day, and Arjuna was ready to ride against Karna — when the field put another enemy in his path. Ashvatthama, the son of Drona, the great teacher who had trained the warriors of both sides, came suddenly against him with a great force of chariots. Like a shore holding back the sea, Arjuna, with Krishna at his side, withstood that furious rush. Then Ashvatthama, mad with rage, covered both heroes with arrows, and those who watched wondered to see Krishna and Arjuna — both of them called Krishna, for both were dark as a rain cloud — standing shrouded in shafts.

Arjuna answered, smiling a little, and called up a celestial weapon. Ashvatthama, born of the priestly class yet a master of arms, turned it aside. Every weapon Arjuna sent against him, he baffled. In that terrible exchange he seemed less like a man than like death itself with open jaws; he filled every quarter of the sky with straight-flying arrows and pierced Krishna three times in the right arm.

Then Arjuna struck down all the horses of his attacker's chariot. The chariot-warriors of Ashvatthama's division fell before Arjuna's arrows, and the ground beneath the two fighters ran red. Neither showed the other any mercy; they rushed at each other again and again. Ashvatthama shook his great bow, plated with gold, pierced Arjuna from every side, and once more bending the bow, struck him hard in the chest with a winged arrow. Wounded deeply, Arjuna answered with his own great bow, Gandiva, showering the son of Drona with arrows until he cut Ashvatthama's bow in two. Ashvatthama seized a spiked mace that struck like thunder and hurled it at Arjuna. Arjuna, still smiling, cut the mace down in mid-air, and it fell to the earth like a mountain split by a thunderbolt.

Maddened now, Drona's son called up the weapon of Indra — a very storm of arrows across the sky. Arjuna strung a weapon created by Indra himself, broke the storm, and buried Ashvatthama's chariot in shafts of his own. Through that hail of arrows the son of Drona came on, and with a mighty weapon of his own he pierced Krishna with a hundred shafts and Arjuna with three hundred small arrows. Arjuna answered, piercing Ashvatthama in all his vital points, pouring arrows on his horses, his driver, and his bowstring, until a broad-headed arrow struck the driver down. Taking up the reins himself, Ashvatthama guided his horses with one hand and fought on with the other, covering Krishna with arrows as he went — a feat of skill that all the watching warriors applauded. Then Arjuna cut the traces of Ashvatthama's horses with a razor-edged arrow. The horses of Drona's son bolted, dragging the chariot away, and a great cry went up from the troops.

The duel was over. The field, which had been a storm around them, fell quiet, and Krishna and Arjuna stood together on the chariot, the charioteer's right arm still marked by Ashvatthama's arrows. Arjuna's bow still hummed in his hand, and he asked to be driven against Karna — Karna, who had wounded their army and their king, whose standard bearing the elephant's rope still moved yonder over the host. But Krishna answered: "Your brother Yudhishthira, the king, has been deeply wounded and cut down by Karna. Go to him first and comfort him. Then, Arjuna, you shall slay Karna."
stories.reflection: The order is revealing: Krishna does not deny Arjuna the duel with Karna — he only insists that the wounded king comes first. In the middle of the war's worst carnage, the charioteer's counsel is still that the brothers should see each other's faces before the last great battle is joined.
stories.content_note: Depicts the intense single combat between Arjuna and Ashvatthama, including arrow wounds to Krishna; described with restraint and no gore.
stories.next_story_tease: And Krishna, taking up the reins, drove Arjuna straight to the side of the wounded king.
stories.hero_scene: On the battlefield, Arjuna and Krishna stand together in the chariot — Krishna with three arrows piercing his right arm — while Ashvatthama's riderless, trace-cut steeds bolt away across the field, and beyond them the distant standard of Karna moves over the host.

stories.title: Krishna Drives Arjuna to Yudhishthira's Side
stories.story:
On the field of Kurukshetra, the war between the five Pandava brothers and their hundred cousins, the Kauravas, had been raging for days — and Arjuna, the Pandavas' finest bowman, whose chariot his cousin Krishna drove, had just done a thing few warriors could claim: in single combat he had defeated the son of Drona, the old master of weapons who had taught both armies how to fight. He should have been the happiest man on the field. Instead he stood in his chariot, bow still outspread in his hands, and searched his own troops for a face he could not find.

Yudhishthira was gone — Yudhishthira, the eldest of the brothers and their king.

Arjuna turned his chariot toward Bhima. "Tell me, where is the king?" Bhima's answer was blunt: Yudhishthira had left the field, his limbs scorched by the arrows of Karna, the great champion of the Kaurava host, and whether he still lived was doubtful.

The words struck Arjuna like a blow. He remembered how the king, though deeply pierced by Drona's arrows, had stayed in the battle, expecting victory, until Drona himself was slain. Now Karna had done what Drona could not, and driven the king from the field, wounded and alone. "Without doubt he has gone to the camp," Arjuna said. "Go quickly, Bhima, and bring me news of him. I will stay here and hold back all our foes."

Bhima shook his head. "Go yourself, Arjuna. If I leave now, every hero on this field will say I ran from the battle." Arjuna gestured at the ranks before his division. "The samsaptakas stand in my way — the warriors who have sworn to conquer or die. I cannot stir until they are dealt with." Then Bhima did what only Bhima could promise: "Rely on my strength. I will fight all the samsaptakas myself. You go, and see the king."

So Arjuna, surrounded by enemies, turned to the one who held the reins and asked for the one thing he had never asked before — to be taken out of the battle. "Drive on, Krishna," he said. "Leave this sea of troops. I must see the king."

Krishna looked at Bhima, and his voice carried the warmth of a man who had watched these brothers all their lives. "This feat is nothing wonderful for you, Bhima. I am going now. Cut down these assembled foes of Arjuna."

Then he shook the reins.

The chariot flew. The horses, swift as Garuda, the king of birds, carried the two cousins across the field at a speed that turned the sea of war into a blur — past the standards, past the shouting, past the last scattered fights — until the noise fell away and the chariot drew up beside a quiet place where a king lay alone on his bed.

Yudhishthira lay there, the marks of Karna's shafts upon him, alone as a man is alone when he has sent his brothers into danger and paid for it with his own body. And then the two of them — the one who held the reins and the one who drew the bow, the pair the poets of the war would call the two Krishnas — stepped down from the chariot.

They did not stand at a distance. They did not wait to be greeted. Krishna and Arjuna walked to the king's bed, and both of them worshipped his feet.

The charioteer of the war, the one who had guided every battle, bowed to the man who had carried the war's heaviest weight. Seeing the king safe and sound, the two were filled with joy, like men who had braced for the worst and found the one they loved alive.

The king raised his head, and his voice was choked with delight. He believed Karna had fallen. He believed the war had turned at last, and he congratulated them both as a man congratulates those who have done the impossible.

He was wrong. But for that moment, on the bed where he lay wounded, the king was happy.
stories.reflection: Krishna, who held the reins through every battle of the war, steps down to worship the feet of the wounded king — reverence flowing upward, not downward. The moment marks the war's real hierarchy: the one who guided it honours the one who carried it.
stories.next_story_tease: But the king rejoiced too soon — Karna was still on the field, and the worst of the day lay ahead.
stories.hero_scene: On the quiet edge of the battlefield, Krishna and Arjuna — the two Krishnas — step down from the chariot and bow to worship the feet of Yudhishthira as he lies wounded on his bed, while the war's noise fades behind them.

stories.title: Krishna Offers Sudarsana to Slay Karna
stories.story:
In the war at Kurukshetra, where the five Pandava brothers fought their hundred cousins, the Kauravas, the duel the whole war had been building toward had finally come. Arjuna, the Pandavas' greatest archer, faced Karna, the champion of the Kaurava host — and the whole field knew that these two would settle what armies could not. Arjuna's chariot was driven by Krishna, his cousin and friend.

Both rode white steeds, and both were at the height of their power. They met like two great elephants locking tusks, and the field trembled under them. Shower after shower of arrows they poured at each other — bows twanging, bow-strings singing, chariot wheels clattering — while the armies of both sides watched in silence. Karna struck first, piercing Arjuna with ten mighty shafts; Arjuna answered with ten of his own, driven into the centre of Karna's chest. The fight left nothing unhurt: the limbs of the two heroes, of their charioteers, of their horses, were cut and bleeding, and the blood ran over the ground like a river no one would drink from.

Arjuna rubbed his arms and the string of Gandiva, his great bow, and then the arrows came in floods — cloth-yard shafts, razor-headed arrows, arrows shaped like a boar's ear, crescent-headed arrows — until they filled the sky like birds coming home to roost in the evening. Every one of them, shower after shower, Karna cut down with arrows of his own.

Both armies, and the beings who watched from the sky, were struck with fear at the sight of that wonderful and terrible encounter. Some among the watchers, carried away with joy, raised their arms and shouted like lions whenever Arjuna rushed at Karna.

The duel went on until the very sun seemed to vanish. Furious now, Arjuna drew Gandiva and loosed a weapon of fire — a blazing thing that covered the earth and the sky, hid the very course of the sun, and set his own body alight with its glow. The robes of the watching warriors caught fire, and they fled, and the sky roared like a bamboo forest burning.

Karna did not flinch. He answered with the weapon of the waters, and great clouds, dark as mountains, gathered on every side and flooded the field. The fire, fierce as it was, was quenched in a moment.

The two looked at each other across the wreckage of their arrows. The warriors of the Pandava host shouted for Arjuna to pierce Karna and cut off his head; the warriors of the Kaurava host shouted for Karna to slay Arjuna and send the Pandavas back to the forests forever.

It was Krishna who broke the silence. From the driver's seat he had watched every exchange, and now his patience ran out. "What is this, Arjuna," he said, "that Karna should succeed in crushing your weapons today?"

The calm of the charioteer had become the wrath of a friend who had watched enough. Krishna held out his hand, and in it turned the Sudarsana — the discus, its edge keen as a razor, the weapon that had felled demons and kings. "Putting forth your might," he said, "strike off the head of this foe of yours with this Sudarsana that I give you — as Indra, king of the gods, struck off the head of his foe Namuci with the thunderbolt."

The discus blazed in the air between them, offered like an answer to a question no one had dared to ask. Through every battle of the war, Krishna had held nothing but the reins; now he offered his own weapon, and the duel hung, waiting.
stories.reflection: Krishna, who came to the war holding nothing but reins, offers his own discus at the moment Arjuna's weapons fail — the wrath of a friend who has watched enough. The offer measures what the war has cost even the one who never lifted a weapon in it.
stories.content_note: Fierce single combat with showers of arrows and a blazing weapon; blood is mentioned without graphic detail.
stories.next_story_tease: But the duel was not to be settled by the discus, and the earth itself would soon swallow the chariot's wheels.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna stands in the chariot holding out the blazing Sudarsana discus to Arjuna, whose exhausted bow-arm hangs low, while Karna's distant chariot waits amid the wreckage of arrows on the darkened field.

stories.title: Krishna Sinks the Chariot
stories.story:
In the great war at Kurukshetra between the five Pandava brothers and their hundred cousins, the Kauravas, no duel had ever mattered like this one. Arjuna, the Pandavas' finest bowman, and Karna, the champion of the Kaurava host, had met at last — and everything, both armies knew, hung on the outcome. Arjuna fought from a chariot driven by Krishna, his cousin and friend.

The fight had begun with Arjuna's weapon careering through the sky like lightning, swelling with power and consuming the Kaurava ranks, until the broken divisions of their army drew back to watch. Then Karna crushed it with showers of gold-winged shafts, using the great foe-killing weapon he had won long ago from Rama of the axe, and turned the fight back. Bending his own loud-sounding bow, whose string could not be broken, he sent shaft after shaft that pierced Arjuna again and again.

So the two closed with each other, and the sky went dark. They struck like two fierce elephants locking tusks. The points of the compass vanished behind their weapons, and the sun itself disappeared beneath the downpour of arrows, until the whole sky was one vast web of shafts with no space between. The men watching from both armies could see nothing but arrows, and no one could tell where the next one would come from. Masters of every weapon, the two wove every manoeuvre they knew, each watching for the other's single lapse — the one opening that would end it.

Now Karna pressed his rival back, now Arjuna drove him in turn. The beings gathered in the sky shouted first "Excellent, O Karna!" and then "Excellent, O Arjuna!" while the earth sank deep beneath the weight of chariots and the trampling of horses and elephants. It was a passage of arms so dreadful that the other warriors on the field could only stand and wonder.

And in that darkness of arrows, something else was waiting for its opening too. The snake Aswasena had long been Arjuna's enemy, and he had hidden himself in the net of arrows above the field, biding his time. Now he let himself be fitted to a shaft, and Karna, bending his great bow, loosed him straight at Arjuna's head.

The shaft blazed as it flew through the sky, alive and burning, aimed to end the duel at a single stroke.

Krishna saw it coming — the way a man who has driven a thousand chariots sees the one arrow among ten thousand that matters.

With great speed and the greatest ease, he pressed the chariot down with his feet. The great car sank about a cubit into the earth — as deep as a man's forearm — and the white horses, white as the rays of the moon, bent their knees and laid themselves down on the ground.

The burning arrow passed low over Arjuna's head, close enough to graze it — and swept away only his diadem.

The crown fell to the earth, and the man who had worn it was still standing. The diadem was the mark by which the whole field knew Arjuna, and Karna's deadliest shaft had torn it from his head and left the head itself untouched. It had met a charioteer who would sink the very ground beneath his friend to keep that head upon his shoulders. In the middle of the greatest battle the world had ever seen, the moment that saved Arjuna came down to a man setting his feet a cubit deeper into the earth.

The chariot rose again, the moon-white horses came back to their feet, and the duel went on — but the opening had passed, and it had passed because of the man holding the reins. Krishna had raised no weapon that day. He had not needed one.
stories.reflection: The episode makes Krishna's loyalty literal: he is not fighting, not speaking, only driving, and yet the whole outcome turns on his feet pressing a chariot into the earth. The divine protection here is not a weapon or a miracle of light but a quick, precise act of a charioteer who will not let his friend be taken.
stories.content_note: Battle violence; an arrow narrowly misses Arjuna.
stories.next_story_tease: But the duel between Karna and Arjuna was not yet decided.

stories.title: Krishna Identifies the Snake Aswasena
stories.subtitle: The snake of Khandava returns as Karna's arrow
stories.story:
All day the duel between Arjuna and Karna had hidden the sun behind a net of arrows. Arjuna, the Pandavas' greatest bowman in the war at Kurukshetra, fought from a chariot driven by Krishna, his cousin and friend; Karna, champion of their hundred cousins, the Kauravas, had matched him shaft for shaft — and had even broken the blazing weapon Arjuna loosed at him. But Karna's own wounds were many. Scorched by Arjuna's arrows, his limbs cut and bleeding, he found at last that he could not prevail — and in that hour he reached for the one shaft he had kept for years, lying alone in its quiver.

He did not know what it was. No one on the field knew.

For there was a snake beneath the earth who had been waiting for this day. His name was Aswasena, and his hatred of Arjuna was older than the war. Years before, when Arjuna fought for Agni, the god of fire, and helped him burn the great forest of Khandava, Aswasena had been in the sky, hidden within his mother's body. Arjuna's arrow slew the mother. The son escaped the flames, pierced the earth in his fury, and hid in the world below, nursing his mother's death and the hatred it planted in him. Now, seeing the fight between Karna and Arjuna, he rose from the lower world, soared up on the power that let him climb the sky, and slipped into Karna's quiver — a living snake in the shape of an arrow.

When Karna set his heart on that single shaft and lifted it out, what he laid on his bowstring was a snake-mouthed arrow, blazing and fierce — the weapon he had long kept for Arjuna's destruction, polished with care and kept in a golden quiver amid sandal dust. He drew it to his ear and aimed it at Arjuna's head.

In that instant the guardians of the world raised their voices and wailed — Indra, the king of the gods, among them — for they saw what no man on the field could see.

Weary from their long exertions, the two heroes looked at each other. The chariot stood sunk in the earth, where Krishna had pressed it down with his feet in the moment the arrow flew. And Krishna, who had seen everything from the first, spoke. "While you stood with your bow at Khandava, serving Agni, the god of fire," he said, "this snake was in the sky, hidden within his mother's body. You slew her. He escaped the flames, and remembering that deed, he comes toward you today for your destruction."

He named him: Aswasena.

Then Krishna told Arjuna to slay the snake, and Arjuna did not ask how. The shaft Karna had loosed was met and cut down, the snake cut off, the old vengeance of Khandava ended on the field of Kurukshetra.

Afterward, when the sky was clear again and the duel stood still, Krishna himself stepped down from the chariot, put his arms beneath it, and raised it from the earth with his own strength. The chariot that had carried them through every battle of the war stood level once more, as if the ground had never swallowed it.

Karna's last weapon was gone. But Karna himself still stood on the field, wounded and failing — and the duel was not over.
stories.reflection: The snake hides in an enemy's quiver and comes for the archer who slew his mother years before — old griefs find their way back to the field in whatever shape they can. Krishna alone reads the arrow for what it is, because he alone remembers the whole history; discernment is memory made present.
stories.content_note: Fierce single combat and a vengeful snake-arrow; described without graphic detail.
stories.next_story_tease: Wounded and failing, Karna still stood on the field — and the end of the duel was yet to come.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna stands beside the chariot sunk in the earth, one arm beneath it lifting the car free, while the severed form of the snake Aswasena falls from the sky and Arjuna lowers his bow on the battlefield.

stories.title: Krishna Urges Arjuna to Slay the Distressed Karna
stories.story:
The war at Kurukshetra between the five Pandava brothers and their hundred cousins, the Kauravas, had narrowed at last to a single duel, and all through that long afternoon the sky over the field had turned into a net of arrows. Arjuna, the Pandavas' greatest bowman, and Karna, the champion of the Kaurava host, had been searching for each other's one mistake, and neither had made it yet. The two hosts had fallen back to watch, for it seemed the whole long war had come down to these two men alone. Arjuna's chariot was driven by Krishna, his cousin and friend.

Early in the fight Arjuna had loosed a weapon that swelled with power and went careering through the air like lightning, consuming the Kaurava ranks, until the broken divisions of the Kauravas fled and stood at a distance, gazing at it. Karna alone held his ground. With showers of gold-winged shafts he baffled that burning weapon while it was still in the sky, and with a great foe-killing weapon of his own — the one he had won from Rama of the axe — he crushed it and pierced Arjuna with keen shafts. Bending his own loud-sounding bow, whose string could not be broken, he shot shower after shower of arrows, and the two closed with each other.

They struck at each other like two fierce elephants locking tusks. The points of the compass vanished behind their weapons and the very sun went invisible; the sky became one vast net of arrows with no space between, and in that dense darkness the armies could make out nothing else. The two masters of weapons kept aiming and shooting, displaying every manoeuvre they knew. Sometimes Karna prevailed over his rival, sometimes Arjuna prevailed, and every warrior on the field was filled with wonder. Even the beings in the sky applauded, crying sometimes "Excellent, O Karna!" and sometimes "Excellent, O Arjuna!" And a serpent named Aswasena, who nursed an old hatred of Arjuna, moved in that darkness of arrows, waiting for his moment.

Then the turn came. The earth had been pressed deep all day under the weight of chariots and the tread of horses and elephants, and now it seemed to turn against one of its own. Karna's chariot wheel sank into the earth, and the ground held it, as though it had at last chosen its side. Karna stood stunned. The man who had never shown his back in battle was held motionless in the open, in the sight of both hosts, and he could not draw his chariot free.

He called out to Arjuna and appealed to his sense of what was right. He was in distress, he said; he had been brought low not by his enemy's hand but by the ground itself. He did not ask for mercy, only for time — the chance to free his wheel and face Arjuna as an equal, as the duty of warriors required. Let Arjuna remember that duty, he urged, and grant him the one moment's respite that a warrior in his place could rightly claim.

Krishna did not let the moment pass. "Why, son of Pandu, have you become so forgetful?" he called out, his voice blazing. "Those who are truly wise never spare their foes, however weak, even for a moment. Slay him, therefore, as Indra, king of the gods, slew the demon Namuci."

Arjuna's arrow answered, and the warrior who had asked for a moment received none. The wheel stayed where the earth held it, and the duel was over.
stories.reflection: The two pleas stand side by side and the account does not step in to say which was right. Karna asks for what dharma owes a man brought low; Krishna answers that a war is no place for such debts, and names Indra and Namuci as the precedent. That the episode ends without resolving the argument is, perhaps, the point: the hardest questions are the ones the source leaves open.
stories.content_note: A warrior is slain in battle; the death is described with restraint.
stories.next_story_tease: But the war's grief was not finished; a mother's curse was about to fall upon Krishna.
stories.hero_scene: Karna standing motionless beside his chariot, its wheel sunk into the earth, calling out to Arjuna while Krishna urges Arjuna to strike, the sky above them dark with a net of arrows.

stories.title: Balarama Tries to Halt the Mace-Duel
stories.story:
The news reached Balarama from the mouths of brahmins — the learned travellers who carried tidings from kingdom to kingdom — telling of the great war at Kurukshetra, where the five Pandava brothers had fought their hundred cousins, the Kauravas, and of the slaughter of the warrior kings. Balarama, Krishna's elder brother, had been journeying through the holy places, and now he listened, and he understood: the burden the earth had carried so long — the weight of kings grown too heavy for the world — was being lifted at last, king by king.

But one duel remained.

Bhima of the Pandavas and Duryodhana of the Kauravas, the two mightiest mace-fighters of their age, had met in their final combat and were beating each other toward death with their iron clubs, the blows ringing out across the field. Balarama set out for Kurukshetra at once, for the slaughter of the kings was done, and he would not see two more lives spent on what was already decided. As he rode, the news was still turning in his mind — the war done, the kings fallen, two champions yet beating each other to death. He drove on with the sound of those iron blows in his ears.

Yudhishthira, the eldest of the Pandavas, saw him coming and went to greet him, the twins Nakula and Sahadeva with him, and Krishna and Arjuna. But Balarama had not come for greetings. His eyes were on the centre of the field, where the two champions stood, maces in hand, enraged, each bent on victory — the last two fighters of a war that had consumed the kings of the earth. All around them lay the silence of a finished slaughter; the great armies were gone, the banners down, and only these two still stood, one against the other, settling what the war had not settled.

"Bhima! Duryodhana!" he called, and his voice carried across the field. "The two of you are of equal strength, equal heroes. Neither of you can win this fight. Desist."

It was the counsel of an honest man, and it was the truth. The two were matched so evenly that victory could be claimed by neither; at the end of such a duel, ruin waited for both. Balarama had no stake in the quarrel of the cousins — he had come only to say what any onlooker with clear eyes could see — and the words he flung across the field were meant to save the lives of both of them.

But the champions did not heed his words. They were bound by enmity, the way kings are bound by the greed of a kingdom; they remembered the insults they had exchanged across the years, and memory held them tighter than any counsel. What Balarama said was reasonable, and neither of them had come to Kurukshetra to be reasonable.

Balarama waited, watching the maces rise and fall, and saw that he could not part them. He was not a man to force his will upon destiny. Accepting what he saw — two champions locked in their duel, deaf to everything but their own hatred — he turned away without another word.

He returned to Dwaraka, leaving the field to the mace and the men who swung it. Behind him, the maces rose and fell, and the last duel of the war went on without him. He had spoken, and been heard, and refused; there was nothing left for a witness to do but leave the field to the two who had chosen it.
stories.reflection: Balarama comes to the last duel as an impartial witness, speaks the truth over the field, and leaves when it is not heard — even the greatest can offer counsel, not compel. The war's ending belongs to the men who chose it and to the hatred that binds them.
stories.next_story_tease: Only the duel of the maces stood between the field and the end of the war.
stories.hero_scene: Balarama stands at the edge of the field, one hand raised, calling to the two mace-wielding champions locked in combat in the centre, while the Pandavas watch and the dust of the duel rises around them.

stories.title: Kunti Asks Only for Remembrance
stories.subtitle: A queen's farewell hymn as Krishna turns toward Dwaraka
stories.story:
The great war was over. The Pandavas — five brothers of the royal house of Hastinapura, the eldest of them Yudhishthira — had won back their kingdom after a long war against their cousins. Krishna, their friend through every battle and every danger before it, had stayed only long enough to see them safe through the war's last terror: the night when an enemy warrior named Ashvatthama loosed his most terrible weapon, and it was turned back before it could destroy them. Now Krishna was turning toward Dwaraka, his own city by the sea. And Kunti, the mother of the five brothers, who had thanked him in her heart through a lifetime of dangers, knew she might not see him again like this, with the world grown quiet.

She had watched him save her sons so many times that the court had lost count of the rescues. Now, as he turned to leave, she came forward and spoke — the mother of kings, with Yudhishthira and his brothers standing silent behind her. What poured out of her was not a plea but a hymn of praise, spoken in the hearing of the whole court.

She bowed to the one she saw hidden in him: the ancient Person behind all things, veiled by his own play, unknowable to the ignorant, imperishable — the goal of the pure-hearted sages. She bowed to Krishna, son of Vasudeva and of Devaki. And she remembered his mother, shut away for years in the prison of Kamsa, the tyrant king of Mathura, and freed at last. Then she remembered her own life. Poison had come to her sons, and the great fire, and the cruel assembly of the dice hall, and the long hardships of exile in the forest, and the weapons of the mightiest warriors of the age. From all of these, again and again, he had freed her and her children.

And then Kunti said the words that made the whole court go still. "May those dangers stay with me forever, teacher of the world," she said, "for it was in danger that I saw you. A man puffed up by birth, by wealth, by learning, by beauty, does not see you at all." She bowed again — to the one who is the wealth of those who own nothing and stands beyond the pull of the world's moods. "I count you as Time itself," she said, "the lord without beginning and without end. No one can read your intention, for you move among us looking like an ordinary man. Even the rope with which a cowherd woman of Vrindavan bound you when you were a child, naughty and crying, black collyrium running down your face — even that was your own play."

People argued, she said, about why he had come to earth at all. Some held that he was born to give glory to the virtuous. Others said Vasudeva had prayed for a son, and so he came to Devaki. Others said he came to lift the burden of the earth, as a boat is lowered onto a drowning sea. Whatever the truth — and the wise could not agree — the troubled of this world heard of his deeds and sang them, chanted them, remembered them, and took joy in them.

Then the hymn found its sorrow. "Will you abandon us today, lord?" she asked. "Will you leave your friends, your servants? What are we, my sons and your own people alike, without you, but a name and a form? This land will not shine as it shines now, once you are gone." And she named him as the old verses name him — Shri Krishna, friend of Arjuna, whose courage has no end.

The court was silent. And Kunti, who in all those years had asked nothing for herself — no kingdom, no wealth, no safety — asked the only thing she wanted. "May my mind stay fixed on you alone, my lord," she said. "Again and again, on you alone."

Krishna, whose every glory she had praised, smiled gently. "So be it," he answered. And he turned back toward the city.
stories.reflection: Kunti's hymn is one of the strangest farewells in the tradition: she does not ask Krishna to stay, only that her remembrance of him stay. Her prayer that dangers might remain forever is not a love of suffering but a confession that it was in danger that she knew him most clearly — gratitude so complete that it can thank even misfortune.
stories.next_story_tease: Krishna granted her prayer, but he would not leave the city that day — there were months of leave-taking still ahead.
stories.hero_scene: Queen Kunti, hands folded in salutation, stands before Krishna in the morning light of Hastinapura as he turns toward his chariot; the Pandava court silent behind her, and Krishna smiling gently as he answers her hymn.
