stories.title: Krishna Departs Hastinapura
stories.subtitle: A city watches its friend leave
stories.story:
It was months before Krishna could bring himself to leave Hastinapura.

The great war had ended with his friends the Pandavas on the throne of their fathers, and Krishna had stayed on in their city — to gladden them, to comfort his sister Subhadra, who still mourned the war's dead, and to let a broken city begin to heal in the presence of someone it trusted completely. Months passed. The wounds of the Kuru house began to close, and still the parting was put off. At last it could be delayed no longer. He took leave of everyone, embraced them one by one, bowed to the elders, and mounted his chariot. The morning was clear, and every person in the city knew this would be the last they would see of him from their own streets for a long while.

And the city could not let him go.

Subhadra, Draupadi, Kunti — Gandhari and old Dhritarashtra, whose own sons had all fallen in the war — none of them could bear the thought of his going. Their eyes followed him and would not turn away. The wise say that those who have tasted true company cannot give it up again; how then could the Pandavas, whose minds were fixed on Krishna, endure his absence? Tears rose in their eyes and were held back, from sheer longing for Devaki's son. No one wanted to be the first to look away.

The whole city came out to see him go. Mridanga drums sounded and conches, bheris and vinas — drums and horns and lutes calling and answering down the length of the royal road. The women of the Kuru house climbed to the roofs of the palaces, desperate for one more sight of him, and the children of the city ran beside the chariot wheels until the road turned. A white umbrella sewn with pearl garlands was raised over his head, and Uddhava — Krishna's closest friend and adviser — and Satyaki, his kinsman, walked beside his chariot, waving long chauri fans. Here and there along the way, the blessings of the brahmins rose over the noise and were heard.

And as the chariot moved through the streets, the people spoke of the one who was leaving. "This is he, surely," they said — "the ancient Person, who alone existed before all distinctions, who sets creation turning again by his own power. His are the feet the sages seek; his deeds are sung in the hidden places of the oldest sacred verses. When kings grow dark with unrighteousness, he comes down." "How blessed is the clan of Yadu," others said, "and how holy the forest of Madhu that raised him. And Kushasthali, his city — the city men now call Dwaraka — dims the glory of heaven itself and makes the earth famous. The women who won him by the price of his own valor, when at the svayamvara — the ceremony where a princess chooses her own husband — he carried off his bride past the fierce king of Chedi and the rest — they make womanhood itself glorious." So the women of the city talked as he passed. The old verses set it down that these were the words heard along the royal road that morning — a whole city praising, as one, the one it loved.

Yudhishthira rode with him part of the way, with the army and the escort to guard him. And at the edge of the city, the Kurus stood at a distance, hardly able to bear the parting, their eyes unblinking on the figure growing smaller down the road.

Krishna passed on. He traveled through the land of the Kurus and through Panchala, through Shurasena and the country along the Yamuna, across the great Maru desert, and through the far provinces of Sauvira and Abhira. And at every kingdom he crossed, the people came out to meet him and did him honor, pressing gifts upon him as he passed — for the road to Dwaraka, though long, ran through a land that had been waiting to see him.
stories.reflection: The verses pause to note that those who have known such company cannot bear to lose it, and the Pandavas, whose minds were fixed on Krishna, could hardly endure the parting. What makes the scene moving is that the grief is not for a king or a deity but for a friend: the city grieves him as a presence that will simply be gone.
stories.next_story_tease: Ahead lay the desert road — and a sea-girt city already decking its gates for his return.

stories.title: Dwaraka Welcomes Krishna Home
stories.subtitle: A conch brings the whole city running
stories.story:
Krishna was coming home. He had been away through the great war, and then through the long months among the Pandavas in Hastinapura, and now the city of Dwaraka, his own city by the sea, heard its lord returning before it saw him.

He was still some way out, crossing into his own prosperous land of Anarta, when he lifted his conch and blew. The white-bellied shell, reddened by his lips, sent out a sound that carried ahead of him like light — a sound that, as the verses say, takes the fear out of the world. And Dwaraka, hearing it, rose and ran to meet him.

The citizens poured through the gates, their faces bright with joy, their voices choked with delight. "We bow to your feet, lord," they cried, "feet that Brahma and Shiva and the kings of the gods themselves worship. Be our welfare — for you alone are our mother, our friend, our husband, our father. When you went away to the Kurus, or to the Madhu people, on visits to friends, how could we live? How could we bear it, with your glance far off — the glance that dries up every sorrow?" So the people spoke, and Krishna heard them all, he who is tender to those who love him. And the joy ran through the city like a tide, from the swept avenues to the humblest doorway with its pot of curds.

The city had been made ready for him as for a festival. Arches of welcome stood raised at the gates and along the roads; the great avenues had been swept clean, the lanes and markets and squares freshened; and at every door were set pots of curds and unbroken rice, fruits and sugarcane. Out of the gates came his own people to meet him: his father Vasudeva, great-hearted; Akrura, the wise elder of the clan; Ugrasena, the old king Krishna had restored to his throne; and Balarama, his elder brother — called Rama as well — with his sons Pradyumna and Charudeshna riding behind, and Samba, the son of Queen Jambavati. The foremost elephant led the procession, and the brahmins chanted blessings of good fortune. The women performers of the city rode out by the hundred in their carriages, eager for his sight; actors and dancers, bards and praise-singers filled the road with song.

Krishna moved among them and did not hurry past. He bowed to the elders and to the brahmins with their wives; he took the hands of his relatives, returning embrace for embrace, smile for smile, glance for glance — the whole long welcome answered in kind. The noble women of Dwaraka watched from the terraces along the royal road, saying that fortune itself lived in his chest, and that their eyes could not drink enough of the sight of him. He passed beneath the white umbrella and the waving fans, showered with flowers from the balconies all the way to his father's house.

There his mothers were waiting — the wives of Vasudeva, with Devaki, who had borne him, at their head. He bowed to them, and they lifted him onto their laps and held him like a child again, their eyes wet with the tears of love. For a long moment the courtyard held only the sound of their weeping.

Only then did he enter his own palace, the house that fulfilled every desire. His wives, who had watched the road for his return all the months he was gone, saw their husband come home, and their hearts broke into festival; with their children about them, with their eyes and their very hearts, they embraced their lord. And the verses close the scene with a quiet marvel: even to those who lived beside him, who saw him in the next room and alone, his two feet were always new.

Dwaraka had him back. The sea-girt city, which had been decked and swept and kept awake while he was away, settled into the long happiness of his presence.
stories.reflection: The citizens' words — 'you alone are our mother, our friend, our husband, our father' — are striking because they come from an entire city, not from a single devotee; a whole people measures its safety by one presence. And the closing marvel, that his feet were always new even to those who lived beside him, says something quiet about devotion: nearness does not exhaust wonder.
stories.next_story_tease: But the wheel of time was turning, and the years of peace were numbered.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna sounding his conch at the approach to Dwaraka, the white sea-girt city rising ahead of him, while citizens stream through the decorated gates with garlands, pots of curds and flowers to welcome him home.

stories.title: Time's Answer to Arjuna
stories.subtitle: Vyasa consoles the grieving archer, and Parikshit is enthroned
stories.story:
Arjuna, the great archer of the five Pandava brothers, had leaned on Krishna through everything. When word came that Krishna had left the world, and his elder brother Balarama with him, Arjuna went to Dwaraka alone.

Dwaraka, Krishna's city by the sea, was a city of the dead. Arjuna performed the last rites for the two brothers and for all the slain. Krishna's eight queens, Rukmini at their head, embraced their lord's body and entered the funeral fire; Revati, holding the body of Balarama, entered it too, and the fire, the old account says, was cool to her. Hearing this, Ugrasena and Vasudeva, Krishna's own father, with Devaki and Rohini, gave themselves to the flames. Arjuna performed their rites as well, and then made the whole city rise and leave — taking Vajra, the young prince of the Yadava line, and leading the thousands of Krishna's wives and all the people slowly away, with tenderness and care.

Behind them, the Sudharman palace and the Parijata tree, which Krishna had once brought down to earth, rose and returned to heaven. That same day the dark age of the world, the Kali age, began; and the ocean rose and covered all of Dwaraka except one small temple of the Yadava deity, which the sea has never washed away. There, they say, Krishna still abides, and whoever visits it is freed from his sins.

Arjuna halted the great company in the Panchanada country, a rich and fertile land. There the robbers of the region saw one lone warrior guarding so many widowed women and so much treasure, and their greed woke. They gathered the lawless Abhiras to them. "Here is Arjuna," they said, "rich and proud of slaying Bhishma and Drona and Karna. He does not know the courage of simple villagers. Up! Take your staves!" And they rushed at the people with cudgels and clods of earth.

"Go back, wretches," Arjuna called, "unless you wish to die." They paid him no heed; they seized the treasure and the women. Arjuna reached for Gandiva, his great heavenly bow — and it would not brace. The string stayed slack, however he strained. The words that called the superhuman weapons would not come back to him. He loosed arrows as best he could, and they only scratched the skin; even the shafts the fire-god Agni had given him were destroyed. He beat at the bandits with the horn of his bow, and they laughed. And before his eyes, the barbarians carried off the women of the Vrishni and Andhaka clans and went their way.

Then the greatest archer of the age broke down. "Alas, alas!" he wept. "I am deserted by my lord!" And in that instant Gandiva and the heavenly weapons, his chariot and his horses, perished before his eyes. "Resistless are the decrees of fate," he said, "which gave feebleness to me and victory to the base. These arms are mine; this fist is mine; I am Arjuna. But without him who stood beside me, all of it is hollow — and without him I am overcome by peasants."

He went on to Mathura and set the young prince Vajra on its throne. There, in a wood, he found the sage Vyasa and bowed at his feet. Vyasa looked at him a long while. "How is it, Arjuna," he asked, "that I see you shorn of your brightness? Have you been beaten by your inferiors in battle?"

Arjuna sighed and told him everything. "Krishna, who was our strength, our heroism, our very brightness, has left us," he said. "Without him we are as weak as straw. Gandiva, famed through three worlds, is foiled by the sticks of peasants; the household of Krishna is carried off by thieves with cudgels. It is not that my brightness is gone — it is a wonder that I live."

Vyasa's answer was gentle, and it was absolute. "Think no more of your disgrace, my son," he said. "Know that time bends all beings the same way: rivers, seas, mountains, gods, men, trees, insects — all are created by time and destroyed by time. Krishna came down to lift the burden of the earth, and that work is done. The kings are slain, the Vrishni race is destroyed; nothing was left for him to do, and so he has departed, his purpose fulfilled. Your defeat by miserable thieves was as much his work as your victories over Bhishma and Karna. It is only the play of the lord of all."

Then Vyasa told him a story. Long ago there was a sage named Ashtavakra, a brahman whose body was bent in eight places. For years he stood in water, meditating. When the nymphs of heaven passed that way, going to a festival on Mount Meru, they praised him. "Ask what you wish," he said. Some asked for the best of husbands, a lord among brahmans. "So be it," he said, and rose from the water. When the nymphs saw how crooked his body was, they laughed, and the sage cursed them: "You shall have the best of men for your husband, but because you laughed at my bent body, you shall afterward fall into the hands of thieves." They begged his pardon, and he softened: in time, he said, they would return to the world of the gods.

"It is because of that curse," Vyasa said, "that the wives of Krishna have now fallen into the hands of the barbarians. Do not grieve over it. All this destruction was worked by the lord of all — and your own end, too, is near, for he has drawn back your strength and your splendor. Death is the end of everyone born; a fall is the end of every rising; union ends in separation; growth tends to decay. Knowing this, the wise are touched by neither grief nor joy. Give everything up, go to the holy forest, and tell Yudhishthira that tomorrow, with his brothers, he must set out on the path of heroes."

Arjuna went back and told his brothers all that he had seen and heard. And the Pandavas placed Parikshit, the young heir of their house, on the throne, and went into the forest.
stories.reflection: Vyasa's consolation rests on a single recognition: Krishna's coming and going alike were the working of time, which gives and takes away without partiality. The Ashtavakra story makes the point gently — even heavenly nymphs were promised to thieves by an old curse — so that Arjuna's defeat loses its sting: it was never his to keep, and never his loss alone.
stories.tradition_note: The Bhagavata Purana gives a somewhat different account of Dwaraka's end and the deaths of the elders; this story follows the Vishnu Purana, as cited in the evidence pack.
stories.content_note: Contains the funeral-pyre deaths of Krishna's queens and family elders after his death, and an attack by robbers; may warrant parental awareness for younger readers.

stories.title: The Pilgrimage to Samanta-panchaka
stories.story:
In the middle of the day, the sun went dark over Dwaraka — and Krishna's people did not read the eclipse as a bad omen. A solar eclipse, everyone knew, was a summons, not a warning: a day when the pious go down to the holy waters, bathe away the dust of their years, and give cows and gifts to the worthy. Every family in the city knew what such a day demanded — the dark sun above, the sacred water ahead, and blessings to be won by those who came with open hands.

The road led to Samanta-panchaka, the field of the Kurus. Long ago, the old verses say, the warrior-sage Parashurama — a Rama of an age long past, the best of all weapon-bearers — had brought the kings of the earth low on that very field, and the five pools he left behind were called Rama's pools, their water counted among the holiest in the land. Krishna went, and his elder brother Balarama, and his father Vasudeva, and Akrura, the wise elder of the clan, and the chief men of the Yadava houses — and behind them half the city of Dwaraka. The road filled with chariots that gleamed like the dwellings of the gods, drawn by swift horses and hung with garlands of gold, so that the whole procession shone as it crossed the plain beneath the darkened sky. It seemed that all the people of the land were on the road too, streaming toward the same field, each pilgrim hoping to leave a lifetime of wrongs behind in the sacred water.

At the field they bathed in Rama's five pools, fasting with their minds gathered close, and then, as the rite required, bathed a second time. They gave cows and gifts, and did all that the day asked of them. And only then did the field show them what the eclipse had truly gathered.

Kings had come from every quarter — from Kamboja and Kaikaya, from Madra and Kunti, from Anarta and Kerala — and with them, kinsmen and friends the Yadavas had not seen in years. Men parted by wars and reigns and the long business of kingdoms fell on one another's necks, their faces opening like lotuses in the joy of meeting, tears running down unchecked. The women of the two houses embraced as well, arm crossing arm, the red festival powder called kumkuma marking each other's shoulders, tears of love bright in their eyes. The youngest bowed to the eldest and were blessed in return, and the elders gave the blessings with both hands, as if they could not let go.

By evening the field had become something rarer than a festival: half the world's families finding one another again. Tents had risen everywhere; the plain was a city of its own. Old quarrels were forgotten at the sight of a familiar face. News was exchanged at every campfire; children born since the last meeting were shown to relatives who wept over them; men who had last met on a battlefield found they could laugh together. The eclipse that had darkened the noon sky had become the excuse for a homecoming no one had dared to arrange.

And then, toward the end of the day, a new dust rose on the road — not the thin dust of chariots but the slower, thicker dust of ox-carts and walking herds. A caravan of cowherds came up out of the haze, men in the rough cloth of the countryside, and a stir ran through the Yadava camp. For among all the kings and kinsmen the field had gathered, these were the faces from the oldest years of Krishna's life: Nanda, the cowherd chief who had raised him, and Yashoda, who had been a mother to him, with the cowherds of Gokula, the village of his boyhood, around them.
stories.reflection: The eclipse gathers what the years have scattered: a day that begins in darkness becomes the occasion for half the world's families to find one another again. Krishna travels to the tirtha like everyone else, and the story's weight falls not on anything he does but on the reunion that his presence draws together.
stories.next_story_tease: Nanda and Yashoda had come to Samanta-panchaka — and the Vrishnis rushed to meet them as if life itself had returned.
stories.hero_scene: Under the eclipsed sun, a long procession of golden chariots crosses the plain toward the five pools of Samanta-panchaka, where kings from many realms and long-separated kinsmen embrace one another with tears of joy.

stories.title: Reunion with Nanda and Yashoda
stories.story:
All through that day, at the holy field of Samanta-panchaka, the great families of the earth had been finding one another again. Now, as the light grew long, the caravan of the cowherds came slowly up the road — ox-carts, dusty men, the lowing of herds — and the Yadavas who went out to meet it came back changed. In the middle of the crowd walked Nanda, the old cowherd chief of Gokula, the village where Krishna and Balarama had grown up, and the Yadavas fell on him as if life itself had returned to their bodies. Vasudeva, Krishna's own father, was the first to reach him. He embraced his old friend, pleased past all words, holding on as a man holds on to something he thought he had lost. Around them the whole clan pressed close, hands reaching out, voices rising and falling, everyone talking at once and no one listening.

Then Krishna and Balarama came forward and bowed low to Nanda and Yashoda, the father and mother who had raised them. With their own hands they seated the two on the seats of honor, and then, speechless with love, embraced them with both arms — the princes of Dwaraka holding the father and mother of Gokula, grown men who had commanded armies pressing their faces into shoulders they had not felt in years.

Yashoda took her two sons onto her lap. They were men now, broad-shouldered and scarred, princes of a city by the sea; on her lap they became again the boys who had crawled after the calves in her courtyard. She held them and said nothing, and the two of them let themselves be held. Around them the cowherds of Gokula stood smiling and wiping their eyes, as if they too had come home.

Then Devaki and Rohini came to Yashoda — Devaki, who had given her sons into other hands when they were smaller than her arm, and Rohini, who had shared those first years of waiting. The three women stood a moment, remembering. "Who could forget that friendship, Yashoda?" they said. "Who could forget what you gave them — the years of tending, the childhood you made safe and bright while we could only wait?" As babies the boys had rested in Yashoda's hands the way the eyelash rests on the eye — placed there, and safe, and afraid of nothing.

Yashoda answered them the way she had always answered: she gave them back their sons, sitting there on her lap, whole and grown. Devaki and Rohini looked at the two princes everyone else in the field saw — and what they saw was the milkmaid's courtyard, the dust of the calf-pens, the little feet running in the sun. Nothing needed to be said. The embrace said it.

Vasudeva watched from a little way off and said nothing. Somewhere in his chest a debt he had never been able to name was being counted again, and he knew that before this gathering ended he would have to speak of it. But not yet. Not while Yashoda's arms were still around her sons.

For the rest of that day, the field of the eclipse was a small Gokula again. The years of separation had shrunk to nothing, and a pilgrimage that had begun as a duty under a darkened sun ended with the oldest, simplest thing in the world: a mother holding her children, and the years falling away from her face. It was the kind of day the elders would tell about for years afterward — the day the whole family was whole again.
stories.reflection: The quiet heart of the reunion is the meeting of the four mothers: Devaki and Rohini, who could not raise the boys, honour Yashoda, who did, and no one needs to say whose claim is greater. The embrace dissolves the old division between the two families in a single gesture.
stories.next_story_tease: But the women of Vraja had come to the field too, and they had waited longest of all to see him.

stories.title: Krishna's Counsel to the Gopis
stories.story:
The gopis of Vraja — the cowherd women of the village where Krishna grew up — had come to Samanta-panchaka like everyone else, to bathe at the great eclipse gathering where all the clans of the land met. But they had come for one face. Krishna had been a boy in their village once; years had passed since he had gone away to the cities, to Mathura and then to Dwaraka. In all that time they had measured the days by his absence: the nights when the flute stayed silent, the mornings when the road to the forest was just a road. They had grown older in his absence, and would not have traded the waiting for anything, because the waiting had kept him near. When at last they stood where he could see them, they did not rush forward. They embraced him in their hearts, and in that inward embrace they reached a stillness that even the great ascetics — those who train their minds in meditation for whole lifetimes — can hardly reach. Their eyes had once cursed their own eyelids for blinking and stealing him from their sight; now their eyes held him, and would not let him go.

Krishna saw them and came to them, drawing them aside to a quiet place away from the crowds — he came to them alone, as he had come to them in the old days in Vraja, without fanfare and without warning. And he asked them, gently: "Do you remember our friendship?" And then: "Or do you think ill of me — do you suspect that I am ungrateful?"

It was not a question they expected. They had come with their longing, not their grievances; in all the years of waiting they had asked nothing of him, only waited. But he did not wait for an answer; he gave them the answer instead.

"As the wind gathers the clouds and scatters them," he said, "as it lifts the dry grass, the cotton, the dust, and lets them fall where it wills, so I bring beings together and carry them apart. I am the one who joins, and I am the one who separates. No meeting lasts by its own strength; every parting that grieves you is woven into the world I wind and unwind. But there is one bond that is not broken — devotion to me. Devotion is what grants immortality to beings. Hold to that, and no separation can touch you. I am the beginning of all beings and their end; I am inside them and outside them; there is nowhere you can go where I am not."

The gopis heard him in the quiet place, with the eclipse-darkened sky above the camp, and their bondage dissolved. The years of longing, the nights of calling his name to the moon, the fear that he had forgotten them — all of it fell away, and they attained him then, in that moment, in a way that no practice could have given them. What he had told them was not that they would never be parted, but that parting itself was his weaving, and that their love of him ran deeper than the weave.

Before they rose, they spoke their answer as a prayer. "May your lotus feet always rise in our minds," they said, "your feet that the wisest of yogis hold in their hearts, the one support for all who have fallen into the well of this world — even for us, who live quietly at home."

He had given them back their friendship, and then he had given them something larger: the knowledge that the friendship had never left them. The gopis returned to their camp walking lightly, as if the road were not there. For the rest of the pilgrimage they moved among the other pilgrims like women who had been shown the end of a long road — having gained in a single hour what a lifetime of seeking can hardly win.
stories.reflection: Krishna answers the gopis' longing not with a promise that they will never be parted, but with the truth that no being is ever really parted from him — he is the beginning, the end, and the inside of all things. Their love, which had looked like grief, turns out to be the one thing that cannot be lost.
stories.next_story_tease: The reunion at Samanta-panchaka could not last forever — soon Nanda would take the road back to Mathura.

stories.title: Nanda's Farewell
stories.story:
The pilgrimage had wound down, camp by camp, and the field of Samanta-panchaka was emptying the way it had filled — in dust and shouting and the slow creak of carts. Only one farewell remained, and it had been going on for three months. Nanda, chief of the cowherds of Vraja — the man who had raised Krishna and his brother Balarama in his own house, safe and loved, as a father raises sons — had stayed all that time, honored with great worship by the Yadavas, Krishna's own clan, with feasts and gifts and the attendance of princes. It was, everyone agreed, a farewell without end. Some of the cowherds joked of settling at the holy place for good, but Nanda knew the road home was waiting. And still the leaving had to come.

On the last day, Vasudeva, Krishna's father by birth, stood before his old friend, and the words he had carried inside him for three months came out wet. The snare called affection, he said, is hard to cast off — harder still when it is weighted with guilt. He told Nanda what he had never told anyone: that blinded by royal splendor, by crowns and palaces and the endless business of a kingdom, he had neglected his oldest friend through all the years he himself could not be there. In the years when it had been in his power, brother, he said, he had done nothing for him — nothing at all, while Nanda had done everything for his sons. He wept as he spoke, and Nanda saw that these were tears the old friend had been saving for years. For Vasudeva, the great ocean of his longing had at last been crossed, and he was not sure he deserved to have crossed it.

"May royal splendor never befall a man who desires his own good," he said, "for it steals the eyes." And yet, he said, wiping his face, the eyes had been given back to him now.

Nanda answered him the way he had answered everything in his long life — not with a speech, but with an embrace. He had done what a friend does: he had raised the boys, kept the friendship, and asked for nothing. That, Vasudeva understood, was the gift that could not be repaid, only honored.

Then came the farewell itself. Nanda's carts were loaded with riches — gifts from Vasudeva, from old King Ugrasena, from Krishna, from Uddhava, Krishna's friend, and from Balarama — so that the caravan that had arrived in the plain cloth of the countryside left carrying the wealth of a kingdom. The cowherds and the cowherdesses of Vraja made ready; the oxen were yoked; children were lifted into the carts; the dust began to rise. Every Yadava family pressed something on the departing guests — cloth, ornaments, cattle — until the carts could hold no more, and Krishna himself walked beside Nanda's cart as far as the edge of the camp.

Nanda climbed up onto his cart, and his heart, worth more than all the gold behind him, stayed where it had always been — at the lotus feet of Govinda, the name the cowherds of Vraja had always used for Krishna. Then the caravan moved off down the road to Mathura, and Krishna and Balarama stood watching until the carts were small against the sky, until the dust settled back into the road.

When the kinsmen had gone, the Vrishnis, his kinsmen from Dwaraka, turned homeward themselves. But for a long while no one spoke. The eclipse had come and gone; the pilgrims had bathed; the gifts had been given. What the field of Samanta-panchaka had truly given them could not be bathed away or loaded onto carts. It stayed in the memory of embraces given and received, and in the sight of an old friend's back moving down the road to Mathura, carrying home a heart that would never leave.
stories.reflection: Vasudeva's lament is a confession that royal splendor can blind a man to his oldest debts, and Nanda's silent reply — the embrace, the refusal to count the cost — is the friendship itself. The riches on the carts matter less than the heart Nanda carried home, fixed on Govinda's lotus feet.
stories.next_story_tease: Back in Dwaraka, the city's sixteen thousand queens were waiting for their lord to come home.

stories.title: Sixteen Thousand Wives, One Beloved
stories.story:
On the edge of Dwaraka, in lakes ringed with blossoming groves, the water itself seemed to be laughing. And in the water was Krishna.

The long years of exile and war were over, and Dwaraka — Krishna's own city, home of his clan, the Yadavas — had settled back into pleasure. Elephants wandered the scented streets, gardens hung heavy with flowers, and music never quite stopped. Krishna had sixteen thousand wives — queens of every great household of Dwaraka — and he was the one beloved of them all. That morning they were in the lakes, and Krishna with them.

The water sports began the way such things always begin: someone splashed, someone shrieked, and in a moment everyone was in the game. The queens ringed him, fine clothes clinging, wet hair loosened and strung with flowers, and tried to douse him; he answered in kind, laughing, until the spray rose like rain. He stood among them as a great elephant stands at the heart of its herd — towering and playful at once, letting himself be caught and then slipping away. Musicians played on the bank — drums, flutes, small cymbals — and the dancers moved with the beat.

To each of the sixteen thousand, the sport felt like a secret. Every woman there was certain of one thing — he is sporting only with me — and each believed she alone held his smile. Strange to say, there was no jealousy among them, for their minds and eyes were fixed on one man, and where the heart is wholly given, no room is left for envy.

Some of the queens cried out in mock terror and clung to him: "O Krishna, I am being drowned — save me!" Others rowed small boats shaped like herons, serpents, and sea-monsters, and some swam on their own strength, and some with water jars. The water itself seemed to enter the game, rising to meet each queen exactly where she stood. His garland was streaked with saffron and his hair fell loose about his face; he gave himself to each game as though it were the only one.

Then, as the afternoon cooled, the play changed. The queens, still in the water, began to sing — songs of longing, strange for women who had been laughing with their lord only moments before, as though he were far away. One sang to the osprey crying over the lake: you call all night and cannot sleep — has love pierced you too, as it has pierced us? Another sang to the shelduck parted from her mate: you weep in the dark, and we weep, for we too have given ourselves wholly to his feet. They sang to the thin moon: are you, too, wasting away from remembering him? They sang to the southern breeze: what have we done that you bring us his memory and nothing else? They sang to the clouds, heavy with rain: you, like us, are bound to the lord of the Yadavas by love, and you spill your tears remembering him. And they sang to a swan as to a messenger: welcome, swan; drink the water, and tell us of Shauri — for Shauri was the name they used for Krishna. Is he well? Does he, who makes friends so quickly, still remember us? For a woman, the songs ended again and again with the same words: there is no refuge but him.

The drums and flutes answered from the bank, and Krishna listened. He was the water they stood in, the breeze they sang to, the one they called to; in his presence they sang of his absence, and their longing was itself the closest embrace. The old tellings say that by such love — constant, single-hearted, poured out in song — those queens reached the highest state.

Evening came down over the lakes, and the queens rose from the water with wet hair and smiling faces, bright as lotuses. The game ended where it had begun: in laughter, in water, in the middle of Dwaraka, where the lord of sixteen thousand hearts was, that day and every day, the single beloved of them all.
stories.reflection: The strangest, most moving thing in this story is that the songs of longing are sung by women who are not separated from Krishna at all — the absence is imagined, and imagining it lets their love pour itself out completely. The story's quiet miracle is that each of the sixteen thousand is given the whole of Krishna, and none of them is diminished.
stories.tradition_note: The Harivamsha sets the same sport in the ocean, whose waters Krishna frees from salt, and adds that the water rose only to the height each woman wished; this account follows the Bhagavata Purana, which places the play in the lakes of Dwaraka.
stories.next_story_tease: Krishna's watchfulness would be tested again soon — on the banks of the Ganga, where a grieving king was coming to meet the Pandavas.

stories.title: Krishna Substitutes an Iron Statue for Bhima
stories.story:
The blind king of Hastinapura was coming to meet the men who had killed his sons — and he was coming with open arms.

The war was over. King Dhritarashtra, whose hundred sons lay dead on the field of Kurukshetra, had set out from his city, grief weighing on him like a stone. It should have been a simple meeting — a nephew going to comfort an uncle — but the whole court watched it with a dread no one spoke aloud. Yudhishthira, now king in his place, heard that his uncle was coming and went out to meet him, taking his brothers and Krishna with him, and Yuyudhana of the Vrishnis and Yuyutsu, the one son of the old king who had fought beside the Pandavas. Draupadi, wife of the five brothers, followed, burning with grief. On the banks of the Ganga they found the ladies of the Bharata court, weeping like a flight of ospreys, their arms raised in anguish, crying out that the king's righteousness was nowhere to be seen, that truth and compassion had gone from the world while fathers and brothers and teachers and sons and friends lay slain. Yudhishthira passed through them in silence and saluted his uncle's feet, and his brothers announced themselves, each giving his own name.

Dhritarashtra embraced Yudhishthira — a reluctant embrace, brief, with a few words of comfort — and then he asked for Bhima. His grief had kindled into something else: a fire, the story says, fanned by the wind of his sorrow, ready to burn everything that came near it, and Bhima most of all. He wanted the man who had killed his son Duryodhana. He wanted to hold Bhima in his arms.

And Krishna knew it. He had known it from the very outset — that was why an iron statue of Bhima, made long ago at Duryodhana's order, had been kept ready. Before the embrace could happen, Krishna quietly drew the real Bhima away and set the statue in his place. The blind king, told that Bhima stood before him, seized it with both arms, thinking it to be Bhima himself in flesh and blood.

The strength of Dhritarashtra was the strength of ten thousand elephants. He crushed the iron Bhima as if it were a reed, shattering it into fragments. But the blow recoiled on him: his own breast was bruised and broken, and blood poured from his mouth. Covered in blood, he fell to the ground like a great flowering tree brought down by the weight of its own blossoms. His charioteer Sanjaya ran to him, raised him, and steadied him. "Do not act so," Sanjaya said. And the old king, his wrath spent at last, wept aloud: "Alas, oh Bhima — alas, oh Bhima!"

Only then did Krishna speak. "Do not grieve, Dhritarashtra," he said. "You have not slain Bhima. That was an iron statue you broke. I saw the rage in you, and I dragged Bhima out of the jaws of Death. There is none equal to you in bodily strength — what man could endure the pressure of your arms? As no one escapes Death itself with his life, so no one comes out safe from your embrace. That statue, made by your son, had been kept ready for this moment. Grief for your sons has pulled your mind away from righteousness, and in that darkness you sought to slay Bhima. But what good would his death have done you? Your sons will not be revived by it. Accept what we have done for the sake of peace, and do not set your heart on grief."

Bhima, who had stood within an arm's length of death, was alive. And on the banks of the Ganga he stood among his brothers — the real Bhima, in flesh and blood — while the blind king wept out his grief and his wrath together.
stories.reflection: Krishna's mercy here works in two steps: he lets the king's rage spend itself against iron rather than flesh, and only then tells the truth. The substitution saves Bhima; the timing saves Dhritarashtra, who is allowed to discover that he is not a murderer and that his grief is not, in the end, a weapon.
stories.content_note: A grieving king crushes an iron statue in his embrace, wounding his own breast and vomiting blood; intense but not graphic.
stories.next_story_tease: The old king's wrath was spent, but his grief still needed one more word from Krishna.

stories.title: Krishna Counsels Dhritarashtra to Govern His Wrath
stories.story:
Dhritarashtra, the blind king of Hastinapura, had been washed of his own blood, and now he sat in silence, with nothing left to him but grief. He had come to the river to meet his nephews, the five Pandavas, after the great war between the two branches of the family had taken his hundred sons; and an hour earlier his grief had nearly turned to murder. He had meant to crush Bhima — the Pandava who had killed his son Duryodhana — in an embrace meant to kill; his strength was the strength of ten thousand elephants. But Krishna had drawn the real Bhima aside and set an iron statue in the king's arms; the embrace that shattered the iron had broken the king's own breast and sent blood pouring from his mouth, and only when his wrath had burned itself out had Krishna told him the truth: you have not slain Bhima. Now the maid-servants had washed the king and dressed his wounds, and Krishna came to him again.

Yudhishthira and his brothers stood a little apart, watching. Krishna did not let the silence soften into comfort. "You have read the Vedas and the scriptures," he said. "You have heard the old histories and everything about the duties of kings. You are learned, possessed of great wisdom, and no longer swayed by strength or weakness. Why, then, do you cherish such wrath, when everything that has overtaken you is the result of your own fault?"

He reminded the king of what had been said to him before the war. Krishna himself had counselled him; so had Bhishma and Drona, Vidura and Sanjaya — the wisest minds of the Kuru court. The king had not followed a word of it, though they had told him plainly that the Pandavas were superior to his own sons in strength and courage. "A king who can see his own faults, and knows the distinction of place and time, obtains great prosperity," Krishna said. "But the man who will not accept the counsel of well-wishers, good or bad, meets with distress, and grieves over the policy he chose himself. You did not keep your soul under restraint; you let Duryodhana rule you. What has come upon you came through your own fault. Observe a different course of life now. Why do you seek to slay Bhima? Recollect your own faults, and govern your wrath."

And then, in the same breath, Krishna turned to the old king's tenderness. He reminded him of the day Duryodhana, from pride, had caused the princess of Panchala — Draupadi, wife of the five Pandavas — to be brought into the assembly hall to shame her. "That mean wretch has been slain by Bhima in just revenge," Krishna said. "Look at your own evil acts, and at the acts of your wicked-souled son. The sons of Pandu are perfectly innocent, and yet you and your son treated them most cruelly."

It is a hard thing to be told, at the end of one's life, that one's sorrow is one's own doing. But Dhritarashtra did not argue. "It is even so," he said. "Everything you say is true. It was parental affection — love for my own sons — that caused me to fall away from righteousness. By good fortune, the mighty Bhima, protected by you, never came within my embrace. Now I am free of wrath and fever, and I long to embrace that hero, the second son of Pandu. When all the kings are dead, when my children are no more, upon the sons of Pandu depend my welfare and my happiness."

And then the old king did what grief had made impossible an hour before. He rose and embraced those princes one by one — Bhima, and Arjuna, whom the old songs call Dhananjaya, and the twins Nakula and Sahadeva, the two sons of Pandu's second wife — the young men he had been ready, an hour before, to destroy. He wept over them, comforted them, and pronounced blessings upon them. The king who had come to the river with murder in his grief left it with his arms around the sons of Pandu.
stories.reflection: Krishna's counsel works because it separates the two things the old king was carrying: the grief, which is real and never rebuked, and the wrath, which is chosen and can be set down. He names Dhritarashtra's fault not to shame him but to give him back the one thing sorrow takes away — the sense that his own choices still matter.
stories.next_story_tease: But beside that same river, another grief was gathering — one that would not answer to counsel.

stories.title: Gandhari Curses Krishna; He Accepts with a Smile
stories.story:
The war was over, and the field of Kurukshetra lay strewn with the dead. Through it walked Gandhari, queen of the blind king Dhritarashtra and mother of the hundred Kuru princes who had fallen in the war, and she saw what a mother sees when the war is over. Her own sons lay dead among the rest, and with them it seemed she had lost everyone's sons. Krishna walked beside her, and she poured it all out to him, pointing from one fallen warrior to the next.

"Look," she said, "there lies the ruler of the Kambojas — that bull-necked hero, lying in the dust though he deserved to rest at ease on soft Kamboja blankets. His wife kneels weeping at the sight of his blood-stained arms, the arms that once were smeared with sandal-paste. Arms strong as iron maces, and yet within their clasp joy never left her for a moment. 'What will be my end,' the sweet-voiced queen cries, 'now that I am deprived of you?' — and she weeps helplessly and trembles."

"Look at the ruler of the Kalingas, lying on the ground with his mighty arms still ringed with golden armlets. Look at the ladies of Magadha, weeping around their lord Jayatsena, their ornaments knocked awry — the long-eyed, sweet-voiced girls whose wailing tears at my heart — women made for costly beds, lying now on the bare ground. Look at that company of lovely women there: worn out with marching and heat, and yet beauty has not left them, like wreaths worn by the gods that do not fade in the sun; only their faces, through toil and the sun's rays, have become like faded lotuses."

"And look — the prince of Kosala, Brihadbala, whose women kneel and draw from his body the arrows with which Abhimanyu, Arjuna's son, pierced him, losing their senses again and again as they do it. There lie the young sons of Dhrishtadyumna, the Pandavas' general — boys of tender years, garlanded with gold, who fell upon the great teacher Drona like insects on a blazing fire — Drona, whose chariot was a chamber of fire, his bow the flame, his shafts and darts and maces the fuel. And the five Kekaya brothers lie with their faces still turned toward the man who slew them, their armour shining like heated gold, their tall standards and chariots and garlands — all of the same bright metal — shedding light over the earth."

Her voice broke. "These wails are tearing my heart," she said. Then she turned from the dead to the one who might have stopped it all. "Since you stood by, indifferent, while the Kurus and the Pandavas slew each other," she said, "therefore you, Krishna, shall be the slayer of your own kinsmen. In the thirty-sixth year from this day, you shall perish by wretched means in the wilderness."

Krishna heard her out, and there was a faint smile on his face as he answered. "There is none in the world, save myself," he said, "that is capable of destroying the Vrishnis."

It was another way of saying that the end she spoke of was already written — and that it would come not from any enemy, but from their own hands. And so the curse was received, not resisted.
stories.reflection: Gandhari speaks from the raw center of grief, and her curse is grief given a shape and a date. Krishna does not defend himself or dispute the blame; he smiles, because he already knows how the Vrishnis will end, and he is not afraid of it.

stories.title: Krishna Rebukes Gandhari
stories.story:
Gandhari had just cursed him, and Krishna had accepted the curse with a smile. Now he stood before her on the field of Kurukshetra, with the grief of a hundred dead sons hanging between them like weather.

Gandhari, mother of the hundred Kaurava brothers, had raised her hands over the battlefield and called down her curse on the man she held responsible for the slaughter: that he would die as her sons had died, at the hands of his own kinsmen. Krishna had taken the words as one takes a blessing. And now, before the pyres of the dead were even built, he spoke.

"Arise, arise, Gandhari," he said. "Do not set your heart on grief. Through your own fault this vast carnage has taken place. Your son Duryodhana was wicked at heart, envious, and swollen with pride. You applauded his wicked deeds and counted them good. He was cruel — hostility itself — and deaf to the counsel of his elders. And you: why do you wish to heap your own faults upon me?"

He did not say that the war had been fate, or that the gods had willed it. The fault, he told her, was hers. Then he spoke of grief itself. "Whoever grieves for what is already past," he said, "only gathers more grief — indulge it, and it doubles." Mourning, he told the mother of the dead, is a fire that feeds on itself.

Then came the harshest words of all. He spoke of the children different mothers bear: the priest's wife bears a son for prayer and penance, the cow her calf for burdens, the mare hers for speed, the serving woman hers for service, the cowherd's wife hers for the herds. "But a princess," Krishna said, "bears sons to be slaughtered."

Gandhari said nothing. The old accounts say her heart was torn by grief, and that she stood silent. Whatever she had expected from Krishna — comfort, apology, the name of the guilty — she received the truth instead, and the truth left her no reply.

Her husband, Dhritarashtra — the blind king of the Kurus — had been listening at her side, and it was he who broke the silence at last. He turned to Yudhishthira, the eldest of the Pandavas, who stood among the survivors. How many, he asked, had fallen? Yudhishthira answered: one billion, six hundred and sixty million, and twenty thousand men had died in the war, and two hundred and forty thousand one hundred and sixty-five had escaped with their lives. Then the king asked where the fallen had gone.

Yudhishthira, who had received the gift of spiritual sight from the sage Lomasa during his years of wandering, could see where each man had gone. Those who had cast off their bodies gladly in fierce battle had reached the worlds of Indra, king of the gods. Those who met death without joy had found the company of heaven's musicians. Those who fell while turning away from the field, or begging for quarter, had reached the world of the hidden ones. The high-souled warriors who scorned to flee, and walked unarmed against armed foes, had won the radiant worlds of Brahma, the creator. And all the rest who died on the field had gone to the far-off northern world of the Uttara-Kurus. To every death, a place.

Then came the work of the living. The king asked about the friendless dead — those with no one to light their pyres — and Yudhishthira gave his order: let no one perish for want of someone to care for them. And so the pyres were built, of sandalwood and aloe and gathered wood, with ghee and oil and perfumes, silken robes, broken chariots, and heaps of weapons for fuel; and the fires were lit.

Duryodhana and his hundred brothers were burned with the rites due to the dead: Shalya, Jayadratha, Abhimanyu — Arjuna's boy — Duhshasana's son, Bhurishrava, Drupada, Virata, Shikhandi, Dhrishtadyumna, and the thousands of the Srinjayas. The smoke of the pyres rose over Kurukshetra, and the field of the great war became, at last, a place of burning and of farewell.
stories.reflection: Krishna's rebuke comes to a woman who has just cursed him, and it refuses to let her grief become a weapon that rewrites what happened. 'A princess bears sons for being slaughtered' is brutal — and it is also the one sentence that could make a queen of the dead stop and hear that her sorrow, however vast, is not the whole story.
stories.next_story_tease: On the road back to Hastinapura, Arjuna would ask Krishna to speak again the teaching he had heard before the war began.

stories.title: Arjuna Asks Krishna to Repeat the Gita
stories.subtitle: Krishna offers the Anugita in its place
stories.story:
Everything Krishna had told him on the battlefield, Arjuna had forgotten.

The great war between the Pandavas and their cousins was over, and Arjuna had his kingdom back. He spent those days in pure joy, doing nothing but keeping company with Krishna in the palace at Hastinapura, in rooms that seemed a piece of heaven, surrounded by relatives and attendants. Yet one thing had begun to trouble him. One day, as the two friends wandered together through that beautiful house, Arjuna turned to Krishna. It was on the eve of battle, he said, that he had first understood how great Krishna was; on that same field he had also seen Krishna's form as the Lord of the universe. But everything Krishna had spoken to him then, out of affection, had slipped from his mind, which was so quick to wander. Again and again he had meant to ask — and now Krishna would soon be leaving for Dwaraka. Would Krishna tell him once more?

Krishna embraced him before he answered. It grieved him, he said, to learn that Arjuna had let slip, out of carelessness, what had been given him. The recollection of that teaching would not come back to him now — he had spoken it while gathered into the deep stillness of yoga, not as men speak from memory, and he could not repeat it in detail. But it had been more than enough, if Arjuna could hold it, to know Brahman, the one reality behind the world. Then Krishna's voice softened into a promise: he would recite an old history upon the same matter, and if Arjuna listened with a heart already shaped by Krishna's teaching, he might yet attain the highest end.

So Krishna began the old history. Once, he said, a brahmana — a sage of the priestly order — had come to them from heaven, from the presence of Brahma the creator, whom the old books call the Grandsire of all beings, and they had honored him as was due. When they asked him about the path of liberation — asked, the brahmana observed, out of compassion for all creatures, and not for his own good — he agreed to speak, asking only that they listen with their whole attention.

The old history concerned a brahmana named Kasyapa, known above all others for knowing what duty requires. Kasyapa had heard of another brahmana who had sounded every depth of the teaching: he knew what the scriptures say of how beings leave this life and return to it, and he held the direct, inward knowledge that yoga gives; he was at home in every branch of learning; he knew the truth about pleasure and pain, and weighed merit against wrong; and he had seen with his own eyes the ends that creatures high and low reach by their deeds. He lived like a man already free — his penance complete, his calm unbroken, every sense his own — and he seemed to blaze with the light of Brahman itself. He could pass anywhere at will, and he could vanish from before the eyes of all. He wandered with invisible siddhas, beings perfected in yoga, and with heaven's musicians, talking with them in places far from the noise of men; and he was as unattached to everything as the wind.

Kasyapa, hearing such things of him, longed to see him. He made his way to the sage, and when he had seen those wonders for himself he fell at the sage's feet with his whole heart, and stayed to wait on the master with deep reverence.

So Krishna spoke in the palace at Hastinapura, with Arjuna before him — and the old history he had promised would unfold, in the days that followed, into the teaching known as the Anugita.
stories.reflection: Krishna's answer to forgotten truth is not a repetition but a story: he cannot summon back the words of the Gita, so he begins an old history, and the Anugita is born from that refusal. Arjuna's fickleness of mind becomes, in a strange way, the occasion for the teaching to be given again in a new form.
stories.tradition_note: The Anugita is the Mahabharata's own sequel to the Gita, and within the text Krishna explains that he cannot repeat the original discourse; the full old history unfolds through the chapters of the Anugita Parva that follow.
stories.next_story_tease: Before long, Krishna would speak his final teaching to a different disciple, at the foot of an ashvattha tree.
stories.hero_scene: In a palace chamber like a piece of heaven, Krishna embraces Arjuna and begins to speak, while Arjuna — who has just confessed that he forgot everything Krishna taught him on the battlefield — listens with bowed head.

stories.title: Krishna's Final Instruction to Uddhava
stories.story:
By the time the Yadava clan — Krishna's own people — had all but destroyed itself, almost no one was left at his side. He had watched the working of his own maya, the great play of the world that he himself had set going, run out to its end. Now he walked down to the bank of the river Sarasvati, sipped its water, and sat down at the foot of an ashvattha tree, the great sacred fig.

There he told Uddhava to go to Badari, the hermitage in the north. Uddhava, the companion who had followed Krishna all his life, found that he could not leave his feet. It was not that he meant to defy the command; it was that the road north led away from Krishna, and that was the one road Uddhava had never learned to take. He lingered, followed at a distance, and waited. Krishna found him there and said: "I know what your heart desires. I grant you what is hard for others to attain."

Uddhava has left his own account of that hour. He saw Krishna seated alone, deep in thought — the one he had sought and loved all his life. Krishna was dark and radiant, free of passion, his eyes peaceful and touched with red, his right foot resting on his left thigh. When Krishna spoke, Uddhava — the friend of the sage Vyasa — bowed low with joy.

"This is your last birth," Krishna told him. "My grace has come to you. What I spoke long ago to Brahma, seated on the lotus born from my navel at the beginning of creation — that is what I give you now."

Uddhava could barely take it in. He had asked for nothing; he had only failed to walk away when he was told to go. Now he was to receive what Krishna had spoken to Brahma at the dawn of the universe. He praised Krishna — the one who acts with no desire of his own; whose birth, and his being before all birth, alike pass all telling; the refuge of the sorrowing, to whom the frightened run from every fear; the one the sacred chants call upon, whose knowledge of himself is whole and unbroken and eternal; the one who, holding the secret of the self, could unfold it fully to another.

All his life, Uddhava saw now, he had been blessed, moment by moment, by Krishna's grace; only at this hour did he understand how much had already been given him. For one who served Krishna's feet, nothing was hard to obtain — not even the four aims men spend their lives seeking: duty, wealth, pleasure, and freedom.

And so, to Uddhava, whose heart lay open, Krishna taught the knowledge of the self, and granted him the state that is hard for others to attain.

It was the final teaching, given at the foot of a tree on the bank of a river, to the one man who could not make himself leave Krishna's feet. The world would long remember the words spoken at Kurukshetra; what Uddhava carried away that day was what came after them — the knowledge of the self, given quietly by a river.
stories.reflection: Uddhava is told to go, and his reward is that he cannot; he receives the supreme state not for asking but for refusing to leave Krishna's feet. The episode quietly suggests that the last grace comes to those who cannot bear separation, even when the Lord himself sends them away.
stories.tradition_note: The account in the third canto is Uddhava's own recollection of the moment; the fuller exposition of the teaching he received is traditionally known as the Uddhava Gita.
locations: the foot of an ashvattha tree

stories.title: Krishna Sends Uddhava to Vrindavan
stories.story:
In the palace at Mathura there were kings and counselors, kinsmen and crowds — but when Krishna wanted comfort carried to the people of his boyhood, he looked past them all. He looked to Uddhava, his dearest friend, whose heart was fixed on Krishna alone.

Uddhava held no office and no rank. What he had was rarer: he had been at Krishna's side through the long years in Mathura, and he had seen how Krishna, the young hero of the city, grew quiet whenever the talk turned to Vrindavan — how a single mention of the village could stop him mid-sentence. Krishna's heart was still there, among the cowherds who had raised him and the women who had loved him, and Uddhava knew it.

One day Krishna called Uddhava to him and gave him a journey. "Go to Vraja," he said — Vraja, the cowherd country of his childhood. "Bring joy to my parents." Nanda and Yashoda had raised him in the village of his boyhood; then the summons of the court of Kamsa — the cruel king of Mathura — had carried him away to the city, and the years since had been long for the people who still loved him there. But Krishna spoke of more than his parents.

"The women of Gokula," he told Uddhava, "have set their minds on me. Their very lives are given up for my sake; for my sake they have abandoned everything — comfort, standing, even their own bodies. To them I am the dearest of all dear ones, and I am far away. They are keeping themselves alive," he said, "with great difficulty — somehow, only just."

Uddhava understood what was being asked of him. Krishna was not sending a herald to deliver orders, or a prince to settle accounts. He was sending his own affection into the village that still sang his name — in the person of the one friend who could speak of him most truly. The women who had given up everything for Krishna were pining, and Krishna, who could have sent anyone, had chosen the one friend who would say the words the way they needed to be said. Uddhava accepted the charge: he would go to Vrindavan and tell Nanda and Yashoda of their son; he would carry Krishna's love to the women of Gokula; and he would not rest until he had done all that could be done to console them.

So he made ready to leave Mathura, carrying the strangest of royal messages: that Krishna, far away, remembered — remembered their songs and their meadows and their faces — and had sent the dearest of his friends to say so. He carried no army and no gifts, only words that would have to be worth the years of waiting. The road to Vrindavan lay open before him, and he set out.
stories.reflection: The message Krishna entrusts to Uddhava is not doctrine but a description of love — minds fixed on him, lives given up for his sake. In sending his dearest friend to console Vrindavan, Krishna sends a part of himself, and comfort travels in both directions.
stories.next_story_tease: He reached Vrindavan as the sun went down, to a welcome he had not expected.

stories.title: Uddhava Arrives in Vrindavan
stories.subtitle: Nanda longs for Krishna as Yashoda weeps
stories.story:
Uddhava, Krishna's messenger from Mathura, reached Vraja — the cowherd country where Krishna had grown up in the care of Nanda and Yashoda — as the sun went down.

The village at dusk was a thing alive. Powerful bulls, scenting the cows, bellowed and fought in the lanes; white calves leaped this way and that, so that the whole settlement seemed dressed in them; and the women sang as they worked, singing the good deeds of Bala and Krishna — Bala being their name for Balarama, Krishna's elder brother — the two brothers the village had raised and lost. Every home bore the marks of worship: the fire, the sun, the guest, the cow, the priest, the ancestors, and the gods, each honored in its turn. Around the settlement the forests stood in full flower, loud with the calling of birds.

Uddhava walked through the lanes slowly, taking it all in — the smoke of the evening fires, the lowing of the cows coming home, the songs rising and falling. So this was the world Krishna spoke of in his quiet moments; no wonder his heart had never quite left it.

When Nanda learned who had come, he hurried out to meet him: Krishna's own companion, a traveler from the city that had taken his son. He embraced Uddhava, honored him as he would have honored Vasudeva, Krishna's father, pressed the finest food the house could offer on him, and settled him on a comfortable couch. Only then, with his guest at rest, did the old man's questions begin to spill out.

"Is our friend well?" he asked — meaning Vasudeva, the son of Shura, who had spent so many years in Kamsa's prison. "By good fortune," Nanda went on, "the sinner Kamsa was killed, with all his followers, by the very evil he had done. But our Krishna — does he remember us? Does he remember his mother, his friends, his playmates? Will Krishna ever come back, even once, to look upon his own people?"

Before Uddhava could answer, Nanda was already answering himself, the memories crowding in. He remembered how Krishna had sheltered them from the forest fire, and from wind and rain, from the great bull and from the serpent. He remembered Krishna's heroic deeds, and that playful sideways glance of his. He remembered the rivers, the mountains, the forests — every one of them adorned by the touch of Krishna's feet. The more he remembered, the more he wondered. Surely Krishna and Rama — for Rama was Balarama's other name — were gods come down to walk among men. Who else could have broken the great bow, tall as three palm trees, as an elephant king snaps a staff? Who else could have brought down Kamsa, strong as ten thousand elephants, together with the two wrestlers and the royal elephant? And the demons of Krishna's boyhood — Pralamba, Dhenuka, Arishta, Trinavarta, Baka — one after another they had fallen to the two brothers in the very fields where Nanda's cattle still grazed.

And as Nanda spoke, Yashoda listened — and wept. She had held herself steady while the messenger spoke of Mathura; it was the boyhood deeds that undid her, the demon fights in the pastures and the fire in the forest, because those were the years when he had still been hers to hold.

So the evening passed in Nanda's house: the honored guest upon the couch, the old cowherd recounting wonders, and the mother of Krishna weeping quietly at the sound of her son's name.
stories.reflection: Nanda's questions run straight to the only thing that matters to him: not what Krishna has conquered, but whether Krishna remembers — his mother, his friends, his playmates. The village keeps Krishna alive by singing his deeds, and the measure of its love is remembrance.
stories.next_story_tease: Only then did Uddhava find the words to speak the message Krishna had entrusted to him.

stories.title: Uddhava Begs Krishna Not to Leave Him Behind
stories.story:
The omens had begun to appear in Dwaraka, Krishna's city by the sea — small ones at first, a strange bird on a rooftop, a vessel of milk soured before its time — and then signs that made the city speak in low voices. Krishna read them all, and grew quiet.

Uddhava, Krishna's dearest friend, had lately returned from Vrindavan, where he had carried Krishna's own message of comfort to the cowherds; he had brought their longing home with him — Nanda's grief, the cowherd women's tears, the old villagers who had pressed his hand as if they had touched Krishna himself. Now, in Dwaraka, he read the omens for what they were. The work Krishna had come to do was done. Krishna meant to leave the world.

Dwaraka seemed to feel it before anyone said a word. The city had grown rich and proud, and its pride had begun to work like a slow fever: feasts that lasted too long, quarrels that flared over a look, young men of the Yadu clans who had forgotten how to fear anything. The elders whispered that the family had grown too great for the earth to hold it, and the omens seemed to say the same. Only Krishna moved through it all untroubled — speaking gently, settling disputes, smiling at children — and Uddhava, watching him, understood that this calm was itself a kind of farewell.

Uddhava found him alone, fell at his feet, and for a long moment could not speak. At last he said: "Krishna, I cannot bear to leave your feet, even for half a moment. Wherever you go, carry me too, to your own abode."

Then, with Krishna's hand resting on his head, everything he had stored up in silence came out. Krishna's pastimes, he said, were the greatest good fortune a human being could meet; nothing in any of the three worlds stood beside them. The bed Krishna had slept in, the seat he had sat on, the roads he had walked, the river pools where he had bathed, his games and his meals, the garlands that had lain on his chest, the scents he wore, his clothes, his ornaments — Uddhava had kept each of them like a secret treasure, and he could not give up the source of them all. Even the ascetics who renounce everything — who throw away wealth and home and name, and wear only the wind for clothing — wander the world with nothing, remembering Krishna and singing his deeds. They never once touched his hand, and they cannot let him go. If the memory of Krishna keeps a man alive who has given up the whole world, what holds the one who held nothing back — who poured his whole life into that one friendship, and was trusted in return with Krishna's deepest errands?

He said all of it with his face against the ground, and when he had finished he lay still, waiting.

Krishna raised him up with his own hands. "What you have said is exactly my own intent," he said. "Brahma, Shiva, and the gods who guard the worlds are longing for my return to heaven. The time has come." He spoke of their longing simply, without triumph, the way one mentions an old appointment kept at last. And he granted Uddhava his prayer — he would not be left behind.

But that was not all he granted. In the quiet of that hour, with the troubled city beyond the walls, Krishna began to instruct him, as a teacher speaks to a disciple he loves — about the self, the world, and the way to freedom. Uddhava had begged to be carried; he received instead something harder and greater: the teaching that would let him stand, and stand alone, after Krishna had gone.
stories.reflection: Uddhava's plea measures devotion not by what a devotee has done but by how near the beloved is: even the sages who have renounced everything cling to the memory of Krishna's deeds, so how could the man who lived beside him bear a moment's separation? And Krishna's answer transforms the request — he grants Uddhava's wish to be carried along, and then gives him something that makes the wish unnecessary: the teaching that lets him stand alone.
stories.next_story_tease: And he began his teaching with a story — of a king who met a wandering sage on a forest road.
stories.hero_scene: In a quiet room in Dwaraka, Uddhava lies prostrate at Krishna's feet, his face against the ground, while Krishna bends to raise him with both hands and the troubled city waits beyond the walls.

stories.title: Yadu Meets the Wandering Avadhuta
stories.story:
"Listen," Krishna said, "and I will tell you what freedom looks like." Uddhava, Krishna's close friend, had asked for teaching, and Krishna answered as he often did — with a story.

There was once a king named Yadu, of the line of Nahusha, who ruled a great kingdom and knew its burdens: ministers who angled for favor, petitions without end, wars that had to be fought to keep the peace. One day his party halted in a forest, and down the road came a wandering brahmin — an avadhuta, a man who had put aside everything: home, family, ritual, even the marks of his order.

The king could not take his eyes off him. The man owned nothing and feared nothing. He moved without hurry, laughed like a child, stood as still as a ghost — and yet there was a serenity in him that Yadu had never seen at court. There every man wore his rank like armor; here was one who wore nothing and needed no armor, and the difference struck the king like a blow.

The world around them was burning, and Yadu thought of it constantly: people consumed by the forest fire of desire and greed, everyone running after what the next man had. His own ministers would have cut each other's throats over a district; the neighboring kings measured friendship in brides and borders; even the ascetics who came to the palace asked for something — a cow, a village, an audience. This man asked for nothing and was afraid of no one, and he walked through the middle of the burning world untouched.

Yadu dismounted and approached him. "Men spend their lives on dharma, wealth, pleasure, and the itch of curiosity," he said, "and burn in that fire all the same. But you are capable, wise, skilled, fortunate; your speech is like nectar; for those who ask, you are the very cause of joy. You act like a child, a madman, a ghost — and yet you are a sage. How did you gain such wisdom?"

The brahmin smiled, the way a man smiles who has been taught by everything he ever met. "O king, I have many gurus. Twenty-four of them. From each one I learn whatever I learn."

And he named them, one after another: earth, wind, sky, water, fire, the moon, the sun; the pigeon, the python, the ocean; the moth, the bee, the elephant, the honey-gatherer; the deer, the fish, Pingala, the osprey; the child, the maiden, the arrow-maker, the serpent, the spider, the cricket.

Yadu stared. Twenty-four teachers — and not one of them a scholar or a sage. Every child knew the sun and the moon were holy, but a python? A fish? A maiden? And Pingala — the name sounded like a woman's, and the king's curiosity sharpened at the thought that she too had taught this man something. He had paid the finest brahmins in the land to instruct him and had mastered the texts and the rituals; here was a penniless wanderer who had studied with rivers and birds.

"Then teach me," Yadu said.

The avadhuta looked at him for a long moment — at the king's ornaments, the armed guard, the fine horse cropping the grass — and it seemed to Yadu that the man was not judging him but weighing something far older: whether the question had come from the king's boredom or from his hunger. Then he nodded, as if he had been waiting for it all along. And he began with the first of his teachers: the earth itself.
stories.reflection: The wonder of the avadhuta is that his wisdom has no human source at all: a king who spent his life being taught by the best of men finds that the deepest freedom was being taught, all along, by the simplest things. The list of twenty-four gurus — rivers and pigeons and a woman named Pingala — quietly reverses the order of the world: the lowliest teacher may hold the greatest lesson.
stories.next_story_tease: And his first lesson came from the earth beneath their feet.

stories.title: The Avadhuta's Lessons from the Elements
stories.story:
A king named Yadu had halted his party on a forest road to question a wandering brahmin — an avadhuta, a renunciate who owned nothing and feared nothing. Yadu had asked how such freedom was won, and the brahmin answered that he kept twenty-four teachers: everything he had ever met. Now the wanderer sat on the bare earth with the king before him, and began with the first of them.

"The earth taught me forbearance," the avadhuta said. "Every being walks upon her — beasts and men, armies in their thousands, the hooves of cattle, the wheels of carts. She is trampled by all of them, morning and evening, and she never once strays from her course. So the wise one, though the world treads on him, does not leave his path."

Yadu thought of how often he had been wronged — by rivals, by fate, by his own temper — and how often he had left the path in fury instead of staying on it. The first lesson had already found its mark.

"The wind taught me detachment," the avadhuta said. "It moves everywhere — through palaces and market streets, through the trees, into every corner of every house — and it clings to nothing it touches. So the sage moves through the world, touching a thousand things and holding on to none."

The wind, the king realized, had taught this man what he had spent his life failing to learn: to be in the middle of things and not be caught by them.

"The sky taught me to remain untouched. Clouds sail through it, rain falls from it, the smoke of a thousand hearths rises into it, birds cross it — and none of them leaves a mark. So the wise one lives among all the beings of the world — moving and still, hidden in each — and is touched by none. The sky is everywhere, and nowhere is it held; and in the same way he sees the one self in all things and knows himself in everything."

"The water taught me purity. It is clear by nature and sweet to the taste, and wherever it flows it makes the place holy — a tirtha, where men come to bathe. So the sage, pure in himself, makes everything around him sacred; people come to him as they come to a river, and the dirt they carry falls from them in his presence."

"The fire taught me to take no stain. Whatever it is given — wood, refuse, offerings, filth — it burns, and takes no stain from any of it. So the sage is not polluted by what he consumes. His light is his own, and the world's dirt does not reach it."

"The moon taught me to wax and to wane. It swells to fullness and thins to a sliver, and both are its own nature. So it is with the body: it rises and falls through birth, youth, age, and death, down to the cremation ground — and all of these belong to the body, not to the self. The wise one watches them as the moon watches its own phases, taking what time brings and letting it go when time takes it."

"The sun taught me the one soul in many bodies. One sun rises on the palace and on the hut, on the king and on the beggar, and gives light to them all alike. So the one self appears in every body; and when a body ends, nothing of that light is lost. The wise one lives in that single sight, seeing himself in every face."

The king sat silent. Seven lessons, and every one drawn from something that had never spoken a word — each as clear as water. He had filled his court with the learned, and none of them had ever told him anything so simply. The avadhuta paused, and when the king leaned forward, he went on — to the eighth of his teachers, the pigeon, and to what love had cost it.
stories.reflection: The seven elemental lessons are striking because each is drawn from a teacher that never spoke: forbearance from the trampled earth, detachment from the wind, purity from water, radiance that takes no stain from fire. And the sun's lesson gathers them all — the one self in many bodies — showing that the elements were never teaching about themselves, but about the single reality reflected in all of them.
stories.next_story_tease: Then he spoke of the pigeon, the eighth of his teachers — and of what love cost it.
