stories.title: The Sun Krishna Has Set
stories.story:
When Vidura put his question — Vidura, the wise minister of the Kuru court, who had come down to the Yamuna to hear the story of Krishna from the man who had known him best — the silence that answered it lasted a long moment. Uddhava, who had served Krishna since he was five years old and had grown old in that service, seemed for a while to have forgotten that anyone was waiting. He sat on the bank of the river with his eyes closed, lost in the sweetness of remembering Krishna's feet, his limbs trembling with love, tears slipping from beneath his lids. Then, slowly, he wiped his eyes, and when he looked up he was smiling.

"The sun has set," he said. "Krishna has set. What good news can I bring to houses stripped of their fortune? Wretched is this world, and more wretched still the Yadavas — who lived with him, ate with him, fought beside him, and never knew him."

This was the grief that had been gathering in Uddhava since the news of Prabhasa reached him. The Yadavas had been no ordinary clan. They were subtle men, masters at reading a glance, mature in counsel, devoted to Krishna alone. And yet his own magic had touched them; the very power by which he had walked among mortals had closed their eyes. They had lived inside the miracle and never once recognised it.

Now that the miracle was over, memory came back to Uddhava in fragments he could not stop. He remembered the Rajasuya of King Yudhishthira — the great sacrifice at which the Pandava king had been crowned — when the three worlds had looked upon Krishna and found their eyes blessed by the sight. He remembered the love that spilled from Krishna's laughing glance during the rasa, the night-dance with the cowherd women of Vrindavan, the look that had given worth to everyone it fell on. Who among the gods, he asked, could ever forget the dust of his lotus feet? At that same sacrifice, even Shishupala — who had hated Krishna all his life — had reached perfection, drawn by that hatred into a fixed gazing at his enemy. And in the great battles, the heroes of the earth had fallen looking upon the lotus of Krishna's face.

That was the strangest part of his sorrow. Enemies had won release by fixing their minds on Krishna, however unwillingly. The whole world had been given the sight of him. Only his own kinsmen — the ones who had been closest — had been struck blind.

He spoke too of how the deathless one had taken birth in Vasudeva's house and played at being a child, and of how Krishna, before setting out on some errand, had bowed at his parents' feet. The memory choked him. "Who could ever forget the dust of his lotus feet?" he said again. "And we — we lived our whole lives beside him."

Vidura listened and asked nothing more. Uddhava, wiping his eyes once more, drew a breath and began to tell it — the long tale that Vidura would carry away with him, and that would be told again and again long after both of them were gone.

He stopped once, and said something strange: that the man seated before him on the riverbank was no ordinary minister, but a soul without equal, a master of the three worlds whose every wish had already been granted. Vidura did not answer. In the world after Krishna, Uddhava seemed to be saying, even the greatest souls went disguised, and only love could recognise them.

The river moved past them, unhurried — the same river that had flowed past the village of his boyhood, where he had grown up among the cowherds. Uddhava's voice steadied as he spoke, as if the telling itself were a kind of returning. The sun had set, but the remembering had begun.
stories.reflection: Uddhava's sorrow is the sorrow of proximity without recognition: the Yadavas had what the whole world longed for and could not see it. The Bhagavata frames its telling through his grief, as if the story of Krishna can only be told properly by someone who has first understood what it cost to be near him and to know him only after he was gone.
stories.next_story_tease: Far to the west, the slow procession leaving Dwaraka was already drawing the eyes of robbers.

stories.title: The Bow That Would Not Tighten
stories.story:
Arjuna, the great archer, found the bodies of Krishna and Balarama and performed the funeral rites for them and for all the slain. The eight queens of Krishna, with Rukmini at their head, embraced the body of their lord and entered the funeral fire. Revati, holding Balarama's body in her arms, climbed the blazing pyre after him, and the fire was cool to her, glad in the touch of her lord. The old Yadava king Ugrasena, and Krishna's father Vasudeva with his wives Devaki and Rohini, gave themselves to the flames as well. When the last rites were done, Arjuna made all the people leave the city, took the young prince Vajra, Krishna's grandson, and led the thousands of Krishna's widowed wives out of Dwaraka, slowly and with care, the whole city behind them.

Behind them the sea rose and swallowed Dwaraka whole. Only the dwelling of the clan's deity stood above the water, and the ocean has never washed it away: Krishna still abides there, and whoever visits that holy shrine is freed of his sins. On the same day the dark-bodied Kali age came down upon the earth. The Sudharman, the great hall of assembly, and the Parijata tree — both brought down from heaven by Krishna — went back where they had come from.

In the country of Panchanada, a rich and fertile spot, Arjuna halted the long column to rest. That halt was his undoing. The robbers of the region saw the widowed women and the great wealth in one man's keeping, and their desires caught fire. They roused the Abhiras, the herdsmen of the countryside. "Here is Arjuna," they said, "immensely rich, guarded only by widowed women, passing confidently among us. His pride is swollen from slaying Bhishma, Drona, Jayadratha, and Karna. He does not know the strength of simple villagers. Up, up! Take your long thick staves!"

They rushed upon the unprotected people with cudgels and clods of earth. Arjuna turned to meet them and called out in derision: "Retire, wretches, ignorant of what is right, unless you are eager to die." They paid him no heed, and seized his treasure and his women.

Then Arjuna braced Gandiva, the great heavenly bow — and it would not tighten. The string stayed slack in his hands, and the incantations of the celestial weapons would not come back to him. He loosed his shafts anyway, and the arrows that had once overthrown kings merely scratched the skin of the herdsmen. The arrows the fire-god Agni had given him at the burning of the Khandava forest, arrows of certain destruction, were themselves destroyed that day and turned against him. He tried to summon the strength of Krishna, the presence that had guided his arm through a hundred wars. It was gone; his arrows flew wide or were brushed aside by peasants. When his quiver was empty he beat at the bandits with the horn of his bow, and they only laughed. And the robbers, before his eyes, carried off all the women of the Vrishni and Andhaka tribes and went their way.

Arjuna wept. "Alas, alas, I am deserted by my lord!" he cried, and in that same instant the bow, the heavenly weapons, his chariot, and his horses perished before him like a gift to a fool. "Resistless are the decrees of fate," he said, "which have laid weakness upon me, robbed me of my illustrious friend, and given victory to the base. These arms are mine, and this fist is mine, and this is my place, and I am Arjuna — but without that righteous aid, all of it is nothing. The valour of Arjuna and the strength of my brother Bhima were his work. Without him I am overcome by peasants."

He made his way to Mathura, and there he placed Vajra on the throne of the Yadava line. In a wood outside the city he found the sage Vyasa and lay prostrate at his feet. Vyasa looked at him for a long time. "How is it," he asked, "that I see you thus shorn of your lustre?"

The question hung in the air. It was the question Arjuna had been asking since Gandiva went slack in his hands: what is an archer, when the presence that strung his bow has left the world? The Kali age had begun, and the first thing it had taken was not a kingdom — it was the strength of the strongest man alive.
stories.reflection: The robbery is not a military defeat but the withdrawal of Krishna's presence made visible. Arjuna's weapons fail not because he has grown weaker but because the source of his strength has left the world — the story's way of saying that the Kali age began as a loss no skill could replace.
stories.next_story_tease: Even as Arjuna wept at Mathura, the gods were gathering in Dwaraka to ask Krishna to come home.

stories.title: The Gods Ask Krishna to Come Home
stories.story:
For a hundred and twenty-five years, Krishna — born into the royal line of the Yadavas to lighten the world's burden — had lived among men as one of them, ruling from Dwaraka, his city by the sea. Now the gods themselves came to that city, to ask him to come home.

They came as witnesses of everything that mattered in the story of the world: Brahma, the eldest of the gods, at their head; Shiva among them; the shining ones of heaven filling the courtyards of the city. And Krishna, who had been born among men and had lived out a man's full span among them, received them the way a host receives old friends.

Brahma spoke for them all. "Righteousness has been established among the good through you," he said, "and among those who keep their word. You came down into the line of Yadu wearing a form without equal. In the dark age that is to come — the Kali age — good men will tell of your deeds for as long as there are tongues to tell them. A hundred and twenty-five years have passed since you came down. Your work for the gods is nearly done, and this clan of yours is almost spent, worn away by the curse the brahmin sages laid upon it. If you think it fitting, Lord, return to your own abode above the world."

Krishna heard them out in silence. When he answered, there was no surprise in his voice, only the calm of a man naming a day he had long known was coming. The earth's burden, he said, was indeed lifted; that work was finished. But the Yadava clan had grown proud — swollen with valour, with prowess, with splendour — and a clan like that could not be left standing in the world like a fire that no one tends. Its destruction, born of the brahmins' curse, had already begun; and when the curse had run its course, he said, he would go.

The gods had their answer, and it was not a refusal. Krishna was not clinging to his life among men; he was waiting for the last duty to be done, the way a lamp waits for the last of its oil. The curse was no enemy stealing upon him from outside — it was the road by which the world itself would set him free. Until it had finished its work, he would stay at his post in Dwaraka, ruling, teaching, waiting.

And so the hour of his leaving was fixed, not by the gods' asking, but by the slow work of the curse. Brahma and the shining ones took their leave of the city of the Yadavas, carrying back to heaven the news that the Lord's time among men had an end now, and that the end was near. Dwaraka went on in its golden light, its halls full of heroes, its streets full of children — and over all of it, unseen, hung the hour that had just been fixed.

The gods had come to ask Krishna to come home, and he had told them, gently, that he would — as soon as the world was done with him. It was the longest goodbye ever spoken, and it had begun.
stories.reflection: The scene fixes the end of Krishna's time on earth not as an accident or a defeat but as a term agreed upon: his life among men lasted exactly as long as the work required. The gods do not command him to return; they ask, as guests ask a host when it is time to leave — and he answers by naming the hour the curse will set.
stories.next_story_tease: The hour Krishna had promised the gods was already drawing close.
stories.hero_scene: The gods of heaven thronging the courtyards of Dwaraka, Brahma at their head and Shiva among them, while Krishna stands before them in the golden light of the city to receive their request.

stories.title: The Hunter Jara Shoots Krishna's Foot
stories.story:
The curse spoken over Krishna's own people had come due at last. The Yadavas — the clan into which the Lord of the universe had been born as a man — had turned on one another at Prabhasa, on the seashore, and destroyed themselves almost to the last man. When it was done, a great silence lay over the shore, and Krishna walked into a forest near the sea and sat down alone. He had watched his elder brother Balarama depart, and he had seen the last of his people fall; there was no one left for him to stay for. The forest was quiet around him, and the sea lay somewhere beyond the trees.

At the foot of a pipal tree he seated himself, and there he sat in meditation, perfectly still, and let his own form change.

It was the form he did not often show: four-armed, bearing on his chest the curled mark called the Shrivatsa, dark as a raincloud, bright with the splendour of molten gold. His face was a smiling lotus framed in dark curls. A yellow cloth girded his waist, a sacred thread crossed his chest; a diadem, bracelets, and armlets adorned him; a garland of forest flowers lay about his body; and his own weapons, alive and embodied, stood about him. He drew his right foot up upon his thigh and rested there, quiet, as if he had come to the end of a long road.

Not far off, an iron arrowhead carried a long story. Long before, an iron club had come into being in the Yadava house — a doom made into metal, foretold to crush the whole race. It had been ground to dust and thrown into the sea, so that its power might be scattered, but the sea gave the dust back as rushes along the shore. And now the last fragment of that iron, hammered into a blade, sat on the shaft of a hunter who had come into the forest in search of deer.

His name was Jara. From a distance he saw Krishna's foot, and he mistook it for the face of a deer. He loosed the arrow, and it lodged in the sole.

He ran forward quickly to claim his prey — and saw what he had done. A four-armed Lord sat there, radiant, and terror took hold of him. He fell at Krishna's feet and begged his pardon. He had loosed the arrow without knowing what he aimed at, he said; let the sin of a poor hunter of deer be forgiven, for even the remembrance of that name, men say, scatters the darkness of ignorance. What he had pierced was a form too great for even Brahma and Rudra and the wisest of the gods to know — and what could a man of no worth say before it?

Krishna forgave him, and spoke to him gently, and raised him to his feet. So the last fragment of the iron that had been made to destroy his whole race found its mark at last — not on a battlefield, but in a quiet forest, by an arrow meant for a deer, loosed by a man who meant no harm and forgiven before he had even finished asking.
stories.reflection: The arrow that ends Krishna's earthly form is forged from the last fragment of the iron that destroyed his people, so that one doom gathers up its own loose ends. A hunter who meant no harm becomes the instrument, and is forgiven, a strange and gentle close to a life spent in the middle of wars.
stories.tradition_note: The Mahabharata describes Krishna lying on the earth in high yoga, pierced at the heel; the Bhagavata Purana, followed here, has him seated at the foot of a pippala tree with his foot drawn up.
stories.content_note: Krishna's earthly form is pierced by an arrow and he departs; the death is described gently.

stories.title: The Last Message to Daruka
stories.story:
The hunter who had shot the arrow could not stop trembling. His name was Jara, and he hunted the forests near Prabhasa. His arrow had struck the foot of a man resting in the grass — and the man was Krishna, the Lord of the universe, who had come down from heaven to live among men. The hour the gods had been promised was upon him.

Krishna looked at the hunter, and his voice was gentle. "Do not be afraid," he said. "Rise. This was my own doing." Then he gave the hunter the last thing he could have expected to hear: "Go, with my leave, to the world of the good." The man whose arrow had brought about his death was not cursed but blessed; the arrow had only done what Krishna himself had arranged. Jara rose, went his way, and was saved.

Then his charioteer Daruka came. Krishna had sent him away, and Daruka, searching for his master's path, had found him at last — at the foot of an ashvattha tree, the great pipal, ringed by the divine weapons of Vishnu, for Krishna and Vishnu are one, which stood blazing guard over their lord. Daruka leapt from the chariot and fell at Krishna's feet, his heart flooding with love, his eyes full of tears.

"Master," he wept, "your lotus feet are hidden from my sight. It is as though my eyes have failed and I have fallen into darkness."

Even as he spoke, the chariot — the one that bore the image of Garuda, the great eagle of heaven, on its banner, the one that had carried Krishna through every war — rose into the air, and the divine weapons rose with it, following their master out of this world.

Krishna looked at his charioteer with the old fondness and gave him the last message he would ever send. "Go to Dwaraka, Daruka," he said. "Tell my kinsmen of their destruction — they have slain one another. Tell them Balarama is gone, and tell them the state I am in. Do not stay in Dwaraka, you or your relatives. Take all your possessions, every one of you, and with Arjuna's help lead the people to Indraprastha. The sea will soon flood the city I have left."

It was a message for a whole city: a people to be moved, a flood to be outrun, a road pointed out to safety. The kinsmen were the Yadavas, his own clan; Balarama was his elder brother; and Arjuna, the Pandava prince who had been his closest friend among men, would come with his chariot to lead the survivors east, to Indraprastha, the city of the Pandavas.

And then, for the charioteer himself, one final word of counsel. "But you, Daruka," Krishna said, "hold to the dharma I have taught you — the right way of living. Be firm in knowledge. Let the pairs of opposites — pleasure and pain, gain and loss — come and go without shaking you; look on all things as one."

Daruka circled his master, bowed again and again, and went on his way to Dwaraka, carrying the last words of Krishna in his heart. Behind him, beneath the pipal tree, the stillest figure in the world remained, guarded by weapons that were no longer there. The last message had been sent; there remained only the last departure — the one that no messenger could carry and no friend could delay.
stories.reflection: The last message is not about Krishna at all but about everyone he is leaving: a people who must move before the sea comes, a hunter forgiven for what he could not know, a charioteer told how to live after his master is gone. Even in leaving, he is arranging the world's safety — and his final counsel to Daruka, to stand firm in knowledge and indifferent to loss and gain, is his whole teaching compressed into a goodbye.
stories.next_story_tease: The last message sent, only Krishna's own departure remained.

stories.title: Krishna's Final Departure
stories.subtitle: The gods watch the Lord leave the earth
stories.story:
Krishna's long life among men was ending. For a hundred and twenty-five years the Lord of the universe had walked the earth as a man; now his people were gone, a hunter's arrow had found him, and the hour he had promised the gods had come. The forest near Prabhasa went quiet in a way forests rarely do.

The birds stopped calling, the deer stopped moving, and the air itself seemed to hold its breath, because the sky above the trees was filling with guests no mortal eye could see. First came the ancestors, then the hosts of heaven — the Siddhas, the Gandharvas, the Vidyadharas — and the great serpents of the deep. All pressed close, eager for a sight none had ever witnessed: the end of a life that had been lived as a gift to the world. Their chariots crowded the sky until it looked like a festival ground at dawn. Flowers began to fall in a steady, unhurried rain, as if the sky itself were making an offering. High above, the drums of heaven sounded on their own, deep and slow.

Below them, Krishna sat where the hunter had found him, in the shadow of a tree. The hunter had knelt there trembling, certain he had done an unforgivable wrong; looking up, he had seen a man in yellow robes, rapt in stillness, his body bearing many arms — and Krishna had comforted him and sent him on his way before he could even finish asking forgiveness. Now the Lord of the world sat alone, his eyes turned inward, holding to one point of stillness while the whole universe gathered to watch him go.

Then he saw Brahma standing before him — Brahma, the grandfather of the worlds, come like everyone else to see the end. That sight was the signal. Krishna drew his glories back into himself, every power he had poured out over a lifetime, the way a tide returns to the sea. Then he closed his lotus eyes.

The fire came then — the fire of yoga, rising from within him. It did not burn the way earthly fire burns; it consumed the way a flame consumes a lamp, taking the body that had walked through Vrindavan and Mathura and Dwaraka and turning it gently into light. The drums of heaven sounded again, louder. Flowers rained from the sky. And when the gods looked once more at the place beneath the tree, there was nothing there at all.

But where had he gone? The gods looked at one another, and even the greatest of them could not trace his path. He had entered his own abode, and that abode is not a place that can be followed to. It was like lightning, the seers said afterward: you see the flash and know it has crossed the whole sky, but once it leaves its cloud no one can say where it has gone. Even the gods stood in the empty forest amazed, holding flowers they had not finished raining down. That was how Krishna left the world — seen, certain, and utterly beyond following.

Other tellings of that hour say the sky blazed with splendour as he rose, filling the whole vault of heaven with light, and the gods — Indra and the twin Ashvinis, Rudra and the Adityas — advanced to receive him, as if heaven itself were coming out to greet a king returning home. The tellings differ in detail; they agree on the wonder.

And then it was over. The flowers settled on the grass. The chariots turned away, one by one. The drums fell silent. The forest was only a forest again, a quiet place with an empty space beneath a tree — and the Lord of the worlds was gone from the earth he had walked for so long.

The earth would feel his absence almost at once: in the city by the sea built around his presence, in the hearts of the women he had left there, and in the sea itself, which seemed to know, before anyone told it, that the one who had held the world together had let go.
stories.reflection: The departure is told as a mystery even the gods cannot witness to its end: they come to see, they rain flowers, and still they cannot trace his path. It is like lightning that leaves its cloud — seen, certain, and utterly beyond following. Krishna leaves the way he lived, in his own time and answerable to no one, and even the last glimpse of him is a gift rather than a right.
stories.tradition_note: The Mahabharata frames the departure as a radiant ascent: Krishna comforts the hunter Jara, then rises filling the sky with splendour, and the gods come to receive him. The Bhagavata keeps the mystery — the body consumed by the fire of yoga, the path untraceable. The telling above follows the Bhagavata as its primary source.
stories.next_story_tease: The moment Krishna vanished, the sea began to stir against the city he had left behind.

stories.title: The Sea Swallows Dwaraka
stories.subtitle: After Krishna leaves, the ocean rises to claim the city
stories.story:
Daruka, Krishna's charioteer, rode into Dwaraka with the news, and the city understood before he finished speaking. He went straight to Vasudeva, Krishna's father, and to Ugrasena, the aged king of the Yadavas, and told them everything: the Yadavas had destroyed one another at Prabhasa, clan against clan, friend against friend, until almost none were left. And Krishna was gone. Balarama, his elder brother, was gone.

The women of the royal house heard it too, and the grief that had been waiting for years finally had its way with them. Devaki, Krishna's mother — who had given up her first children to a tyrant's fear and had spent a lifetime loving her sons from a careful distance — gave up her life then. Rohini, Balarama's mother, gave up hers. Vasudeva, the father who had carried his newborn son through a stormy night to safety, looked at a world in which neither of his sons would ever come home, and he too let go of life — not in fire, but in the simple inability to go on breathing in a world without them.

The queens took the other road. With Rukmini at their head, they pressed close to the body of their lord — Hari, as the old books name him, the Lord they had married — and walked with him into the funeral fire. The city that had been the joy of the world watched its mothers and wives choose death over a life without him.

Arjuna, the Pandava prince who had been Krishna's dearest friend, arrived as he had been summoned — too late to save anyone, and just in time to bury them. He walked through the ruined halls of Dwaraka and performed the last rites for the dead of Krishna's house, one after another, until the rites ran together. Then he gathered what was left of the city — the women, the children, the elders — and prepared to lead them away.

That was when the sea rose. It did not storm. It did not crash against the walls. It simply came, calmly and completely, like water filling a footprint. The ocean — that home of sharks and alligators — flooded over Dwaraka and all its wealth, swallowing the golden city whole. Whatever ground they crossed, the ocean covered immediately behind them. They walked faster and faster, looking back at the water at their heels, and the wonder of it struck even their grief. "Wonderful is the course of fate," they said to one another, and pressed on.

Only one thing did the sea refuse to take. The Lord's own dwelling stood above the rising water and would not be washed away — the house where Krishna had lived, the shrine that marked the place of his earthly play. The flood took the city and the streets that had known his footsteps, and left that one house standing, as if the ocean itself knew better than to touch the home of the one who had made it.

And as the people walked away from the drowning city, they saw two more things leave the earth. The Sudharman assembly hall and the Parijata tree — the two gifts of heaven that Krishna had brought down to Dwaraka — rose out of the water and returned to heaven. And on the same day that Krishna departed from the earth, the seers said, the dark Kali age — the age of quarrel — came down upon the world.

Arjuna led the survivors slowly and tenderly until they reached Indraprastha, the city of the Pandavas. There he placed Vajra — the surviving heir of the Vrishnis, the clan into which Krishna had been born — on the throne as king. An era ended at Prabhasa; another, smaller and quieter, began in Indraprastha.

The sea never gave Dwaraka back. But the Lord's own dwelling still stood in the water, and the seers said it would stand forever — because Krishna still abides there, even today, in the place where he carried on his life on earth. Whoever visits that holy shrine, they said, is freed from all his sins. The city was gone; the Lord's presence was not.
stories.reflection: The city that had been the joy of the world became, in a single day, a memory under water — all but the one dwelling that had housed the Lord himself. The Bhagavata and the Vishnu Purana agree on that stubborn detail: the sea could take everything else, but not the house where Krishna had lived. Some things the flood cannot reach.
stories.tradition_note: The Bhagavata says Vasudeva, Devaki and Rohini gave up their lives out of grief at being separated from Krishna and Balarama; the Vishnu Purana has them, with Ugrasena, enter the flames, and adds that Arjuna found the bodies of Krishna and Balarama and performed the rites for them. The telling above follows the Bhagavata as its primary source, keeping the Vishnu Purana's closing image of the dwelling the sea could not wash away.
stories.content_note: Deaths by fire and by grief, and the drowning of a city; described with restraint, but the episode may warrant parental awareness for younger listeners.
stories.next_story_tease: Yet one farewell had happened before the flood, and it had still to be told: the last time Krishna himself walked through Dwaraka.

stories.title: Krishna Entrusts the Women to Vasudeva
stories.subtitle: One last walk through the city before the end
stories.story:
Before the sea rose, before the last pyres burned, Krishna came back to Dwaraka one final time. The city was still standing, but it was no longer a city. The men were gone — the Yadavas had destroyed one another at Prabhasa — and the streets that had once rung with their voices now belonged to the women, the children, and the very old, who moved through the empty avenues like people in a dream.

Krishna had not come to stay. He had sent his charioteer Daruka riding to the court of the Kurus with the news of the slaughter and a summons for Arjuna, the Pandava prince who was his dearest friend. He had watched Vabhru — a young kinsman, the last survivor of the fighting — fall to the iron bolt that had pursued the cursed Yadavas to the very end. And Balarama, his elder brother, was waiting for him at the edge of the forest. There was only one thing left to do in the city, and he had come back to do it.

He went to his father.

Vasudeva, who had lived to see his sons become the lords of the earth, looked at his son and heard the words that ended everything. "Protect all the ladies of our house," Krishna told him, "until Arjuna comes. He will come, and he will take charge of them. At the edge of the forest, Balarama is waiting for me. I shall meet him today. I have seen this great slaughter of the Yadavas, just as I once saw the slaughter of the greatest warriors of the Kuru line. I cannot bear to look on this city of the Yadavas when the Yadavas are no longer in it. Know that I am going into the woods, to live there as a hermit, with Balarama beside me."

He had given his father a task — protect the women until Arjuna came — and a task was the one gift that could hold a man upright when everything else had been taken from him.

Then Krishna bowed and touched his father's feet with his head — the reverence of a son for the father who had carried him across a river on a night of storm — and he left quickly, because farewells that last too long become unbearable.

He had not reached the gate when the sound came after him: a loud wail of sorrow rising from the ladies and children of his house, a cry that followed him down the street like a second shadow. Krishna stopped. He retraced his footsteps, walked back through the courtyard, and stood before the weeping women.

"Arjuna will come here," he said. "That foremost of men will lift this grief from you." That was all he could promise them, and it was everything he had left to give.

He had sent for the one man on earth he trusted to carry his family forward, and he had told them so, plainly and gently. Then he turned and left again, and this time he did not stop. He walked out of the palace and out of the city, through the streets of the Dwaraka he had built and loved, past the golden towers and the gardens he would never see again, toward the forest where his elder brother sat waiting in solitude.

The women stood in the courtyard behind him, holding the promise he had left them, watching the doorway long after he was gone. He had come into the city one last time to make sure that those he left behind would be cared for — to bow to his father, to answer their wailing with a promise. Then he walked out of Dwaraka for the last time, into the forest, into the silence, toward the end that was waiting for him beneath a tree.
stories.reflection: Krishna's last acts in Dwaraka are entirely for other people: he gives his father a task that will keep him upright, he promises the weeping women that Arjuna will come, and he turns back, one last time, to answer their grief. The son touches his father's feet even as the father has lost everything he had; the farewell is a gift to the ones left behind.

stories.title: Vrikasura's Lethal Boon
stories.subtitle: The demon who asked Shiva for the power to kill with a touch
stories.story:
On a road one day, the demon Vrikasura met the sage Narada. Vrikasura, the son of Shakuni, was the kind of being who had never once been told no. Narada, a wandering sage who knew the roads to every god, looked at him and offered a piece of advice. “Worship Girisha, the god of the mountain,” he said. “Do that, and you will succeed quickly.”

The demon took the advice the way fire takes dry grass. He went to Kedara, the mountain shrine of Shiva, and began a penance of terrible intensity. He stood without moving. He fasted until his body was a shadow. He burned in the fire of his own austerity — the sort of penance that makes the earth itself uneasy. When a demon practices self-denial, he is not seeking purity. He is seeking power.

For seven days he waited, and the god did not come. On the seventh day, out of that despair, Shiva rose before him — fire rising from fire, the most compassionate of the gods, moved by the sight of even a demon’s suffering. “Enough,” Shiva said. “Choose a boon from me. Whatever you wish, I will give it to you.”

Vrikasura had thought of nothing else for seven days. He knew exactly what he wanted. “Whoever’s head I touch,” he said, “let him die.”

Even the patient god flinched. It was a gift of death held in one outstretched hand, and it would bring fear to every living being. Shiva’s face darkened, yet he granted it — reluctantly, the way a man gives a knife to a child because he has promised. A boon once offered cannot be taken back. A god’s word is a god’s word.

Vrikasura stood in the mountain light, flexing his hand, feeling the new power settle into his palm like a second skin. Then he decided to make sure the boon truly worked. He reached out and tried to place his hand on Shiva’s own head.

Shiva fled.

The destroyer of worlds ran. He ran trembling, seized with terror, pursued by the demon and by his own gift. Vrikasura came after him, hand outstretched, and Shiva ran across the earth to its farthest ends; when there was no more earth, he ran through the heavens. The gods watched them pass — Indra and the kings of the celestial realms — and sat in silence, because not one of them knew any remedy. There is no counterspell for a boon granted by Shiva himself.

At last Shiva reached the end of his flight: Vaikuntha, the home of Vishnu — the lord whom the old books also call Narayana — and the last shelter of those who have given up the world. There Vishnu sat waiting, blazing like a fire, wearing the sacred thread and deerskin of a wandering holy man. He was the destroyer of affliction, and he had seen Shiva’s distress long before Shiva reached his door.

Shiva, the refuge of the world, had found his own refuge. And behind him, still running, hand outstretched, came the demon whose touch meant death — into the presence of the one being in all the worlds who could do something about it.
stories.reflection: The most compassionate of gods grants the most terrible of boons, and then must run from his own gift: the story turns generosity inside out. Vrikasura asks for power over every head but his own, and the terror is that Shiva cannot break his word even to save himself. A knot tied that tightly can only be untied by someone from outside.
stories.tradition_note: The Bhagavata frames the episode with Narada's advice sending Vrikasura to worship Shiva; the same tale is told with variations in other Puranas. The sequel, Vishnu's rescue of Shiva, is told in the next episode.
stories.next_story_tease: But Vrikasura had chased Shiva to the one refuge his boon could not enter — the abode of Narayana.
stories.hero_scene: The mountain shrine of Kedara: the emaciated demon Vrikasura kneeling in penance as Shiva rises before him like fire from fire, one hand raised to grant the boon while the demon's eyes fix on him with a terrible intent.

stories.title: The Boon That Tested Its Own Giver
stories.story:
The demon Vrikasura, son of Shakuni, stood at the gate of Vaikuntha, the home of Vishnu, and bellowed for the god hiding inside. A little while before, he had won a terrible gift from Shiva: whoever’s head he touched would die. He had meant to test that gift on Shiva’s own head, and Shiva had fled before him — across the earth, through the heavens, and at last through this very gate, into the one refuge that never turns away anyone who comes pursued.

Inside, no terror waited for him. A young brahmachari came out to meet him — a wandering student, staff in hand, a deerskin over his shoulder — glowing like low fire, his face mild and open, as though fear had never touched it. He greeted Vrikasura by name and asked why a victor like him looked so spent, and where he was rushing.

The young man was Vishnu himself, the lord of the house Vrikasura had come to, though the demon had no way of knowing it.

Vrikasura, worn out and vain, told him everything: the penance, the boon, and how he meant to test its truth on Shiva’s own head. The young man listened, and a kindly doubt creased his brow.

“Forgive me,” he said, “but that cannot be. I have heard that the great god Shiva is compassionate — but even compassion has its limits. Such a power, given to a demon, over life itself? No. You have been deceived, or you deceive yourself.”

The demon swore it was true. The young man shook his head, still gentle. “Then you have nothing to fear from proving it,” he said. “Place your hand on your own head. If you live, the tale was always a tale. If you do not — well, then the boon was real after all.”

It was said so smoothly, so kindly, that the words seemed to take the breath out of the demon’s rage. He had chased a god across the world wanting to prove his power, and here at last was a listener who doubted it. He forgot Shiva. He forgot everything but the insult of being disbelieved. He raised his hand and brought it down on his own head. The skull split, and Vrikasura fell where he stood — dead in that instant, struck down by the very power he had meant for another.

For a moment Vaikuntha was still. Then flowers rained down from every direction, released by the gods who had watched, helpless, from the edges of the sky. Shiva, freed at last, stepped out of hiding and stood before the young man. “O Lord,” he said, “what creature that has wronged the great has ever survived? This one offended against a god, and his own gift destroyed him. He was never killed by you. He was killed by what he carried.”

Vishnu received the praise the way he received everything — quietly, without claiming it. The terror that had emptied the heavens was over. Before long, Shiva set out for his own mountain, and Vaikuntha grew quiet again beneath the fallen flowers.
stories.reflection: Vishnu wins without lifting a weapon, by letting the asura's own boon answer for him. There is an exactness to the justice: the power Vrikasura meant to aim at a god had been aimed at himself from the moment he received it, and the gentlest of disguises carried the heaviest of truths.
stories.content_note: A demon dies when his own hand splits his skull; the moment is described with restraint.
stories.next_story_tease: The question that had opened the tale still stood, and the sages would soon put the three great gods themselves to the test.

stories.title: Bhrigu Tests the Three Gods
stories.story:
Which of the three great gods was greatest — Brahma, who made the worlds; Shiva, who unmakes them; or Vishnu, who keeps them safe? The sages who gathered to settle the question could not agree, and argument after argument came to nothing. At last they resolved to settle it not with words but with a test. They chose one of their own, the sage Bhrigu, and sent him out with a single instruction: offer no bow, no hymn, and no word of honor to any of the three, and watch what happened. A god who could not bear a slight, they reasoned, was in the end no greater than the man who offered it.

Bhrigu went first to Brahmaloka, the heaven of Brahma the creator — who happened to be his own father. He walked in and stood before the god and said nothing: no prostration, no praise, not a single syllable of respect. Anger rose in Brahma, hot and gathering, ready to pour out. Then he looked at the man standing silent before him, his own son, and he held it down. He let the insult pass unanswered.

Next Bhrigu climbed to Kailasa, the mountain home of Shiva. Again he offered nothing: no greeting, no honor, no sign that he stood before a god at all. Shiva’s anger did not wait to be mastered. It rose at once, and his trident was already lifting to strike when his wife, the goddess Parvati, threw herself at his feet and spoke soft words to him, and slowly the storm in him went still.

Last of all, Bhrigu came to Vaikuntha, the home of Vishnu. There he found the god lying at ease, the goddess of fortune resting against his chest. Bhrigu walked straight up to him and, without a word, drove his foot into that chest.

Vishnu rose at once from his couch — not to strike back, but to bow. He bent his head to the sage and asked his forgiveness. “Let the touch of the sage’s foot purify me,” he said, “and all who depend on me. Today your foot has made me the one true home of Lakshmi, the goddess of fortune who rests upon this chest.”

Bhrigu stood silent. This was not the answer he had come prepared to receive, and it undid him. He had expected, at best, a god who could master his temper. He had found instead a god who seemed not to have one — who met a blow not with patience but with welcome, as though the foot that struck him had come bearing a gift.

He returned to the assembly of sages and told them what he had seen, and they listened in wonder as the doubt they had carried fell away. In Vishnu, Bhrigu told them, dwelt everything a soul could ask of a god — righteousness, wisdom, and freedom from desire, and the true home of peace and fearlessness. And so the question was answered at last — not by the one who raged, not by the one who mastered his rage, but by the one in whom no rage rose at all.
stories.reflection: The sages set out to measure power and instead measured restraint. Two gods burned at an insult; the third apologized to the foot that struck him — and that, Bhrigu reported back, is where greatness actually lives. The test was meant to find strength, and it found the thing that most looks like weakness: the man who does not hit back.
